A digital director named Cassie Young faced body-shaming from a personal trainer after politely declining his wedding-day fitness offer. When the trainer pressured her to lose weight, Young publicly shared their exchange on Facebook, emphasizing that body positivity is about self-acceptance and happiness. Her post resonated widely, garnering support from many who agreed that appearance should not define self-worth.

The world's first all-Disney dating website, Mousemingle.com, launched recently. Created by Dave Tavres, a self-proclaimed "software geek" from Culver City, the site caters to Disney enthusiasts. Users can check boxes for their favorite Disney songs, shopping habits, and "Disney nerd level" to find matches. Anyone can view profiles and photos, but private messages require a $12.55 monthly membership. Tavres, who previously worked on the Disneyland Railroad, aimed to connect single Disney fans who live in areas without nearby Disney parks. The site hopes to help passionate Disney fans find partners who share their interests.

Moses Malone, a three-time NBA MVP and key figure in the Philadelphia 76ers' 1983 championship team, passed away at the age of 60. Known for his ferocious rebounding and iconic presence, Malone led the league in rebounds per game for five consecutive seasons. After being acquired by the 76ers in 1982, he won MVP honors in Houston the previous season. Billy Cunningham, the head coach at the time, emphasized the physical presence Malone brought to the team. Malone's contributions to the 76ers are remembered as integral to the team's history, with the organization honoring his legacy as a genuine icon.

In a remote area of Cass County, Missouri, the FBI has assisted in the discovery of human remains, including a second skull, near where Kara Kopetsky and Jessica Runions went missing. The Missouri State Highway Patrol has closed 6.5 miles of State Route Y for the search, which could continue until Wednesday. Kopetsky, 17, vanished in 2007, and Runions, 21, disappeared in 2016. Both families, particularly Rhonda Beckford and Jamie Runions, have been searching for answers and are hopeful for resolution. Runions was last seen with Kylr Yust, who has been charged with burning her vehicle, but has not faced charges related to her disappearance. Beckford and Runions have become close, sharing the bond of missing their daughters. Yust has a history of violence, including animal abuse and domestic violence. The families continue to search for their daughters and seek justice.

Kate Gosselin, once a reality TV star, has landed a new job as a coupon blogger for CouponCabin.com, focusing on money-saving tips for families. This move, while unexpected, could help her support her eight children. Gosselin sees coupons as "free money in your pocket" and is excited to share her expertise. Her first post will cover navigating Black Friday, with future topics including budgeting for large families and holiday shopping. This job might provide a temporary solution while keeping her off the TV screen, potentially allowing her to explore other opportunities.

The New England Patriots have launched a comprehensive website to refute the findings of the Ted Wells report on the DeflateGate scandal, portraying the investigation as an unjust attack. The website, wellsreportcontext.com, includes a 20,000-word rebuttal authored by Daniel L. Goldberg, a Patriots lawyer. It challenges the scientific evidence and the interpretation of text messages between team employees Jim McNally and John Jastremski. The Patriots argue that the halftime PSI measurements of their footballs were consistent with the Ideal Gas Law, blaming the temperature drop for the lower pressure. They also dispute the sequence of events during halftime, suggesting the Colts’ footballs were measured after the Patriots’ were re-inflated. The Patriots accuse the NFL of making unfounded assumptions and manipulating the evidence to support their case. They claim the NFL’s lawyers told Exponent, their scientific consultants, to assume certain timings and conditions that skewed the results. The website also disputes the NFL’s interpretation of text

Six Sydney women, not bridesmaids, arrived at a wedding reception all wearing the same A$160 dress, prompting amused confusion and eventual bonding. The incident, reminiscent of the 1993 play, led to a Facebook post by Debbie Speranza that garnered over 39,000 likes and 9,500 comments. The women, initially laughing at the coincidence, ended up dancing the night away together.

Mitt Romney stated in an interview that his views on abortion rights are more lenient than those of the Republican Party platform, supporting abortion in cases of rape, incest, and to protect the life of the mother. The Republican Party is convening its national convention in Tampa, Florida, where it will adopt a platform calling for a constitutional amendment banning abortion with no exceptions. Romney's position is likely to face scrutiny from conservatives, as his stance on the health of the mother could be seen as a broader exception. His comments come amid increased Democratic attacks on the Republican ticket over reproductive rights, partly due to the strong views of his running mate, Paul Ryan, and the controversial remarks of GOP Senate candidate Todd Akin on rape and abortion. Romney downplayed the issue, saying it is a matter for the Supreme Court and not a political distraction.

A controversial teacher, Rafe Esquith, known for his work with underprivileged students and numerous accolades, faces allegations of sexual misconduct, including inappropriate comments and emails to students, leading to his removal and eventual firing from his position. The Los Angeles Unified School District released 66-page documents detailing these claims, which paint Esquith as a predator, despite no criminal charges. The allegations include inappropriate jokes, inappropriate content screenings, and explicit emails to students, raising questions about the teacher's fitness and the district's handling of the situation.

More than 400 people reported falling ill after eating at a Chipotle restaurant in Powell, Ohio, according to a website tracking foodborne illnesses. Chipotle closed the Powell location on Monday following reports of customer and employee illnesses. The Delaware General Health District is investigating, having received 518 inquiries related to the possible outbreak. The restaurant was previously inspected on Thursday and found to have violations related to food temperature and proper cooling of lettuce. Chipotle plans to reopen the restaurant on Tuesday after a deep clean. The company stated they are taking the reports seriously and cooperating with local health officials.

Gwyneth Paltrow, 38, and mother of two, showcases her toned and stretch-mark-free physique in a topless photo shoot for Vanity Fair. The actress, known for her dedication to yoga and healthy eating, appears youthful and fit, wearing only Louis Vuitton jewelry and fishnets. Her natural makeup and smoky eyes complement her demure pose. Paltrow, who regularly rises at 4:30 AM for her routine, has launched a lifestyle website, GOOP, sharing tips for a better life, though it has faced criticism for being unrealistic. Her appearance on the Glee tour and upcoming projects with her personal trainer Tracy Anderson highlight her continued involvement in various entertainment and wellness endeavors.

A Houston Tex-Mex restaurant, El Tiempo Cantina, faced backlash after posting a photo of Attorney General Jeff Sessions dining at their establishment, leading to the shutdown of their social media accounts. The original post, which thanked Sessions for his visit, was quickly deleted amid calls for a boycott. Owner Roland Laurenzo clarified that the photo did not represent support for Sessions' policies, particularly his stance on separating children from parents. Laurenzo stated that Sessions was served without knowledge of his identity and the post was made without his approval. Despite the clarification, the incident sparked intense criticism and even death threats. El Tiempo Cantina now hopes that customers will understand their stance on immigration policies.

A 25-year-old woman riding a Divvy bike in Chicago's Avondale neighborhood died in a crash with a flatbed truck, believed to be the first fatality involving U.S. bike-share programs. The incident occurred near Sacramento and Belmont avenues, with the woman taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center in critical condition, where she later passed away. The Chicago Department of Transportation and Divvy expressed condolences to the rider's family. This event highlights the need for enhanced bike infrastructure safety. A study by the Mineta Transportation Institute found that collision and injury rates for bike-sharing are lower than for regular bicyclists, attributed to the design of shared bikes, which promote stability and limited speeds.

A 12-year-old student in Florida faces seven felony charges and one misdemeanor charge after six middle school students ingested THC-infused gummy candies during gym class and required hospitalization. The candies, which contain 100 milligrams of THC, were shared among two boys and four girls. The 12-year-old denies consuming any himself. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd expresses concern over the 12-year-old's possession and distribution of the illegal drug near a school. The students experienced symptoms such as stomachaches and dizziness. The incident highlights the dangers of marijuana-infused edibles, especially when they resemble common candies.

Hillary Clinton's visit to the Iowa State Fair this weekend showcased a marked change in her approach compared to her 2008 campaign. This time, she embraced the crowds, shaking hands, taking selfies, and engaging with Iowans on a personal level. Clinton's security detail, known for their plaid shirts, struggled to manage the dense crowds. She met with a young boy and his cow, listened to personal stories, and even munched on a pork chop. Clinton's supporters noted a difference in her demeanor, with one saying, "She’s having a good weekend." Despite the positive interactions, Clinton did not participate in the traditional soapbox event, which some saw as a missed opportunity. Her visit highlighted her effort to connect with "everyday Americans," a key challenge from her previous campaign.

An elderly Massachusetts man, Nicholas Salerno, faces a charge of soliciting a prostitute after allegedly paying a 48-year-old woman, Karen Proia, $100 for a sex act in his home earlier this summer. Salerno reported to Orleans police that a necklace was missing after Proia left. The necklace was found at a South Yarmouth pawn shop. An officer informed Salerno he would be charged with soliciting a prostitute, to which Salerno responded, "I don't give a (expletive). I'm 90 years old..." Both Proia and Salerno pleaded not guilty during arraignments.

Michael Schumacher's medical files, stolen from his hospital in Grenoble, are being offered for sale to the media, his manager has announced. The files, containing details of surgical procedures, are reportedly being sold for around €50,000. Schumacher, a 45-year-old former Formula One racing driver, sustained life-threatening injuries in a skiing accident six months ago. He was transferred from Grenoble to University Hospital Lausanne in France last week after coming out of a medically induced coma. His manager, Sabine Kehm, warned that both the purchase and publication of such documents are forbidden and that criminal charges will be pressed against any unauthorized disclosure. The theft has been reported, and authorities are involved.

A new study suggests that getting a flu shot may lower the risk of heart problems, including heart attacks and strokes, especially for those with a history of heart disease. Analyzing data from 12 randomized clinical trials, researchers found that individuals who received the flu vaccine were 36% less likely to experience a major cardiovascular event compared to those who did not. For those with recent heart issues, the risk reduction was even more significant, with a 55% lower likelihood of experiencing another heart event. The study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, indicates that flu shots could be a valuable tool in preventing heart problems, particularly for high-risk groups.

At least nine undocumented immigrants have died after a Walmart employee reported a man asking for water, leading to the discovery of dozens severely injured in the back of a non-functioning air conditioning tractor-trailer in Texas. The incident, described as a human trafficking crime, involved 31 injured survivors, with two minors hospitalized. Authorities are investigating the trailer's origin and duration of the journey. The U.S. Attorney's Office has charged the driver, James Matthew Bradley Jr., with transporting undocumented immigrants. The case highlights ongoing issues with human smuggling and calls for comprehensive immigration reform.

The KFC Double Down Chicken Sandwich, finally available, is a letdown. Despite initial excitement, the sandwich is described as a "total dud." The chicken is stringy and lacks tenderness, while the cheese interferes with the mild chicken flavor. Bacon is present but not prominent. A ketchup, mustard, mayo hybrid sauce adds little to the taste. While filling, the sandwich cries out for sides, and its small size belies its $5 price. Rating: 2 out of 5.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has initiated a preliminary investigation into allegations of crimes against humanity committed by Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte during his anti-drugs campaign. ICC prosecutor Fatou Bensouda stated that the inquiry will examine events since July 1, 2016, in the context of the "war on drugs." Duterte's spokesperson, Harry Roque, dismissed the investigation as a waste of resources, arguing that many of the allegations predate the Philippines' ratification of the ICC in 2011. Bensouda, however, specifically referenced killings since July 2016. The ICC defines crimes against humanity as "serious violations committed as part of a large-scale attack against any civilian population." Human rights groups and opposition politicians view the ICC's move as a significant step toward accountability for Duterte's actions.

A man doused himself with gasoline and set himself on fire in St. Peter's Square in Vatican City. He is in critical condition, having suffered serious burns to the upper part of his body. A Jesuit priest initially tried to smother the flames with his frock and jacket. Two police officers later arrived and extinguished the fire using a fire extinguisher. The Vatican has not disclosed the man's motives, though they found a piece of paper with his daughter's phone number. The incident echoes a similar case from 15 years ago, when Alfredo Ormando set himself ablaze to protest the Church's stance on homosexuality.

Orexigen Therapeutics Inc. saw its stock surge after winning the first U.S. panel recommendation for its weight-loss drug Contrave, doubling its share price. The FDA advisory committee voted that the drug's weight-loss benefits outweigh its side effects, allowing a large study on cardiovascular risk to wait until after approval. This decision contrasts with the rejections of Arena Pharmaceuticals Inc.'s and Vivus Inc.'s similar drugs, Qnexa and lorcaserin, respectively. Analysts predict potential sales of $1 billion or more for each approved drug. The FDA will make a final decision by January 31.

An Arizona family faced with a tragic loss found unexpected kindness from two Delta pilots. Jay W. Short, a 56-year-old father of three who passed away from lung cancer, wished to be buried with his family in Bolivar, Tennessee. His wife booked flights for the family to travel from Phoenix to Memphis for the funeral. A 90-minute delay caused by cargo door damage left the family with just seven minutes to catch their connecting flight in Minneapolis. Desperate to make the funeral, they waved to the pilots and crew, pleading not to take off. The family missed their flight and was told to take a later one to Atlanta, driving from there to Tennessee. However, Delta pilots Capt. Adam Cohen and his first officer turned the plane around, allowing the family to board and attend the funeral. The pilots' act of kindness was praised by the family, who expressed gratitude for the rare gesture in the airline industry.

Former Berkshire Hathaway executive David Sokol violated the company’s insider-trading rules and misled Warren Buffett about his personal stake in Lubrizol Corp., according to a scathing report from the firm’s board. Sokol’s actions may add fuel to an ongoing Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) probe. The board stated it may sue Sokol to recover his $3 million trading profit and seek damages for harm to the company’s reputation. Sokol’s high-profile attorney disputes the board’s report, claiming Sokol acted with honesty and integrity. The report paints a picture of Sokol deliberately misleading Buffett and highlights the potential legal and reputational consequences for both Sokol and Berkshire Hathaway.

Human Rights Foundation warned Hilary Swank and Jean-Claude Van Damme before they attended a lavish birthday party for Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, who is accused of human rights abuses. The party, held on October 5th, included performances by Swank, Van Damme, and Vanessa-Mae, and was criticized by Human Rights Watch for legitimizing a "brutal leader and his regime." Swank's manager initially said she would not attend, but she and Van Damme were photographed at the event. Human Rights Watch urged the stars to avoid supporting Kadyrov, who has been linked to abductions, torture, and executions in Chechnya.

Michele Bachmann's claims about State Department aide Huma Abedin and Democratic Rep. Keith Ellison being tied to the Muslim Brotherhood have sparked a mixed reaction. While her supporters in the exurbs north of the Twin Cities remain staunch in their support, the incident has faced widespread criticism from both parties. Bachmann's base seems galvanized by the controversy, viewing it as part of her mission to expose alleged Muslim infiltration in the government. Her political star has risen once again on the far right, despite previous setbacks. However, this move has irritated House Republican leaders and tarnished the party's brand. Democrats are now targeting Bachmann for defeat, focusing on a moderate alternative in Jim Graves. Bachmann insists the matter needs investigation, though she faces significant backlash for her claims.

Las Vegas shooting videos reveal the harrowing decision concertgoers faced when the gunshots started. Those in front of the stage dropped to their stomachs, but this position offered less protection against the shooter's elevated vantage point. Audio recordings suggest at least one of the weapons used by the alleged shooter, Stephen Paddock, may have been capable of burst fire, discharging multiple bullets with a single trigger pull. This capability, though federally regulated, raises questions about the weapons' modifications and the ease of obtaining such firearms. Sheriff Joseph Lombardo reported that 16 rifles and a handgun were found in Paddock’s hotel room, including AR-15-style rifles. The exact weapons used remain unclear.

Lou Ferrigno is recovering after a pneumonia vaccination went wrong. The 67-year-old Incredible Hulk actor shared the news on social media, revealing he ended up in the hospital with fluid in his bicep after what he believes was an incorrect shot. Ferrigno advised his followers to be cautious when receiving shots and to watch the needle properly. He attended an event the night he was released from the hospital. Despite the incident, Ferrigno remains optimistic and has several acting and fitness projects lined up.

If the Republicans are still uncertain about pursuing a government shutdown, they should reconsider, suggests former Reagan budget director David Stockman. Stockman, known for his hardline fiscal views, advocates for a shutdown to force President Obama to fold and secure $60 billion in spending cuts. He views the current political climate as ripe for a shutdown, predicting that Obama will capitulate quickly. Stockman also criticizes the GOP's strategy, especially the inclusion of non-budgetary policy riders, and argues that the economic impact of a shutdown is exaggerated. He foresees a long period of economic struggle due to high national debt and criticizes the Ryan budget for its long-term focus and lack of immediate fiscal solutions.

Iran's Islamic Penal Code, detailed in Book Five, outlines comprehensive legal frameworks for various offenses, including crimes against national security, religious values, property, and individuals. It mandates severe punishments for offenses such as espionage, terrorism, and theft, with sentences ranging from fines to life imprisonment and even the death penalty. The code also covers offenses related to public morality, family rights, and economic crimes, emphasizing strict penalties for breaches of trust and public order. Notably, the code allows for mitigating circumstances in certain cases, but overall, it emphasizes harsh punishments to maintain social and religious order.

A group of senior scientists and clinicians has called for urgent investigation into the potential role of viruses and bacteria in causing Alzheimer's disease, as detailed in an editorial published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. The editorial suggests that microbes, including the herpes virus, chlamydia bacteria, and spirochaete, are major contributors to the disease. The authors argue that there is substantial evidence linking these microbes to Alzheimer's, including their presence in the brains of elderly people and their association with specific genetic factors. They propose that further research, including clinical trials of antimicrobial treatments, is warranted to explore this hypothesis. The editorial highlights the need to reassess the current focus on amyloid plaque buildup as the primary cause of Alzheimer's, suggesting that targeting microbes could potentially slow or halt disease progression.

Chinese authorities confirmed a case where a woman was forced to have a late-term abortion due to failing to pay a fine for violating the country's one-child policy, amid widespread outrage. The Shaanxi provincial government acknowledged the incident and promised to take action against the perpetrators, stating it violated regulations against late-term abortions. Rights groups and activists have long criticized the policy, with one group citing the case as an example of ongoing violence against women. The incident, which gained attention through online photos, highlights the continued controversy surrounding China's strict family planning measures.

Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, an early Trump supporter and possible candidate for a top government post, presented a detailed plan to the president-elect during their meeting. The plan includes updating and reintroducing the National Security Entry-Exit Registration System (NSEERS) for immigrants from "high-risk" areas, asking "extreme vetting questions" about support for Sharia law and the U.S. Constitution, and reducing the intake of Syrian refugees. The document, visible in a photograph taken during the meeting, also calls for increased border security measures. Kobach's plan reflects his long-standing advocacy for strict immigration policies and could position him for a high-level role in the Trump administration.

France will temporarily close its embassies and schools in 20 countries on Friday due to a French satirical magazine's publication of cartoons of the Prophet Mohammad, aimed at a film mocking the prophet, potentially escalating tensions. The magazine, Charlie Hebdo, published these cartoons amid ongoing outrage over the anti-Islam film, which has sparked violent protests globally. French authorities and Muslim leaders urged restraint, with Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault rejecting a planned protest against the film in Paris. The magazine's latest issue, featuring nude cartoons of the Prophet, has drawn criticism from Muslim leaders but is defended as a stand for free speech. Security measures are being increased at French diplomatic offices in the Muslim world.

Country music superstar Carrie Underwood helped a 12-year-old fan make a special memory during her concert in Louisville, Ky., by bringing him onstage for a kiss. After warning the boy that her husband was in the arena, Underwood asked, "OK, how are we going to do this?" The brave fan replied, "Lip to lip." Underwood obliged, giving him a kiss on the lips. She later thanked the boy and the Louisville audience on Twitter. Underwood's "Blown Away Tour" will include home state shows in Oklahoma City and Tulsa.

Catherine Zeta-Jones, 41, has checked into a mental health facility for a brief stay to treat her Bipolar II Disorder. Her publicist confirms that after dealing with the stress of the past year, including her husband Michael Douglas's throat cancer treatment and legal battles, Zeta-Jones has found herself in need of some expert care. While her stay is not related to substance abuse, her publicist notes that she is feeling great and looking forward to starting work on her upcoming films. Zeta-Jones and Douglas, 66, have been through significant challenges together, including Douglas's cancer diagnosis and legal issues, which have drawn the couple closer.

Three surfers have died after getting into difficulties in the sea off Mawgan Porth beach in Cornwall. Seven surfers, including four children, were helped from the water at around 1:30 pm on Sunday due to a rip current. The three adults, a man in his 50s from outside the Devon and Cornwall area and two men and a woman in their 40s from Cornwall, were later pronounced dead after being airlifted to the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. The four children were rescued and described as "walking wounded." Local conditions were described as "not as bad as it can be" but some currents were "slightly more dangerous than usual." Rip currents can be dangerous for surfers, swimmers, and bodyboarders, and people without the necessary water skills can be at risk if they panic or exhaust themselves swimming against the flow.

Vanderbilt University will remove the name "Confederate" from its residence hall, renaming it Memorial Hall after raising $1.2 million to repay a 1933 donation from the United Daughters of the Confederacy. The university's chancellor, Nicholas S. Zeppos, stated that the name change is to address the hall's status as a "symbol and a reminder of racism, slavery, and the Civil War." The decision comes as universities across the country reassess historical names and symbols, with some, like Middle Tennessee State University, considering renaming buildings named after Confederate figures. Vanderbilt's move is seen as a step towards a more inclusive campus environment, although it faces criticism from those who argue it erases history.

The estate of the late artist Dash Snow is suing McDonald’s for using his signature graffiti tag, "SACE," without permission in multiple restaurants, claiming copyright and trademark infringement. Snow, who passed away in 2009, was an anti-commercial artist who avoided associations with corporate culture. His estate argues that McDonald’s use of his work could harm the value of his original artworks and is attempting to capitalize on his reputation. The lawsuit, filed in October 2016, alleges that McDonald’s refused to remove the graffiti tag after being asked to do so in June 2016.

Congressional leaders and President Obama called for a return to negotiations to avert the fiscal cliff, but talks had already broken down earlier in the week, reports the Wall Street Journal. House Speaker John Boehner’s backup plan collapsed Thursday night, leaving the White House and congressional Republicans at an impasse. The Journal’s reconstruction of the negotiations reveals deep divisions, with Boehner struggling to keep his party in line and Obama facing resistance from his own side. Both leaders failed to find common ground on key issues, including tax rates and spending cuts. Despite the breakdown, both sides expect a small package to be agreed upon, deferring the battle until next year. The article highlights the tension between the two parties and the challenges they face in reaching a deal to avoid the fiscal cliff.

A professor at Leipzig University in Germany apologized for denying an internship to an Indian student due to the "rape problem in India," after the German ambassador strongly condemned the incident. The professor, Annette G Beck-Sickinger, admitted the decision was a "misunderstanding" and claimed the university does not discriminate against Indian students. However, another student came forward, alleging Beck-Sickinger had also rejected his PhD application on similar grounds. The German ambassador criticized the professor's oversimplifying and discriminating generalization, urging her to learn more about India's diversity and women empowerment efforts. The incident sparked a debate on gender equality and violence against women in India, with the documentary "India's Daughter" banned in the country despite its global screening.

In a groundbreaking procedure, doctors in Toronto performed the world's first in-utero surgery to treat a severe congenital heart defect in a fetus. Kristine Barry, 25, and her husband Christopher Havill, 27, learned their baby Sebastian had a life-threatening condition called complete transposition of the great arteries (TGA) and closed heart chambers. To save Sebastian, doctors at the Hospital for Sick Children and Mount Sinai Hospital devised a plan to insert a balloon through Barry's uterus to create a hole in Sebastian's heart, allowing blood to circulate properly. The surgery was successful, and Barry gave birth to a healthy Sebastian five days later. Sebastian then underwent open-heart surgery to correct his heart's structure. Now a healthy two-month-old, Sebastian's parents are grateful for the medical team's efforts, which they say could have been life-threatening if not for the in-utero procedure.

Baltimore Ravens cornerback Tray Walker, 23, has died from injuries sustained in a motorcycle crash in Miami. Walker, who was riding a motorbike without a helmet, collided with a Ford Escape on Thursday night. The crash occurred in Miami without any signs of alcohol or drug involvement, and police do not believe it was a racing incident. Walker, a native of Miami and a 2015 fourth-round draft pick, was wearing a Ravens jersey and dark clothing. His death has deeply affected the Ravens team, with Coach John Harbaugh expressing his sorrow and sharing memories of Walker's positive impact on the team. Fellow players, including C.J. Mosley, Steve Smith Sr., and Za'Darius Smith, have expressed their grief and shared personal anecdotes about Walker, highlighting his smile and dedication to the team. The Ravens organization has extended their condolences to Walker's family and friends.

A man named Grim LeRogue, who changed his name from Joe Rogan, ran onto the field at Yankee Stadium with five pictures, including one of Alex Rodriguez with an X over his face and a message threatening him. LeRogue, 33, also carried a picture of Cameron Diaz with a message expressing his desire to be with her. He was tackled by security and charged with assault and interfering with a sporting event. LeRogue, who has a history of arrests, was taken to Lincoln Hospital for a psychiatric evaluation. His mother expressed disbelief at his actions, stating that while he had a troubled past, he is now 33 and mature.

Chris Christie on "Piers Morgan Tonight" expressed frustration with Warren Buffett's calls for higher taxes, saying Buffett should "just write a check and shut up." Christie is tired of hearing about Buffett's complaints and suggests he contribute directly if he wants to give more to the government. Christie emphasized his role as governor is to serve all New Jerseyans, not engage in class warfare.

The San Francisco home from the 1993 film "Mrs. Doubtfire" was targeted by a suspicious fire on Monday night. Police were called to the property on Broadway and Steiner Street around 8 p.m. after someone tried to set fire to the home's garage door and front door, possibly using an accelerant. No suspects have been identified. The home, now owned by a doctor who has performed facial feminization surgeries, was the setting for the movie starring Robin Williams. The owner reported issues with a former client but stated the incident does not appear to be a hate crime.

The National Portrait Gallery unveiled portraits of former President Barack Obama and former First Lady Michelle Obama. Barack Obama's portrait, painted by Kehinde Wiley, features him sitting against a backdrop of green foliage, while Michelle Obama's portrait, by Amy Sherald, shows her in a flowing, patterned dress with a thoughtful expression. Both artists are African-American, with Wiley known for his vibrant, large-scale paintings of African-Americans and Sherald for her unique style that underscores themes of social justice. The Obamas chose the artists after considering over two dozen portfolios, and the portraits will be open to public viewing starting Tuesday.

Richard Carpenter, representing the Carpenters' estate, has filed a lawsuit against Universal Music Group and A&M Records, alleging that the music companies have underpaid them in digital royalties. The lawsuit seeks at least $2 million in compensatory damages. According to the Carpenters, the record labels improperly classified revenue from digital downloads as sales of records, resulting in a lower royalty rate. They also claim undercounted digital downloads and applied an incorrect base price to CD sales. The case is similar to a previous lawsuit involving Eminem, where the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that digital downloads are a licensing of master recordings rather than a sale of records. Richard Carpenter stated that he is looking forward to proving the allegations in court.

IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn, 62, faces charges of attempted rape and other sexual assault offenses in New York, dealing a blow to his presidential ambitions. The scandal, which unfolded after a maid accused him of sexually assaulting her in his $3,000-a-night suite at the Sofitel hotel, forced him to flee a plane bound for Paris and led to his arrest. Strauss-Kahn's wife, Anne Sinclair, defended him, but the charges could result in up to 20 years in prison. The incident threatens to undermine the IMF's leadership and Strauss-Kahn's political career, as he was seen as a frontrunner for the French presidency. His arrest also raises questions about the IMF's handling of his previous misconduct, including an affair with a subordinate in 2008. Strauss-Kahn's legal team is working to cast doubt on the allegations, but the case has already caused delays in IMF meetings and could further damage his reputation.

The International AIDS Conference, set to begin in Melbourne, mourns the loss of several attendees, including renowned HIV researcher Joep Lange and WHO staff member Glenn Thomas, who were aboard the Malaysia Airlines flight shot down over Ukraine. The conference organizers express deep sorrow and offer condolences to the families of the victims. Many attendees, activists, and researchers, who were en route to the conference, have lost colleagues and friends. The tragedy casts a somber shadow over the upcoming event, with organizers planning a "Silent Walk" in central Amsterdam to honor the victims.

Federal air marshals have been secretly observing specific American travelers on domestic flights under a previously undisclosed program called "Quiet Skies," according to a report by The Boston Globe. Thousands of unsuspecting Americans have been subjected to targeted airport and in-flight surveillance by small teams of armed, undercover air marshals since the program began in March. The Transportation Security Administration acknowledged the Quiet Skies program, declining to specify how passengers are targeted or if any arrests have resulted from the initiative, but stated it has been in existence since 2010. Air marshals follow about 35 Quiet Skies targets a day, observing them on a flight and recording behaviors such as fidgeting, using a laptop or smartphone, sweating heavily, or sleeping. TSA insists the program does not single out travelers based on race, religion, or nationality, but privacy advocates are concerned about potential constitutional issues and the use of unreliable techniques to monitor travelers.

A customer was refused service at Chinatown Coffee Co. in Washington, D.C., when he ordered three shots of espresso over ice. The barista, citing that it would "ruin" the espresso, refused to make the drink, leading to an uncomfortable exchange. This incident, reminiscent of a similar controversy at Murky Coffee in 2008, sparked a debate about customer rights and coffee shop policies. The barista's refusal and subsequent comment, "Aww… did I just ruin your day?" added an insulting twist, leaving the customer disappointed. The customer's response, "You’re goddamned right you can’t stop me," highlights the tension between customer preferences and establishment rules.

A global email virus with the subject "Here you have" caused disruptions at various organizations including NASA, Comcast, and Disney. The threat, which McAfee referred to as a virus, Trojan, and worm, spread through links in emails, but can only infect computers if users click the link. Security experts advise against clicking unknown links and keeping antivirus software up to date. The virus, linked to a cyber-jihad group, spread widely, affecting multiple companies and government agencies. While the risk for home users is low, the incident highlights the importance of email security.

A 2006 letter from then-Archbishop Leonardo Sandri, now a top Vatican cardinal, confirms that the Holy See received information in 2000 about the sexual misconduct of now-resigned U.S. Cardinal Theodore McCarrick, lending credibility to accusations of a cover-up at the highest levels of the Roman Catholic Church. The letter, published by Catholic News Service, refers to a 2000 letter from Father Boniface Ramsay, who informed the Vatican about complaints from seminarians regarding McCarrick's behavior. Archbishop Sandri's acknowledgment of the 2000 letter suggests the Vatican was aware of the allegations early on, potentially implicating Benedict's papacy for failing to act on the information. Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano, in his expose, cited Ramsay's 2000 letter and accused church officials, including Pope Francis, of failing to address the abuse and power misuse by McCarrick.

Two students were injured in a shooting outside Frederick High School during a junior varsity basketball game Wednesday night. Police have not identified any suspects or motives and continue to search the area. The victims, one 14 and the other 15, were flown to a Baltimore hospital for non-life-threatening injuries. Frederick High and nearby West Frederick Middle School were closed Thursday for a police investigation, while other schools remained open. Students were questioned and released to their parents. Police believe the shooter or shooters fled on foot and targeted the victims. The shooting raised concerns about safety and prompted additional security measures at schools.

Steven Spielberg's "Bridge of Spies" is a complex Cold War drama that challenges the audience to trust its slow-burn narrative and intricate details. The film follows Brooklyn lawyer James B. Donovan (Tom Hanks), who is thrust into negotiating the release of a captured American U-2 pilot, Francis Gary Powers (Austin Stowell), in exchange for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel (Mark Rylance). Spielberg and screenwriters Joel and Ethan Coen, along with Matt Charman, weave a thoughtful meditation on doing the right thing, embodied in the friendship between Abel and Donovan. Donovan's character is portrayed as a real person with doubts and runny nose, avoiding the hyperbole of the great man myth. Mark Rylance delivers a standout performance as Abel, making him sympathetic despite his role as a Soviet agent. The film's focus on Abel contrasts with near indifference to Powers and another American student, emphasizing the moral drama's depth. Directed by Spielberg, the film is a lean, purpose

The revival of Gilmore Girls is officially moving forward, with Netflix confirming the production of four 90-minute movies. The original cast, including Lauren Graham, Alexis Bledel, Kelly Bishop, Scott Patterson, Sean Gunn, and Keiko Agena, will reprise their roles. Creator Amy Sherman-Palladino and her husband Daniel Palladino will write and direct the films, which are set in the present day and span a calendar year, each covering a different season. This revival aims to provide closure for fans, as Sherman-Palladino was not involved in the show's final season. The exact title and premiere date remain undisclosed.

Two more suspected drug-smuggling tunnels linking warehouses in Tijuana and San Diego have been uncovered by U.S. and Mexican authorities, and a 73-year-old California woman is accused of being the logistics manager for one passageway. No drugs or other contraband were found in the tunnels, which featured lights, rails, wooden supports, and ventilation. The passages, costing millions to build, were the sixth and seventh super tunnels found between Tijuana and San Diego since 2010. The first tunnel, about 600 yards long, was found in an industrial park in Otay Mesa, San Diego. On Wednesday, Glennys Rodriguez, a U.S. citizen from Chula Vista, was arrested and faces federal charges of conspiring to maintain a drug-involved premises. The second, more sophisticated tunnel, stretching about 700 yards, was unearthed by Mexican investigators following leads from U.S. counterparts. Authorities aim to shut down these elaborate

President Obama warned that the global economic recovery remains fragile, urging continued spending to support growth. The Group of 20 agreed to halve annual deficits within three years and stabilize overall debt by 2016, though the U.S. preferred a more cautious approach. The final statement acknowledged the need for balanced fiscal sustainability and growth, with countries charting their own unique paths. Strong emerging markets like China were urged to boost local spending and demand. Advanced surplus countries committed to narrowing trade gaps, particularly in Europe. The G-20 also discussed banking regulations but could not agree on a global bank tax. Despite divisions, leaders emphasized the need to avoid synchronized fiscal adjustments that could harm recovery.

Ivanka Trump used a personal email account to send hundreds of messages discussing official White House business in 2017, officials confirm. The discovery alarmed some advisers, who feared similarities to Hillary Clinton's personal email use during her tenure as secretary of state. Trump's lawyer says she was not familiar with the rules and did not create a private server, but critics argue her father's campaign against Clinton's email use was hypocritical. The White House says she stopped using her personal account after being briefed on the rules and turned over her emails for preservation. Critics call for an investigation into whether she violated federal records rules.

President Donald Trump's longtime financial gatekeeper, Allen Weisselberg, was granted immunity by federal prosecutors in New York during the Michael Cohen investigation. According to two sources, Weisselberg is identified as "Executive 1" in the criminal information filed by prosecutors against Cohen. Prosecutors allege Cohen sent an invoice to Weisselberg for a payment meant to reimburse Cohen for a $130,000 payment to adult-film star Stormy Daniels. Weisselberg then directed another executive to pay from a trust, categorizing it as a legal expense. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York declined to comment. Weisselberg, 70, has worked for the Trump Organization since the 1970s and was also treasurer of the president's charitable foundation, which has faced legal issues. Cohen mentioned Weisselberg's name in a recorded phone conversation with Trump about a payment to suppress a story about the president's alleged relationship with Playboy

Thais queue up outside the Grand Palace to sign condolence books as the country enters a year of mourning for King Bhumibol Adulyadej. The Commerce Ministry warns traders against price hikes on black mourning attire and sends inspectors to monitor markets. Traders report brisk sales but deny price gouging, with some selling black shirts for 120-130 baht. Many Thais, including shoppers in Bangkok, wear black in honor of the late king.

A fight over a break room light at Philadelphia International Airport turned deadly, resulting in the stabbing death of one worker. The incident occurred around 11:30 a.m. in a secure area of Terminal E, involving three workers employed by Worldwide Flight Services, a cleaning contractor for Frontier Airlines. One man turned off a light, angering another who then got into an argument. A third worker pulled out a knife and stabbed one of the men, 28-year-old Aaron Jenkins, fatally. The alleged attacker, 35-year-old Kevin Emanuel, and the other involved worker fled but were apprehended by police. The weapon, believed to be a box cutter, was not recovered. The incident did not disrupt airport operations.

Many Afghan army units are running out of key equipment, including Humvees, due to their inability to repair or find replacements. After a tough fighting season, Afghan soldiers find that a significant portion of their vital equipment is broken and cannot be easily replaced. The Afghan army, which started doing the bulk of the fighting, is now struggling to maintain and repair its vehicles. The U.S. military, which previously handled repairs, stopped doing so as part of the transition process. However, with the Afghan supply chain still undeveloped and the Defense Ministry hobbled by corruption, army units across the country are not getting the gear and parts they need. This issue affects not only regular army units but also special forces teams. The lack of functional equipment restricts the army's ability to conduct operations, with some units forced to walk long distances or use less-protected vehicles. The Afghan Defense Ministry has acknowledged these problems but has seen limited progress in addressing them. U.S. officials say they are aware of

Sen. Marco Rubio (R., Fla.) suggested his decision on whether to run again for his Senate seat would not be made until the weekend at the earliest. The shooting massacre in Orlando on Sunday had led Rubio to consider how he might best serve the country. Friends for 20 years, Rubio and Florida Lt. Gov. Carlos Lopez-Cantera had an unusually frank conversation about their political futures. Lopez-Cantera, who has been running for his Senate seat for over a year, encouraged Rubio to reconsider running. Despite Rubio’s initial resistance, the conversation removed one of the biggest obstacles to Rubio running again: a longtime friendship that he wouldn’t want to ruin due to political ambition. The filing deadline for the race is June 24. Polling shows Rubio is the strongest Republican in a potential race against the Democrats’ strongest candidate, Rep. Patrick Murphy, in a contest that could decide control of the Senate. The Republican Senate race is crowded, and the full-court press to recruit

Melissa McCarthy's career took a hit with "Identity Thief," a comedy that critics found unfunny and predictable. The film follows Jason Bateman's character, Sandy, whose identity is stolen by McCarthy's Diana, a Florida shopaholic. Despite McCarthy's talent, the script by Craig Mazin and Jerry Eeten fails to deliver laughs, with the movie relying on clichés and predictable plot twists. Director Seth Gordon's efforts to create a road movie with action sequences fall flat, and the film's attempts at sentimentality are seen as forced. McCarthy's character, Diana, is portrayed as an obnoxious sociopath, and the movie's treatment of obesity is seen as insensitive. Overall, "Identity Thief" is a disappointing entry in McCarthy's filmography, overshadowing her previous comedic successes.

A Jefferson County judge dismissed the capital murder charge against Gabe Watson, ending his prosecution in the death of his wife, Tina, during their honeymoon scuba diving in Australia in 2003. Judge Tommy Nail ruled there was insufficient evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Watson intentionally killed his wife for monetary gain. The prosecution claimed Watson discussed insurance policies with his wife before the trip and tried to collect on insurance after her death. However, the only eyewitness testified that Watson was trying to save his wife's life. The judge's decision came after a two-week trial and before the defense presented its case. Gabe Watson's father expressed relief, hoping his son could start healing and rebuilding his life.

In the aftermath of the San Bernardino shootings, investigators pieced together that Syed Rizwan Farook, a co-worker of the victims, left a work meeting 20 minutes before the attack and matched the description of a gunman. Farook and his wife, Tashfeen Malik, killed 14 people and wounded 21 others before dying in a shootout with police. The attack occurred at the Inland Regional Center during a holiday gathering. Farook and Malik had reportedly practiced at a local gun range for a year and made financial plans for their family. They left their 6-month-old daughter with Farook’s mother. Investigators are examining a $28,500 deposit to Farook’s account in the weeks before the attack, which may have been for their family. FBI investigators also suggest Farook may have discussed staging an attack as early as 2012.

This year's Democratic National Convention in Charlotte, North Carolina, features a mix of key political figures and issues. Bill Clinton is set to deliver a speech endorsing Barack Obama, potentially overshadowing the current president. The relationship between the two, once strained, has mended as they face a common foe in Mitt Romney. Elizabeth Warren, a rising star in the Democratic Party, is scheduled to speak, highlighting the competitive Senate race in Massachusetts against Republican Scott Brown. The convention aims to emphasize Obama's economic policies and his ability to handle the economy, contrasting him with Romney. Weather conditions and the overall atmosphere of the convention are also points of interest, with Charlotte's bustling streets and relaxed security measures creating a different vibe compared to the previous Republican National Convention.

In a study that challenges conventional wisdom, researchers found that sending romantic emails can be more effective than leaving voicemail messages. Using psychophysiological measures from college-age participants, the study showed that email senders were more emotionally aroused and used stronger, more thoughtful language compared to those who left voicemails. The researchers suggest that email allows senders to modify and carefully craft messages, potentially increasing emotional content. This finding contradicts the belief that digital communication is poor for conveying emotions and supports the idea that the choice of medium can significantly influence the content and impact of the message.

Two women in their 70s, Denice Juneski and Linda Jourdeans, discovered they were switched at birth in 1945 after DNA tests revealed their true family connections. Denice, who lives in Eagan, Minnesota, took a DNA test on the genealogy website 23andMe, leading to the surprising discovery. Linda’s niece noticed Denice on her own DNA report, prompting both women to take DNA tests, which confirmed they were switched. Born on the same day in 1945 at Bethesda Hospital in St. Paul, Denice Mary Mayer and Linda Jean Nielsen unknowingly walked in each other’s footsteps for 72 years. Family photos and anecdotes support the DNA results, showing how they fit into different family dynamics. Since their discovery, the women have met several times and plan to attend a reunion with both families.

Taylor Swift's social media accounts were hacked on January 27, with hackers threatening to release nude photos in exchange for bitcoins. Swift, however, dismissed the claims, telling fans to "have fun" finding any. The incident occurred as Swift was in Maui with Haim sisters. She also used the hack as an opportunity to address a bullied fan named Caillou, encouraging her to not let negative words affect her. Swift's belly button was revealed in a bikini photo from Maui, settling the mystery of whether it's an inny or outy. The article also mentions Swift's upcoming album "Reputation" and its storm-related motifs.

A man named Willie Corey Godbolt, 35, allegedly carried out a shooting spree in Mississippi that left eight people dead, including a Lincoln County deputy, and two boys. Godbolt, who had an argument with his estranged wife over their children, told The Clarion-Ledger he intended to "suicide by cop." He was arrested in Brookhaven after a seven-hour manhunt. Godbolt's stepfather-in-law recounted that Godbolt shot and killed three family members in their home. The shooting also took the lives of two boys and their mother in another location. Godbolt was treated for a gunshot wound and taken to a Jackson hospital. Lincoln County Sheriff Steve Rushing described the community's grief over the loss of Deputy William Durr, a two-year veteran of the department and a local favorite among children. Governor Phil Bryant asked for prayers for the victims and their families.

Tesla is working to understand the facts of a fatal accident involving a Model X on March 23, with the company emphasizing the safety benefits of its Autopilot feature. Autopilot was engaged with adaptive cruise control at minimum follow distance when the driver did not respond to several hands-on warnings before the collision. The crash was severe due to a previously undetected, severely damaged crash attenuator on the highway. Internal data shows Tesla vehicles equipped with Autopilot hardware are 3.7 times less likely to be involved in fatal accidents compared to non-autonomous vehicles. Tesla maintains that Autopilot improves safety for occupants, pedestrians, and cyclists, despite not preventing all accidents. The company is cooperating with investigators and has released photos of the damaged crash attenuator, which had not been replaced after a prior accident.

Performers for an all-male dance revue on the Las Vegas Strip thwarted a gunman seen stealing property inside the dancers' locker room at the Excalibur hotel-casino on March 18, 2014. The suspect, believed to be between 25 and 35 years old, was caught after a struggle during which he fired a .44 Magnum handgun, striking a wall but not anyone. The dancers subdued him, and he was later booked into Clark County Detention Center on charges of attempted murder with a deadly weapon, attempted robbery with a deadly weapon, and burglary with a deadly weapon. The show remained on schedule the following day.

Researchers have discovered what they believe to be the oldest fortified settlement in North America, Fort Caroline, built by the French in 1564. Historian Fletcher Crowe and Professor Anita Spring claim the fort is located on an island at the mouth of the Altamaha River, two miles southeast of Darien, Georgia, not near Jacksonville, Florida, as previously thought. Their findings were announced at an international conference in Florida. The location of Fort Caroline has been a mystery for over 150 years. Crowe and Spring used 16th-century maps and trade routes to pinpoint the site. They argue that the fort’s destruction by Spanish troops in 1565, which has been linked to Jacksonville, can be explained by the fort’s actual location on the Georgia coast. The site has not yet been excavated, and further research is planned.

Jonathan Pollard, a convicted spy for Israel who has served 29 years of a life sentence, will be released from federal prison on November 20, exactly 30 years after his arrest. Pollard's lawyers successfully argued that he met the legal standards for parole, including good behavior in prison and no threat of returning to espionage. The release could help ease tensions between the U.S. and Israel, particularly regarding the Iran nuclear deal. President Obama's administration has stated that Pollard's parole was granted according to standard procedures and is not connected to foreign policy considerations.

As the 2014 Sochi Olympics begin, the U.S. team features both seasoned veterans and fresh faces. Notable athletes to watch include Mikaela Shiffrin in alpine skiing and Shaun White, who withdrew from the slopestyle event to focus on the halfpipe. White's decision highlights concerns over the safety of the slopestyle course, which has already injured several competitors. The addition of 12 new events, including slopestyle snowboarding and women's ski jumping, brings the total medal events to 98. Despite security concerns, Russian deputy prime minister Dmitry Kozak reassures that the level of threat in Sochi is no worse than in other major cities. The opening ceremony approaches, promising to showcase Russia's blend of history and modernity to an expected 65 heads of state and government.

The mysterious DVD that arrived at the door of RJ Cipriani and his wife Greice Santo contained a chilling message: pay up or face a gruesome fate. Inside, a man in a balaclava threatened the couple, warning them to settle a $2.5 million debt to a US cocaine kingpin with links to Mexican and South American cartels. The DVD showed two men being beheaded, one with a chainsaw and the other with a butcher's knife. Cipriani, a former professional gambler known as Robin Hood 702, became a key witness in the case against Owen Hanson, a former USC athlete turned accused drug lord. Hanson was sentenced to 21 years in prison after pleading guilty to racketeering and conspiracy to distribute drugs. The case against Hanson was built on evidence that included threats, beheading videos, and a $702,000 cash find. Hanson's lavish lifestyle and criminal activities were exposed, leading to

President Donald Trump called acting National Park Service director Michael T. Reynolds on Saturday to complain about a retweet from the agency’s official Twitter account that compared the size of the crowd at his inauguration to Barack Obama’s in 2009. The call, confirmed by White House deputy press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders, highlights Trump’s focus on the crowd size controversy and his proactive approach to addressing perceived issues. Acting director Reynolds was instructed to provide additional crowd photos to support Trump’s claim that the attendance was much larger than reported. The incident underscores the tension between the new administration and career government employees, particularly at the National Park Service, as the agency faced internal directives to restrict social media communications following the inauguration.

Archaeologists uncovered two skeletons holding hands at a 1,000-year-old "lost" chapel in Hallaton, Leicestershire. Found by the Hallaton Fieldwork Group over four years, the pair, believed to be of similar age, were buried in the 14th century. University of Leicester archaeologist Vicky Score, who leads the project, says the site might have been a special burial place for pilgrims or the sick. Among other findings, a man was killed by a sharp object, possibly in battle, and another young male was buried with his legs raised, suggesting a disease. The chapel, located after local historian John Morrison's research, may fill a gap in the historical record between Roman and medieval periods.

Scott Weiland's ex-wife Mary Forsberg has filed documents in Los Angeles asking to be named the executor of his will, TMZ reports. Forsberg, who was his second wife and mother of his two children, filed a will with Weiland's signature as proof, written in April 2007, around the time their marriage was falling apart and Weiland was battling addiction. Weiland's estate is estimated to be about $2 million, and he also created a trust with undisclosed assets. His third wife Jamie Wachtel was with him for two years before his death and could still contest Forsberg's filing.

The U.S. House of Representatives voted Friday to defund Planned Parenthood for a one-year period, passing the bill 241-187. The vote came after months of intense focus on the organization following the release of undercover videos that activists claim show violations of federal laws prohibiting the sale of fetal tissue for profit and restricting certain abortion procedures. Despite the nearly party-line vote, neither bill is likely to become law as Senate Democrats have filibustered similar measures, and President Obama has indicated he would veto both. The votes were aimed at appeasing conservatives who have threatened a government shutdown over the organization. However, Democrats argue the bill is an attack on women's health care and that other health-care providers would be unable to absorb all of Planned Parenthood’s patients. The bills were brought to the House floor amid a deadline to fund the government, but neither side indicated a shutdown would force them to change their stance.

President Barack Obama's White House Honey Brown Ale, believed to be the first beer brewed on the White House grounds, was revealed with a recipe and brewing video. The beer, inspired by home brewers, includes light malt extract, amber crystal malt, honey, gypsum, yeast, and corn sugar. White House press secretary Jay Carney announced the recipe on Twitter, and White House chef Sam Kass, who brews the beer in the White House kitchen, stated that the president paid for the materials. The White House also released a recipe for a honey porter and a honey blonde. The brewing process involves steeping grains, adding malt extract and honey, boiling with hops, cooling, fermenting, and bottling. The honey gives the beer a rich aroma and finish but doesn't sweeten it.

President Trump claimed he turned down an interview and photo shoot for Time magazine's "Person of the Year" issue, stating that "probably" being named the title was not good enough. Time magazine later clarified that Trump was indeed named Person of the Year for the second year in a row but denied the need for an interview and photo shoot. Trump frequently boasts about his Time cover appearances, though he has falsely claimed to hold the record. The magazine will announce its Person of the Year on December 6.

A 4-year-old cancer patient named Jillian Massey, from Coopersburg, Pennsylvania, who was diagnosed with brain cancer in April and spent six months in the hospital, decided to give back to her friends by collecting 50 gifts for them at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia. Her Amazon wish list went viral, and with the help of her mother's colleagues at a homebuilding company, the drive expanded to over 3,000 toys. Jillian is excited to bring cheer to her friends when the toys are delivered on Monday.

A North Korean soldier, identified only by the family name Oh, who defected across the DMZ to South Korea on November 13, is recovering in a Seoul hospital after sustaining multiple gunshot wounds. The 24-year-old, described as a quiet, pleasant man, has nightmares about being sent back to the North. Surgeon John Cook-Jong Lee, who has been treating Oh, says the defector has shown signs of depression and PTSD. Lee has been playing South Korean pop music and American TV shows like "The Transporter" and "CSI" for Oh to help him recover. Oh has undergone three surgeries, including the removal of 10-inch-long parasitic worms from his intestines. He has also been diagnosed with tuberculosis and hepatitis B. The North Korean military has reportedly replaced guards in the area where the defection occurred, and South Korean and U.S. soldiers involved in the rescue have been decorated.

If you swim at 10 different U.S. beaches, you could encounter bacteria that might cause stomach bugs, conjunctivitis, or other illnesses. New research from the National Resources Defense Council (NRDC) found that 10% of the country’s coastal and lakefront beaches fail to meet the Environmental Protection Agency’s water-safety standards. The main culprits are stormwater runoff and untreated sewage, which annually affect 3.5 million Americans. Federal law mandates states to test beach water and respond when bacteria levels are too high. In 2012, nearly 2,000 beaches in New York and New Jersey were closed due to pollution. Rainfall and drought conditions further complicate water quality issues, especially in California, where 9% of water quality samples failed to meet the EPA’s swimmer safety threshold, putting the state on par with the national average. Green infrastructure solutions could help manage stormwater runoff and reduce pollution.

World of Beer is offering an internship where you can travel the world, drink beer, and get paid $12,000 for four months. The company, with 77 locations nationwide, is looking for three interns to visit breweries and beer festivals, writing about their experiences. The internship covers travel, food, and lodging expenses. Applicants, who must be 21, can apply by submitting a video or in person at specific locations. The top ten applications will have Skype interviews, with three interns ultimately selected for the unique opportunity.

A New York City subway station has reopened after 17 years, symbolizing the city's resilience following the 9/11 attacks. The WTC Cortlandt station, part of the 1 train route, was buried in debris when the World Trade Center towers collapsed. After extensive construction, the fully accessible station, costing $181.8 million, now features state-of-the-art technology, including an air ventilation system and fewer columns for better passenger flow. Its walls are adorned with a white marble mosaic, quoting text from the US Declaration of Independence and the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights, underscoring the station's significance as a symbol of recovery and human rights.

More American mothers are older and better educated than they were two decades ago, according to a study by the Pew Research Center. In 2008, 14% of newborn mothers were 35 or older, up from 10% in 1990. Half of mothers surveyed said parenthood "just happened." The study also found that 41% of births were to unmarried women in 2008, up from 28% in 1990. Improvements in medical care and fertility treatments, along with delayed marriage and childbearing to pursue education, contributed to these trends. Women in their 30s are more likely to have multiples, and older mothers are more likely to raise children in stable marriages. The study suggests that the rise of single motherhood is significant and challenges societal norms.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is likely to serve a third term after voters gave his conservative team a surprising second place in the national election, with a new centrist party founded by television celebrity Yair Lapid emerging as a key player. Lapid's Yesh Atid party emphasized kitchen-table issues like class size and apartment prices and ran a campaign that resonated with the middle class. Netanyahu's Likud-Beiteinu ticket won 31 seats, while Lapid's Yesh Atid took 19. The traditional blocs were evenly divided, with 60 seats for right-wing and religious parties and 60 for center, left, and Arab-dominated factions. Netanyahu called Lapid shortly after the polls closed and offered to work with him, while Lapid indicated he was open to working with Netanyahu but emphasized the need for a broad coalition to address Israel's challenges.
