As Ron Paul gains momentum in the Republican race, questions arise about his past involvement in publishing newsletters containing racist and conspiracy theories. Critics argue that his exclusion from the Republican Jewish Coalition’s forum was justified due to these views, which include claims that the majority of black men are semi-criminal and that AIDS was created in a U.S. government laboratory. Paul’s campaign maintains he did not write or authorize the content, but his failure to fully account for the newsletters raises concerns about his judgment and the nature of his political movement. The controversy highlights the tension between Paul’s libertarian ideology and his association with extremist views, potentially impacting his viability as a presidential candidate.

A 45-year-old man was arrested after a standoff lasting over eight hours in Brunswick, Ohio, in connection with the deaths of three women in North Royalton. The suspect was subdued with a Taser after entering a house in the 3300 block of Valley Forge Drive. The deaths of 45-year-old Suzanne Taylor and her two daughters, 21-year-old Taylor Pifer and 18-year-old Kylie Pifer, were found in their North Royalton home on Sunday evening. Police believe the killings were targeted, as there were no signs of forced entry. The mother and daughters' bodies were under the covers, almost as if they had been tucked in bed. A knife was used in one death, but the cause of the other women's deaths remains under investigation. No arrests have been made, and police are treating the case as tragic.

A routine traffic stop in South Seattle early Sunday turned into a miraculous childbirth. Officer Anthony Reynolds pulled over a speeding car for running red lights when the driver, Abdul Abdashiek, informed Reynolds that his wife, Maly Yusuf, was in labor. Reynolds called for an ambulance, but the baby decided to arrive before medics. With the help of the mother, officers cleared the baby's airway, ensuring she could breathe. The ambulance arrived shortly after, transporting mother and child to a nearby hospital, both in stable condition. The family later thanked the officers, calling their daughter Hadaya, meaning "gift," and expressing their gratitude.

In Port-au-Prince, Haiti, desperate survivors were using pickup trucks as ambulances and doors as stretchers to rescue the injured following Tuesday's earthquake. Aid from around the world began arriving, including an Air China plane with a Chinese search-and-rescue team, medics, and supplies, and three French planes with aid and a mobile hospital. The U.S. and other nations pledged food, water, and medical supplies to assist the impoverished nation, where the Red Cross estimated 3 million people, a third of the population, needed emergency relief. In the streets, survivors set up camps amid piles of salvaged goods, including food from the rubble. Doctors Without Borders treated wounded at two hospitals that survived the quake and set up tent clinics elsewhere. President Barack Obama promised an all-out rescue and humanitarian effort, including the military and civilian emergency teams from across the U.S. The aircraft carrier USS Carl Vinson was expected to arrive, and the Navy ordered the amphibious assault ship USS B

Moe’s Southwest Grill has overtaken Chipotle to become America’s favorite Mexican-inspired fast casual restaurant chain, according to a new Harris Poll. Chipotle, which had topped the poll for the last three years, failed to even make the top four this time. The Denver-based chain has been struggling with food-borne illnesses, including a norovirus outbreak and E. coli incidents, leading to a 30% decline in sales and a 33% drop in stock price. Moe’s, with 600 locations, achieved its first-place ranking and demonstrated the largest increase in brand equity among all restaurants measured. Taco Bell, Qdoba Mexican Grill, and Baja Fresh Mexican Grill also outperformed Chipotle in the poll. Moe’s attributes its success to its willingness to listen to customer feedback and adapt to their needs. Despite Chipotle’s efforts to regain its reputation, the company faces stiff competition from other fast-casual Mexican chains.

Frances Bean Cobain's estranged husband, Isaiah Silva, is seeking a significant monthly spousal support payment of $25,000 from her, according to documents. Silva claims he left a stable job to marry Frances and supported her child from a previous relationship, while Frances has access to her father Kurt Cobain's estate worth an estimated $100 million. Frances argues that the Cobain money is hers alone and has not agreed to a prenuptial agreement. The case is heading towards a legal battle over the guitar from Nirvana's 1993 "MTV Unplugged" concert, with Frances and Isaiah taking opposing stances on its ownership.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds, known for their privacy, have unexpectedly split after two years of marriage, shocking friends. "No one had any idea this was coming," a close friend of Johansson tells me. The couple, who rarely spoke about their relationship in public, kept their personal life extremely private. Their statement emphasized love and kindness, while stressing the importance of privacy. Reynolds, who had to promote his film "Green Lantern" during the first half of 2011, faced the challenge of avoiding personal questions.

A Delaware family became seriously ill during a vacation at a U.S. Virgin Islands resort, leaving three members hospitalized for weeks. Federal officials confirmed the presence of methyl bromide, a banned pesticide, in the villa where the family stayed. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Justice Department are investigating the use of the toxic chemical at the Sirenusa Condominium Resort in Cruz Bay, St. John. The Esmond family, including father Steve, teenage sons, and mother Theresa, fell ill on March 20, with the boys in critical condition. The EPA banned methyl bromide for indoor residential use in 1984 due to health concerns. The chemical has been used in other units at the resort in the past year, raising questions about its proper application. Terminix, the pest control company, is under criminal investigation. Sea Glass Vacations, the rental agent, has terminated its contract with Terminix. The EPA continues to test and monitor the property to prevent future

The 5th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that hospital-like structural requirements for Texas abortion clinics can go into effect, which will cause all but seven or eight clinics to close. This decision, part of a 2013 law that also banned abortion after 20 weeks, mandated physicians to have hospital admitting privileges, and tightened regulations on abortion-inducing drugs, could leave women in rural areas hundreds of miles away from an abortion provider. Nancy Northup, CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said, "Not since before Roe v. Wade has a law or court decision had the potential to devastate access to reproductive health care on such a sweeping scale." Texas will be able to enforce the restrictions in about three weeks unless the Supreme Court intervenes.

Russian actor Steven Seagal has been appointed as a "special representative" for US-Russian humanitarian ties, according to a statement from Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Seagal's role will focus on promoting relations in the humanitarian sphere, including culture and public and youth exchanges. This appointment, similar to UN goodwill ambassador positions, highlights Seagal's close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin and his support for Putin's government. Seagal has previously praised Putin as a "great world leader" and defended him against election meddling allegations.

A 59-year-old Kansas man died after his motorcycle collided with a black cow on a blacktopped rural road Friday night. Kansas Highway Patrol trooper Brant Birney said there were no witnesses and it is unclear if Zordel was speeding or if the cow suddenly appeared. Zordel, who was not wearing a helmet, was pronounced dead at the scene about 6.5 miles south of Interstate 70 near Russell. No one else was injured in the accident.

For 40 years, Bill Bresnan has written his wife, Kris, a love letter every day, accumulating over 10,000 notes in 25 boxes. These letters document their daily lives and express his deep affection, always ending with "I love you, my darling." The couple shares their relationship secrets, emphasizing the importance of daily communication and shared experiences. They maintain a simple routine of candlelit dinners and romantic outings, like reenacting scenes from "Summertime." Bresnan's daily letters have become a cherished part of their 40-year journey, serving as a reminder of their commitment and love. Despite challenges, they prioritize open dialogue and never go to bed angry, ensuring their relationship remains strong and fulfilling.

A beauty queen who was too old to compete has filed a lawsuit against the state and national pageant organizations, seeking $3 million in damages and reinstatement of her titles. Amanda Longacre, who was crowned Miss Delaware in June, was disqualified after it was discovered she turned 25 on October 22, violating Miss America's age requirement. The lawsuit claims that other contestants were similarly disqualified and that the organizations knowingly recruited ineligible participants. Longacre seeks restoration of her titles, scholarships, and a waiver to compete for Miss America in September. The Miss America Organization denies the lawsuit's merit.

The Arcade Fire's single "We Used to Wait" comes to life in a unique, interactive website called "The Wilderness Downtown." By entering your childhood address, the site creates a personalized experience blending video, animation, and satellite imagery, all set to the band's music. This innovative use of technology and Google Maps data offers a nostalgic journey down memory lane, potentially paving the way for future interactive music experiences online.

Autopsy results reveal that seven of the eight victims in the killings of a southern Ohio family were shot multiple times, with some showing signs of a struggle before their deaths. The victims, all members of the Rhoden family, were found in four separate homes in Piketon, a rural community east of Cincinnati. Authorities have found marijuana growing operations at three of the crime scenes but have not ruled out other motives. More than 300 tips have been received, and 79 pieces of evidence have been sent to a state crime lab for analysis. A $25,000 reward has been offered for information leading to the arrest of the suspect or suspects.

Google has launched a wedding planning site to help consumers create websites, edit photos, and plan their weddings using templates in Google Sites, Docs, and Picnik. The site, launched for Valentine's Day, includes tips from wedding planner Michelle Rago and a sweepstakes offering $25,000 and Rago's wedding planning expertise. This move by Google aims to integrate more deeply into consumers' lives, following previous attempts like Google Health, while raising privacy concerns.

MasterCard is introducing a new system that allows customers to use selfies and fingerprints for online payment security, replacing traditional passwords. The company confirmed this move at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, following successful trials in the U.S. and the Netherlands. Ann Cairns, head of international markets for MasterCard, stated that biometric checks enhance security. The system will launch in the U.K. and will be available in the U.S., Canada, and several European countries this summer. Users will download an application to their devices, which will prompt them to take a selfie and blink to verify their identity. MasterCard claims 92% of test subjects preferred this method over passwords. Ajay Bhalla, head of MasterCard's safety and security division, emphasized the convenience and security benefits of biometric authentication, noting that passwords are often weak and easily compromised. The company asserts that its other security measures will prevent or detect suspicious behavior, and the biometric data will not be transmitted in a form that

Donald Trump faced criticism for his handling of a question at a town hall event in Rochester, New Hampshire, where a man asked about getting rid of Muslims and claimed President Barack Obama is Muslim. Trump did not directly address the claim about Obama. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest condemned the incident, and Democratic candidates and party leaders harshly criticized Trump's response, calling it racist and morally lacking. Trump's campaign manager later stated that Trump did not hear the question about Obama's religion but focused on the mention of training camps. The incident highlights ongoing controversies surrounding Trump's rhetoric and handling of sensitive issues.

Ricky Gervais, known for his biting humor, hosted the 73rd Golden Globes, delivering a monologue filled with sharp jabs at Hollywood celebrities. He mocked Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, Roman Polanski, Jennifer Lawrence, Jeffrey Tambor, and Ben Affleck, among others. Gervais' jokes ranged from criticizing Jennifer Lawrence's advocacy for equal pay to questioning the credibility of The Martian's comedy status. His introduction of Mel Gibson included a bleeped-out question that hinted at a controversial past. Gervais' performance was both offensive and entertaining, leaving no one out of his comedic crossfire.

A Pembroke Pines police officer was allegedly denied service at an Arby's restaurant because she is a cop, sparking a controversy and calls for a national boycott from the police union. The incident occurred when a manager allegedly told the officer she was not served because she is a police officer. The Pembroke Pines Police Chief called the behavior "offensive and appalled" and demanded an apology from Arby's. Arby's CEO apologized and offered free meals to local police officers, but the police union is still pushing for firings of the involved employees. The Arby's manager's grandfather believes it was a misunderstanding and not a serious issue. The incident highlights tensions between law enforcement and businesses, with the police union viewing it as a lack of respect and a need for stronger leadership.

Speaker John Boehner insists that any debt-ceiling increase must come with significant entitlement cuts and no tax increases, as he and Democratic leaders meet at the White House to discuss averting a government default. Boehner argues that the House will not pass a bill raising taxes on job creators and demands that any deal include substantial spending cuts larger than the debt-limit increase. He also calls for a balanced-budget amendment. Despite Obama's praise for Boehner's willingness to explore a "grand bargain" that includes entitlement cuts and new revenue, the two leaders remain at odds over tax increases and the extent of entitlement reform.

During a House Science, Space, and Technology Committee hearing, Rep. Mo Brooks (R-Ala.) questioned the primary cause of rising sea levels, rejecting the notion that global warming is responsible. Instead, he proposed alternative factors such as erosion and silt deposition from major rivers. Brooks cited the White Cliffs of Dover and the erosion of California coastlines as examples of natural processes that could contribute to sea level rise. He also disputed a recent study showing the Antarctic ice sheet is shrinking, claiming that satellite data is unreliable and that ice quantity is actually increasing. Brooks emphasized the importance of geological factors over climate change, arguing that erosion has been the primary cause of sea level rise throughout Earth's history. His comments sparked debate, with climate scientist Philip Duffy countering that human activities, particularly greenhouse gas emissions, are the main drivers of current sea level rise.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid postponed a 1am procedural vote on his debt ceiling plan, giving negotiations with Republicans more time. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and other Democratic leaders emerged from a closed-door meeting late Sunday, with Reid hopeful of a vote tonight. The framework could trigger significant defense cuts, problematic for many Republican House members. Senate Republicans failed to break the 60-vote threshold to end debate on Reid’s $2.2 trillion debt ceiling bill. Both sides expressed optimism, with Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell stating they were “very close” to a deal. Democrats remain concerned about their priorities getting lost in the process.

New Zealand may consider raising cigarette prices to $100 a packet by 2020 as part of efforts to reduce smoking, according to a government discussion paper. The Health Ministry aims for the country to be smoke-free by 2025 and is exploring various measures, including a 30% initial price hike followed by 10% annual increases. However, Prime Minister John Key warns that such a move could fuel a black market. Associate Health Minister Tariana Turia supports whatever measures are necessary to achieve the smoke-free goal.

Virginia officials are warning residents about the presence of giant hogweed, an invasive plant that can cause severe burns and even blindness. Found in Clarke County, this plant, native to the Caucasus region, has toxic sap that, when exposed to sunlight, can lead to painful blisters and long-lasting scars. The Massey Herbarium at Virginia Tech reported the discovery of about 30 giant hogweed plants. Environmental officials advise against using weed-whackers to remove the plant due to the risk of sap splattering. Effective removal methods include physical removal or using herbicides like glyphosate or triclopyr. Long-term monitoring is crucial, as seeds can remain viable in the soil for up to 15 years.

PricewaterhouseCoopers, the auditing firm responsible for the Oscars, took full responsibility for the Best Picture flub, stating they did not act quickly enough to correct the mistake. Brian Cullinan, one of the accountants, accidentally handed the wrong envelope to Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway, leading to the incorrect announcement of La La Land as the Best Picture winner. PwC apologized for the error and expressed gratitude to those involved for their graciousness. The company's U.S. chairman, Tim Ryan, acknowledged the mistake and the disappointment it caused. PwC is under review for its future role in the Oscars process, with potential changes including a two-auditor system at each stage entrance. The incident also raised questions about Cullinan's use of social media, as he had posted a photo of Emma Stone just before the mix-up.

A fan named Craig Mandell has launched a crowdfunding campaign called "Don't Let Nickel Back" to prevent the Canadian band Nickelback from playing in London. The goal is to raise $1,000 to send emails to Nickelback's management discouraging them from scheduling any gigs in the city. For every dollar donated, Mandell will send one email; a $5 donation gets a "slightly more forceful email," and a $50 donation includes an attached mp3 of Nickelback's music. Mandell envisions thousands of music lovers not having to witness a Nickelback concert in London, which he deems "glorious." All funds will go to charity or therapy for those affected by the band. Meanwhile, a different crowdfunding campaign successfully brought Foo Fighters to Cornwall, England, raising £150,000 in just two days.

True Grit is a beautifully crafted Western drama that brings Charles Portis's 1968 novel to life with Joel and Ethan Coen's signature blend of classic structure and fresh ideas. Jeff Bridges stars as U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn, a serious and tough one-eyed man hired by 14-year-old Mattie Ross to find her father's killer. Mattie, played by newcomer Hailee Steinfeld, embarks on a journey with Rooster and a Texas Ranger named LaBoeuf, played by Matt Damon, to the Indian territory that would become Oklahoma. The Coens and cinematographer Roger Deakins create a haunting and poetic atmosphere, making every scene feel rich and meaningful. Bridges delivers a nuanced performance, and Steinfeld is sturdy and convincing. Damon adds sly humor. The film is both funny and heroic, proving that it stands tall in the shadow of John Wayne's 1969 version.

A group of motorcycle club members in St. Paul helped a widow find her husband's wedding ring after he died in a motorcycle accident. Rhonda Thill, whose husband Randy Thill was killed in a June 2014 crash, couldn't bear to lose his ring, too. A friend contacted the State Patrol, but they couldn't find the ring. A search by Thill's father and brother with a metal detector also failed. Tim Allen, a friend of the Thills, organized a search with the Sober Soldiers motorcycle club. They followed the tow truck to the crash site and searched a 100-foot stretch of road. Jay Stevens found the ring pushed into the soil behind a weed. The group returned to Rhonda Thill's house, where she held her head down until Allen showed her the ring on his finger. Thill was moved by the kindness of strangers who helped her find closure.

A live-in nanny who was fired from the Bracamontes' home in Upland, California, has agreed to leave by July 4, but the family is skeptical. Diane Stretton, 64, has been living in the Bracamontes' home since March, helping care for their three children in exchange for room and board. After several weeks, Stretton stopped working and refused to leave, claiming health issues. The Bracamontes fired her on June 6 but she has remained in the house. Stretton now says she will leave by July 4, but only if certain conditions are met, such as the media leaving and a heat wave passing. The family plans to be away for the holiday, but will have other family members house-sitting. Stretton's past includes multiple lawsuits, many of which were against her own family members.

A federal judge granted a temporary stay of deportation for Pablo Villavicencio, a 35-year-old Ecuadorean pizza deliveryman, blocking his immediate removal to Ecuador. Villavicencio was arrested while making a delivery to Fort Hamilton Army base in Brooklyn and was found to have an active warrant for immigration law violations. His wife, Sandra Chica, an American citizen, and their two young daughters, born in the U.S., fear separation. Legal Aid Society attorneys argue for a fair hearing and Villavicencio's potential path to permanent residency. New York Governor Andrew Cuomo called for an investigation into ICE's conduct, citing concerns over the speed and cruelty of Villavicencio's detention.

With Laura Linney in the lead role, "The Big C" aims to bring humor to the topic of cancer, but struggles to balance the dark reality with lighthearted comedy. Linney's character, Cathy, a schoolteacher with a year to live, decides to keep her condition secret, opting instead for a life filled with practical jokes and risky behaviors. The show's attempts to portray a relatable character navigating terminal illness are undermined by a series of over-the-top and inconsistent supporting characters. Linney's performance, while commendable, is hampered by a script that forces her to constantly smile and joke about her impending death. Despite some clever writing and strong performances, the show's approach to handling the subject matter feels forced and unnatural, leading to a disjointed viewing experience.

A nephew killed his uncle in a shootout over a prized pet fighting rooster near Decatur, Tenn., early Wednesday morning. Timothy Dewayne Johnson, 52, was found dead in the driveway, while his seriously wounded nephew, Larry Eugene Johnson Jr., 28, was inside the trailer. The rooster, named "Bubba," was found tied to a chair outside the trailer. Timothy Johnson confronted Larry about the alleged theft of the rooster, leading to a gunfight where Larry shot his uncle four times. Larry was hospitalized with two broken ribs, a punctured lung, and a bullet still inside him. The district attorney's office will present the case to the Meigs County grand jury after completing the autopsy and toxicology tests.

The death of 17-year-old Kendrick Johnson, found wedged in a rolled-up gym mat, has been re-examined by a private pathologist, challenging the state medical examiners' conclusion that it was an accident. Johnson's parents, who never accepted the official explanation, had his body exhumed and a second autopsy performed. The new findings revealed that Johnson's organs were missing, stuffed with newspaper, raising further doubts about the circumstances of his death. A former FBI agent has reviewed death scene imagery and questioned the official account, suggesting foul play. Federal prosecutors are considering reopening the case, but for now, the local sheriff's office maintains the death was accidental.

President Obama demanded daily meetings with House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to resolve a budget impasse or face continuous White House sessions until an agreement is reached. Obama stated his team is ready to meet for as long as necessary to finalize a deal, warning that inaction would be inexcusable. Boehner and Reid met later, but no agreement emerged, with Boehner maintaining the White House and Senate Democrats need to accept deeper spending cuts. The government faces a potential shutdown by the end of the week, and Obama ruled out further short-term funding extensions. Republicans in the House have proposed a one-week funding plan and are pushing for significant spending cuts and policy riders.

British officials criticized President Donald Trump for his comments on the London subway attack, with Prime Minister Theresa May calling his rhetoric "unhelpful." Trump tweeted that the attackers had been "in the sights of Scotland Yard" and that law enforcement needed to be "proactive." National security adviser H.R. McMaster attempted to clarify Trump's comments, stating he was referring to law enforcement in general. Trump also used the attack to criticize the Obama administration and justify his travel ban on people from predominantly Muslim countries. The White House later said Trump had called May to offer support and express sympathy.

A significant portion of Americans nearing retirement age have postponed their retirement plans due to the Great Recession, according to a Federal Reserve report. About 40% of people aged 45 and over who were not yet retired have pushed back their retirement dates. The report highlights that lower-income individuals are particularly affected, with 54% of those earning under $25,000 reporting no retirement savings or pension. Only one-fourth of respondents are actively planning for their retirement, and a concerning 14% of those aged 45 or older admitted they do not know how they will cover expenses in retirement. The lack of retirement savings is exacerbated by limited access to retirement plans, with only 37% of part-time workers having access compared to 75% of full-time workers. Many plan to rely on Social Security, continue working, or take on part-time jobs in retirement. The report underscores the need for better financial education and planning among Americans.

Ariel Winter, the 19-year-old star of Modern Family, has sparked controversy by wearing a glamorous gold minidress to a recent event, drawing criticism from some who deemed her outfit overdressed. In response, Winter defended her choice, posting on Instagram, "Why TF does anyone care that I didn’t dress casual like everyone else for the panel? Why do I have to be like everyone else? Why can’t people just let other people feel good about themselves and do what they want?" She emphasized, "WEAR WHATEVER YOU WANT PEOPLE!" Winter's statement encourages self-expression and confidence, urging individuals to wear what makes them feel good.

Japanese novelist Haruki Murakami is offering to answer any questions from readers on his publisher's website, "Murakami's Place," from January 15 to 31. This is a rare opportunity for fans to communicate directly with the reclusive author, who is known for his surreal and critically acclaimed works. Murakami, 65, will address a wide range of topics, from literature to his interests in running, cats, and baseball, while also tackling more personal queries. His responses will be published from late January to March. Murakami has previously been a favorite for the Nobel Prize in Literature but is notoriously private, making this engagement with readers a significant departure from his usual media shyness.

President Obama's recent airstrikes in Syria mark a significant reversal of his previous stance against American involvement in the country's civil war. The attacks, targeting both Islamic State and the Khorasan Group, come after a swift sequence of events in Iraq where Islamic State fighters routed Iraqi forces and posed a threat to Baghdad. This shift raises questions about the potential for an ever-escalating U.S. military role in Syria and Iraq. While the attacks are seen as a necessary response to the threat posed by Islamic State, concerns remain about the clarity of the strategy and achievable goals. The case for such an intervention has yet to be fully made.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in a case where a convicted killer in Illinois argued that prosecutors improperly focused on his silence during the trial, potentially influencing the jury's decision to sentence him to death. Ronald Mikos, a foot doctor, was convicted in 2005 for shooting a disabled nurse to prevent her from testifying against him in a Medicare fraud trial. His lawyers objected to the prosecution's tactic of highlighting his silence as evidence of lack of remorse. The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Mikos's death sentence. In a separate case, federal prosecutors announced they would seek the death penalty for Brendt Christensen, a former University of Illinois graduate student accused of kidnapping, torturing, and killing a visiting Chinese scholar. Christensen is also charged with a 2013 sexual assault and has claimed to have additional victims. The decision to seek the death penalty, which requires approval from the U.S. Attorney General, will delay his trial

Wal-Mart faces a U.S. Justice Department investigation into bribery allegations in its Mexican subsidiary, potentially threatening the company's expansion and corporate image. The New York Times reported that Wal-Mart de Mexico paid over $24 million in bribes to secure construction permits. Despite a whistleblower alert in 2005, the company shut down the investigation without reporting to law enforcement. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, which has ties to Wal-Mart, has been lobbying to loosen the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Wal-Mart shares fell nearly 5%, and lawmakers are calling for a meeting with company executives. The investigation could result in significant penalties and slow Wal-Mart’s growth in Mexico.

A Nevada couple who appeared on the reality TV show "Ghost Adventures" were found dead in a barricaded Sparks apartment after a standoff. Police responded to a hostage situation involving the couple's adult daughter and found Mark and Debby Constantino dead inside. The couple had been featured on the Travel Channel series in recent years, including episodes at the Mustang Ranch brothel and the Goldfield Hotel. Police had been tracking the daughter's cellphone to locate her, leading them to the Sparks apartment. The incident began when police found a man dead in a northwest Reno home and learned that the daughter and her estranged husband, Mark Constantino, were missing. Officers heard several shots and negotiations before using explosives to enter the apartment, where they found the couple deceased. Debby Constantino had previously been a victim in a kidnapping and domestic incident involving her husband.

Depending on your feelings about Whitney Houston, the Motown-era musical "Sparkle" will either feel like a fond (and sometimes cringe-inducing) farewell to an old friend, or a wholly unremarkable entry in the star-is-born genre. Houston, who shot the film just a few months before her death in February, gets a moment of glory in a scene where she belts out a powerful performance in a church. However, the rest of the film is a plodding story that often seems like a straightforward Supremes biopic, with cardboard dialogue and a now-worn "Behind the Music" trajectory. The remake of a 1976 film starring a young Irene Cara, "Sparkle" tells the story of three sisters, Sparkle, Sister, and Dee, who try to make it as a girl group in Detroit's Motown scene. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, a conservative icon and the longest-serving member of the current court, was found dead at a West Texas ranch. His death, which occurred in his sleep, sets the stage for a contentious political battle over his replacement. President Obama vowed to nominate a successor, but Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell argued the vacancy should remain open until the next president. Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, on the other hand, called for immediate action to avoid a year-long vacancy. Scalia's death will significantly impact ongoing cases, potentially leading to 4-4 splits and no precedents being set. His legacy includes his influential originalist approach to constitutional interpretation and his sharp, often controversial opinions. The sudden absence of Scalia on the court will have far-reaching implications for future decisions and the balance of power.

A Catholic priest in the Philippines was suspended and forced to repent after he rode a hoverboard during Christmas Eve Mass, drawing criticism from his diocese. Footage of the incident, where the priest rode up and down the church nave singing, went viral. The diocese deemed the action inappropriate, stating it is not a personal celebration where one can introduce new elements to gain attention. The priest acknowledged his mistake and promised not to repeat it, spending time reflecting on the incident.

A 14-year-old girl fell from a stopped gondola ride at Six Flags Amusement Park in Queensbury, New York, on Saturday night. She landed in a crowd gathered below who attempted to catch her. The girl, from Greenwood, Delaware, was treated by park emergency medical staff and taken to Albany Medical Center in stable condition with no serious injuries. The ride was inspected and found to be in proper working order. A 47-year-old man from Schenectady, who was a park guest, was treated and released for a back injury sustained while trying to catch the girl. The park has closed the attraction for a thorough review.

Mitt Romney released his 2010 and 2011 tax returns, showing he pays a lower effective tax rate than many top wage-earners. Romney earns most of his income from investments, dividends, and interest, resulting in an effective tax rate of 13.9% in 2010 and an estimated 15.4% in 2011. President Obama will use the "Buffett rule" in his State of the Union address to ensure the ultra-wealthy pay their "fair share" of taxes. Romney’s tax returns highlight the disparity between his income and that of most Americans, potentially hurting his chances in the general election. His tax rates are lower than those of President Obama and his closest Republican rival, Newt Gingrich. The release of his returns comes after Romney faced pressure from rivals to disclose his finances, and he hopes it will help him regain footing in the Republican race.

SpaceX successfully launched a classified U.S. spy agency mission, NROL-76, from Kennedy Space Center on May 1, 2017, then landed the Falcon 9 rocket’s first stage for potential reuse. The 230-foot rocket blasted off at 7:15 a.m. ET, carrying a National Reconnaissance Office satellite. The mission faced a sensor issue that scrubbed a first attempt on the previous day. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk noted the launch was a good outcome despite high-altitude wind shear. The first stage executed a series of maneuvers, deploying fins and firing engines to return to Landing Zone 1 at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. This was SpaceX’s first dedicated mission for the NRO and marked a significant step in its reusable rocket program. The company has now recovered the first stage of a Falcon for the 10th time, with plans to lease a facility to accommodate more boosters.

Josh Duggar, former executive director of the Family Research Council and star of 19 Kids and Counting, is facing new allegations of using another man's image on dating and social media sites, including Ashley Madison. Matthew McCarthy, a DJ and photographer, claims Duggar used his face on several profiles, including one on OkCupid. McCarthy says the connection has been humiliating, with people sending him harassing messages. McCarthy is now suing Duggar for the wrongful use of his image and damages. The OkCupid profile, which has since been taken down, lists Duggar as a "strictly monogamous" man looking for "casual sex," despite Duggar not having graduated college. While there is no definitive proof linking the profile to Duggar, the timing and location of the profile's activity raise questions. Duggar has not responded to these allegations.

UC Irvine faced backlash after rescinding admission offers to about 500 students this year due to transcript and grade discrepancies, exceeding enrollment expectations. Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Thomas Parham acknowledged "missteps" and assured swift corrections. Of the 499 withdrawn offers, 63 students had their appeals reinstated. Students complained of confusion and anxiety, with some, like Simran Chopra, alleging their transcripts were submitted on time. Parham emphasized that all meeting terms and conditions would be admitted, and over-enrollment was not a factor in withdrawals.

The scandal involving former CIA Director David Petraeus has expanded to include Marine General John Allen, the top U.S. commander in Afghanistan. Defense Secretary Leon Panetta has placed Allen's nomination as NATO Supreme Allied Commander on hold pending an investigation into alleged inappropriate communications between Allen and Jill Kelley, a Tampa socialite. Kelley, who is an unpaid social liaison at MacDill Air Force Base, had previously complained to the FBI about harassing emails, which led to the investigation of Petraeus and his biographer, Paula Broadwell. While Allen has denied any wrongdoing and stated he never shared classified information with Kelley, the investigation continues, raising questions about the potential impact on Allen's nomination.

Tony Curtis, the legendary actor known for his roles in films like "Some Like It Hot" and "Spartacus," disinherited his five children in his final will, written five months before his death from cardiac arrest at 85. Instead, he left his estate to his widow, Jill Vandenberg Curtis. One of his children attempted to contest the will but was unsuccessful. Curtis acknowledged his children's existence in the will but stated he had intentionally chosen not to provide for them. His daughter Jamie Lee Curtis, who eulogized him at his funeral, expressed shock and sadness at being cut out of the will. Curtis's widow maintained that his wishes were private family matters.

Four families of American hostages who were killed by the Islamic State have jointly written a letter to President Obama, urging the administration to use all appropriate means to find and bring home missing journalist Austin Tice. Tice, who was captured in Syria in 2012, is the last unaccounted-for American in that region. The families, including those of Kayla Mueller, James Foley, Steven Sotloff, and Peter Kassig, express their ongoing grief and ask the president to prioritize Tice's case, emphasizing that they are not asking for any compromise on national security. They remind Obama of his previous promises and implore him to act urgently to bring Tice home.

A video game allowing players to simulate a school shooting was set to release on Steam but was removed by Valve Corporation after controversy. The game, developed by Revived Games and published by ACID, drew criticism from activists and lawmakers. Valve stated the developer, Ata Berdiyev, had a history of customer abuse and manipulation. The game's description aimed to distance itself from promoting violence but faced backlash for its controversial nature.

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi stated she will not trade with President Donald Trump for his border wall, calling it a "manhood issue" for him. Pelosi emphasized Democrats support border security but prefer to strengthen existing measures as part of a comprehensive immigration overhaul. She warned against allowing Trump to claim Democrats are not interested in protecting the border. Pelosi's stance likely won't matter much in the House, where Republicans have enough votes to pass the $5 billion wall funding request. Senate Democrats, however, could be a real obstacle. Pelosi projected confidence about being elected speaker if Democrats win the House majority in November. She highlighted key priorities for Democrats, including lowering health care costs, increasing paychecks, and protecting Dreamers. Pelosi also reiterated her view that impeachment is divisive and that Democrats will hold Trump and his administration accountable.

Adam Wainwright's gesture of respect to Derek Jeter during the 2014 All-Star Game turned into a public relations nightmare. As Jeter stepped to the plate, Wainwright placed his glove on the mound and stepped back, letting Jeter have a moment. However, after giving up a double, a triple, and a home run, Wainwright admitted he was going to "give him a couple of pipe shots." His candid comments sparked controversy and criticism, with Wainwright calling himself an "idiot" and expressing regret. The incident highlighted the challenges of the "This One Counts" initiative, which ties home-field advantage in the World Series to the All-Star Game's outcome. Wainwright's experience may prompt MLB to reconsider the event's format and purpose.

A Chinese tourist was fined $1,000 and a $30 court processing fee for walking off the boardwalk in the Mammoth Hot Springs thermal area at Yellowstone National Park. The witness reported seeing the individual break through the fragile travertine crust and collect thermal water, likely for medicinal purposes. Park rangers issued a federal violation notice and emphasized the importance of staying on designated trails and boardwalks for visitor safety and to protect the park's natural resources. This incident comes after several other recent cases where tourists got into trouble, including a 23-year-old man who fell into a hot spring and died in the Norris Geyser Basin. Park officials urge visitors to follow regulations to prevent further damage and potential injuries.

In Taiwan, the consumption of betel nuts, a habit involving the chewing of nuts wrapped in leaves and often containing harmful ingredients, is linked to high rates of oral cancer. Despite its cultural significance and use as a stimulant, betel nuts pose significant health risks, including oral cancer and other diseases. The Taiwanese government is taking action, offering subsidies to farmers to replace betel nut palms with other crops and providing free screenings and programs to help people quit the habit. However, the tradition remains deeply ingrained, and its long-term effects continue to impact public health.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton ruled out running for president in 2012 or 2016 during interviews in New Zealand, stating she is very pleased with her role as Secretary of State. Clinton emphasized she has no plans to run for the top U.S. office despite speculation, adding that the U.S. should be ready for a female president. She noted that countries like New Zealand and Australia, which have elected women to high offices, are examples of progress. Clinton also defended President Barack Obama, suggesting his decisions, though unpopular at times, were necessary for the well-being of the American people. Her comments came during a nearly two-week Asia-Pacific tour, with New Zealand being the second-to-last stop before concluding in Australia.

The Treasury Department warned that restructuring Solyndra's $535 million government loan might be illegal, but the Energy Department proceeded anyway, according to newly released emails. Despite concerns from the White House and Treasury, officials pushed to support the failing solar company. Solyndra's loan was approved by Energy Secretary Steven Chu, and Steven Spinner, an Energy Department official with a conflict of interest due to his wife's law firm representing Solyndra, advocated for the loan's approval. Spinner's emails show he urged quick approval and pushed for high-profile White House involvement. The restructuring now likely means taxpayers will bear most of the loss. The emails reveal disagreements between Energy and Treasury officials about the legality and oversight of the loan, adding to the controversy surrounding Solyndra's bankruptcy.

President Obama delivered a speech in Afghanistan outlining his plan for a responsible withdrawal of troops, emphasizing national self-interest and realism. Critics argue that his strategy lacks a clear path to victory and may lead to further stratification and discontent. Obama's speech was criticized for being rushed and lacking compelling reasons for escalation, while also downplaying the dysfunction within the Afghan government. Despite the challenges, Obama maintained a centrist stance, facing bad choices due to the Bush-Cheney administration's incompetence. His supporters acknowledge the tough decision but remain disappointed, hoping for better solutions through ongoing activism.

A Georgia man, Alvin Cross Jr., texted his probation officer asking if they had any drugs, leading to a raid and his arrest for cocaine possession. He pleaded guilty and will serve one year in prison. This highlights the potential consequences of sending messages to the wrong person, especially when under supervision.

The report from the bipartisan Commission on Wartime Contracting in Iraq and Afghanistan highlights significant issues with the federal government's reliance on contractors in conflict zones, estimating tens of billions of dollars in wasted funds. The commission calls for major reforms, including creating special teams of federal workers to monitor projects and restricting contractors' roles in hiring other contractors. It also criticizes poor planning, oversight, and criminal behavior that contribute to waste. The report's recommendations aim to improve accountability and ensure better use of resources in future military operations.

A mother of two from the United Kingdom died from sepsis after scratching her hand while gardening, her family has revealed. Lucinda Smith, 43, visited her GP after feeling pain in her shoulder following the minor scrape in March. The doctor diagnosed a trapped nerve and prescribed anti-depressants, advising her to see a physiotherapist. Three days later, Smith's condition worsened, and she experienced swelling, vomiting, and increased pain. She was admitted to Basildon Hospital where a blood test confirmed she had sepsis. Despite immediate treatment, she died two days later due to organ failure. Her family believes she could have been saved if she had been given a test and had her blood pressure taken when she first complained of feeling unwell. The inquest ruled her death was caused by toxic shock from sepsis. The condition can affect anyone but is more common in seniors and those with weakened immune systems. Early treatment with antibiotics and fluids improves survival chances.

A 60-year-old man died after his vehicle broke down on a remote track in Western Australia's Goldfields region, prompting him to walk 48 kilometers for help with only a small container of water. He was found dead two kilometers from Windidda Station, 200 kilometers east of Wiluna, by searchers who had rescued the woman who left the vehicle the following day. Police stated there were no suspicious circumstances and a report would be prepared for the coroner. Authorities urged travelers to stay with their vehicles if they break down or become lost, as searchers can more easily spot vehicles from the air than individuals. They also recommended carrying a three-day supply of food and water, ensuring vehicles are in good condition, and using emergency beacons or phones. Travellers should inform others of their plans and expected arrival times.

Nearly two dozen Islamist women and girls, some as young as 15, received heavy prison sentences for protesting, as Egypt's military-backed government cracked down on secular demonstrators under a new anti-protest law. The harsh sentences and police brutality against female activists, reminiscent of the Mubarak era, signal a return to authoritarian tactics. The sentences sparked criticism and protests, with the Muslim Brotherhood vowing to increase its opposition. The new law banning public gatherings without police permits has intensified tensions, as secular and Islamist groups find common ground in their opposition to the government's actions.

At least 45 people, including 15 children, have died after an illegally constructed building collapsed in Mumbai, India. About 70 people were injured, and many are feared trapped. The building, which was under construction and had four floors already occupied, collapsed on Thursday evening. Rescue efforts continue, with dozens injured and search for survivors ongoing. Authorities say the builder used substandard materials and lacked an occupation certificate. The incident highlights the issue of illegal construction in India, where poor building practices and high demand for housing lead to such collapses. At least 20 people remain missing, and police are searching for the builders to arrest them.

A 12-year-old girl on the brink of suicide was saved by a rookie police officer during a routine patrol in Southern California. Officer Chris Perez, who had been on the South Pasadena Police force for only a year, approached the girl calmly as she clung to a 6-inch ledge on the York Bridge, ready to jump. The girl, upset by her living conditions at a group home, was crying and desperate. Perez built trust through patient conversation, eventually hugging the girl and dragging her back over the ledge to safety. Paramedics arrived to assist, and the girl was taken into custody for a medical evaluation. Officer Perez, though reluctant to call himself a hero, expressed relief at his parents' approval of his actions.

Camp John Waters, set for September 2017 in Kent, Connecticut, invites fans of the cult filmmaker to experience a weekend of debauchery and fun. Activities include screenings of John Waters' films, 'Blood Mary Bingo,' Hairspray karaoke, burlesque lessons, and a costume contest judged by the "Prince of Puke." Participants can also enjoy a one-man show by Waters, a Q&A session, and a chance to purchase his new book, "Make Trouble," with an autographed copy included. Additional alcohol is available for an extra fee. This camp promises a mix of camp traditions and Waters' signature campiness, offering a unique experience for both longtime fans and newcomers.

Five children, including two 1-year-old twins, died in a fire that swept through a house in Youngstown, Ohio, late Sunday night. The only survivor was their mother, who managed to jump out of a second-floor window. Firefighters found flames throughout the first floor and were able to rescue three of the children, but they later died at a hospital. The mother was taken to a hospital with injuries and is in stable but critical condition. The fire, which began on the first floor, is being investigated by state and local officials, who so far have no indication that it was suspicious. The house, a two-story ranch built in 1924, was owned by Lindsey Maggie and Lindsey Henry of Campbell. The tragedy occurred just two weeks before Christmas, leaving the community and firefighters deeply affected.

Microsoft unveiled its new motion-control system, Kinect, during a Cirque du Soleil performance, finally giving it a name after a year of anticipation. The system allows users to play games and interact with the Xbox 360 console through gestures and spoken commands without needing a controller. The event showcased various games, including a yoga/tai chi game, a soccer game, a racing game, Kinect Sports with sports like boxing, bowling, and soccer, a dance game, and Kinectimals featuring virtual interaction with animals. The system also demonstrated dashboard apps for photo browsing and live video chats. While the event was impressive, the details about pricing and availability were not disclosed, with more information expected at the following day's press conference.

Lawyers for Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev argue his trial should have been held outside the city due to widespread outrage and unrelenting publicity, and that he deserves a new trial elsewhere. They claim jurors couldn't avoid media coverage and that the "crime of violence" term applied to Tsarnaev's actions is now questionable. Despite being sentenced to death in June for the 2013 bombings that killed three and injured over 260, Tsarnaev has become the 62nd inmate on federal death row. His fate, however, will likely take years to resolve, with the process potentially taking at least 10 years.

Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders plans to introduce a bill aimed at eliminating for-profit prisons, expanding a national conversation on social justice and prison reform. The "Justice Is Not For Sale" Act, co-sponsored by Rep. Raul Grijalva, would ban private prisons within three years, reduce high fees for prisoner services, reinstate the federal parole system, and decrease immigrant detention center populations. Sanders argues that the private prison industry creates a "perverse incentive" to increase incarceration rates, citing studies that suggest private prisons do not save money and may increase recidivism. The bill seeks to address the disproportionate number of black and Hispanic individuals in the prison system and aims to lower the overall prison population by focusing on rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

A Miami doctor named Arturo Carvajal sued a Houston's restaurant for not teaching him how to properly eat an artichoke, leading to severe abdominal pain and hospitalization. Carvajal, who ordered a grilled artichoke special at the restaurant in May 2009, claims the server failed to explain that only the inside portion of the leaf is digestible. After consuming the entire artichoke, Carvajal suffered "severe abdominal pain and discomfort," and an exploratory laparotomy revealed artichoke leaves lodged in his bowel. He seeks unspecified damages for bodily injury, pain and suffering, disability, disfigurement, and medical expenses. The restaurant's general counsel calls the lawsuit a "silly notion" and says the company will defend itself vigorously.

Police issued an Amber Alert for a 2-year-old boy who was reportedly taken by force, along with his mother, from a home in Des Moines. The alleged abduction involved a 65-year-old paternal grandmother and a 46-year-old woman known to the mother. The mother managed to escape but was unable to retrieve her child. The boy's father was questioned by detectives but was not charged. The child was found safe after his babysitter, John Truong, recognized the Amber Alert and contacted authorities. The suspects, Alyssa Chang and Vien Nguyen, were taken into custody and face multiple felony charges.

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2 retained its box office lead for a fourth consecutive weekend, earning $11.3 million. In contrast, Warner Bros.' In the Heart of the Sea, a $100 million production about the real-life whale ship disaster that inspired Moby-Dick, flopped with just $11 million in its opening. The film, directed by Ron Howard and starring Chris Hemsworth, struggled to attract audiences, particularly older viewers. It faced stiff competition from holdovers like The Good Dinosaur and Creed, which maintained their positions. The Big Short, a critically acclaimed film about the 2008 housing crisis, debuted strongly with $720,000 from eight theaters, driven by Golden Globe nominations. With Star Wars: The Force Awakens set to debut, the upcoming weeks promise to be highly competitive.

Scientists from the U.S. and Denmark are using a helicopter-mounted electromagnetic system to map the underground hydrothermal features of Yellowstone National Park for the first time. The device, resembling a giant hula hoop, will record voltage signals to distinguish between solid earth, "rotten" sulfuric rock, and water. This survey aims to visualize the geology and water flow down to about 1,500 feet, filling in gaps about the geysers and hydrothermal explosions. The project, expected to take at least four weeks, will help understand the plumbing system feeding thermal features like Old Faithful and potentially assist park administrators in future development planning.

In the Guadalupe-Nipomo Dunes, remnants of a massive Hollywood set from the 1920s film "The Ten Commandments" have remained buried for nearly a century. The set, built for Cecil B. DeMille, included sphinxes, statues, and other Egyptian-themed props. In recent years, one sphinx was discovered and is now on display. Now, a company is using aerial photography to locate more artifacts from the same set. Archaeologists hope to uncover more pieces before the sands shift too much, preserving a piece of early Hollywood history.

The U.S. government faced criticism for its six-month ban on deepwater drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, with Transocean Ltd. president Steven Newman arguing for immediate resumption of operations. Judge Martin Feldman in New Orleans blocked the moratorium, stating it could cause significant economic harm. Interior Secretary Ken Salazar announced a new order would be issued, emphasizing the need for a pause due to ongoing oil spill issues. The moratorium halted drilling in waters over 500 feet deep and prevented new permits. A lawsuit by a drilling equipment company challenged the ban's legality, arguing it lacked evidence of existing risks. Louisiana Governor Bobby Jindal and Senator Mary Landrieu urged against appealing the ruling, citing the industry's importance. Meanwhile, cleanup efforts showed some progress, but long-term environmental impacts remained uncertain.

An aircraft with 54 people on board crashed in Indonesia's remote Papua region on Sunday, the latest in a series of aviation disasters in the country. The Trigana Air flight lost contact with air traffic control as it flew from Jayapura to Oksibil. Local residents reported the plane crashed into Tangok mountain. The aircraft, an ATR 42-300, was carrying 44 adult passengers, five crew, and five children and infants. Search efforts were hampered by bad weather and rugged terrain. Trigana Air, which has a history of safety incidents and is on the EU's banned carrier list, operates 14 aircraft with an average age of 26.6 years. The crash site is in a remote, mountainous area, making rescue operations challenging. Indonesia's president called for the country to "pray together" for the victims.

The Thomas Jefferson Memorial is facing a new challenge with the growth of biofilm on its dome, a problem not unique to this monument. Biofilm, a colony of microscopic organisms including algae, bacteria, and fungi, has darkened the once-white rotunda, affecting other memorials like the Lincoln Memorial and even ancient sites worldwide. National Park Service officials are studying the biofilm's impact on stone and testing various cleaning methods, emphasizing the need for treatments that do not harm the marble. The issue is particularly pronounced on the Jefferson Memorial's dome, base, and pediment, and may be related to decreased air pollution and the microclimate near the memorial. While some biofilm can be removed, it may regrow, making long-term preservation strategies crucial.

Talia Jane, a customer service representative at Yelp, penned an open letter to CEO Jeremy Stoppelman detailing her struggles with low pay and high living costs in San Francisco. The letter, titled "An Open Letter To My CEO," went viral, leading to Jane's immediate termination. Jane criticized the company for offering low wages, forcing employees to take on second jobs and live with family to make ends meet. She also highlighted issues like high utility bills and the difficulty of affording basic necessities. After Jane's firing, Stoppelman acknowledged the high cost of living in San Francisco but maintained that the termination was not related to the letter. The incident sparked debate about corporate responsibility and the challenges faced by employees in high-cost tech hubs.

At least 16 people have died in severe storms that hit Texas and Oklahoma, with flooding and tornadoes causing widespread damage. In Texas, the Blanco River surged into vacation homes, creating dangerous situations for residents. The city of Wharton issued a voluntary evacuation notice for homes near the Colorado River, which was expected to rise above flood stage. In Parker County, a voluntary evacuation order was issued for 250 homes along the Brazos River. In Houston, 1,400 structures suffered severe damage, and six deaths were reported. Meanwhile, in Dallas, over 200 people were rescued from flash flooding, with nearly 7 inches of rain falling on the city. The storms, which caused the wettest May on record, also led to power outages and flight cancellations. President Obama pledged federal support for the affected areas.

Charlie Sheen, who recently disclosed his HIV-positive status, had been developing a new sitcom. Despite his diagnosis, Sheen expressed confidence that it wouldn't affect his career, citing discussions with Sony TV executives who seemed interested in working with him again. However, the revelation of his condition may face legal challenges from former sexual partners. Sheen's previous sitcom, "Anger Management," was produced without his colleagues' knowledge of his HIV status, and the industry was aware of his condition for some time. This information adds context to Sheen's claims of extorting $10 million to keep his diagnosis secret and his belief that his career won't be impacted by his HIV status.

Casey Anthony's parents, George and Cindy Anthony, have broken their silence two months after their daughter's acquittal and granted an interview to Dr. Phil McGraw. In excerpts aired on NBC's Today show, Cindy defends her MySpace message and the smell in Casey's car, while George expresses his disbelief about Caylee's disappearance. The full interview, paid for by McGraw's production company and Casey's Fund, will air on Dr. Phil's TV show.

At least four people died and several were injured early Wednesday when a bus carrying passengers from El Paso, Texas, to Los Angeles overturned after hitting steel pipes scattered on the eastbound 10 Freeway near Blythe, California. The pipes had been spilled by a jackknifed truck earlier in the night. Ana Perez, a mother traveling with her 12-day-old baby, described the horrific scene, saying the bus rolled over and she held her baby tightly to avoid separation. Rescuers helped passengers from the overturned bus, with some injured being airlifted to hospitals. The freeway was closed for several hours. The truck driver and bus driver were not injured. The bus was operated by El Paso-Los Angeles Limousine Express Inc., and the truck by VG Transport. Both companies had no significant safety violations in recent years.

In Saudi Arabia, the ancient port center of Al-Balad in Jeddah, a UNESCO Cultural Heritage Site, faces challenges in preserving its historical buildings due to fire and disrepair. To address these issues, FalconViz, a Saudi-based 3D surveying and mapping firm, employs advanced drone technology and Autodesk software. This method allows for efficient and accurate documentation of Al-Balad's unique architectural features, including cut coral stones and intricately hand-carved rawashin-style latticed windows. By creating detailed 3D models, FalconViz supports various applications such as fire safety simulations and emergency response planning. The technology not only aids in the preservation of cultural heritage but also enhances modern urban infrastructure planning and development.

Two men from Albuquerque, N.M., may have plotted to kill Justin Bieber and his bodyguard, according to a New Mexico state police investigation. Mark Staake, 41, and his nephew Tanner Ruane, 23, were arrested after an alleged plot to murder four people, including Bieber, was uncovered. The plot involved strangling victims with a paisley tie and castrating them, with a bounty of $2,500 offered for each testicle. Justin Bieber's management stated they take every precaution to protect the singer and his fans. Staake and Ruane were arrested after Staake missed a highway exit and was detained by a U.S. border agent, while Ruane was later apprehended in New York.

Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad announced plans to release two American men, Shane Bauer and Josh Fattal, convicted on spy-related charges, and grant them a "unilateral pardon." Each man is required to pay $500,000 in bail, the same amount set for Sarah Shourd, the third American arrested with them in 2009. Ahmadinejad stated they will be free to choose how they return to the United States. The decision could ease tensions between Iran and the U.S., coming weeks before Ahmadinejad's visit to the U.N. General Assembly.

Before Kelsey Grammer was out of his teens, he experienced more loss than most people do in a lifetime. Growing up, he lived with his mother and grandfather, who he lost at age 11. Two years later, his father was shot and set on fire, with the killer found not guilty by reason of insanity. At just 20, his sister was brutally raped and murdered, and Grammer had to identify the body. In 1980, his two half-brothers died in a scuba diving accident in St. Thomas. These early life traumas provide a stark contrast to the glamorous and successful career Grammer has since built.

This year's 38th annual List of Words Banished from the Queen's English for Misuse, Overuse, and General Uselessness, compiled by Lake Superior State University, features "spoiler alert" as the most nominated term, followed by "fiscal cliff," "superfood," "guru," "job creators," and "double down." The list, which has survived for nearly four decades and includes around 900 words or phrases, is submitted through the university's Facebook page. Spokesman Tom Pink notes that while the list aims to highlight words that have outlived their usefulness, some terms like "viral," "amazing," and "LOL" persist in everyday language. The list continues to generate interest and discussion each year, with nominations coming from the United States, Canada, and beyond.

Astana, the capital of Kazakhstan, is emerging as a promising travel destination, thanks to its ambitious architecture and upcoming Expo 2017. The city, known for its space-age structures like the Bayterek Tower and the Palace of Peace and Reconciliation, designed by Norman Foster, is positioning itself as a modern hub in Central Asia. With two major hotel chains, the Ritz Carlton and St Regis, set to open, Astana aims to attract more international visitors. The Expo, focusing on "future energy," will showcase Kazakhstan’s potential and enhance the city’s global profile. Beyond its futuristic skyline, Astana offers a blend of Soviet and modern architecture, reflecting its unique history and culture. The city also provides access to Kazakhstan’s vast natural landscapes, making it an appealing destination for adventure and cultural exploration.

Henri Bendel, an upscale retailer with a 123-year history, will close all 23 of its stores, including its iconic Fifth Avenue location in New York, by January 2019 due to declining sales. L Brands, the parent company that acquired Bendel in 1985, announced the closures to focus on larger brands like Victoria's Secret and Bath & Body Works. Bendel's sales last year were approximately $85 million, making up a small portion of L Brands' $12.6 billion revenue. Founded by Henri Willis Bendel in 1895, the store was known for its designer purses and shoes and was one of the first luxury retailers to open an "upper Fifth Avenue address" in 1913.

The family of Kayla Mueller, a 26-year-old American aid worker held by ISIS, received confirmation of her death after ISIS sent them photographs of her body. Mueller was kidnapped in 2013 while working in Syria. Her parents initially refused to believe her death and demanded proof from ISIS. The U.S. government authenticated the photographs, which showed bruises but did not confirm the cause of death. President Obama expressed condolences to her family and stated that the U.S. would bring ISIS members to justice. Mueller's family released a letter she wrote from captivity, expressing her dedication to helping those in need and her hope to relieve suffering. Her death highlights the ongoing risks faced by aid workers in conflict zones.

North Korea attempted to launch an intermediate-range missile on the birthday of its "eternal president," Kim Il Sung, but the launch failed, according to South Korean military officials. The missile, believed to be a Musudan, deviated from a normal trajectory. Despite the failure, North Korea continues to test various missile systems, aiming to develop longer-range capabilities that could eventually target the U.S. mainland. The failed launch occurred on a day of significant importance in North Korea, adding to the embarrassment for leader Kim Jong Un. Analysts suggest that the regime may attempt another test, possibly including a nuclear test, to bolster its military capabilities and legitimacy ahead of a key party congress. The international community, including China, has condemned the launch and emphasized the need for continued pressure on North Korea through sanctions.

A 9-year-old boy with cerebral palsy and epilepsy, named Lakhan Kale, was tethered to a bus stop in Mumbai by his grandmother so she could work, drawing outrage and leading to his placement in a shelter. Lakhan, who cannot hear or speak, was left unattended while his grandmother sold toys and garlands on the roadside. After a photograph of him tied to the bus stop was published, local authorities intervened, and Lakhan was admitted to The Children's Aid Society. The incident highlights the lack of resources for disabled children in India, with activists calling for more government support and residential centers.

Chef Mario Batali faces criminal investigation for alleged sexual misconduct, including groping and assault of female employees at his New York City restaurant, The Spotted Pig. In a 60 Minutes segment, several women recount incidents of harassment and assault, highlighting a culture of powerlessness and fear of retaliation. Batali has stepped away from his restaurant empire, acknowledging past inappropriate behavior. The Spotted Pig, co-owned by Batali and Ken Friedman, lacked a full-time human resources department, making it difficult for employees to report incidents. The investigation spans multiple years and restaurants, with Batali denying some specific allegations.

Reports of sexual abuse of nuns by priests, including rape, are emerging globally, highlighting a long-standing issue within the Catholic Church. Several nuns have come forward, sharing their experiences, which include priests demanding sex in exchange for permissions or certifications and exploiting nuns' cultural conditioning of subservience. The problem is particularly acute in Africa, where the prevalence of HIV/AIDS has made nuns perceived as "safe" targets. Despite reports dating back to the 1990s, the issue has remained largely under the radar. Now, buoyed by the #MeToo movement, some nuns are speaking out, detailing cases in Europe, Africa, South America, and Asia. The Catholic Church has not taken clear measures to address the problem, with victims often reluctant to report abuse due to fear of disbelief and local church leaders reluctant to acknowledge the issue. The extent of the abuse remains unclear, but it is evident that the church's culture of secrecy and the imbalance of power between n

White House national security adviser James Jones says Americans will feel "a certain shock" when they read an unclassified report on the missed clues that could have prevented the alleged Christmas Day bomber from boarding the plane. President Obama is alarmed that available information, such as patterns of behavior, was not acted upon. The White House plans to release the report on Thursday. The suspect, Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, who faces life in prison if convicted, has told investigators he was trained and equipped in Yemen by a group affiliated with al-Qaeda. His father had warned American officials about his son's extremist ideology, but Abdulmutallab's visa was not revoked and he was not placed on the "no-fly" list. The remedies involve "tweaks" rather than the overhaul that followed the Sept. 11 attacks, according to Jones.

Yahoo is attempting to distance itself from the controversy surrounding its new policy against remote work. In a statement to The New York Times, the company asserts that the ban is not reflective of broader industry trends but is instead tailored to Yahoo's specific needs. The policy aims to foster camaraderie, intensity, and creativity through physical interaction and to eliminate underperforming employees. While the ban has caused some grumbling from Yahoo employees who previously enjoyed remote work, many insiders support the move, believing it necessary to reinvigorate the company. Yahoo's new CEO, Marissa Mayer, is not backing down, and the controversy highlights her leadership abilities in making tough, unpopular decisions. Despite criticism that the policy may disrupt work-life balance, especially for women, and that it could lead to the loss of valuable employees, Mayer maintains that the policy is essential for Yahoo's turnaround.

Louisiana prison officials considered illegally obtaining a lethal-injection drug from an Oklahoma pharmacy for the execution of convicted child killer Christopher Sepulvado, according to newly released state documents. The Apothecary Shoppe, a compounding pharmacy not licensed in Louisiana, was suspected of supplying pentobarbital for recent executions in Oklahoma and Missouri. State documents revealed an email from the pharmacy to a Louisiana prison official, raising questions about the legality and transparency of the drug procurement process. Sepulvado’s lawyers argue that condemned inmates have a right to know how they will be executed, highlighting the ongoing secrecy and potential risks associated with using unregulated compounding pharmacies. The case underscores the broader crisis in obtaining execution drugs, with states increasingly turning to unlicensed suppliers and facing legal challenges over the methods used.

Madonna has lost a legal battle to prevent the auction of several personal items, including a letter from her former boyfriend Tupac Shakur and a pair of her panties. A Manhattan judge ruled that the items, which were originally up for auction last year, can now be sold. Madonna had filed a temporary restraining order against the auction house, Gotta Have Rock and Roll, claiming she was unaware the items were no longer in her possession. The judge sided with the auction house, stating that Madonna had misdirected her legal action. The auction, which includes personal photos and another letter in which Madonna describes Whitney Houston and Sharon Stone as "horribly mediocre," will resume in July.

Ben Carson, facing criticism for his limited foreign policy knowledge, is visiting Jordan to gain firsthand experience by touring a refugee camp and interacting with children. This move aims to strengthen his campaign and address concerns about his preparedness for the role. His recent support has waned, particularly in Iowa, where Donald Trump and Ted Cruz have taken the lead. Carson has previously opposed accepting Syrian refugees and faced scrutiny for comparing security concerns to a "rabid dog." His trip to Jordan is seen as an effort to demonstrate a deeper understanding of the issues.

Andrew Breitbart, known for his controversial and often incendiary statements, died unexpectedly just weeks before revealing what he claimed were incriminating videos of President Obama from his college years. Breitbart's death sparked numerous conspiracy theories, with some suggesting he was murdered by political opponents. Twitter, a platform Breitbart frequently used, became a hub for such theories, ranging from Obama's involvement in his death to the contents of the supposed tapes. Critics argue that these theories exemplify the very type of conspiracy-driven rhetoric Breitbart himself promoted.

Elon Musk announced his intention to take Tesla private at $420 per share, a move aimed at benefiting shareholders and advancing Tesla's mission. Musk notified the Tesla board on August 2nd and shared funding discussions with the Saudi Arabian sovereign wealth fund, which expressed strong support. Musk made a public announcement to ensure all shareholders had the same information, despite initial concerns about transparency. The funding for the buyout is contingent on due diligence and approvals. Musk is engaging advisors to explore potential structures and options, with a special board committee to evaluate any final proposal. The process will involve obtaining regulatory approvals and presenting the plan to Tesla shareholders for a vote.

A Texas state trooper was killed during a traffic stop on Thursday, with the suspect apprehended more than 100 miles away in a neighboring county. The Harris County Sheriff's Office announced that the suspect, identified as Dabrett Black, 32, of Linsdale, Texas, was taken into custody in Waller County. The trooper, whose identity has not been disclosed, was shot and killed with a rifle during the traffic stop on Interstate 45 near Fairfield, about 90 miles south of Dallas. The suspect fled the scene. Hours later, shots were reportedly fired in Hempstead, about 110 miles south of Fairfield, before the suspect was apprehended. U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz offered prayers for the trooper's family, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott called the killing a "heinous crime" and extended condolences to the trooper's family.

Eight people, including five juveniles, were wounded in a shooting at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Park during the MLK Day celebration in Liberty City, Miami-Dade. Police blocked off NW 32nd Avenue and questioned two suspects, recovering two firearms. The victims, aged 11 to 30, were treated with five in stable condition and one in critical condition. Two juveniles were grazed and released on the scene.

A new three-year study from Vanderbilt University’s National Center on Performance Incentives in Nashville found that significant bonuses for teachers to raise student test scores do not significantly improve student performance.
