Scientists and Energy Department employees are concerned about a request by the Trump transition team for names of individuals who have worked on climate change issues. The Energy Department has refused to provide names, emphasizing the importance of respecting the professional and scientific integrity of its workforce. This request has raised fears of potential retaliation against those who have supported climate science and policies under the Obama administration. Congress members have expressed alarm, warning of possible retribution and intimidation tactics. The Energy Department's refusal to comply could signal potential friction between the new leadership and existing staff.

Sen. Marco Rubio says he will not vote for the comprehensive immigration reform bill he helped draft unless significant changes are made, specifically in the area of border security. Rubio told radio host Hugh Hewitt that the bill needs stronger border security measures to prevent future illegal immigration. He stated that if the necessary amendments do not pass, he will vote against the bill. The bill's supporters hope to pass it by July 4, but Rubio emphasizes the importance of thorough debate and amendments to ensure the bill's success.

During an interview on The Colbert Report, Pussy Riot members Nadya Tolokonnikova and Masha Alyokhina showcased their wit and humor, despite conducting the conversation through a translator. Their responses were sharp and often hilarious, as they discussed their imprisonment and release, took jabs at Putin, and offered commentary on Russia’s anti-gay laws. The interview highlighted how humor can transcend language barriers, with their jokes and insights hanging on every word.

A key step in decommissioning Japan's Fukushima nuclear plant began, with operators starting to remove protective covers from one of the reactors. The covers, installed in 2011 to prevent radioactive materials from escaping, will be fully dismantled by the end of next year, with the extraction of 292 spent fuel rods to follow in 2020. Meanwhile, the Japanese government approved a larger compensation package of 7.07 trillion yen for the Fukushima crisis, as tens of thousands of evacuees remain in temporary housing more than four years after the disaster.

The legal team representing the Guinean hotel maid who accused former IMF chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn of sexual assault has enlisted French lawyer Thibault de Montbrial to locate any past victims of Strauss-Kahn. De Montbrial, known for his work on high-profile French cases, is being brought in to help the New York-based lawyers dig up evidence. Strauss-Kahn, 62, remains under house arrest and faces up to 25 years in prison if convicted on charges of attempted rape, sex abuse, a criminal sex act, unlawful imprisonment, and forcible touching. His defense team has asked the prosecution if they plan to discuss any past claims of unwanted sexual advances during the trial.

Iran's president-elect Hassan Rouhani has called for an end to government and clergy interference in private lives, increased internet freedom, and more open state media. Rouhani, who won in a surprise election, aims to foster moderation and better relations abroad. He addressed fellow clergymen, emphasizing a strong government should not interfere in people's lives but rather focus on improving trust and offering services. Rouhani supports loosening internet controls and criticizes state broadcaster IRIB for ignoring domestic issues. He opposes gender segregation and supports women's rights, stating that virtue should not be questioned by clothing compliance. Rouhani's vision faces challenges from hardliners and an economy affected by international sanctions, requiring patience and gradual change.

The debate over the effectiveness of hashtag activism, particularly in the context of the #BringBackOurGirls campaign for Nigerian schoolgirls kidnapped by Boko Haram, highlights the complexities of using social media for social change. While some argue that such campaigns can raise awareness and pressure leaders into action, others, like D.A. Lovell, caution that they may offer a false sense of accomplishment and obscure the need for more substantive efforts. Lovell suggests that true impact requires deeper engagement and strategic action beyond mere online support. The article also critiques the perceived bias in media coverage, noting that similar atrocities in other parts of the world receive less attention. Despite criticisms, hashtag activism has shown potential to influence policy and public discourse, as evidenced by increased international involvement and support for the Nigerian girls.

A 1-ton European science satellite, GOCE, re-entered Earth's atmosphere and mostly burned up, with debris likely landing in the southern Atlantic Ocean, officials say. The satellite, known for its sleek design, ran out of fuel and began descending from its low orbit. About 25% of the satellite was expected to survive re-entry, with its composite materials potentially enduring the intense heat. GOCE was launched in 2009 to map Earth's gravity and had completed its mission before its uncontrolled re-entry. Tracking data suggests the satellite broke up and any surviving pieces fell into the South Atlantic, just off the coast of South America.

A metal detectorist helped a couple recover an engagement ring that fell into a pond, turning a failed proposal into a successful one. Seth Dixon and Ruth Salas were planning to propose to Ruth at Loose Park Pond but the ring accidentally fell through a bridge into the water. Michael Long, who had a metal detector, heard about the couple's misfortune and decided to help. After two days of searching, Long found the ring and returned it to the couple. The couple's story went viral, leading to an appearance on Jimmy Kimmel Live! where they received a new ring.

National Library of Medicine, the world's largest medical library, is collecting and archiving web content to document the histories of health and medicine. University of California at San Diego researcher Albert Lin is leading the Valley of the Khans Project, which uses online volunteers to sift through high-resolution satellite images of Mongolia for ancient structures and artifacts, including potential burial sites of Genghis Khan and his descendants. Over 7,000 volunteers worldwide help by tagging images as "roads," "rivers," "modern structures," "ancient structures," or "other." This citizen science approach, part of a broader trend in engaging the public in scientific research, highlights how technology can enhance scientific discoveries while making the process more accessible and engaging for participants.

Hurricane Harvey, forecasted to be a Category 3 storm, is expected to make landfall along the Texas Gulf Coast, bringing catastrophic flooding and heavy rainfall. The storm's slow movement and favorable conditions, including warm water temperatures and weak upper-level winds, could result in up to 40 inches of rain in some areas, potentially causing life-threatening flooding. Governor Greg Abbott activated 700 service members to assist with rescue and recovery efforts, while residents were advised to prepare or evacuate. The storm's potential to stall over Texas for days poses a significant threat, with meteorologists warning of unprecedented flooding that could render parts of the region uninhabitable for weeks. President Donald Trump pledged federal assistance, emphasizing the importance of prioritizing life safety.

A young Golden Retriever named Fergus, found as a stray with severe chemical burns down his back, is receiving treatment for potential infection at the Animal Medical Center. The Lancaster Animal Shelter initially believed Fergus had been set on fire, but further investigation revealed acid was poured down his body. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors has offered a $25,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the perpetrator. At least seven dogs, including Fergus, have been found with similar injuries in the Antelope Valley and surrounding areas. Authorities are investigating whether the injuries were accidental or intentional crimes. A GoFundMe page has raised over $19,000 for Fergus's medical care, and PETA has offered a $2,500 reward for information.

Most psychologists agree that basic personality traits remain stable throughout life, but research suggests that personality becomes more stable in the 20s through the 50s before tapering off in old age. A study involving 4,000 men and women aged 20 to 80 found that personality stability followed a bell curve, peaking in middle age. Certain traits like conscientiousness, openness, and honesty-humility showed similar stability levels in the oldest participants as in the youngest. Neuroticism levels increased in the 30s but decreased in the 50s, being replaced by conscientiousness, openness, and honesty-humility.

The lawyers for Adel Daoud, a 19-year-old charged with plotting to bomb a Chicago bar, are questioning why the government is not acknowledging whether evidence in his case was obtained through a controversial surveillance program. The government, they argue, is trying to avoid a constitutional challenge to the program, which allows the interception of foreign targets' communications without individual warrants. The case highlights the broader debate over the reach of government surveillance and its impact on privacy rights.

A new study challenges the common belief that pyroclastic flows from supervolcanoes move at extremely high speeds, suggesting they might travel at more manageable, street-like speeds of about 10 to 45 miles per hour. By analyzing rocks trapped in volcanic ash from the 18.8 million-year-old Silver Creek caldera eruption in Arizona, researchers found that the ash flow could pick up and move large rocks, indicating a dense, slow-moving flow. This finding implies that people living near a supervolcano might have a few hours to evacuate once an eruption begins, potentially offering a chance to escape. However, the study emphasizes that volcano monitoring and early evacuation remain the most effective ways to ensure safety.

A respected religious counselor in New York's ultra-Orthodox Jewish community, Nechemya Weberman, was convicted of repeatedly sexually abusing a young girl who had come to him for guidance. The 54-year-old was found guilty of 59 counts, including sustained sex abuse of a child and sexual abuse, facing up to 25 years in prison. The victim, now 18, testified that the abuse lasted three years, involving various acts of sexual abuse during therapy sessions meant to help her become more religious. The case highlighted the strict rules and social customs of the Satmar Hasidic sect, where questioning faith or customs is forbidden, and the community has its own systems for handling disputes. Defense attorneys argued that the case was based on "he said, she said" and that the girl was a liar. The conviction was seen as a potential turning point for ultra-Orthodox victims of sexual abuse, with the district attorney stating that such abuse will not be swept under

Charlotte-Mecklenburg police released body and dash cam footage of the fatal shooting of Keith Lamont Scott, sparking ongoing protests. Chief Kerr Putney announced the release at a news conference, stating that other footage would be released later. The videos show Scott exiting his vehicle and falling to the ground, but do not clearly show if he was holding a gun. Scott’s family maintains he was unarmed. The police say Scott was shot after not following commands to drop a gun, but the family disputes this. The release of the videos did not satisfy the family, who say they are left with more questions than answers. The footage shows Scott rolling a marijuana "blunt" in his car, which police say contributed to the encounter. The police also released photos of the gun and holster they recovered from the scene. The shooting ignited several nights of protests in Charlotte, with the state declaring a state of emergency after violence and arrests.

A 105-year-old Japanese man named Hidekichi Miyazaki broke his own record for the oldest competitive sprinter at a competition in Kyoto, Japan. Miyazaki, nicknamed the "Golden Bolt" after Usain Bolt, ran the 100-meter dash in just 42.22 seconds, setting a world record in the over-105 age category. Born in 1910, Miyazaki showed no signs of slowing down, expressing disappointment with his time but satisfaction at finishing the race. He dreams of someday competing against Bolt and continues to train diligently, crediting his health to willpower and regular exercise. Despite his age, Miyazaki plans to continue running for a few more years, aiming to improve his performance and inspire others.

White House social media director Dan Scavino shared a video of what he said was a waterlogged Miami International Airport on Sunday, as Hurricane Irma approached southern Florida. The airport quickly corrected Scavino, who then deleted the tweet, acknowledging the mistake. Scavino had been sharing Hurricane Irma-related content with President Donald Trump and Vice President Mike Pence hourly. The video, which appeared on YouTube and other sites more than a week earlier, was actually from Mexico City, not Miami. The White House did not respond to questions about how Scavino verified the posts or if Trump was using the information.

A political party in Pakistan, led by former cricket star Imran Khan, has revealed what it claims is the identity of the CIA's top spy in the country as part of an escalating campaign against U.S. drone strikes. The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party named the CIA station chief in a letter to police, demanding he be held accountable for a recent drone strike that killed five militants, including senior Haqqani Network commanders. John Brennan, the CIA director, was also named in the letter. The PTI's move comes amid growing controversy over drone attacks, with the party's leader and other officials strongly opposing the strikes as a violation of Pakistan's sovereignty and a source of civilian casualties. The revelation could complicate U.S.-Pakistan relations, as it is rare for a CIA station chief's cover to be blown.

Obamacare's popularity is on the rise as President Trump pushes for its repeal, according to a new Politico/Morning Consult poll. Among registered voters, 45% approve of the law, while 45% disapprove, marking a seven-point increase in support since early January. The poll, which surveyed 2,013 registered voters over three days, also found that more voters favor keeping key provisions of Obamacare than repealing them. Eight out of nine specific ACA provisions garnered majority support, with the individual mandate being the only exception, with 57% wanting it repealed. The findings suggest that while Trump and Republicans aim to repeal Obamacare, public sentiment may make it challenging to achieve a complete overhaul.

A 17-year-old student at a competitive New York City high school, Omotayo Adeoye, was found dead in the Hudson River after being caught cheating on a German exam. The incident occurred on Thursday, with Adeoye allegedly writing a suicide note on her test before leaving the school and walking to the river. She placed her school ID on a rock and jumped into the water, where she was found by bystanders. The teacher who confronted her, Eva Malikova, reportedly screamed in anguish afterward. Adeoye, a promising student who played basketball and soccer, was described as intelligent and funny by her friends. Her father informed police that she did not know how to swim. The school launched an investigation into the incident, and the Department of Education promised a new focus on student mental health awareness.

Edward Snowden, the former National Security Agency contractor who leaked details of U.S. surveillance programs, is evading U.S. authorities and seeking asylum in Ecuador. After a night in Moscow’s airport, Snowden was expected to fly to Cuba and then to Venezuela. The U.S. is urging Russia to hand him over, but Snowden’s whereabouts remain unclear. Ecuador’s foreign minister stated his government is considering Snowden’s asylum request, while President Rafael Correa warned against U.S. pressure. The U.S. has revoked Snowden’s passport and is pressuring countries like Russia, Cuba, and Venezuela to cooperate. Snowden’s journey highlights the tension between the U.S. and countries like China, which was pleased with the revelations about American surveillance. The U.S. is also facing criticism for its own cyber espionage practices, as revealed by Snowden’s leaks.

The FBI is considering possible domestic terrorism charges against the individual accused of shooting a guard at the conservative Family Research Council. The FBI defines domestic terrorism as "Americans attacking Americans based on U.S.-based extremist ideologies." Currently, the FBI is hunting down seven people charged with such crimes, five of whom are women.

During the World Cup, residents in Samara, Russia, are being asked to shower in pairs to conserve water for visiting fans, reports the utility company Samarskiye Kommunalniye Systemy. The increased water usage is due to both the ongoing football tournament and a recent heat wave, straining the city's water supply.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints took a step toward transparency on March 26, 1830, the 185th anniversary of the publication of the Book of Mormon, by unveiling the first published pictures of a small sacred stone believed by founder Joseph Smith to have helped in its translation. The stone, described as smooth, brown, and egg-sized, was part of the third volume of the Joseph Smith Papers, which also included the first printer's manuscript of the Book of Mormon. The church historian Steven E. Snow displayed the stone at a Salt Lake City news conference, aiming to provide visual evidence and enhance understanding of the religion's origins. The move reflects the church's efforts to address curiosity and misinformation in the digital age, as its membership has grown to 15 million over the past three decades.

A photo from a College at Brockport party showing a dog doing a keg stand went viral, leading to an investigation and arrests. The image, shared on Twitter by @SUNYPartyStory, showed a black Labrador Retriever being held by its hind legs with a beer keg's nozzle in its mouth. Brockport Police arrested Robert Yates of Brockport, charging him with torturing and injuring animals. The dog, named Mya, was taken into protective custody but appeared to be in good condition. Shane Oliver, also a student, was charged for holding the dog. The incident occurred off-campus, and the College at Brockport stated it would investigate and take appropriate action, though details about student discipline were limited due to student privacy laws.

Dr. Conrad Murray, convicted of involuntary manslaughter in Michael Jackson's death, is to remain in jail pending sentencing, his attorney argued. Murray faces up to four years in prison and the loss of his medical license. The jury found him guilty after a nine-hour deliberation over two days, citing his deceptive and incompetent actions, including administering propofol and delaying emergency calls. Murray's own words from a post-incident police interview admitted to giving Jackson propofol, but experts suggested he may have lied about the dosage. Murray will be assigned a single cell for his own protection and an escort during his time in jail.

A retrospective review of 32 catastrophic pole-vault injuries from 1982 to 1998 found that 31 resulted in fatal or permanent head injuries, while one caused paraplegia. Common mechanisms included landing with the body on the landing pad and the head on the ground, getting stranded in the vault box, and missing the landing pad entirely. Recommendations include increasing landing pad size and ensuring soft surfaces around them. Other injury prevention strategies are discussed, focusing on reducing the risk of lower back and leg injuries during the plant/takeoff phase.

An 18-year-old Florida man is recovering after being bitten on the lip by a cottonmouth snake he was keeping in a pillowcase on his bed. The snake, also known as a water moccasin, escaped and bit him when he tried to recapture it. The bite from a cottonmouth can be deadly, causing massive swelling. The man was rushed to Tampa General Hospital, where his condition improved and he is expected to recover. He had illegally captured the snake and was not permitted to possess it. The snake was euthanized for proper identification and treatment. Cottonmouths, part of the viper family, are venomous and usually found in swamp-like habitats. They have a reputation for defending themselves when threatened.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has devised an unconventional plan to avoid demolishing 30 illegally constructed apartments in the Ulpana settlement outpost in the West Bank. Instead of destroying the buildings, the government intends to dismantle and reassemble the structures elsewhere. This approach, while intended to ease the impact on settlers, is seen as costly and impractical by construction experts. Netanyahu's plan aims to sidestep the Supreme Court order to demolish the settlement, which was built on privately owned Palestinian land. The relocation process, involving complex engineering and substantial financial resources, is estimated to cost millions of dollars. The move has sparked criticism from legal and human rights groups, who argue that it defies the court ruling and sets a dangerous precedent for future evictions. Despite the government's efforts to compensate settlers with new housing, the plan faces significant challenges and may not be completed by the July 1 deadline set by the court.

One-year-old Lucas Warren, from Dalton, Georgia, has been named the 2018 Gerber Baby, making history as the first child with Down syndrome to win the title since 2010. Lucas's outgoing personality and happy expression won over the Gerber team. His parents, Jason and Cortney Warren, hope this will shed light on the special needs community and help individuals with special needs be accepted. The Warrens received a $50,000 cash prize, and Lucas's year will be documented on Gerber's social media. Cortney Warren emphasizes that Lucas is "always Lucas first" and hopes he will be proud of himself in the future.

Zambian Vice-President Guy Scott, a white man, has become Africa's first white head of state in decades, following the death of President Michael Sata. Scott, who regularly stood in for Sata at official events, now faces the challenge of leading the country through its complex relationship with China. Sata, known as "King Cobra," was a controversial figure who won the presidency on an anti-Chinese platform but Scott acknowledges the need to recalibrate the relationship with China, citing issues such as poor management and worker conditions. Scott's rise to power comes with the expectation of maintaining Sata's legacy while navigating the country's economic and political landscape.

American aid worker Kayla Mueller, held captive by ISIS in Syria, endured brutal treatment including torture, sexual abuse, and forced labor. Despite her suffering, she maintained hope and selflessly supported fellow hostages. Mueller was reportedly raped by ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi and passed up an escape opportunity to help Yazidi girls. Her fellow captives praised her strength and faith. Mueller's family, aided by proof-of-life messages, attempted negotiations with ISIS but faced delays and obstacles. In February 2015, ISIS claimed she died in a Jordanian airstrike, though U.S. officials confirmed her death later.

Writer Zinzi Clemmons has announced she will no longer write for Lena Dunham and Jenni Konner’s online feminist newsletter Lenny Letter due to Dunham and her friends' "well-known racism." Clemmons, who has known Dunham since college, says she previously avoided Dunham's social circle due to their "hipster-racism," which often uses sarcasm as a cover. Clemmons cites an incident where a friend experienced sexual assault by a member of Dunham's circle, mirroring a similar experience she witnessed. Clemmons encourages other writers, especially women of color, to leave Lenny Letter in response to Dunham's initial support of Murray Miller, who was accused of sexual assault.

Artist Marni Kotak is transforming the Microscope Gallery into a home-birth center for her upcoming exhibition "The Birth of Baby X," which will document the birth of her child from conception through college and beyond. The gallery will serve as a birthing space, complete with a shower, shag carpeting, and artwork related to her pregnancy. Kotak's performances often focus on real-life experiences, and this project aims to highlight the authenticity of human life and birth. The exhibition runs from October 8 to November 7, with the gallery remaining open if the birth occurs during the show.

Pope Francis, the first Latin American and the first non-European pope in over 1,200 years, reportedly turned to religion after being rejected by his childhood sweetheart when they were both 12 years old. His sister expressed concern about his "infinite loneliness" in his new role, while Francis himself jokingly declined the papacy, citing the distance and the large responsibility. Despite his reluctance, he was elected on Wednesday, succeeding Pope Benedict XVI, who stepped down last month. The new pope inherits a church facing various challenges, including a priest shortage, a sexual abuse crisis, and growing competition from evangelical churches in the Southern Hemisphere.

Anne Hathaway's choice of dress for the Oscars was not her first pick. She initially intended to wear a pink Valentino gown but opted for a Prada column dress instead, citing a last-minute decision due to a similar dress worn by her co-star Amanda Seyfried. Hathaway, a longtime fan of Valentino, expresses regret over the change, though she remains pleased with her final selection.

Taylor Swift's $50,000 donation to a GoFundMe campaign for a young cancer patient named Naomi prompted the platform to raise its donation limit from $15,000 to $50,000. Swift, known for her philanthropic efforts, donated the maximum amount allowed in four separate transactions after hearing about Naomi's situation and her upcoming missed concert. The GoFundMe CEO, Rob Solomon, praised Swift's generosity and its potential to inspire future donations. Naomi and her family expressed gratitude through a video response, touched by Swift's support during their difficult time.

President Barack Obama emerges from the Democratic conventions with a clearer path to victory, according to top advisers to Mitt Romney. The Romney campaign, while pleasantly surprised by Obama’s lackluster prime-time performance, fell short of expectations and now faces a tough map, with Ohio leaning heavily in Obama’s favor. Both campaigns anticipate little movement in national polls before the first debate on October 3, focusing instead on Obama’s ability to connect with voters and present solutions. The Romney campaign plans a negative ad strategy, but Obama officials remain confident in their small but important lead in battleground states. The article suggests that Obama’s post-convention polling gains may indicate a more substantial lead than initially thought, with the potential for a significant bounce once the full impact of the conventions is reflected in the polls.

Four of the five people killed in the operation that killed Osama bin Laden were unarmed, according to U.S. officials. The initial claims that bin Laden had fired at the Navy SEALs and used his wife as a human shield have been revised. The operation was described as a precision mission with the SEALs moving through the compound methodically. Bin Laden was found in his bedroom with weapons within reach but was unarmed when shot. The SEALs also found stashes of weapons and barricades, suggesting the compound was prepared for a prolonged standoff. The raid resulted in the capture of 22 women and children, and the team gathered computers, hard drives, and other documents for intelligence analysis. President Obama decided not to release photos of bin Laden's body, citing concerns about potential propaganda use.

Pink, 38, was thrilled to be featured on the cover of PEOPLE's 2018 Beautiful Issue, sharing the spotlight with her 15-month-old son Jameson Moon and 6-year-old daughter Willow Sage. Upon learning the news, she joked about avoiding eye contact for the week. Pink attributes her cover deal to her children, musing that Jameson might be upset about his first cover. She also discussed her parenting philosophy, emphasizing affection and letting her kids know they can count on her. Pink's daughter Willow, however, remains unconvinced, expressing that she still feels ugly despite Pink's efforts. Pink believes in teaching her children to follow rules while also knowing when to break them. The issue, rebranded as "The Beautiful Issue," features celebrities without makeup and highlights diverse beauty standards.

U.S. Ambassador to Syria Robert Ford visited the town of Hama to show support for protesters, despite Syrian government accusations of unauthorized entry. Ford met with residents and visited a hospital treating the injured. More than 500,000 protesters gathered in Hama on Friday, marking the largest demonstration yet. The U.S. summoned the Syrian ambassador after reports that embassy staff filmed protests against the crackdown. Syrian authorities accused the U.S. of interfering and escalating the situation.

Star Wars actor Mark Hamill took to Twitter to defend net neutrality, clashing with Republican Senator Ted Cruz. In a tweet, Hamill mocked Cruz's spelling of his name, saying, "Thanks for smarm-spaining it to me I know politics can be confusing, but you'd have more credibility if you spelled my name correctly. I mean IT'S RIGHT THERE IN FRONT OF YOU!" This exchange occurred as the Federal Communications Commission voted to repeal net neutrality rules, which protect internet freedom. Hamill, known for his role as Luke Skywalker, used his platform to criticize the decision, highlighting the potential negative impacts on various industries.

Seth Owen, an 18-year-old co-valedictorian from Jacksonville, Florida, faces a financial challenge to attend Georgetown University due to his parents' refusal to support his tuition after discovering his homosexuality. Despite maintaining a 4.61 GPA and being accepted to Georgetown, Owen's financial aid package was insufficient because it was based on his parents' expected contribution, which they no longer provide. His former biology teacher, Jane Martin, launched a GoFundMe campaign to raise $20,000 for Owen's tuition, which has surpassed $50,000, covering his first year's expenses. Owen plans to use the support to become a defense attorney for teens, emphasizing the importance of standing up for oneself and seeking help when facing adversity.

Jake Perry, an 85-year-old plumber from Austin, Texas, is known for his dedication to cats, having adopted and rehomed hundreds of them over the years. Perry believes his cats' long lives are due to a combination of a special diet, mental stimulation, and lots of love. His cats, including the world-record holders Granpa Rexs Allen and Creme Puff, often enjoy homemade breakfasts, nature documentaries, and even cat-friendly holiday celebrations. While the scientific basis for Perry's methods is questionable, sterilization is believed to play a significant role in extending cat lifespans. Perry's dedication to his cats extends beyond their lifetimes, as he has buried 47 of them in his backyard and plans to open a pet cemetery. His own health and the well-being of his last cat, Cowboy, remain a focus as he contemplates his future.

Deputy Defense Secretary Robert Work highlighted China's rapid advancements in military technology, emphasizing the need for the U.S. to develop new capabilities to maintain its military superiority. Speaking at a conference, Work noted China's progress in stealth aircraft, advanced missiles, and electronic warfare equipment, indicating a serious challenge to U.S. military dominance. While seeking a constructive relationship, the Pentagon acknowledges the competitive aspects of their military rivalry, particularly in technological development. Work also discussed the importance of hedging against potential international competition, citing a Harvard study on rising powers and established powers. The U.S. aims to develop new technologies, such as directed energy weapons, to counter China's advancements and maintain its strategic edge.

The U.S. shellfish industry, particularly geoduck clams from the Pacific Northwest, faces an unprecedented ban by China, cutting off a $270 million industry from its largest export market. China cited high levels of arsenic and a toxin causing paralytic shellfish poisoning in recent shipments. The ban, effective last week and indefinite, affects clams, oysters, and other two-shelled bivalves from Washington, Oregon, Alaska, and Northern California. U.S. officials are seeking to identify the exact source of contamination and negotiate with China to reopen trade. The ban has severely impacted geoduck harvesters and farmers, with many facing job losses and reduced operations. Geoduck farmers and harvesters are turning to politicians and government officials, including Governor Jay Inslee, to overturn the ban and find alternative markets.

Tom Hiddleston, known for his roles in film and theater, earned his first Emmy nomination for his performance in AMC's miniseries "The Night Manager." Hiddleston expressed delight over the nomination and highlighted the strong performances of his co-stars and the series itself. Despite the excitement, Hiddleston's new relationship with Taylor Swift remains a topic of interest. He confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that his relationship with Swift is genuine and not a publicity stunt, emphasizing their happiness together. Hiddleston is set to celebrate his nomination with co-stars from "Thor: Ragnarok" and is looking forward to attending the Emmy Awards.

Archaeologists analyzing DNA from an underwater site off the Isle of Wight have discovered evidence of wheat cultivation 8,000 years ago, 2,000 years before agriculture became established in Britain. The findings suggest that Stone Age Britons engaged in trade or other interactions with Neolithic farmers in southern Europe, challenging the conventional view of isolated hunter-gatherers. The DNA, extracted from 8,000-year-old sediment cores, indicates that wheat was imported to Britain, likely through the English Channel, which was narrower and shallower at the time. This discovery highlights the sophistication of prehistoric communities and the existence of trade networks long before the widespread adoption of farming in Britain.

The Obamas have purchased a Kalorama mansion they had been renting since leaving the White House, for $8.1 million. The eight-bedroom, nine-and-a-half-bath home, built in 1921 and renovated in 2011, will serve as their residence while their 15-year-old daughter Sasha finishes high school at Sidwell Friends. The purchase makes sense given their planned two-and-a-half-year stay in Washington. The former first couple will continue to be neighbors with President Trump’s daughter Ivanka and Jared Kushner, who live a few blocks away.

Dark Web marketplaces offer lifetime access to popular streaming services like Netflix and Spotify for a fraction of their regular subscription costs. McAfee Labs reported that stolen accounts from services such as HBO NOW, HBO GO, and premium sports services can be purchased for under $10. Some sellers even provide a "guarantee" of lifetime access, with one marketplace boasting its own help desk. These accounts likely stem from both stolen credit-card and account information. To protect your data, use unique, strong passwords and enable two-factor authentication.

Local TV news anchor Greg Kelly, son of NYPD Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly, was cleared of rape charges after Manhattan prosecutors reviewed the evidence. Kelly, who had been off the air since the accusations surfaced, expressed gratitude for the exoneration. The investigation, conducted by the Manhattan District Attorney's office, found no evidence to support the rape allegations. Kelly's accuser, a 28-year-old paralegal, claimed she was raped after a night of drinking with Kelly, but her story was inconsistent with text messages and other evidence. Kelly promised to return to his anchor chair soon.

Democrats may be losing their historic advantage in electing women to office, as Republican women are making significant gains in primary elections. With five Republican women nominated for Senate this cycle, compared to four Democrats, the momentum is shifting towards the GOP. While some argue the trend is exaggerated, the number of female Republican candidates, especially in key races, could lead to a more balanced representation in Congress. The "Palin effect" is credited with boosting several female candidates, but the absence of Hillary Clinton as a frontrunner is noted. The trend extends to governorships, where the number of female governors is now evenly split between parties. The documentary "Fire From the Heartland" capitalizes on this phenomenon, highlighting the rise of conservative women in politics.

A woman fleeing police through a pasture was chased down by a dozen cows, leading her to officers and arrest, according to the Sanford Police Department. Jennifer Anne Kaufman, 46, was riding in a stolen Subaru SUV being pursued by officers. The vehicle crashed near a pasture, and Kaufman and another occupant, Jamie Michael Young, 46, fled into the pasture. Young was chased down by a K9 unit, but Kaufman made it deeper. Then, a herd of cows, numbering over a dozen, chased Kaufman to a fence where authorities were waiting. Kaufman was charged with petit theft, possession of cocaine, possession of drug paraphernalia, trespassing, resisting arrest, and violation of probation.

The death toll from Japan's earthquake and tsunami surpassed 10,000, with thousands still missing. Radiation concerns spread as iodine-131 was detected in tap water and certain vegetables, prompting bans and shortages. In Tokyo, residents stocked up on bottled water, while farmers faced uncertainty about their produce. The Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant continued to struggle, with workers battling to prevent further radiation leaks.

Amazon offers a "Pay to Quit" program to warehouse workers, providing up to $5,000 in severance to those who leave their jobs, aiming to retain employees who truly want to work for the company. This program, first introduced by Amazon subsidiary Zappos, encourages workers to reflect on their job satisfaction and potentially move on if they are not content. Amazon also supports employee education through its "Career Choice" program, covering up to 95% of tuition costs for courses in demand fields, such as airplane mechanics or nursing, regardless of relevance to Amazon. These initiatives reflect Amazon's focus on employee well-being and choice, ensuring the company only retains committed workers while providing opportunities for skill development and career advancement.

A Minnesota judge overseeing Prince's estate narrowed down potential heirs, ruling out nearly 30 claimants while ordering genetic testing for six purported family members, including Prince's sister and three half-siblings. The judge's order excludes five unidentified individuals with questionable claims and dismisses several others, leaving the inheritance of Prince's estimated $300 million estate to be determined among the tested relatives.

Islamists clashed with protesters outside Egypt's presidential palace on Wednesday, as Vice President Mahmoud Mekky proposed a way to end the constitutional crisis. Stones and petrol bombs were exchanged between the two sides, with 23 people reportedly wounded. Mursi returned to work after a day of protest. Mekky suggested amendments to disputed articles in the constitution could be agreed with the opposition, then submitted to the next parliament. The opposition blamed Mursi for the violence and called for dialogue if he scrapped his November 22 decree and postponed the referendum. Many Egyptians seek an end to political upheaval, which has harmed the economy. The Muslim Brotherhood called for a protest outside the palace, describing the opposition's actions as "oppressive abuses." The army, which took over after Mubarak, has not intervened in politics. Investors are hopeful that the crisis may soon ease, with stocks rising.

Tiger Woods' recent performances at the U.S. Open and the Memorial Tournament have raised doubts among those still holding onto his past glory. Woods opened with an 80 in the first round at Chambers Bay, and despite showing some improvement in the third round, he still finished 16-over par, missing the cut. His struggles have led to comparisons with aging athletes like Willie Mays, who lost his consistency in later years. Woods' career has been marked by numerous injuries and a significant decline since 2008, when his sex scandal became public. Despite his past achievements, his current form suggests he may never regain his former status as the best golfer in the world.

A Mississippi man, Joshua Vallum, was sentenced to 49 years in prison on May 15, 2017, for the first-ever conviction under federal hate crime charges for killing a transgender woman. U.S. District Judge Louis Guirola Jr. sentenced Vallum for the 2015 killing of 17-year-old Mercedes Williamson, marking the first case prosecuted under the federal Hate Crimes Prevention Act for a victim targeted because of gender identity. Prosecutors stated Vallum shocked Williamson with a stun gun, stabbed her, and beat her to death to prevent fellow Latin Kings gang members from discovering their sexual relationship, which was against gang rules. Vallum pleaded guilty in December and also faces a life sentence for a state murder charge. The case drew national attention from LGBT advocates and the Justice Department, with U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions emphasizing the importance of holding accountable those who commit violent acts against transgender individuals. Public defenders highlighted Vallum's troubled childhood, including

Donald Trump's presidency, marked by his embrace of untruth and alternative facts, poses a significant threat to American democracy and the nation's moral standing. His policies, while often variations of classic Republican positions, are executed with a reckless disregard for truth and the rule of law, making their impact potentially disastrous. Trump's presidency is characterized by his unpredictability, petulance, and self-regard, which could lead to severe consequences, including the erosion of public education, environmental degradation, and the weakening of the U.S. relationship with other nations. His lack of respect for institutions and his promotion of conspiracy theories and racist memes further undermine the integrity of the democratic process. The challenge now lies in opposing his agenda while defending the rule of law and the principles of a free society.

Students returned to Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, for the first time since the Valentine's Day shooting that killed 17 people, facing a new policy of leaving backpacks at home. About 50 armed officers were present to ensure safety. Dick's Sporting Goods announced it would stop selling assault-style rifles and raise the minimum age for gun purchases to 21. A student leader, David Hogg, expressed fear over seeing armed police and continued advocating for an assault weapon ban. Survivors and their families returned to the school, with some planning to wear maroon to honor the victims. A legislative hearing discussed raising the age limit for buying long guns and allowing deputized teachers to carry concealed weapons in classrooms, though the school's superintendent opposed the latter measure.

A massive ice jam on the Yukon River in Galena, Alaska, caused severe flooding, forcing the evacuation of several hundred residents. The ice jam, which began flooding the town on Sunday, showed signs of weakening by Wednesday, with chunks breaking off and water levels rising downstream. The National Guard evacuated 32 people and 19 dogs to Fairbanks, while other residents stayed behind, camping at the airport or in former Air Force barracks. The flooding has left Galena without power, fresh water, and cell phone reception, with many homes submerged and cars floating. The town faces the risk of a flash flood as the ice jam is expected to break, potentially flooding the downriver community of Koyukuk. The National Weather Service expects the ice jam to break by late Wednesday or Thursday, with a surge of water expected to reach Koyukuk by Thursday afternoon.

A woman who owns a business claiming to be California's largest landlord of marijuana businesses has sued the city of San Bernardino to overturn its new pot regulation ordinance. The lawsuit, filed by Stephanie Smith, owner of Bubba Likes Tortillas, argues the ordinance could create monopolies and prevent her from renting property to pot growers. The dispute stems from a December raid where 35,000 marijuana plants were seized from buildings she owns. The new rules bar anyone, including property owners, from the commercial cannabis business if they have violated local or state laws related to the industry or failed to report income from it. Smith fears the ordinance could disqualify her tenants and her company from obtaining licenses, violating due process and potentially creating monopolies. San Bernardino's ordinance allows only 17 commercial marijuana businesses, but there are 19 different types of licenses available. The city council approved the ordinance to replace a voter-approved measure invalidated by a judge.

Rep. Allen West, a Florida Republican, spoke at a GOP dinner, calling Democrats' message of equality, economic dependency, and enslaving the entrepreneurial spirit "not going to resonate with Florida citizens." He challenged Democrats to "bring it on" in the upcoming elections. Meanwhile, Florida's Republican legislature is reportedly pushing through a redistricting plan that could put West at risk, with one of Mitt Romney's spokesmen, Will Weatherford, leading the effort. West's district is set to lose significant support, and a deal has been made to finalize and push through these maps quickly. Despite attempts to downplay the situation, insiders suggest this is a targeted move against West, a rising Tea Party star.

The Buffalo Bills have hired Kathryn Smith as a quality control assistant, making her the first full-time female assistant coach in NFL history. Smith will work under special teams coordinator Danny Crossman. Head coach Rex Ryan praised Smith, noting her outstanding job over the past seven years and her strong commitment. Ryan also mentioned consulting with Bruce Arians, who was the first NFL head coach to hire a female assistant coach. Smith has spent 14 years in the NFL, previously working as an administrative assistant and assistant to the head coach for the New York Jets. Her hiring marks a significant step in gender equality in the NFL.

The South Carolina deputy who forcefully removed a student from class by flipping and tossing her across a classroom has been fired, Richland County Sheriff Leon Lott announced. Videos of the incident, which went viral, showed the officer, Ben Fields, using excessive force against a black female student. Lott stated that Fields' actions were "not acceptable" and that he did not follow proper training and procedure. Fields' lawyer defended his client, stating that his actions were justified and lawful. The student suffered injuries, including a cast on her arm and neck and back injuries. The incident has sparked debate over the use of police in schools and raised concerns about racial bias. The FBI and Justice Department have opened investigations into whether civil rights were violated. Lott emphasized that while the student's behavior was disruptive, it did not justify the officer's actions.

Former President George W. Bush and Bill Clinton, along with other political figures, have weighed in on the killing of Osama bin Laden. Bush called it a "momentous achievement" that marks a victory for America and the fight against terror. Clinton congratulated President Obama and the military and intelligence communities. Other leaders, including Mitt Romney, John McCain, and Nancy Pelosi, also expressed support and gratitude for the operation, emphasizing the importance of continuing the fight against terrorism. Mike Huckabee, founder of Huck PAC, highlighted the significance of the moment and the enduring commitment to justice.

The Hollywood Sign Trust plans to enhance surveillance to prevent future pranks after a New Year's Day incident where the sign read "Hollyweed" for a brief period. The non-profit organization, responsible for maintaining the landmark, stated that while the surveillance system is constantly evolving, improvements are needed to better deter unwanted visitors. The incident, which involved hanging tarps over the sign, remains unsolved, with no suspect identified. The sign was restored by mid-morning, and the trust will review the security system to ensure the safety of the neighborhood and visitors.

A senior U.S. Secret Service agent, Kerry O'Grady, faced scrutiny after posting on Facebook that she would not take a bullet for President Donald Trump, sparking an investigation by the Secret Service. O'Grady's posts, including one where she stated she would prefer jail time over supporting Trump, drew complaints and attention. The Secret Service confirmed it was taking "appropriate action" but declined to comment further. O'Grady acknowledged she deleted the posts after a few days and maintained her commitment to her duties, despite her political views. Her actions raised questions about the balance between personal beliefs and professional obligations within the Secret Service.

JPMorgan Chase reduced CEO Jamie Dimon's 2012 compensation by 50%, reflecting the bank's multibillion-dollar trading loss. Despite record profits and strong revenue growth, the board cut Dimon's total compensation to $11.5 million from $23 million. The decision aimed to hold Dimon accountable for oversight failures. The bank reported a $5.7 billion fourth-quarter profit, up 53% year-over-year, and $21.3 billion in annual earnings. JPMorgan also faced legal challenges and regulatory scrutiny, including a $8.5 billion settlement with federal regulators over foreclosure practices.

A film crew working on the Gregg Allman biopic "Midnight Rider" was struck by a train on a railroad trestle in Wayne County, Georgia, killing one crew member and injuring seven others. The incident occurred when the crew, from Meddin Studios in Savannah, Georgia, was filming on tracks without permission from the railroad. The train, owned by CSX Railroad, struck a mattress and other equipment, causing the fatal accident. The victim, 27-year-old Sarah Elizabeth Jones from Atlanta, was identified by the sheriff's department. The film production company, Open Road Films, stated it still plans to release the movie in the U.S. but did not provide a release date. The investigation is ongoing, with cooperation from CSX Railroad and the film crew.

Johnny Cash's boyhood home in Dyess, Arkansas, has been added to the National Register of Historic Places. Initially nominated in December, the nomination was returned in January with recommendations to emphasize the home's impact on Cash's musical development. The revised nomination, submitted in April, highlights the property's association with the Dyess Resettlement Colony and its influence on Cash's early life and career. The five-room farmhouse, built in 1934, was part of the Federal Emergency Relief Administration's efforts to help families during the Great Depression. Cash lived in the house from age 3 through high school, a period he credited as foundational to his musical journey. Arkansas State University, which owns the property, spent $575,000 on its restoration and now visitors can walk in the footsteps of the future "Man in Black."

In a California court, a 17-year-old girl detailed years of abuse she and 12 siblings suffered in a house where they were shackled to beds, choked, and went unbathed for long periods. The girl, in a childlike voice, called 911, pleading for help for her sisters. David and Louise Turpin, the parents, have pleaded not guilty to charges including torture and child abuse. The 13 siblings, ages 2 to 29, lived in isolation, with signs of starvation and neglect evident. The oldest adult child weighed just 82 pounds. The children were locked up as punishment, beaten, and denied basic necessities like toys and games. The girl planned her escape for two years, fearing for her life when her father choked her. The case drew worldwide attention, highlighting severe neglect hidden behind a seemingly normal family facade.

Central Texas high school student Macie Martinez, a Lake Travis junior and softball team trainer, recovered with a light-hearted attitude after being struck by lightning. One week post-incident, she joked on social media about her "cool scar," using imagery of lightning bolts. Her mother described the terrifying moment when Macie screamed upon opening the refrigerator door. Macie suffered nerve damage, temporary paralysis, and ongoing fatigue. Despite these challenges, she maintains a positive outlook, and her family uses nicknames like "Sparky" to keep spirits high. The lightning strike also caused significant damage to household items, but Macie's health and her coffee maker remain the priorities.

Barry Byron Mills, the notorious leader of the Aryan Brotherhood prison gang, died in July 2023 at the age of 70 in a supermax federal prison in Florence, Colorado. Mills, known as "Baron," was serving multiple life sentences for murder convictions. His influence extended across the United States, particularly in the Bay Area and Northern California. Mills was known for his brutal killings and his ability to orchestrate criminal activities from his cell, including a failed decapitation attempt while in federal custody. He was also involved in a race war between prison gangs and a notorious protection deal with John Gotti. Mills' death does not appear suspicious, but an autopsy is pending.

The U.S. ambassador to Libya, Chris Stevens, and three other Americans were killed in an attack on the U.S. Consulate in Benghazi, Libya, by a mob angry over an anti-Islam film. The film, produced by a California real estate developer, was posted online and depicted the Prophet Muhammad in a mocking manner. U.S. President Barack Obama condemned the attack and ordered increased security for diplomatic personnel worldwide. The Libyan government apologized for the attack and vowed to bring the attackers to justice. The incident highlighted the ongoing lawlessness in post-revolution Libya and Egypt, where protesters also attacked U.S. embassies in Cairo, expressing anger over the film. The deaths of the U.S. diplomats underscored the risks faced by foreign service officers in the field.

U.S. President Barack Obama's attendance at an annual summit of Southeast Asian leaders in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, thrust him into the center of the region's most contentious dispute: the long-standing territorial conflicts in the South China Sea, particularly between China and its neighbors. The inability to resolve these disputes has become a major obstacle for the 10-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) as it aims to establish an EU-like economic community by the end of 2015. Behind closed doors, the Chinese and Philippine leaders pressed their claims, while others called for restraint. The dispute, and Obama's presence, highlighted how ASEAN has become a key battleground for influence in Asia, with the U.S. pushing its "Pacific pivot" and China acting to protect its interests. The lack of consensus among ASEAN countries over the maritime disputes has pushed much of the bloc's other work to the sidelines. At a conference in Malmö, Sweden, the Dalai Lama, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989, stated that Europe should help refugees but that they should ultimately return to rebuild their own countries. He said, "Europe belongs to the Europeans," and advised that refugees should be received, helped, and educated, but ultimately develop their own nations. This comes amid Sweden's struggles with an increase in violent crimes and refugee-related incidents, particularly in Malmö. The Dalai Lama's comments echo his previous statements about refugees in Germany, emphasizing temporary admission and the goal of returning refugees to their homelands.

Zsa Zsa Gabor, the Hungarian-American socialite and actress known for her wit and quick comebacks, died at the age of 99. Gabor was famous for her sharp remarks and memorable quotes, such as "I’m a great housekeeper. Every time I get a divorce, I keep the house" and "You can say I’m full of s—t — but don’t say I’m old." Her quotes often addressed her frequent marriages and divorces, with one remark stating, "Husbands are like fires. They go out when unattended." Other notable quotes include "I never hated a man enough to give him his diamonds back" and "A girl must marry for love, and keep on marrying until she finds it." Gabor's sharp tongue and memorable one-liners continue to be celebrated in the entertainment industry.

A couple who received a wedding gift advising them not to open it until their "first disagreement" finally opened it nine years later. The gift contained wine glasses and personal notes with cash, instructing them to buy flowers, pizza, and other items. However, the real value lay in the lessons learned over the years—tolerance, understanding, compromise, and patience—teaching them that the tools for a strong, healthy marriage are within themselves.

President Donald Trump is calling for Russia to be reinstated to the Group of Seven (G-7), a leading group of industrialized nations. Trump made this statement on the eve of the G-7 summit in Canada, where he will face criticism from allies over new U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum imports. The move is seen as an attempt to improve relations with Russia and further his campaign promises on trade. However, this suggestion has drawn criticism from U.S. lawmakers and allies, who argue that Russia's annexation of Crimea and support for separatists in Ukraine make it unworthy of rejoining the group. Trump's stance highlights the growing divide between the U.S. and its closest allies, and raises questions about his approach to foreign policy.

A lawyer for a woman who says Bill Cosby sexually abused her when she was 15 has stated in a recent court filing that he has interviewed two witnesses who corroborate her story. The lawyer, Marc Strecker, wrote in a sworn declaration that he has reviewed photographs of his client, Judy Huth, with Cosby at the Playboy Mansion in the mid-1970s, the place and time she says the abuse happened. Huth's sexual battery lawsuit against Cosby comes amid a flurry of allegations that he drugged and sexually assaulted more than a dozen women. Cosby's attorney, Martin Singer, is seeking to dismiss the suit and has called it an extortion attempt, arguing that Huth tried to sell her story to a tabloid 10 years ago. Strecker's declaration does not provide details about how the witnesses corroborate Huth's story, but her lawsuit states she and a 16-year-old female friend were taken to the Playboy Mansion by Cosby sometime around 1

An 8-year-old Jack Russell Terrier named Knuckles has a unique talent that has gained him internet fame. Whenever he hears the "Law & Order" theme song, Knuckles starts to howl along, much to the amusement of his owner, Daniel Serna of Los Angeles. Serna noticed Knuckles' behavior shortly after bringing him home years ago. A video of Knuckles singing along to the theme song has garnered nearly 10,000 views on YouTube. The behavior is not unique to Knuckles, as other dogs have been recorded howling to the same tune. Experts suggest that the high-pitched and staccato nature of the music might trigger a response in dogs' auditory nerves, causing them to howl. While some owners are amused by their dogs' reactions, others are concerned about the potential strain on their pets' ears.

A study published in PLOS ONE has identified a unique chemical cocktail emitted by decomposing human bodies, distinguishing them from other animals. Researchers analyzed volatile organic compounds (VOCs) released during the decomposition of six human and 26 animal remains over six months in a laboratory setting. Using principal component analysis (PCA), they found eight compounds—ethyl propionate, propyl propionate, propyl butyrate, ethyl pentanoate, pyridine, diethyl disulfide, methyl(methylthio)ethyl disulfide, and 3-methylthio-1-propanol—that were specific to humans and pigs. Five esters—3-methylbutyl pentanoate, 3-methylbutyl 3-methylbutyrate, 3-methylbutyl 2-methylbutyrate, butyl pentanoate, and propyl hexanoate—were unique to pigs. These findings could help train cadaver dogs more effectively

A local English pub and restaurant is maintaining its traditional holiday schedule, with several days closed for Christmas and New Year's observances. The establishment, known for its simple and hearty meals, will be closed from Boxing Day through New Year's Day, reopening on January 2nd for a regular morning service. The pub expresses holiday wishes to its patrons, looking forward to serving a Sunday roast in the New Year.

Jessica Hayes, 38, from Fort Wayne, Indiana, became the Fort Wayne-South Bend Diocese's first consecrated virgin in 25 years, marrying Jesus Christ in a ceremony at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception. Hayes, a high school theology teacher, made this decision after years of prayer and soul-searching. She faced the same challenges as any bride, such as finding the perfect wedding dress, ensuring it was appropriate for her vow to remain a virgin for Christ, and making sure her guests had a good time. Hayes believes that all people are called to marriage, but in her case, it is to Christ. She hopes her experience will inspire others to consider this vocation. Hayes will continue to live as a lay person but is now married to Jesus, making a public commitment to serve the church.

LeBron James added another ring to his collection, marrying Savannah Brinson at a private ceremony in San Diego. About 200 guests attended the Saturday event, part of a three-day celebration. James, a four-time NBA MVP, and Brinson, with whom he has two sons, have been together since high school. The wedding, with intense security, was a closely guarded secret, even from some guests. No details were released, and no phones were allowed. The couple's focus was on ensuring Savannah's day was perfect. James and the Miami Heat will soon open training camp, with the team aiming to defend their recent championship.

First lady Melania Trump told ABC News that she has expressed concerns about people in her husband's administration whom she did not trust. During an interview in Africa, she also claimed to be one of the most bullied people in the world, which has motivated her "Be Best" campaign aimed at addressing cyberbullying. When pressed on her assertion, she softened her statement, saying she could be considered one of the most bullied. Trump discussed how bullying has affected her personally and why her initiative focuses on social media and online behavior, especially for children.

One of two men convicted for stealing two paintings from the Van Gogh Museum in 2002, Octave Durham, recently shared his story with the Telegraaf. Durham and his accomplice Henk B. initially aimed to steal Sunflowers and The Potato Eaters but failed due to security and the size of the latter. They ended up taking Seafront at Scheveningen and Congregation leaving the Reformed Church in Nuenen. These paintings were later recovered by Italian authorities and returned to the Netherlands. Durham refused to disclose how much the Italian mafia paid for the paintings. After failed attempts to sell the stolen works in the Netherlands, they were eventually sold to the mafia. Durham had long denied involvement in the Amsterdam museum heist, which led to his 2005 conviction and 3.5-year prison sentence. In January, a court ruled the paintings could be released and returned to the Netherlands.

CBS News revamped "The Early Show" with a complete makeover, replacing co-hosts Harry Smith and Maggie Rodriguez with Chris Wragge and Erica Hill, who will start Jan. 3. Weather forecaster Dave Price is also leaving for Marysol Castro from ABC's "Good Morning America." CBS News President Sean McManus believes the new team will help the show grow, though ratings haven't improved much despite previous changes. Smith, with the longest tenure, will stay at CBS as a news reporter and primary substitute. The new anchors bring a different chemistry, with Hill and Wragge already working well together on Saturday mornings.

It's a big moment for Chicago Cubs fans as their team aims to end an 108-year championship drought. A number of high-profile celebrities have shown support, including Bill Murray, Pearl Jam's Eddie Vedder, and NBA stars Dwayne Wade and Jimmy Butler. Even hockey players from the Blackhawks joined in, singing "Take me out to the ball game" during a game. The Curse of the Billy Goat, a long-standing superstition that the Cubs would never win a World Series, has persisted for decades. However, the Cubs finally broke the curse in 2016, winning the World Series for the first time since 1908. Attempts to reverse the curse through various means, like bringing goats to Wrigley Field, have been made over the years, but the team's historic victory in 2016 marked the end of this legendary sports curse.

Syrian opposition activists report that the Islamic State group has captured several towns near the Turkey border, displacing other rebel forces. The group's expansion continues as it secures more territory in Syria. Meanwhile, France has announced it will supply arms to Kurdish forces fighting Sunni extremists, marking a shift in their policy. The United States has also increased its involvement, deploying troops to Iraq and directly arming Kurdish fighters. The situation in Iraqi Kurdistan is described as "catastrophic," with the Islamic State group threatening the region and targeting minorities.

Aimee Copeland, a 24-year-old Georgia graduate student, has spoken for the first time since being hospitalized with necrotizing fasciitis. Her father, Andy Copeland, announced on Facebook that "Our baby can talk" on what they are calling "Aimee Day." Aimee developed the flesh-eating disease after falling from a homemade zip line and cutting her leg. She has already lost her left leg, other foot, and both hands due to the infection. While she is still in critical condition, she has begun breathing on her own and was able to sit up in a chair on Thursday.

Beneath Yellowstone National Park lies a supervolcano, capable of erupting with catastrophic force. Recent research suggests that the magma reservoir feeding this supervolcano is about 2.5 times larger than previously estimated, and the entire process leading to a supereruption may occur in just decades, much faster than previously thought. This revelation challenges previous assumptions that such eruptions require millennia of preparation. Scientists analyzed crystals from the park’s last supereruption, dating back 631,000 years, and found evidence of a rapid temperature increase and the introduction of barium, hinting at a magma injection event as the trigger. While the risk of an imminent eruption remains low, understanding these processes could aid in developing better warning systems for future events.

Syria's capital, Damascus, is increasingly feeling the impact of the ongoing civil war, reports The New York Times. Once a city of routine and normalcy, it now faces checkpoints, curfews, and a scarcity of basic goods. Traffic jams and kidnappings are common, and the once vibrant nightlife has ceased. The government's grip on the city is tenuous, with rebels slowly encroaching on its outskirts. The city's residents, caught between opposing forces, are grappling with the reality of war. As the conflict drags on, fears of a full-scale siege and the potential for sectarian strife among the Alawite community, which supports the Assad regime, are growing. Meanwhile, the economic toll on Syria's wealthy, who have long supported the regime, is mounting, with businesses damaged and operations disrupted. The regime's reliance on air power and the shabiha militia has exacerbated the situation, leading to increased civilian casualties and further strain on the economy.

Autopsy reports released on the bodies of Christina Anderson and her 8-year-old son Ethan, found in the burning property of James DiMaggio, reveal extensive injuries. Christina, 44, died from blunt-force trauma to the head, with multiple impact sites and signs of binding and tape. Ethan's body, found in the charred house, showed signs of burns and fractures, though the cause of the fractures could not be determined. DiMaggio, who killed the family and kidnapped their daughter Hannah, was shot and killed by FBI agents in Idaho. Hannah was rescued and returned to her family.

Two students were shot at a Philadelphia high school gymnasium, with one in critical condition and the other in stable condition. Police say a 17-year-old boy was shot in the shoulder, and an 18-year-old girl was hit in the bicep. The girl was discharged from the hospital, while the boy remains hospitalized. The shooting occurred when a student pulled out a handgun inside the school's gymnasium, though it is unclear if the weapon was intentionally fired. A 15-year-old student was initially taken into custody but was later released and not charged. Police identified a 16-year-old boy as a suspect but did not believe he was the shooter. A 17-year-old boy turned himself in and was charged with two counts of aggravated assault. The school was placed on lockdown, and students were searched before being released. Police are investigating how the gun was brought into the school.

Before Robert Bales was accused of killing 16 Afghan civilians, he was remembered by neighbors as a family man and "good guy." His wife, Karilyn, wrote on her blog about his disappointment over not getting a promotion and expressed relief that they could move on. Bales faced legal troubles, including a hit-and-run accident and an assault charge. His military record showed commendations for his service but also financial struggles and marital issues. The Army alleges Bales left his base, shot the civilians, and tried to burn their bodies. His lawyer, John Henry Browne, disputes claims of alcohol or marital problems and says Bales is a "very mild-mannered person." The case has strained relations between the U.S. and Afghanistan and raised concerns about the mental health of veterans.

Chris Martin, in his first interview since his "conscious uncoupling" from Gwyneth Paltrow, revealed that his personal issues played a significant role in the end of their 10-year marriage. Speaking to BBC Radio 1's Zane Lowe, Martin stated, "About two years ago I was a mess really because I can't enjoy the things that we are good at and I can't enjoy the great things around me because I'm burdened by this. I've got to not blame anyone else and make some changes." He explained, "I wouldn't use the word breakdown, this was more a realization about trying to grow up. If you can't open yourself up, you can't appreciate the wonder inside. You can be with someone wonderful, but because of your own issues you cannot let that be celebrated in the right way." Martin's new album, Ghost Stories, reflects his journey towards vulnerability and honesty, as he said, "What Ghost Stories means to me

American cities and recycling companies are facing a significant challenge as China, traditionally the largest buyer of their exported recyclables, has stopped accepting certain types of waste, including many plastics. This change, part of China's Operation Green Fence, has left recycling depots in the U.S. with stockpiles of mixed plastics that cannot be sold. The restrictions target low-grade, mixed plastics such as disposable coffee cup lids, PVC pipes, and garden planters. This shift has forced U.S. recyclers to sort their materials more meticulously, with some companies like Far West Fibers now needing to manage multiple bins for different types of plastic. The lack of alternative buyers is causing concern among U.S. cities, which have made commitments to recycle but may struggle to find new markets for the now-unwanted materials.

A South Carolina woman, Lana Clayton, has been charged with murder after allegedly poisoning her husband, Stephen Clayton, with tetrahydrozoline from eye drops over a three-day period. Authorities found a high amount of the chemical in Stephen Clayton's body after his July 21 death. Lana Clayton is also charged with tampering with a drug product or food. She has no prior criminal record. The couple lived in an upscale home valued at $822,000 on Lake Wylie. Stephen Clayton was known for his generosity and mentoring children. The arrest has shocked friends and neighbors.

Josh Vandiver and Henry Velandia, a same-sex couple who married in Connecticut, face the risk of Velandia being deported to Venezuela due to the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act, which defines marriage as between a man and a woman for all federal laws, including immigration regulations. Velandia, who is from Venezuela, applied for a work visa but had his application denied, and his current visa has expired. Vandiver, a Princeton Ph.D. student, cannot sponsor Velandia's application for legal residency. The couple is fighting for the repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act and appealing to members of Congress to cease deportation hearings against foreign-born spouses of U.S. citizens. They have gained over 1,000 supporters through a Facebook group and are hoping for a delay in Velandia's deportation while the U.S. Supreme Court rules on the Defense of Marriage Act. Legal experts suggest their chances are slim.

Rep. Darrell Issa escalated the legal battle over Fast and Furious by directly accusing President Barack Obama of either abusing his power by withholding information or having his aides conspire with Justice Department officials to manage the aftermath of the failed ATF gun-walking program. Issa's letter to Obama, to be released the next day, charged that either the president or his most senior advisors were involved in managing Operation Fast & Furious and its fallout, or that the president was asserting a presidential power unjustified solely for the purpose of obstructing a congressional investigation. Issa's move is unlikely to force action by the president but is sure to build drama before the House votes on whether to hold Attorney General Eric Holder in contempt of Congress for refusing to turn over documents. Democrats are portraying the Republican contempt motion as an assault on minority rights, while Republicans accuse Holder and the Obama administration of stonewalling Congress. Florida International University's Pi Kappa Alpha fraternity chapter has been suspended following the discovery of a private Facebook page containing explicit content and references to hazing, drug sales, and derogatory comments. The page, which reportedly had about 70 posts, was exposed through an anonymous email sent to media outlets and university administrators. The posts included drug offers, hazing boasts, and offensive content targeting women and rival fraternities. FIU is investigating potential violations of its code of student conduct, and the fraternity has been ordered to cease all meetings and events. This suspension comes amid a history of disciplinary actions against the chapter, including alcohol violations and hazing incidents. The case highlights ongoing issues within Greek life, with experts noting the potential influence of fraternities on student recruitment and alumni donations.

Six men, aged 28 to 49, are hospitalized after participating in a Phase I clinical trial of an experimental drug in France. One man is brain dead, while three others could face permanent brain damage, according to the chief neurosurgeon at the Rennes hospital. The drug, manufactured by Portuguese company Bial, was administered orally as part of a trial conducted by the French clinic Biotrial. The trial has been suspended, and all volunteers have been recalled. The health ministry is investigating the incident, and the drug is described as a FAAH inhibitor meant to act on the body’s endocannabinoid system. The trial began in July, and no drug currently on the market is implicated. All clinical trials carry some risk, but incidents like this are rare.

A Chinese baby girl, born at just 23 weeks gestation and weighing 660 grams, has defied medical odds by surviving her first week of life. Doctors in Chongqing, southwest China, performed an emergency operation to correct a problem with the mother's cervix, saving the tiny infant who was initially given little chance of survival. The baby, nicknamed "chopstick girl" due to her height, is currently in intensive care, facing challenges from underdeveloped organs and veins. This "miracle baby" has captured the attention of local media and medical professionals, highlighting the extraordinary resilience of premature infants.

In a groundbreaking study, researchers from the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics have identified a word that appears to be universally understood across diverse languages and cultures: "huh?". This word, used to seek clarification when one does not understand what has been said, shows remarkable consistency in form and function in languages from five continents. The team analyzed "huh?" in 10 languages, including Dutch, Icelandic, Mandarin Chinese, Siwu, and Murrinh-Patha, and found that it is nearly identical in each, often consisting of a low-front central vowel with a questioning intonation. This uniformity suggests that "huh?" may have developed independently in different languages due to similar communicative needs, rather than being an innate biological trait. The researchers propose that the word's minimal effort and questioning prosody make it an efficient tool for initiating repair in conversations, adapting to local linguistic systems while maintaining a core form.
