When a wedding was canceled 40 days before the ceremony, the Fowlers of Atlanta decided to donate the reception to the homeless instead of canceling everything. They contacted Hosea Feed the Hungry, a local nonprofit, and arranged for 200 homeless women, children, and families to attend the event at the Villa Christina restaurant. The celebration included outdoor appetizers, face painting, juggling, and a room for children. Adults enjoyed a meal of salmon and chicken, while children had chicken fingers, French fries, and fresh fruit. The Fowlers were deeply moved by the positive impact of the event, and they hope to make it an annual tradition.

Mitt Romney, the 2012 Republican presidential nominee and current U.S. Senate candidate in Utah, predicts that President Donald Trump will win re-election in 2020 and secure the Republican nomination easily. Romney, who previously criticized Trump harshly during the 2016 campaign, now believes Trump's political fortunes are bolstered by an improving economy and the likelihood of Democrats nominating an outside-the-mainstream candidate. Romney, who faces a June 26 runoff for the GOP nomination against Mike Kennedy, a conservative state representative, has softened his stance on Trump and praised some of his early actions as president. The remarks were made during Romney's annual gathering of top Republicans and wealthy political donors in Deer Valley, Utah.

A 23-year-old hotel worker named Jason Garnett experienced a 17-hour erection that left him in pain and embarrassment. Waking up with an erection on a Friday morning, Garnett initially dismissed it but by lunchtime realized something was amiss. After unsuccessful attempts to relieve the condition with an ice bath and jogging, he sought help from a roommate, who alerted hospital staff. Diagnosed with priapism, doctors drained two pints of blood from his penis and administered 24 injections to reduce blood flow. The ordeal was excruciating, with Garnett describing the pain as "10 out of 10." Despite the discomfort, his condition is now resolved, though his penis appears "war-torn," with visible bruising.

Schlitterbahn Waterparks and Resorts announced that the Verrückt waterslide, which was closed since a tragic accident that killed 10-year-old Caleb Schwab, will be permanently removed once the investigation is concluded and court permission is granted. The company, which has been heartbroken over the tragedy, stated that the slide's removal is the only proper course of action. Verrückt, billed as the world's tallest waterslide, has been closed since the incident on August 7, 2016, when Caleb died and two women suffered facial injuries. The company remains committed to the safety of its staff and guests and is cooperating with investigative teams and the families involved.

The body of 36-year-old Marie Joseph was found floating in a state-run pool in Fall River on Tuesday night, prompting the temporary closure of all 30 state-operated deep-water pools for safety reviews. Joseph's body was discovered after teenagers entered the pool area at 10 p.m. on Tuesday and reported a body. She had not been reported missing and was last seen swimming with friends on Sunday. A 9-year-old boy who was at the pool with Joseph on Sunday recounted that she had an accident on a water slide and did not resurface. The cause of death is under investigation, and an autopsy is pending. The Fall River Police Chief stated that the sequence of events after Joseph went underwater is unclear. The state Department of Conservation and Recreation has placed the pool staff on administrative leave and expressed condolences to Joseph's family.

Federal authorities arrested 24 suspected hackers in a two-year undercover operation targeting online financial fraud involving stolen credit card and bank information. The operation, known as Operation Card Shop, involved participants from 13 countries and prevented potential losses of over $205 million on more than 411,000 compromised consumer credit and debit cards. The FBI created a fake carding forum called "Carder Profit" to lure hackers, which was shut down in May. Among those arrested were Mir Islam, known as "JoshTheGod," who was charged with trafficking 50,000 stolen credit card numbers, and Joshua Hicks, known as "OxideDox." The operation highlights the international nature of cybercrime and the efforts to combat it.

Nebraska executed Carey Dean Moore on Tuesday at the State Penitentiary. The execution timeline shows Moore arriving in the execution chamber at 10:24 a.m., with four media witnesses present. Four drugs were administered: diazepam, fentanyl, cisatracurium besylate, and potassium chloride. Moore appeared to speak to his witnesses, showed signs of breathing difficulties, and eventually went still. He was pronounced dead at 10:47 a.m. by the coroner.

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor (R-Va.) announced he will step down from his leadership post at the end of July after losing his primary to tea party challenger Dave Brat. Cantor, who had been considered a potential successor to Speaker John Boehner, endorsed Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) to take over as majority leader. McCarthy, currently the majority whip, is expected to face competition from Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas), chairman of the powerful House Rules Committee. Sessions, who began rallying support immediately, argues he can unite the conference. Rep. Jeb Hensarling (R-Texas), chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, is also considering a bid. The race for whip, which would open if McCarthy wins majority leader, is also heating up, with Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.) challenging Rep. Peter Roskam (R-Ill.). Rep. Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) and others have ruled themselves out of contention. The leadership transition

President Donald Trump has nominated Robert Wilkie, the current acting Veterans Affairs secretary, to become the department’s permanent leader, following the withdrawal of the nomination of Ronny Jackson due to workplace conduct issues. Wilkie, who has been leading the VA in an acting capacity since March and was previously confirmed by the Senate for a Pentagon post, will face a smoother path to confirmation compared to Jackson. Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs Chairman Johnny Isakson and House panel chairman Phil Roe both expressed support for Wilkie’s nomination. Wilkie’s appointment comes amid ongoing challenges at the VA, including high-profile departures and ethics scandals. His nomination could potentially face scrutiny due to his involvement in the 2016 Republican platform debate, which is under investigation by special counsel Robert Mueller.

Senators and lawmakers are calling for more women in the Secret Service to prevent incidents like the recent prostitution scandal in Colombia. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Rep. Carolyn Maloney (D-N.Y.) both suggested that a more diverse Secret Service could have avoided the situation. Collins noted the agency's low female representation at 11%, while Maloney emphasized the need for diversity, including more women and minorities. Additionally, Marco Rubio stated he will respect Mitt Romney's vice-presidential process, indicating a shift from his previous stance. He expressed support for Jeb Bush for the position. Meanwhile, Sen. Joe Lieberman announced he will stay out of the 2012 presidential race, enjoying the break from campaigning. President Obama is reportedly "apoplectic" over wasteful spending at the GSA, with one of his top advisers saying the administration acted quickly to address the issue. Finally, Sen. Tom Coburn praised the Secret Service's director, Mark Sullivan, and

Hillary Clinton’s campaign clarified that her team read every email before deciding to delete or turn over those deemed work-related or personal. This comes after Clinton admitted that over 30,000 emails were deleted as personal, while nearly 32,000 work-related emails were handed over to the State Department. Clinton’s spokesman stated that the previous fact sheet did not adequately convey that every email was read. House Speaker John Boehner is expected to launch a new investigation into Clinton’s email practices as Secretary of State, including her admission of deleting thousands of emails. Critics question who gets to decide what is personal and what is public, and whether Clinton’s lawyers made the correct determinations. Clinton’s team detailed a multi-step process for sorting emails, but did not specify how many were read. The State Department acknowledged that automatic archiving of emails for senior officials began only recently, raising questions about the preservation of important emails.

A suicide bomber killed the deputy governor of Kandahar province and wounded three of his bodyguards in a targeted attack in Kandahar, south of Kabul. The Taliban claimed responsibility, marking a resurgence of high-profile assassinations of public servants that had subsided in recent months. The attack raised concerns about the security of government officials and the stability of Kandahar, a key Taliban stronghold. Afghan President Hamid Karzai and U.S. Ambassador Karl Eikenberry condemned the assassination. The incident occurred as NATO and Afghan forces aim to improve governance and public services in Kandahar, but such killings undermine these efforts.

According to an analysis by the University of Toulouse's Young-Ho Eom, Frank Sinatra is the most important person in the English-language Wikipedia, followed by Michael Jackson and Pope Pius XII. This surprising result comes from a study that used methods similar to Google's PageRank algorithm to determine the importance of individuals based on the number of Wikipedia pages linking to them. The study, considering all 24 major language editions of Wikipedia, found that Adolf Hitler was the most important figure overall, with Michael Jackson in second place and Madonna in third. The research aimed to uncover biases in the attention given to historical figures, noting that most important figures are born in Western countries after the 17th century and are male. However, each Wikipedia edition highlights local figures, emphasizing the importance of local contributions.

Congressional reactions to President Trump's Syria strikes were mixed, with some lawmakers supporting the action while others raised constitutional concerns. House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin offered backing, but both called for further action to be approved by Congress. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer supported the strikes but urged a strategy and engagement with Congress. Libertarian-minded Republicans like Sens. Mike Lee and Rand Paul criticized the decision to launch strikes without congressional authorization. Meanwhile, Republican defense hawks, including Sens. John McCain and Lindsey Graham, praised Trump's action. The article also mentions criticism of MSNBC anchor Brian Williams for his comments during live coverage of the strikes, which some found insensitive given the context.

University of Virginia President Teresa Sullivan suspended all campus fraternities and sororities following a Rolling Stone article detailing an alleged 2012 gang rape at a Phi Kappa Psi fraternity party. The article, which also criticized the university's response to sexual assault allegations, sparked outrage and calls for action from students, faculty, and alumni. In response, Sullivan announced a seven-week suspension of Greek-letter organizations and called for a review of the university’s sexual misconduct policy. She urged community members to come forward with information to the police and emphasized the need for institutional and cultural change. The suspension of fraternity and sorority activities will continue until January 9th, with the university planning to convene groups of students, faculty, and alumni to discuss further steps.

Baby names with personal meaning, such as family names and inspiring role models, dominate the 2013 list from BabyCenter, with Jackson and Sophia maintaining top spots for boys and girls, respectively. Names from "Duck Dynasty," "Homeland," and reality TV shows like "Girls" also see significant increases. Celebrities like Kanye and George (for girls) boost their names' popularity, while those of criticized figures decline. The full list includes Jackson, Aiden, Liam, Noah for boys and Sophia, Emma, Olivia, Isabella for girls.

School systems in New York and Los Angeles both received bomb threats today, but only Los Angeles took the threat seriously, closing 640,000 students for the day. The threats, sent via email and similar in content, were deemed hoaxes by authorities. New York officials dismissed the threat as "outlandish," while Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti defended the decision to close schools, stating the precaution was necessary given recent events. The threats included details that suggested they were not credible, such as the use of inappropriate email addresses and misspellings. Despite the closure, Los Angeles schools will reopen on Wednesday after thorough searches.

A Tennessee lawmaker is upset after discovering an email from the Tennessee Virtual Academy suggesting teachers delete failing grades from students' records. The email, sent by the school's vice principal to middle school teachers, instructs them to remove grades from the computer system to improve the school's appearance. Lawmakers are concerned this practice may be hiding poor student performance. The Tennessee Virtual Academy, a for-profit online public school, is among the worst in the state according to standardized test results. The school's principal says the goal is to more accurately reflect students' current progress, but critics argue this is grade fixing. The school has faced scrutiny over its performance and enrollment, with a bill proposed to cap its student numbers.

Houston Texans defensive end J.J. Watt is out for the season after suffering a tibial plateau fracture in a game against the Kansas City Chiefs. Head coach Bill O'Brien confirmed the injury and stated that Watt will not return, while also noting that outside linebacker Whitney Mercilus will miss the remainder of the season due to a torn pectoral muscle. Watt, a three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year, is a key player for the Texans and his absence will significantly impact the team's defense.

Detectives investigating the attempted murders of Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia believe the pair were poisoned with a nerve agent at the front door of his Salisbury home. The highest concentration of the nerve agent was found on the front door, according to police. Counter-terrorism detectives will continue to focus their inquiries on the home address for weeks or months. More than 130 people could have been exposed to the nerve agent, and the UK government suspects the Russian state was behind the attack. In response, over 150 Russian officials have been expelled from multiple countries, and the UK is considering further measures, including a ban on the City of London from selling Russian sovereign debt. Public health experts are working to determine if the attack poses a long-term risk to Salisbury residents, who will receive a £1m support package.

Millennial workers, ages 18 to 35, are just as likely to stick with their employers as their older counterparts in Generation X were when they were young adults, according to recently released government data. College-educated Millennials have longer track records with their employers than their Gen X counterparts did in 2000. One factor contributing to this trend is the relatively high levels of education among Millennials, which is typically associated with longer tenure. However, the longer tenure of college-educated Millennials does not necessarily translate into higher wages or more job security. These findings challenge the "job-hopping Millennial" characterization. The trend is different among less-educated young adults, who have similar job tenure to their Gen X counterparts. This suggests that the "job-hopping" narrative may not apply to the broader Millennial workforce.

A young woman who broadcast the beating and racial taunting of a man on Facebook Live has been arrested with three others in connection with the attack in Chicago. The 30-minute video shows a man tied up and verbally and physically abused by his attackers, who shouted racial slurs and made political statements. The victim, an 18-year-old with special needs, was found wandering a Chicago street and was so traumatized that it took most of the night for him to calm down and talk to police. The suspects, two men and two women, are in custody awaiting formal charges, which are expected to be filed the next day. Hate crime charges are under consideration due to the racial and political nature of the attack. The incident has drawn intense scrutiny, coming as Chicago faces a grim milestone of 762 homicides in 2016.

New fathers, particularly those around age 25, tend to gain weight after their first child is born, according to a study of over 10,000 men. Men who lived with their children gained an average of about 4.4 pounds, while those who did not live with their children gained about 3.3 pounds. This is an increase of 2.6 percent for resident dads and 2 percent for non-resident dads. By contrast, men who remained non-fathers lost an average of 1.4 pounds over the same period. The study, published in the American Journal of Men's Health, suggests that fatherhood can affect men's health, beyond the known effects of marriage. New fathers may face challenges in maintaining their health due to changes in lifestyle and eating habits. Pediatricians can play a crucial role in counseling new fathers about their health.

The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration report on the IRS's handling of 501(c)(4) applications reveals the agency used inappropriate criteria based on names and policy positions, leading to delays and unnecessary requests for donor information. While the report stops short of accusing the IRS of bias, it highlights ineffective management and a politically biased test that was used and then quietly recreated. Despite these issues, the report finds no evidence of intentional wrongdoing and recommends improvements to the application process. The IRS has agreed to implement seven of the nine recommendations, showing a commitment to addressing the problems, though some disagreements remain.

A 15-year study of emergency room visits found that self-inflicted injuries, including attempted suicides and drug overdoses, have significantly increased among U.S. girls. The sharpest rise was seen in girls aged 10 to 14, nearly tripling from 2009 to 2015. Rates among older teen girls were the highest, at 633 visits per 100,000 in 2015. Boys' rates remained relatively stable. Drug overdoses and intentional cutting with sharp objects were the most common methods. The study, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, suggests a need for increased prevention efforts, including helping at-risk youth feel less isolated and teaching coping skills.

Peaceful protesters in Madison, Wisconsin, rallied on the streets following the fatal shooting of an unarmed black 19-year-old by a white police officer, with chants of "Black Lives Matter." The city's police chief, Mike Koval, acknowledged the community's anger and assured demonstrators of his department's commitment to protecting their rights, urging restraint. The shooting occurred when Officer Matt Kenny, a 12-year veteran, entered an apartment after responding to a disturbance call. Koval stated Kenny was injured, but the details were not clear. Tony Robinson, the 19-year-old victim, had a prior conviction for armed robbery but Koval declined to discuss his background. The shooting took place days after the U.S. Justice Department declined to charge Darren Wilson, the officer who shot Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri. The Madison Police Department placed Kenny on administrative leave pending an investigation by the state's Division of Criminal Investigation. Mayor Paul Soglin promised transparency in the investigation's results. Over

Donald Trump, speaking at a campaign rally in Tennessee, defended Second Amendment rights and suggested that arming teachers could have prevented the Oregon community college shooting. His comments came three days after nine people were killed in the Oregon shooting. Trump, who has a concealed carry permit in New York, said he would respond with force if attacked, comparing himself to the action hero Charles Bronson in the film "Death Wish." He criticized "gun-free zones" and argued that mental health issues, not gun laws, are the root cause of mass shootings. Trump's positions on gun control have evolved, and he now aligns with the National Rifle Association. He also discussed his tax plan, emphasizing his ability to cut costs and arguing that major tax cuts would benefit the economy.

Anthony Weiner, the former U.S. Representative who faced multiple sexting scandals, is set to plead guilty in federal court on May 19, 2017, for sending obscene material to a minor. Weiner, who resigned from Congress in 2011 after a lewd photo of his crotch was leaked, will face a sentence of 21 to 27 months in prison. His plea stems from online communications with a 15-year-old girl in 2015. Weiner acknowledged engaging in sexually explicit conversations and sharing explicit images, stating, "I have a sickness, but I do not have an excuse." His wife, Huma Abedin, a top aide to Hillary Clinton, separated from him in 2016 after new sexting allegations emerged. The case gained renewed attention when FBI agents seized Weiner’s laptop, leading to the discovery of emails between Clinton and Abedin, which contributed to Clinton’s loss in the 20

Arizona State University permanently revoked the recognition of the Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity after it hosted a Martin Luther King Jr. holiday party with racially insensitive themes, including posing in basketball jerseys and flashing gang signs. The university stated the party violated its student code of conduct, specifically for engaging in discriminatory activities, violating alcohol rules, and off-campus conduct that may present a risk. This is the second time ASU has expelled a fraternity chapter in less than a year, following incidents involving Sigma Alpha Epsilon. The local chapter is no longer affiliated with the university, cannot recruit members or hold meetings on campus, and will face further student discipline investigations.

Satellite images and testimonies from defectors reveal that North Korea's political prisoner camps, which have imprisoned entire families for generations, continue to grow despite international attention. These camps, where conditions are akin to slavery, have seen a significant increase in size since 2001, according to Amnesty International. The camps house an estimated 200,000 people, many of whom were imprisoned due to "guilt by association." Former prisoners describe inhumane treatment, starvation, and mass executions. The camps are so secretive that even with modern technology, information about them is scarce, making it difficult to address the ongoing human rights abuses. The harsh reality of the North Korean regime, which imprisons families for generations and allows thousands to die of starvation, challenges the public's imagination and response.

A 23-year-old immigrant who had received protection under the Obama-era Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Seattle, potentially marking the first such detention under the Trump administration. Daniel Ramirez Medina, with no criminal record, was taken into custody along with his father, though the reason for his father's arrest remains unclear. Ramirez had been granted temporary permission to live and work legally in the U.S. under DACA, which shields young immigrants brought to the country illegally as children. His detention has sparked concerns among immigrant rights groups, who fear a broader crackdown on DACA recipients. Lawyers for Ramirez argue that his constitutional rights were violated and have filed a lawsuit seeking his release. The case highlights the uncertainty surrounding the future of DACA recipients under the Trump administration.

In Oregon, lawmakers are considering a new tax on coffee beans and ground coffee, aiming to raise funds for alternative education programs and support for primary schools, reports KOIN 6 News. The bill, if passed, would impose a five-cent tax per pound on wholesale coffee and direct half the revenue to the Oregon Military Department for the Oregon National Guard Youth Challenge Program, while the other half would fund grants for alternative high school and primary school reading programs. However, the proposal faces opposition from House Republicans, who argue it's a new tax increase that Oregonians won't support. The bill's fate remains uncertain in the face of a $1.8 billion budget gap.

Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz remains optimistic despite China's slowing economy, planning to open more than one new store daily for the next five years in the world's second-largest economy. By 2021, the company aims to have nearly 5,000 stores across China, marking a significant investment in the market. Schultz recalls the early challenges of educating Chinese customers about coffee rituals and acknowledges initial skepticism from Wall Street. However, he attributes the company's success to early investments and a focus on operating stores with Starbucks personnel. Schultz believes China will eventually surpass the U.S. as Starbucks' largest market, highlighting the brand's continued growth and relevance in the country.

Once again, Barron Trump has faced criticism for his casual attire during a public appearance, sparking a debate about the expectations for the president's son. Conservative news outlet the Daily Caller criticized Barron for wearing a T-shirt and shorts while boarding Air Force One, suggesting he should "dress like he's in the White House." In response, numerous political figures and celebrities, including former first daughter Chelsea Clinton, defended Barron, urging the media to respect his privacy. The White House also asked for media restraint, stating Barron is a minor and deserves a private childhood. Chelsea Clinton's tweets emphasized the importance of supporting all children, while Barron's mother, Melania Trump, thanked Clinton for her support. The controversy highlights the ongoing tension between public scrutiny and the desire to protect the president's children.

NASCAR has asked its fans to refrain from displaying the Confederate flag at its races, issuing a statement signed by tracks hosting the Sprint Cup, Xfinity, and Camping World Truck series. The Daytona International Speedway will offer a flag exchange for the upcoming Coke Zero 400. NASCAR Chairman Brian France expressed a desire to eliminate the Confederate flag from its events. The statement aims to create a fan-friendly, welcoming atmosphere free of offensive symbols. Fans are encouraged to wave the American flag instead, especially for the nation's birthday. Tracks will not sell officially licensed merchandise with the Confederate flag symbol and support removing the flag from the South Carolina Capitol grounds.

Three children in Salinas, California, were found severely abused and malnourished in their home, prompting authorities to intervene and place them in protective custody. The 8-year-old girl was reportedly chained to the floor to prevent her from obtaining food, while the two younger boys, aged 3 and 5, were also found in poor health. Their mothers, Eraca Dawn Craig, 31, and Christian Jessica Deanda, 44, were arrested on multiple child abuse charges after a welfare check revealed the children's dire conditions. The home was described as cluttered and dirty, with little food available. The girls were legally adopted, while the younger boy is the biological son of one of the women. Both mothers are former correctional officers and businesswomen, with online profiles detailing their professional and personal lives. The case is particularly heinous, with the 8-year-old girl described as looking like a "concentration camp" victim.

A Federal Court judge, Robin Camp, has resigned following a recommendation from the Canadian Judicial Council to remove him from the bench due to his conduct in a 2014 sexual assault trial. Camp faced criticism for comments he made during the trial, including asking the complainant why she couldn't keep her knees together and expressing views on the law of consent. The council's report stated that Camp's conduct was so destructive of judicial impartiality and integrity that public confidence was sufficiently undermined. Despite undergoing counseling and further training, the council recommended his removal, and he resigned to avoid the formal process. Camp's case highlights the need for better training of judges in handling sexual assault cases, as similar issues continue to arise in other jurisdictions.

Three new films, each adapted from a novel by a popular author, explore the complexities of marriage and the media's role in scrutinizing it. "Gone Girl," directed by David Fincher, delves into the mystery surrounding Nick (Ben Affleck) and Amy Dunne (Rosamund Pike), whose marriage unravels under the spotlight of media speculation. The film, praised for its suspenseful storytelling and razor-sharp wit, keeps audiences guessing until its final moments. Despite its strengths, "Gone Girl" falters near the end, losing its coherence and emotional impact. Fincher's direction and the performances of Affleck and Pike, along with a supporting cast that includes Tyler Perry and Carrie Coon, elevate the narrative. However, the film's reliance on a well-known source material limits its potential for innovation.

Scientists in East Africa plan to use trained African giant pouched rats to screen for tuberculosis among prison inmates in Tanzania and Mozambique. These rats, already trained to detect landmines, can identify TB in sputum samples with near-perfect accuracy. The rats can screen 100 samples in 20 minutes, compared to a lab technician's four-day process. With funding from USAID, APOPO aims to expand the rat screening program to prisons, shantytowns, and other high-risk areas, potentially saving lives and reducing costs. TB rates are 10 times higher in prisons than the general population, highlighting the need for efficient screening methods.

All 54 people on board a Trigana Air Service plane were killed when it crashed into a mountain in Indonesia's Papua province, the latest in a series of aviation disasters in the country, officials reported. The plane, which was flying from Jayapura to Oksibil, lost contact with air traffic control about half an hour into its scheduled 42-minute flight. Rescuers reached the crash site on Tuesday after being hindered by rugged, forested terrain and bad weather. The plane's black boxes were found intact, providing crucial data for the investigation. The victims, including four postal workers carrying government aid, were mostly Indonesian nationals. The airline, known for its safety issues, has had 14 serious incidents since its inception in 1991. The crash site, located at an altitude of about 8,500 feet, highlights the challenges of search and rescue operations in the remote and mountainous region.

Enthusiasm at the Democratic National Convention on Tuesday night was notably higher than at the previous Republican convention, according to various media outlets. Journalists noted a more energetic atmosphere in the hall, with CNN's David Gergen stating it was more palpable than at the Republican convention. Michelle Obama's speech about her husband and the Obama family drove a significant number of tweets, with her line "Being president doesn't change who you are. It reveals who you are." sparking widespread discussion. The convention as a whole sparked over 3 million tweets by the end of its first night, nearly matching the 4 million mark set by the Republican convention.

The Angry Birds Movie soared to the top of the box office with a $39 million opening, according to comScore estimates, as family audiences flocked to see the animated adaptation of the popular app game. The film, budgeted at $73 million, nabbed the third-best animated debut of the year, behind Zootopia and Kung Fu Panda 3. Captain America: Civil War, starring Chris Evans and Robert Downey Jr., dropped to second place with $33.1 million, bringing its domestic total to $347.4 million and just over $1 billion worldwide. Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising debuted in third place with $21.8 million, while The Nice Guys, starring Ryan Gosling and Russell Crowe, claimed fourth place with $11.3 million. Disney's live-action The Jungle Book rounded out the top five with $11 million, having swung to a wild $327.5 million since

The latest iPad, unveiled by Apple, offers significant improvements over its predecessor, including a stunning display, faster speed, and 4G LTE capabilities. The new iPad boasts a retina display with four times the number of pixels compared to the previous model, making text and images appear much sharper and more vibrant. Apple has also enhanced the rear camera, allowing for high-definition video recording and improved photo quality. Additionally, the device supports 4G LTE, providing faster internet speeds comparable to home broadband. Despite these upgrades, the new iPad maintains the same battery life as its predecessor, ensuring users can enjoy long hours of use without recharging. While the iPad 2 remains available at a lower price point, the new model is a compelling choice for those seeking the best tablet experience, offering a combination of stunning visuals, speed, and connectivity.

An Indian public official, A.K. Verma, was dismissed from his Central Public Works Department (CPWD) job after taking earned leave in December 1990 and failing to return. Verma, who joined CPWD as an assistant executive engineer in 1980, defied orders to report to work and continued extending his leave without authorization. An inquiry in 1992 found him guilty of "wilful absence from duty," but no further action was taken until 2017, when Urban Development Minister M.Venkaiah Naidu intervened. Verma's dismissal aims to streamline CPWD operations and ensure accountability. India's notoriously work-shy bureaucracy has faced criticism for absenteeism, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi implementing measures like real-time attendance tracking to improve attendance.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stated in a New Year's speech that a nuclear launch button is always on his desk and the entire U.S. is within range of North Korean nuclear weapons, emphasizing that these are realities, not threats. However, he also offered a potential olive branch to South Korea, suggesting openness to dialogue and considering sending a delegation to the upcoming Winter Olympics in South Korea. Kim emphasized the focus on mass-producing nuclear warheads and missiles for operational deployment, but vowed not to use nuclear weapons unless sovereignty or interests are threatened. Kim's speech marked a shift in tone towards South Korea, potentially aiming to improve ties and create a rift between South Korea and the U.S. President Trump responded cautiously, indicating that the U.S. will see how North Korea's actions unfold.

Environmental activists often criticize bottled water for its perceived wastefulness, but a new study commissioned by the International Bottled Water Association (IBWA) reveals that producing one liter of bottled water in North America requires only 1.39 liters of water, less than the global average for soda (2.02 liters) and significantly less than beer (4 liters) and hard alcohol (34.55 liters). This finding, according to the IBWA, demonstrates that bottled water is more efficient in water use compared to other packaged beverages. However, water activists argue that the study overlooks the broader water footprint, which includes the water used for packaging. The Water Footprint Network's Ertug Ercin points out that packaging can use up to six or seven times the water contained in the bottle, considering the water used for drilling for oil to make plastic and for paper. While the IBWA acknowledges the difficulty in fully accounting for all water usage, it emphasizes the industry's commitment

Madonna's MDNA tour faces new controversy in Poland, where a Catholic youth group is calling for the pop star's August 1 performance to be canceled. The group, known as the Youth Crusade, argues that Madonna's provocative stage shows, which have included flashing and burning crosses, are disrespectful to the city's World War Two remembrance day. The group has launched an online petition to rally support for their cause. Despite the controversy, Madonna's tour continues, with performances in London and other European cities drawing mixed reactions from fans.

The US has begun deploying the first parts of a controversial missile defense system in South Korea, with the Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system designed to protect against threats from North Korea. This move comes a day after North Korea launched four ballistic missiles, breaking international sanctions. However, the deployment has angered many on the Korean peninsula and around the region, including China. South Korean media suggest operations to install a THaad battery have begun, with some parts flown from the US to an air base near Seoul. Chinese foreign spokesman Geng Shuang stated that China opposes the deployment and would "resolutely take necessary measures to defend our own security interests." The THaad system is designed to shoot down short and medium-range ballistic missiles in the terminal phase of their flight, using hit-to-kill technology. Its deployment is controversial, with domestic opposition in South Korea and concerns internationally, particularly from China, who worry about the system's powerful X-band radars. Drinking alcohol before a woman's first pregnancy may increase her risk of breast cancer and benign breast disease, according to a new study. The risk increased by 11 percent for every 10 grams of alcohol consumed daily, equivalent to about six drinks per week, compared to nondrinkers. The study, published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, analyzed data from over 91,000 women who participated in the Nurses' Health Study II. Women who consumed about one drink daily also had a 16 percent higher risk of proliferative benign breast disease, a risk factor for breast cancer. The link between alcohol consumption and breast cancer risk was consistent regardless of whether women drank after their first pregnancy. The researchers suggest that breast tissue is particularly susceptible to environmental exposures between the onset of menstruation and first pregnancy due to rapid cellular proliferation. They recommend reducing alcohol intake, especially before first pregnancy, to lower breast cancer risk.

During a rally in North Dakota, President Trump emphasized the importance of maintaining Republican control of the Senate, particularly in light of Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy's retirement. Trump stated that Kennedy's departure makes Senate control "one of the vital issues of our time," and he highlighted the potential impact on future Supreme Court nominations. He criticized Democratic Senator Heidi Heitkamp, who voted to confirm Trump's first Supreme Court nominee, Neil Gorsuch, and predicted that she would oppose any new conservative nominee. Trump also mentioned that he would seek a nominee with "intellect" who could serve for decades. The retirement of Kennedy has increased pressure on red-state Democrats in upcoming midterm elections, as their votes could determine the ideological balance of the Supreme Court.

The Democratic National Committee contacted the FBI after detecting what it believed was a sophisticated attempt to hack into its voter database, but later determined it was an unauthorized "simulated phishing test," according to a Democratic source. The fraudulent login page was designed to mimic the access page for the Votebuilder database, potentially tricking users into handing over their login details. The DNC, along with a cloud service provider and a security research firm, believe they thwarted a potential attack. The incident highlights ongoing threats to election security as the midterms approach, with political groups and government organizations remaining vigilant against potential hacks and foreign interference.

A tourist ferry capsized on a reservoir near Medellin, Colombia, on Sunday, leaving nine dead and 28 missing. The four-story El Almirante ferry, reportedly packed with about 170 passengers for the holiday weekend, sank rapidly. Rescuers, including firefighters and air force pilots, searched for survivors. Survivors described people crawling down from the fourth-floor roof as the boat began to sink. Preliminary reports indicated 99 people were rescued, and 40 found their way to shore. It's unclear what caused the boat to sink, but it appeared to be overloaded, and no one was wearing life vests. The reservoir is a popular weekend destination, especially busy during holiday weekends.

The Occupy Oakland movement, which gained momentum after an Iraq War veteran was injured in a clash with police, descended into chaos as protesters broke into a vacant building, shattered windows, and set fires. Police responded with tear gas and flash-bang grenades, making dozens of arrests. While most of the day's protest was peaceful, late-night events saw masked vandals throw rocks, metal pipes, and Molotov cocktails. The clashes hospitalized three protesters and left several officers with minor injuries. Protesters and police clashed near the Occupy Oakland encampment, with some protesters arguing the police escalated the situation. The night's actions highlighted the growing tension between the movement and law enforcement, as well as the challenges in maintaining a peaceful protest.

An Illinois man, Angel Gonzalez, was released after spending 20 years in prison for a rape and abduction conviction that was later thrown out due to DNA evidence. Gonzalez, 41, was also cleared of a separate property damage charge that had kept him incarcerated. He was freed on Tuesday night after prosecutors in Lake County, Illinois, asked a judge to vacate his conviction. Gonzalez's exoneration came after DNA tests revealed that the evidence matched two unidentified men, not Gonzalez. The Innocence Project, which has been working on his case, praised the prosecutor for his prompt action. Gonzalez, who is a Mexican national, had his immigration status cleared, allowing him to remain in the country. Upon release, Gonzalez expressed gratitude to his supporters and family, and looked forward to resuming his hobbies, including painting.

Russian military intelligence officer Anatoliy Chepiga, identified by Bellingcat as one of the suspects in the Salisbury nerve agent attack, has a decorated history and was awarded the Hero of the Russian Federation. Chepiga, who used the cover identity Ruslan Boshirov, served in the 14th Spetsnaz Brigade in Khabarovsk and was involved in multiple operations, including in Chechnya. He was relocated to Moscow and given a false identity, suggesting he was assigned a high-level, clandestine mission. The UK government has long accused Chepiga and his partner, Alexander Petrov, of being GRU agents involved in the attack. Chepiga's partner, Petrov, claimed they were tourists visiting Salisbury, but Bellingcat's investigation provides strong evidence linking Chepiga to the operation. The revelation challenges both the suspects' and Russian officials' claims, highlighting the complexity of the case and the ongoing tensions between the UK and Russia.

The Fourth Kind, starring Milla Jovovich, claims to be a re-enactment of real events in Alaska involving alien abductions. Directed by Olatunde Osunsanmi, the film mixes found footage with dramatizations, featuring Jovovich as a hypnotherapist who investigates patients' mysterious experiences. The movie, set in a town in Bulgaria, aims to create suspense through split screens and levitating patients, but relies heavily on familiar horror tropes. Jovovich delivers a strong performance, but the film's hybrid approach fails to fully immerse the viewer. Despite some scares, the concept and execution earn a C grade.

Alabama State Senator Shadrack McGill's wife, Heather, has posted a fiery warning on her husband's official Facebook page, addressing women who have allegedly been sending him private photos and soliciting his attention. She claims multiple women, some of whom she suspects are not real, have been contacting her husband while children are present. Heather McGill, describing herself as "blessed to be the wife of a God fearing, hard working, ministry minded, loving father and husband," threatens to publicly expose these women if they continue. Her post has garnered over 300 likes and numerous supportive comments. Senator McGill, while not directly addressing the issue, thanked his wife for her support and expressed pride in her actions. He also mentioned past incidents, including unsolicited visits from strippers during his last campaign and subsequent Facebook account hijackings.

Ohio State quarterback Terrelle Pryor and four other Buckeyes—running back Dan Herron, wide receiver DeVier Posey, offensive lineman Mike Adams, and defensive end Solomon Thomas—will be suspended from the first five games of the 2011 season for NCAA violations, including selling championship rings, jerseys, and awards, and receiving improper benefits from a tattoo parlor. All six players will be eligible to play in the Sugar Bowl against Arkansas. The violations came to light during a federal probe into the affairs of a local tattoo parlor owner. Ohio State coach Jim Tressel and athletic director Gene Smith expressed regret and plan to appeal the suspensions.

Three months after an Ohio woman kicked out part of a door to end nearly a decade of captivity, a former school bus driver who kidnapped three women and subjected them to years of sexual and physical abuse was sentenced to life in prison plus 1,000 years. Ariel Castro, 53, pleaded guilty to 937 counts, including murder and kidnapping. During the sentencing, law enforcement agents testified to the horrific conditions in Castro’s home, where he chained his victims in the basement, fed them only one meal a day, and provided plastic toilets that were infrequently emptied. Castro used his children to lure the women into his home, exploiting their trust. The women were raped repeatedly and suffered multiple forced miscarriages. In his plea deal, Castro admitted to his crimes but insisted he was not a violent sexual predator. Despite his attempts to show remorse, the judge emphasized that Castro would never be released.

Osama bin Laden's youngest wife, Amal Ahmad Abdul Fateh, provided detailed testimony to Pakistani investigators about the nine years she spent with the al-Qaeda leader in Pakistan. Her account, contained in a police report, reveals that bin Laden moved among five safe houses and fathered four children, at least two of whom were born in a government hospital. The report, while containing some paraphrased details, highlights the challenges faced by Western intelligence in tracking bin Laden's movements. The three widows and two children of bin Laden are currently under house arrest in Islamabad, with the possibility of facing charges related to breaking Pakistani immigration laws. The report suggests that bin Laden and his family evaded detection by frequently changing locations and using local Pashtun hosts. The youngest wife's cooperation with investigators may provide valuable insights into bin Laden's movements and the support network that allowed him to remain undetected for so long.

The average American woman now weighs as much as the average American man weighed in the 1960s, according to CDC data. Both U.S. men and women have gained significant weight since 1960, with men adding nearly 30 pounds and women gaining about 18.5 percent in weight. The average American man now weighs 195.5 pounds, while the average woman weighs 166.2 pounds. Both sexes have also gained about an inch in height over the same period.

The weight gain is attributed to three main factors: eating less healthy food, consuming more food, and engaging in less physical activity. The average American is 33 pounds heavier than the average Frenchman and 70 pounds heavier than the average Bangladeshi. If every country had the same weight distribution as the U.S., the world would be 58 million tons fatter, highlighting the critical need to address population fatness for world food

The investigation into the discovery of a missing five-year-old Virginia boy's body in a septic tank is progressing, with authorities emphasizing the focus will be on facts and physical evidence rather than speculation. The body of Noah Thomas, found Thursday afternoon in Dublin, Va., is pending autopsy results, which will help explain what happened to him. The boy was last seen by his mother on Sunday morning, when he was reported missing after she awoke from a two-hour nap to find him gone. Police are not releasing many details and are urging the public to come forward with any information or tips. The FBI is providing forensic support, and the cause of death remains unknown. A candlelight vigil is planned to remember Noah Thomas.

When 12-year-old Charlie Le Quesne picked up a demo iPhone 4S in a UK Tesco store, Siri, the voice-controlled personal assistant, reportedly let loose with a string of profanity. Le Quesne's mother, Kim, was reportedly taken aback when Siri responded to a simple question with "Shut the f*** up, you ugly t***." Tesco launched an investigation and sent the phone back to Apple for diagnosis. Staff suggested the offensive phrase might have been entered as the user's name during setup. The incident raises questions about potential tampering and whether Siri's responses could be influenced by setup instructions.

A key Shiite political bloc, led by Muqtada al-Sadr, has thrown its support behind Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, potentially breaking a months-long deadlock over Iraq's next government. This move, seen as a strategic shift by al-Sadr, could significantly bolster al-Maliki's chances of securing a third term. Al-Maliki's political coalition, which narrowly lost to the Iraqiya bloc in March elections, now has enough support to form a government, though it still needs to secure backing from the Kurdish parties and other smaller groups. The U.S. administration, while welcoming a resolution, remains concerned about al-Sadr's influence and his movement's close ties to Iran. The endorsement by al-Sadr, who has historically opposed al-Maliki, highlights the complex and shifting alliances in Iraq's political landscape.

President Donald Trump sent a $25,000 personal check to the family of a fallen soldier the same day that The Washington Post reported he had promised the soldier's father a personal donation during a June condolence call but never followed through, CNN reports. The White House confirmed the check was sent, though a spokesperson said it had been "in the pipeline" since the President's conversation with the father. The timing raised questions, and a White House official defended the gesture as a "generous and sincere" personal act. The incident comes amid ongoing controversy over how presidents handle condolence calls to families of those killed in action and Trump's feud with a Democratic congresswoman over his call with the widow of Sgt. La David Johnson, who was killed in Niger. Trump denied saying the serviceman "knew what he signed up for, but I guess it still hurt." A Virginia Beach man faces animal abuse charges after allegedly shooting and burying his 15-year-old dog, Allie, on the Oceanfront. Michael Whalen says he ended Allie's life due to severe seizures caused by Cushing's disease, describing the experience as emotionally devastating. Whalen buried Allie at 85th Street, but a resident discovered her body on February 10. He now hopes to clear his name and highlight euthanasia rights. Whalen's attorney argues he acted appropriately as a pet owner.

In the face of criticism, filmmakers Kirby Dick and Amy Ziering maintain their documentary "The Hunting Ground" accurately portrays the crisis of campus sexual assault. The film, which premiered at Sundance, highlights cases like Kamilah Willingham, a Harvard Law student sexually assaulted by Brandon Winston, and Erica Kinsman, a Florida State University student raped by Jameis Winston. Despite Winston's legal threats and Harvard Law School faculty's complaints about the film's portrayal, Dick and Ziering stand by their work, arguing it brings necessary attention to the issue. Legal challenges and counterarguments underscore the contentious nature of addressing campus sexual assault.

A meteorologist with over 20 years of experience has sued CBS Corporation and its Los Angeles affiliates, KCAL and KCBS, for age and gender discrimination. Kyle Hunter claims he was repeatedly passed over for weather broadcaster positions because CBS prefers hiring young, attractive women, despite his qualifications. Hunter, represented by attorney Gloria Allred, seeks unspecified damages and argues that CBS is using these women to attract more male viewers. The lawsuit alleges Hunter was denied opportunities for positions vacated by male meteorologists and that CBS had to lower its educational requirements to hire women without meteorological backgrounds. CBS denies the allegations, stating the claims are based on "gross misstatements of fact."

Japanese whisky has shocked the industry by topping the 2015 World Whisky Bible, with the Yamazaki Single Malt Sherry Cask 2013 scoring a perfect 97.5 out of 100, reports the Telegraph. This marks the first time a Scottish malt has failed to make the top five, and the first year a Japanese whisky has claimed the highest accolade in the 12-year history of the review. Whisky expert Jim Murray praised the Yamazaki's "nose of exquisite boldness" and "light, teasing spice," but warned Scottish distilleries they need to improve to compete. Only 18,000 bottles of the winning whisky were produced, making it a rare find for whisky-lovers.

"The Giver," based on Lois Lowry's 1993 novel, explores a dystopian future where a young boy, Jonas (Brenton Thwaites), is chosen to be the Receiver of Memory, learning the painful and joyful history of a society that has sacrificed individuality for sameness. The film, directed by Phillip Noyce and featuring a cast including Jeff Bridges, Meryl Streep, and Katie Holmes, finds its place in a crowded field of young-adult dystopian adaptations. While the movie offers a poignant coming-of-age story, it struggles to match the innovative spirit of its source material and the emotional depth of its predecessor. The adaptation, though well-acted and visually engaging, seems somewhat predictable and heavy-handed, lacking the ambiguity and complexity of the book. Nonetheless, it serves as a respectful and faithful adaptation, appealing to fans of the original and the genre alike.

Jacksonville International Airport was shut down for nearly five hours, stranding incoming passengers on the tarmac after police found two suspicious packages. One package was deemed "destructive" and had to be deactivated offsite by a bomb squad. The airport was evacuated shortly after 6 p.m. Tuesday, with some incoming planes held up on the tarmac until buses could arrive to pick up passengers. No flights were allowed to take off following the evacuation. Individual airlines will determine how to restart their operations. Passengers on inbound flights were bused to offsite hotels as transportation became available. The delay was cumbersome but passengers remained calm, with one passenger, Arlie Gentry, arriving on a flight from New York via Baltimore and experiencing the evacuation firsthand.

In the Indian town of Sadiya, an unknown species of highly aggressive spiders has caused panic and fatalities. The spiders, which appeared during a Bihu festival on May 8, bit multiple residents, leading to hospital overcrowding. Two individuals, Purnakanta Buragohain and an unnamed schoolboy, died from their bites. Scientists from Dibrugarh University and Gauhati University arrived to investigate, identifying the spiders as potentially new and aggressive but unable to definitively name them. The spiders' sudden appearance and behavior remain unexplained, raising concerns about their origin and potential spread. Local authorities have struggled to manage the situation, lacking resources and expertise. British naturalist Dr. Vejay Singh suggests environmental factors might have triggered the swarm.

French air strikes forced Islamist guerrillas to retreat from key towns in northern Mali, while rebels seized a small western town, highlighting the challenges ahead in restoring order. French jets targeted Douentza and Gao, killing at least 60 insurgents. Despite the offensive, Islamists struck back by taking Diabaly, 250 miles north of Bamako. French Defense Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian acknowledged a "difficult" situation in the west, where rebels are well-armed. France secured new international support, including logistical aid from the US and troop commitments from African nations. However, Malian troops, trained by the US, faced significant challenges, with some Tuareg commanders defecting to the rebels. The UN Security Council expressed unanimous support for France's military intervention, while aid workers reported civilian casualties and displacement.

It looks like a cross between a Pac-Man ghost and a Pokémon creature, but this adorable little octopus, yet to be named, might just earn "adorable" as part of its scientific identity. A postdoctoral fellow at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, Stephanie Bush, suggests naming it Opisthoteuthis Adorabilis due to its cuteness. This rare cephalopod, part of the Opisthoteuthis genus, is known for its distinctive webbing between tentacles, allowing it to float like a parachute while using fins on its mantle to steer. The naming process, involving publishing papers and distributing specimens to museums, is lengthy and complex. Bush discovered key distinctions between this species and Opisthoteuthis californiana, the pink flapjack octopus from "Finding Nemo," after working on the Monterey Bay Aquarium’s Tentacles exhibit. Hillary Clinton delivered a harsh rebuke to Donald Trump at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, emphasizing the importance of community and togetherness over Trump's "I alone can fix it" approach. Clinton highlighted her campaign slogan, "Stronger Together," and contrasted it with Trump's semi-authoritarian stance, assailing him for his business career and manufacturing jobs overseas. She criticized Trump's inability to handle even minor provocations and his rhetoric, stating, "America is great because America is good." Clinton outlined her "bold agenda" for improving lives, including debt-free college education, immigration reform, and campaign-finance reform. She also acknowledged Bernie Sanders's campaign, praising his focus on economic and social justice issues and reaching out to his supporters.

Three law enforcement agencies searched for a 19-year-old Johns Creek man named Aftab M. Aslam since he was reported missing on April 27. His family received a text message stating he had been kidnapped, but investigators found that Aslam had purchased the phone used to send the message. Now, Aslam has returned home unharmed, telling police he left on his own for personal reasons. Charges have not been filed yet as investigators verify his account.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 continues with a metal object found near Augusta, Australia, confirmed not to be from the missing plane. Despite extensive searches, no clear debris has been identified, and the ocean is full of garbage, complicating the search. The Bluefin-21 underwater drone has scanned over 90% of the search area without success. Weather conditions and ocean garbage have hindered efforts, but authorities are planning to use more powerful sonar equipment. Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott emphasizes that the search will continue until every possible area is thoroughly examined, despite the lack of findings.

Scientists have reevaluated the age of Homo floresiensis, the "hobbit" humans discovered in Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores. The latest analysis, published in Nature, suggests the hobbits lived between 100,000 and 60,000 years ago, with their stone tools dating back to around 190,000 to 50,000 years ago. This new timeline indicates they likely did not coexist with modern humans, who arrived in the region about 50,000 years ago. The hobbits, standing about 3.5 feet tall and weighing around 75 pounds, were a unique species with small brains, resembling early hominins and chimpanzees. The reevaluation was based on more extensive excavations and five independent dating methods, addressing earlier confusion due to the cave's complex geological layers. The NFL will use Arabic numerals for Super Bowl 50, marking the first time since Super Bowl IV that Roman numerals will not be used. The league's decision, after 44 years of using Roman numerals, was made to avoid the unappealing appearance of the letter "L." The 50th Super Bowl logo features the number "50" in gold, symbolizing the game's golden anniversary and its location in the "Golden State." The league plans to revert to Roman numerals for Super Bowl LI in 2017.

Former state senator Brian Joyce was arrested and charged with over 100 counts, including racketeering, wire fraud, extortion, and money laundering. Joyce, who served as a Democrat from Milton, is accused of using his legislative position for personal gain by accepting bribes and kickbacks from various entities. The 102-page indictment alleges Joyce secretly profited from his role as a state senator by exerting influence on local and state officials in exchange for financial benefits. Joyce’s attorney maintains his innocence and questions the validity of the charges. The case highlights a significant fall from grace for Joyce, who had previously held a leadership position in the Senate and had faced earlier allegations of conflicts of interest.

A new mother who accidentally smothered her 10-day-old baby in a hospital bed has filed an $8.6 million lawsuit against Portland Adventist Medical Center. The lawsuit claims the hospital was at fault for medicating the breastfeeding mother, putting the infant in her bed without supervision, and not having clear policies or enforcement on the dangers of the combination. Monica Thompson, the mother, dozed off with her medicated newborn and awoke to find the baby unresponsive. The baby suffered catastrophic brain damage and was removed from life support six days later. The lawsuit also seeks compensation for the mother's emotional distress.

Yawning might not be about getting more oxygen or being bored; it could be your brain cooling down. A study by researchers at the University of Vienna found that people yawn more frequently when the temperature is around 20°C, which is optimal for brain cooling. Yawning frequency decreased when temperatures were either very high (around 37°C) or very low (freezing). This suggests that yawning helps regulate brain temperature to improve alertness and mental efficiency. The study, which compared pedestrian behavior in Vienna during summer and winter with a similar study in Arizona, supports the thermoregulatory theory of yawning, indicating that it is constrained to an optimal thermal zone.

The Women's Convention, set for October 27-29 in Detroit, aims to bring together activists and leaders to share strategies and build on the momentum from the Women's March. Organizers, including co-chairs of the Women's March, initially announced that Senator Bernie Sanders would open the event, sparking controversy. Critics argue that a woman should open the convention to set a precedent and reinforce the movement's focus on women's issues. Despite the backlash, organizers defended their choice, stating that Sanders is a "fierce champion of women's rights" and highlighting the many female speakers scheduled. The convention will feature workshops, training sessions, and speeches from notable women and men, focusing on collective liberation for women of all backgrounds.

A pregnant woman in Fort Dodge, Iowa, was held at gunpoint by police after refusing to pull over her speeding car on the way to the hospital. Rachel and Ben Kohnen were driving at 85 mph in a 55 mph zone when an officer pursued them. They did not stop, leading to tire spikes being deployed, which forced them to halt. Rachel Kohnen gave birth to their fourth child, a nearly 10-pound baby named Hazel, about an hour after being escorted to the hospital. The couple tried to call 911 but faced communication issues due to Rachel's contractions. No charges have been filed against them.

Protesters staged a topless demonstration in St. Peter's Square to oppose the Vatican's stance on gay adoption, while in Paris, hundreds of thousands joined a march against same-sex marriage. The Vatican's newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano, defended the traditional family unit, stating that no one has the "right" to children claimed by gay couples seeking adoption. In response, four women from the Ukrainian Femen group removed their tops, displaying slogans like "In Gay We Trust" and "Homophobes shut up." The protest drew angry reactions from some pilgrims, but police quickly removed the activists. The Vatican has increasingly voiced opposition to gay marriage, with Pope Benedict XVI reaffirming the Church's stance in December.

The State Department faced criticism and deleted a tweet that was seen as sexist and patronizing, apologizing afterward. The tweet, sent from the @TravelGov account, read, "Not a ‘10’ in the US? Then not a 10 overseas. Beware of being lured into buying expensive drinks or worse—being robbed. #springbreakingbadly." The department later deleted the tweet and issued a two-part apology, acknowledging that it had come off negatively and emphasizing its intention to warn travelers about scams.

Bangladesh's anti-terrorism unit has arrested Farabi Shafiur Rahman, a suspect in the killing of U.S. blogger Avijit Roy, who was hacked to death in Dhaka. Rahman, previously jailed for ties to the extremist Hizbut Tahrir group, was arrested at a bus stop in Dhaka and had allegedly threatened Roy in social media posts. He posted photos of the crime scene shortly after the attack. Rahman had previously called for Roy's death on Facebook. The murder of Roy, who was an engineer of Bangladeshi origin, comes amid a crackdown on hardline Islamist groups, which have increased activities in recent years. Bangladesh ranks 146th among 180 countries in press freedom, according to Reporters Without Borders.

President Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping are meeting at the Sunnylands estate in California, aiming to improve relations and address cybersecurity concerns. Obama seeks to build a personal rapport with Xi, while Xi pushes for a new model of major country relationship, emphasizing peaceful development and avoiding conflict. Both leaders discuss military-to-military relations and economic cooperation. Obama highlights the importance of setting common rules for cybersecurity, while Xi stresses the need for mutual understanding and cooperation. The informal setting of the summit is seen as a historic opportunity to reset the U.S.-China relationship, with expectations high for a productive outcome.

President Obama denied in an exclusive interview with ABC News that he was "tense" during a recent encounter with Arizona Governor Jan Brewer, contradicting Brewer's description of the meeting. Obama said, "I'm usually accused of not being intense enough, right, too relaxed." Brewer had previously accused Obama of being "somewhat thin-skinned and a little tense" during their 2010 meeting. Obama added, "Last time we met, she wasn't fully satisfied. But, you know, I think this is a classic example of things getting blown out of proportion." He also emphasized his determination to fight for a second term, stating, "How much do you want it? Badly, because I think the country needs it." Obama criticized his Republican opponents, particularly Mitt Romney, Newt Gingrich, and Rick Santorum, for their "rhetorical flourishes" and "failed political philosophy," arguing that their approach had resulted in a "huge crash" that lost jobs.

Actor Mark Wahlberg is seeking a pardon from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts for a 1988 assault conviction, hoping to clear his criminal record and become a better role model. In his application to the Massachusetts Board of Pardons, Wahlberg, now 43, expresses remorse for his actions on April 8, 1988, when he hit a man over the head with a stick and caused him to lose vision in one eye. He served 45 days in prison for the assault and other charges. Wahlberg states he has dedicated himself to becoming a better person and has engaged in philanthropic efforts, including founding the Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation and supporting the Dorchester Boys and Girls Club. He hopes a pardon will recognize his personal improvement and serve as an example of redemption.

Nestle has failed to convince European judges that it can trademark the shape of its iconic four-fingered KitKat bar in the UK. The European Court of Justice ruled that Nestle must prove the public relies solely on the shape to identify the snack, a requirement difficult to meet when the bar also bears a brand name. This ruling, part of a decade-long legal battle between Nestle and Cadbury, clears the way for competitors to produce similar-shaped chocolate bars. Both companies expressed satisfaction with the decision, but the case will now return to the UK High Court for a final ruling. The dispute highlights the challenges of trademarking product shapes and the ongoing "chocolate wars" between the two confectionery giants.

U.S. President Barack Obama urged world leaders at the Nuclear Security Summit in Washington to enhance security measures for nuclear facilities to prevent "madmen" like ISIS from obtaining nuclear materials or developing "dirty bombs." Obama highlighted the persistent threat of nuclear terrorism despite progress in reducing such risks. He emphasized that no group had succeeded in obtaining bomb materials, but al Qaeda and ISIS posed significant concerns. Obama noted that 102 countries had ratified an amendment to a nuclear security treaty, reducing the risk of nuclear theft and smuggling. The summit also addressed Iran's nuclear deal, which Obama called a "substantial success," and discussed the need to secure nuclear materials to avoid them falling into the wrong hands. The absence of Russian President Vladimir Putin and Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif due to regional tensions and a bombing in Lahore, respectively, was noted. Obama warned that complacency was dangerous and that the world must continue efforts to reduce nuclear threats.

Katie Couric addressed a controversial comment she made on Watch What Happens Live in 2012, where she jokingly said Matt Lauer used to pinch her on the ass. Appearing on the show with host Andy Cohen, Couric clarified that the comment was meant as a joke and apologized for any misunderstanding. Couric, who was fired from the Today show in 2017 for alleged inappropriate behavior, also discussed the ongoing allegations against Lauer, stating that some reports may be exaggerated. She defended Lauer's alleged use of a door lock button as a mere privacy feature and not indicative of misconduct.

If you're in the mood for a Michael Bay-style action flick with a dash of true crime, Pain & Gain delivers. Mark Wahlberg stars as Daniel Lugo, a personal trainer who, after a stint in prison, sets his sights on a life of luxury, fueled by a sense of entitlement and the advice of a self-help guru. The film, while not subtle, stays close to the facts, offering two hours of sweat, blood, and Bayesque excess. Wahlberg is matched by Anthony Mackie and Dwayne Johnson, who bring their own brand of craziness to the mix. The result is a movie that might leave you questioning whether it's a monumentally stupid film or a brilliant exploration of stupidity itself.

Five men have been arrested in connection with the alleged abduction and rape of a Japanese woman who was held captive for over a month in eastern India, police said. The woman, a 23-year-old research student, was reportedly lured by a man posing as a tour guide to travel to the Gaya district, where she was held and repeatedly raped by the men. She managed to escape and file a complaint with the Japanese consulate in Kolkata. The police suspect an organized gang was involved, with some members reportedly fluent in Japanese. This case adds to a growing number of high-profile rape cases in India, prompting stricter laws but continuing public outrage over violence against women.

A drug-sniffing German shepherd named Sombra, known as "Shadow," has been moved to a safer location after Colombia's most powerful drug gang, the Urabeños, placed a significant bounty on her head. Sombra, credited with sniffing out over nine tons of cocaine and leading to 245 arrests, was originally based in Turbo, a key trafficking point. The Urabeños, offering a reward of up to $70,000 for her capture or death, are retaliating against her successful drug detections. To ensure her safety, Sombra was transferred to Bogotá's international airport, where she will now be accompanied by additional security.

A 9-year-old girl named Zianna Oliphant addressed Charlotte City Council, expressing her feelings about police treatment of African-Americans, including the fatal shooting of Keith Lamont Scott. Her emotional speech, which went viral, highlighted the ongoing tensions between the black community and law enforcement. Zianna, who was nervous but decided to speak, emphasized that black people should not have to protest because they are being treated unfairly. Her mother, Precious Oliphant, was proud of her daughter's courage and noted that Zianna and her brother are involved in a police youth league, highlighting the complex relationship between the community and police. Zianna's speech and the protests following Scott's shooting have put pressure on city officials to address the issues of police use of force and racial discrimination.

On the Fourth of July, Rep. Beto O’Rourke performed with Willie Nelson at the singer’s annual country music festival, drawing both cheers and boos. O’Rourke, facing a tight Senate race against Republican Ted Cruz, used the event to express hope for a more inclusive America. The musician’s support of O’Rourke has sparked controversy among some of Nelson’s traditional country music fans, who accuse him of aligning with a “socialist” agenda. Despite the backlash, Nelson stands by O’Rourke, citing shared concerns and the candidate’s integrity. The singer will headline a September rally and concert for O’Rourke, featuring other musicians like Leon Bridges and Lukas Nelson.

Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's Nobel Peace Prize winner, embarked on her first trip to Europe in nearly a quarter century, formally accepting the prize that launched her global prominence two decades ago. During her 17-day visit, which includes stops in Norway, Britain, Ireland, and France, Suu Kyi urged foreign governments not to form joint ventures with her country's state-owned oil and gas company until it improves transparency and accountability. She briefly fell ill at a press conference in Bern but attended a cocktail reception. Suu Kyi also received a standing ovation at the International Labour Organization, where she highlighted the need for responsible investment to aid Myanmar's transition from nearly 50 years of military rule. She expressed cautious support for Western oil firms like Total, while emphasizing the importance of transparency in contracts.

A 54-year-old Florida man was arrested after allegedly trying to perform an exorcism on his 80-year-old live-in girlfriend, holding her down and removing phone batteries to prevent her from calling for help. Deputies found the elderly woman bruised and scratched outside their shared home. The man, David Benes, was arrested on charges of battery on a person 65 or older and false imprisonment. He is currently in jail.

Arizona's new abortion law, set to take effect Thursday, bans most abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy, even in cases where a fetus has a fatal defect. The law, which defines gestational age from the first day of the woman's last period, effectively bans abortions starting at 18 weeks. Eight other states have similar bans, but Arizona is the only one to push the ban back to 18 weeks. The law requires doctors to offer information about perinatal hospice services to women considering abortion due to a fatal fetal abnormality and mandates the state maintain a website list of organizations that provide such services. These organizations, like MISS Foundation and Embrace, offer counseling, comfort, and support to families, including helping develop birth plans, attending births, organizing meals, and preparing for every outcome. However, these organizations worry they may be overwhelmed as more women are required to continue pregnancies. The law aims to support families but also faces challenges in providing adequate resources.

Bitcoin's price rebounded above $9,000 after positive discussions at a G-20 meeting, while German researchers uncovered links to child pornography within the cryptocurrency's blockchain, raising legal concerns. The blockchain, intended as an immutable ledger of transactions, can store non-financial data, potentially making its possession illegal in some jurisdictions. This discovery could hinder Bitcoin's mainstream acceptance, despite its decreasing use in illegal transactions.

Lois Riess, 56, from Blooming Prairie, Minnesota, is now suspected of killing 59-year-old Pamela Hutchinson, 59, of Bradenton, Florida, because the two women looked alike. Riess, who is already wanted for the murder of her husband, David Riess, in March, targeted Hutchinson and stole her identity. After killing Hutchinson, Riess took her white 2005 Acura TL with Florida license plate Y37TAA. The car has been spotted in Louisiana and Corpus Christi, Texas. Riess's 2005 white Cadillac Escalade was found abandoned in a Florida park. She is wanted for murder, grand theft of a motor vehicle, and grand theft and criminal use of personal identification. U.S. Marshals are actively searching for Riess, who is considered armed and dangerous. Authorities believe Riess's mode of operation is to befriend women who resemble her and steal their identities.
