Despite speculation that Al Gore might run for president in 2016, Gore's advisers say he has no plans to challenge Hillary Clinton. Gore spokeswoman Betsy McManus told POLITICO that Gore is focused on climate change. However, some Democrats are discussing the possibility of Gore running, citing Clinton's troubles with email controversies and flagging poll numbers. Gore, who won the popular vote but lost the presidency in 2000, has not shown any interest in a run and has largely stayed out of politics since then. His potential candidacy is seen as a serious option if Clinton falters, alongside Joe Biden.

A 15-year study of over 530,000 British women found that those who had their appendix or tonsils removed, particularly both, are more likely to get pregnant and do so sooner than the general population. Researchers at the University of Dundee analyzed medical records and discovered that women who had undergone appendectomies, tonsillectomies, or both had higher pregnancy rates—134, 149, and 143 pregnancies per 100, respectively, compared to 131 in those who hadn't had any procedures. The findings challenge the long-held belief that appendectomies can damage fertility due to potential scar tissue. Experts suggest the increased fertility could be due to reduced inflammation or behavioral factors like increased sexual activity. Further research is needed to determine the exact reasons behind this link, but the study aims to reassure women that having these surgeries won't negatively impact their chances of getting pregnant.

Bryson DeChambeau won the Northern Trust golf tournament with a four-shot victory, moving to the top of the FedEx Cup standings and securing a strong position for the Tour Championship. His victory, coming after a strong performance at The Northern Trust, puts him in contention for a captain's pick for the U.S. Ryder Cup team. Tony Finau finished second, making a statement for a potential captain's pick as well. Tiger Woods, despite a solid showing, finished 40th, 14 shots behind the winner. DeChambeau expressed his ambitions for both the Ryder Cup and the FedEx Cup, while Woods focused on his recent improved play and his relationship with President Donald Trump, emphasizing the importance of respecting the office.

Obama states there is increasing recognition that law enforcement practices are not always "colorblind," citing the incidents in Ferguson and the death of Eric Garner as key factors in raising awareness.

James Cameron successfully completed a solo dive to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the deepest point on Earth, in his submersible Deepsea Challenger. Cameron, known for his adventurous spirit and filmmaking prowess, described the journey as a "heckuva ride" and spent over two hours exploring the alien-like environment before resurfacing. The descent took 156 minutes, but due to a hydraulic fluid leak, Cameron decided to end his mission early, cutting his time on the ocean floor short. Despite the limited time, Cameron managed to collect samples and capture footage of the deep-sea environment. His mission, part of the Deep Sea Challenge, highlights the dangers and challenges of exploring such extreme depths, including the risks of implosion, freezing, fire, and entanglement. Cameron's bravery and preparation made this historic solo dive possible, and he hinted at the possibility of future dives to the Challenger Deep.

The Pentagon's official Twitter account mistakenly retweeted a call for President Trump to resign, a move quickly disavowed by the Department of Defense. The erroneous retweet, made by an "authorized operator," came from an activist account @proudresister, which also sells anti-Trump merchandise. Pentagon spokesman Col. Rob Manning and press secretary Dana White both clarified that the retweet did not reflect the Department of Defense's stance. The incident follows a series of sexual misconduct allegations against various figures in Washington and Hollywood.

A remarkable Milwaukee woman, Mary Agnes Mullaney, better known as "Pink," left behind an extraordinary legacy through her obituary. The obituary, filled with colorful and practical advice, showcases her devotion to others. Excerpts include: "Go to church with a chicken sandwich in your purse. Cry at the consecration, every time. Give the chicken sandwich to your homeless friend after mass." Her family and friends remember her as a gentle, kind person who touched many lives. The obituary serves as a testament to her life, encouraging others to continue her lessons of kindness and generosity.

A fight over crab legs at a Manchester buffet led to two arrests after a physical altercation, with a 21-year-old man suffering a cut lip and broken tooth. His mother used pepper spray to protect him, resulting in no charges against her. Clifford Knight, 46, and Lataya Knight, 38, were arrested; Clifford faces third-degree assault and disorderly conduct, while Lataya is charged with disorderly conduct and threatening. Both are husband and wife and were released on bail with court dates set for April 14. The Manchester Fire Department responded to vent the restaurant, and it was temporarily closed by the Health Department.

In an era where image editing is ubiquitous, people are increasingly seeking plastic surgery to resemble their heavily edited selfies, a phenomenon dubbed "Snapchat dysmorphia." Doctors are noticing this trend, where patients bring in their own edited photos, asking to look more like their filtered versions. This practice is causing concern among experts, who fear it may negatively impact self-esteem and trigger body dysmorphic disorder, a mental illness on the obsessive-compulsive spectrum. The ease of editing tools, such as Snapchat filters and Facetune, has made these unattainable beauty standards accessible to anyone, blurring the line between reality and fantasy. While traditional cosmetic procedures cannot replicate the instant fixes seen in edited photos, patients often demand unrealistic results, leading to disappointment and potential psychological issues. This trend highlights the pervasive influence of social media on beauty standards and self-perception, with the constant exposure to idealized images potentially leading to dissatisfaction and even dangerous behaviors.

The Baltic Sea is home to numerous shipwrecks, with around 1,000 known objects in German waters alone. German maritime expert Thomas Dehling notes that many of these wrecks date back to the two World Wars, with some as old as the 15th or 16th century. Shipwrecks are regularly surveyed, particularly those that could pose a danger to navigation. Divers must be cautious due to fishing nets often entangled in the wrecks. The Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency charts and manages these objects, but does not publicize their exact locations to prevent unauthorized diving. New shipwrecks are still discovered each year using modern technology.

The Boy Scouts of America is proposing to lift the ban on gay youth members but maintain a prohibition on gay adults from leading troops, a compromise aimed at ending a long-standing controversy. The proposal will be voted on by the organization's National Council at a meeting in Texas the week of May 20. This move comes after surveys showed that a majority of members supported allowing gay youth members but not gay adult leaders. Gay rights groups welcomed the change for youth but criticized the exclusion of gay adults, while conservative groups and some churches opposed the proposal. The decision reflects the ongoing debate over gay rights in the United States and the challenges faced by the century-old organization in balancing tradition and modern values.

A former investment analyst has quit his job to play fantasy football full-time, illustrating the growing financial significance of fantasy sports. With an estimated 36 million participants in the U.S. and Canada, fantasy sports have become a substantial industry. Drew Dinkmeyer, who now dedicates himself to daily fantasy games, explains that his earnings from these games, combined with income from writing and hosting, support his lifestyle. He compares his approach to day-trading, where players select undervalued players based on their performance predictions. This shift indicates the potential for fantasy sports to offer a viable career path for enthusiasts.

Saturday Night Live opened the show with a sketch mocking Rush Limbaugh's radio show, featuring Taran Killam as the cranky host who berated bizarre sponsors like "Depends For Racists" for abandoning him after his controversial comments about Georgetown student Sandra Fluke. The sketch, while amusing in its absurdity, felt repetitive and stretched beyond the length of Limbaugh's actual show. The episode highlighted the broader advertiser exodus, with 98 companies, including major brands like Ford, GM, and Allstate, pulling their ads from Limbaugh's program and others due to his offensive content.

Barnes & Noble may be phasing out its 3G Nook model, according to Engadget, which cites "hard evidence from within B&N." The company is reportedly encouraging retail partners to not send out bulk requests for the Nook 3G, as there may not be sufficient quantities to fulfill those orders. While the Nook 3G sold well during the holidays, it's unclear if this move signals the end of the 3G model or if Barnes & Noble will continue to offer both Wi-Fi and 3G versions. Some industry insiders suggest that Barnes & Noble may be losing money on its e-ink readers and could be looking to release a more cost-effective product. However, a Barnes & Noble representative told Engadget that the Nook 3G remains on sale and that the company does not comment on rumors.

Kris Humphries plans to seek a legal separation from Kim Kardashian, sources tell PEOPLE. Humphries intends to annul the marriage instead of pursuing a divorce, aiming to clear his record of ever being married to the reality star. This change of heart comes shortly after Kardashian's trip to Minnesota, where she met with Humphries and the pastor who married them. Humphries initially wanted to sign the divorce papers but now seems to be reconsidering. Meanwhile, Daniel Craig criticizes the Kardashian family for making careers out of their private lives, calling them "f***ing idiots" in a recent interview with GQ magazine. Despite his successful career, Craig remains unsatisfied and constantly seeks improvement.

A 25-year-old man was arrested after allegedly posing as a Hurricane Harvey evacuee and enrolling as a freshman at a Dallas ISD high school. Principal Chris Bayer of Hillcrest High School said the school immediately notified district and local authorities once it became aware of the student enrolled under false pretenses. The man, Sidney Bouvier Gilstrap-Portley, enrolled at Hillcrest as Rashun Richardson and even played for the basketball team, scoring 17 points in a playoff game. He had previously enrolled at Skyline High School. District spokeswoman Robyn Harris confirmed that when a student enrolls claiming to be homeless or an evacuee due to a natural disaster, federal law exempts them from requiring documents. The incident has raised concerns about the need for improved verification processes when accepting students in times of need.

The Bank of England will unveil its first plastic banknote, the new Winston Churchill £5, at Blenheim Palace on Thursday, marking the start of a shift to polymer notes. These notes, which will feature Winston Churchill, Jane Austen, and JMW Turner, are expected to be more durable, secure, and environmentally friendly than paper notes. The move to plastic will cost shops and banks up to £236 million due to the need for recalibrating or replacing ATMs and vending machines. Over 30 countries already use polymer notes, and the Bank of England claims the new notes will offset higher production costs and save an estimated £100 million.

Amazon's Amazon Flex program, which uses independent contractors to handle last-mile deliveries, operates with minimal oversight and faces scrutiny over potential labor law violations. Drivers are hired through a simple application process and minimal training, earning between $18 and $25 per hour. The program is expanding rapidly, but faces challenges such as misaligned block times and package numbers, and a cap on weekly hours. Drivers often compete fiercely for blocks, leading to physical altercations. Flex’s terms of service include an arbitration agreement that prevents drivers from joining class-action lawsuits, making it difficult to address widespread issues. Legal experts argue that Amazon may be misclassifying drivers as independent contractors to avoid providing benefits, raising concerns about labor law compliance. The program’s secretive nature and lack of public awareness make it challenging for regulators to address potential issues, leaving drivers with few avenues for recourse.

A Florida man, William Reiss, survived Hurricane Irma only to be killed by a FEMA contractor he had befriended for storm damage assessments. Reiss, 68, was shot four times by 18-year-old Gerjuan Jackson, who also wounded Reiss’s roommate, Kenneth Maier, who later died. Jackson, along with accomplices Kenley Campbell and Darril Rankin, stole up to 25 guns and a TV from Reiss’s home before burning his truck and selling the stolen items. Jackson admitted to shooting Reiss and Maier. All three suspects were charged with first-degree murder and other crimes. Kenneth Maier, 57, who had initially flagged down passersby after the shooting, later died from his injuries.

Milwaukee County is grappling with an unprecedented drug crisis, with 70 probable drug overdose deaths in just seven weeks, according to the chief medical examiner's office. Adam Peterson, 29, the son of Milwaukee County's chief medical examiner Dr. Brian Peterson, died from a suspected drug overdose at a friend's apartment. The medical examiner's office reports that this year is on track to surpass the previous five years in heroin-related deaths, with the number of overdose deaths already exceeding the number of homicides in the past four years. Dr. Peterson, who heads the Milwaukee County Medical Examiner's Office, shared at a recent opioid round-table discussion that one in three cases autopsied in a month earlier this year were overdose cases. The ages of the deceased ranged from 1 year old to 63 years old, with tragic cases like a 1-year-old found dead from methadone poisoning. An Egyptian court has sentenced 528 supporters of ousted President Mohammed Morsi to death for their alleged participation in an attack on a police station in Minya in August, which resulted in a police officer's death. The UN human rights commissioner condemned the decision, calling it "rife with procedural irregularities" and a breach of international human rights law. The defendants were found guilty in a single session lasting less than an hour, with most of them not present and their defense lawyers boycotting the trial. The verdicts have sparked widespread international criticism, with the U.S. State Department and European Union urging Egypt to ensure fair trials. The court will issue its final verdict on April 28 after Egypt's grand mufti ratifies the death sentences. In a separate trial, 683 Morsi supporters, including the Muslim Brotherhood's general guide, Mohammed Badie, and the chairman of its Freedom and Justice Party, Saad al-Katatni, went on trial on

Mandy Patinkin, star of "The Princess Bride," has received numerous emails showing images of Ted Cruz's face superimposed over his character Inigo Montoya in scenes from the film. Cruz, a big fan of the movie, has been reciting lines from it on the campaign trail, including the famous "Allo, my name is Inigo Montoya. You killed my father. Prepare to die." Patinkin is concerned that Cruz's portrayal of Inigo Montoya, a character who seeks revenge and ultimately finds love, does not reflect the movie's core message of love and hope. Patinkin urges Cruz to consider creating "hope, optimism and love" instead of spreading fear and hatred. Cruz's campaign spokeswoman defended his use of the movie, stating that he is "a huge fan of the film and the actors in it" and that "having some fun with a cult classic like 'The Princess Bride' should be something we can all get behind, politics aside

First lady Michelle Obama promoted healthy eating on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno, bringing him nutritious snacks like apples and sweet potato fries. Obama, who is supporting her "Let's Move!" campaign, managed to convince Leno to try a pizza made with vegetables. During the interview, Obama hinted at her husband's singing abilities, noting that he sings to her often and enjoys classics like Al Green and Marvin Gaye. She downplayed any political implications when discussing Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney's performance of "America the Beautiful." Obama stated that she and President Obama aim to do their best each day, hoping their efforts will speak for themselves. She is currently on a two-day swing through California promoting healthy eating and fitness for kids while helping Democrats raise money for upcoming elections.

Rapper Kevin Gates was sentenced to 180 days in jail after a jury found him guilty of misdemeanor battery for kicking a fan during a concert in Lakeland, Florida. The incident, captured on video, occurred in August 2015 when Gates was filmed kicking Miranda Dixon, 18, in the chest. Dixon testified that she had grabbed Gates' pants twice, but Gates admitted to kicking her in self-defense. Defense attorney Jose Baez argued that Gates' kick was in response to Dixon's battery. The judge sentenced Gates to triple the requested 60 days, with one year of probation and fines.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive. These data are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. By including location information in tweets, users can enhance their social media posts. This feature allows for more precise tracking and sharing of locations, both on the web and through third-party apps. The Internet Archive aims to archive pages as they are created and the pages they reference, ensuring that broken links can be fixed and the original intent of page authors can be preserved.

Three years after her acquittal in the murder of her 2-year-old daughter Caylee, Casey Anthony continues to live in seclusion due to public hatred, according to her former defense attorney Cheney Mason. Mason, who joined the case pro bono, shared that Anthony is working as a housekeeper and clerk in her undisclosed Florida location. She avoids public spaces and has few social interactions, maintaining a guarded and aloof demeanor. Mason's new book, "Justice in America," delves into the case's legal and media aspects, providing behind-the-scenes insights. Anthony, who was acquitted of first-degree murder but convicted of providing false information to law enforcement, remains estranged from her family and friends, focusing on keeping her life as private as possible.

Oscar-winning actress Cate Blanchett is set to star as Lucille Ball in an authorized biopic, with Aaron Sorkin penning the script. The project, produced by Lucie Arnaz and Desi Arnaz Jr. alongside Escape Artists, aims to chronicle Ball's 20-year marriage to Desi Arnaz. While Sorkin has not officially committed, the studio is eager to proceed. Ball, known for her roles in iconic TV sitcoms and numerous awards, will be brought to life on screen, with Blanchett's recent filmography including roles in "Cinderella," "Carol," "Truth," and "Knight of Cups."

In the run-up to the Iran nuclear deal, the Obama administration agreed to release or drop charges against 21 Iranian nationals, including seven in the U.S. and 14 fugitives abroad. These men were accused of posing national security threats, including involvement in illegal procurement networks supplying Iran with U.S. military technology. The Justice Department and federal agents were shocked and angry at the deal, which they believed undermined their counterproliferation efforts. The Obama administration justified the swap as a one-time humanitarian gesture, but critics argue it weakened the U.S. position on Iran. The fallout has left key investigations stalled, and some federal officials say the deal has damaged the infrastructure built to enforce laws against Iran.

A newly discovered dinosaur from northeastern China, named Caihong juji, had iridescent feathers that may have glimmered like a rainbow, according to a study published in Nature Communications. The dinosaur, about the size of a duck, lived 161 million years ago and had a bird-like body with feathers suitable for flight. However, it also had a crested head resembling Velociraptor. The well-preserved fossil revealed the presence of melanosomes, the pigment-containing organelles, in the feathers, suggesting the dinosaur's head, chest, and parts of its tail had a metallic sheen. This discovery, along with the finding of iridescent feathers in the dinosaur Microraptor, indicates two different ways small raptor dinosaurs developed iridescence before the origin of birds. The exact function of these colorful feathers remains uncertain, but they may have served as social or sexual cues.

A Texas prison escapee who fled 16 years ago has been captured in Mexico and is awaiting extradition to complete his sentence. Juan Salaz, 37, escaped from the Garza East prison in Beeville, Texas, in 1997 by climbing over three 16-foot razor-wire topped fences. He was serving three concurrent 35-year sentences for aggravated kidnapping with a deadly weapon and two counts of attempted capital murder of a police officer. Salaz is also facing a felony escape charge. The hunt for him involved the U.S. Marshals Service, the Texas prison system's Office of Inspector General, and Mexican law enforcement agencies. Salaz had been suspected of being in the Monterrey, Mexico, area for the past three years.

Solving Sudoku puzzles led to seizures in a 25-year-old German man who survived an avalanche and subsequent hypoxia. After an oxygen-deprived brain, the man experienced muscle twitches when speaking and walking. In the hospital, he began having clonic seizures in his left arm while attempting to solve a Sudoku puzzle. Doctors found that his intense three-dimensional imagination, used to solve Sudoku, overactivated a brain region, causing seizures. These seizures ceased when he stopped solving Sudoku. The case highlights reflex epilepsy triggered by external stimuli and the brain's complex network systems.

The Dallas Morning News, known for its conservative lean and long-standing tradition of endorsing Republican candidates, broke with its history by endorsing Hillary Clinton over Donald Trump. The newspaper's editorial board cited Trump's exploitation of fear and racism, his lack of preparedness, and his impulsive behavior as reasons for their decision. This move, coming from a traditionally Republican stronghold, could potentially sway undecided voters. Research suggests that unusual endorsements by newspapers can influence readers, especially those who closely follow the editorial pages. The Dallas Morning News' endorsement could be particularly impactful given its conservative readership, potentially altering the political landscape in key swing states like Texas.

A new method that tans skin without using ultraviolet radiation has shown promise in human skin samples, potentially leading to a lotion or cream that could protect fair-skinned individuals from skin cancer. The drug, tested in a 2006 study on mice, activates melanin production in human skin samples, creating a natural tan that absorbs UV radiation. This approach differs from current self-tanning products, which merely stain the skin and offer minimal protection. Researchers hope this discovery could prevent skin cancer and even slow skin aging. The drug works by mimicking the chemical reactions triggered by UV light, producing real melanin in a UV-independent manner. While the method could potentially benefit redheads, who typically do not tan, it remains in early stages of development, requiring further safety testing and commercialization.

The family of Stephon Clark, a 22-year-old black man fatally shot by Sacramento police, is grieving his loss. Clark's girlfriend, Salena Manni, and his two sons, Aiden and Ciaro, are heartbroken. Manni describes Clark as the love of her life and says he was a changed man who had recently improved his life. Clark's family and friends have started a memorial fund to support them. The police initially said Clark was armed with a "tool bar" but later clarified he was holding a cellphone. Body camera footage shows Clark breaking windows before being confronted by officers. He was shot 20 times and pronounced dead at the scene. No weapon was found. The incident has sparked protests and calls for justice, with community leaders demanding transparency and accountability.

A major winter storm brought heavy snow, strong winds, and frigid temperatures to the Northeast, causing travel disruptions and forcing school closures. Snow totals reached up to 2 feet in some areas, with New York City expecting up to 7 inches. Airlines canceled thousands of flights due to low visibility and dangerous conditions. Governors in New York and New Jersey declared states of emergency, urging residents to stay home. Massachusetts and New York closed major highways, while Amtrak and some train services operated on modified schedules. The storm tested the new mayor of New York City, Bill de Blasio, and posed challenges for Boston's outgoing mayor, Thomas Menino. Cold temperatures and wind chills could cause frostbite in just 30 minutes, prompting warnings to dress warmly. Snowplows and salt spreaders worked to clear roads, and outreach teams helped homeless individuals. The storm extended holiday breaks for some students and created a logjam in air travel schedules across the country.

A 25-year-old woman from Wyandotte gave birth in a bathroom at work and tried to hide the dead baby in her desk drawer, police said. The discovery was made at Ceva Logistics in Redford Township around 11:19 a.m. on Tuesday. Employees found blood in a bathroom stall and called 911. The woman, a temporary employee of Level Professional Services, was taken to a hospital, where the baby was pronounced dead. Police are investigating whether the mother is responsible for the baby's death and are awaiting autopsy results. The company offered grief counseling to its employees.

A charter school in San Antonio assigned a worksheet to middle school students asking them to list the "positive" and "negative" aspects of slavery, sparking outrage and an apology from the school. The assignment, titled "The Life of Slaves: A Balanced View," was posted on social media by a concerned parent. Great Hearts Monte Vista Charter School placed the teacher on leave and removed the textbook used for the assignment. The school plans to audit the textbook and provide additional lessons on the topic. Superintendent Aaron Kindel stated, "It was a clear mistake and we sincerely apologize for the insensitive nature of this offense." The incident has drawn attention from local lawmakers and educators, emphasizing the need for sensitive historical instruction.

Dunkin' Donuts is renaming itself "Dunkin'" to emphasize its focus on coffee and other beverages, starting in January. The change will appear on ads, packages, and signage at new and remodeled U.S. stores, as well as social media accounts. The company, which has over 12,500 global locations, aims to modernize its brand and appeal to younger customers by simplifying its menu and adding mobile ordering options. Beverages, especially coffee, now make up 60% of U.S. sales. Dunkin' tested the shortened name in California and Massachusetts before rolling it out company-wide. The company plans to open 1,000 new U.S. stores by the end of 2020.

Oracle Team USA secured an incredible comeback to win the America's Cup in a winner-take-all race, defeating Emirates Team New Zealand. Skipper James Spithill and his crew pulled off one of the most impressive comebacks in sailing history, overcoming an 8-1 deficit to win the best-of-17 series. Despite facing stiff penalties, Oracle's catamaran proved faster, especially as the competition progressed. The final race showcased Oracle's speed, with Spithill steering the boat past Dean Barker and his team. Oracle's victory, which included rallying from seven-point deficits, kept the America's Cup trophy in the United States.

In a controversial move, Michael Moore and MoveOn.Org have produced an ad featuring Mary J. Blige, Q-Tip, and Julianne Moore, calling on voters to re-elect President Obama. The ad, titled "Yes We Plan," highlights Obama's stance on women's rights and health care. However, the ad's message takes a dark turn, with one speaker threatening to "burn this mother f**ker down" if Romney wins, and another vowing to "give him the world's biggest c**k punch." The final speaker promises to "watch us all having sex," adding an unsettling tone to the campaign message.

Russian spy Anna Chapman posed provocatively in the Russian version of Maxim magazine, according to Reuters. The Kremlin has celebrated the case to boost the prestige of its intelligence services, despite the spy ring's failure to secure major intelligence before their arrests in the United States. Russian President Dmitry Medvedev awarded the group of spies the country's highest state honors. The photographs and an interview with Chapman will appear in the next issue of Maxim, which has included her in its list of Russia's 100 sexiest women.

Reality TV star Tila Tequila has shockingly embraced Nazi ideology, posting a photoshopped image of herself in front of Auschwitz with a swastika armband and SS uniform, calling herself "Hitila" in a new song. She claims to sympathize with Hitler, arguing his history was rewritten after World War II. Tequila also expresses anti-Semitic views, blaming Jews for worldwide genocide. Her sudden conversion from Judaism to Nazism has sparked outrage and confusion.

In Florida, over 7,000 lawsuits linked to smoking-related injuries and deaths continue, benefiting from the 2006 Engle ruling that established tobacco companies sold defective and unreasonably dangerous cigarettes. The latest verdict, from Bronson, Florida, awarded $80 million in damages, with $72 million in punitive damages, to the family of a two-pack-a-day smoker who died of lung cancer. The jury found R.J. Reynolds 90% at fault. This verdict reverses recent defense wins for the tobacco industry in Engle cases.

California has agreed to end its practice of isolating imprisoned gang leaders indefinitely, restricting a policy that kept hundreds of inmates in segregation for a decade or longer. This move, influenced by criticism from President Obama and Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy, aims to align California with more mainstream practices while still addressing security concerns. The settlement limits the duration of solitary confinement and introduces new restrictive custody units for inmates who refuse rehabilitation programs or repeatedly break rules. It also addresses the safety of inmates like 71-year-old Hugo Pinell, who was killed shortly after being released from isolation. The changes are part of a broader movement away from solitary confinement, with advocates hoping this will serve as an example for other states to follow.

Fox & Friends co-host Brian Kilmeade defended President Trump's border policies, stating that at least American children are not being separated from their parents. Kilmeade argued that someone needs to address the issue of illegal immigration and that migrants from other countries should not be prioritized over American citizens. MSNBC's Stephanie Ruhle criticized Kilmeade's comments, highlighting the inconsistency in his stance.

The U.S. is to provide non-lethal aid, including medical supplies and food, to the Syrian opposition for the first time, Secretary of State John Kerry announced at a meeting of the "Friends of Syria" group in Rome. This comes as the Obama administration doubles its support to the opposition’s civilian council, aiming to bolster their governance and services in rebel-controlled areas. The European Union has also amended its arms embargo to allow the supply of non-lethal military equipment to the rebels. However, the aid stops short of weapons, disappointing many in the opposition who argue that the lack of arms is hampering their ability to defeat government forces. Despite the new support, opposition leaders remain frustrated, with some postponing talks to choose a leader for a provisional government. The U.S. and its allies are now working to ensure that all countries providing aid are coordinating their efforts effectively.

A federal judge ruled that the District of Columbia and Maryland may proceed with a lawsuit against President Trump, alleging that his business dealings have violated the Constitution’s ban on receiving improper “emoluments” or payments from individual states and foreign governments. U.S. District Judge Peter J. Messitte in Maryland stated that the plaintiffs, Maryland Attorney General Brian E. Frosh and District of Columbia Attorney General Karl A. Racine, have legal standing to sue the president. The judge cited examples of government clients patronizing the Washington hotel, which the president continues to hold a financial interest in, potentially to the detriment of competitors and taxpayers. The ruling narrows the lawsuit’s scope to the Washington hotel and allows the plaintiffs to seek internal documents from the Trump Organization to determine how much money the hotel has taken in from state and foreign governments. The Justice Department, representing the president, did not immediately say whether it would appeal. Frosh and Racine plan to seek the president’s financial documents and tax returns as

Hundreds of thousands of Egyptians filled Cairo's Tahrir Square and other cities on Sunday, calling for the removal of Islamist President Mohammed Morsi on the anniversary of his one-year tenure. Opponents, waving flags and chanting "Leave!" demanded early elections and accused Morsi of failing to uphold democratic values. Meanwhile, Morsi's supporters, fearing violence, gathered in protective gear near the presidential palace. Both sides warned of potential clashes, with Morsi's opponents questioning his legitimacy and his supporters rejecting calls for compromise. The scale of the protests surpassed expectations, with tens of thousands more participating than initially predicted. As tensions escalated, the military remained a key player, with Defense Minister Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi hinting at possible intervention. The outcome of this confrontation could significantly shape Egypt's political future.

A Republican candidate for Maine's House of Representatives, Leslie Gibson, withdrew from the race after facing backlash for insulting Parkland shooting survivors Emma González and David Hogg. Gibson, who called González a "skinhead lesbian" and Hogg a "bald-faced liar," faced criticism from both Democrats and Republicans. In response, two other candidates, Democrat Eryn Gilchrist and Republican Thomas Martin Jr., entered the race. Gilchrist, in particular, decided to run because she was "horrified and embarrassed" at the prospect of Gibson representing her. Martin also entered the race after reading Gibson's comments. Gibson apologized to González but still stepped down, stating it was "the best thing for everybody."

San Francisco's Millennium Tower, which has sunk 17 inches and tilted 14 inches since 2006, now faces another significant issue: a large crack in a window on the 36th floor. The crack, discovered over the Labor Day weekend, has prompted officials to require building engineers to assess the extent of repairs needed and investigate the condition of the glass panel and adjacent curtain wall system by September 7, 2018. The crack, which residents heard creaking and popping sounds before appearing, raises concerns about the building's stability. City Supervisor Aaron Peskin notes that the window, designed to withstand hurricane force winds, could pose a safety hazard if it were to fail completely. The crack has led to the temporary closure of part of the sidewalk below the tower. The issue adds to a long list of problems for the 58-story building, including ongoing lawsuits from residents and questions about who is responsible for the sinking and tilting.

Ten volunteer firefighters from Fairmont and Orrum, along with a Maxton police officer and a Department of Corrections worker, have been arrested for setting numerous fires in abandoned homes and woods in Robeson County over a two-year period. The charges include 90 arson-related counts and more are expected. Sheriff Ken Sealey stated that the investigation began after a tip and has involved the Robeson County Sheriff's Office, State Bureau of Investigation, Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, and the NC Forestry Service. Each defendant faces various counts of arson and conspiracy, with bond amounts ranging from $100,000 to $200,000. The fires have cost taxpayers thousands of dollars in response costs.

A low dose of the antidepressant fluoxetine, found in sewage from human use, can make female starlings less attractive to males, according to a study in the journal Current Biology. Male starlings sang less and were more aggressive towards fluoxetine-treated females compared to controls. The drug had no effect on female courtship behavior or reproductive physiology. This suggests that environmental concentrations of pharmaceuticals can alter important traits related to individual fitness and population dynamics in wildlife.

A new study reveals that modern sperm whales may have descended from a single female, challenging our understanding of their genetic diversity. Analyzing mitochondrial DNA from 1,633 whales, researchers found low genetic diversity, hinting at a single "Eve" whale who lived around 80,000 years ago. This finding, published in Molecular Ecology, suggests that despite sperm whales' large size and global distribution, their genetic makeup is surprisingly homogeneous. The study also highlights the interplay of natural selection, genetic drift, geographic isolation, and mating systems in shaping genetic diversity. Female philopatry, or the tendency for females to stay in their birth social groups, appears to play a significant role in sperm whale genetics, though its importance varies by ocean and social group. This research underscores the vulnerability of sperm whale populations to environmental changes and the need for broader social interactions to maintain genetic diversity.

More than 150,000 gallons of water tainted with toxic firefighting chemicals was released into the Colorado Springs Utilities sewer system from a Peterson Air Force Base training area, raising concerns about potential contamination downstream. The discharge, discovered on October 12, contained perfluorinated compounds, linked to health issues like kidney and liver damage and cancer. The chemicals flowed through the wastewater treatment plant and into Fountain Creek, potentially affecting communities downstream. The Air Force is investigating the cause, but the chemicals are not regulated, and the plant lacks the capacity to remove them. Colorado Springs Utilities confirmed there was no immediate threat to drinking water, but residents in affected areas are concerned about long-term health impacts.

Former President George W. Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney appeared together for the first time since leaving office to celebrate the groundbreaking of the George W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum on the Southern Methodist University campus in Dallas. The event, attended by hundreds of Bush administration alumni, marked a return to the public stage for Bush, who has been largely out of the spotlight since 2009. Bush emphasized his commitment to advancing the causes of human freedom, global health, economic growth, and education reform through the library and a new public policy institute. Cheney, appearing gaunt and frail after heart surgery, praised Bush’s leadership and defended the administration’s record. Both men reaffirmed their friendship despite their final disagreement over the pardon of former chief of staff I. Lewis Libby.

SkyMall, the in-flight shopping catalog that once offered novelty items like garden gnomes and cat beds, has filed for bankruptcy, blaming the rise of e-commerce and the shift to electronic devices among travelers. The company, which generated about $15.8 million in revenue in the first nine months of 2014, saw its business decline as passengers increasingly turned to their smartphones and laptops for entertainment. With contracts from major airlines like Delta and Southwest expiring, SkyMall struggled to compete with the convenience and lower prices offered by online retailers. Despite its quirky and often absurd product offerings, SkyMall became a nostalgic comfort for unaccompanied children and a tradition for families during holidays. Its bankruptcy marks the end of an era for in-flight retail, as the industry continues to adapt to the digital age.

Rescuers are committed to ensuring the safe extraction of 12 boys and their soccer coach from a flooded cave in northern Thailand, with no risks taken, according to an official. The boys and coach, aged between 11 and 16, and their 25-year-old coach were found alive after 10 days trapped inside the cave on July 3. Seven divers, including a doctor and a nurse, joined the group inside the caves. Authorities are considering how best to bring the group to safety, with the governor stating, "Whoever has zero risk first can leave the cave first." More heavy rain could see water levels rise and threaten the air pocket where the group has taken refuge. The boys have received their first food and medical treatment in 10 days, with none in serious condition. Rescuers are also providing entertainment and keeping the boys occupied. The Thai military says the boys would need to learn to dive or wait up to four months for flooding to

A new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found no direct link between antidepressant use during pregnancy and an increased risk of heart defects in babies. The research, which analyzed data from nearly a million women, contradicts previous studies that suggested early prenatal exposure to certain antidepressants, particularly paroxetine (Paxil), might increase the risk of heart malformations. The latest findings were based on a more focused approach, considering various factors that could interfere with the data. The study, which included data from 46 U.S. states and Washington, D.C., from 2000 to 2007, aimed to re-examine the evidence and found that while antidepressants are commonly used by pregnant women, there is no significant association with heart defects in infants.

Howard Stern believes that Donald Trump will struggle as president, considering it potentially detrimental to Trump's mental health. Stern, a longtime friend of Trump despite political differences, suggests Trump's desire for people to cheer for him may be at odds with the realities of the presidency. Trump has frequently appeared on Stern's radio show, engaging in crude discussions typical of the shock-jock's program. Stern, an advocate for Hillary Clinton, recalls a time when Trump supported her and doubts the sincerity of his political shifts. He also criticizes Trump's recent hostility towards Hollywood and the media, noting that such attitudes are not beneficial for a president.

The parents of a 3-year-old girl who went missing after being left outside have hired attorneys and are no longer cooperating with investigators, according to an attorney. Sini Mathews, the girl's mother, is "distraught" over her daughter's disappearance, her attorney Kent Starr said. The parents have two attorneys to avoid any potential conflict of interest. The girl, named Sherin Mathews, was reportedly last seen at 3 a.m. by her father, Wesley Mathews, who told investigators she was left outside to stand by a tree after not drinking her milk. Mathews was arrested Saturday on a child endangerment charge and released on $250,000 bond. The girl's mother was reportedly asleep during the incident and is not facing charges. The FBI and Richardson police have been searching the area and seized three vehicles from the family. An Amber Alert was issued but later discontinued. Sherin is still considered missing, and the search continues.

Los Angeles has become the largest U.S. city to raise its minimum wage to $15 an hour, passing a bill by a 14-1 vote. The city council's decision, part of a broader national effort to reduce poverty, will see the minimum wage increase to $10.50 in July 2016, with gradual increases reaching $15 by July 2020. Small businesses with 25 or fewer employees will have a modified schedule. Opponents warn of potential job losses and higher prices. The move follows similar actions in Seattle and San Francisco, with New York and Chicago also considering $15 minimum wage proposals. Advocates hope the increase will improve the lives of low-wage workers and set a national precedent.

The Baltimore Ravens expressed deep gratitude towards NFL officials following a crucial game, as they benefited from several key calls that secured their victory. Key moments included a controversial pass interference call that gave the Ravens a critical first down, and a questionable holding penalty on the opposing team that set up a game-winning field goal. These officiating decisions were seen as pivotal in the Ravens' 27-24 win, which not only secured their playoff spot but also highlighted the significant impact of officiating in high-stakes games.

More than 40 people were injured, including seven high school students and one teacher who died, after an avalanche struck during a climbing event near Nasu Onsen ski resort north of Tokyo. The incident occurred as 40 students and eight teachers from seven high schools were training in accumulated snow. Avalanche warnings were in effect due to heavy snowfall and rising temperatures. Rescue efforts were hampered by bad weather, and the self-defense force was called in to assist. The climbing trip, part of a three-day event, was scheduled to end about two and a half hours after the avalanche. An investigation is underway to determine if the deaths resulted from professional negligence.

At a House Oversight Committee hearing, the deputy director of the White House’s Office of National Drug Control Policy, Michael Botticelli, faced questioning about the harms of marijuana in comparison to alcohol and prescription drugs. Rep. Gerry Connolly (D-VA) pointed out that marijuana-related deaths are very rare, while alcohol and prescription drugs cause hundreds of thousands of deaths annually. Botticelli admitted that marijuana is less deadly than these substances but maintained that it is still a dangerous drug. Despite President Obama’s recent comments suggesting that marijuana is not as harmful as alcohol, the administration remains opposed to state-based efforts to legalize marijuana, stating that the Department of Justice’s responsibility to enforce the Controlled Substances Act remains unchanged. The hearing highlighted the ongoing conflict between federal drug policy and state-level legalization efforts, as well as concerns about the disparate impact of federal enforcement policies on minorities.

Researchers have developed sperm-inspired micro-robots that can be controlled using magnetic fields, reports Live Science. These tiny devices, about six times longer than a human sperm, consist of a flexible body and a metal-coated head. By applying a magnetic field, the robots can be made to "swim" forward and steered towards a fixed point. This technology could have applications in medical fields such as targeted drug delivery and in vitro fertilization. The robots, created using a simple fabrication method, could potentially be miniaturized further for even more precise tasks.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has turned to Serbian horse placenta healer Marijana Kovacevic to address his team's injury crisis, with defenders Glen Johnson and Fabio Aurelio among the latest high-profile players to travel to Belgrade for treatment. Kovacevic, whose methods have gained significant attention following Arsenal striker Robin van Persie's visit, now works on a recommendation basis and charges up to €3,000 for her unorthodox therapy, which involves horse placenta fluids and electrolysis. Despite skepticism, Benitez has placed his trust in Kovacevic, with other clubs reportedly giving their blessing to players seeking her help. The Liverpool manager faces ongoing concerns over injuries to key players, including Steven Gerrard and Fernando Torres, as the team struggles to maintain form.

Indian customs officials investigating a bomb scare at Kolkata's international airport found 12 gold bars hidden in lunch boxes in the toilets of a Jet Airways plane, triggering a smuggling probe. The gold bars, each weighing 1 kg, were worth 73.68 million rupees ($1.18 million). The plane had arrived from Patna but usually operates between Dubai and Mumbai, a key gold trading hub. Customs officials say five cases involving 100 kg of gold have been detected over two months. They believe they catch only about 10% of the total smuggling, with many groups evading detection. The finance minister acknowledged a slight rise in smuggling but noted that no one can bring in more than 5 kg of gold without being detected. Airport staff are now on alert for passengers lingering in the loo and educating themselves on aircraft maps to spot suspicious behavior.

A teenager, Shana Grice, was murdered by her ex-boyfriend, Michael Lane, after repeatedly complaining to police about his stalking and harassment. Despite multiple reports, including one where she was given a fixed penalty notice for wasting police time, Lane was not held accountable. On the day of her death, Grice reported receiving heavy-breathing calls, but the case was left on file. Lane denies murder, claiming he found Grice's body and did not know it was dead. He admits to leaving a note and installing a tracker but denies setting the room on fire. The trial continues, with Lane admitting to lying in previous police interviews.

Oklahoma congressional candidate Tim Murray has contested the primary election victory of incumbent Representative Frank Lucas, claiming that Lucas is a look-alike and was executed in Ukraine. Murray's campaign website details his theory, but Lucas's office confirms his continued existence. Murray received only 5.2% of the vote, while Lucas won with 82.8%. The Oklahoma State Election Board is monitoring the situation, with Murray having until 5 p.m. to file a formal petition. Murray's claims echo the plot of the 1993 movie "Dave," and he contrasts his candidacy with the use of look-alikes.

Meet Mark Block, Herman Cain's top adviser and the newest YouTube sensation in the 2012 presidential campaign. Block stars in a bizarre 5-10 second video, puffing on a cigarette as he speaks patriotically about Cain's campaign. "We’ve run a campaign like nobody’s ever seen," Block says, before revealing the smoking shot that has sparked debate. The video ends with a close-up of Herman Cain smiling. Block's campaign defense? "There was no subliminal message. In fact, I personally would encourage people not to smoke." However, the smoking scene has raised questions about its purpose and whether it was a deliberate marketing move or a spontaneous decision.

Decades-old DNA led to the arrests of two men in connection with the shotgun slayings of two girls in California over 40 years ago. Authorities arrested Larry Don Patterson, 65, in Oklahoma and William Lloyd Harbour, 65, in California after comparing their DNA with semen found on one of the victims, 13-year-old Doris Karen Derryberry. The 12-year-old Valerie Janice Lane was also killed. The girls were reported missing after failing to return from a shopping trip in 1973. Their bodies were found shot at close range in a wooded area near Marysville. Both men will face murder charges. The case remained unsolved until 2014 when DNA testing linked the suspects to the victims.

A petition aimed at Electronic Arts (EA) to counter anti-gay boycott groups was hit with spam attacks, with duplicate comments and fake signatures flooding the AllOut.org website. The petition, supporting the inclusion of gay characters in EA games, received over 60,000 legitimate signatures but was temporarily disabled due to the spam. AllOut.org denied any contact with EA and stated their campaign was to support EA's decision to include LGBT options in their games. The organization is investigating the source of the spam, with no evidence pointing to EA or any coordinated effort. Despite skepticism from some, AllOut.org insists they acted independently and are focused on raising awareness for LGBT rights.

Authorities in Davidson, North Carolina, are reexamining the death of Sarah Catherine Long, initially ruled a suicide, after uncovering inconsistencies. Long was found dead on July 23 with a gunshot wound to her left temple, and a .357 Taurus revolver in her left hand, despite being right-handed. A search warrant revealed that Long's lover, William Becker, produced documents showing she left him her $1 million fortune. Neighbors reported hearing a loud noise and seeing Long with a man on July 19, the last day she was seen alive. Long's doctor confirmed she did not have cervical cancer, contradicting Becker's claims. Police are investigating whether Long was drugged and are awaiting forensic results. No arrests have been made, and a person of interest is under scrutiny.

Saudi media outlets Al-Hayat and Sabq.org mistakenly reported a satirical column by Andy Borowitz, believing that President Obama admitted to Congress he is Muslim. Borowitz's joke suggested Obama might be willing to concede his birthplace is negotiable. Despite Obama's repeated statements of being Christian, the article notes that many suspect him of being secretly Muslim. Both newspapers picked up the humorous "quote," leading to confusion.

Stay away from microwaves, iPhone users. The newly released iOS 8, despite its impressive features like app extensions and improved keyboard options, does not allow wireless charging via microwave, as a 4chan hoax suggested. Fake "Wave" ads on Twitter and Reddit have misled some into trying to charge their phones in the microwave for 60 to 70 seconds, potentially damaging their devices. While it's unclear how many fell for the prank, several people posted photos of damaged iPhones and burned microwaves, likely as jokes.

The World Health Organization (WHO) declared Cuba the first country globally to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV and syphilis. In 2013, only two children in Cuba were born with HIV, and five with syphilis. Cuba's success highlights the feasibility of universal access and health coverage in achieving such public health goals. The WHO and Pan American Health Organization credit Cuba's early prenatal care, HIV and syphilis testing, and treatment for infected mothers as key factors. This achievement encourages other countries to redouble their efforts in preventing mother-to-child transmission of these diseases.

A Minnesota doctor, Dr. Michael Todd Schulenberg, treated Prince twice in the month before his death, including the day before he was found unconscious in an elevator at Paisley Park. Search warrants revealed Schulenberg's involvement and that he prescribed Prince medications, though the specific drugs are unknown. Schulenberg no longer works at the North Memorial Medical Center where he treated Prince. Authorities are investigating whether Prince died from an overdose and whether a doctor was prescribing him drugs in the weeks leading up to his death. A search warrant was carried out at North Memorial Medical Center, and investigators also interviewed Kirk Anthony Johnson, a close associate of Prince's who was present when Prince's body was found. The investigation continues, with no foul play or suicide suspected.

The Instant Pot, a multi-functional kitchen appliance that combines the features of a pressure cooker, slow cooker, rice cooker, and yogurt maker, has become a top-selling product on Amazon, both in Canada and the U.S. Its success is attributed to its ability to provide quick, healthy, and convenient meal solutions for busy families. Inventor Robert Wang, a former Nortel engineer, developed the Instant Pot to address the time-crunch faced by modern-day cooks. The device's smart features, including pressure sensors and a microprocessor, ensure that food is cooked perfectly without the risk of burning or exploding. Despite its technical advancements, the Instant Pot's popularity is largely driven by word-of-mouth and the enthusiasm of its user community, which has grown to over 750,000 members on Facebook. The appliance's versatility, from making risotto to cooking beans, has made it a must-have for many home cooks. As the Instant Pot continues to evolve with new functions and features

A man arrested in Nicaragua is suspected of killing 22-year-old nursing student Haley Anderson from Long Island. Orlando Tercero, Anderson's ex-boyfriend, was detained after allegedly fleeing the U.S. via a flight from JFK to Nicaragua. Police found Anderson's body during a welfare check at a home near her college campus. The circumstances of her death remain unclear, but authorities believe Tercero had a previous romantic relationship with Anderson. His arrest and transfer to a Nicaraguan prison are part of an ongoing investigation.

India's foreign ministry has lodged a complaint with Saudi Arabian authorities following an alleged "brutal" attack on a 58-year-old Indian domestic worker in Riyadh. Kasturi Munirathinam's right arm was reportedly amputated by her Saudi employer after she complained to police about harassment and poor treatment. Munirathinam is recovering in a hospital, and her family is seeking compensation and medical expenses from the Saudi family. Indian Foreign Minister Sushma Swaraj expressed strong disapproval, stating that such treatment is unacceptable and that the Indian embassy is in contact with the victim. The family claims Munirathinam was not allowed to speak to her relatives, was forced to work long hours, and was not given proper food. The incident has drawn attention to the widespread abuse and poor treatment faced by Indian domestic workers in the Middle East.

Electronic road signs in the Dallas area were hacked, displaying messages related to the 2016 presidential race and work cancellations. Messages included "Donald Trump is a shape-shifting lizard," "Bernie for president," and "Work is canceled. Go back home." The signs, typically used for construction warnings, were altered by someone who manually changed the messages at the control panels. Texas Department of Transportation officials say hacking these signs is a third-degree felony and can result in prison time. The signs were found along Interstate 30 and nearby roads in west Dallas.

Rescue efforts in the aftermath of a massive mudslide in Washington state have yielded no more signs of life, officials said Sunday. The slide, which killed at least eight people and destroyed dozens of homes, left many people missing. Authorities confirmed eight dead during a community meeting, raising the death toll from four the previous day. Searchers heard voices from buried structures on Saturday night but heard no more on Sunday. Emergency officials said they were working off a "soft list" of 108 unaccounted-for individuals, though the actual number of victims is likely lower. The slide, spanning nearly a square mile, buried a mile-long stretch of Highway 530 under 20 feet of mud. With no positive news, relatives of the missing gathered at the Darrington Community Center, handing photos to rescue personnel in hopes of finding unconscious survivors. The mudslide, caused by saturated ground from heavy rain, also critically injured several people, including an infant. Authorities warned of potential downstream

A 18-year-old hiker named Chloe Jakubowski and others were injured when ice and debris collapsed in the Big Four Ice Caves in Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. Jakubowski, along with friends, was inside the cave when a loud crack and subsequent icefall scattered visitors. Jakubowski helped others and suffered minor injuries. Rescue efforts were delayed for 45 minutes due to poor cellphone reception. One person died, and five were injured, with three adults in critical and serious conditions, and two girls with minor injuries. The cave area remains closed indefinitely due to dangerous conditions, as warm weather weakens the caves. Authorities warn that the caves are prone to collapse and advise visitors to stay on the trail.

A team from Point Loma Nazarene University (PLNU) is raising $40,000 to fund a scholarship for survivors of human trafficking through a crowdfunding campaign. The campaign, named "The Beauty for Ashes Fund," aims to provide a college education as a means of long-term rehabilitation. Sex and labor trafficking have reached epidemic proportions, with PLNU's Center for Justice and Reconciliation working to address this issue. The university believes that a Christian education can transform survivors from victims to thrivers. The funds will primarily cover tuition, room, and board, with smaller portions allocated for vocational discernment and administrative support. Donations are tax deductible, and the campaign will fund students as early as September 2015. PLNU encourages supporters to share the campaign on social media and contact them for more ways to get involved.

U.S. fighter jets and drones conducted airstrikes against ISIS targets in northern Iraq, marking the first direct military action against the militant group since the capture of Iraq's second-largest city. The strikes, which targeted ISIS artillery units and a convoy near the Kurdish regional capital of Irbil, came as the group also seized control of Iraq's largest hydroelectric dam. The U.S. also carried out airdrops of food and water to stranded Yazidis on Mount Sinjar, while officials welcomed the U.S. intervention, calling for greater international involvement to confront the crisis. President Obama authorized the airstrikes to protect American personnel and prevent potential genocide, but emphasized there would be no buildup of U.S. combat troops in Iraq.

Buffalo Bills wide receiver Stevie Johnson sparked controversy by joking that North Korea should target Foxboro, Massachusetts, home of the New England Patriots, if they were to launch a nuclear attack. His tweets drew criticism from Patriots fans but also highlighted the lack of serious concern many Americans have regarding North Korea's nuclear threats. Johnson later apologized, stating he had respect for all NFL teams.

In a recent survey, one in three Americans admitted to lying about money to their spouses, while another third said they had been deceived. The survey, commissioned by ForbesWoman and the National Endowment for Financial Education (NEFE) and conducted by Harris Interactive, found that the leading money crimes were hiding cash, minor purchases, and bills. Significant numbers of people admitted to hiding major purchases, keeping secret bank accounts, and lying about debt or earnings. Financial infidelity can lead to arguments, less trust, and in severe cases, divorce or separation. Experts warn that small lies often compound over time, causing significant damage to relationships. The issue of financial infidelity affects people across all income levels, and some experts suggest that having more money can lead to more elaborate schemes. Financial experts advise couples to have open money talks early in their relationship and use tax season as a nonthreatening way to gain a better grasp of shared finances.

A Houston restaurant customer was asked to leave after calling a bartender a "twerp" on Twitter, marking one of the first instances of a diner being ejected for online behavior. The incident at Down House involved Allison Matsu, who posted a negative tweet during her visit. General Manager Forrest DeSpain, who runs the restaurant's Twitter account, called Matsu and asked her to leave. Matsu responded with a series of tweets expressing her distress. The case raises questions about the importance of physical versus virtual patrons to a restaurant's reputation and operations.

A "Put 'Em in a Coffin" prank gone wrong left a Houston man's BMW with a $4,000 repair bill. The latest internet meme involves teenagers doing a backward dive onto cars, causing damage. James McHugh's home security camera captured seven young men jumping on his white BMW and his wife's car at Plaza del Sol Park. "You work hard, and then to have that much money washed away for 10 seconds of laughter," McHugh said, expressing frustration over the incident.

The only US soldier known to still be living in North Korea after defecting more than five decades ago, James Joseph Dresnok, died last year, pledging his loyalty to "great leader Kim Jong-un," his sons have said. Dresnok, who crossed the demilitarized zone in 1962, was among a handful of American servicemen to desert following the Korean War. His sons, appearing in a video on the state-run Uriminzokkiri website, confirmed their father had a fatal stroke in November. They expressed devotion to Kim Jong-un and warned against US military threats, stating that North Korea would "wipe the land of the US from the earth for ever" if war breaks out. Dresnok's sons, born in North Korea, also highlighted his satisfaction with life in Pyongyang, where citizens enjoy better standards of living compared to other parts of the isolated country.

In a groundbreaking study, researchers found microplastics in the stool samples of eight individuals from around the world, indicating that microplastics are likely widespread in the human food chain. Every participant tested positive for microplastics, with an average of 20 particles per 10 grams of stool. The study, led by Dr. Philipp Schwabl from the Medical University of Vienna, detected up to nine different types of plastic particles ranging from 50 to 500 micrometers. Commonly found plastics included polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate, often used in plastic bottles and packaging. Participants reported consuming plastic-wrapped foods and drinking from plastic bottles, suggesting these as sources of exposure. The study highlights the need for further research to understand the health implications of microplastics in the human gut, as they could affect the immune response and potentially transmit toxic chemicals or pathogens.

Dennis Rodman, the controversial former NBA player, is back in North Korea, drawing attention for his frequent visits to the reclusive country. Rodman, who calls North Korean leader Kim Jong Un his "friend for life," is traveling as a private citizen and says his purpose is to promote sports and open doors. His trips have been criticized for potentially undermining US safety warnings and for his failure to address human rights issues. US Under Secretary of State Thomas Shannon expressed concern, stating that the US wishes Rodman well but advises against travel to North Korea for safety reasons. Rodman's latest visit comes during heightened tensions between the US and North Korea, and he hopes his presence can help bridge the gap between the two countries.

U.S. President Barack Obama and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continue to navigate a complex and often contentious relationship, particularly regarding the ongoing negotiations with Iran over its nuclear program. Obama defends his diplomatic efforts, emphasizing the potential for a deal that would significantly constrain Iran’s nuclear capabilities, while Netanyahu warns of the dangers of a "bad deal" that could allow Iran to develop nuclear weapons. The upcoming speech by Netanyahu to a joint meeting of Congress is expected to highlight these differences, with critics arguing it could undermine the Iran talks and damage U.S.-Israeli relations. Despite tensions, both leaders acknowledge the importance of maintaining a strategic alliance, with Obama expressing a desire to see the talks succeed while Netanyahu remains skeptical of any agreement. The high-stakes negotiations, involving the United States, Iran, and other world powers, continue to shape the broader geopolitical landscape in the Middle East.

Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto announced plans to overhaul municipal police forces, facing criticism over the disappearance of 43 trainee teachers in Iguala. The plan includes putting local police units under federal control, dissolving them if infiltrated by drug cartels, and establishing a single nationwide emergency number. The reforms will initially target four violent states: Guerrero, Michoacan, Jalisco, and Tamaulipas. Pena Nieto's measures follow public outrage over the students' disappearance and the alleged involvement of local police and the mayor.

Ex-Pirelli model Christina Estrada secured a record-breaking £75 million divorce settlement from her Saudi businessman ex-husband Sheikh Walid Juffali after arguing for "reasonable needs" including luxury homes and cars. Estrada, 54, claimed she needed £1 million annually for clothes, including £40,000 for fur coats and £109,000 for haute couture dresses. Juffali, worth an estimated £8 billion, denied the extravagant claims, stating his net worth was closer to £113.8 million. The settlement, including assets worth £22 million, still fell short of Estrada's initial £309,000 request.

The European Chess Union (ECU) has implemented a dress code for chess tournaments, addressing concerns about players' attire during games. General Secretary Sava Stoisavljevic explains that the rules, which include restrictions on décolletage and short skirts, aim to maintain a professional appearance and avoid distractions. While some players and spectators have commented on the new regulations, no player has reported being distracted. The ECU's dress code for women chess players includes rules on shirt buttons and skirt length, with penalties for non-compliance, such as exclusion from prize-giving ceremonies. The rules are part of a broader effort to improve the image of chess and ensure players adhere to a code of casual dressing appropriate for the sport.

The House Oversight Committee has denied a request from the White House for more information on payments made to former national security adviser Michael Flynn from foreign governments, including the Kremlin-backed RT and other Russian firms. The White House claims it does not have all the documents, but the committee chairman and ranking Democrat suggest Flynn may have violated federal law by not disclosing these payments when seeking his security clearance. Flynn is under investigation for possible ties to Russia and is facing scrutiny over his financial disclosures and communications with foreign officials. The Oversight Committee is pressing for more transparency and accountability, while the White House maintains it has provided all requested documents.

The world's longest and highest glass-bottom bridge is set to open next month in Zhangjiajie, Hunan, China, offering thrill-seekers panoramic views from nearly 1,000 feet above the ground. This bridge, spanning over 1,400 feet and 20 feet wide, can accommodate up to 800 people at once. To reassure safety concerns, the bridge's creators invited BBC reporter Dan Simmons to test the panels by striking them with a sledgehammer, which showed no structural damage. Plans include adding a bungee jump, making it the world's highest once completed. The bridge, designed by Israeli architect Haim Dotan, aims to attract visitors to the scenic Wulingyuan area, which inspired the movie Avatar.

One of the strongest earthquakes in modern Caribbean history struck off the coast of Honduras on Tuesday night, triggering tsunami warnings that were later cancelled. The magnitude 7.6 quake, felt across northern Central America, caused no immediate damage or casualties. Shaking was reported in Honduras, Mexico, and other nearby areas, with some homes experiencing cracks. Tsunami advisories were issued for several Caribbean islands and Central American coasts but no significant waves were observed. The earthquake, one of the largest in the region's recorded history, was centered in the sea about 125 miles north-northeast of Barra Patuca, Honduras, and 188 miles southwest of George Town, Cayman Islands, at a depth of 6 miles.

Exiled filmmaker Roman Polanski is seeking to unseal secret testimony that could potentially end his decades-old child rape case and allow him to return to the United States, his lawyer, Harland Braun, told The Post. Polanski's plea deal with the original Los Angeles prosecutor, Roger Gunson, included a 42-day stay at Chino State Prison, but Judge Laurence Rittenband later changed his mind and ordered Polanski to serve up to 50 years. Polanski fled the U.S. and has lived in Paris since 1978. In 2009, he was captured in Switzerland and spent over 300 days in jail as U.S. authorities tried to extradite him. Braun now wants the court to honor the original plea deal and allow Polanski to travel freely.

Searchers investigating signals detected by a Chinese ship and an Australian naval vessel are treating the leads cautiously, as they have found no confirmation that the signals are from the missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. The Chinese ship Haixun 01 reported picking up signals twice on Friday and Saturday, while the Australian vessel Ocean Shield is pursuing a separate acoustic noise. Authorities say the signals are "an important and encouraging lead," but urge caution as they continue to search a vast area in the southern Indian Ocean. Up to 10 military planes, two civil aircraft, and 13 ships will assist in Sunday's search, focusing on three separate areas northwest of Perth. The race against time intensifies as the batteries on the plane's black boxes are predicted to run out soon, with day 30 marking the critical point.

American manufacturing faces an identity crisis, as many iconic products are no longer strictly "Made in the U.S.A." Despite 61% of Americans preferring to buy American-made items, only 75% of consumed goods are actually produced domestically. This discrepancy raises questions about the true "American" status of brands like Budweiser, Coors, Chevrolet Silverado, and Levi's, which have significant foreign ties. Even seemingly American products like American Girl dolls and Craftsman tools often have components or production lines abroad. The Chevrolet Silverado and Ford F-150, while partially assembled in the U.S., rely on global supply chains. Rawlings baseballs, while long-standing, manufacture their products in Costa Rica. Levi's, once a symbol of American craftsmanship, now sources its jeans from multiple countries. American Girl dolls, owned by Mattel, produce their products in China. Craftsman tools, once a proud American brand, now label some products as "Made in China."

A 30-year-old Maryland man faces murder charges after accidentally shooting his friend during a test of a bulletproof vest, a video of the incident shows. Mark Ramiro shot Darnell Mitchell, 28, who had been bragging he was about to take a "deuce deuce in the chest" before the fatal shot. Mitchell suffered a gunshot wound above the vest and died at the hospital. Ramiro is charged with first- and second-degree murder and weapons violations. The shooting was recorded by a third person's video camera in the basement of Ramiro's home.

The FBI profile of Adam Lanza, released in 2014, reveals that he meticulously planned the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, which occurred on December 14, 2012, over 21 months. Lanza, who weighed only 111 pounds at the time of his death, had an "extremely rigid and inflexible worldview" and was described as lonely and socially awkward. He communicated with an unidentified woman online for over two years, during which he expressed a fascination with past shootings and documented mass killers in a spreadsheet. Lanza's relationship with his mother, Nancy, deteriorated significantly in the weeks leading up to the attack, with Nancy noting that Adam had not left his room for three months and only communicated via email. The FBI found no evidence that Lanza viewed the shooting as a video game. His interest in children, categorized as pedophilia, was noted but not linked to any actions. Lanza's online communications also revealed his dissatisfaction

In a dramatic turn of events, a graphic designer named Lilian Lepère, who had taken refuge inside a printing facility in Dammartin-en-Goele, northeast of Paris, provided crucial information to police that helped end the standoff with the Charlie Hebdo attackers. Lepère, hiding under a sink in the canteen, sent text messages with tactical details to the authorities, allowing them to plan the assault. Meanwhile, in Paris, a separate hostage situation unfolded at a kosher supermarket where Amedy Coulibaly held several people captive. The siege ended with the deaths of both attackers, but four hostages also lost their lives. The operation to neutralize the suspects involved intense negotiations and a coordinated effort by security forces, leading to the resolution of both crises.

In her first public update in over three months, Jahi McMath's mother, Nailah Winkfield, shared a photo on Facebook, stating that Jahi is "as healthy and beautiful as ever, proving the naysayers wrong." Winkfield thanked supporters for their prayers and love, adding that Jahi is a "fighter, A warrior, A blessed child." The family moved Jahi to an unidentified long-term care facility in New Jersey in 2014, where she has been on life support since being declared brain dead in 2013. Jahi's case drew intense media attention and raised awareness about brain death. Winkfield's family is suing the hospital for allegedly botched surgery and pressuring them to donate Jahi's organs.

A class-action lawsuit has been filed against Spin Master over the popular holiday toy Hatchimals, which failed to hatch for many children. The lawsuit, filed by Jodie Hejduk on behalf of a class of affected consumers, alleges that the toy did not function as advertised and was part of a "bait-and-switch marketing scheme." Spin Master released Hatchimals in October 2016, and the toys quickly became highly sought after, leading to long lines and inflated prices on secondary markets. However, many parents reported that their children's toys did not hatch, leading to frustration and disappointment. Spin Master responded by providing troubleshooting support and replacement products for some consumers, but the lawsuit claims the company failed to adequately address the issues. The case highlights the challenges of managing high demand and the potential consequences when a product fails to meet expectations.
