Ramer, a member of the Poarch Creek Band of Indians, wore the feather despite not signing the contract. Other Native seniors faced different outcomes: one wore a feather necklace without issue, while the other two did not wear a feather at all. Ramer was not given her diploma and had to turn in her cap and gown. She spoke with the interim headmaster, who said he would give her the diploma if it were up to him, but it requires board approval. The school's actions have drawn criticism from the community and a former teacher.

President Obama's push for the American Jobs Act has faced significant challenges, including a lack of bipartisan support and internal Democratic opposition. Despite claiming the bill was non-controversial and supported by both parties, the reality is that Democrats in the House and Senate are hesitant to raise taxes on wealthier Americans and corporations, especially as they face re-election in 13 months. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid prioritized a bill to punish China over currency valuation, indicating a shift in legislative focus. The White House's strategy of blaming Congress for the economic situation has backfired, as Democrats are now bailing on the president. This shift reflects a broader re-evaluation of Obama's approach, moving away from his initial efforts to engage with business and Republicans towards a more populist stance. The article highlights the political challenges Obama faces as he attempts to revive his economic agenda ahead of the 2012 elections.

A car plowed into a group of children outside a primary school in Huludao, northeastern China, on Thursday, killing five and injuring 18, a local government spokesman said. The driver was taken into custody after the crash around noon. Security camera footage showed the vehicle swerving into a line of children crossing the street in front of their school. The cause is under investigation. In recent years, China has faced several deadly attacks at schools and other public places, often carried out by individuals with mental health issues or a desire to settle scores.

A large U.S. study using data from 17 states found that farmers, lumberjacks, and fishermen had the highest suicide rates, while librarians and educators had the lowest. The highest rates were seen in manual laborers working in isolation and facing unstable employment, such as carpenters, miners, and electricians. In contrast, health care professionals had an 80% lower suicide rate compared to the highest-risk occupations. The study, based on 2012 data, highlights significant differences in suicide rates across various occupations, emphasizing the need for targeted prevention strategies.

"The Mummy," the first in Universal's "Dark Universe" franchise, is a bloated, convoluted mess that fails to live up to its classic 1932 predecessor. Directed by Alex Kurtzman and written by a team including David Koepp, the film is a hodgepodge of borrowed elements from other horror and sci-fi movies, including "American Werewolf in London," "Lifeforce," and "Evil Dead." Tom Cruise stars as Nick Morton, a tomb raider who uncovers the sarcophagus of the mummy Ahmanet (Sofia Boutella), setting off a series of chase scenes and supernatural events. Russell Crowe plays Dr. Henry Jekyll, a character who struggles to serve multiple roles within the story. Despite the star power and potential for thrilling action sequences, the film's convoluted plot and lackluster chemistry between Cruise and co-star Annabelle Wallis make it a forgettable entry in the franchise

Starting May 23, new California lawyers will swear to be courteous and dignified, as part of a revised oath approved by the California Supreme Court. The change, proposed by the American Board of Trial Advocates and the State Bar of California, adds a civility pledge to the existing constitutional support and professional duty oath. The new requirement aims to remind lawyers to conduct themselves with dignity, courtesy, and integrity, particularly in dealings with clients, other attorneys, and judges. While some critics question its effectiveness, proponents believe it will serve as a general reminder of positive professional behavior.

Sally Struthers, best known for her role as Gloria Stivic in "All in the Family" and later for charity ads, has been arrested for drunk driving in Maine, reports TMZ. Struthers, 65, was pulled over at 12:30 AM in Ogunquit and charged with operating under the influence. She posted $160 bail and was cooperative with law enforcement, who say no drugs were involved. Struthers is currently performing in the musical "9 to 5" at the Ogunquit Playhouse and maintains her innocence through a public statement. Her arraignment is set for December 14.

Bernie Sanders is relying on small donations from supporters like Donna Mae Litowitz, a Miami Beach retiree who gave $10,000 to his campaign. Unlike other candidates, Sanders has refused to accept support from super PACs, instead focusing on small donors and grassroots support. This strategy has helped him build a formidable war chest, raising more money in gifts of $200 or less than any other candidate. While he still lags behind Hillary Clinton in overall fundraising, his small-dollar support appears significantly higher than Obama's in 2008 and more than any other candidate this cycle. Sanders' campaign manager says it's "absolutely possible to win without the super PACs" and that the campaign is running a more frugal operation.

Police in Delhi have arrested Abu Jindal, also known as Syed Zabiuddin, a key figure in the planning of the 2008 Mumbai attacks that claimed 165 lives. Described as the "handler" of the 10 gunmen involved, Jindal is being held in police custody. He is believed to have directed the terrorists from a Karachi control room and was responsible for their weapon training and Hindi language familiarization. Jindal was involved in previous attacks, including one in Ahmedabad in 2006 and the Aurangabad arms haul the same year. His arrest is seen as a significant breakthrough in the investigation and could provide insights into the current structure and plans of Pakistan-based terror groups.

The 2017 BrandZ™ Top 100 Most Valuable Global Brands increased 8% in brand value year-on-year, reaching $3.6 trillion, with technology brands driving significant growth. Retail led the category value growth, increasing 14%, largely due to e-commerce giants Amazon and Alibaba. Aguila, Coca-Cola, and Pampers topped the Brand Contribution metric. US brands, now comprising 71% of the Global Top 100 value, saw a 12% increase, while other brands declined 1%. China's brand value rose 937% over 12 years, with 13 Chinese brands now in the Global Top 100. Technology brands, accounting for 54% of the 2017 Global Top 100 value, grew 16% year-on-year, compared to a 4% increase for other brands. Newcomers like YouTube, HPE

Marvel Comics co-founder Joan Lee, wife of Stan Lee for 69 years, has passed away at the age of 93 in Los Angeles. A spokesperson for the family confirmed she died peacefully surrounded by her loved ones. Joan, a former British hat model, married Stan on December 5, 1947, and together they had two children: Joan Celia (J.C.) and Jan, who died shortly after birth. The couple met when Stan was supposed to take Joan's friend on a blind date. Joan inspired Stan during his early career and is credited with encouraging him to create the Fantastic Four. After a brief marriage to an American soldier during World War II, Joan moved to New York with Stan, where they worked for Timely/Atlas Comics, now known as Marvel Comics. The Lees relocated to California in 1981, and Joan supported Stan's work in developing Marvel TV and film projects. She voiced characters in animated Marvel shows and made a

Amanda Knox, now 26, has stated she will become a fugitive if convicted of murder in Italy, according to an interview with the Italian newspaper La Repubblica. Knox, who was previously acquitted but had her conviction reinstated, faces a retrial in Florence. She maintains she will not return to Italy if found guilty, fearing another prison term. The case, which has been controversial and lengthy, is expected to conclude with a verdict on January 30. Knox's legal team hopes for an exoneration, while the Kercher family's lawyer, Francesco Maresca, expects the court to uphold the original conviction.

Ted Haggard, former pastor of New Life Church and founder of the National Association of Evangelicals, is set to appear on the upcoming ABC reality show "Celebrity Wife Swap." The show, which is based on a British version and similar to "Wife Swap," involves Haggard and actor Gary Busey swapping partners for a short time. The Haggards and Busey will swap spouses at the GLBT Pride Center in Colorado Springs. Haggard, who faced a sex and drug scandal in 2006, has since returned to the ministry as pastor of St. James, a new nondenominational church. Busey, a born-again Christian and active minister with Promise Keepers, is no stranger to reality TV, having appeared on shows like "Celebrity Rehab" and "Celebrity Apprentice." The show is scheduled to shoot on Thursday, with Haggard refusing to comment.

A 150-year-old chestnut tree that comforted Anne Frank during her hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam during World War II has fallen due to heavy wind and rain. The tree, mentioned in her diary and widely known as "The Anne Frank Tree," had developed fungus and was set to be felled in 2007 due to safety concerns. However, a steel support system installed to save it failed, and the tree fell, damaging nearby gardens but not injuring anyone. Despite efforts to preserve it, the tree's fall is seen as a natural occurrence. Many clones of the tree have been planted, but it is uncertain if a replacement will be placed in the same spot. The tree's significance in Frank's diary and its fall highlight the fragility of historical symbols.

Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, held captive by Hamas for over five years, was freed in a prisoner swap and reunited with his family. Shalit, now 25, appeared thin and weary at his home in Mitzpe Hila, Israel, after enduring harsh conditions in captivity. His father, Noam, said Shalit would need time to recover from both physical and psychological wounds. Shalit expressed relief at being free but also fear about potential future conflicts. The release of 477 Palestinian prisoners into Gaza and the West Bank sparked celebrations among Palestinians, while Israel warned that any released prisoners returning to violence would face consequences. The deal, criticized by some in Israel, marked the largest prisoner exchange in decades and could strengthen Hamas politically.

Bernie Sanders supports President Obama's executive action on gun control, emphasizing the need to strengthen background checks, eliminate the gun show loophole, and address mental health issues. Meanwhile, the New York City subway token, a symbol of the city's history, is set to end its working life, with the final version of the token no longer valid for subway rides as of May 4, 2015. Despite its impending demise, the token remains a cherished symbol of New York, sold in various forms as souvenirs and collectibles. The transition to the MetroCard has saved the Metropolitan Transportation Authority significant handling costs, but the token's legacy continues through its cultural significance and the debate over its replacement.

A car bombing at the Corinthia Hotel in Tripoli killed 10 people, including an American and four Europeans, in an attack claimed by the Libyan affiliate of the Islamic State group. The group said the attack was in retaliation for the 2013 abduction and death of Abu Anas al-Libi, a Libyan Qaeda operative. The hotel, a hub for foreign tourists and embassies, was largely empty at the time. Five guards were also killed, and two attackers were reportedly killed in a standoff. The attack highlighted ongoing instability in Libya, where competing militias and political factions vie for control.

Five Southern California high school students, including a pair of sisters and best friends, died in a fiery car crash on their way to the beach, friends said. The victims were three girls and two boys from two high schools in the Irvine Unified School District. The driver, 17-year-old Abdulrahman Alyahyan, a senior at University High School, was identified. The Infiniti sedan veered off the road and hit a tree, splitting the car in two and causing it to catch fire. Speed was believed to be a factor. The crash killed four of the teens immediately, and one was declared dead at a hospital. The coroner used fingerprints to identify two of the bodies. The victims were described as close friends who bonded over their immigrant experiences. The crash occurred on a popular bypass with a 55 mph speed limit. School officials and friends expressed shock and sorrow over the loss of five vibrant teenagers.

Bristol Palin, now 20 and a single mother to her 2-year-old son Tripp, is set to release her memoir "Not Afraid of Life," offering an intimate look into her life, from her upbringing in Alaska to her experiences as her mother Sarah Palin gained political prominence. The book delves into her teenage pregnancy, her relationship with her child's father, and her time on "Dancing with the Stars." Bristol speaks candidly about her aspirations and the deep religious faith that guides her. In a recent interview, she shared that she is adjusting well to her new life in Arizona and expressed happiness for her son's well-being. The memoir promises to provide new insights into Bristol's journey and values.

Arizona Senator Jon Kyl, a three-term Republican and the Senate's No. 2 Republican leader, announced he will not seek re-election at the end of his term in 2012. Kyl, who has never lost an election and is 68 years old, said he wants to focus on helping his allies and new Republicans get elected during his remaining time in office. His retirement, along with four other senators scheduled for re-election in 2012, could create an opportunity for Democrats to gain a seat in Arizona. Kyl's departure will leave a gap in the Senate, particularly in finance and defense policy areas. Potential replacements include Rep. Gabby Giffords, Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano, and Rep. Jeff Flake. Democrats see this as a "prime pick-up opportunity" in Arizona.

Google's autocomplete feature has been altered to remove some but not all offensive suggestions, following outcry over antisemitic, sexist, and racist entries. The company claims it acted swiftly after being notified, though it did not comment on why certain results were changed while others were not. Academics warn that right-wing propagandists are effectively controlling search results, with hate sites dominating queries about Muslims, Jews, Hitler, and women. Google's response is seen as inadequate, with critics calling for more transparency and editorial oversight. The issue highlights the power and potential misuse of search algorithms, raising concerns about the democratic distribution of information and the impact on public opinion.

A rare Jackson Pollock painting, valued at up to $10 million, is set to be auctioned in Scottsdale, Arizona, after a 18-month investigation by Josh Levine of J. Levine Auction & Appraisal. The painting, found in a Sun City garage, was believed to have been passed down through the estate of Jenifer Gordon, a friend of Clement Greenberg and Peggy Guggenheim, both influential in promoting Pollock's work. Forensic reports confirmed the authenticity of the piece, with no pigments or binding media introduced after Pollock's death. Levine spent tens of thousands of dollars on research and authentication, including hiring private investigators. The painting will be auctioned on June 20, with Levine expecting it to sell for at least $10 million.

The world's first "three-parent baby" was born five months ago to Jordanian parents, using a new in vitro fertilization technique to avoid passing defective mitochondrial DNA to the child. The baby, a boy, was created using a spindle nuclear transfer method, where the nucleus from the mother's egg was removed and inserted into a donor's egg, which was then fertilized with the father's sperm. This technique was necessary because the mother carries mitochondrial DNA mutations for Leigh syndrome, a fatal neurological disorder. The birth represents a significant step forward in reproductive medicine, though it has sparked debates about safety and ethics. Critics argue it could pave the way for "designer babies" and raise concerns about the long-term effects on future generations. The UK has approved a similar technique, but the birth in Mexico occurred because the procedure is not yet legally approved in the US.

Rates of Alzheimer's disease and other types of dementia appear to have declined significantly since 2000, according to a new study published in JAMA Internal Medicine. Researchers analyzed data from over 21,000 Americans aged 65 and older, finding that the prevalence of dementia dropped from 11.6% in 2000 to 8.8% in 2012. An increase in educational attainment, with more people completing high school and college, may be a key factor. Better management of cardiovascular risk factors, such as diabetes and high blood pressure, also contributed. However, the study notes that the full set of social, behavioral, and medical factors contributing to the decline is still uncertain. The findings suggest that population brain health may have improved, but the number of people with dementia is expected to rise as the population ages.

A study in the journal PLOS One found that men who perform poorly in video games are more likely to harass female players, while skilled players tend to be more amiable. Researchers observed 163 plays of Halo 3 and noted that male players generally treated each other politely, but those who were less skilled and performing worse than their peers were more likely to make nasty comments to female gamers. This behavior aligns with evolutionary theory, suggesting that lower-status males may increase female-directed hostility to maintain their social rank in the face of a competitive threat. Higher-skilled players, who have less to fear from hierarchical reorganization, were more positive towards female teammates. The study highlights the importance of considering an evolutionary perspective when exploring factors that affect male hostility towards women in competitive environments.

On Data Privacy Day, Facebook introduces two new security features: a secured connection for HTTPS browsing and social authentication for account verification. The secured connection allows users to access Facebook entirely over HTTPS, enhancing data security, especially when using public Wi-Fi. Social authentication uses friends' photos to verify user identities, adding a social layer to account security. While these features aim to protect user data, they require users to manually enable them and may not be fully rolled out for some time. Facebook emphasizes the importance of staying in control of personal information and encourages users to visit the Facebook Security Page for more information.

A pregnant server in Delaware noticed two young girls applying for jobs at her restaurant and became suspicious due to their young age and lack of contact information. Lisa Stephenson, 26, and her Facebook search led to the discovery of two missing Maine teens, helping to bring them home safely. The girls had stolen a car and traveled through several states, facing dangerous situations. Stephenson's actions were praised as heroic by the girls' families.

Britain's Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will marry at Windsor Castle's St. George's Chapel in May, Kensington Palace announced. The 15th-century chapel is more intimate than Westminster Abbey, where Harry's brother William married Kate Middleton in 2011. Markle, an American actress, will be baptized in the Church of England and become a British citizen, though the process will take several years. The couple, who have been dating for about a year and a half, announced their engagement on Monday. Harry proposed over a roast chicken dinner at his London home, after months of keeping their long-distance relationship private. The choice of St. George's Chapel follows royal tradition, as it was the venue for Prince Peter Phillips' wedding in 2008. Markle's divorced status will not pose an obstacle to a church wedding, as the Church of England permits divorcees to remarry. Kristina Chesterman, a 21-year-old nursing student, tragically died in September after being hit by a suspected drunk driver. Her organs saved five lives, including Susan Vieira, a 64-year-old retired nurse who received her heart. Despite the anonymous nature of organ donation, Vieira discovered her connection to Chesterman through a newspaper article about Chesterman's bucket list. The two families met, and Vieira plans to honor Chesterman by completing her bucket list items. Chesterman's mother, Sandra, believes her daughter's heart is with Vieira, bringing comfort and a sense of continuity. Chesterman's legacy continues to inspire others to fulfill her unfulfilled dreams.

A heartwarming Christmas ad from Polish e-commerce giant Allegro has gone viral, touching the hearts of millions. The ad tells the story of a grandfather who learns English to reconnect with his family living abroad. This tale resonates with many Poles who have migrated for work, often leaving behind family ties. The ad poses a fundamental question about life's purpose, prompting viewers to reflect on their own desires. The viral response highlights the power of technology in bridging physical distances and strengthening familial bonds.

President Obama urged Congress to pass a small package of spending cuts and tax changes to delay the sequester, deep spending reductions set to begin March 1, for a few months. Obama said Congress should act to postpone the cuts to find a "smarter solution." Without action, the sequester, worth $1.2 trillion over a decade, will take effect, causing anxiety among government workers and contractors. Obama favored a broader deal of spending cuts and tax changes, including closing tax loopholes for the wealthy. House Speaker John Boehner opposed any tax increases and insisted on spending cuts and reforms to balance the budget in 10 years. The sequester, designed to force significant deficit reduction, will slash $1.2 trillion in domestic and defense spending over 10 years, with some programs exempt. The fiscal cliff deal postponed the sequester for two months.

Martin Shkreli, the 32-year-old CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals, has become the most hated man in America after raising the price of the drug Daraprim by 5,000%, sparking outrage and even death threats. Shkreli's controversial move has drawn criticism from patients' rights groups, politicians, and social media users. Despite the backlash, Shkreli has defended the price hike, arguing that the drug was previously unprofitable and that the increased price would allow for improvements to the 62-year-old drug. However, after intense public pressure, Shkreli agreed to lower the price to an "affordable level." The incident has brought attention to the broader issue of skyrocketing generic drug prices, which have increased by thousands of percent in recent years. While Shkreli's actions may have prompted some reform, the real challenge lies in achieving lasting changes to address the root causes of these price hikes.

Sacha Baron Cohen has offered to pay fines for six Czech tourists who were arrested in Kazakhstan for wearing mankinis inspired by his character Borat. The tourists, fined 22,500 Tenge ($67.7) each for "minor hooliganism," posed for photos in the capital city of Astana. Cohen responded on Facebook, asking the tourists to contact him with proof of their identity so he can cover the fines. The incident has sparked mixed reactions on Kazakh social media, with some supporting and others criticizing Baron Cohen's intervention.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is set to officially announce his presidential bid on Monday, marking the beginning of his campaign to become the first Republican candidate in the 2016 race. Cruz, known for his conservative stance and confrontational style, plans to launch his candidacy outright without forming an exploratory committee, aiming to raise between $40 million and $50 million. His strategy hinges on appealing to the Republican base, particularly the tea party and social conservative wings, to build a coalition against the establishment candidate. Critics argue that Cruz faces challenges in raising high-dollar donations and may struggle with comparisons to President Obama. Despite potential difficulties, Cruz's campaign is expected to attract significant support from his base, potentially making him competitive in early primary states like Iowa. However, analysts suggest he may face an uphill battle in a general election, trailing likely Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton in early polls.

Greek Parliament appeared close to approving unpopular austerity measures amid intense political maneuvering and violent protests. Prime Minister George A. Papandreou, with a five-vote majority, faces opposition from his Socialist Party base and the New Democracy opposition. A key lawmaker, Thomas Robopoulos, switched his vote to support the measures, citing national interest. Meanwhile, unions began a 48-hour general strike, leading to clashes with riot police. The measures, including wage cuts, tax increases, and privatizations, are crucial for unlocking $17 billion in aid to prevent default. European officials, including Olli Rehn, emphasized the urgency of passing the measures to avoid immediate default. The demonstrations reflect deep dissatisfaction with the government's handling of the economic crisis, with protesters calling for better terms in the bailout negotiations.

The Internet Archive has been archiving websites and blogs of 17 Russian political and cultural figures, including opposition leaders and activists, as well as eight websites focusing on political and human rights issues. This archive captures content from figures like Oleg Kashin, Aleksei Navalnyi, and Boris Nemtsov, who have expressed opposition to Vladimir Putin's policies. Sites like Civil Platform and Traitor.net are also included, reflecting the political climate in Russia. Meanwhile, a viral YouTube video shows birds flying in formation resembling Vladimir Putin's face near the Brooklyn Bridge, sparking speculation and debate in Russia about its meaning.

After the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, wildlife in the exclusion zone has thrived, with populations of elk, roe deer, red deer, wild boar, and wolves now comparable to or exceeding those in nearby uncontaminated nature reserves, a study in Current Biology reports. Researchers found that the mere absence of human activity, including hunting and forestry, has had a more significant positive impact on wildlife than radiation exposure. The study, led by Jim Smith of the University of Portsmouth, analyzed long-term census data and found that large mammal populations in the Chernobyl exclusion zone are likely higher than before the accident. This suggests that human habitation and activities are more detrimental to wildlife than radiation, highlighting the resilience of nature when freed from human interference.

An elderly couple and their son died or were injured after a swarm of bees attacked them on their remote ranch in south Texas. William Steele, 95, and his wife Myrtle, 92, died, while their son Richard, 67, was stung multiple times. The attack occurred as they tried to clean a hunting cabin, likely after moving a wood stove that exposed a beehive. Richard drove 15 miles to call for help, but by the time deputies arrived, they were stung but managed to assist the injured couple. The bees, likely Africanized honey bees, are common in the area and known for their aggression. Myrtle was airlifted to a hospital where she died, while Richard was hospitalized but later released. The hive was not removed from the home, and the species of bees was not identified.

A Michigan nurse, Iris Zink, donated a kidney to her longtime patient, Ginny Holcomb, when Holcomb was diagnosed with kidney cancer. Zink, a nurse practitioner who has treated Holcomb for over 15 years, did not hesitate to offer her kidney. After a year of testing, the two were found to be a perfect match and underwent the transplant in July. Both women now consider each other integral parts of their lives, with Zink saying, "We're bonded for life; she's got part of me in her," and Holcomb responding, "It's a beautiful thing to have someone else's body part in you." The pair hopes their story inspires others to consider organ donation.

Research InMotion (RIM), the company behind BlackBerry, is expected to report a net loss for its first fiscal quarter, marking a significant downturn for the once-dominant smartphone brand. Analysts predict a net loss of 3 cents per share on $3.1 billion in revenue, compared to a profit of $1.33 per share on nearly $5 billion in revenue from the same period last year. The company's troubles are expected to continue, with RIM's market value having fallen to under $5 billion, a fraction of its peak. Former executives reveal a split in leadership, with co-CEOs Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie pursuing different strategies, leading to internal conflicts and missteps. RIM's focus on maintaining its core email functionality while struggling to compete with touch-screen devices like the iPhone and Android phones has left it behind. The company's attempts to diversify through licensing its technology and developing the BlackBerry 10 operating system have not yielded

A heist occurred at a jewelry store in Santa Fe's historic plaza during a holiday tree-lighting festival, with thieves stealing over $1 million in jewelry. Police are seeking help to identify a woman and two men who scouted the store for weeks before the theft. The jewelry was taken between 5:15 and 5:30 p.m. on a Friday, while the store was busy with customers. The store owner, Ala Shawabkeh, did not notice the items missing until later. Police are distributing images of the suspects and asking for public assistance.

North Carolina lawmakers have approved a bill that significantly expands where concealed handguns can be carried. The bill, passed by both the House and Senate, allows concealed-carry permit holders to bring weapons into bars and restaurants that serve alcohol, as long as alcohol is not being consumed. It also permits storing firearms in locked cars on public school and university campuses and allows guns in public recreation areas. The final version of the bill maintains the current handgun purchase permit system but restricts local sheriffs' ability to limit the number of permits issued to individuals annually and requires them to document permit denials. The measure now awaits Governor Pat McCrory's signature or veto.

A 14-year-old boy, known as "El Ponchis," was arrested in Cuernavaca, Mexico, as he tried to flee to his native California with his sisters. He allegedly worked as a paid assassin for the South Pacific drug cartel since he was 11, admitting to participating in at least four decapitations. The teen claimed he acted under threat and was drugged. His arrest came after rumors of a child hit man circulated, with a YouTube video allegedly showing him next to corpses and guns. The boy's sisters were also detained, with one reportedly acting as a decoy and the other as a girlfriend of a cartel boss. The case highlights the involvement of minors in drug cartel activities and the increasing violence in Mexico.

A British makeup artist named Bethany Townsend, who suffers from Crohn's disease, has gained attention for posing in a bikini with her colostomy bags. Initially fitted with the bags in 2010 after her bowel ruptured, Townsend felt insecure about them for years. On a Christmas vacation in Mexico, her husband encouraged her to wear a bikini, and she decided to share a photo of herself with the Crohn's and Colitis UK Facebook page. The photo, which has been viewed over nine million times, has inspired Bethany to return to modeling, a career she had abandoned after the surgery. Her story highlights the power of body positivity and the impact of sharing personal experiences to inspire others.

Ku Klux Klan members and their supporters gathered in Charlottesville, Virginia, to protest the city council’s decision to remove a statue honoring Confederate General Robert E. Lee. The rally, held in Justice Park, faced a large counterprotest, with about 1,000 people jeering the Klansmen and chanting “shame.” Police in riot gear escorted the Klansmen to and from the rally, separating them from the counterprotesters. After the rally, police arrested several people and used gas canisters to disperse the remaining counterprotesters. The city had prepared for potential unrest, deploying hundreds of law enforcement officers. The rally highlighted ongoing tensions over Confederate monuments and the city’s efforts to rename parks and remove statues.

A young schoolteacher with a rare form of amnesia, Hannah Upp, went missing on St. Thomas in the U.S. Virgin Islands on September 14, just as Hurricane Maria struck the region. Upp, 32, has experienced two previous episodes of dissociative fugue, a condition that causes people to forget who they are for days or months at a time. Her latest disappearance is particularly concerning as it coincides with the aftermath of Hurricane Irma, which devastated the island, and as residents prepare for Hurricane Maria. Upp was last seen leaving her apartment, and her car was later found in a parking lot at Sapphire Beach, where her sandals, sarong, and dress were also discovered. Her colleagues and friends have been searching for her, posting fliers and checking hospitals, but the search has been complicated by poor cellphone service and the chaos of the hurricanes. Democrats are embracing super PACs after their successful use in 2012, despite reservations about big money's impact on politics. Following a three-day secret meeting of major donors and officials from liberal outside groups, plans are underway to establish a permanent network of officially blessed independent groups that can compete with well-funded Republican counterparts. The event, part of the annual winter conference of the Democracy Alliance, featured presentations by top Obama campaign and administration officials. Democrats are now more willing to participate in the wave of unlimited political spending, with some new megadonors pledging to be quicker to respond in future elections. However, state regulators are cracking down on tax-exempt advocacy groups that engage in campaigns without revealing their financial backers, highlighting the tension between federal and state campaign finance rules.

A 22-year-old father who jumped into the Connecticut River from the Arrigoni Bridge in Middletown late Sunday night may have taken his 7-month-old son with him, police say. The baby's mother called 911, reporting the child was crying in the background as her husband threatened suicide. The father, Tony Moreno, was pulled from the river and taken to the hospital, where his condition was initially listed as serious but improved. Police are searching for the baby, now classified as a recovery mission due to the challenging river conditions. Community members gathered for a candlelight vigil, and a Facebook group has gained support from over 1,500 people. Police are investigating and expect to file charges.

A decomposing body was found inside a column at a supermarket in Lancaster, and investigators believe it may be a suspect who escaped from a traffic stop earlier in the week. The body, believed to be that of Raymundo Rivera, 35, was discovered in a pillar at WinCo Foods on Saturday afternoon. The store manager reported a strong odor, leading to the discovery of a shoe and leg inside the column. The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department is investigating and believes the body may belong to a suspect who escaped after a chase, possibly hiding in the store and getting stuck in the column. An autopsy is pending to determine the exact cause of death.

A humpback whale and its calf managed to free themselves after getting stranded on a sandbar off Stradbroke Island, east of Brisbane. Initially reported on Thursday night, the mother and calf were spotted on a sandbar near Dunwich. The calf was seen nudging its mother to help her into deeper water. About 40 minutes after getting stuck, the whale successfully dislodged itself. Queensland Parks and Wildlife Services (QPWS) personnel were on standby to assist, but the whale and its calf were able to swim away to the open sea. The incident highlights the common presence of whales on the Queensland coast during birthing season.

President Trump has expanded the definition of "fake news" to include any reporting he disagrees with, from negative polls to factual corrections, alarming free-speech advocates. In a tweet, he linked to an article listing 16 "fake news" stories, but most were merely mistaken or framed negatively. The term's broadening threatens journalistic integrity and could be seen as an attempt to undermine the press. Trump's critics liken his use of "fake news" to the n-word, an ugly insult that journalists should avoid unless they can prove intentional lying.

At Busch Stadium during a key Interleague game, Royals reliever Peter Moylan faced the Cardinals with a 5-4 lead in the bottom of the sixth. Suddenly, a small cat ran onto the field, stopping by center fielder Lorenzo Cain before being chased off by a stadium employee. The distraction did not last long, as Yadier Molina hit a game-changing grand slam, giving the Cardinals an 8-5 lead and a crucial win. The victory helped the Cardinals leap into second place in the NL Central, just a game and a half behind the Cubs. Cardinals manager Mike Matheny joked, "I'm not a cat person, but I sure like that one." The incident brought back memories of the "Rally Squirrel" that had previously boosted the Cardinals' spirits.

Sen. Robert Menendez faces growing controversy over allegations of a questionable friendship with a Florida eye doctor, Dr. Salomon Melgen, who is under investigation for Medicare fraud. The allegations include improper flights to the Dominican Republic and alleged patronizing of prostitutes, including underage girls. Despite these accusations, Menendez has denied all wrongdoing, and top Democrats, including Majority Leader Harry Reid, are backing him. Reid expressed confidence in Menendez, stating he is a leader in immigration reform and will do a "wonderful job." However, the Senate Ethics Committee is investigating the case, and party leaders are waiting for the committee's findings before taking any action. Menendez has repaid $58,500 to cover the cost of two personal flights to the Dominican Republic on Melgen's private jet. The New York Times reported that Menendez tried to intervene on behalf of Melgen's company regarding a port-security contract with the Dominican government.

The three Cleveland women rescued from over a decade of captivity have expressed gratitude for the public's support while requesting privacy as they recover. Their attorneys released a letter on their behalf, thanking well-wishers for their generosity and support. The Cleveland Courage Fund has raised over $825,000 to directly benefit the survivors. The women are focused on reconnecting with their families and rebuilding their lives, with the fund aiding in their needs.

The U.N. Security Council called for a cease-fire in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict centered on Gaza, with a statement approved by all 15 members. The statement, which is not legally binding, calls for de-escalation, restoration of calm, and resumption of direct negotiations aimed at a two-state solution. Palestinian U.N. envoy Riyad Mansour stressed the need for immediate implementation. British Foreign Secretary William Hague and U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry are meeting to discuss a halt to the fighting. The council statement expresses concern for civilians and calls for respect of international humanitarian law. The U.S. supports Israel's right to defend itself but remains concerned about further escalation. The Israeli military has entered Gaza for the first time, ordering residents to leave their homes for safety. The conflict has resulted in at least 156 casualties.

A Florida landscaper, Jason Falbo, 24, was charged with nine counts of animal cruelty after deliberately running over a family of Muscovy ducklings with his riding mower. The incident occurred in Wellington, with the family of 11 ducklings losing nine to Falbo's mower. The mother duck and four ducklings managed to escape to a nearby lake, but two drowned. The family witnessed the horrific event, leaving them devastated. Falbo, who had previously been arrested for domestic battery, is being held on $27,000 bail and faces up to three years of probation. The family is using this experience to teach their 7-year-old son about the value of life and the cruelty of some people.

California drivers can legally use their hand-held cellphones to read maps while driving, according to a state appeals court ruling. The court overturned a $165 fine on Fresno man Steven Spriggs, who was ticketed for looking at a map on his iPhone 4 while stuck in traffic. The court ruled that the law prohibiting people from talking on cellphones without a hands-free device does not apply to using the phone for navigation. Texting while driving remains illegal. Spriggs hopes the ruling prompts legislators to revisit and clarify the law.

Eight Paraguayan bus drivers and one of their wives have nailed themselves to crosses in a union protest over sackings, reports AFP. The gruesome demonstration began 20 days ago near the bus terminal in Luque, 12km outside Asuncion. The drivers were allegedly fired for asking for medical benefits and overtime pay. Union leader Juan Villalba says they will continue until all eight are reinstated. The drivers' wives are also taking turns to be nailed to crosses. The manager of the bus company says five drivers will be re-hired, but the group is refusing to return until all are reinstated.

A 24-year-old father, Anthony Powell, has been sentenced to 60 years in prison for the fatal beating of his three-year-old son, Tristan, over potty-training accidents. Powell admitted to striking the child multiple times, including one instance where he picked up Tristan like a rag doll after knocking him to the ground.

Donald Trump is set to become the 45th president of the United States, despite receiving nearly 3 million fewer votes than Hillary Clinton. Clinton won the popular vote by 2.86 million votes, with a total of 65,844,610 votes compared to Trump’s 62,979,636. Other candidates garnered 7,804,213 votes. The Electoral College, however, secured Trump’s victory with 306 electoral votes, compared to Clinton’s 232. This makes Clinton the second Democrat to lose the presidency while winning the popular vote in the last five elections, following Al Gore’s loss in 2000.

On Thursday night, Jimmy Kimmel addressed the closure of Toys'R'Us, joking that the store was closing and offering Babies'R'Us for adoption. Kimmel then had an unexpected visitor: Geoffrey the Giraffe, the Toys'R'Us mascot. Geoffrey expressed his disappointment, blaming customers for buying toys online and causing him to lose his job. Kimmel tried to comfort Geoffrey, who was drunk and singing the old "I'm a Toys'R'Us Kid" jingle. Kimmel's security guard escorted Geoffrey out, and Kimmel wished him well.

The 2016 Republican presidential hopefuls weighed in on the Confederate battle flag controversy in South Carolina, with some calling for its immediate removal and others expressing caution. Mitt Romney, the 2012 Republican nominee, tweeted his support for taking down the flag. Other candidates, including Jeb Bush and Scott Walker, offered more measured responses, focusing on the debate within South Carolina. The flag's presence has become a contentious issue following the Charleston church shooting, where the accused killer was found with the flag in his possession. The candidates' varying stances reflect the complexities of the cultural and political landscape surrounding the flag's symbolism and its removal.

Billionaire heiress Casey Johnson's life spiraled out of control in her final months, living in squalor and battling diabetes while surrounded by drug abuse and financial troubles. Johnson, daughter of New York Jets owner Woody Johnson, was found dead in Los Angeles on December 31st. Her family said she had been in and out of intensive care due to diabetes but insisted she was not neglecting her insulin treatment. Friends described Johnson's descent into drug addiction, including OxyContin, Klonopin, Adderall, marijuana, ecstasy, and cocaine. Her family tried to get her into rehab but she checked out early and relapsed. Johnson's last known communication was a tweet on December 29th. Toxicology tests could take up to six weeks. J.J. Abrams has assembled a diverse cast for "Star Wars: Episode VII," which is set for release on December 18, 2015. Returning original stars Harrison Ford, Carrie Fisher, and Mark Hamill are joined by newcomers such as Adam Driver, Daisy Ridley, and Andy Serkis. The eclectic mix includes veteran actors like Max von Sydow and fresh faces like John Boyega and Domhnall Gleeson. The cast list balances established talent with fresh resumes, ensuring a mix of recognized and unknown actors. The film aims to bring the beloved saga forward while introducing new characters to the Star Wars universe.

Astronaut Peggy Whitson, who set a new record for the most cumulative time in space by an American with 665 days, safely returned to Earth on September 2, 2017, aboard the Soyuz MS-04 spacecraft. Whitson, along with NASA astronaut Jack Fischer and Russian cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin, spent 136 days aboard the International Space Station. Their Soyuz undocked from the space station at 5:58 p.m. EDT and landed at 9:21 p.m. EDT (1321 GMT on September 3) in Kazakhstan. Whitson's 288-day mission broke her previous record and made her the first woman to spend over 660 cumulative days in space. Fischer and Yurchikhin, who arrived in April, spent 136 days in space. A political action committee called Trump Has Tiny Hands PAC was launched to mock Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump over his hand size, which has become a campaign topic. The PAC was initiated by Henry Kraemer from Portland, Oregon. During a debate, Marco Rubio mocked Trump's hands, leading Trump to defend himself and accuse Rubio of lying. Kraemer started the PAC to highlight the inconsistency of Trump denying having "tiny baby hands." The PAC's name and mission reflect the ongoing joke about Trump's hand size, with Trump himself frequently defending the size of his hands and even boasting about his golfing abilities. The issue has become a recurring point of contention in the campaign, with both sides engaging in playful banter.

Vermont lawmakers are using a provocative strategy to push for marijuana legalization: a bill that would reinstate alcohol prohibition. Reps. Jean O'Sullivan and Christopher Pearson introduced House Bill 502, which would make possession of alcohol punishable by up to 30 years in prison and fines of $1 million. The lawmakers argue that since marijuana is less dangerous and is still illegal, alcohol, which is more dangerous, should be banned as well. This bill is part of an effort to highlight the scientific consensus that marijuana is far safer than alcohol and to generate support for legalizing marijuana in Vermont. While O'Sullivan acknowledges the bill's irony, she hopes it will draw attention to the financial benefits of legalizing marijuana, such as potential tax revenue to address the state's budget deficit. The bill has not yet been acted upon in the Statehouse.

Supporters quickly rebuilt a memorial for Michael Brown after it was destroyed by a vehicle on Christmas Day in Ferguson, Missouri. The memorial, located near where Brown was shot and killed, was rebuilt by morning after photos on social media showed it had been run over. Ferguson Police Department's public relations officer, Officer Timothy Zoll, was placed on unpaid leave after he falsely claimed no crime had been reported and then admitted to misleading his superiors. The incident highlights ongoing tensions in Ferguson, where a national conversation about race and policing has centered around the shooting of Brown by Officer Darren Wilson.

In Thailand, elephants are trained to step on tourists' backs as a form of stress relief, despite the potentially unsettling experience of having a large animal place its foot on your back after seeing a wild snake. Meanwhile, snakes of various sizes show a preference for exploring unconventional areas like faces, as captured in a disturbing video. While the snakes used are nonvenomous, their tickling might not be as soothing as intended.

President Obama delivered a critical speech at American University, urging Congress to support the Iran nuclear deal and warning that rejecting it would lead to another war in the Middle East. Obama compared opponents of the deal to those who supported the Iraq War, arguing that the same people are now opposing diplomacy with Iran. He emphasized that the deal is the strongest nonproliferation agreement ever negotiated and that walking away from it would undermine America’s credibility as a leader of diplomacy. Obama also highlighted that every nation that has weighed in on the deal has backed it, except for Israel. He stressed that the alternative to the deal is conflict, with the U.S. losing “something more precious,” America’s credibility as a leader of diplomacy. The White House is working to build support among undecided lawmakers, including House Democrats, while facing criticism from Republicans who argue that the deal is too weak and that economic sanctions on Iran should be maintained.

Wayne Flynt, a professor emeritus of history at Auburn University and Harper Lee's longtime friend, provides insights into Lee's life and work in his new book "Mockingbird Songs: My Friendship With Harper Lee." The book, set to release on May 2, includes letters from Lee to Flynt, offering a glimpse into her thoughts and feelings. Lee is known to have called Truman Capote a "compulsive liar" in a 2006 letter, revealing the strain in their friendship due to Lee's success with "To Kill a Mockingbird." Flynt's book also discusses Lee's fear of obsessive fans and her nervousness before public appearances. Additionally, it addresses Lee's role in Capote's "In Cold Blood" and her mixed feelings about the publication of "Go Set a Watchman."

A missing California woman, Jamie Tull, 33, was found alive after vanishing for nearly three weeks. She was discovered by searchers near Le Grand, about a mile from where she crashed her car. Tull survived by eating a few bugs and drinking from a dirty cattle trough, according to authorities. She told rescuers she did not want to be found and was trying to reach Yosemite. Tull, a former public elementary school teacher struggling with emotional issues, was dehydrated and badly sunburned when found. She was taken to a nearby hospital for medical treatment.

A 71-year-old veteran died after collapsing in the cafeteria at the Raymond G. Murphy VA Medical Center in Albuquerque, 500 yards from the emergency room. Despite being within walking distance, it took 30 minutes for an ambulance to arrive, as staff followed protocol to call 911. Kirtland Air Force Medical Group personnel performed CPR until the ambulance arrived. The incident highlights ongoing issues with wait times and emergency response at VA facilities, amid widespread reports of veterans facing long delays and even deaths while on waiting lists. The VA's policy on responding to medical emergencies outside the main hospital building is under review. The death has drawn criticism and calls for reform, as the VA faces scrutiny for systemic failures and a struggling health system.

The Mexican attorney for "affluenza" teen Ethan Couch says a decision on his client's deportation could take months, reports FoxNews.com. Couch, 18, and his mother Tonya were detained in Puerto Vallarta after a video surfaced allegedly showing Ethan drinking at a party. Tonya was deported to the U.S. early Thursday, while Ethan remains in a Mexico City immigration detention center. His attorney, Fernando Benitez, argues that Couch's constitutional and civil rights may have been violated and that his crimes in the U.S. should not affect Mexican officials. A judge is considering Couch's detention, with a decision potentially taking up to 90 days. Benitez hopes to meet with Ethan next week. Tonya Couch is facing a felony charge in Texas and is being held on a $1 million bond.

Right-wing news site The Daily Caller is running a gun giveaway contest, offering new registrants a chance to win a free handgun engraved with the Bill of Rights. The gun's manufacturer, Jim Pontillo, has criticized American progressives for promoting communism and claimed that those calling for secession are acting in the Founding tradition. Pontillo's website also features extreme right-wing rhetoric, including claims that firearm ownership opposes liberal philosophies. The giveaway is part of The Daily Caller's "Guns and Gear" section, which largely reprints NRA content.

Clarissa Dickson Wright, known for her role as one half of the TV cooking duo "Two Fat Ladies," passed away at the age of 66 in Edinburgh. A brilliant cook and food historian, she was celebrated for her eccentric personality and strong opinions. Her career spanned from her early days as a barrister to her successful cooking shows and books. Despite her fame, she faced personal struggles, including alcoholism and financial difficulties. Known for her fiery temper and outspoken nature, Dickson Wright was a champion of traditional British cuisine and countryside pursuits, often engaging in controversial debates. Her legacy includes not only her culinary contributions but also her unique and influential presence in the world of television cooking.

A woman with an extremely drug-resistant form of tuberculosis has traveled across multiple states before seeking treatment, prompting health officials to trace her contacts. The patient, whose identity is not disclosed, was diagnosed with XDR-TB after traveling from India to the United States, passing through Chicago O'Hare airport. She was initially treated in a Chicago-area hospital before being transferred to the National Institutes of Health for specialized care. Health authorities are conducting contact tracing to identify individuals who may have been in close proximity to her, emphasizing the importance of proper infection control measures. XDR-TB is rare but poses significant challenges due to its resistance to most TB drugs, with treatment potentially lasting years and costing hundreds of thousands of dollars. The case highlights the ongoing threat of drug-resistant TB and the need for vigilant public health responses.

Thousands of U.S. soldiers are facing financial strain after the Pentagon ordered them to repay thousands of dollars in signing bonuses paid during the height of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. The bonuses, meant to retain troops, were improperly distributed, leading to overpayments, especially in the California National Guard. Soldiers like Van Meter, who served in Iraq, refinanced their mortgages to pay back $46,000. Critics argue the repayments are unfair, citing the stress and financial strain on service members. The California National Guard states it has no authority to waive the debts but is advocating for veterans through the process.

A passenger on an Alaska Airlines flight from New York's JFK Airport to Seattle attempted to open a rear door mid-flight, leading to an emergency landing at the Minneapolis-St. Paul Airport. The door could not be opened due to air pressure differences. Crew members decided to divert the flight after the unruly passenger's behavior escalated. He was arrested upon landing and taken to Fairview Southdale Hospital for evaluation. The flight eventually arrived at Sea-Tac Airport around 1 p.m. Pacific time.

George Lucas has chosen Chicago over Los Angeles and San Francisco to house his $1 billion interactive museum, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art. Mayor Rahm Emanuel won the competition, offering a 17-acre site between Soldier Field and McCormick Place. The museum, set to open in 2018, will feature a collection of art and movie memorabilia, including Norman Rockwell paintings and Darth Vader costumes. Emanuel praised the decision, highlighting its potential to create jobs and attract tourists. However, open-space advocates are concerned about the museum's location on lakefront land.

Nathaniel Marston, a former star of the soap opera One Life to Live, was involved in a severe car accident and is fighting for his life. His mother, Elizabeth Jackson, shared updates on his condition, describing his injuries as traumatic, including a broken and fractured neck, broken shoulder, broken ribs, and a collapsed lung. Nathaniel was not wearing a seatbelt and was ejected from the vehicle. Despite the severity of his injuries, doctors initially suggested he might be paralyzed from the neck down and require a ventilator. However, he showed signs of improvement, communicating with his mother and undergoing surgery with a chance of regaining upper body movement and possibly walking again. The family and friends have been supporting him with prayers and positive thoughts. A memorial service will be held in multiple locations.

Saturday Night Live's opening skit featured a standout performance by Aidy Bryant as Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who was both comically oblivious and impressively over-the-top, singing and dancing through a musical number with a Demi Lovato tune. The sketch also showcased a shift in approach for Donald Trump impersonations, moving beyond his incompetence to explore the surreal and nightmarish aspects of his presidency. Meanwhile, Larry David's monologue drew mixed reactions, with some finding his concentration camp jokes offensive while others defended them as a form of Jewish humor. The episode's other highlights included a bizarre shower scene with Alec Baldwin as Trump, Alex Moffat as Manafort, and Kate McKinnon as Jeff Sessions, alluding to the chaos and absurdity of the current political landscape.

The latest Transformers installment, "Age of Extinction," is a three-hour spectacle that leaves little to no room for depth or meaningful storytelling. Director Michael Bay, known for his penchant for "blowing things up real good," delivers another mindless, chaotic affair that prioritizes explosions and CGI over coherent plot and character development. Mark Wahlberg, in a more prominent role than in previous films, struggles to elevate a script that is repetitive and soulless. The film's action, while technically impressive, is overwhelming and exhausting, making it a hard sell for any viewer seeking substance. With its relentless focus on destruction and a convoluted narrative, "Age of Extinction" is a testament to blockbuster moviemaking at its worst, promising to make so much money that a fifth installment is almost guaranteed.

President Donald Trump and congressional lawmakers signaled on Tuesday that more steps are needed to rein in North Korea's nuclear program despite the UN Security Council's unanimous vote to pass additional sanctions. Trump noted the 15-0 UN vote but said it was "just another very small step" and suggested it might not have much impact. State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert said the UN resolution was the strongest set of sanctions so far. North Korea's Foreign Ministry condemned the sanctions, calling them a "heinous provocation." Lawmakers expressed frustration that the US isn't exerting greater pressure on China to stop North Korea's nuclear development. Both Republicans and Democrats criticized Trump's belligerent comments and tweets. US officials are pushing China and Russia to do more to rein in North Korea, with Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin saying the US has "more tools in our toolbox" to put additional sanctions on North Korea. President Donald Trump abruptly replaced Reince Priebus as chief of staff with Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly, ending a turbulent six-month tenure marked by infighting and legislative setbacks. Priebus, who reportedly resigned privately on Thursday, told CNN that he was pleased with the change, stating, "A president has a right to hit a reset button. I think it's a good time to hit the reset button." Trump praised Kelly, calling him "a Great American... and a Great Leader," and noted Kelly's success at Homeland Security. The move followed months of speculation about Priebus's departure and came amid reports of infighting, particularly after communications director Anthony Scaramucci's controversial comments. While Priebus left under the radar, his vehicle split from the motorcade and departed alone from the tarmac, while Trump and Kelly were still on Air Force One. Priebus will work with Kelly on a transition for the next couple of weeks.

Every weekday for seven months, UPS worker Trenton Lewis has been walking five miles from his home in Little Rock, Arkansas, to his 4 a.m. shift, no matter the weather. Lewis, 21, started this routine to support his daughter and ensure he never missed work. His coworkers, Kenneth and Patricia Bryant, noticed his dedication and decided to help. They collected $1,900 from other employees and surprised Lewis with a car. On a Facebook Live video, Lewis was shocked to receive the keys, calling it his first car. Now, he leaves for work at 3:30 a.m., allowing him more rest and fewer daily walks.

The parents and attorneys of Dylan Noble held a news conference in Fresno, California, on July 7, 2016, denying claims that their son was depressed or unhappy when he was fatally shot by police after a traffic stop on June 25. Body-camera footage released by the Fresno Police Department shows officers repeatedly shooting the unarmed 19-year-old, including multiple shots fired while he was lying on his back and barely moving. The video captures Noble repeatedly ignoring commands to show his hands and get on the ground. After watching the footage, Noble's father said the officers "just wanted to shoot him," calling their actions "trigger-happy." The family has filed a lawsuit against the city, alleging excessive force. The release of the video came amid heightened tensions following the police shootings of Alton Sterling and Philando Castile, which sparked nationwide protests. A major blizzard is expected to hit the Northeastern U.S., potentially dumping up to 3 feet of snow from New York City to Boston and beyond, beginning Friday. Forecasters warn of dangerous conditions, including heavy snow, strong winds, and the possibility of widespread power failures. Residents stocked up on supplies, while schools and some businesses canceled operations for Friday. Airlines canceled over 2,600 flights, and Amtrak suspended service. Blizzard warnings were issued for parts of New Jersey, New York's Long Island, and portions of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut. Authorities urged residents to prepare and stay off the roads during the storm.

A white woman at a soccer game in St. Johns County, Florida, called police on a black father who was coaching his son from the sidelines, sparking outrage as the latest incident in a series where white people have called 911 on black people for no reason. The father, whose identity has not been revealed, was only speaking to his son and not the referee when a field marshal, dubbed "Golfcart Gail," approached and demanded he stop. When he tried to leave, she called police, claiming he was being aggressive. Deputies arrived but found no wrongdoing and did not detain the father. The incident, captured on video by a witness, highlights ongoing tensions and accusations of racial profiling. The field marshal's actions were defended by the Ponte Vedra Athletic Association, which said such calls are rare and usually not necessary.

President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump have paid respects to former President George H.W. Bush at the U.S. Capitol, where Bush is lying in state. Trump, who has a fractured relationship with the Bush family, visited the Capitol Rotunda with Melania, though he skipped an earlier service. Bush, who died at 94, will lie in state until Wednesday morning, after which he will attend an invitation-only funeral service at Washington National Cathedral. The public can visit Bush’s casket until then. Bush’s son, former President George W. Bush, and other family members were among those present. The elder Bush will be buried in his presidential library in Texas.

A memorial at Warren Hills' football stadium honored Evan Murray, a three-sport athlete and senior who died after being injured during a home football game against Summit. Faculty, students, friends, and family gathered to mourn and remember the teenager who touched many lives. "Everyone honored him, and they should because he deserves it," said Anthony Veneziano, a classmate. Murray was known for his leadership and character, described by baseball coach Mike Quinto as a "young gentleman" and "one of the best leaders." The Warren Hills community, already grieving recent tragedies, is struggling to come to terms with Murray's death. Grief counselors were made available for students. "We lost a fine kid," said Warren Hills coach Larry Dubiel.

Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad met with Egypt's President Mohamed Mursi during the Non-Aligned Movement summit in Tehran, marking the first visit by an Egyptian leader to Iran since 1979. Ahmadinejad, addressing heads of state from developing countries, reaffirmed Iran's commitment to peaceful nuclear energy while criticizing the United Nations Security Council as illogical and unjust. Mursi, in his speech, called for support of the Syrian people in their struggle against an oppressive regime, prompting a walkout by the Syrian delegation. The summit's final declaration is expected to express concern over the violence in Syria and support efforts by the U.N.-Arab League envoy to resolve the conflict. U.N. Secretary General Ban Ki-moon urged Iran to take concrete steps to prove its nuclear work is peaceful and criticized Iran's human rights record. David Letterman's former CBS news producer, Robert "Joe" Halderman, faces a criminal case after being indicted for attempting to extort $2 million. Halderman is set to appear in a Manhattan court for the first hearing, where he is expected to challenge the prosecution rather than accept a plea deal, according to his attorney. Since his indictment, Halderman has raised $100,000 for his defense fund, indicating his intention to go to trial. The case, which involves potential charges of attempted grand larceny, could result in up to 15 years in state prison if Halderman is found guilty. Legal analyst Dan Abrams predicts that the defense attorney may use the hearing to attack Letterman's character and push for a trial. Meanwhile, Levi Johnston, the father of Sarah Palin's grandson, is receiving a "Crossover Star Award" from Fleshbot for his transformation from a future son-in-law to a Playgirl pinup model,

A town in Italy has banned wood-burning pizza stoves to combat severe air pollution. The measure, enacted by Mayor Antonio Falcone of San Vitaliano, aims to reduce particulate matter levels. The town, located north of Naples, experienced 114 days of unsafe air last year. The ban, effective until June 2016, allows exceptions for stoves with filtration systems. Local pizzerias and artisanal bakeries face fines for non-compliance. Residents and business owners protest, questioning the ban's necessity amid claims that other factors may contribute more significantly to pollution.

South Korean opposition lawmakers set a new world record for the longest combined filibuster, speaking for 192 hours and 25 minutes to block an anti-terrorism bill. The filibuster, which began on February 23, ended on March 2, with the last speaker, Rep. Lee Jong-kul, delivering a 12-hour and 31-minute speech. Thirty-nine lawmakers participated, with each speaking for extended periods, including reading from George Orwell's "1984." The filibuster aimed to prevent the bill from passing, claiming it would infringe on personal freedoms. Despite the opposition, the bill was eventually passed, as the ruling party controlled a majority in the National Assembly.

A local news station in the Bay Area shared an image of Nia Wilson holding what looked like a gun during a broadcast about her murder, drawing outrage from viewers. Nia Wilson, an 18-year-old high school student, was killed and her sister critically injured by a knife-wielding suspect. The suspect, John Lee Cowell, was arrested the following day. Critics argue that the image was used to demean the victim and perpetuate harmful narratives about Black individuals, invoking the #IfTheyGunnedMeDown hashtag. Local news stations are facing criticism for their portrayal of Black victims and the impact such images can have on public perception and justice.

Republican leaders are cautioning their members to avoid any disruptive behavior during President Obama's final State of the Union address, drawing parallels to former Rep. Joe Wilson's "You lie!" outburst during Obama's previous address. House Minority Whip Eric Cantor hopes for a dignified evening, while Rep. Joe Wilson promises to be a "gentleman" but will instead deliver a live response on Facebook. The DCCC has challenged Wilson on his intentions. Meanwhile, Republican representatives have criticized Obama's agenda, with Rep. Jeb Hensarling agreeing with 80% of what Obama says but disagreeing with 80% of what he does. Grover Norquist's Americans for Tax Reform even offered a mocking "Bingo" card for the address, highlighting Obama's signature phrases and policy proposals.

Michele Bachmann's campaign has been marked by several physical confrontations with reporters, raising questions about the intensity of its media management. In less than two months, Bachmann's staff has reportedly become embroiled in at least five incidents involving pushing, shoving, and even alleged threats. These encounters have included incidents where staffers pushed ABC News reporter Brian Ross and CNN's Don Lemon into a cart. The campaign justifies this aggressive approach by citing security concerns for the popular, controversial candidate. However, the intensity of these interactions stands out, especially in Iowa, where media access is typically more open. The campaign's most aggressive aide, a former Secret Service agent, frequently makes physical contact with reporters. While the campaign maintains that this is necessary for safety, the number and intensity of these incidents have drawn scrutiny and raised concerns about the balance between security and press freedom.

Captain Francesco Schettino, facing charges of manslaughter and abandoning ship, returned to the wreck of the Costa Concordia for the first time as part of his trial. The ship hit a reef near the island of Giglio in January 2012, resulting in the loss of 32 lives. Schettino denies the charges and maintains he stayed to help passengers. He was accompanied by court-appointed experts and attended a health-and-safety briefing before boarding a small boat to the wreck. Schettino criticized the "media frenzy" surrounding his visit and insisted he is not a coward. His return stirred mixed emotions among locals, some tired of the story and others seeking closure. The complex salvage operation to right the ship took 18 hours and involved 500 engineers and divers.

A new MRI study identifies a unique brain region in humans, the lateral frontal pole prefrontal cortex, which may be crucial for analyzing alternative decisions and may not have an equivalent in macaque monkeys. This region, part of the ventrolateral frontal cortex, helps in strategic planning and decision-making, as well as "multi-tasking." Researchers from Oxford University divided the human ventrolateral frontal cortex into 12 distinct areas, each with its own pattern of connections to other brain regions. Comparing human and monkey brain scans, they found that while the overall structure is similar, the human brain has this unique lateral frontal pole prefrontal cortex. Additionally, the auditory parts of the human brain are more connected to the prefrontal cortex, potentially explaining our ability to understand and generate speech, unlike monkeys. This study, published in Neuron, highlights the differences between human and primate brains and could aid in understanding psychiatric diseases.

A 31-year-old photography teacher at El Dorado High School in Placentia was found hanging in her classroom by students on Monday morning. The teacher, Jillian Jacobson, was discovered around 8:40 a.m. after another teacher unlocked her locked classroom. Students initially tried to enter but found the door locked, leading them to seek help from a nearby teacher. Jacobson was pronounced dead at the scene after paramedics arrived. The school district is providing grief counselors for students and staff. This incident marks the second tragedy at the school in a year, following the death of a 16-year-old student in a skateboarding accident.

Twenty years after the Ms. Foundation launched Take Our Daughters to Work Day, it's time to shift the focus to encouraging girls to become leaders. The mission of demystifying the workplace has been accomplished, as women now make up half the US workforce. What girls need now is exposure to the C-suite, where corporate chiefs work, to understand the daily responsibilities and rewards of leadership. Companies should introduce girls to top-ranking women, explain leadership roles, and provide ongoing support through sponsorship initiatives. These efforts need to extend beyond a single day in April, as the lack of women in top leadership positions is costing companies talent and undermining social equality. Real change will come when girls are brought inside the halls of power to lead in the future.

President Obama left a summit with world leaders after two days of intense lobbying, with some expressions of support for a strong U.S. response to Syria's alleged chemical weapons use, but short of an international coalition that might help persuade reluctant lawmakers. Obama had hoped to build pressure on Congress as it considers authorizing missile strikes against Syria. Before leaving for Washington, he said he would make his case in a White House address on Tuesday, acknowledging the divisive nature of the plans both abroad and at home. The summit produced a joint statement from 10 countries, including the U.S., calling for Assad to be held accountable for the alleged nerve gas attack but not explicitly supporting military action or promising participation. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Assad's closest ally, did not endorse the statement. Obama and Putin had a lengthy discussion about Syria, but did not break their impasse. The U.S. plan for limited and not open-ended strikes remains unpopular in the U.S., with the Senate set to take the first

John McCain's memorial services excluded President Donald Trump and former vice presidential running mate Sarah Palin, sources tell PEOPLE. The family, particularly widow Cindy McCain, is reportedly protective of John's legacy and memory, with disinvitations sent through intermediaries. While Trump and McCain had a public feud, sources say Palin's exclusion is more due to respect for the McCain family. The focus now shifts to replacing McCain in the Senate, with speculation that Cindy McCain might be a candidate for the position. Meanwhile, Trump's inner circle is increasingly targeting social media and search engines, claiming bias against conservatives, potentially leading to the creation of conservative alternatives.

Taylor Swift has officially announced her sixth studio album, Reputation, set for release on November 10. The singer revealed the cover art, featuring a black and white photo of herself with wet hair and dark lipstick, standing amid fake newspaper headlines repeating "Taylor Swift." This comes after a series of videos featuring a slithering snake, an animal often associated with Swift. Swift's camp claimed credit for a song that reportedly led to her split with Calvin Harris, causing Harris to go on a Twitter rant against her and sparking a social media backlash from his supporters.

Gambian President Yahya Jammeh has announced that all death row prisoners will be executed by mid-September, sparking condemnation from human rights groups. Jammeh, who last executed an inmate about 30 years ago, stated that by the middle of next month, all death sentences would be carried out. The tiny West African nation currently has 44 people on death row, including two women. Amnesty International and other rights organizations have criticized the execution order, citing concerns about unfair trials and the use of the death penalty against political opponents. Jammeh's announcement has drawn international attention and condemnation, with the French government urging Gambia to maintain its de facto moratorium on executions.

Karl Lagerfeld transformed Paris' Grand Palais into a "Chanel Shopping Center" for his fall-winter 2014-2015 ready-to-wear show, creating an immersive supermarket experience. Models pushed trolleys and picked up branded products like "Tweed cola" and "Maison Gabrielle" wine, while guests were encouraged to help themselves to the merchandise. The collection featured oversized tweed jackets, shiny pants, and comfortable jogging suits, blending luxury with everyday wear. Despite the elaborate setup, the show ended with guests looting the set, highlighting the disconnect between the designer's vision and reality. Rihanna and Keira Knightley attended the show, entering a cordon after the presentation. The event showcased Lagerfeld's ability to blend high fashion with pop culture, though the chaotic aftermath suggested the concept may have been too ambitious.

Two American hikers jailed in Iran since 2009 were freed from prison on Wednesday and reunited with their families in Oman. Shane Bauer and Joshua Fattal, both 29, were released after spending more than two years in prison on charges of illegal entry and espionage. They were arrested while hiking in the mountainous region near the border between Iraq and Iran. The release came a day before Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was set to address the U.N. General Assembly, potentially as a goodwill gesture. President Obama praised the release as a "wonderful day" for the men's families. Oman reportedly paid $1 million bail for their release. The men, who denied being spies, were convicted of espionage charges in a closed trial. Their release was seen as a positive gesture ahead of the U.N. meeting.

Americans generally have a favorable view of most states, with Hawaii topping the list and California bringing up the rear.
