Police in Florida are pursuing misdemeanor charges against five teenagers for failing to report a man's death after they recorded and mocked his drowning. The teens, aged 14 to 16, were seen laughing and recording the incident as 31-year-old Jamel Dunn struggled in a Cocoa pond. Initially, authorities said no charges would be filed, but after hours of discussion with the State Attorney's Office, they decided to use Florida Statute 406.12, typically for medical examiners, to charge the teens with not reporting a death. The teens' actions, described as "utterly inhumane and cruel," have sparked discussions about potential new legislation requiring assistance in such situations.

Mollie Tibbetts' brother Jake encouraged students to make new friends at a vigil held on the University of Iowa campus to honor his sister. The event focused on Tibbetts' positive impact, with attendees remembering her smile and her advocacy for mental health. Tibbetts, a psychology student, would have started her sophomore year on the same day she went missing. The vigil highlighted the community's support and the thousands who came together to remember her. Meanwhile, Cristhian Bahena Rivera, the man charged with first-degree murder in Tibbetts' case, worked at Yarrabee Farms for four years under a different name. The Lang family, who owned the farm, expressed shock and received threats after learning of Rivera's true identity. Rivera's employment records and his alleged confession to following Tibbetts and dumping her body in a cornfield have raised questions about the farm's hiring practices and the broader issue of undocumented workers.

Five defendants being taken to trial for robbery and murder in a Moscow court tried to escape by seizing weapons from their guards, resulting in three deaths and two serious injuries, Reuters reports. The incident occurred when the five defendants, accused of being part of a "Grand Theft Auto Gang" responsible for a series of vehicle thefts and murders, tried to escape in a lift at the Moscow Regional Court. Three defendants were shot dead by Russian national guard officers, while the other two were seriously wounded. Three law enforcement officers were also injured, one with a gunshot wound. One of the group members had previously fought for ISIS in Syria, according to official TV channel Rossiya 24.

A tsunami advisory issued shortly after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Japan's Ryukyu Islands was canceled, with no reports of tsunami damage, the Japan Meteorological Agency reported. The quake, centered 10 kilometers deep and 85 kilometers from Okinawa, was felt on the island, with shaking lasting about 15 seconds. About 20,000 U.S. troops are stationed on Okinawa. An iReporter described the quake as lasting longer than usual but noted no significant damage or disruption to daily life. The U.S. Geological Survey reported the quake's magnitude at 7.3. Local officials reported no injuries or major damage, and operations at the Nishihara refinery continued normally.

After nearly two decades of "don't ask, don't tell," gay U.S. military members now have a new social network, Out Military, where they can communicate openly. Launched just over a week ago, the site aims to provide a platform for gay and lesbian service members to connect, despite the current lack of specific implementation rules. With only 53 members so far, the site's creators hope it will grow as the new policy takes effect. Some members, like Kristin Orta of the Florida National Guard, see it as a step towards serving openly, while others, like Vietnam veteran Bill Royal, hope it will help those who have suffered abuse. The site's creator, John McKinnon, encourages joining but advises against posting revealing information until the repeal is fully implemented.

A 20-year-old man accused of fatally shooting a Weymouth police officer and an innocent bystander could face murder charges. Emanuel Lopes, who was out on pre-trial release for drug offenses, is accused of using the officer's service weapon to kill Officer Michael Chesna, a six-year veteran of the force. Lopes also shot and killed 77-year-old Vera Adams after spotting her through a sliding glass door. The officer was responding to a report of a driver who had crashed a BMW, which Lopes was allegedly vandalizing. Lopes was hospitalized after exchanging gunfire with responding officers. The incident occurred on the sixth anniversary of Chesna joining the Weymouth police force. Lopes has a history of mental health issues and drug-related offenses, including resisting arrest and property damage. His mother had previously taken out a restraining order against him.

A TV news segment in New Mexico swabbed a handful of men's beards and sent the samples to a microbiologist for analysis. The results, according to the microbiologist, John Golobic, showed that some beards contained bacteria similar to those found in fecal matter. However, this does not necessarily mean the beards are as dirty as toilets. Human skin naturally hosts a diverse range of microbes, and some types of gut bacteria can be present on the skin. There are no proper scientific studies suggesting beards are as dirty as toilets. A couple of studies found that beards may reduce the likelihood of certain pathogens and that bearded men shed more bacteria than clean-shaven men. Regardless, the importance of wearing face coverings during sterile procedures remains crucial.

Two Tennessee high school basketball teams, Riverdale and Smyrna, were banned from the postseason and fined for intentionally losing a game to avoid playing the top-ranked team and improve their chances of advancing to the state tournament, according to the TSSAA. Both schools were placed on restrictive probation for the rest of the school year and the next. The referee reported intentional turnovers, missed free throws, and players stepping over midcourt. The TSSAA executive director said the teams "made a mockery" of the game and that high school athletic programs are meant to teach ethics, integrity, and sportsmanship. Both principals apologized for their teams' actions.

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-No Man's Land) faced criticism from fellow Republicans this week, with Sen. James Inhofe, the conservative website Redstate.com, Glenn Beck, and Rep. Pete Hoekstra all taking him to task. Graham, however, remains focused on his principles rather than his colleagues' approval. His latest offer to Obama—to close Guantanamo Bay in exchange for trying 9/11 suspects in military tribunals—reflects his commitment to pragmatic compromise over ideological purity. Graham's stance could provide a way out of the current impasse, but it also risks alienating his party. His willingness to challenge his colleagues and Obama's administration shows a commitment to what he believes is in the best interests of the country, despite potential political costs.

The connection between dreams and sex is explored in a study published in the journal Dreaming, which found that sleeping on the stomach with arms raised above the head increases the likelihood of experiencing erotic dreams. According to the research, 70% of women and 100% of men have overtly sexual dreams, with common themes including "sex," "being tied up," "being unable to move," and "being locked up." The study, involving 670 students who self-reported their dreams and sleeping positions, suggests that the position puts pressure on the genitals, potentially mixing external stimuli into our internal narratives during sleep. Lead researcher Kai-Ching Yu posits that the brain during sleep is not entirely detached from the external world, incorporating stimuli into dream content. While this position may increase the chances of erotic dreams, it is also noted as one of the worst for sleep due to potential lower back pain.

A Russian researcher at the Bellingshausen station in Antarctica has been charged with attempted murder after allegedly stabbing a colleague in the dining room with a knife. The incident, which reportedly occurred on October 9, may have stemmed from the pair's prolonged cohabitation at the remote base. Sergey Savitsky, the accused, is currently under house arrest until December 8 and has cooperated with authorities. The injured colleague has been taken to a hospital in Chile. The Bellingshausen station, established in 1968, is one of several research facilities on King George Island, with jurisdiction over crimes typically handled by the researcher's home country.

Global stocks opened weak on Monday, with the S&P 500 experiencing its worst start to a year in over a decade. The U.S. market saw a significant drop, led by declines in financial, health-care, and consumer discretionary sectors. China’s poor economic report and heightened tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia contributed to the global sell-off. Investors shifted towards safer assets like gold and Treasurys. The Dow Jones fell 276 points, while the Nasdaq dropped 104 points. The circuit-breaker system in China, activated due to a 7% slide in the Shanghai Composite, halted trading for the day. European markets also declined. Analysts suggest this volatility could continue in 2016 due to ongoing economic uncertainties and geopolitical tensions.

CNN host Piers Morgan discussed his interview with Alex Jones, the conservative radio host and gun advocate, who went on a rant during the segment. Morgan described Jones's "vitriol, hatred, and zealotry" as "really quite scary" and expressed concern about Jones's level of influence. The interview, which Morgan called a "big, long rant," included Jones's conspiracy theories and premonitions of a 1776-like rebellion, while Morgan attempted a calm and civil conversation. Jones's show and websites have a significant online presence, allowing him to spur gun sales and ammunition purchases through fear. Morgan emphasized the importance of continuing the gun control debate, stating that the issue must remain "boiling along" until politicians take action.

Pippa Middleton, sister of the Duchess of Cambridge, is set to launch a book deal worth £400,000, sparking debate over her qualifications. The book, due to be released next autumn, will offer advice on hosting perfect parties. Despite her family's party-planning business, critics question her expertise, citing past controversies and her reliance on royal connections. The deal, negotiated by her agent, highlights the bidding war for her work, but some Britons are upset by the perceived cashing-in on royal status.

A woman was killed after getting too close to the tracks while taking photographs of a Union Pacific steam locomotive in Henderson, Colorado. The 21-car train, known as the 'Denver Post Special,' was returning from a day-long trip to Cheyenne Frontier Days in Wyoming when the incident occurred. The train had just arrived at the 124th Avenue crossing near Henderson at about 7:45 p.m. on Saturday. Union Pacific is leading the investigation, and passengers were bused back to Denver. Steam Engine 844, a historic locomotive, was involved in the incident.

Investigators are re-examining conversations detected by U.S. intelligence agencies in spring 2015 that captured Russian government officials discussing associates of Donald Trump, according to current and former U.S. officials. This move is prompted by revelations that the president’s eldest son met with a Russian lawyer last year. The younger Trump said the meeting with the Russian lawyer yielded no useful information about Hillary Clinton, instead turning into a discussion about a Russian-American diplomatic dispute. The timing of these events and Trump’s positions that summer, including openness to lifting sanctions on Russia and suggesting he might not defend NATO allies, have raised questions about potential Russian influence. Trump said he did not know about the June 2016 meeting with the Russian lawyer until a few days ago and did not fault his son for holding the meeting. Trump also said he directly asked Russian President Vladimir Putin if he was involved in Russian meddling in the presidential campaign and that Putin denied any involvement. Chris Brown will return to jail for a month after being arrested on Friday for violating his probation. On Monday, a judge cited his "inability to stay out of trouble" as grounds to keep him locked up until April 23. Brown, 25, was arrested based on a warrant issued by probation officials and held without bail. TMZ reports that the singer was kicked out of a Malibu rehab center for violating unspecified "internal rules." Brown was ordered to spend 90 days in a residential facility in November for anger-management issues after an incident in which he threw a rock through his mother's car window. He was discharged from a rehab facility after two weeks in early October following an alleged assault in Washington, D.C. Brown is due back in court on April 17, when a judge will determine whether he committed criminal assault in that incident. The Malibu rehab facility revealed in court documents that Brown suffered from PTSD and bipolar disorder. He was thrown out of the Malibu

Author R.L. Stine, known for his scary stories for children, announced he will write a new Halloween tale exclusively on Twitter. He plans to share the story live on the platform, encouraging followers to join in. This is not the first time Stine has used Twitter for his spooky content, with previous tales shared over multiple tweets. His latest book, "A Nightmare on Clown Street," is set for release in February. Despite his age and preference for physical books, Stine maintains a significant social media presence, with over 133,000 Twitter followers. He will also take over Scholastic’s Twitter feed for a Halloween-themed Q&A on Thursday.

A 2-year-old boy brought to a Wichita hospital with an octopus stuck in his throat has shown improvement, police say. The boy, in good condition, was not breathing when his 36-year-old boyfriend performed CPR at home. Doctors removed the 2-inch octopus from the child’s throat. The octopus, intended for sushi, was not a pet. The boy’s 21-year-old mother told police she returned home from work to find the incident. The boy’s 36-year-old boyfriend was arrested on suspicion of child abuse and released on bond. Police continue to investigate.

In recent years, many Americans have fallen victim to data breaches, with prominent companies like Adidas, Best Buy, Delta, Kmart, Macy’s, and Sears among those affected in 2018, reports the Identity Theft Resource Center. Between January 1, 2005, and August 31, 2018, there have been 9,395 breaches compromising over 1.1 billion records. Despite increased security measures, the Trump administration's new cybersecurity plan, which includes more aggressive offensive measures against foreign cyberattacks, has not fully thwarted evolving criminal strategies. WalletHub analyzed the 50 states and the District of Columbia, ranking Nevada as the most vulnerable to identity theft and fraud, while states like Hawaii and South Dakota are the least vulnerable. The analysis considered metrics such as identity-theft complaints, average loss due to fraud, and policy measures in place. Tips for protecting personal information include emphasizing email security, signing up for credit monitoring

A Chilean mother, Sindy Melany Ortiz, claims a hospital is limiting her access to her newborn due to her admission of smoking marijuana to alleviate arm pain. Ortiz says she is only permitted to see her daughter for two hours daily and cannot breastfeed her. Hospital officials in Talcahuano state they were following protocol after tests indicated potential risks to the baby. The case highlights the current legal status of marijuana in Chile, where personal use is allowed but selling or growing the drug is illegal. A bill to decriminalize personal use and cultivation, currently allowing up to 10 grams of cannabis and six plants, is pending approval.

New research suggests that repeatedly losing and regaining weight, known as weight cycling or "yo-yo dieting," may increase the risk of death from heart disease among postmenopausal women who were of normal weight at the start of the study. Among 158,063 postmenopausal women followed for 11.4 years, women who lost and regained weight had about three and a half times higher risk for sudden cardiac death than women whose weight remained stable. Weight cycling was also associated with a 66% increased risk for coronary heart disease deaths in these normal-weight women. However, no increase in either type of death occurred among overweight or obese women reporting weight cycling, or among women who gained or lost weight but did not cycle. The study highlights the potential dangers of yo-yo dieting, especially for women who start out at a normal weight, and underscores the need for further research to understand the underlying mechanisms.

Mitt Romney will not participate in the December 27th debate scheduled by Donald Trump, opting instead to focus on campaigning in key early states. Romney told Fox News he informed Trump of his decision and will instead attend two other debates in December. Ron Paul and Jon Huntsman have also declined, while Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum have confirmed their attendance.

Anonymous has intensified its campaign against ISIS following the Paris attacks, releasing a list of over 1,000 Twitter accounts suspected to be used by supporters. The group's actions are part of a broader effort to disrupt the terror group's online presence, including previous work to take down websites and social media accounts. A YouTube video declared "war" on ISIS, warning of "massive cyberattacks." While Anonymous claims to degrade ISIS's digital capabilities, experts question the effectiveness of such tactics, noting that ISIS supporters can easily recreate accounts and that Anonymous's actions might disrupt law enforcement investigations.

Former President Bill Clinton earned $75.6 million in speaking fees since leaving office in 2001, with his most lucrative year coming in 2010 when he made $10.7 million from 52 paid speeches. Clinton's earnings have been significantly influenced by international engagements, with nearly half of his 2010 earnings coming from 18 speeches in 13 countries. His domestic earnings were from 34 speeches in eight states and the District of Columbia. Clinton's average earnings per speech have been $181,000, with the majority of his earnings, $44.9 million, coming from 215 overseas events in 48 countries. His most popular destinations outside the U.S. include Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Sending a Christmas card can leave a lasting impression, as demonstrated by Andrew Simes and Queen Elizabeth II. Simes continued a tradition started by his grandfather, who sent cards to the Queen every holiday season from 1952 until his death in 2011. In 1972, their paths crossed at a reception in Turkey, where the Queen remembered his grandfather and joked about the cards. After Simes took over the tradition, he received a letter from Buckingham Palace expressing condolences upon his grandfather's passing and thanking him for his continued correspondence. Wishing everyone a magical Christmas, Simes continues to send his cards, with a special place reserved for the Queen.

A 10-year-old boy was bitten by a shark in Daytona Beach Shores, Florida, on Wednesday, marking the fourth reported shark bite in Volusia County this year. The boy suffered minor injuries and was treated on the beach. This incident comes as shark attacks have increased in the area, with 11 attacks reported in the state this summer, the most in one year since 1935. Experts suggest that better reporting and more people in the water, combined with warmer ocean temperatures and fish migrations, may be contributing factors. However, the overall risk remains low, with shark attacks still far less common than those caused by humans. Beachgoers are advised to stay in groups and avoid areas near fishing piers where sharks may congregate.

After three years together, Derek Jeter and Minka Kelly have called off their relationship, according to sources. The couple, who first got together around May 2008, remains friends and still cares for each other. Minka is currently shooting the ABC reboot of Charlie's Angels in Miami, while Derek is busy with the New York Yankees. Despite facing rumors of splits and engagements, the couple couldn't make it work. Both stars are expected to find new love if they desire.

A woman who fled with her 8-year-old daughter during a custody dispute turned herself in to face trial after a decade on the run. Genevieve Kelley, 50, disappeared with her daughter, Mary, into Central America in 2004 after attempting to prove her ex-husband, Mark Nunes, had harmed the child. Nunes was never charged with a crime. After Mary turned 18, Kelley contacted authorities and agreed to face a jury on her custodial interference charge, stating her daughter is safe. U.S. Marshals investigated numerous tips over the years. Kelley surrendered in Lancaster, New Hampshire, and was arrested. Her lawyer argues she would not be a flight risk and wants a trial to clear her name. Mark Nunes remains hopeful of reuniting with his daughter and learning more about her. U.S. Marshal David Cargill Jr. expressed hope that Mary is safe.

A 17-year-old high school senior, Jacqueline Gomez, was found dead in a north Houston hotel room the morning after her prom at MacArthur High School. Her boyfriend discovered her unresponsive in their 8th-floor room at the Hyatt Hotel around 11 a.m. on Saturday. Police are investigating whether alcohol or prescription painkillers were involved, but the cause of death remains unclear. Friends remember Gomez as a hardworking student who planned to take classes at Lone Star College. The incident has left her classmates and friends in shock and seeking answers.

A letter containing a substance tested positive for ricin at the Washington, D.C., office of Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.). The letter was intercepted at an off-site Senate mail facility and was immediately quarantined. Capitol Police hazardous material personnel responded to the scene. Senate Sergeant at Arms Terrance Gainer stated that the letter had a Memphis, Tennessee, postmark and no return address. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid confirmed the presence of ricin after laboratory tests. Further testing is needed as initial field tests can be inconsistent. The letter was addressed to Sen. Wicker, and a protective detail has been assigned to him. Senate offices have been instructed to be vigilant for similar letters. The incident highlights the ongoing security measures in place since the 2001 anthrax attacks.

Norway's Prime Minister Erna Solberg issued an official government apology to women who were mistreated in the 1940s due to relationships with German soldiers during World War II. Up to 50,000 Norwegian women are thought to have had intimate relations with German soldiers, and many faced harsh reprisals after Norway's liberation in 1945, including job dismissals, detentions, expulsions, and loss of nationality. The government acknowledged that these women were treated undignifiedly and violated the principle that no citizen should be punished without trial. Solberg's apology came at an event marking the 70th anniversary of the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Historian Guri Hjeltnes noted that Norwegian authorities violated fundamental rights, and many of the women directly affected are no longer alive, but the apology also benefits their families and children.

An FBI agent was shot in the shoulder while conducting surveillance in Brooklyn on Saturday afternoon, sources tell CBS2. The agent was working a drug investigation in Canarsie when a suspect driving a BMW approached and fired into his vehicle around 3:30 p.m. Despite being struck, the agent managed to return fire, hitting one of the suspects. The wounded suspect was arrested after seeking treatment at Kingsbrook Jewish Medical Center. The second suspect was captured outside a nearby business on Remsen Avenue. The agent's injuries are not believed to be life-threatening. NYPD Chief of Department Terence Monahan tweeted that no suspects remain at large and expressed wishes for the agent's speedy recovery. The investigation is ongoing, and it is unclear if the suspects were aware the agent was an FBI officer.

A magnitude-6.0 earthquake struck the Napa Valley early Sunday, causing damage to buildings and wine cellars, with some 250 people injured and 70 buildings red-tagged as unsafe. Cleanup efforts were underway, but challenges remained, including water shortages and school closures. Wineries reported significant damage, with wine barrels and bottles spilled and broken, but the extent of the damage varied across the region. Despite the severity, many residents expressed gratitude that the quake was not worse, and recovery efforts were expected to be a long process.

The U.S. economy added 215,000 jobs in March, driven by gains in construction, retail, and health care industries. Despite the increase, the unemployment rate ticked up to 5% from 4.9%, mainly because more Americans entered the job market. Steady hiring continues to boost wages, which rose 2.3% from a year earlier. Job growth suggests employers remain optimistic about business prospects, even as overall economic growth has slowed. Construction firms added 37,000 jobs, partly due to warmer weather, while manufacturing and mining lost jobs. Consumer spending, which is crucial for growth, has been tepid, with a savings rate rising to 5.4% in February. Other economic indicators show mixed signals, with manufacturing potentially stabilizing and home sales declining.

Pepsi pulled an ad featuring Kendall Jenner after it was widely criticized for trivializing social justice protests. The ad showed Jenner joining a group of smiling protesters and handing a can of Pepsi to a police officer, who took a sip. Pepsi said they "missed the mark" and apologized, removing the content and halting further rollout. Critics called the ad "gloriously tone-deaf," comparing it to a photo of a Black Lives Matter protester approaching an officer in Baton Rouge. Late-night comedian Stephen Colbert mocked the ad, highlighting its trivialization of the protest movement and the absurdity of Jenner's role.

Gretchen Carlson and Fox News reached a $20 million settlement, with Fox issuing a public apology for not treating Carlson with the respect and dignity she deserved. The settlement comes after a series of sexual harassment allegations against Roger Ailes, Fox News's former chairman, led to his ousting. Ailes denied all accusations. The Murdochs, Rupert's sons, initially launched an internal investigation but have since focused on retaining key anchors and navigating the post-Ailes landscape. The settlement marks a significant chapter in the Ailes scandal, though the broader culture of Fox News remains largely unexamined.

In the wake of the Florida school shooting, the National Rifle Association (NRA) leader Wayne LaPierre spoke at a conservative conference, accusing gun control advocates of wanting to destroy American liberty. LaPierre called for increased school security, including arming teachers, and criticized the FBI for failing to prevent the shooting. He also attacked Democrats and the media, saying they were exploiting the tragedy for political gain. Meanwhile, Vice President Mike Pence took a more conciliatory tone, praising Trump's calls for background checks and restrictions on bump stocks. The NRA's response highlights the ongoing political divide over gun control, with the group pushing back against calls for stricter regulations and advocating for more armed security.

Spanish police have arrested at least one person in connection with the discovery of what is believed to be the bodies of Dutch international volleyball player Ingrid Visser and her partner Lodewijk Severin. The bodies were found in a shallow grave in a lemon grove near Alquerías, about 12 kilometers from Murcia. Identification is pending DNA testing. The couple disappeared on May 13 and were last seen in Murcia. Their rental car was later found on a street. Police believe the murders may be business-related and that there were "certain business disagreements" between the couple and the suspects. An ex-director of a Spanish volleyball club, Juan Cuenca Lorente, and two other Romanian men were among those arrested.

Rupert Murdoch met with the family of murdered schoolgirl Milly Dowler and offered a "full and sincere apology." Dowler's family lawyer described Murdoch as humbled and sincere, but emphasized that actions must follow words. Rebekah Brooks, former editor of the News of the World and now CEO of News International, resigned, facing pressure from British politicians. James Murdoch signaled a new strategy for dealing with the crisis, installing a new CEO, Tom Mockridge. The scandal has led to the closure of the News of the World, a multimillion-pound payout to the Dowler family, and a criminal investigation by British police. The FBI is also investigating possible hacking of 9/11 victims' phones.

Mark Cuban, known for his outspoken nature, recently admitted to having his own prejudices in a video interview with Inc. magazine. He stated that if he sees a black kid in a hoodie late at night, he would cross the street, and if he sees a white man with tattoos, he would do the same. Cuban acknowledged that everyone has some form of prejudice and emphasized the importance of controlling these biases. His comments sparked debate, with some supporting his candidness and others criticizing his examples as insensitive. Cuban stood by his statements, arguing that addressing and working through these biases is crucial. The incident also highlighted the ongoing challenges in the NBA regarding race and ownership, as Cuban is one of the 30 owners who will decide Sterling's fate.

Devo, the seminal new wave band, lost a founding member, Bob Casale, who passed away at 61. Bob Casale, known as "Bob 2," was a key figure in the group's sound and visual style. His brother, bandmate Gerald Casale, praised his contributions, noting his role in the band's early days and his work as an audio engineer. Devo, formed in the midst of cultural upheaval, has continued to tour and create, with Bob Casale's involvement in recent years. His death comes as a shock to the band, with Mark Mothersbaugh expressing his loss and highlighting Bob's contributions to their work over decades.

A 21-year-old man, Scott Bertics, killed his former girlfriend, Clare Orton, and then himself at her home in Walnut Creek using two homemade "ghost guns" he built from parts he ordered online, police said. Neither gun had a serial number, making them untraceable. Bertics, a former Stanford University student, took a leave of absence after the fall 2014 quarter. Orton was an honors student at San Diego State University and an athlete. The incident highlights the ease with which unregistered guns can be assembled from mail-ordered parts, despite efforts to regulate such purchases.

A Vancouver museum featuring the St. Roch, the first ship to circumnavigate North America, offers a unique look into maritime history. The museum, located in Vanier Park, includes exhibits on British Columbia's seafaring tradition, model ships, and interactive areas like Pirates Cove and the Discovery Center. While some find the exhibits engaging and educational, others criticize the high admission price and the presence of sexually explicit scrimshaw on display, which they argue is inappropriate for children. The St. Roch, a former RCMP vessel, is the main attraction, allowing visitors to explore the inside of the ship and learn about its historic voyages. The museum also hosts events like "Pirate Parties" for children.

A 14-month-old girl survived a fall from a fifth-story window in a Bronx apartment after wearing a heavily cushioned winter coat, authorities and neighbors said. The child, Xania Samuels, was rushed to Jacobi Hospital with head trauma but is expected to survive. Her father said the girl insisted on wearing her favorite pink coat on a hot day, which might have cushioned her fall. The incident occurred when the father was giving the girl’s twin brother a bath while the mother was at a Laundromat. There were no window guards on the building’s upper floors, and previous complaints to the landlord were ignored. The child fell at 11:29 am, but it took at least 7 minutes before anyone realized she had fallen. An emergency medical technician found the lifeless infant on the pavement and called for help. The father later screamed from the window when he realized what had happened. (No charges were filed against the parents.)

During the busy summer travel season, the TSA offers tips to help travelers move through airport security faster. Pittsburgh International Airport is allowing non-ticketed patrons to access the airside terminal's shops, restaurants, and gates starting September 5th, with approval from the TSA. Passengers will need to check in at a special desk, show a valid ID, and undergo security screening. The TSA supports this change but notes no additional staff has been hired, and there are no plans to expand the program. The union representing flight attendants at American Airlines criticizes the decision, warning it could decrease airport safety and lead to longer security lines, causing flyers to miss their flights.

Cory Booker, the mayor of Newark, won the Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate seat in New Jersey, defeating his three rivals with a significant margin. Booker will face Steve Lonegan, the Republican primary winner, in the October 16 special election to replace the late Frank Lautenberg. The race was marked by intense attacks from Booker’s opponents, who struggled to shift the focus onto their own qualifications. Despite these challenges, Booker’s record in Newark and his pragmatic approach to governance resonated with voters. His campaign emphasized his ability to work across the aisle, highlighting his relationship with Republican Governor Chris Christie. With a strong financial backing and support from the Democratic establishment, including celebrities like Oprah Winfrey, Booker secured a decisive victory. His victory speech emphasized his commitment to working for all New Jersey residents and finding common ground.

Fashion designer Peter Nygard claims to have reversed his aging process through stem cell therapy, according to reports. Nygard, a Bahamian resident, says he has been receiving stem cell treatments for four years and that a study from the University of Miami supports his claim of rejuvenation. He advocates for stem cell research in the Bahamas and has been examining potential sites in Freeport for a stem cell clinic. Nygard's interest in Freeport has received backing from local business leaders, while his plans for a clinic at his Lyford Cay property faced opposition. His push for stem cell research and therapy in the Bahamas has sparked debate on the ethical and practical implications of the technology.

Louisville guard Kevin Ware suffered a gruesome leg injury during a closely watched NCAA tournament game against Duke, causing his teammates to weep. Ware's right leg broke in two places, with the bone sticking out six inches, as he tried to block a shot. The injury, which prompted CBS to stop showing replays, left Ware in critical condition but he underwent successful surgery. Louisville went on to win the game, 85-63, and advance to the Final Four. Ware hopes to return to support his team in Atlanta, his hometown. Dr. Frederick Azar described the injury as a "bending fracture," similar to former Louisville running back Michael Bush's injury. Ware's recovery will depend on the type of hardware used during surgery, with a full return to play potentially taking 6-8 months.

Boulder police and prosecutors plan new DNA tests on key evidence in the 1996 unsolved murder of 6-year-old JonBenét Ramsey, following a joint Camera/9NEWS investigation revealing flaws in previous DNA testing. Boulder County District Attorney Stan Garnett and Boulder Police Chief Greg Testa confirmed discussions with the Colorado Bureau of Investigation (CBI) about using new, more sophisticated DNA testing kits required by the FBI's Combined DNA Index System. These tests aim to address ambiguities in the 2008 DNA results, which cleared the Ramseys but are now disputed by forensic experts. The new tests could involve Y-STR testing to identify male contributors to mixed samples, potentially shedding light on the case.

After days of escalating violence, Palestinian and Israeli authorities have agreed to a truce and to stop all military operations, an Egyptian intelligence official announced. The agreement, mediated by Egypt, aims to halt the fighting that has left seven people dead in Gaza and more than 36 rockets fired into Israel. The U.N. Secretary-General expressed grave concern over the violence, urging both sides to cease attacks. Despite the truce, conflicting reports from both sides about casualties and incidents of rocket fire persist, raising doubts about its sustainability. The latest round of violence, the worst in Gaza in months, highlights the ongoing tensions despite diplomatic efforts to revive peace talks.

Six people were killed and at least 13 others injured when a building being demolished collapsed onto a Salvation Army thrift store in Philadelphia. The collapse occurred around 10:40 a.m., trapping people inside the store. Rescuers pulled a 61-year-old woman from the rubble alive after 13 hours. The building's demolition was permitted, but questions remain about inspections and potential violations. The incident raised concerns about safety regulations and oversight in demolition projects.

When Huguette Clark's will was filed, plans for her estate to be transformed into a museum in Santa Barbara excited art lovers. However, a New York judge suspended Clark's attorney and accountant as her executors, citing accusations of massive tax fraud. The public administrator's office alleged that attorney Wallace Bock and accountant Irving Kamsler caused Clark's estate to lose over $50 million through false tax returns and unauthorized gifts. Bock and Kamsler were removed as executors, but may seek reinstatement. The case highlights the ethical concerns surrounding Clark's long-term care and the handling of her extensive fortune.

Sandy Hook Elementary students returned to class on Thursday at a nearby middle school in Monroe, Conn., where they will remain until their old school is no longer a crime scene. The 400-plus students, who had not been back to school since the Dec. 14 massacre, were excited to reconnect with friends and teachers after three weeks of mourning. The former Chalk Hill Middle School was refurnished for the students, with old desks, backpacks, and lunch boxes brought in to make the new surroundings familiar. The new principal, Donna Page, who retired from Sandy Hook in 2010, agreed to return after the previous principal, Dawn Hochsprung, was killed. Security was visible, but officials aimed to make the day as normal as possible, with counselors and therapy dogs on hand. Connecticut Governor Dannel Malloy announced a commission to address school security, mental health services, and gun laws to prevent such tragedies in the future.

Bodybuilder Rich Piana collapsed while getting a haircut from his girlfriend and was found with 20 bottles of steroids in his Florida home, according to a police report obtained by TMZ Sports. Emergency responders administered Narcan but were unable to revive him, and he was placed in a medically induced coma. Piana's girlfriend, Chanel, believes he was clean from opiate addiction but had a history of steroid use. She stated he has been using steroids for over 20 years and had a slightly enlarged heart. Piana is still alive and fighting, but his girlfriend asks for prayers.

The half marathon has seen a significant surge in popularity, becoming the fastest-growing standard distance among U.S. road races in 2013. With an estimated 1.96 million finishers, a 6% increase from 2012, it set a new record. The growth is largely attributed to increased female participation, with women making up 61% of finishers, up from 53% in 2006. Despite a slight decline in male participation percentages, the absolute number of male finishers continues to rise. Notably, the half marathon's popularity extends beyond the U.S., with the three largest races held in Sweden, Great Britain, and France. The race's growing appeal is evident in its rapid expansion over the past quarter-century, with the number of finishers increasing more than sixfold since 1990.

Portland police have decided to reopen their investigation into sexual assault allegations against former Vice President Al Gore, citing procedural mistakes in the original 2009 case. According to Portland Police Chief Michael Reese, command-level supervisors should have reviewed the case and made the decision on whether to move forward after the complainant approached the bureau for a second time. In 2006, an attorney representing the accuser, Portland massage therapist Molly Hagerty, contacted Portland police. Detectives attempted to meet with Hagerty three times, but these meetings were cancelled by her attorney. The lawyer informed detectives that Hagerty was pursuing a civil lawsuit, leading the case to be cleared due to her lack of cooperation. Reese emphasized the bureau's responsibility to both parties involved and requested public patience during the investigation.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, designed to safeguard seeds against disasters, recently faced unexpected water intrusion due to melting permafrost. Despite initial concerns, the seeds themselves remained safe. The facility, built to withstand natural and man-made disasters, has been operating for over nine years. Water occasionally enters the tunnel leading to the vault but is managed by pumping systems. Recent events highlight the vault's vulnerability to climate change, prompting discussions on further waterproofing measures. The Seed Vault continues to store backups of seeds from global seed banks, aiming to preserve crop diversity.

A 30-year-old hospital technician in Uganda has died from Marburg hemorrhagic fever, a rare and deadly virus closely related to Ebola. Health officials have quarantined about 80 people who came into contact with the victim, including 60 healthcare workers. Testing on 11 potential cases came back negative, including the victim's brother. Marburg causes symptoms similar to Ebola, including fever, headache, and internal or external bleeding, with a fatality rate ranging from 23% to 90%. The virus is spread through direct contact with the blood, tissues, or bodily fluids of an infected person or animal. Previous outbreaks have occurred in Europe, Uganda, and Angola. While there is no specific treatment or vaccine, supportive therapy can help manage complications. The Ugandan government has experience dealing with such outbreaks and has put in place surveillance and control measures.

A man in Amritsar, Punjab, ate 40 knives over two months and only sought medical help due to stomach pain, weight loss, and a low appetite. Doctors conducted a five-hour surgery to remove the metal objects from his stomach. The patient reportedly felt an urge to eat the knives. Dr. Jitendra Malhotra, who performed the surgery, stated, "This was very unnerving. Have never witnessed something like this in my career as a doctor." The patient is now stable.

French prosecutors have filed preliminary murder and terrorism charges against Abdelkader Merah, the 29-year-old brother of Mohamed Merah, who was killed by police after a 30-hour siege in Toulouse. Abdelkader Merah denies helping his 23-year-old brother commit the attacks that killed seven people, including three Jewish schoolchildren, a rabbi, and three paratroopers. Preliminary charges under French law suggest a strong reason to suspect a crime was committed but allow for more investigation time. Abdelkader Merah is suspected of complicity in murder, theft, and involvement in a terrorist enterprise. He has denied being proud of his brother's actions and claims he was only present when Mohamed stole a scooter used in the attacks. Abdelkader's lawyer states he "strongly condemns" his brother's actions. Mohamed Merah died in a shoot-out with police, admitting to killing three soldiers and three children at a Jewish school. The United States ended a 75-year losing streak against Mexico, earning a 1-0 victory in Mexico City. Michael Orozco Fiscal scored the winning goal in the 80th minute, and Tim Howard made crucial late saves to secure the win. The U.S. dominated for much of the match despite Mexico's 15-6 shot advantage and 10 corner kicks. Coach Jurgen Klinsmann's team showed resilience and improved defensive organization, marking a significant milestone in U.S. soccer history. The victory, achieved with a makeshift roster due to injuries and European club commitments, boosted team morale and confidence for upcoming World Cup qualifiers.

California will no longer bar all registered sex offenders from living within 2,000 feet of a school or park, instead applying such restrictions on a case-by-case basis. The move comes after a state Supreme Court ruling this month affecting San Diego County, which found that "Jessica’s Law" was unconstitutional and did not protect the public. The change is expected to leave the restrictions in place for offenders who sexually abused children, while relaxing the rules for some others. Existing restrictions will remain in place while the corrections department reviews the cases of thousands of sex-offender parolees to decide if the residency law should still apply. That review is expected to take two months. California has 6,000 sex offender parolees living in communities across the state who are required to register for life with police and disclose their address on a publicly searchable database, established under "Megan’s Law."

China is reinforcing its northern border with North Korea amid heightened tensions, preparing for potential crises, including U.S. military strikes. Recent reports on Chinese military and government websites indicate new border defense brigades are conducting patrols, and the area is under 24-hour surveillance. Beijing's concerns focus on a potential influx of North Korean refugees, given the region's dense population and economic importance. Analysts warn that instability on the Korean Peninsula could strain China's resources and security. Despite repeated condemnations of North Korea's weapons testing, China's influence over its ally is limited, leading to frustration among all parties involved.

A new report from She Should Run and the Center for Responsive Politics highlights the persistent gender gap in political donations, showing that women contributed just 26% of total federal political contributions in 2010, down from 31% in 2008 and 27% in 2006. Female candidates, however, are better fundraisers, raising more money than their male counterparts. The report suggests that women may not see the connection between politics and social change, and are deterred by the perceived "dirty" nature of politics. Despite this, female candidates are outperforming male ones in fundraising, raising approximately $100,000 more on average. The report recommends making the connection between women’s political contributions and the issues they care about to encourage more women to get involved and run for office.

Mount Everest faces ongoing challenges with overcrowding, unstable weather, and geography, as highlighted by recent incidents and decisions. Over 300 climbers were preparing for the 2014 season, but after a deadly avalanche killed 16 Sherpas, one of the largest commercial operators, Himalayan Experience, decided to cancel its expedition, shocking the base camp. The avalanche, which occurred on April 18th, was the deadliest in Everest's history, and it has reignited discussions about the risks faced by Sherpas. The fatality rate among Sherpas working on Everest is significantly higher than in traditionally dangerous professions like commercial fishing and military combat. Despite improvements in safety measures for Western climbers, the job remains perilous for Sherpas, who carry the majority of the physical and financial burden. The Nepali government and Sherpas are currently negotiating demands for better compensation and working conditions, reflecting the growing tension and awareness of the risks involved.

Newt Gingrich launched his latest presidential campaign with the slogan "Win the Future," which Obama later adopted for his own use. Gingrich registered "American Solutions for Winning the Future" with the IRS in 2006, using it as his main political arm. Despite Obama co-opting the phrase, Gingrich's campaign spokesman says they think it's "great" and plan to debate whose policies will actually win the future.

Bill Cosby faces a sexual assault trial in Pennsylvania, with Andrea Constand as the sole accuser. Constand, now 44, alleges Cosby drugged and assaulted her in 2004, while Cosby claims the encounter was consensual. The trial hinges on Constand's testimony and her account of the events, as Cosby plans not to testify. Other potential witnesses include a former assistant to Cosby's agent and a psychologist to discuss the behavior of sex-abuse victims. The case has broader implications, potentially encouraging other victims to come forward and addressing the challenges of prosecuting sexual assault cases with limited forensic evidence.

A small bowl purchased at a garage sale for $3 turned out to be a 1,000-year-old Chinese Ding ware, selling for $2.2 million at Sotheby’s. The family kept the bowl for years before consulting experts, who brought it to Sotheby’s, which estimated a $200,000 to $300,000 price. London art dealer Giuseppe Eskenazi outbid four others for the Northern Song dynasty bowl, known for its thin potting, fine white body, and ivory-colored glaze. Only one other bowl of the same form and decoration exists, in the British Museum. The Ding wares were among the 'five great wares' of the Song dynasty, often mimicking precious materials like gold and silver. The bowl, from the Hebei province, is described as ornamental, possibly created to resemble more elaborate wares found in palaces.

A fugitive murder suspect, Masaaki Osaka, has been arrested after more than 45 years on the run, police in Japan announced. Osaka, 67, is accused of setting a 21-year-old police officer on fire during a Tokyo street protest in November 1971. He was identified through DNA tests after being arrested in a Hiroshima apartment belonging to the Japan Revolutionary Communist League (JRCL). No other suspected criminal in Japan has evaded arrest for as long. Japan has no statute of limitations for murder, with the 15-year limit abolished in 2010. Osaka initially faced charges of obstructing police before his true identity was confirmed. He has appeared on wanted posters for decades and is alleged to have remained on the run due to assistance from sympathetic party associates.

A California woman, Michelle Hadley, was exonerated after spending nearly four months in jail for crimes she never committed, including attempted forcible rape and stalking. Hadley was accused by Angela Maria Diaz, who had married Hadley's ex-boyfriend and was framed for the crimes. Diaz falsely reported threatening emails and rape fantasies to police, leading to Hadley's multiple arrests. Prosecutors now charge Diaz with 22 counts of falsely reporting crimes, kidnapping, false imprisonment, perjury, and forgery. Hadley, who was released in October, is relieved and considers the ordeal a nightmare. The case highlights the dangers of social media and online impersonations, according to the district attorney.

Jodie Foster, 51, is attending Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and embracing a 12-step program to support her girlfriend Alexandra Hedison, a recovered alcoholic, according to a friend. The two, who have been dating for months, are both now sober and considering a commitment ceremony. Meanwhile, Ellen DeGeneres is reportedly advising Jodie against marriage, fearing Alexandra might be headed for the same struggles Ellen faced with Portia de Rossi. Ellen, whose own marriage is reportedly troubled, may be offering this advice out of concern for Jodie's well-being.

Playboy, the iconic men's magazine, is set to drop fully nude female photography from its pages as part of a redesign. The move, announced by Playboy's CEO Scott Flanders, aims to appeal to a broader and younger audience in both print and online. Flanders cited the ubiquity of online pornography as a reason for the change, stating, "You're now one click away from every sex act imaginable for free. It's just passé at this juncture." Despite the potential alienation of long-time subscribers, Playboy plans to continue featuring women in provocative poses. The change will take effect in February with the March issue.

California Assembly Member Ian Calderon introduced legislation calling for straws to be offered only upon request in sit-down restaurants. The bill, Assembly Bill 1884, aims to reduce plastic waste by raising awareness of the environmental impacts of single-use plastic straws. Currently, providing a straw without a request could result in fines or jail time, though Calderon plans to amend the penalties. The law would not ban plastic straws but seeks to encourage a "straws-upon-request" policy to lessen environmental damage from plastic waste in landfills, waterways, and oceans. Approximately 500 million straws are used daily in the U.S., and only 9% of plastic is recycled, with straws often ending up in marine environments.

A Dutch father, Hans de Borst, who lost his 17-year-old daughter, Elsemiek, in the downed Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, wrote an emotional open letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, blaming him for the tragedy. De Borst expressed anger and grief, stating, "Thank you very much Mister Putin, leaders of the separatists or the Ukraine government for murdering my loved and only child, Elsemiek de Borst." He described his daughter's aspirations and how her life was cut short. The letter highlights the personal impact of the disaster and the father's frustration with the political situation.

Kentucky family court judge W. Mitchell Nance has disqualified himself from hearing adoption cases involving gay parents, citing personal bias. Nance's order, issued after being assigned to a case involving same-sex couples seeking to adopt, has drawn criticism from legal experts who view it as discriminatory. The decision comes amid ongoing debates over LGBTQ+ rights and judicial ethics.

A community town hall in Dearborn, Michigan, is organized to challenge anti-Arab and anti-Muslim bias, particularly in response to the "Jessica Mokdad Human Rights Conference" by Pamela Geller and Robert Spencer. The conference, named after a young Arab American girl killed in Warren, is seen as exploiting her tragedy to promote a bigoted agenda. Local organizations, including the Arab American Institute, are hosting the town hall to directly address the narrative of the conference and discuss how to respond to continued attacks on the community. The event, held on the same day as the conference, aims to foster a community conversation on diversity and freedom of religion.

Former President George W. Bush has canceled a planned visit to Switzerland due to legal threats and protests over alleged torture. Bush was set to speak at a Jewish charity gala in Geneva but the event organizers decided against his participation for security reasons, citing concerns about criminal complaints against him for torture. Human rights groups, including the New York-based Human Rights Watch and the International Federation of Human Rights, had filed complaints against Bush for his involvement in waterboarding and other alleged mistreatment of detainees. Swiss parliament member Dominique Baettig called for Bush's arrest if he entered the country. Despite Bush's defense of waterboarding in his memoirs, most human rights experts consider it a form of torture. Bush's visit cancellation reflects growing pressure on former leaders to face accountability for alleged war crimes and human rights abuses.

Syria's ongoing civil war has created a refugee crisis of unprecedented scale, with over 2 million people fleeing the conflict, according to the United Nations. The crisis, described as the most challenging of its kind in a generation, has strained resources in neighboring countries like Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, and Iraq. As the conflict drags on, governments and international organizations are preparing for a prolonged displacement. Zakaria Deeb, a Syrian refugee in Turkey, expresses uncertainty about the war's end, having fled his home a year ago due to fighting between rebels and government forces. The influx of refugees has raised concerns about potential instability in host countries and the risk of conflict spillover. Turkey, which has hosted over 80,000 refugees, faces pressure to expand its capacity and manage the increasing number of arrivals. The situation highlights the complexity and humanitarian challenges of the Syrian conflict, with no end in sight.

Former Louisiana Governor Edwin Edwards, 86, announced his comeback bid for Congress, aiming to represent the 6th District. Edwards, known for his colorful political career and time in prison, stated he believes he can win despite his past. He plans to focus on improving healthcare access, particularly through Medicaid expansion, and addressing infrastructure concerns. Edwards faces a challenging race in a Republican-leaning district, with over a dozen candidates already vying for the seat. His announcement has drawn mixed reactions, with some viewing it as a publicity stunt.

Wisconsin Republican Frank Lasee, a state senator, faces questions about his residency as he seeks to replace retiring Rep. Reid Ribble in the 8th District. Lasee lists a De Pere apartment as his voting address but until recently, his condo was available for rent on Airbnb. This has raised doubts about his actual residence. Lasee's wife owns a $262,000 home in Ryan's district, adding to the confusion. Lasee has a "crazy" living arrangement, splitting time between De Pere and Racine. He removed the Airbnb listing, but local conservative radio host Jerry Bader brought attention to the issue. Democrats had previously complained about Lasee's residency, but now Republicans are raising questions. Lasee is running against businessman Mike Gallagher, who has a significant fundraising advantage.

An 86-year-old Indian environmental activist, GD Agarwal, died after more than 15 weeks of a hunger strike to protest government inaction on cleaning the Ganges river. Agarwal, who held a PhD in environmental engineering, began his fast in Haridwar on June 22, demanding a law to protect the river and the cancellation of hydroelectric projects that destroyed its natural flow. His death prompted tributes from activists and political leaders, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressing sadness over the loss. Agarwal's passion for saving the Ganges and the country will be remembered, according to Modi. His death has sparked calls for an independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding his forced hospitalization and subsequent passing.

Federal and state officials are investigating the shooting deaths of four male sea otters, a federally protected species, found washed up on beaches near Santa Cruz over eight days. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service announced a $10,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and conviction of the responsible party. Three otters were found between August 12-19, and a fourth on August 20, with a suspected gunshot wound. Finding multiple shot sea otters in such a short time frame is unusual, said Ashley Spratt of the Fish and Wildlife Service. Sea otters, once hunted nearly to extinction, are protected by the Marine Mammal Protection Act, California state law, and the Endangered Species Act. Killing a sea otter can result in fines up to $100,000 and a jail sentence. Wildlife officials urge the public to report any information to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Suspected serial killer Todd Kohlhepp confessed to the 2003 murders of four people at a motorcycle shop in Chesnee, South Carolina, and is now suspected in the deaths of as many as seven individuals. Kohlhepp, 45, was seen walking the property with investigators and led them to where he said two other bodies are buried. The body of Charles Carver, the boyfriend of a kidnapped woman, was identified as one of the victims. The woman, whose name is not disclosed due to Kohlhepp being a sex offender, was found chained in a storage container on Kohlhepp's 95-acre property. Kohlhepp, who was released from prison in 2001 after a 14-year-old rape conviction, has a history of anger and violence. His real estate business in South Carolina was built after his release.
