Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) disclosed that Sergio Marchionne, the company's former CEO, had been treated for a serious illness at University Hospital Zurich for over a year before his death. The hospital stated that despite advanced medical treatments, Marchionne passed away. FCA maintained that it was unaware of his health condition, citing medical privacy as the reason. The company only became aware of Marchionne's serious deterioration on July 20 and announced his replacement as CEO the following day. Marchionne, known for his role in reviving Fiat and Chrysler, died at the age of 66. His death drew tributes from industry peers and colleagues.

Workers at a Goodyear tire factory in northern France have held two managers captive, preventing them from leaving the plant amid plans to close the facility. The managers, the production director Michel Dheilly and human resources chief Bernard Glesser, have been confined inside the Amiens plant since a Monday morning incident. The dispute over the plant's future has been ongoing for five years, with the union pushing for generous redundancy packages. The plant's closure has faced numerous obstacles, including violent protests and government concerns. While boss-nappings were more common during the financial crisis, such actions are generally not prosecuted in France, provided the managers are released within a week. The managers have reportedly been given water and allowed to use their mobile phones. Goodyear stated that the move was inopportune and counterproductive, focusing on the future of affected employees.

Oscar-winning actress Jodie Foster and her photographer girlfriend Alexandra Hedison have tied the knot, PEOPLE confirms. The couple, who have been dating for almost a year, exchanged vows in a private ceremony. Foster, 51, had previously addressed her sexuality in a Golden Globe speech, hinting at her long history of being open about her relationship with Cydney Bernard. E! Online was the first to report the news of the wedding.

YouTube comedy vloggers Liza Koshy and David Dobrik, known for their popular content and combined 21 million subscribers, have announced a breakup in a heartfelt video. The couple, who have been together since 2015, split six months ago due to growing distance and busy schedules. They emphasize their amicable separation and mutual respect, despite the surprise reaction from fans. The video showcases their genuine emotions and continued friendship, offering insight into the challenges of maintaining relationships in the public eye. While the split may initially shock their audience, industry experts suggest it could have little impact on their individual careers and future collaborations.

A study from Australian researchers suggests that bearded men are more likely to hold sexist views than their clean-shaven counterparts. In the survey, more than 500 men aged 18 to 72 were divided into groups based on facial hair, and those with any form of facial hair were found to agree more with hostile sexist statements. Only about a third of the participants did not express any sexist attitudes. The researchers propose that beards may appeal to men with more patriarchal views as a way to reinforce their perceived masculinity and dominance. Higher levels of education were associated with less hostile sexism but more benevolent sexism.

Mark Salling, best known for his role as Noah "Puck" Puckerman on "Glee," was arrested for possession of child pornography. Law enforcement sources report finding "hundreds" of images on his computer during a search warrant at his Sunland, California home. Salling was arrested by the Los Angeles Police Department's Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force Unit and is currently in custody with bail set at $20,000. This isn't Salling's first legal trouble; in 2013, he settled a $2.7 million lawsuit from an ex-girlfriend alleging sexual battery. Salling's representatives have not commented on the latest charges.

Several people in Bennington have reported being attacked by a squirrel over the last few weeks, according to the Bennington Banner. Kevin McDonald, of 15 East Street, said he was shoveling snow when the squirrel jumped onto him, scratching his back and shoulders. He threw the animal off but it jumped back onto his arms twice. A local game warden, Travis Buttle, has spoken to two people about the attacking squirrel, one of whom was bitten on the back of the neck and is undergoing a rabies vaccination series. Buttle advises anyone attacked by a squirrel or any animal to consult a doctor. The squirrel's attacks appear to be unprovoked, and it is possible the squirrel was raised as a pet and lost its fear of humans.

India's government has released a booklet advising pregnant women to avoid meat, eggs, and lustful thoughts, among other unconventional suggestions. The Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy, part of the government's ministry promoting traditional healing practices, compiled the "Mother and Child Care" booklet. It includes advice such as staying away from desire, anger, attachment, hatred, and lust, being with good people, and hanging pictures of beautiful babies. Critics argue these recommendations are unscientific and could be harmful, particularly given India's high maternal mortality rate. Doctors emphasize the importance of a nutritious diet, especially protein-rich foods like meat and eggs, and safe sexual practices during pregnancy. They warn that such advice could exacerbate malnutrition and anemia, worsening maternal and infant health outcomes in a country where poverty and patriarchal norms often limit women's access to proper nutrition and healthcare.

A new analysis of more than two dozen studies found toxic chemicals in 90% of household dust samples taken from 14 states. The research, published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology, adds to a growing body of evidence showing the dangers posed by exposure to a wide range of chemicals commonly found in household goods. These chemicals, including phthalates, phenols, flame retardants, and perfluoroalkyl substances, are present in everyday items such as toys, cosmetics, furniture, and food packaging. The study highlights the need for manufacturers to replace harmful chemicals with safer alternatives and for regulatory changes to better protect public health. Individuals can reduce exposure by washing hands frequently, using HEPA vacuums, and avoiding products containing harmful chemicals.

A former CIA agent has revealed his role in tipping off South Africa's apartheid regime to Nelson Mandela's whereabouts, leading to Mandela's 27-year imprisonment. This disclosure has sparked calls for the United States to apologize and for the CIA to come clean about its involvement. Mandla Mandela, the grandson of the former president, demanded a full disclosure and suggested the U.S. should face censure by the United Nations. The CIA operative, Donald Rickard, justified his actions by viewing Mandela as "the world’s most dangerous communist outside of the Soviet Union." Rickard, now 88, passed away, leaving behind six children and a legacy of service and adventure.

Nokia, facing significant challenges in the smartphone market, has announced plans to cut an additional 10,000 jobs, bringing the total job cuts since CEO Stephen Elop took over in 2010 to over 40,000. The company's stock price has fallen 18%, pushing Nokia's market value below $10 billion. Elop's overhaul includes closing production and research sites in Finland, Germany, and Canada, and executive departures. Nokia's second-quarter adjusted operating margin at the devices unit is expected to be worse than a loss equivalent to 3% of revenue, down from previous projections. The company aims to reduce expenses and improve its financial position, with plans to bring annual expenses at its devices business to about 3 billion euros by the end of 2013. Despite efforts to challenge Apple and Android with its Lumia smartphones, Nokia continues to struggle, with its market share declining and cash burn increasing.

Four years ago, Liu Wen entered a modeling contest in China to win a computer for school. Now, she will be the first Victoria's Secret model of Asian descent to walk the runway in the company's fashion show. Wen, 21, from Hunan province, China, was discovered at a regular modeling call and has since walked for top designers like Anna Sui and Dolce & Gabbana. Her success marks a growing trend for Asian models in the fashion industry, following in the footsteps of Devon Aoki. Wen, who previously studied to be a teacher, is now enjoying the modeling bug but remains open to returning to education. The Victoria's Secret fashion show, known for its elaborate costumes and high standards, requires months of preparation, including extensive makeup and hair styling. Models like Selita Ebanks share stories of the rigorous backstage process, highlighting the dedication and skill required to perform on the runway.

Mitt Romney leads President Obama by 3 points nationally according to the Gallup daily tracking poll, which shows Romney at 50% and Obama at 47%. However, Obama retains a 1-point advantage among registered voters. The poll, a rolling seven-day average, includes data from the second presidential debate but only two days from the foreign-policy debate. Other polls show a closer race, with Obama leading in battleground states like Ohio. The term "momentum" in political coverage often refers to a candidate gaining ground and likely to continue doing so. However, recent data suggests that Romney’s gains after the Denver debate may have peaked, with Obama showing slight improvement in the FiveThirtyEight model. The Ohio polls, while showing a close race, indicate that Obama has maintained a lead since the Denver debate, suggesting the race may be stabilizing.

To satisfy a peculiar obsession, a data-driven experiment was conducted with 1,050 fortune cookies, revealing 676 unique fortunes and 556 unique lucky numbers. Despite the sample size, the distribution of first letters in sentences differs from standard English. Fortune cookie numbers showed a higher winning rate compared to random numbers, hinting at potential manipulation or coincidence. The back of the cookies contained 173 Mandarin vocabulary words and phrases, mostly related to food, suggesting limited language learning potential. The majority of fortunes focused on the recipient, with themes of success, character, and happiness, indicating a personal rather than predictive nature. The experiment also highlighted the reuse of common phrases and the potential for algorithmic generation of new fortunes, adding a layer of novelty and unpredictability.

A British judge officially declared the infamous aristocrat Lord Lucan dead, nearly 42 years after his disappearance following the murder of his children's nanny. This ruling allows Lord Lucan's son, George Bingham, to inherit the family title and become the Eighth Earl of Lucan. Lord Lucan vanished in 1974 after the murder of Sandra Rivett, the nanny, and his wife Lady Lucan was assaulted. Despite numerous unverified sightings and various theories about his whereabouts, Lord Lucan was never found. The latest development brings closure to the long-standing mystery surrounding the fate of the missing peer. Berriman, the son of the murdered nanny, expressed mixed feelings about the ruling, emphasizing the ongoing quest for justice for his mother.

Michael Jordan and wife Yvette Prieto are expecting identical twin girls, E! News confirms. The former Chicago Bulls star, now 50, is set to become a father for the fourth time. Jordan and Yvette, a Cuban-American model, tied the knot in a lavish ceremony in Palm Beach, Florida, in April 2013, after five years of dating. The couple, who already have three grown children from Jordan's previous marriage, are due in April.

A 20-year-old man from Brooklyn, Chanel Lewis, has been arrested in connection with the strangulation death of Karina Vetrano, a 30-year-old jogger found dead in a secluded marsh near her Queens home on August 2. Chief of Detectives Robert Boyce stated that DNA evidence, including material found under Vetrano's fingernails and on her phone and neck, led to Lewis's arrest. Vetrano's father discovered her badly beaten body after she failed to return from her run. Lewis is facing a murder charge, carrying a penalty of 25 years to life in prison if convicted.

After 26 years on the run, Gustavo Falcon, one of the "Cocaine Cowboys," was arrested while biking with his wife near Kissimmee, Florida. U.S. Marshals had been surveilling his rental property in the Orlando-Kissimmee area and confirmed his identity during a bike ride. Falcon, 55, had been living under assumed names and was found to have fraudulent driver’s licenses. He faces charges of conspiracy to import cocaine and is being held without bond. His brother, Augusto "Willie" Falcon, and fellow drug kingpin Salvador "Sal" Magluta were previously convicted and are serving lengthy prison sentences.

International outrage over the massacre in Houla continues to mount, with Turkey and Japan expelling Syrian diplomats in a coordinated protest. The U.N. Human Rights Council plans a special session to address the killings, which included 49 children and 34 women. Syria's government denies responsibility, blaming "armed terrorists." Diplomatic efforts by Kofi Annan have yielded little progress, as violence persists. Russia, a key ally, rules out any Security Council action that could lead to foreign military intervention. The U.N. observer mission confirms another multiple killing, with 13 bodies found in Deir al-Zour. The situation in Syria is described as a "low point," with fears of a proxy conflict escalating.

As Brittany Murphy's tragic death unfolded, Redbox faced an eerie and challenging situation. The DVD rental company had to remove box art images from its kiosks nationwide for Murphy's latest film, "Deadline," which features her character lying lifeless in a bathtub. Murphy's sudden collapse in her Hollywood Hills home and subsequent death prompted Redbox to quickly address the issue, with staff beginning to remove the artwork and hoping to complete the task by January 1. The box art was also pulled from the company's website. Murphy's role in the straight-to-DVD horror thriller involves a screenwriter who travels to a haunted Victorian mansion, only to uncover videos that lead to a psychological breakdown.

A federal judge in St. Louis ruled that Carl and Janice Duffner must plant turf grass in their yard, despite Janice Duffner's severe grass allergies. If they fail, fines could exceed $200,000 or even lead to prison time. Represented by the Freedom Center of Missouri, the Duffners are appealing, as they argue the city's ordinance is overly punitive and violates their property rights. The case could potentially reach the U.S. Supreme Court. St. Peters, Missouri, passed an ordinance in 2008 requiring homeowners to cover at least 50% of their yards with turf grass, a rule the Duffners have consistently refused to follow.

A lawyer representing a boy who accused former Penn State football coach Jerry Sandusky of sexual abuse said his client and other alleged victims plan to testify at a Dec. 13 hearing, marking the first time they will publicly confront Sandusky. The client, known as Victim 1, is expected to appear at the Centre County Court hearing, though Sandusky could waive his right to an open hearing. Sandusky is charged with 40 criminal counts related to alleged abuse of eight boys over 15 years through his charity, The Second Mile. Sandusky's lawyer, Joseph Amendola, has suggested some victims might recant their allegations.

A 13-year-old boy from Eagan died after being accidentally shot by his 15-year-old brother with their father's handgun during a game of "cops and robbers," police said. The incident occurred on January 25, 2015, when the 15-year-old initially told emergency dispatchers his brother had accidentally stabbed himself with a knife. Upon further questioning, he admitted to police that he had unintentionally fired the weapon, striking his brother in the chest. The 11-year-old sister was uninjured and did not witness the shooting. The boys had recently discovered their father owned a 9mm pistol, which was unloaded but with a loaded magazine nearby. The gun was thought to be unloaded when the 15-year-old loaded it and chased his brother during the game. The case is under investigation, and the results will be presented to the Dakota County Attorney’s Office for review. No arrests are anticipated, but the incident highlights the

A San Francisco man named Trent Arsenault has fathered 14 children through his internet sperm donation business, which the FDA has ordered to cease operations due to improper procedures. Arsenault, a 37-year-old tech worker, openly shares his sperm donations on amateur porn sites, posting over 100 videos of himself masturbating into sterile cups. He claims his "donorsexual" lifestyle boosts his sperm count and helps him assist three childless couples per month. Arsenault's activities have sparked controversy, with supporters praising his altruism and detractors criticizing his lack of transparency with potential parents. The case highlights the lack of regulation in the sperm donation industry and raises questions about the ethics of online sperm sharing.

San Diego is implementing power-washing and extended restroom hours to combat a hepatitis A outbreak among the homeless, while also planning temporary shelters. Crews began power-washing downtown sidewalks with a bleach and chlorine solution on Monday, with cleanings set for Wednesday and Friday, repeating every other week. The city is extending the hours of 14 Balboa Park restrooms to 24/7 starting Tuesday. Mayor Kevin Faulconer expects to announce a plan this week to set up multiple large tents equipped with restrooms, showers, and hand-washing stations for hundreds of homeless people. The city aims to house the growing homeless population, identifying three downtown areas for regular cleanings and planning three temporary shelters. While the solutions are not perfect, they are seen as necessary steps to address the outbreak and provide immediate relief.

A Florida man, Alan Miller McCarty, was found guilty of threatening to kill a judge and other officials after a trial where he loudly insulted and interrupted the presiding judge. McCarty, 36, was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his threats against Circuit Judge Matt Foxman and dispatchers. During the trial, McCarty was kept in a small room with one-way glass, where he continued to yell and curse at the judge and witnesses. He was arrested after making phone threats to Judge Stasia Warren, who ruled in an earlier custody case involving McCarty. The jury found McCarty guilty of threats or extortion and corruption by threat. Despite his outbursts, the jury took about 30 minutes to reach a guilty verdict.

Google's ambitious plan to digitize the world's books faces a significant legal setback as a federal judge rejects a $125 million settlement with authors and publishers. The decision, citing concerns over copyright, antitrust, and privacy, leaves Google's massive digital library project in legal limbo. The judge suggests revising the agreement to an "opt-in" model, which could address some of the concerns. Google's project, championed by co-founder Larry Page, aims to make millions of books widely available but has faced opposition from rivals, the Justice Department, and copyright experts. The setback forces Google and the authors to decide whether to resume their legal battle or negotiate a new settlement, with Google still committed to making more books discoverable online.

Roshonara Choudhry, the woman who attempted to murder Labour MP Stephen Timms by stabbing him twice during an advice surgery, cited revolutionmuslim.com as one of the sites that radicalized her. The website, hosted in the US, lists MPs who voted for the Iraq war and calls Choudhry a "mujaahidah," or holy warrior. It includes instructions for Muslims to kill these MPs, along with details of their surgery times and locations. The site also features a video guide on how to purchase a £15 kitchen knife from Tesco Direct. British officials are urging US authorities to take action against similar sites.

The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER), a monumental fusion reactor project, faces significant challenges according to a recent assessment. Spanning a hundred feet tall and weighing twenty-three thousand tons, ITER aims to simulate the conditions of a star on Earth, generating immense heat and energy through the fusion of hydrogen atoms. However, the project's leadership, management, and governance have been criticized, potentially jeopardizing its future funding and progress. The ITER Council, after reviewing the report, restricted its readership, highlighting the severity of the issues. Backers may reconsider their support due to these challenges, putting the ambitious project's timeline and success at risk.

In 1966, Roger Watson and Dave Brown, both from northwest Detroit, were drafted on the same day and trained together in Fort Hood, Texas. They became friends but separated before serving in Vietnam. After the war, Roger settled in Berkley, Michigan, while Dave returned home. Roger's neighbor, Peggy Brown, eventually revealed they were married to each other, leading to a 18-year-long reunion. The two men, now retired, met at their chain-link fence, sharing stories and realizing their long-lost friendship.

Actress Angela Lansbury has apologized for comments she made about women sometimes "taking blame" for sexual harassment, stating she is "devastated" by the backlash. In a statement, Lansbury clarified that she believes there is "no excuse whatsoever for men to harass women in an abusive sexual manner" and that she is a strong supporter of women's rights. She expressed frustration that her comments were taken out of context and blamed on her generation or age. Lansbury's remarks, made during an interview, sparked criticism from groups like Rape Crisis England & Wales, which emphasized that victim-blaming attitudes are harmful. Actress Patricia Arquette and designer Donna Karan also criticized Lansbury's comments, with Arquette stating, "It doesn't matter how young or old, how beautiful or homely. Rapists rape. End of story."

Videos released by Rosemont police depict Kenneka Jenkins staggering alone through a deserted hotel kitchen, the last time she is seen alive. Though the footage does not capture her entering the walk-in freezer where her body was found, it shows no one else entered the area until her body was discovered. The videos, released after days of speculation and pressure from community activists, show Jenkins, initially steady, becoming increasingly disoriented. She is last seen tottering through an empty kitchen, disappearing around a corner. The same surveillance camera next picks up activity at 8:34 p.m., when a person briefly enters the frame, looks around, and leaves. No one else enters until 12:23 a.m. when a man goes around the same corner, returning with a police officer. Jenkins was pronounced dead at 12:48 a.m. The case has drawn intense speculation, with many suggesting she was murdered, but police are conducting a death investigation, not a homicide probe

The United States has deployed 80 troops to Chad to assist in the search for over 200 kidnapped Nigerian schoolgirls, a significant escalation in the global effort to find them. These forces, largely Air Force personnel, will conduct surveillance and operate drones but will not engage in ground searches. The deployment aims to support intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions over northern Nigeria and surrounding areas. This move comes as the United States has already sent a team of eight experts to Nigeria to advise on the recovery effort, with U.S. surveillance drones already searching for the girls since May 11. The search area is vast, roughly the size of West Virginia, and is described as dense forest, making the mission challenging. The U.S. government has emphasized the difficulty of the task, likening it to finding a needle in a jungle. Meanwhile, Nigeria has asked the United Nations to designate Boko Haram as a terrorist group, which could enable international sanctions. The U.S. State Department condemned

A woman named Rebekah Martinez, 22, from Fresno, was reported missing in Humboldt County on November 18, 2017. Her mother filed a missing person's report after Martinez went missing while working on a marijuana farm. Martinez was later found on the reality TV show "The Bachelor," which led to her removal from the California Department of Justice's missing persons list. She has been active on social media since going missing, often tweeting about her appearance on the show. The Humboldt County Sheriff's Office confirmed Martinez was not missing and removed her from the list.

The National Credit Union Administration sued JPMorgan Securities and Bear Stearns & Co over $3.6 billion in mortgage securities the bank allegedly sold to credit unions that collapsed due to losses from the securities. This lawsuit is the largest such action by the regulator to date and adds to ongoing cases against JPMorgan related to Bear Stearns. In October, the New York Attorney General sued JPMorgan, alleging that Bear Stearns deceived investors buying mortgage-backed securities in 2006 and 2007. JPMorgan's CEO, Jamie Dimon, criticized the government's actions, stating the company lost billions in Bear Stearns-related costs. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Kansas, seeks to recover losses related to the failure of credit unions seized by the regulator during the financial crisis.

Barrett Township in Pennsylvania has canceled Halloween activities, including trick-or-treating, due to the ongoing manhunt for accused cop killer Eric Frein. The town, which normally hosts a large Halloween parade and 5K Scarecrow Race, postponed these events indefinitely as police search nearby woods. "This parade is probably one of the biggest events that the town has every year," said Ralph Megliola, chairman of the township's Board of Supervisors. Instead, a "trunk-or-treat" event will be held at a Catholic school parking lot. The manhunt, now in its fourth week, has increased police presence and concerns among residents, who worry about Frein's potential escape during Halloween activities.

MIT is hosting a "Make the Breast Pump Not Suck" hackathon to improve breast pump technology and make the experience less awkward. The event, aimed at 150 engineers, designers, parents, public health researchers, and lactation consultants, seeks to address issues like loud motors, complex designs, and lack of privacy. Problems with current breast pumps include noise, multiple parts, cleaning difficulties, and the inability to pump while lying down. MIT hopes to innovate to support working mothers and improve maternal health, with prizes for the most promising projects. The hackathon aims to catalyze innovation in maternal and pediatric health and provide better support for families.

A 24-year-old woman from Dallas is under house arrest after attempting to transport high-tech night vision scopes to Russia without a license. Federal officials found the scopes, including a Raptor 4X Night Vision Weapons Sight, in her luggage at JFK International Airport in New York. She faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted. The case has drawn comparisons to the recent arrest of Anna Chapman, a suspected Russian spy, though the two women are not known to have any connection. Chapman and nine others were part of a spy ring busted in the U.S. and later deported in a "spy swap" exchange.

A 66-year-old Appalachian Trail hiker, Geraldine Largay, survived for nearly a month after getting lost in Franklin County, Maine, in July 2013. She documented her final days in a journal and tried to send text messages to her husband, but poor cell reception prevented communication. Largay set up a campsite and attempted to signal for help. Her remains and personal effects, including her journal and cellphone, were found more than two years later by the Maine Warden Service. The extensive search, one of the most costly in state history, was based on limited clues, including a photo of Largay taken by another hiker. Largay died from a lack of food and water and environmental exposure. Her family and friends described her as an experienced hiker but noted her poor sense of direction.

European leaders hailed Greece's approval of austerity measures as a step towards managing the debt crisis, but many economists and Greeks remain skeptical. Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany and other officials expressed optimism, urging Greek lawmakers to pass the measures and allowing for a second bailout package. However, critics argue that the measures will only buy Greece time and that significant constitutional changes are needed. Greece's parliament is set to vote on the measures, with violent protests and strikes ongoing. While some opposition lawmakers have backed the plan, others remain opposed, raising concerns about the government's ability to implement the measures. Analysts warn that even if the measures pass, Greece still faces challenges in implementing them and ensuring long-term economic sustainability.

The 115th Congress, with Republicans in control of both the House and Senate, is set to dismantle eight years of Democratic policies, including the Affordable Care Act, and pursue a conservative agenda. Key priorities include repealing Obamacare, implementing a tax overhaul, and reversing Obama-era environmental regulations. Democrats will try to block these efforts by swaying public opinion and using their Senate majority to filibuster legislation. Internal Republican disagreements, such as how to handle Russian interference in the election, may complicate their agenda. The new Congress also faces the challenge of confirming Trump's cabinet picks, with some Democrats likely to oppose controversial nominees.

Following five healthy habits—never smoking, maintaining a healthy body-mass index, engaging in moderate to vigorous exercise, limiting alcohol intake, and eating a healthy diet—could add more than a decade to your life expectancy, according to a new study published in Circulation. Among adults aged 50, adhering to these factors was linked to 14 additional years of life expectancy for women and 12.2 years for men, compared to those who did not follow any of them. These habits significantly reduce the risk of dying from the leading causes of death in the U.S., such as cardiovascular disease and cancer. The study, based on data from over 122,000 participants, suggests that lifestyle changes can greatly impact longevity, with the main takeaway being the substantial health benefits from simple behavioral modifications.

San Francisco Supervisor Scott Wiener disclosed that he takes Truvada, a daily antiviral pill, to reduce his risk of contracting HIV. This practice, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), can lower the risk of infection by up to 99% when taken daily. Wiener's public announcement aims to raise awareness about PrEP, a strategy recommended by public health authorities and part of New York's plan to reduce new HIV infections. Wiener, representing a district heavily impacted by HIV, emphasizes the importance of using multiple prevention methods, including condoms, alongside PrEP. He addresses concerns about adherence and potential increases in risky behavior, citing research that shows PrEP does not lead to increased risky sexual behavior. Wiener highlights the need for broader access to PrEP, especially for those who are uninsured or underinsured, to reduce health disparities. His disclosure is seen as a step towards reducing stigma and encouraging more people to consider PrEP as a viable HIV prevention tool

Elon Musk's Boring Company has received a permit for preliminary work at a site in Washington, D.C., potentially paving the way for a high-speed Hyperloop system connecting New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and D.C. in just 29 minutes. The exact location of the permit is a parking lot at 53 New York Avenue NE, near the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. While the permit is a small step, it could lead to the construction of a network of stations and tunnels. The D.C. government is considering what additional permits are needed, and the project has received backing from the White House and Maryland officials. The Hyperloop would use pods with up to 16 people or individual cars, moving on electric sleds through a system of vacuum tubes. Stations would be modest in size and numerous, unlike traditional train stations. Critics, however, question the feasibility and cost of such a project.

A mechanical failure at a swing ride called the Zumur at Connecticut's Norwalk Oyster Festival sent 13 people, including 12 children, to hospitals on Sunday. The ride, which swings riders in an elliptical motion, suddenly stopped mid-air, causing passengers to collide and fall. Authorities say no one was ejected from the ride. The festival's organizer, the Norwalk Seaport Association, directed the ride's operator, Stewart Amusement, to shut down the entire ride area until state inspectors completed a check. The ride is inspected daily by its own staff, weekly by state and local inspectors, and annually by engineers and insurance inspectors. Stewart Amusement is cooperating with the investigation and plans to have the machine taken apart for inspection. The incident raises questions about the safety oversight of portable rides, with some experts calling for federal oversight and consistent inspection guidelines across the country.

Crystal Palace's team bus was vandalized by their own fans before a 1-0 Premier League win over Middlesbrough. Fans mistakenly thought it was Middlesbrough's bus and spray-painted it with red, white, and blue graffiti, causing an estimated £40,000 in damages. The bus had been loaned to Crystal Palace by the club for Middlesbrough's visit to Selhurst Park. Palace informed the police and used another bus for the game, securing valuable points to move out of the bottom three.

George Zimmerman still believes he was a victim when he shot and killed Trayvon Martin, according to a CNN interview. He says he wouldn't change his actions, but wishes he had stayed home that night. Zimmerman maintains his faith in God as the ultimate judge and hopes to become a lawyer to prevent similar injustices. Since his acquittal, he has faced legal troubles, including speeding tickets and threats from his new girlfriend. He also used his notoriety to sell paintings and even agreed to a boxing match, which was canceled. Zimmerman continues to receive death threats and says those who call him a racist don't know his family members are black. He claims most people get a different perspective on him when they meet him one-on-one.

Major League Baseball is considering a rule change that would eliminate the four-pitch intentional walk in favor of a dugout signal, aiming to speed up games. While some see this as a minor tweak, others lament the loss of the dramatic intentional walk, which can be botched or exploited by batters. The change is expected to have minimal impact on game pace, with intentional walks taking up only about 35 seconds per game on average. Fans and commentators have suggested creative alternatives for the new signal, adding a touch of humor to the discussion.

Authorities arrested 56-year-old Cesar Sayoc in Florida in connection with over a dozen suspected pipe bombs sent to prominent Democrats and CNN offices. A fingerprint from a package to Rep. Maxine Waters helped identify Sayoc, who was arrested at an AutoZone in Plantation. His van, adorned with images of Trump and Vice President Pence, was seized. Sayoc faces up to 48 years in prison. DNA evidence and his cell phone also linked him to the devices. Sayoc had a history of arrests, including a 2002 bomb threat. He was initially cooperative after his arrest, saying the bombs wouldn't hurt anyone. Additional suspicious packages were found for Sen. Cory Booker, former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper, and billionaire Tom Steyer. The FBI said the devices were not hoax and were intended to cause harm. President Trump praised law enforcement's swift action.

Dinosaurs might not have roared like their Hollywood portrayals suggest, according to new research. Scientists argue that these ancient creatures likely produced low, throaty sounds similar to those made by modern birds like pigeons or ostriches. The study, published in the journal Evolution, analyzed vocal data from living archosaurs—birds and crocodiles—which include dinosaurs. Researchers found that closed-mouth vocalizations, common among large-bodied birds, could have evolved in dinosaurs as well. These sounds, produced by pushing air into an esophageal pouch, are quieter and lower in pitch compared to sounds made through an open beak. The findings suggest that dinosaurs may have used these vocalizations for mating or territorial displays, adding a new dimension to our understanding of their behavior and communication.

Last night during the Super Bowl halftime show, Red Hot Chili Peppers performed "Give It Away" without amplifying their bass, leading to speculation and criticism. Flea, the band's bassist, addressed the issue in a statement on the band's website, explaining that they chose to play along with a pre-recorded track to maintain the authenticity of the performance. Flea defended the decision, stating that the band aspires to grow as musicians and songwriters, and that they wanted to bring their unique spirit to the event. Despite the controversy, Flea expressed that he would do it all the same way again.

The Republican field for the 2016 White House race is expanding, with the number of candidates approaching a historic high. This could complicate Chris Christie’s bid for the nomination. With only the top 10 candidates invited to Fox News and CNN debates, Christie, currently in eighth place, faces a tight race to secure a spot. The large field and closely competitive rankings suggest that candidates will need to employ more aggressive strategies to gain media attention and improve poll numbers. Christie, known for his confrontational style, is already using attacks on rivals like Rand Paul and Jeb Bush to define his position. As the race stretches into the summer, experts predict a prolonged campaign, potentially lasting until the convention in July, due to the influence of outside money and the lack of a clear frontrunner. This could impact New Jersey’s primary, which is scheduled for June.

Scientists have discovered that early neornithischian dinosaurs, a group previously thought to be scaly, also had feathers, challenging the previous belief that feathers were unique to theropods and their bird descendants. The discovery of Kulindadromeus zabaikalicus in Siberia, a 150-million-year-old creature, shows that feather-like structures were widespread among dinosaurs. This suggests that all dinosaurs, including plant-eating ornithischians, may have had some form of feather covering, potentially indicating that the common ancestor of all dinosaurs also had feathers. The find, published in Science, indicates that the origin of feathers may be much earlier than previously thought, and that dinosaurs may have initially used feathers for insulation and signaling before they evolved for flight.

A 12-year-old Arkansas girl named Kali Hardig has made remarkable progress after battling a rare and often-fatal brain-eating amoeba infection. Kali, who contracted the Naegleria fowleri amoeba, is now able to say a few words, including "yes," "no," "Hi mama," "daddy," and "nanny." Doctors attribute her survival to early detection and experimental treatment. Kali was diagnosed after a trip to an Arkansas water park. The infection, which enters the body through the nose while swimming, causes primary amebic meningoencephalitis, leading to severe symptoms and brain damage. Despite the infection's rarity, Kali is one of only three known survivors in the U.S. since 1962. She remains at Arkansas Children's Hospital for ongoing therapy and is expected to recover with continued support.

The 2018 midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant Republican victory, surprising many in the media who have consistently predicted Democratic gains. Columns by Barry Casselman and Scott Adams highlight the media's self-deception and consistent mispredictions regarding President Trump and his administration. The media's false narratives on the Republican Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which were intended to convince Americans of higher taxes, backfired as the act proved beneficial to taxpayers. This discrepancy between media predictions and reality will likely impact voter sentiment, potentially leading to a strong Republican performance in the midterms. The article suggests that the media's bias and misinformation could result in a decisive election outcome, with voters choosing between higher taxes and a stronger economy.

New York's attorney general is investigating whether energy drink makers, including PepsiCo, Monster Beverage, and Living Essentials, are misleading consumers with their marketing and advertising practices. The investigation, which began in July, focuses on whether the companies overstated the benefits of ingredients like B-vitamins, taurine, and ginseng while understating the role of caffeine. Energy drinks, which have become a fast-growing segment of the beverage market, are regulated more loosely than traditional sodas. Critics argue that the main active ingredient is caffeine, and the investigation could lead to changes in labeling and marketing practices if the companies are found to be in violation of state laws.

Japanese legal adulthood begins at 20, but a Twitter user's parents decided to make the transition more formal by sending a "Notice of Expiration of Child-Rearing Services" on his 20th birthday. The document outlines new responsibilities and financial expectations, such as making monthly payments for rent, utilities, and groceries, and paying interest on any loans. It also reminds him of adult responsibilities like paying national pension contributions and avoiding drunk driving. The user, @zamayuma1004, humorously notes he has been paying the monthly amount since last year and plans to contribute more to help his parents. This case highlights the unique approach to transitioning to adulthood in Japan, where many young adults continue to live with their parents until marriage or starting a job.

Twitter is expanding its tweet format to include "expanded tweets," allowing for richer content within the 140-character limit. These expanded tweets can include headlines, snippets, photos, and other media, making them up to 410 characters in total. Initially, only select partners like The New York Times, Wall Street Journal, BuzzFeed, TMZ, and WWE are included, but Twitter plans to expand this to more sites over time. This change aims to enhance user experience by providing more context and engaging content directly within tweets, making Twitter a more comprehensive source for news and information. Critics argue that this move could dilute Twitter's essence, but proponents see it as a natural evolution that keeps the platform relevant in an increasingly multimedia landscape.

Megyn Kelly is reportedly no longer a client of CAA and will not be represented by UTA, as she has hired attorney Bryan Freedman for settlement talks with NBC. The controversy over her comments about blackface during her show "Megyn Kelly Today" has led to her show potentially ending soon. Kelly's show will not air on Thursday, and she is unlikely to return. The fallout includes cast members and producers of Netflix's "House of Cards" pulling out of guest appearances on her show. Kelly apologized for her comments, but the incident has raised questions about her future at NBC and her contract negotiations.

San Diego's city council voted to ban drinking in the water to stop "floatopia" parties, which have exploited a loophole in the city's beach drinking ban. These parties, held in small bays, attract hundreds of people who drink while floating on rafts and inner-tubes. The council aims to prevent drownings and injuries from broken bottles. Despite concerns that the ban could hurt tourism, the council voted unanimously to enforce the new rule immediately. The ban does not apply to drinking on boats.

Sir Roger Bannister, the first person to run a mile in under four minutes, passed away at the age of 88. His historic time of 3 minutes 59.4 seconds, achieved in 1954, marked a significant milestone in athletics. Bannister also won a gold medal in the mile at the 1954 Commonwealth Games and later became a renowned neurologist. He was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2011. Bannister's achievement inspired many athletes, and IAAF president Lord Coe expressed deep sadness at his passing. Bannister's record stood for just 46 days before being broken by John Landy. The current world record holder is Moroccan Hicham El Guerrouj, who ran a mile in 3:43.13 in 1999.

At least four people died when a newly installed pedestrian bridge collapsed at Florida International University, crushing several vehicles. The bridge, intended to provide a safer crossing over a busy road, was under construction and not expected to open until 2019. Rescue efforts continued into the night, with at least nine injured people taken to hospitals. Miami-Dade Fire Chief Dave Downey confirmed four deaths, while Miami-Dade Police Chief Juan Perez said eight vehicles were trapped under the rubble. The collapse occurred during a stress test, but the exact cause remains unclear. Florida Governor Rick Scott and Senator Marco Rubio promised thorough investigations. The bridge was built by MCM Construction and designed by FIGG Bridge Design, both companies with past safety violations. The collapse has raised questions about the safety of innovative construction methods.

Virginia's outgoing governor, Terry McAuliffe, played a prank on his successor, newly inaugurated Democrat Ralph Northam, by leaving pillowcases emblazoned with McAuliffe's face and the phrase "Sleep when you're dead" for Northam and his wife to use in the governor's mansion. Northam found the pillowcases and several photos of McAuliffe around the residence, and even received an early morning alarm clock trick. These pranks are common in Virginia, where the governorship changes hands every four years. Previous outgoing governors have left similar surprises for their successors, such as a stuffed bear and hidden cellphones.

A new owner, Jerome and Nancy Kohlberg, has acquired the Vineyard Gazette, along with its real estate, from Richard Reston, the paper's publisher since 1988, who is retiring. The sale includes $2 million for the newspaper and $1.5 million for the Gazette's real estate. The Boston Globe reported on the transaction. Meanwhile, Peter Wallsten's hiring at The Post was highlighted, with memos noting his expertise in uncovering stories. The California Supreme Court ruled that SF Weekly must pay $21 million in damages to the Bay Guardian for competitive advertising practices. The Lowell Thomas Travel Journalism Competition recognized top travel journalists and publications, with awards given to magazines like Afar, the Washington Post, and San Francisco Chronicle, as well as online sites and travel books. Andrew McCarthy, a travel journalist, won the Travel Journalist of the Year award. The competition, now in its 26th year, honored excellence in travel writing and storytelling.

Wealthy Americans are flocking to warm climates and low-tax states, according to IRS data analyzed by Forbes. Top destinations for the rich include Collier County, Florida, Greene County, Georgia, and Nassau County, Florida. These areas offer tax advantages and a desirable lifestyle, with Florida counties particularly attractive due to their lack of income tax. Conversely, wealthy individuals are leaving high-tax states like California, New Jersey, and New York, seeking more affordable living conditions. This trend highlights the growing importance of tax policies and cost of living in affluent residents' relocation decisions.

During a CNN panel discussion on the Jemele Hill controversy, sports radio host Clay Travis made an unexpected and controversial statement, declaring his belief in "the First Amendment and boobs." This comment, which took the conversation in an unexpected direction, left CNN anchor Brooke Baldwin stunned. Baldwin clarified Travis's statement, asking if he meant "boobs" or "booze." Travis confirmed he meant "boobs," and Baldwin, visibly irritated, ended the interview early. The incident sparked widespread criticism of Travis and praise for Baldwin's handling of the situation.

A report finds that two Salt Lake City police officers who forcibly arrested a nurse who refused to draw blood from an unconscious patient violated police codes of conduct. Bodycam footage showed Detective Jeff Payne dragging and handcuffing Nurse Alex Wubbels after she said his request for a blood sample was against policy. Wubbels screamed "I've done nothing wrong!" as she was dragged away. The hospital said she acted correctly. The incident is "unacceptable" and not reflective of the city or police department, Salt Lake City Mayor Jackie Biskupski said. Both officers have been placed on administrative leave and will respond to the allegations within 20 days. The police department amended its policy to match the hospital's.

In a CNN debate, Ron Paul faced a hypothetical question about a man who becomes ill and is uninsured, potentially leading to his death. The crowd's response surprised Rep. Paul, who emphasized the role of community and non-government institutions in healthcare. Following the debate, Texas Governor Rick Perry expressed being "taken aback" by the crowd's reaction, emphasizing the Republican Party's stance on life and support for in-state tuition for illegal immigrants. Perry defended his policy, stating it was about education and opportunities for children brought to the U.S. illegally. During the debate, both Michele Bachmann and Rick Santorum criticized Perry's stance on the Gardasil vaccine, with Bachmann citing a case of mental retardation allegedly caused by the vaccine. Perry dismissed these claims, comparing them to debunked theories about vaccinations and autism.

The wife of late artist Thomas Kinkade and trustee of his estate have filed a temporary restraining order against his live-in girlfriend, Amy Pinto-Walsh, to prevent her from disclosing confidential information about Kinkade and his businesses. Kinkade, known as the "Painter of Light," died in April, and Pinto-Walsh spoke to a local newspaper about his death, contradicting the family's account of natural causes. The restraining order seeks to prevent Pinto-Walsh from making negative statements or publishing information about the Kinkade family and businesses, including trade secrets. A judge will hear the case on April 24.

Secretary of State Rex Tillerson may be considering resignation due to growing frustrations with the Trump administration. Friends outside Washington have reported a noticeable increase in his frustration, potentially leading to a "Rexit" sooner than originally speculated. Tillerson has faced criticism for his absence on the world stage and has clashed with the White House over issues like Iran policy and personnel. His public statements and actions, such as his criticism of Trump's rebuke of Attorney General Jeff Sessions, have further strained his relationship with the administration. Despite his frustrations, Tillerson has expressed a desire to stay until the end of the year to complete the reorganization of the State Department.

Rapper Snoop Dogg received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, thanking himself and several important figures in his life, including his wife Shante Broadus, DJ Warren G, Dr. Dre, Jimmy Kimmel, and Quincy Jones. During his speech, Snoop highlighted his hard work and dedication, stating, "I want to thank me for believing in me; I want to thank me for doing all this hard work; I want to thank me for having no days off; I want to thank me for never quitting; I want to thank me for always being a giver, and trying to give more than I receive; I want to thank me for doing more right than wrong; I want to thank me for being me at all times." Snoop Dogg has had a successful career, selling over 23.5 million albums in the United States and 37 million albums worldwide, and has received numerous Grammy nominations. He has also expanded his career into various other fields

Oklahoma has experienced a forty-fold increase in earthquakes between 2008 and 2013, likely triggered by massive injections of wastewater from the oil and gas industry, according to a new study published in Science. Researchers linked a swarm of tremors around the town of Jones to four high-volume wastewater wells, suggesting that the disposal of water could be responsible for a significant portion of the state’s seismic activity. The study indicates that wastewater injection sites, used to dispose of toxic water from oil drilling and fracking, may induce relatively strong earthquakes even at considerable distances. This finding challenges previous assumptions about the limited impact of such wells on seismic events.

In a groundbreaking discovery, archaeologists have identified the world's earliest known winemaking, dating back 8,000 years to the Neolithic period in Georgia. Chemical analysis of pottery shards from the ancient villages of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora revealed tartaric acid and other wine residues, confirming the production of wine as early as 6,000 B.C. These findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, push back the known origins of modern-style viticulture by up to 1,000 years. The Eurasian grapevine, the ancestor of nearly all modern wine varieties, was likely cultivated in the region. The wine was likely produced in large jars, similar to the qvevri method still used in Georgia today. This discovery highlights the sophistication of early human civilizations and their innovative horticultural techniques.

Facebook has updated its Community Standards to provide more clarity on what types of posts are not allowed on the platform, aiming to balance free sharing of information with maintaining a safe environment. The company's goal is to give people a place to share and connect freely and openly, while addressing concerns about violent or offensive content. The updated standards cover topics such as self-injury, dangerous organizations, bullying and harassment, criminal activity, sexual violence and exploitation, nudity, hate speech, and violence and graphic content. Facebook will still rely on users to report violations, with review teams examining each report before a decision is made. The process can take up to 48 hours for safety-related matters. Facebook also publishes a Global Government Requests Report, detailing government requests for content removal and account data, to maintain transparency.

Florida's busiest airport, Orlando International, is set to become the first in the U.S. to require facial scans for all international arriving and departing passengers, including U.S. citizens. The move alarms privacy advocates who argue there are no formal rules for handling the data and no clear guidelines if a passenger is wrongly prevented from boarding. Currently, face scans are used at some airports for departing international flights but not for all travelers. The Orlando program will compare the scanned image to a Department of Homeland Security database to verify identities. U.S. citizens can opt out, but a notice suggests they may be required to provide photographs. Privacy experts raise concerns about the accuracy of facial recognition technology, particularly for racial minorities, women, and children. Senators have called for formal rules before expanding the program.

Malaysian and international officials are investigating the possibility that one of the pilots of missing Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 deliberately crashed the plane. The search area for the missing aircraft has expanded to include 11 countries, stretching from Kazakhstan to the Indian Ocean. U.S. intelligence officials suggest that the pilots may have been responsible for the plane's disappearance. Malaysian police have searched the homes of both pilots, including a flight simulator from the captain's home, as part of the investigation. The plane's last communication was at 8:11 a.m. on March 8, 2014, and it is believed to have flown for six and a half hours after that. Authorities are also looking into the backgrounds of passengers and crew members to determine if any had flight training or connections to terrorist groups. The search efforts have involved multiple countries, with India suspending its operations until new search areas are identified.

Actor Tom Sizemore is accused of touching an 11-year-old girl's genitals during a 2003 movie shoot in Utah. The Hollywood Reporter states that Sizemore, then 42, was sent home after the child actress told her mother about the alleged incident. Months later, he returned for reshoots in Malibu. Sizemore has never been accused of molestation before. He is known for his roles in action films and dramas, including Saving Private Ryan and Black Hawk Down. The incident has been kept private until now, coming to light in the wake of the Harvey Weinstein scandal. Sizemore's representatives have not commented on the allegations.

An Austrian climber had his thumb severed during a fall on El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. After dropping about 80 feet and landing on a small ledge, the thumb was recovered by the climber's partner, who then called for emergency assistance. Park rangers conducted a complex, high-angle rescue, using a helicopter to extract the climber and transport him to a hospital where his thumb was successfully reattached. This rescue highlights the skill and dedication of Yosemite National Park's Search and Rescue team.

Movie star Ewan McGregor, 46, and actress Mary Elizabeth Winstead, 32, were spotted sharing a passionate kiss and leaving a busy London cafe together on a motorbike. The pair, who play lovers in the TV show Fargo, were seen deep in conversation for over an hour at The Good Life Eatery in St John’s Wood, North West London. McGregor's wife Eve Mavrakis, 51, and their four daughters have been married since 1995. Meanwhile, Winstead recently split from her husband Riley Stearns, her teenage sweetheart. Both stars have been linked romantically in the past, but this latest sighting has sparked speculation about a potential affair.

Carson Daly, host of a radio show, faced criticism after making comments that some found offensive, particularly to the LGBT community. Following dialogue with GLAAD, Daly issued a statement apologizing for his words, which he said were unintentional and offensive. He expressed his support for LGBT rights and commitment to being an ally. Daly's original comments and subsequent apology can be seen in his Twitter post, where he admitted to making a mistake and offending others. GLAAD stated they look forward to Daly continuing to fight for LGBT equality.

A mother named Estella Havisham gained widespread attention for her creative punishment of her 13-year-old son, Aaron. After he lied about doing homework and was disrespectful, Estella took away his belongings and set up a "rental" system where he would have to pay for his room, utilities, and food, as well as do daily chores. The incident went viral, with over 80,000 shares on Facebook. While some praised Estella's tough-love approach, others criticized her for embarrassing her son publicly. Despite the controversy, Estella believes her actions were effective, stating that her relationship with Aaron remained strong and he showed remorse.

An American, Arturo Pierre Martinez, 29, of El Paso, Texas, denounced the U.S. political and economic system in a press conference in North Korea. Martinez, who entered the country illegally, was presented to the media by North Korean authorities. His mother, Patricia Eugenia Martinez, explained that her son, who is bipolar, previously attempted to enter North Korea by swimming across a river but was returned to the U.S. and placed in a psychiatric hospital. She said Martinez left the U.S. without permission and entered China before crossing into North Korea. In his statement, Martinez criticized U.S. policies, including the Iraq War, and accused the U.S. electoral system of benefiting the wealthy. He also discussed various conspiracy theories. The legal status of Martinez in North Korea remains unclear.

A Southwest Airlines flight from San Francisco to Phoenix experienced an unexpected arrival when a passenger gave birth shortly after takeoff. The plane diverted to Los Angeles International Airport for medical assistance, where the mother and newborn were taken to a hospital in good condition. The flight crew and on-board medical professionals helped with the delivery, and passengers applauded the arrival of the new baby. The baby's gender was not disclosed, and the other 111 passengers continued their journey on another plane, arriving more than two hours behind schedule. This incident isn't the first time a baby has been born mid-flight on a Southwest Airlines flight.

In a small Illinois town, Rick Odell Smith, 43, entered a home early Wednesday morning and shot and killed a grandmother, a young couple, and three small children. He also seriously wounded a 6-year-old girl, who was taken to a hospital in critical condition. After the shooting, Smith carried the injured girl to a neighbor's home and fled in his white sedan. He was pursued by police and died in a gunfight. The victims were identified as Joanne Sinclair, 67; her granddaughter Brittany Luark, 23; her boyfriend Roy Ralston, 29; and their children, Nolan Ralston, 5, and Brantley Ralston, 1. The 6-year-old girl's name is Kassidy Ralston. Police found a shotgun, a scoped rifle, and a hunting knife at the scene. Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska says her views on same-sex marriage are "evolving" and that she is reviewing her stance "very closely." Murkowski, who has previously voted for constitutional amendments defining marriage as between one man and one woman, now acknowledges a "change afoot in this country" regarding marriage. She cites her young sons' attitudes as influencing her perspective, noting that they find the question of gay marriage "old hat." Murkowski's position may depend on feedback from her constituents in Alaska, who voted to ban same-sex marriages in 1998. She believes there are more pressing issues than same-sex marriage, such as sequestration. Murkowski's evolving stance follows similar changes by other Republicans, including Rob Portman, who reversed his position after learning his son is gay.

The new commissioner of New York City's jail system, Joseph Ponte, faced criticism for sending up to 47 mentally ill inmates into 23-hour confinement without mental health clinician approval. Ponte claimed the move aimed to reduce jailhouse violence, but board members argued it jeopardized inmate health, especially for those on heat-sensitive medications. At least one inmate experienced a seizure. Ponte acknowledged the move violated city rules designed for prisoner safety. The city's jail system houses nearly 40% of inmates with mental health diagnoses, and Ponte highlighted the ongoing issue of high-risk inmates driving violence on Rikers Island.

Two pro-life county commissioners in Oregon reacted with horror to a Vancouver newspaper story claiming aborted fetuses from British Columbia are routinely shipped to a waste-to-energy incinerator near Portland, where they are incinerated to generate electricity. The story, which caught local officials off guard, prompted them to temporarily halt all biomedical waste shipments and amend local ordinances to bar future shipments containing fetal tissue. Marion County officials expressed disgust over the alleged practice, emphasizing the importance of drawing a line on respectful disposal of remains. The controversy highlights the complex and often controversial issue of medical waste disposal, with the Oregon incinerator processing 550 tons of municipal solid waste daily, including a small portion of medical waste.

Yahoo is preparing to confirm a massive data breach affecting 200 million user accounts, according to sources. The breach, which could be worse than previously reported, may have implications for Yahoo's $4.8 billion sale to Verizon. The company is expected to disclose details of the hack, which may lead to legal action and government investigations. The deal is moving towards completion but could face renegotiation or cancellation if the scale of the liability becomes apparent. Yahoo's CEO, Marissa Mayer, faces another setback as the tech giant struggles to turn around its business.

A woman was carjacked while trying to help crash victims on Interstate 4 near Daytona Beach early Saturday. The 34-year-old woman stopped to assist those involved in a crash when three young men, described as black males in their teens or early 20s, jumped out of a stolen car and took her 2012 Ford Mustang convertible. The suspects also loaded an unresponsive woman, believed to be in her teens or early 20s with short dreadlocks, a red hooded sweatshirt, brown jeans, and black shoes, into the stolen car before driving away. The stolen vehicle is a dark blue Ford Mustang convertible with a Florida tag V83-4QC, black vinyl top, and no window tint. Deputies are actively searching for the suspects and the stolen car.

Some Democrats are in no hurry to pass immigration legislation, as they believe a compromise with Republicans might take the edge off an issue that is crucial to Hispanics, who gave Obama 71% of their votes in the 2012 presidential election. The fate of the legislation rests largely with House Speaker John Boehner, who must decide whether to bring a bill to the full House. The Senate passed an immigration bill in June that included a path to citizenship for the country’s estimated 11 million undocumented workers. While some lawmakers and business groups are lobbying for legislation, internal political dynamics and skepticism of President Obama within the House Republican Conference are making it difficult to pass any immigration reform before the end of the year. The House has just 19 days in session before the end of 2013, and any immigration bill needs significant House Republican support. Motorcyclists in New Jersey may legally lane split, though the practice isn't encouraged, according to the state's driver's manual. New Jersey police can cite riders for failure to keep right if they lane split. Advocacy groups argue lane splitting can improve safety and efficiency, while the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration suggests further study. California recently passed a bill allowing the California Highway Patrol to establish guidelines for safe lane splitting, making it the first state to formalize the practice.

Veterinarian John Robb faces legal battles and personal struggles after losing his hospital to Banfield Pet Hospital, a large chain criticized for its one-size-fits-all approach to pet care. Robb, a born-again Christian, believes he was unfairly targeted for reducing vaccine doses for small dogs, a violation of Banfield protocol and Connecticut law. Banfield, now owned by Mars Inc., has been accused of pushing unnecessary vaccines and treatments, leading to lawsuits and ethical concerns among former employees and pet owners. Despite legal setbacks, Robb continues to fight, using social media to rally support and raise awareness about what he sees as corporate greed in the pet care industry.

The U.S. military is investigating photos obtained by TMZ showing Marines burning and posing next to dead bodies of what appear to be Iraqi insurgents in Fallujah in 2004. The photos, which include images of Marines pouring gasoline and setting bodies on fire, have triggered a Marine Corps investigation. Pentagon officials say the actions depicted violate the Uniform Code of Military Justice and could still result in prosecution, even years later. The full set of 41 photos, also containing images of Marines rifling through pockets of corpses and a dog eating a body, has been turned over to the military for review. Commander Bill Speaks of the Department of Defense stated that the photos do not represent the actions of the majority of service members who served in Iraq and Afghanistan.

The New York Stock Exchange, a cornerstone of American capitalism for 220 years, is set to be acquired by IntercontinentalExchange Inc. in an $8.2 billion deal, signaling a shift towards electronic trading dominance. If approved, the combined entity would own 14 stock and futures exchanges and five clearing operations, surpassing any rival in market scope. This merger underscores the shift from traditional floor trading to electronic platforms and the exchanges' push to expand their operations globally. Shares of NYSE Euronext surged more than 21 percent in after-hours trading, reflecting investor optimism. However, the deal may face regulatory scrutiny and opposition from other exchanges.

Walter Scott, a father of four, was killed by a North Charleston police officer after a traffic stop, sparking national headlines. Scott had a history of failing to pay child support, which led to multiple jail terms and the loss of his job. Despite these setbacks, he attempted to turn his life around through a program called "Father to Father," but his child support debts continued to accumulate. Critics argue that the use of jail to enforce child support payments traps poor men in a cycle of debt and unemployment. In South Carolina, a state grant called "Operation Work" aims to help fathers find ways to support their families, offering job training and suspending child support payments during enrollment. Walter Scott's death has highlighted the broader issue of how punitive policies for unpaid child support may contribute to cycles of poverty and incarceration.

Taylor Swift and Justin Bieber teamed up for a surprise performance on Taylor's Speak Now tour, but the MTV prank series "Punk'd" is bringing back the celebrity pranks with a new episode featuring the two friends. Justin reportedly surprised Taylor onstage during a Los Angeles stop of her tour, performing his hit "Baby" with her. The first episode of the show's return is set to air, with Justin taking the role of prankster against Taylor. Fans can tune in to see what mischief unfolds.

Ahmed Wali Karzai, the powerful half-brother of Afghan President Hamid Karzai and a key figure in the southern province of Kandahar, was assassinated by a trusted family security guard, creating a dangerous power vacuum. His death raises questions about the stability of security gains in Kandahar and the future of the U.S. military mission. Although accused of corruption and ties to the opium trade, Wali Karzai was seen as a stabilizing force and a critical ally in the fight against the Taliban. His assassination complicates the U.S. strategy, as his influence was deeply intertwined with local tribal dynamics and the U.S. military's efforts to maintain control. The U.S. military and Afghan officials are now grappling with the implications of his death and the potential for increased Taliban influence in the region.

A new round of advertisements from Colorado's health insurance exchange supporters has sparked controversy, featuring risqué and party-oriented content aimed at young adults. In one ad, a woman holding birth-control pills says, "OMG, he's hot! Let's hope he's as easy to get as this birth control." Critics argue the ads belittle women and detract from serious health issues, while supporters defend them as effective in raising awareness. The ads, part of the "Got Insurance?" campaign, also include images of young people doing keg stands and shots, drawing mixed reactions and debate over their approach to promoting the Affordable Care Act.

The fleece vest, often in black and from outdoor clothing retailer Patagonia, has become the unofficial uniform for venture capitalists in Silicon Valley. No one knows exactly how this trend started, but it is now an inescapable sight in the region. Venture capitalists like Reid Hoffman, Marc Benioff, and Joanne Wilson have been spotted wearing these vests. Several theories suggest the practicality of layering in the Bay Area's unpredictable weather as a primary reason for their popularity. Patagonia attributes the trend to the quality of their vests, which are seen as representing quality without being pretentious. The trend has even spread to New York's Silicon Alley, where general partners like Henry McNamara own a fleece vest. San Francisco International Airport now has a vending machine selling Uniqlo down vests, which are popular among visiting venture capitalists. The vending machine, part of Uniqlo's "Uniqlo To Go" initiative, has become a source of humor for Twitter users.

A series of leaked Twitter messages from Sarah Palin’s aide Rebecca Mansour reveal her critical views of conservative figures and even her own boss’s daughter, Bristol Palin. Mansour called Erick Erickson, editor-in-chief of RedState, a "total douchebag" and criticized Mitt Romney supporters as an "AstroTurf brigade." In one message, Mansour suggested mailing a "dead fish" to a political opponent. The most damaging messages focus on Bristol Palin, with Mansour predicting she would be "held at arm’s length" by her mother. These messages, sent to an online acquaintance, highlight internal dynamics and strategic calculations within Palin’s campaign. Mansour initially denied sending the messages but later admitted to them, leading to questions about her role and status within SarahPAC.

A 15-year-old girl, Daejona M. Holmes, has been certified as an adult and charged with two counts of second-degree murder, two counts of armed criminal action, and tampering with physical evidence in the fatal shootings of her parents. Police were called to a home in the 5000 block of Belmeade Road on April 9, where they found Daejona's parents, Kinderly Holmes and Brian Starr, dead from gunshot wounds. Daejona initially told police that a robbery had occurred and her parents were shot. Her story later changed to claiming her father shot her mother, and she shot her father. The investigation revealed online searches for "scary movies where kids kill parents," rap lyrics about wanting her father dead, and a video of Daejona holding a gun and dancing. A California man, Rudy Kurniawan, was convicted of fraud for selling counterfeit wines worth millions, becoming the first person tried and convicted for selling fake wines in the U.S. Kurniawan, known for his exceptional palate and ability to find rare wines, was found guilty of wire and postal fraud. He was accused of blending younger wines with older, lower-quality ones and re-bottling them with counterfeit labels. Wine experts from Domaine Ponsot and Domaine Roumier testified that several bottles Kurniawan sold were forgeries. Kurniawan, who had been living illegally in the U.S. since 2003, faced up to 40 years in prison. His defense argued he was being made a scapegoat, but the jury found him guilty.

Hurricane Irma's eyewall has reached the Florida Keys, with the storm's center positioned about 30 miles south of Key West. Forecasters warn against shooting at the storm, as it won't alter its path and could have dangerous side effects. Irma, a Category 4 hurricane with sustained winds near 130 mph, is moving northwest at 8 mph. The storm's approach has led to widespread power outages, with Florida Power & Light reporting about 430,000 customers without power. Authorities urge residents in the Keys to remain indoors until the storm passes, as conditions can become deceptively calm during the eye of the hurricane. Meanwhile, the Dutch king is flying to the Caribbean to visit survivors evacuated from St. Maarten, while Dutch marines and troops are working to restore infrastructure and distribute aid.

A woman was arrested after allegedly jumping on stage at a music festival in Hayward and attacking 73-year-old musician Lester Chambers, who dedicated a song to Trayvon Martin. The woman, identified as 43-year-old Dinalynn Andrews Potter, reportedly yelled "it's all your fault" before shoving Chambers. Eyewitnesses and police believe the attack was racially motivated. Andrews Potter was arrested on suspicion of battery and could face additional charges. Chambers, a former member of The Chambers Brothers, was taken to the hospital but has since been released. His son says Chambers has bruised ribs and nerve damage. The incident occurred after Chambers dedicated Curtis Mayfield's "People Get Ready" to Martin, who was shot by George Zimmerman.

Colin Kaepernick has filed a collusion grievance against the NFL, alleging that he remains unsigned due to a conspiracy by league owners following his anthem protests. Kaepernick’s attorney, Mark Geragos, stated that they pursued every avenue with NFL teams before filing the grievance. The NFL Players Association will support Kaepernick. Kaepernick, who opted out of his contract with the San Francisco 49ers, was the first NFL player to kneel during the national anthem to protest racial injustice, sparking a national conversation and ongoing protests by other players. Despite his strong performance in 2016, Kaepernick has received little interest from teams in 2017.

The Saudi government has unveiled ambitious plans to diversify its economy and reduce its dependence on oil, aiming to transform the kingdom into a global investment power. Deputy Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman announced that state oil company Saudi Aramco will be valued at over $2 trillion and plans to sell less than 5% of its shares through an initial public offering (IPO). The Public Investment Fund will be raised to $2 trillion, and a green card system will allow expatriate Arabs and Muslims to live and work long-term in Saudi Arabia. The plan includes increasing non-oil revenue, boosting women's participation in the workforce, and investing in domestic manufacturing. Prince Mohammed emphasized that the vision aims to ensure Saudi Arabia can survive without oil by 2020, despite oil accounting for 70% of government revenues. The reforms, while promising, face challenges in implementation and may not address all concerns, particularly regarding education reform and potential economic disruption.

A Bridgewater woman, Casey Giles, 37, is accused of using children's drawings to smuggle prescription drugs, specifically Suboxone, to her boyfriend, Michael Gill, 38, who is incarcerated in the Somerset County Jail. Mail addressed to Gill was inspected on June 15, and K-9 Apex, a detection dog, indicated the presence of Suboxone hidden in the drawings. More mail with suspected Suboxone was found on June 20 and June 28. Giles was charged with third-degree possession with intent to distribute a controlled dangerous substance and remanded to jail with a $20,000 bail.
