He filed a lawsuit under the Americans with Disabilities Act, seeking damages and ensuring such discrimination does not occur again. Six Flags declined to comment on the ongoing lawsuit.

South Korea's political scandal, centered on the close relationship between President Park Geun-hye and her longtime friend Choi Soon-sil, has led to Park's impeachment. The scandal began when Ko Young-tae, a former national fencer and Villomillo accessory brand founder, allegedly exposed their relationship after a fight over a puppy in 2014. Ko collected evidence, including CCTV footage of Choi treating presidential aides as her personal servants, and shared it with local media. This revelation, along with the discovery of a tablet containing drafts of Park's speeches, sparked public outrage. Park admitted to giving inappropriate government access to Choi but denied corruption charges. The scandal has implicated numerous high-profile figures and marked the first time a South Korean president faced impeachment.

The relationship between Mike Pence and his wife Karen has become a focal point of his political career, particularly since his ascension to the role of Vice President. In 2002, Pence reportedly stated that he never eats alone with a woman other than his wife and avoids events with alcohol if she is not present, a practice often referred to as the "Billy Graham rule" among evangelicals. This has sparked both criticism and defense. Critics argue that Pence’s adherence to these rules is indicative of a broader issue of limiting women’s roles and autonomy, while Pence’s defenders claim it is a personal choice and a matter of self-preservation. The nickname "Mother" that Pence uses for his wife has also drawn attention, with some considering it quaint and others finding it outdated and potentially sexist. Overall, the Pences' relationship has become a significant aspect of public discourse surrounding Pence’s political ideology and personal conduct.

Former President George H.W. Bush, 92, and his wife Barbara, 91, are hospitalized at Houston Methodist Hospital. Bush is in the ICU for an acute respiratory issue from pneumonia, while Barbara was admitted for fatigue and coughing, later diagnosed as viral bronchitis. Both are expected to return home soon, with Bush possibly discharged by the weekend. President Obama expressed well wishes for the couple, calling them "as fine a couple as we know."

Quinnipiac University's latest national poll indicates that President Barack Obama is viewed as the worst president since World War II by 33% of American voters, with George W. Bush following closely at 28%. Ronald Reagan is seen as the best president, with 35% of voters rating him top. Obama is considered better than Bush by 39% to 40%, with gender and party lines showing significant divides. Economic issues are a major concern, with 35% citing them as the most pressing problem. Obama's handling of the economy, health care, and foreign policy receives mixed reviews, while his competence and attention to his administration's work are generally viewed negatively. The poll also reveals that 45% of voters believe the country would have been better off under Mitt Romney in 2012, compared to 38% who think it would have been worse.

Demi Lovato, 18, has been quietly dating Ryan Phillippe, 36, according to E! News. The couple started seeing each other casually, but their relationship intensified. Phillippe, a divorced father of three, is currently the father of a 2-week-old daughter, Kai. Lovato was unaware of Phillippe's new paternity until it occurred. The promotion of Lovato's new single "Skyscraper" has been keeping her busy, potentially affecting the progression of their relationship. Phillippe's representatives deny any relationship with Lovato, stating he is "totally single."

In a desolate post-apocalyptic world, Denzel Washington's Eli, a mysterious man with a sacred mission, wanders through a bleak landscape, battling savages and protecting a young girl named Solara. The film, directed by the Hughes brothers, struggles with a heavy religious message and uneven performances. While Washington's stoic portrayal of Eli is compelling, the story feels overwrought and the action scenes lack excitement. Gary Oldman's villainous Carnegie adds some tension, but the overall experience is marred by its didactic tone and drab visuals. The Hughes brothers, known for their visceral and psychological prowess, fall short here, creating a film that is more of a cautionary tale than an engaging adventure.

A 35-year-old middle school teacher named Cary Joseph Heath was arrested on a capital murder charge after two of his neighbors were found fatally shot early Sunday morning in North Texas, according to police. Heath, who is employed as an eighth-grade science teacher at Permenter Middle School in Cedar Hill, was booked on a $1 million bond. Police have not released a motive or the names of the victims, who were longtime residents. Heath has been placed on administrative leave from the Cedar Hill Independent School District. A man initially detained for questioning was not arrested. Parents expressed concern over the incident, as Heath was around children daily.

Sen. Scott Brown (R-Mass.) expressed relief that Elizabeth Warren (D) did not pose nude for a magazine to pay for college, referencing his own past. Brown made the comment on a Boston radio station, laughing and saying "Thank God!" Brown emphasized his own struggles, mentioning financial hardships during his upbringing. Warren, who graduated from the University of Houston and Rutgers, did not take off her clothes but instead borrowed money and worked part-time. Despite the incident, Warren remains a strong contender in the race against Brown. Brown's comments drew criticism from the Massachusetts Democratic Party, who called them inappropriate.

A superhero-themed funeral was held for 6-year-old Jacob Hall, who died after being shot at Townville Elementary School. His mother, Renae Hall, said the service would honor Jacob, who "wanted to save everybody" like his favorite Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. The funeral at Oakdale Baptist Church featured a small blue casket with Batman stickers, and mourners were encouraged to dress as superheroes. Jacob's great-aunt, Rebecca Hunnicutt, said, "We want to honor Jacob, celebrate Jacob, in a way he would love." A Batmobile driven by John Buckland, dressed as Batman, attended the service. The 14-year-old accused of the shooting faces multiple charges.

Donald Trump repeatedly claims the Obama administration wants to take in 200,000 Syrian refugees, a figure far from accurate. Trump's campaign often uses this statistic to fuel fears about potential terrorist threats. However, the actual number of Syrian refugees the U.S. plans to accept is much lower. President Obama has directed the U.S. to accept at least 10,000 Syrian refugees in the next year, a significant increase from previous years but far from the 200,000 Trump cites. Trump's insistence on this number, without basis, contributes to his campaign's divisive rhetoric and stokes fears among his supporters. His repeated use of this statistic, despite its inaccuracy, highlights the tactics he employs to gain support and attention.

Burger King is changing its slogan to "Be Your Way," moving away from the long-standing "Have It Your Way" tagline. The new slogan, set to debut in U.S. marketing campaigns, aims to emphasize individuality and self-expression. Burger King's senior vice president of global brand management, Fernando Machado, explains that the new slogan reflects a broader lifestyle connection rather than just customization. This shift comes as fast-food chains compete to appeal to younger, more discerning customers who value authenticity and uniqueness. However, the effectiveness of this new approach remains to be seen, as other chains like McDonald's and Taco Bell have also updated their slogans to stay relevant.

A manhunt for former LAPD officer Christopher Dorner, who is accused of killing one police officer and injuring two others, continues with no clear direction of his whereabouts. Dorner, 33, is believed to have a vendetta against the LAPD and has published an online manifesto detailing his grievances and threats. Authorities are concerned about his knowledge of police tactics and the possibility that he may be heavily armed, including with a powerful .50 caliber rifle. Dorner's last known movements included an attempt to hijack a yacht and the discovery of his burning vehicle on a mountain road. The search involves over 200 empty cabins and has led to a widespread lockdown in Big Bear, California. Dorner's background includes a troubled career with the LAPD and a military service that provided extensive combat and counter-terrorism training. His firing from the LAPD in 2008 was the catalyst for his alleged revenge killings.

Marine experts in Sydney, Australia, successfully rescued a critically endangered grey nurse shark from choking to death. The shark's gills were wrapped in an elastic cord, causing it to struggle for breath. A team from SeaLife sanctuary and aquarium used a clear plastic shark sock to capture the shark and bring it to the surface. A veterinarian cut away the cord and administered antibiotics to prevent infection. The shark was able to swim away, with the wound expected to heal in about a month. This rescue is significant as only an estimated 1,500 grey nurse sharks remain off the Australian coast.

On Tuesday, President Obama signed a bill authorizing a prestigious Congressional Gold Medal for Nisei veterans, recognizing their service and sacrifice during World War II. These Japanese Americans, born to immigrant parents, fought overseas while their families were interned in camps. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, an all-Japanese-American unit, became the most decorated Army unit of its size and length of service, with the 100th Battalion and Military Intelligence Service also honored. Art Iwasaki and Kenji Yaguchi, among other veterans, recount their experiences, highlighting the challenges and the pride they felt in serving their country. The Congressional Gold Medal, one of the highest civilian honors, will be awarded to over 6,000 Nisei veterans, acknowledging their bravery and contributions to the nation's security and interests.

The University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) campus may house up to 7,000 bodies, primarily of former patients of the Mississippi State Lunatic Asylum, which operated from 1855 to 1935. UMMC has discovered 1,000 bodies and plans to build a parking garage, but the discovery has halted these plans due to the high cost of reburial—approximately $3,000 per body, totaling $21 million. Instead, UMMC is considering an in-house exhumation and memorial project, which could cost $400,000 annually for at least eight years. The project aims to create a visitors’ center and a lab for studying the remains, potentially making Mississippi a national center for historical records on health in the pre-modern period. Researchers have already begun examining the remains, revealing insights into the lives of the patients, including evidence of nutritional deficiencies and diseases.

A forklift driver from North Wales became the first person to survive swimming across the Hoover Dam reservoir in the United States. Arron Hughes, 28, made the daring swim during a stag do in Las Vegas. Hughes swam from Arizona to Nevada, covering the quarter-mile distance in about 30 minutes. He escaped being dragged under only because nine of the ten hydroelectric turbines were not in operation. Hughes was arrested and fined $330 for his stunt. Despite the risk, Hughes says he had no idea it was prohibited and was simply trying to cool off. His swim has generated mixed opinions, with friends calling him a legend and his parents initially reacting with concern. Hughes admits the swim was "drink fuelled" and is an adrenaline junkie who has performed other daring stunts.

New England Patriots receiver Julian Edelman received an Instagram message warning about a potential school shooting, leading to the arrest of a 14-year-old boy in Port Huron, Michigan. The boy admitted to making the threat and police found two rifles at his home, which belong to his grandfather. He is charged with making a false report of a terrorist threat.

Starbucks is relocating its bottled-water operation out of California due to the severe drought, moving Ethos production to Pennsylvania. The company aims to find a new water source for the West Coast. Starbucks emphasizes its commitment to global responsibility and water conservation efforts, reducing water usage by over 25% in California stores. Previously, Ethos water from Baxter, California, was sourced from private springs in an area classified as "exceptional drought." Critics argue that bottled water companies, including Starbucks, are profiting from scarce water resources during a time of crisis. The decision comes as California faces mandatory 25% urban water reductions and the fourth year of drought.

A new study suggests that counting moles on the arm could help estimate the total number of moles on the entire body, aiding in identifying individuals at higher risk for melanoma. Researchers at King's College London analyzed data from 3,694 female Caucasian twins and found that the number of moles on the right arm was the best predictor of the total body mole count. Women with more than seven moles on their right arm were nine times more likely to have more than 50 moles on their entire body, while those with more than 11 moles on the right arm were more likely to have over 100 moles. The study, funded by the Wellcome Trust, was replicated in a wider sample of male and female participants from a UK melanoma case-control study, identifying the arm as the most predictive site for a full body mole count. This method could help GPs quickly assess melanoma risk, allowing for more targeted monitoring and intervention.

Nelson Mandela's children and grandchildren have launched a court case against prominent South Africans, including advocate George Bizos, businessman Tokyo Sexwale, and lawyer Bally Chuene, challenging their roles as directors of two companies established to manage proceeds from the sale of Mandela's handprints. The companies, Harmonieux Investment Holdings and Magnifique Investment Holdings, are estimated to hold over R15 million. Mandela's daughters, Makaziwe and Zenani, argue that Bizos, Sexwale, and Chuene were never properly appointed as directors and should be removed. They claim the trio has not fulfilled their duties with due care and skill. Bizos and Sexwale deny the allegations, stating they were appointed by Mandela five years ago. The case highlights a long-standing dispute over the control and management of Mandela's legacy.

At least 95 women and girls have accused former Michigan State University doctor Larry Nassar of sexual assault, dating back to 1992. The mediation phase in lawsuits related to Nassar could be extended by 30 days, as attorneys seek to reach a settlement. As of October, 140 women and girls have filed lawsuits, and 120 have reported Nassar to police. Michigan State University has faced significant legal fees, with its outside law firms billing the university over $4 million. Aly Raisman, a six-time Olympic medalist, has confirmed she was sexually abused by Nassar, joining McKayla Maroney and Jamie Dantzscher in alleging abuse. Raisman called for sweeping changes within the sport, expressing anger and frustration over the handling of abuse allegations. USA Gymnastics, Nassar's former employer, has faced criticism for its response to the scandal, including the resignation of its CEO.

A woman walking her dogs in South Australia was severely bitten by a koala, requiring hospitalization and 12 stitches. The incident occurred when the koala, feeling threatened, latched onto the woman's leg while the dogs were being attacked. Despite the injury, the woman does not blame the koala. Experts advise keeping a safe distance from wild koalas and warn that they can defend themselves with sharp teeth and claws.

Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou, who has ties to Vancouver and owns properties there, is fighting for bail while awaiting an extradition hearing to the U.S. on fraud charges related to alleged violations of sanctions against Iran. Meng’s legal team argues she should be released based on her strong connection to Canada, owning two homes in Vancouver, and health concerns. She faces potential severe penalties if found guilty. The case has strained relations between Canada and China, with China demanding Meng’s immediate release. Meng’s defense highlights her family’s long-standing connection to Vancouver and her commitment to Huawei’s reputation. Meanwhile, the U.S. government alleges she misled banks about Huawei’s control of Skycom, a company operating in Iran, and claims she put banks at risk of violating U.S. sanctions.

Tennessee banking executives Matt Daniels and Tim Williams have each offered a $10,000 reward for information leading to the return of 9-year-old Carlie Trent, who was abducted by her uncle Gary Simpson. Simpson, 57, took Carlie from her school on May 4th under the pretense that her father was in an accident. The TBI has shared a list of items Simpson purchased before the abduction, including a pink and purple blanket, lipstick, and a bikini, suggesting he intended to take Carlie to a remote location. Authorities are still searching for Carlie and Simpson, with an Amber Alert active in Tennessee. The TBI has received over 1,200 tips but has not yet found any credible leads. Simpson is being held on a $1 million bond and is on suicide watch in solitary confinement.

The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Texas on Tuesday night, freezing a lower court opinion that had invalidated two congressional districts and state house districts in four counties. This means the current state electoral maps will stay in effect pending appeal. The ruling is a victory for Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who argued that the lower court opinion would have thrown the electoral process into disarray. The four liberal justices on the court noted that they would have denied Texas' request. The decision is a setback for civil rights groups, who had noted that none of the additional congressional seats drawn to favor the state's growing Hispanic population were used to favor minority candidates. The ruling, which was 5-4, was seen as an indication of the influence of Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, Trump's nominee to the Supreme Court. Texas has been losing in federal courts over its election practices, with four separate cases ruling that the state discriminated against minorities in drawing districts, requiring ID for voters, and regulating voter assistance.

A Boston-area man, Daniel Morley, is accused of threatening to blow up an airplane and had materials to build a pressure-cooker bomb before the Boston Marathon bombing, according to his mother's statements in a recently unsealed police affidavit. No links have been established between Morley and the Boston Marathon attack. He is accused of assaulting his mother and her boyfriend and making an airplane hijacking threat. Police found a pressure cooker, bomb-making materials, ammunition, and other items in his home. Morley is undergoing psychiatric evaluation and is scheduled for court.

The Nunes memo, a document created by House Intelligence Committee staff, alleges FBI abuse of surveillance authority, particularly in seeking a secret court order to monitor a former Trump campaign adviser. Despite FBI and Justice Department objections, President Trump approved the memo's release, citing the public interest. The memo details several alleged issues, including the FBI's use of a politically biased dossier by Christopher Steele, which was funded by the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, and the omission of this information in FISA applications. It also highlights potential conflicts of interest involving FBI officials and the Steele dossier. The memo suggests that the FBI's surveillance process may have been compromised by political motivations.

U.S. comedian Arsenio Hall is suing singer Sinead O'Connor for defamation, seeking damages of "not less than" $5 million. O'Connor accused Hall of supplying Prince with drugs "over the decades" and of spiking her with drugs in a Facebook post. Hall's lawyers deny the claims, stating he hasn't had contact with O'Connor for 25 years and denies supplying Prince with drugs.

Martin Tripp, a former Tesla technician, has filed a countersuit against the company, alleging that Tesla is not living up to its environmental mission and is generating large amounts of waste. Tripp claims Tesla reuses damaged battery parts and lacks traceability in its part tracking. Tesla, in response, has accused Tripp of hacking and stealing confidential data, and has filed a lawsuit against him. Tripp denies hacking and claims he was a whistleblower, leaking information to a Business Insider reporter out of environmental and safety concerns. Tesla's claims of receiving a threat of a mass shooting from a "friend of Tripp" are disputed, with Tripp alleging defamation and seeking at least $1 million in damages. The lawsuit comes amid Tesla's ongoing production challenges and financial pressures.

Augustus "Gus" Lee, a University of Richmond football player and Paul VI Catholic High School graduate, was found dead in his car on December 11, 2018. His family has decided to donate his brain to the Veterans Administration-Boston University-Concussion Legacy Foundation Brain Bank, a repository studying traumatic brain injuries and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Lee's mother, Phyllis Lee, expressed concern about the potential link between his death and a brain injury from contact sports. Lee played football, lacrosse, and track in high school and was a redshirt freshman defensive back at Richmond. He struggled with homesickness and the rigorous training regimen during his freshman year but showed improvement by spring practice. Lee's death came after he reported feeling lonely and stressed, prompting a mental health evaluation. The cause of death was reported as suicide by asphyxiation. Lee's family and teammates mourn his loss, with Richmond's coach and president expressing their condolences

Police in Los Angeles and Philadelphia cleared Occupy encampments early Wednesday, arresting hundreds of protesters. In Los Angeles, over 200 people were arrested as police dismantled a two-month-old camp outside City Hall. Demonstrators chanted and some defied orders to leave. In Philadelphia, about 50 protesters were arrested after occupying their site for nearly two months to make room for a $50 million renovation project. Both cities aimed to minimize disruption by conducting operations in the early morning hours.

Robin Thicke has been making it clear he's not ready to give up on his marriage to Paula Patton. After announcing their separation, Thicke performed in Virginia and dedicated a song to his estranged wife, telling the crowd he's trying to get her back. He also told TMZ he's just trying to figure things out. Despite the split, Thicke wore his wedding ring and continued to perform songs about Patton. Meanwhile, Patton has been sending Thicke expensive floral arrangements, possibly in an attempt to win him back. The couple's son Julian was involved in a minor car accident with Patton and her mother and assistant, adding another layer of drama to their ongoing custody battle.

Some researchers argue that laws restricting the use of psychedelic drugs like LSD and psilocybin hinder scientific progress and prevent understanding of their potential therapeutic benefits. These drugs, once used in medical research, are now largely off-limits due to legal restrictions. Critics say these laws, enacted in the 1960s and 1970s, have impeded vital research into the drugs' functions and therapeutic uses. Proponents of lifting these restrictions argue that psychedelic drugs could offer significant medical benefits, such as treating depression, anxiety, and addiction, and even aiding in understanding the nature of consciousness. However, the illegal status of these substances makes it challenging to conduct research and obtain funding, limiting the scope of current studies.

John Heath, 68, from Bridgewater, pleaded not guilty to the 1984 murder of his wife, Elizabeth, whose remains were found in a well under a barn in Newtown in 2010. Heath, who is being held on $1 million bond, was arrested after a moving truck was spotted at his home. Elizabeth, 30 at the time of her disappearance, was reported missing days after Heath filed for divorce. Her body was discovered wrapped in bedding and placed head-first into a cistern. Heath told police she had left with $600, but friends and family doubted his story. He is a Vietnam veteran with a volatile temper. The case is set for a probable cause hearing in May.

Hope Hicks, former White House communications director, has been named executive vice president and chief communications officer for New Fox, the company to emerge after 21st Century Fox sells assets to Disney. She will report to Viet Dinh, Fox’s chief legal and policy officer. Danny O’Brien, previously with GE Transportation, has also been appointed as executive vice president and head of government relations. Hicks will succeed Julie Henderson as communications chief for Rupert Murdoch’s media empire. Hicks, who left the White House in February amid probes into Russian interference in the 2016 election, will be based in Los Angeles. Her appointment further ties Fox News to the Trump administration.

The bodies of Canadian Francesca Matus, 52, and American Drew DeVoursney, 36, were found in a sugarcane field in Belize on Monday. Matus, from Ontario, and DeVoursney, from Georgia, were last seen leaving a bar in Corozal on April 25. Their friend, Joe Milholen, found their SUV abandoned in a cane field near Paraiso on Sunday. Police are investigating the deaths as homicides, with DeVoursney's mother stating they were found with duct tape around their wrists. Matus was scheduled to return to Canada on Wednesday, but neither she nor her vehicle were at her home when Milholen arrived. The Canadian government has advised Canadians to exercise caution in Belize due to high rates of violent crime.

JPMorgan Chase's trading losses have surged beyond the initial $2 billion estimate, reaching at least $3 billion, according to sources familiar with the situation. The losses are attributed to a complex hedging strategy that backfired, with JPMorgan's Chief Investment Office making large bets on credit derivatives. The bank's Chief Executive Jamie Dimon acknowledged that additional losses could occur, but the exact amount remains uncertain. The Federal Reserve is examining the losses and the risk-taking practices of JPMorgan's chief investment office. While JPMorgan's overall financial health remains strong, the trading losses have reignited debates about banking regulation and the appropriateness of such large-scale trading activities within a federally insured institution.

Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain has released an unexpected album of gospel music, titled "Sunday Morning," which has appeared online. The 13-track album, published 15 years ago, features Cain's soulful vocals and includes a standout track, "This is the Day," which is described as a fun, danceable song. While the Cain campaign has not officially commented on the album, it is being distributed by GLC Music, Selah Sound Production, and Melodic Praise Records. The release of this music, which comes as Cain's campaign is gaining traction, has sparked interest and speculation among media outlets.

Congressional leaders made progress Thursday toward a deal to fund the government through next fall and extend a one-year cut in the payroll tax rate for 160 million workers, aiming to avoid a partial shutdown at midnight Friday. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) and House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) expressed optimism about swift compromise. The $1 trillion spending bill, expected to be approved by both chambers, would keep federal agencies operating. Sticking points remained on financing the payroll tax extension and unemployment benefits, with negotiations on a two-month extension ongoing. Leaders hoped to finalize both measures before the year-end, avoiding a government shutdown and maintaining middle-class tax relief.

Paul Manafort, former Trump campaign chairman, filed a lawsuit Wednesday challenging the authority of special counsel Robert Mueller, alleging Mueller's indictment of Manafort on money laundering and tax charges exceeded legal boundaries. The lawsuit, filed in Washington federal court, questions the May appointment by Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein, which authorized Mueller to investigate potential links between the Russian government and the Trump campaign, as well as any related matters. Manafort's attorneys argue Mueller's charges, which stem from his work for a pro-Russian Ukrainian political party, are unrelated to the 2016 campaign. The Justice Department dismissed the lawsuit as frivolous.

A 93-year-old former Nazi SS guard, Oskar Groening, testified during his trial for being an accessory to the murder of at least 300,000 Jews at Auschwitz. Groening, known as the "accountant of Auschwitz," described the arrival of trains at the death camp, noting that two trains would sometimes have to wait while the first was processed. Most passengers were gassed immediately. Groening stated he had no direct role in killings but acknowledged "moral guilt." He described the scene as "very orderly" and "not strenuous" for him. Survivors, like Eva Kor, testified about their experiences, including being torn from their families and subjected to horrific experiments. Kor emphasized that her forgiveness did not absolve the perpetrators and called for them to take responsibility. The charges against Groening relate to the period between May and July 1944 when 425,000 Jews from Hungary were taken to Auschwitz.

A key Hawaii lawmaker and Honolulu police have agreed to remove a longstanding exemption that allowed officers to have sex with prostitutes, the AP reports. State Sen. Clayton Hee, head of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said the exemption was contrary to popular opinion. Police are okay with making it illegal for officers to have sex with prostitutes, as long as undercover officers can still verbally offer sex to make arrests. Police spokeswoman Teresa Bell stated that officers have never been allowed to have sex with prostitutes under departmental rules, so making it illegal won't change how officers operate. The bill passed the House without the clause that would have made sex with prostitutes illegal for officers, after police lobbied to have it removed. At a Senate hearing, lawmakers and the public expressed outrage at the exemption, with Hee vowing to make the practice illegal. The version of the bill moving through Hee's committee will remove sexual penetration from the police exemption, leaving police with the ability to solicit sex in investigations. Bell said officers

Former NAACP chapter president Rachel Dolezal appeared on NBC News, questioning whether she is part of a white family and denying allegations that she lied about her racial identity. Dolezal stated she has not had a DNA test and does not know if Larry and Ruthanne, the couple who exposed her, are her biological parents. She emphasized her identification as "more black than white" and rejected the term "transracial," arguing that being white does not describe who she is. Dolezal defended her actions, stating that she never backed down and that her identity is complex. The interview sparked a national debate about racial identity, with some supporting her message and others condemning her methods. Dolezal’s claims about her family and upbringing have been challenged by relatives, creating a contentious narrative about her past and motivations.

Summer 2015 saw numerous celebrity breakups, and Avril Lavigne and Chad Kroeger, known for his band Nickelback, are the latest to announce their separation after two years of marriage. Lavigne revealed the news on Instagram. Both artists have faced health challenges, with Lavigne battling Lyme disease and Kroeger having vocal cord issues.

A former Siberian police officer, Mikhail Popkov, nicknamed the "Werewolf," has confessed to 59 additional murders, bringing his total to 81, making him Russia's most prolific killer. Between 1992 and 2010, Popkov attacked and killed women he considered immoral, often offering them rides before taking them to remote locations where he used axes, knives, or screwdrivers. He was already serving a life sentence for 22 murders. Popkov claims he wanted to "cleanse" the streets of prostitutes. Confessions and evidence suggest he killed women in the Angarsk and Irkutsk regions, with victims ranging in age from 17 to 38. His confessions are ongoing, and authorities expect to charge him in 12 more cases. If confirmed, Popkov's total would surpass that of the worst-known Soviet and Russian serial killers.

Gracie Gold, a two-time U.S. figure skating champion and 2014 Olympic team bronze medalist, announced she will take time off before the 2018 Olympics to seek professional help for "recent struggles on and off the ice." Gold, 22, has struggled with her performance, finishing sixth at the 2016 U.S. Championships and missing the 2017 World Championships. She cited her passion for skating as remaining strong but acknowledged the need for professional assistance. Gold's decision comes just four days after Russian Olympic champion Julia Lipnitskaya announced her retirement due to anorexia. The U.S. Olympic figure skating trials are scheduled for early January, with the 2018 Winter Olympics starting in February.

A Prince George's County police officer was killed in a shootout outside a district station in Landover on Sunday, in what the police chief called an unprovoked attack. Officer Jacai Colson, a four-year department veteran, was shot and died after several officers engaged the suspect. The suspect was wounded and taken to a hospital in stable condition. Two brothers, Malik and Michael Ford, were arrested in connection with the shooting. Police Chief Henry P. Stawinski III praised Colson's bravery and described him as a "cop's cop." The shooting occurred in Landover, about 10 miles northeast of downtown Washington, D.C. Flags were ordered to fly at half-staff by Maryland Governor Larry Hogan.

George A. Romero, the "father of modern horror films" and creator of the iconic "Night of the Living Dead," passed away at 77 after a brief battle with lung cancer. His low-budget films, including "Dawn of the Dead" and "Land of the Dead," significantly influenced the zombie genre and popular culture. Romero's work often carried social commentary, and he directed several Stephen King adaptations. He died peacefully in his sleep, surrounded by his family. Romero's legacy continues to endure, with Pittsburgh hosting an annual Zombie Fest in his honor.

NASA astronaut Jeanette Epps, who was set to become the first African-American crew member on the International Space Station, was unexpectedly reassigned from her June mission. Her brother believes the decision stems from "oppressive racism and misogyny" within NASA. Despite NASA's refusal to provide a reason, Epps will now work at the Astronaut Office at Johnson Space Center and await another potential flight assignment. Her removal from the mission, announced on January 18, has sparked a petition calling for her reinstatement. Epps, part of the 2009 astronaut class, was inspired to become an astronaut after watching Sally Ride become the first American woman in space in 1983.

A 10-year-old girl was airlifted from Six Flags Magic Mountain amusement park in Valencia, California, after collapsing near the Revolution ride. She later died at a hospital, though the exact cause is pending an autopsy. The ride, a roller coaster with a 90-foot vertical loop reaching 55 mph, was temporarily closed for review. Magic Mountain stated the incident was not related to the ride's operation and that over 45 million visitors have safely ridden it since 1976. The park expressed condolences to the girl's family.

Pop star Lady Gaga attended a Silicon Valley fundraiser for President Barack Obama, held at Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg's home. Wearing a black, sleeveless gown and high heels, Gaga mingled with Silicon Valley elites, who paid up to $35,800 per couple for the event. Though Gaga aimed to meet Obama to discuss bullying, the White House press corps report notes that Obama did not acknowledge her during his eight-minute speech. Gaga's presence was hard to miss, towering over guests in her towering bouffant hairstyle adorned with a black veil.

A maniacal carjacker led police on a wild chase through Los Angeles during rush hour, driving a suspected stolen car at high speeds and crashing into at least six vehicles. The chase ended when he was shot by police as he tried to steal another car. The suspect, identified as a 20- to 30-year-old man, was arrested in hospital with multiple gunshot wounds. He had collided with cars and forced a 22-year-old woman out of her vehicle at gunpoint. Police described his actions as callous and dangerous, but no one was killed.

Cambridge University is seeking the world's first Lego professor of play, development, and learning, funded by the LEGO Foundation. The professor will lead the Centre for Research on Play in Education, Development and Learning (PEDAL), focusing on the role of play in children's education and development. This unique position, with a competitive salary, aims to enhance understanding of play's benefits and support evidence-based policy and practice globally. Applications, requiring a letter of application, research plans, CV, and referee details, close on January 20, 2017. The LEGO Foundation is committed to funding this role indefinitely, emphasizing the importance of play in education and development.

State Rep. Daniel B. Winslow, a former judge and Romney aide, officially entered the race for the U.S. Senate special election to replace John Kerry, becoming the first Republican to do so. Winslow plans to donate $100,000 and expects costs between $4 million and $6 million. He will resign from his law firm and meet with Republicans in Washington. Other potential Republican candidates include Bruce E. Tarr, Sean Bielat, Gabriel Gomez, and Jon Fetherston. Democrats are vying between Reps. Edward J. Markey and Stephen F. Lynch. Candidates must gather 10,000 signatures by February 27 to make the April 30 ballot.

In 1961, a B-52 bomber carrying two 4-megaton hydrogen bombs broke apart over North Carolina, leading to a near-disaster that could have resulted in a nuclear explosion. Newly released documents reveal that one bomb's arming mechanism switched from "safe" to "armed" upon impact, while the other bomb, though it deployed a parachute, was also close to detonating due to a single low-voltage switch preventing its explosion. The incident, detailed in Eric Schlosser's book "Command and Control," highlights the narrow margin between safety and catastrophe in the handling of nuclear weapons. Had the bombs detonated, the destruction could have been catastrophic, with a blast 260 times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb. The US Air Force narrowly averted a nuclear disaster, with only one switch preventing the second bomb from exploding. This incident, along with other nuclear accidents, underscores the risks associated with nuclear weapons and the importance of safety protocols.

Inventor Charles Hall, 71, is reviving the waterbed with a redesigned version that aims to address past issues while retaining the comfort and support of the original. Hall, who first introduced the waterbed concept in 1968, plans to launch the updated model later this year. The new waterbed features a foam collar around the water bladder, a spandex cover for a floating sensation, and a fiber insert to quell waves. It also includes an improved temperature control system. The bed will be available in queen and king sizes, with a complete system priced around $2,000. Hall hopes to tap into a potential resurgence, particularly among millennials, with his friend Keith Koening, president of City Furniture, set to test-market the beds in Florida. Hall believes the waterbed could make a comeback, offering a blend of comfort and nostalgia for both older and younger generations.

The complex journey of William Morgan, an American who fought alongside Fidel Castro during the Cuban Revolution, highlights the intricate web of loyalty and betrayal. Morgan, initially seen as a hero to many Cubans, later became a double agent, working covertly for the U.S. government. His life took a dramatic turn when he orchestrated a counter-revolutionary plot against the Castro regime, which ultimately failed and led to his stripping of U.S. citizenship. Despite facing significant risks and a bounty on his head, Morgan continued to support the Cuban revolution, eventually becoming a revered figure on the island. His story, intertwined with his wife Olga’s unwavering support, underscores the personal and political complexities of the Cold War era.

Simone Biles, a 2016 Olympic gold medalist, has joined other gymnasts in accusing former USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar of sexual abuse, adding her #MeToo statement on social media. Nassar, who treated young hopefuls and Olympic champions, is facing a weeklong sentencing hearing where nearly 100 victims will share their stories. Biles, like McKayla Maroney, Aly Raisman, and Gabby Douglas, says she was molested by Nassar under the guise of medical treatment. She expresses that she is no longer afraid to speak out and that the abuse was not her fault. The hearing will include victim impact statements from elite athletes and ordinary patients, many of whom blame USA Gymnastics and Michigan State University for enabling Nassar's abuse. USA Gymnastics has promised to support Biles and others who have come forward, while facing criticism for its handling of abuse allegations. The case highlights the #MeToo movement's

Denver Broncos player Kenny McKinley, who was the University of South Carolina’s all-time leader in receptions and a standout in college football, was found dead at his home in Colorado in an apparent suicide. McKinley, 23, was a fifth-round draft pick in 2009 and played eight games for the Broncos, primarily on special teams. The Broncos and his former college coach, Steve Spurrier, expressed shock and sadness over his death. McKinley’s agent described him as having a big heart and a positive outlook. The Broncos will hold a team meeting to address McKinley’s passing, and grief counselors will be available. This tragic event marks the third death involving an active Broncos player in the past four years.

Hollywood icon Carrie Fisher, best known for her role as Princess Leia in the "Star Wars" saga, has passed away at the age of 60 after suffering a heart attack during a flight from London to Los Angeles. Fisher's death has left fans and colleagues in shock, with many taking to social media to express their grief and share memories. Fisher was an acclaimed author and script doctor, and her openness about mental health struggles helped break down stigma. She also left a legacy of quirky, self-aware fashion choices and a love for her dog Gary, who accompanied her on red carpet events and social media. Fisher's impact on pop culture and her enduring popularity as a "geek girl" role model are evident in the outpouring of tributes and reactions from both fans and fellow actors.

A new poll from Morning Consult reveals that Supreme Leader Snoke is the most hated Star Wars character of all time, with only 26% favorability. Jar Jar Binks, Mace Windu, Kylo Ren, Emperor Palpatine, and Jyn Erso also rank low in the poll. In contrast, Leia, Luke Skywalker, Chewbacca, Yoda, and R2-D2 receive high favorability ratings. The poll surveyed 2,200 people and also found that 53% of respondents do not consider Star Wars to be political, while 41% of those who do find the series' political tone bothersome. The poll provides insights into fan preferences and political perceptions of the Star Wars universe.

Within seconds of seeing a new face, we form judgments about approachability, dominance, and attractiveness. A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences used 1,000 internet photos to develop a model predicting these first impressions based on facial features. Volunteers rated the faces on 16 social traits, which boiled down to three main impressions: approachability, dominance, and attractiveness. The researchers then created cartoon faces to test their model, finding that the computer-generated faces accurately reflected human perceptions. This model could help in creating more convincing characters for animation or improving first impressions in professional or personal contexts.

Groupon's stock price has been volatile, with institutional investors selling off shares as soon as they can after the IPO. The stock started trading around $30, up from the $20 IPO price, but its future is uncertain. Groupon's growth is decelerating, and this could lead to a significant decline in the stock price if the growth rate stabilizes negatively. The company is already operating at a break-even point, and cutting marketing costs will likely slow growth further. While Groupon has a large user base and a global presence, its near-term upside appears limited. Long-term, Groupon could potentially double in value, but the risk/reward profile is not compelling given the current valuation. As of now, the stock seems overvalued, and investors should be cautious.

Dallas Cowboys coach Jason Garrett's news conference focused solely on recently cut wide receiver Lucky Whitehead, with Garrett repeatedly standing by the team's decision to cut him despite questions and challenges from reporters. Garrett emphasized that the decision was in the best interest of the Dallas Cowboys and that the team would move forward, declining to address any other football-related questions.

Google's security bounty programs have been quite lucrative, with over $2 million paid to more than 300 researchers in 2015. Notable recipients include Sanmay Ved, who briefly owned Google.com before it was returned, and Tomasz Bojarski, who discovered 70 bugs. Android joined the Security Reward program in 2015, resulting in payments over $200,000. Google also introduced Vulnerability Research Grants to support researchers, with one example involving Kamil Histamullin, who found an issue in YouTube Creator Studio and received an additional $5,000 reward.

A Minnesota restaurant owner upset over the St. Cloud mall stabbing posted a "Muslims Get Out" sign outside his Treats Family Restaurant in Lonsdale, MN. The sign has led to some backlash, but the owner says business is up and he has no plans to take down the sign. He believes it's time for people to "stand up" against what he sees as extremism. A local resident criticized the sign, saying it could give Lonsdale a negative image. The restaurant offers ice cream and cooked food items, with mixed reviews. While the ice cream is positively received, the cooked food is described as gritty, greasy, and lacking flavor. Service is noted to be poor, and the atmosphere is described as unpleasant.

Retired federal judge Vaughn Walker, who ruled California's same-sex marriage ban unconstitutional, spoke publicly for the first time since his retirement, defending his decision and addressing personal questions. Walker stated that his sexuality is not relevant to his judicial role and that it would be inappropriate to recuse himself based on his sexual orientation. He also discussed his desire for higher courts to review his ruling on its merits. Walker, known for his independent thinking and past rulings, expressed his hope that his decision stands. He advocated for televised trials as a means to ensure public transparency in the judicial process.

New cases of diabetes have begun to decline in the United States for the first time in decades, according to a CDC report. The number of new cases dropped from 1.7 million in 2008 to 1.4 million in 2014. This marks the first significant decrease in diabetes incidence in 25 years, though the overall number of Americans living with diabetes remains high, affecting about 21.9 million people. Public health officials attribute this trend to improved prevention efforts, including promoting healthier lifestyles and better dietary habits. However, the incidence rate is still 60% higher than it was in the early 1990s, indicating a long way to go in addressing the diabetes epidemic.

Bolivia has rejected a donation of 100,000 chickens from Bill Gates, stating that the billionaire philanthropist should apologize for not knowing Bolivia already has enough poultry. Minister César Cocaric criticized the gift, saying Bolivia does not need external help to produce chickens and eggs. Bolivia's poultry industry has grown significantly, with per capita egg consumption increasing by 13% and chicken meat consumption rising by 35% over the past five years. The Cooperativa Agropecuaria Integral San Juan de Yapacaní focuses on poultry, producing about 20 million eggs monthly. Gates' initiative aims to help high-poverty countries, but Bolivia views it as an insult, emphasizing its self-sufficiency in poultry production.

Rescue workers in Genoa found the bodies of three more people, bringing the death toll to 43, following the collapse of the Morandi bridge. The last reported missing individuals were members of the same family found in a crushed car. The bridge, a key route linking Genoa to the A10 motorway and the French border, gave way during heavy rainfall, sparking a debate on Italy's infrastructure. The bridge's operator, Autostrade per l'Italia, has set up funds for victims' families and to assist those displaced. The government has launched a commission to investigate the cause and plans a large-scale infrastructure maintenance program. The engineer who designed the bridge, Riccardo Morandi, had warned of corrosion risks decades ago, suggesting the collapse may have been preventable.

Inmates at the Century Regional Detention Facility are reportedly sick of Lindsay Lohan's presence, according to a relative of an inmate. "She's not treated like if it was anyone else going to jail," the relative says. "If they even want to bring her new clothes or bring her anything, they put the whole facility on lockdown." Despite the claims, Los Angeles Sheriff's spokesman Steve Whitmore denies any special treatment. Lindsay Lohan's lawyer Shawn Chapman Holley says she is doing well and her outlook is positive. Lohan is serving a 90-day sentence for violating her probation and is expected to be released early due to jail overcrowding.

When Matt Lauer of The Today Show asked General Motors CEO Mary Barra about balancing her demanding job and being a mother, she responded gracefully, highlighting her support system. Male CEOs, however, rarely face such questions. MongoDB CEO Max Schireson recently stepped down after realizing he couldn't balance his demanding role and family responsibilities. His decision to remain a vice chairman and spend more time with his children sparked positive reactions, but also highlighted the double standards in the "having it all" debate. Schireson's experience and Scheryl Sandberg's encouragement to "lean in" underscore the need for a more balanced approach to work-life integration, regardless of gender. As more men like Schireson question their roles, it signals a shift towards recognizing the importance of family in leadership.

Chris Christie and Mike Huckabee miss the main debate stage for Fox Business Network, falling just short of the 2.5 percent threshold in four major polls. Both will participate in the undercard debate, a blow to their campaigns. Christie, who previously appeared on the main debate stage, received 2 percent support in the Fox News poll. Huckabee, a former Fox News host, secured 4 percent support. The main debate will feature eight remaining Republican candidates, including Donald Trump, Ben Carson, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, Jeb Bush, Carly Fiorina, John Kasich, and Rand Paul. The undercard debate will include Christie, Huckabee, Bobby Jindal, and Rick Santorum.

The NBA imposed a lifetime ban and $2.5 million fine on Donald Sterling for racist remarks, while his girlfriend V. Stiviano expressed sadness over the decision. Sterling's team, the Los Angeles Clippers, staged a silent protest during Game 5 of the playoffs, with players wearing red T-shirts inside out. Coach Doc Rivers informed the team of Sterling's punishment during a morning shoot-around, and the Clippers went on to win 113-103 against the Golden State Warriors. The victory gave the Clippers a 3-2 series lead. Players and fans supported the decision, seeing it as a step towards a safer and more inclusive environment.

A Playmobil pirate ship set has sparked controversy over instructions that include putting a neck shackle on a dark-skinned figurine, resembling a slave. Ida Lockett of Sacramento, California, noticed the instructions when assembling the toy with her 5-year-old son, who received it as a birthday gift. Lockett considers the toy and its assembly directions racist, stating that the figurine's neck cuff/shackle is clearly a slave collar. The set, which includes a dungeon, retails for $89.99. Playmobil defended the toy, saying it was intended to represent a historical context of a former slave pirate. However, the NAACP in Sacramento called for the toy to be banned. Not everyone agrees, with some arguing that pirates took slaves and that children can use their imagination to play with the toy in any way they choose.

A 3-year-old boy and his 1-year-old brother survived a single-vehicle crash that killed their mother in south Arkansas for an estimated two days. The older boy, identified as Kylen, managed to exit the wrecked car, find his way to a state highway, and was eventually found by authorities after a 911 call. He appeared traumatized and was in poor condition, with cuts and scrapes. Kylen's one-year-old brother remained in the car, strapped in his seat. Both boys showed signs of dehydration but are expected to recover. The mother, Lisa Holliman, 25, was not seen since going grocery shopping on Thursday. The cause of the accident is under investigation. (The older boy's actions are described as miraculous by his grandfather.)

The internet worldwide has experienced a significant slowdown due to the largest cyber-attack of its kind, targeting Spamhaus, a non-profit organization that filters spam and unwanted content. The attack, which has lasted over a week, uses a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) tactic, flooding Spamhaus's Domain Name System (DNS) servers with traffic. Experts warn that the conflict between Spamhaus and Cyberbunker, a Dutch web host, could escalate to affect banking and email systems. Five national cyber-police forces are investigating the attacks, which peaked at 300 Gbps, significantly higher than usual. The attack's power is likened to a motorway jam, with the potential to "decapitate" internet infrastructure. Spamhaus, supported by major internet companies, has managed to cope with the attack by distributing its infrastructure globally. The attacks have also targeted companies providing data connections to Spamhaus and CloudFlare, which helped by absorbing the traffic. Experts stress the difficulty in

Archaeologists have finally located the 16th-century Spanish fort San Marcos, one of several forts built on the Santa Elena settlement, on what is now Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island. For over 20 years, researchers had been searching for the fort, using advanced technology like ground-penetrating radar and magnetometers. The general location was known from historical documents archived in Spain, but the exact site remained elusive until recent improvements in data interpretation techniques. The fort, founded in 1577 by Pedro Menendez Marquez, was built in just six days with pre-made large pieces to protect against Native American attacks. Archaeologists are mapping the entire town of Santa Elena, which included about 60 homes, a church, shops, and taverns, and believe they have found the locations of several key structures. The breakthrough came after multiple failed attempts and is set to be published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports. This discovery will enhance understanding of

Florida Representative Brad Drake proposed a bill to end lethal injection as the method of execution, instead allowing death row inmates to choose between electrocution or a firing squad. Drake said the idea came from a conversation with a constituent at a Waffle House. He argued that lethal injection allows inmates to die in their sleep, while other methods would force them to contemplate their punishment. The Florida Legislature will consider the bill during the 2012 session. Critics argue that the bill would cause embarrassment and raise ethical concerns.

In southern Guangdong Province, two officials were arrested for purchasing stolen corpses to meet government cremation quotas, according to Chinese media reports. In June, a resident in Guangxi reported his grandfather's body was stolen from a graveyard. Police apprehended a grave robber in July who admitted to stealing over 20 corpses and selling them to the officials. The officials, in charge of funeral management reform, bought the bodies to fulfill monthly cremation targets. The practice has sparked controversy, as traditional burial beliefs clash with government policies aimed at saving land. Further investigation is ongoing.

The Obama administration announced a one-year delay in enforcing the employer mandate of the Affordable Care Act, pushing the requirement for larger employers to provide coverage or pay penalties to 2015. This delay, made to give businesses more time to comply, was seen as a significant concession to employer groups and a potential political move to avoid backlash ahead of the 2014 midterm elections. While the White House emphasized the delay would not affect other provisions of the law, such as the establishment of health insurance exchanges, critics argued it created a "backdoor" for employers to drop coverage and dump employees into the exchanges. The decision faced mixed reactions, with some Democrats praising it as a sign of flexibility, while Republicans used it as evidence of the law's flaws and called for its repeal.

Online dating platforms have transformed the way people meet partners, potentially breaking down social barriers and strengthening marriages, according to research. Traditional social networks are characterized by strong ties with close friends and weak ties with distant connections. However, online dating introduces complete strangers into these networks, creating new pathways and increasing interracial marriages. The study by Josue Ortega and Philipp Hergovich models the impact of online dating on social networks, predicting significant racial integration and stronger marriages. The rise of online dating, particularly apps like Tinder, coincides with a sharp increase in interracial marriages in the U.S., suggesting a direct link between the two. This research highlights the profound societal changes brought about by digital match-making services.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad plans to visit North Korea and meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, potentially the first meeting between Kim and another head of state in Pyongyang, according to North Korean state media. Assad made the comments on May 30 while receiving the credentials of North Korean Ambassador Mun Jong Nam. Syria and North Korea maintain good relations and both face international isolation. Assad expressed support for Kim's policies and the reunification of Korea. The visit comes as international attention focuses on the upcoming summit between Kim and U.S. President Donald Trump scheduled for June 12 in Singapore.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz apologized after making a joke about Vice President Joe Biden at a Michigan Republican dinner, drawing criticism due to the timing, as Biden's son Beau had recently died from brain cancer. Cruz said, "Vice President Joe Biden, you know the nice thing? You don't need a punch line," and continued with, "The next party you're at, just walk up to someone and say, 'Vice President Joe Biden' and just close your mouth. They will crack up laughing." He later issued an apology on Facebook, stating it was a mistake to use the old joke during Biden's time of grief and expressing prayers for the Biden family.

On the evening of Tuesday, November 17, and into the morning of Wednesday, November 18, the Leonid meteor shower will peak, creating a host of shooting stars. The event, caused by bits of ice and rock burning in Earth’s atmosphere, will be visible above the eastern horizon around midnight in the U.S. Head out after sunset on Tuesday, November 17, and look east from a dark site away from street lights. NASA predicts one meteor every four minutes, and the crescent moon will provide a darker sky for better visibility. However, cloud cover may obstruct views in a good portion of the U.S. The Leonids happen annually around November 17 as the Earth passes through the debris field of the comet Tempel-Tuttle.

The largest diamond ever found in North America has been discovered at the Diavik mine in Canada’s Northwest Territories by Dominion Diamond Mines and Rio Tinto Group. Weighing in at 552 carats, this yellow gem is nearly three times the size of the previous largest diamond found in Canada. While the Diavik mine is known for producing high-quality diamonds, such a large gem is unusual for this region. Dominion Chief Executive Officer Shane Durgin stated the diamond is gem quality, suitable for jewelry, but did not provide further details on its value. The discovery is the seventh-largest diamond found this century and ranks among the 30 largest diamonds ever unearthed. The largest diamond ever found, the 3,106-carat Cullinan, was discovered in South Africa in 1905. This significant find comes at a good time for Dominion, which has been facing management changes and considering expansion projects.

In a small Ohio town, long-time residents Rick and Cindy Krlich claim to have endured over 5,000 honks from passing cars over the past seven years. ABC News' "20/20" attempted to bring peace and reconciliation by hosting a barbecue, but the event did little to resolve the ongoing dispute. Rick Krlich alleges that John Clemente, the former fire chief, and his family orchestrated the campaign of horn honking as retaliation for a failed real estate deal in 2007. Surveillance cameras installed by the Krlichs have captured numerous incidents, including horn honking by firemen and police officers. John Clemente and his wife deny instigating the honking, instead blaming Rick Krlich for bringing it on himself. Despite numerous complaints and legal actions, including 40 lawsuits, the Krlichs say police have failed to investigate or take action. The "20/20" team invited all parties to a barbecue, hoping

North Korea's Kim Jong Il appointed his youngest son, Kim Jong Un, as a four-star general, signaling his potential succession. This move, confirmed in state media, is seen as a step to establish the Kim family's third generation of leadership. Kim Jong Un, believed to be in his late 20s and educated in Switzerland, has so far remained hidden from the public eye. Analysts view this as a strong indication that Kim Jong Il is preparing to pass power to his son, though Kim Jong Un's lack of experience raises concerns. The appointment also aligns with the "songun" policy, emphasizing military-first governance. Kim Jong Il's sister, Kim Kyong Hui, was also promoted to a four-star general, suggesting she may play a role in the succession process. The Workers' Party convention, North Korea's largest political gathering in decades, further underscores the importance of this transition.

Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz researched suicide methods and cockpit door security on his tablet in the days before the crash, according to Düsseldorf prosecutors. The co-pilot, suspected of deliberately crashing the plane, had locked the captain out of the cockpit. Investigators found a tablet with search terms related to medical treatment and suicide, as well as 40 damaged cellphones at the crash site. The discovery of the second black box, the flight data recorder, should provide more details on Lubitz's actions. A new task force will examine cockpit door mechanisms and pilot medical procedures.

About 80% of the caravan members are from Honduras, fleeing poverty, political unrest, and violence following the disputed election of Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández. The group, organized by Pueblos Sin Fronteras, aims to reach the US, hoping for asylum or to cross undetected. The large number of migrants has overwhelmed towns they've stopped in. Organizers hope the group's size will deter authorities and criminals. Conditions are tough, with migrants walking long distances under heat and risking attacks. Some plan to cross into Mexico legally, while others aim for the US. The caravan is self-organized, with security, food, and logistics committees. Despite risks, the migrants see it as a safer option than traveling alone.

Mel B is still wearing her wedding ring from Stephen Belafonte despite filing for divorce, flaunting a 7-carat, $300,000 diamond that she received in 2014. The divorce documents reveal a decade of abuse, including physical assaults, emotional manipulation, and threats of releasing sex tapes. Belafonte is accused of beating Mel, forcing her into sexual encounters, and threatening to expose their intimate videos to ruin her career and family. Despite multiple incidents where friends and colleagues witnessed her injuries, authorities were not alerted. Mel B recently obtained a restraining order, forcing Belafonte to leave the family home and stay away from her and their three children.

British businessman Krishna Maharaj, who has spent 27 years in a Florida prison for double murders he claims he did not commit, is seeking a retrial with new evidence. Lawyers plan to call 53 witnesses and present 498 documents to support his case. Maharaj was sentenced to death in 1987 for the 1986 murders of his business partner Derrick Moo Young and Young’s son Duane in Miami. The case involves allegations of a drug-money hit ordered by Pablo Escobar, with new witnesses claiming Maharaj was framed. Maharaj’s lawyers argue that the Moo Youngs were involved in money laundering for the Medellin cartel, which led to their murders. A full evidentiary hearing is set for April 24, where Judge William Thomas will decide if Maharaj should be granted a new trial based on the new evidence.

Anonymous street artists in Los Angeles posted posters depicting Meryl Streep with the phrase "She knew" near her home and other locations, suggesting she was aware of Harvey Weinstein's alleged sexual misconduct. Streep responded that she did not know about Weinstein's crimes, either in the 1990s or in subsequent decades. Rose McGowan, who was allegedly raped by Weinstein, criticized Streep for her past association with the producer. McGowan argued that Streep should wear black at the Golden Globes to protest sexual harassment, while Streep maintained she was not complicit and was working to change the power structure in Hollywood. Actress Amber Tamblyn also defended Streep, stating she did not support McGowan's criticism.

Two daycare workers, Lizandra Cosme, 32, and Susana Gonzalez, 27, have been charged after surveillance footage allegedly showed Cosme burning five toddlers with a hot glue gun while Gonzalez laughed nearby. The incident occurred at the Children’s Learning Place in Chicago on December 1. Cosme, who was caring for 16 children at the time, applied hot glue to the hands and arms of three girls and two boys, causing them to grimace in pain, according to prosecutors. Gonzalez was charged with causing the circumstances of child endangerment. Both women are facing multiple counts of aggravated battery of a child. The daycare center terminated the two employees and is cooperating with an investigation by the Department of Children and Family Services.

Burberry has announced it will stop destroying unsellable products and will no longer use real fur, marking a significant step towards sustainability. This move aligns with the company's broader responsibility agenda aimed at driving positive change, reducing waste, and impacting one million people. Burberry has already been reusing, repairing, donating, or recycling unsellable products and plans to expand these efforts. The company is also partnering with Elvis & Kresse to transform leather offcuts into new products and has established the Burberry Material Futures Research Group to develop sustainable materials. Burberry's commitment to social and environmental responsibility is reflected in its inclusion in the Dow Jones Sustainability Index for the third consecutive year.

The enigmatic Benny Anders, a key player in the Phi Slamma Jamma era of the University of Houston's basketball team in the 1980s, was recently located in the Detroit area. Anders, known for his flamboyant style and colorful quotes, vanished from public view after a stint in the NBA and a gun-related incident. A documentary filmmaker, Chip Rives, tracked him down with the help of former teammate Eric Davis. Anders, now working in a restaurant and looking younger than his 350-pound reputation, appeared in the documentary "Phi Slama Jama," which will air later this fall. He ended the film with the statement, "A brotherly love is a very powerful thing."

President Trump has indicated he is open to offering a path to citizenship for some younger undocumented immigrants known as "dreamers" as part of an immigration deal being negotiated by Congress. Trump's support for citizenship is contingent on securing $25 billion for a border wall and $5 billion for additional border security upgrades. This potential shift signals a major change from Trump's previous hard-line stance on immigration. The White House plans to release a complete framework on Monday, which would grant immediate provisional legal status to DACA recipients and allow them to pursue full citizenship over 10 to 12 years. Lawmakers face a Feb. 8 deadline for a must-pass spending bill, and Democrats have said they will not support a long-term deal without addressing the future of the DACA program. Trump's proposal is limited to the 690,000 immigrants who were enrolled in DACA when it was terminated.
