The incident occurred near the Philippines, within China's claimed waters, and is one of the most serious between the two militaries in recent years. President-elect Donald Trump criticized China's actions on Twitter, suggesting the U.S. might not want the drone back. The U.S. and China are already at odds over Taiwan and China's militarization of the South China Sea.

World leaders and citizens from various countries reacted to Donald Trump's unexpected victory in the U.S. presidential election, expressing a mix of concern, hope, and uncertainty. In Mexico, the peso's value dropped sharply, causing anxiety among citizens. In Indonesia, some questioned the implications for their relationship with the U.S. China's state media portrayed the election as a crisis for U.S. democracy. In South Korea, Park Geun-hye's victory was seen as a potential shift in U.S.-Korea relations. In Europe, leaders from Germany, France, and the United Kingdom offered congratulations and stressed the importance of maintaining trans-Atlantic ties. Russia welcomed the opportunity to restore good relations, while Turkey called for the extradition of a U.S.-based cleric. In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu welcomed the new president, while Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas expressed hope for peace. The global financial markets showed initial volatility, with stock prices rallying and bond yields increasing, as investors grappled with the implications

A Cook County judge did not set bail for Chicago police Officer Jason Van Dyke, who was charged with first-degree murder in the shooting death of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald. The judge watched silent dashcam footage of the shooting before setting Van Dyke's bail at $1.5 million, allowing him to post $150,000 and leave Cook County Jail. The dashcam video showed Van Dyke firing 16 shots at McDonald, most after the teen had fallen. Demonstrations and protests against police brutality continued, with activists calling for the police superintendent's resignation. Van Dyke's attorney argued the video was not the full story and that the officer believed his actions were justified.

An off-duty California Highway Patrol sergeant returned over $120,000 in cash she found on a roadway in Concord, California, to its rightful owner after making a U-turn to retrieve two bank deposit bags. The sergeant, who asked not to be identified, immediately alerted authorities after finding stacks of $100 bills in the bags. She was praised by her superiors for her integrity, stating it was an opportunity to set a good example for her children. The CHP Golden Gate Division Chief highlighted her actions, noting that too often, officers do not report such finds, believing they are simply doing their job.

Hurricane Harvey has caused widespread damage and power outages along the Texas coast, with nearly 300,000 customers affected. The storm, initially a Category 4 hurricane, has been downgraded to a Category 1 but continues to dump heavy rain, leading to potential catastrophic flooding. In Rockport, one of the hardest-hit areas, the high school roof collapsed, and multiple residents were injured when a senior living complex roof caved in. Emergency services are hampered by communication issues and power outages, making initial damage assessments difficult. President Trump has commended FEMA's response and is closely monitoring the situation from Camp David. Flooding is expected to continue for days, with some areas potentially receiving up to 40 inches of rain.

Archaeologists will use ground-penetrating radar to search for King Harold II's remains in the grounds of Waltham Abbey Church, potentially rewriting history. The same team that discovered Richard III under a Leicester car park is now investigating whether Harold, the last Saxon king, survived the Battle of Hastings and lived as a hermit for 40 years. An amateur historian, Peter Burke, believes Harold may have escaped death and was later buried at Waltham Abbey. The scan, funded by Burke, aims to find Harold's body, which could change historical records. If successful, the search may require excavation due to the site's consecrated status.

Kim Kardashian West was robbed at gunpoint in a private Paris residence, with men disguised as police making off with millions of pounds worth of jewelry. The 35-year-old reality TV star was "badly shaken but physically unharmed" after being tied up in the flat's bathroom. Five armed men, still at large, stole a jewelry box worth €6 million and a ring worth €4 million, as well as mobile phones. The incident took place early Monday morning, with Kardashian West giving a statement to police before flying out of France. Her husband, Kanye West, had abruptly ended his performance at the Meadows music and arts festival in New York on Sunday night, citing a "family emergency." The robbery sparked criticism from political opponents to the Socialist government, with Nathalie Kosciusko-Morizet calling for a general emergency on security in the French capital. Paris has been a special place for the Kardashian West couple, who spent the weekend there before their 201

Boston Marathon bombing suspects Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev befriended a brain-damaged anti-U.S. government conspiracy theorist through their mother's health care aide job years before the deadly attack, according to a lawyer representing the theorist. The lawyer, Jason Rosenberg, said the brothers got to know Donald Larking, who has had brain damage since being shot in 1974, while substituting for their mother to help care for his wife. Larking shared publications with the brothers, discussing theories that the 9/11 attacks and the Sandy Hook shooting didn't happen or that the U.S. government was behind them. The Tsarnaev brothers, ethnic Chechens from Russia, took Larking to their mosque, where he converted to Islam. Rosenberg said he doesn't think Larking influenced the brothers but may have made them feel they weren't alone in their beliefs.

Cleanup crews are working inside the Air Route Control Center in Aurora after a fire, smoke, and water left it in disarray. Brian Howard, 36, of Naperville, has been charged with destroying aircraft or aircraft facilities after allegedly setting a fire in the basement of an Aurora FAA facility, cutting radar feeds, and damaging the communications system, causing a ground stop at Chicago's O'Hare and Midway international airports. Howard had intimate knowledge of the building and its radar system and had faced a transfer to Hawaii. The fire caused significant flight delays and cancellations, with airlines urging travelers to check the status of their flights. The FAA is assessing the damage and determining how long it will take to fix the facility.

United Airlines has introduced a new boarding process to reduce congestion and improve efficiency at the gate. The changes, which will be implemented across all United gates starting this week, involve reducing the number of boarding lanes from five to two. Elite and priority passengers will board through lane 1, while other passengers will use lane 2. The airline is also launching push notifications for those with the United mobile app to alert them when boarding begins, aiming to reduce the need for passengers to wait in line. This new system follows similar changes made by American and Delta Airlines in early 2017. United says customer feedback was a key factor in developing the new process, which aims to reduce waiting times and improve the overall boarding experience.

Ireland overwhelmingly approved same-sex marriage in a historic referendum, becoming the first country to legalize it via popular vote. With 62% voting "Yes," the decision marked a significant social shift in a traditionally Catholic nation that only decriminalized homosexuality two decades ago. Celebrations erupted in Dublin Castle, where results were displayed, and a senator proposed to her partner on national television. Prime Minister Enda Kenny hailed the outcome as a "social revolution," while the Catholic Church faced challenges in its dominance. The victory, supported by all political parties and celebrities, reflects a transformation in Ireland's social landscape, with youth playing a crucial role in the high turnout. International leaders, including Hillary Clinton and Ellen DeGeneres, congratulated Ireland on its achievement.

A curious two-spotted octopus in the Santa Monica Pier Aquarium in California caused a surprise when it disassembled a water recycling valve and directed a tube to release 200 gallons of seawater for about 10 hours, according to the Los Angeles Times. The aquarium's education manager, Tara Treiber, explained that octopuses are very intelligent creatures, capable of problem-solving and memory retention. Jennifer Mather, a comparative psychologist who has studied octopuses for 35 years, shared that octopuses can navigate mazes, solve problems, and exhibit personalities. They also engage in playful behaviors, such as blowing water jets at pill bottles, and use different techniques to open prey, showing adaptability and intelligence.

House Republicans have moved to impeach IRS Commissioner John Koskinen, accusing him of violating the public trust and misleading Congress. Oversight Committee Chairman Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah) introduced an impeachment resolution, arguing that Koskinen failed to comply with a congressional subpoena, destroyed backup tapes containing potentially relevant documents, and misled lawmakers about the missing emails. Democrats, including Rep. Elijah Cummings (D-Md.), criticized the move as political grandstanding and a waste of taxpayer money. The IRS maintains it has fully cooperated with all investigations.

Florida police captured a 12-foot, 120-pound Burmese python that neighbors suspect was preying on cats in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood. The snake, found hidden in waist-high brush, killed one cat and may have been responsible for the recent disappearances of several others. The python, banned in Florida since 2012, belonged to an owner with a license to keep it.

A doctor who was the target of a former colleague who opened fire at Bronx Lebanon Hospital on June 30, 2017, said he was surprised to be singled out. Dr. Kamran Ahmed, who specializes in early detection and treatment of dementia, said he had worked with the shooter, Dr. Henry Bello, but Bello had never argued with him. Bello, who was forced out in 2015 amid a sexual harassment scandal, had vowed to return to the hospital to kill Ahmed. Bello arrived at the hospital with an assault rifle hidden under his lab coat and shot Dr. Tracy Sin-Yee Tam, a family medicine doctor, among others. Tam's neighbor described her as a sweet girl who would always help others. Bello died from a self-inflicted gunshot, and detectives found the gun box in his Bronx home.

Al Qaeda claimed responsibility for the kidnapping of Warren Weinstein, a 70-year-old American aid worker in Pakistan in August, and issued demands for his release. In a video message, Al Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri stated that Weinstein would be freed if the U.S. halted airstrikes in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, and Yemen, and released all al-Qaeda and Taliban suspects worldwide. Weinstein, who worked for the U.S.-based consulting firm J.E. Austin Associates in Pakistan, was abducted by armed men from his home in Lahore. His health had been deteriorating, with a history of heart problems.

The Boy Scouts of America has revoked the charter of a Seattle-area church troop for keeping an openly gay Scoutmaster, Geoff McGrath. The organization informed leaders and parents that Rainier Beach United Methodist Church can no longer host Troop 98 and its Cub Scout pack due to McGrath's continued leadership. Boy Scouts spokesman Deron Smith stated that the church no longer adheres to BSA policies, including the ban on gay adults. The church's pastor, Rev. Monica Corsaro, plans to keep McGrath and the youth group intact, offering alternative programs. This decision is seen as the first since the BSA's policy change in 2013, which allowed gay youth but not adults.

A Seattle-based investigative reporter returned from El Salvador with claims that U.S. Secret Service agents and military specialists visited a strip club and engaged in heavy drinking and solicitation of sexual favors before President Obama’s 2011 trip to El Salvador. The subcontractor who provided security details witnessed the agents' behavior and says some took escorts back to their hotel rooms. The strip club owner confirmed a large number of U.S. agents visited his establishment over multiple nights. This incident, occurring a year before the Cartagena, Colombia, scandal, has raised questions about the agency's culture and practices. The Secret Service is investigating the claims, and lawmakers are calling for an independent review.

Just days into his role as President Trump’s national security adviser, Michael Flynn faced a crisis that led to his resignation. During a meeting with FBI agents, he was reportedly found to have been less than forthcoming about his conversations with Russia’s ambassador. This revelation, along with ongoing investigations, ultimately prompted Flynn’s resignation, raising questions about the trust and transparency within the Trump administration. Flynn’s fall from grace came amid broader concerns about potential ties between the Trump campaign and Russia, as new reports emerged suggesting that members of the campaign had contact with Russian officials. The controversy has sparked calls for a wider investigation into the Trump administration’s dealings with Russia, while also highlighting the challenges of maintaining national security in the face of political pressure and leaks.

Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro faces a confusing and potentially staged attack by a rogue police helicopter that fired on the Supreme Court and Interior Ministry. The incident, which Maduro called a "terrorist attack," involved a stolen blue police helicopter carrying an anti-government banner. Oscar Perez, identified as the pilot, claimed to represent a coalition of security and civilian officials against Maduro's "tyranny." The helicopter dropped four Israeli-made grenades and fired 15 shots, but no one was injured. Maduro vowed to capture the pilot and recover the stolen helicopter, while critics suspected the attack as a government ploy to justify repression. The event adds to Venezuela's political and economic crisis, with ongoing protests and a constitutional assembly vote looming.

A Moldovan dancer who was on the bridge of the Costa Concordia with Captain Francesco Schettino testified that she was his lover, adding to the captain's manslaughter trial. Schettino, facing charges of manslaughter and abandoning ship, risks up to 20 years in prison if convicted. The dancer, Domnica Cemortan, admitted to being romantically involved with the captain and was on the ship when it crashed into a reef off Italy in 2012, killing 32 people. She helped passengers evacuate and took the captain's laptop before they both left the ship in separate lifeboats. The trial, expected to hear evidence from about 1,000 survivors and crew, is ongoing in Grosseto, Italy.

Twenty-four-year-old Nick Stoeberl from California holds the record for the longest tongue in the world, measuring 10.1 cm (3.97 in) from the tip to the middle of the closed top lip. His record-breaking tongue earned him a spot in the new Guinness World Records 2015 book. Stoeberl discovered his unusual feature as a child when imitating Gene Simmons of KISS. He boasts about his tongue, mentioning he can lick his nose and even his elbow. The record previously belonged to British man Stephen Taylor, whose tongue measured 9.8 cm. The 60th anniversary edition of the Guinness World Records book is now available, featuring Stoeberl's record and other incredible feats.

ABC is bringing the Connor family back to television with a new revival of the iconic sitcom Roseanne. Network president Channing Dungey announced the eight-episode midseason order during the 2017 Upfronts week. The reboot, set to debut midseason, will feature the original cast including Roseanne Barr, John Goodman, Sara Gilbert, Laurie Metcalf, Michael Fishman, and Lecy Goranson, with Sarah Chalke returning in a different role. The show will explore the economic challenges faced by the working-class Connor family in 2018, continuing to address the issues that made the original series a hit. The revival is part of ABC's strategy to appeal to working-class middle America following the 2016 presidential election.

Last Week Tonight's Oliver took a serious look at Donald Trump's proposed border wall with Mexico, highlighting several issues. The cost is a major concern, with estimates ranging from $4 billion to $25 billion, far beyond Trump's initial claims. Mexico has rejected the idea of funding. Geographically, the wall faces challenges, particularly where the border is the Rio Grande, leading to previous fencing projects that obstructed US territory. Effectiveness is questionable, as many unauthorized immigrants enter legally and could easily circumvent a wall. Trump's rhetoric about the wall keeping out criminals and rapists is contradicted by data showing immigrants are less likely to commit crimes. Oliver humorously proposed buying $75 electric waffle irons for every American as a better use of funds, noting the wall would be significantly stupider than this alternative.

A Cobb County police lieutenant who was recorded on video during a traffic stop saying "we only shoot black people" is being fired, the police chief said Thursday. Dashcam video from July 2016 shows a white officer interrupting a woman and saying, "But you're not black. Remember, we only shoot black people." Cobb County Police Chief Mike Register, who has known Abbott for years, said the comments were inexcusable and not indicative of the values he wants to instill in the department. Abbott, who had been an officer for 28 years, was placed on administrative leave while the department investigated the video. Register's decision to fire Abbott has been applauded by black community leaders, who see it as a step towards addressing deeper issues of police conduct and race relations in the department.

Cypriot officials are investigating reports of a meteor that may have exploded overhead with a loud bang, causing the ground to shake. Eyewitnesses reported a blue glow and a loud noise, with some hearing the ground vibrate. Police and authorities are searching for any remnants of the object. No casualties or damage were reported, and the civil aviation authority confirmed all flights operated normally. The incident, which was visible across a wide area of the island, is being examined to determine if it was indeed a meteorite.

The mayor of Venice, Luigi Brugnaro, has vowed to investigate and punish a restaurant that charged four Japanese tourists an eye-watering €1,100 for a meal. The tourists complained to police after receiving the bill at a restaurant near St Mark's Square. Even other tourists dining nearby faced high costs, paying €350 for seafood pasta. Brugnaro promised to examine the case and take action if the complaint is confirmed. Local residents' groups are warning tourists to be cautious, as such incidents are not uncommon. The mayor has been vocal about protecting Venice's reputation, defending local businesses and urging tourists to spend more. However, critics argue his attitude towards tourists is misplaced and could harm Venice's image.

Experts from UNESCO have concluded that a wreck off the coast of Haiti is not the Santa Maria, the flagship of Christopher Columbus. The UNESCO team found that artifacts from the site, including metal fasteners, indicate a ship from a later period, not the 15th century Santa Maria. In May, underwater archaeologist Barry Clifford had claimed to have found the Santa Maria, stating that all evidence pointed to the site being the famous ship. However, the UNESCO experts say the wreck is likely from the late 17th or 18th century. The Santa Maria ran aground near Haiti in December 1492 during Columbus's first voyage to the Americas. Clifford's claim was based on the ship's size, location, and what he believed to be a 15th-century cannon. The UNESCO report suggests the Santa Maria might be buried under sediment on what used to be seabed and is now coastal marshland. The organization plans to search for the Santa Maria in various

Tiffany & Co. cites protests outside Trump Tower as a factor in slowing sales at its flagship New York store, according to its latest financial results. The company reported a 1% increase in worldwide net sales to $949 million, but noted a 2% decline in comparable store sales in the United States. While the impact on sales at its Fifth Avenue location is minimal, Tiffany remains cautious about potential future effects from ongoing protests and increased security measures in the area. The company's shares rose 8% following the release of these results, marking their highest level in 15 months.

Some U.S.-purchased weapons ended up in the hands of Islamic State fighters within two months, according to a report by Conflict Armament Research. The report, based on three years of documentation of weapons recovered from ISIS, found that one anti-tank missile sold to the U.S. Army made its way to ISIS in just 59 days. This highlights the risks of supplying weapons to unprepared or poorly trained groups, as many weapons obtained by Syrian rebel groups supported by the U.S. were diverted to ISIS. The report also details the diverse origins of ISIS' arsenal, including European Union, Russian, and Chinese weapons, with older weapons like Mauser rifles from Nazi Germany also found in their caches.

John McCone, an industrialist and engineer, took over as CIA director in 1961, tasked with restoring order after the Bay of Pigs fiasco. Despite his outsider status, he aimed to prevent future intelligence failures. After JFK’s assassination in 1963, McCone stayed in his role, testifying before the Warren Commission that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone. However, a 2013 CIA report reveals McCone and other senior officials withheld critical information, including past CIA plots to assassinate Fidel Castro, potentially involving the Mafia. This cover-up may have prevented the commission from investigating Oswald’s possible ties to Cuba. The CIA’s acknowledgment, half a century later, highlights the extent of the cover-up and its implications for the official narrative of the assassination.

Rosie O'Donnell revealed she had a secret heart attack last week, sharing the experience in a poem on her blog. She describes feeling chest pain, nausea, and a general sense of discomfort but did not call 911, citing that 50% of women experiencing heart attacks do not seek help. O'Donnell ended up having a "widow maker" heart attack, with a 99% blockage in her LAD artery, and was treated with a stent. She warns other women to recognize heart attack symptoms and to call 911 immediately.

A new book titled "Sex at Dawn" challenges the traditional view of monogamous marriage, suggesting it is a recent and unnatural development. Co-authors Neal McDonough and Cacilda Jethá argue that humans are biologically and culturally predisposed to non-monogamous relationships, drawing evidence from human physiology, primate behavior, and pre-agricultural societies. They propose that the modern emphasis on lifelong monogamy and sexual exclusivity may be detrimental to marital stability and happiness. The authors also explore the implications of these ideas for different genders and sexual orientations, suggesting that gay men may have a more realistic understanding of relationships. Overall, the book aims to foster a more open and tolerant discussion about human sexuality and its role in marriage.

A U.S. judge ruled that Nomura Holdings Inc. and Royal Bank of Scotland Group Plc may face $500 million in damages for selling defective mortgage-backed securities to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac before the 2008 financial crisis. The judge, in a 361-page opinion, said the banks misled the government-sponsored enterprises and set a damages formula that could result in the government winning about half its original $1 billion claim. The ruling may encourage other banks to settle similar claims. Nomura and RBS are expected to appeal the decision. The case is the first to reach trial out of 18 filed by the Federal Housing Finance Agency over $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

A suspect in freeway shootings in Phoenix, Arizona, has been released from jail after a judge reduced his bond to zero, allowing him to return home under electronic monitoring. Defense lawyers argue that ballistic tests cast doubt on authorities' claim that their client, Leslie Merritt Jr., was responsible for the four freeway shootings. Merritt's bond was previously set at $1 million. The judge set a May 18 court date and emphasized the importance of Merritt's presence. Merritt's lawyers have raised questions about evidence and suggested that the real culprit might still be at large.

In the chaos of Libya's conflict, thousands of prisoners vanished, their fates uncertain. Faraj, a rebel fighter, was among the thousands missing after joining the battle in March. The Transitional National Council estimates nearly 60,000 more Libyans disappeared during the six-month conflict. Many remain in underground prisons or possibly mass graves, leaving families in despair. At Abu Salim prison in Tripoli, Abdul Rauf, held for 48 days, recounted his ordeal, including daily beatings and forced use of a bottle as a latrine. His reunion with family members brought tears and joy, but the search for the missing continues. Meanwhile, Muneer Masoud Own described the gruesome slaughter of nearly 150 prisoners by Gadhafi forces as rebels approached Tripoli. The warehouse where he was held, filled with the stench of human waste, became a mass grave, with only a few survivors. The bodies, charred and unrecognizable,

Libyan leader Moammar Gaddafi, in an interview with BBC, ABC, and the Sunday Times, dismissed reports of protests and insisted he is loved by all Libyans, who would die to protect him. He denied any intention to step down and accused the West of abandoning Libya and seeking to colonize it. Gaddafi blamed al Qaeda for the protests and accused his opponents of using drugs. He also dismissed reports of aerial bombardments and chemical weapons, insisting he is not besieged in Tripoli. U.S. Ambassador to the UN Susan Rice called Gaddafi "delusional" for laughing while civilians are being killed. Meanwhile, the international community, including the U.S. and EU, imposed sanctions and called for his departure.

The U.S. has contingency plans to secure Syria's chemical weapons depots if necessary, amid President Obama's warning that any use or movement of such weapons would trigger military action. Pentagon officials are focusing on protecting or destroying stockpiles that could fall into the hands of rebel fighters or militant groups. Syria is believed to possess hundreds of tons of sarin, mustard gas, and VX nerve agents, stored in bunkers and production facilities. While the Syrian government denies using chemical weapons against its people, it has stated they could be used if foreign troops intervene. The U.S. is closely monitoring the sites but acknowledges some materials could be relocated without detection.

Demi Moore's evening started with a birthday party for a friend, but ended with a trip to the hospital. Moore, 49, hosted a party for a few girlfriends at her Beverly Hills home, but the evening took a concerning turn. Sources say Moore was acting "pretty hyper" and "acting crazy," leaving the party several times. After a dessert, Moore reportedly began convulsing and acting like she was having a seizure, leading a friend to call 911. Paramedics rushed her to a nearby hospital. Moore is now seeking treatment for anorexia and substance abuse, including Adderall use. Her publicist stated she is getting help "to treat her exhaustion and improve her overall health." Meanwhile, Ashton Kutcher, 33, has been partying in Brazil and has not commented publicly on Moore's hospitalization.

Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, and JPMorgan Chase announced a partnership on Tuesday to cut health-care costs and improve services for their U.S. employees, potentially disrupting the health-care industry. The new company, free from profit-making incentives, will initially focus on technology solutions to simplify the health-care system. Executives from each company, including Amazon's Jeff Bezos, Berkshire's Warren Buffett, and JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon, emphasized the complexity of the health-care system and their commitment to finding solutions. The move could significantly impact health-care companies, with shares of several firms falling sharply. Analysts see this as a step towards disrupting the traditional health-care system, but remain cautious about the potential for meaningful cost reductions.

Frank Taaffe, a former outspoken supporter of George Zimmerman, has testified before a grand jury that he received a call from an unknown number shortly after Zimmerman shot and killed Trayvon Martin, in which the caller made racially charged comments about Martin. Taaffe, who previously defended Zimmerman on national television, now believes Zimmerman may have racially targeted Martin and should have not followed him. Taaffe's change of heart came after the deaths of his two sons, allowing him to identify more with the Martin family. He hopes his testimony will make amends with the Martin family and clear his conscience.

The condition of Yulia Skripal, daughter of a former Russian spy, is improving rapidly, while her father remains critically ill after both were poisoned with a nerve agent in Salisbury. Doctors report Yulia, 33, is no longer in critical condition and is receiving ongoing care. Her father, Sergei Skripal, 66, is still in critical but stable condition. Salisbury District Hospital's medical director praised the staff for their care. The nerve agent, identified as Novichok, was likely smeared on Sergei Skripal's front door, with the highest concentration found there. The investigation, involving over 5,000 hours of CCTV footage and 500 witnesses, continues. Cordons have been placed around a children's play area near the Skripals' home as a precaution. Russia has responded to the expulsions of its diplomats by expelling an equal number and closing the British Council in Russia.

Utah's San Juan County has declared a state of emergency and plans to storm National Park Service barricades, reopening park areas to the public. County commissioners, citing economic concerns for local businesses, have mobilized deputies, search and rescue volunteers, and other resources. They seek financial assistance from the state and plan to explain their actions as being in the best public interest. Governor Gary Herbert is prepared to support the county's efforts. The county, which depends heavily on visitors to its National Park and Monument areas, faces legal challenges but remains determined to reopen these sites.

A Bronxville man, William McCormack, is suing Lawrence Hospital Center after undergoing what he claims was a repeat appendectomy a year after a supposed successful operation at the same facility. McCormack, 43, says he experienced severe stomach pain in early March 2013, leading to an emergency appendectomy at Adirondack Medical Center in Saranac Lake. The lawsuit alleges that during the second operation, it was discovered that his appendix was never removed and was still inside him. The hospital and surgeon, Dr. Michael Kerin, are being sued for unspecified damages. Lawrence Hospital declined to comment on the pending litigation, while the surgeon's website lists him as a former director of surgery at the hospital.

Actor George Takei faced backlash for calling Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas a "clown in blackface," a term Takei claimed was non-racist theater lingo. Fans criticized Takei, arguing his comments were insensitive and condescending. Takei's defense that blackface is part of a racist history was seen as contradictory. His suggestion that Thomas has abandoned his African American heritage due to his views on slavery and internment was met with outrage. The incident highlighted the tension between Hollywood actors and the broader public on issues of race and identity.

A Jacksonville, Florida, pediatric dentist, Dr. Howard Schneider, is facing multiple lawsuits and an ongoing investigation for alleged abuse and fraud. Four plaintiffs have filed a class-action lawsuit against Schneider, accusing him of assault, battery, false imprisonment, and intentionally inflicting severe emotional distress. The lawsuit claims Schneider’s practice was a "house of horrors" where children were physically and psychologically tortured. Parents describe incidents of children being strapped down, left with visible injuries, and subjected to unnecessary procedures. Schneider has a history of similar allegations, including two previous incidents where the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office was called to his practice. The Florida Attorney General's Office is investigating Schneider for Medicaid fraud, alleging he billed for non-medically necessary procedures and performed excessive extractions. Despite these claims, Schneider maintains his innocence and claims the allegations are false. A third psychologist has been appointed to evaluate his mental competence for the upcoming trial, which is set for November.

Samantha Ronson, Lindsay Lohan's on-again-off-again girlfriend, was arrested on suspicion of DUI in Baker, California, Monday morning. Ronson, a 33-year-old DJ, was pulled over for speeding and initially refused a breathalyzer test, leading to her arrest and a stint in the Barstow jail. However, she eventually took a breathalyzer test at the jail and was released several hours later. The District Attorney’s office will decide whether to file charges against her in a day or two. Ronson had been DJing at the Lavo nightclub in Las Vegas the night before.

The president of the Brevard Hall of Fame, John Tice, wants to move Jim Morrison's remains from his Paris gravesite to Melbourne, Florida, his birthplace. Morrison, the controversial lead singer of The Doors, died in 1971. Tice hopes to contact Paris cemetery officials and organize a fundraising drive for the potential relocation. Morrison's display at the Brevard Hall of Fame includes posters, records, and a framed copy of his will. While some in the community support the idea, others may be skeptical. Tice is still waiting to hear back from officials in Paris.

A Michigan woman, Kimberly Pappas, 25, faces trial for the murder of her newborn son, allegedly suffocating him and hiding his remains in a desk drawer at work. Pappas, who delivered the baby in a bathroom stall at CEVA Logistics on March 31, initially told coworkers she had miscarried. An autopsy revealed the child died of suffocation, having lived 20 to 30 minutes. Pappas was found mentally competent and is charged with first-degree premeditated murder, felony murder, and first-degree child abuse. Her trial is set for August 31 in Wayne County Circuit Court.

Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and senior White House adviser, appeared before Senate Intelligence Committee staff for a closed-door meeting, emphasizing his innocence in any collusion with Russia. He stated, “I did not collude, nor do I know of anyone else in the campaign who did so,” and claimed he had no improper contacts with Russia. Kushner’s statement, released before the meeting, detailed four interactions with Russian officials during the campaign and transition, but denied any improper actions. The meeting lasted nearly three hours, and Kushner did not answer reporters' questions after returning to the White House. He also addressed a Reuters report claiming he had two calls with the Russian ambassador, Sergey Kislyak, between April and November 2016, stating he had no such recollection and that his phone records did not support the claim.

Did You Hear About the Morgans?, starring Hugh Grant and Sarah Jessica Parker, is a romantic comedy that fails to deliver much in the way of laughs or engagement. Critics find the film's premise and execution to be painfully dull. The plot revolves around a Manhattan power couple, the Morgans, who are thrust into witness protection after witnessing a murder. Their relocation to Wyoming is portrayed with an awkwardness that highlights the film's shortcomings. While Grant and Parker are game, their characters' dependency on technology and general privilege are not effectively used for humor. The script, directed by Marc Lawrence, lacks the wit and depth to elevate the familiar rom-com tropes. The movie's formulaic structure and lackluster execution make it a forgettable entry in the genre.

Attorney General Jeff Sessions was authorized by the FBI to be investigated for possible perjury in 2017 over his congressional testimony that he had no contacts with Russians, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. Sessions had previously acknowledged meeting the Russian ambassador during the campaign and being aware of campaign adviser George Papadopoulos's Russian ties. The FBI investigation, which was known to Sessions, was initiated after a request from lawmakers. Andrew McCabe, then FBI deputy director, oversaw the investigation, which later led to McCabe's firing for "lack of candor." Sessions fired McCabe just before his retirement, jeopardizing his pension. Sessions's lawyer stated that he is not under investigation for perjury.
