Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton announced plans to expand funding for community health care centers and reaffirm her support for a public-option insurance plan within Obamacare, aiming to court Bernie Sanders supporters ahead of his possible endorsement. Clinton's proposal would double funding for primary care services at Federally Qualified Health Centers and offer individuals below Medicare age the option to opt into the program at age 55. This comes as Clinton and Sanders are working to find common ground, with Clinton's healthcare plan now more closely aligned with Sanders' proposals. Sanders praised Clinton's announcement, seeing it as a significant step toward universal healthcare. The Democratic Party's platform committee in Orlando failed to adopt strong language opposing the Trans-Pacific Partnership, disappointing Sanders' supporters but signaling a growing compromise between the two campaigns.

Donald Trump's planned contribution to the Republican National Convention, scheduled for Monday, has been canceled due to Tropical Storm Isaac. The real estate mogul was set to deliver a "big surprise" but will likely miss the event, according to his spokesman Michael Cohen. The convention, originally planned for four days, is now shortened to three, with full proceedings rescheduled for Tuesday. Despite the weather, Republican officials aim to frame President Obama's leadership as a failure, focusing on issues like a stagnant economy and increasing debt. However, the storm poses a risk of a perceived celebratory atmosphere amid hurricane warnings, potentially damaging the GOP's image. The shortened schedule also affects other planned appearances, including Donald Trump's, due to scheduling conflicts. Republican strategists emphasize Romney's managerial skills and his ability to connect with voters, while the Obama campaign counters with a video highlighting Romney's inconsistent positions. The Romney campaign faces challenges, including the fallout from Rep. Todd Akin's controversial comments on rape, which have drawn criticism

Archaeologists have uncovered pieces of flint tools dropped more than 4,300 years ago in a house near Marden Henge, a giant ditch and bank enclosure in Wiltshire. The rectangular building, one of the best-preserved Neolithic structures in the UK, is believed to have been used for great gatherings and feasts. The site, part of the enormous Marden Henge, also produced finds such as flint arrowheads, decorated pottery, and a Roman brooch. The henge, larger than Avebury or Stonehenge, was likely used to display wealth and power. The open day at the site will feature tours and activities, part of the national festival of archaeology.

Four people, including a prominent East Hampton builder known for constructing luxury homes for celebrities, were presumed dead after a small plane crashed off the coast of Long Island. Bernard Krupinski, 70, his wife Bonnie Krupinski, 70, their 22-year-old grandson William Maerov, and 47-year-old pilot Jon Dollard were on board the Piper PA31 Navajo aircraft when it went down about a mile offshore near Indian Wells Beach in Amagansett around 2:50 p.m. on Saturday. The plane was en route to East Hampton Airport when it encountered severe thunderstorms, leading to the crash. The cause of the crash is under investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board. The Krupinskis were well-known in the Hamptons for their philanthropy and business, with Bernard Krupinski having built homes for clients such as Martha Stewart and Billy Joel. Two bodies were recovered, but the identities of the deceased were

A 17-year-old boy who went missing after leaving his high school prom on April 14 is still unaccounted for. Orofino police launched an investigation after Kristian Perez, who had signed out of the prom at 9:32 p.m., did not return home. Perez's tuxedo jacket, one shoe, and a broken cell phone were found near the prom location. A canine tracking team suggested he may have entered a vehicle after walking west from the National Guard Armory. Police have a search warrant for his cell phone records to find any clues. The public is asked to contact the Orofino Police Department with any information.

The Accountant, starring Ben Affleck, opened at No. 1 with $24.7 million, outperforming expectations for a moderately budgeted film. Audiences gave it an A grade at CinemaScore, while critics rated it at 51% on Rotten Tomatoes. Kevin Hart's live comedy concert film, Kevin Hart: What Now?, took second place with $11.98 million, already covering its $10 million production budget. Thriller The Girl on the Train, starring Emily Blunt, placed third with $11.97 million. Max Steel, a sci-fi adventure, failed to make the top 10, earning only $2.2 million. The Birth of a Nation dropped sharply in its second weekend, earning $2.7 million.

A Wisconsin woman, Cindy Cox, has filed a lawsuit against online retailer Accessory Outlet, alleging that the company threatened her with a $250 penalty and collection actions if she attempted to complain about a non-delivered $40 iPhone case. The lawsuit, handled by Public Citizen, argues that Accessory Outlet's terms of sale are unreasonable and unenforceable, preventing customers from speaking publicly about their transactions or contacting credit card companies. Cox claims the company used threatening emails and demanded she pay the fine or face negative marks on her credit. Accessory Outlet's terms also include a clause requiring binding arbitration in New York City for any disputes, even after the 90-day period. The company has faced scrutiny for its "A+" rating from the Better Business Bureau, which has since been revoked, and other false endorsements.

Alabama Democrat Doug Jones has won the U.S. Senate election, defeating Republican Roy Moore, a former Supreme Court justice embroiled in sexual misconduct allegations. Jones's victory, seen as a blow to President Trump, narrows the Republican Senate majority to 51-49. Moore's supporters rallied behind him, while Jones benefited from national Democratic support. The race's significance is heightened amid national discussions of sexual misconduct, with Moore facing multiple allegations of inappropriate behavior with teenage girls in the 1970s. Despite these controversies, Trump and the Republican Party backed Moore, emphasizing the importance of maintaining the seat. Jones's win in a traditionally Republican state energizes the Democratic Party, which hopes to capitalize on anti-Trump sentiment for upcoming midterm elections.

McDreamy is back on the market. After 15 years of marriage, Patrick Dempsey and his wife Jillian Fink are calling it quits, according to Page Six. "It is with careful consideration and mutual respect that we have decided to end our marriage," the couple said in a statement, prioritizing their children's wellbeing. Fink, who filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences, is reportedly seeking joint custody and spousal and child support. The couple, who tied the knot in 1999 and have three children together, are asking for privacy during this sensitive time.

Pete Davidson's joke about proposing to Maggie Rogers during a "Saturday Night Live" promo video has Ariana Grande upset. The comedian's ex-fiancée, who recently ended her whirlwind romance with him, took to Twitter to express her dissatisfaction. Grande wrote, "For somebody who claims to hate relevancy u sure love clinging to it huh," referencing the engagement and breakup. The tweet comes after Davidson made a similar joke during a comedy show, suggesting he's not taking their split seriously. Grande has been keeping busy with her "Sweetener" world tour and seems to be moving on, while Davidson continues to make light of their relationship on stage.

For the first time in history, complications from preterm birth have become the leading cause of death for young children under five globally, according to new findings published in The Lancet. Preterm birth complications accounted for nearly 1.1 million deaths out of an estimated 6.3 million deaths of children under five in 2013. Direct complications from preterm births caused 965,000 deaths in the first 28 days of life, with an additional 125,000 deaths between one month and five years. The countries with the highest numbers of preterm birth deaths include India, Nigeria, Pakistan, and Democratic Republic of the Congo. The U.S. ranks 141st worst, with 28.1% of under-five deaths due to preterm birth complications. Efforts to address this issue include new research initiatives, global health partnerships, and increased funding. World Prematurity Day, observed on November 17

IKEA is recalling about 27 million chests and dressers due to the risk of tipping and crushing children if not properly anchored to the wall. Two children have died from Malm chests tipping over since 2014, and the company is aware of three additional deaths involving other models since 1989. Consumers are advised to order or pick up free wall anchoring kits from IKEA stores or their website. The Consumer Product Safety Commission is urging the furniture industry to make more stable furniture, with IKEA to lead given their significant market share. About 7 million Malm chests and 20 million other IKEA chests and dressers are part of this nationwide repair program. IKEA's U.S. commercial manager stated the company is "deeply saddened" by the deaths and hopes to prevent further tragedies.

Reality TV star Tila Tequila attended an alt-right conference in Washington DC, where she gave a Nazi salute and praised Adolf Hitler, sparking outrage. Tequila defended her actions, claiming she was just trolling and joking around. She expressed concerns about the entertainment industry being "owned by Jews" and called for "breaking down" what she sees as a "corporate" machine. Tequila also discussed her flat Earth beliefs and supported Donald Trump's presidency. Maggiano's Little Italy, the restaurant hosting the event, issued an apology after an attendee made a Sieg Heil salute, donating $10,000 to the Anti-Defamation League.

George Talley, who worked at General Motors and owned several Corvettes, thought his 1979 model stolen over three decades ago in Detroit was lost forever. However, the car was recently found in Mississippi. Michigan State Police traced the vehicle using a suspicious VIN number and confirmed Talley, now 71 and retired, is still the rightful owner. GM’s Executive Vice President, Mark Reuss, heard about the story on the radio and offered to cover the cost of bringing the still-running, 47,000-mile Corvette back to Michigan. Talley expressed relief and gratitude, saying, "It’s a lucky day. When I get that car here in that driveway, we’ll go from there."

CBS News is in the process of determining who will replace Bob Schieffer as the host of "Face the Nation." Network President David Rhodes has not yet settled on a successor, but a shortlist of candidates is being considered. Internally, Major Garrett, the network's chief White House correspondent, and Norah O'Donnell, the co-anchor of "CBS This Morning," are among the likely contenders. Outside talent being considered includes Jake Tapper from CNN and Jonathan Karl from ABC News, though both are believed to be under contract. The decision is seen as crucial for positioning the show for the 2016 presidential campaign season, as Schieffer's departure comes with increased pressure to ensure the program remains competitive.

A queen bee became trapped in the back of a 4x4, leading to a 48-hour chase by a swarm of around 20,000 bees. The bees followed the car after the queen got stuck in the boot. Park rangers and beekeepers helped contain the swarm, but the queen was inadvertently left behind. The bees continued to chase the car, covering it again the next day. The incident drew attention from passersby, causing concern about potential danger to people and the bees.

Academy Award-winning actor Tom Hanks has once again provided the White House press corps with a new espresso machine, continuing his tradition of supporting the media during their often grueling work. The machine, a replacement for the one he gifted in 2010, was found in the press area of the White House with a note encouraging the press to "Keep up the good fight for Truth, Justice, and the American Way. Especially for the Truth Part." The note, featuring an illustration of American troops, was a reminder of Hanks's longstanding support for the press, which he first demonstrated during the Bush administration when he noticed the lack of a coffee maker in the press break room.

JPMorgan Chase & Co. disclosed a $5.8 billion trading loss in its chief investment office, larger than expected, which has complicated efforts by CEO Jamie Dimon to restore investor confidence. The loss, caused by traders possibly hiding problems in a portfolio, has driven second-quarter profit down 9 percent. Dimon faces scrutiny over the loss, which has reduced the firm's market value by $39.7 billion since April 5. The bank is also under investigation for potential market manipulation and interest-rate fixing. Dimon is meeting analysts to address concerns, and the company is clawing back compensation from responsible individuals.

Celebrities and public figures have expressed their displeasure with the possibility of Donald Trump winning the presidency by threatening to leave the United States. Rev. Al Sharpton, Whoopi Goldberg, Raven-Symone, and others have stated they would move if Trump is elected. The backlash includes social media posts and public statements from actors, comedians, and other public personalities. Donald Trump's sons, Eric and Donald Jr., responded by offering to cover the airfare for those celebrities. Meanwhile, Rosie O'Donnell has been embroiled in a long-standing feud with Trump, with both exchanging insults and making personal attacks over the years, including during the 2016 presidential campaign and beyond.

Lindsay Lohan had an unexpected visit from actor and producer Ben Affleck while she was in rehab at Cliffside Malibu, RadarOnline.com reports. Affleck, a former substance abuser himself, came to check on Lohan and discuss the possibility of her starring in his upcoming film Live by Night. Lohan was reportedly excited about the potential role, though a source close to the movie maintains she is not being considered. The article also mentions a recently released Oprah Winfrey interview promo featuring Lohan discussing her addiction and the challenges of turning her life around.

A former Chicago police officer, William Whitley, 61, pleaded guilty to sex trafficking a minor after using out-of-state condoms, federal prosecutors argue. Whitley paid a 14-year-old girl for sex, and she provided intimate details about their encounters, including the specific condom brands used. This interstate commerce element, along with his use of a phone, allowed charges to be brought in federal court. Whitley also admitted to paying for sex with three other teenage girls and taking explicit photos of them. He faces at least 10 years in prison and must register as a sex offender.

Administration lawyers have proposed four options for restructuring the NSA's phone-surveillance program to the White House, according to officials. These options include letting phone companies retain the data, another government agency like the FBI or Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court take control, a non-government and non-telecommunications entity manage the data, or scrapping the program altogether. Obama is leaning towards the first two options but a decision has yet to be made.

Congress is racing against time to avoid a government shutdown, with House Speaker John Boehner pushing a plan to fund federal agencies through December 15, including conditions to delay the Affordable Care Act for a year and repeal a medical device tax. Senate Democrats, led by Majority Leader Harry Reid, are set to reject these changes, and President Obama is expected to veto such a bill. Boehner’s move to delay the health law for a year is seen as a compromise between his party’s demands and Democrats’ stance. Senate Democrats plan to table amendments to delay the health law and repeal the medical device tax, likely leading to a government shutdown if the House fails to pass a clean funding bill. The House and Senate may opt for a short-term funding measure to buy more time, or a partial government shutdown could occur, affecting over 700,000 jobs in the Washington region and causing economic losses estimated at $200 million daily.

Premier Wen Jiabao of China encouraged North Korea to allow market mechanisms to help revamp its economy, during a meeting with Jang Song-thaek, the powerful uncle of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. Jang's visit to China, following his powerful position, signals a potential easing of tensions between the two countries. Wen also recommended economic growth through improved laws and regulations, business investment, and customs service reforms. President Hu Jintao also met with Jang, showing support for North Korea's new leadership. China and North Korea have been working to intensify economic cooperation through development zones, with North Korea receiving around $300 million in non-financial direct investment from Chinese companies. Despite strained relations due to North Korea's rocket launch, China remains North Korea's most important ally and continues to support its economic reforms.

Dove has launched a new campaign featuring body wash bottles in various shapes and sizes to celebrate body diversity, but the initiative has been met with criticism and humor on social media. The campaign aims to highlight that beauty comes in all shapes and sizes, with six exclusive bottle designs representing this diversity. However, many women are unimpressed, finding the idea silly or condescending. While Dove claims the bottles are a celebration of individuality, some users have pointed out that the bottles might inadvertently reinforce the idea that there is a "best" body type. The campaign has sparked a mix of amusement and skepticism, with users sharing their existing bottles that already match their body types. Critics argue that Dove's attempt to promote body positivity through product design is incoherent and may backfire, reinforcing rather than challenging beauty norms. The article raises questions about the effectiveness of such campaigns and whether they truly empower women or simply exploit their insecurities.

Police in San Antonio, Texas, fatally shot Gilbert Flores, 41, after a 20-minute struggle during a domestic disturbance call. According to authorities, Flores, who had a criminal past, was armed and resisted arrest. Two Bexar County Sheriff deputies used non-lethal weapons unsuccessfully before shooting Flores in the driveway of a northwest San Antonio home. A passerby captured the incident on video, showing Flores with his hands up as deputies shot him. Sheriff Susan Pamerleau said the video raises concerns, but the investigation is ongoing. District Attorney Nicholas LaHood called the video troubling. Deputies Greg Vasquez and Robert Sanchez, with over 10 years of experience each, were placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation.

A St. Louis jury awarded a California woman over $70 million in damages, concluding that Johnson & Johnson's baby powder caused her ovarian cancer. This verdict follows two other St. Louis cases that resulted in $72 million and $55 million awards earlier this year. Johnson & Johnson maintains the safety of its talc products and plans to appeal the latest verdict, citing scientific evidence supporting their safety. However, plaintiffs' attorneys argue that the company ignored decades of research linking talcum powder to ovarian cancer and failed to warn consumers. The case highlights ongoing legal battles and public debate over the potential health risks associated with long-term talcum powder use.

Researchers have discovered that interbreeding between two malaria mosquito species in Mali has led to the creation of a hybrid mosquito that is resistant to insecticide-treated bed nets. This hybrid mosquito, a result of increased insecticide exposure, is considered "super" due to its ability to survive exposure to insecticides. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, provides evidence that environmental changes, such as the introduction of insecticides, can alter the evolutionary relationship between species, leading to the rapid evolution of insecticide resistance. This development highlights the urgent need for new and effective malaria vector control strategies, including the exploration of new insecticides, biological agents, and genetic manipulation of mosquitoes.

Steven Spielberg's adaptation of Roald Dahl's children's book, The BFG, struggled at the box office during the Independence Day weekend, earning only $22.3 million in North America. Despite a $140 million budget and high expectations, the film faced challenges in appealing to both children and adults. Critics praised Mark Rylance's performance as the Big Friendly Giant but noted that the movie lacked the visual spectacle and emotional depth to fully captivate audiences. The BFG's lukewarm reception can be attributed to its mixed reviews, lack of recognizable stars, and the timing of its release, which coincided with the success of Finding Dory. While the film may still perform well internationally, its domestic performance suggests that Spielberg's family-friendly fare may have lost some of its appeal.

A Washington, D.C., police officer challenged a 17-year-old girl to a dance-off in a park, surprising the teen with the request. The officer, who was responding to a fight, saw Aaliya Taylor dancing to "Watch Me (Whip/Nae Nae)" and invited her to compete. The encounter left Aaliya surprised but impressed, hugging the officer and saying, "We need more cops like you." The video of their dance-off, posted on Facebook, has been viewed over 279,000 times. Mayor Muriel Bowser praised the officer's efforts, tweeting that D.C. has "innovative ways to keep our community #saferstrongerDC."

The Toronto Zoo is investigating after a video surfaced online showing a woman jumping over a protective fence to retrieve a hat inside a tiger's pen. The woman can be seen climbing down the fence and reaching for the hat while a tiger, separated by a second fence, lunges toward her. After recovering the hat, she hops back over to a group of onlookers. The zoo's spokesperson, Jennifer Tracey, says the incident is very irresponsible and could have resulted in a serious injury. No zoo staff were present when the incident occurred, and the zoo is seeking witnesses. Violating the zoo's by-laws could result in a long-term ban or a fine of up to $2,000. The zoo is encouraging anyone with information to come forward.

A 29-year-old man from Southern California has been charged with murder in the death of a 63-year-old woman who was mauled to death by a pack of pit bulls earlier this month. Pamela Devitt, a retired office manager, was jogging in the Mojave Desert when she was attacked. She suffered approximately 150 to 200 puncture wounds and died en route to the hospital. When a deputy arrived, he found one of the dogs still mauling Devitt. The deputy fired two shots to subdue the dogs. Authorities charged the dogs' owner, Alex Donald Jackson, with murder after finding evidence that he was aware of the dogs' vicious nature and had received at least three other reports of attacks. Jackson is also facing charges related to a marijuana operation at his home. The eight dogs, six pit bulls and two mixed breeds, were taken into custody and are likely to be euthanized.

Trayvon Martin's parents and the Trayvon Martin Foundation held a ceremony at Florida Memorial University to honor their son and the work the foundation is doing to help families affected by violent crime. The university provided the foundation with a space to house artwork and memorabilia depicting Martin, including a hooded sweatshirt, symbolizing his memory. The event, which included prayers and speeches, emphasized the need for positive change and understanding. Martin's father highlighted the impact of Martin's death on the nation and the importance of addressing gun violence. The foundation's office, open to the public, serves as a reflection space and a platform for brainstorming ways to reduce crime and promote peace.

Purdue Pharma, the company behind OxyContin and currently facing over 1,000 lawsuits for its alleged role in the opioid crisis, has been awarded a patent for a new formulation of buprenorphine, a medication used to treat opioid addiction. Dr. Richard Sackler, a family member of the Purdue founders, is listed as one of the inventors. The patent describes a faster-dissolving wafer form of buprenorphine, which could potentially reduce the risk of drug diversion. Critics argue that this patent could enable the family to benefit financially from the addiction crisis they are accused of fueling. Meanwhile, the company is attempting to present itself as part of the solution by backing safer prescribing efforts and donating to law enforcement initiatives.

Toilet paper rolls are getting narrower, cardboard tubes are expanding, and the number of sheets per roll is decreasing, while the sheets themselves are becoming smaller. Despite these changes, Americans use an average of 46 sheets of toilet paper daily. Consumer Reports tested toilet paper for strength, softness, disintegration, and tearing ease, identifying two top picks. White Cloud 3-Ply Ultra, sold at Walmart, was named a Best Buy, scoring excellent in strength and softness, and very good in disintegration and tearing ease. Charmin Ultra Strong, though costly, also made the list due to its excellent tearing ease and good scores in other attributes. Other brands like Scott 1000 and Marcal Small Steps received lower ratings for softness and tearing ease. Consumers are advised not to rely solely on brand names when choosing toilet paper.

An iguana electrocuted itself on a power line, causing a power outage at The Palms Care Center in Lauderdale Lakes and forcing 20 patients to be moved to hospitals as a precaution. Battalion Chief spokesman Michael Kane reported that the facility was running on generator power but only half of the building was effectively cooled. Firefighters arranged for backup cooling and moved residents to parts of the building with working air conditioning. Electricity was restored by late Friday, and patients were set to return to the nursing home by early Saturday. The facility is licensed for 120 beds.

Hillary Clinton, viewed as a frontrunner for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016, criticized stricter voter ID laws and a Supreme Court decision that struck down a key component of the Voting Rights Act in a speech at the American Bar Association. Clinton argued that new voting obstacles often disguise a non-existent "election fraud" epidemic and threatened to undermine the Voting Rights Act's progress. She urged the Justice Department to enforce remaining voting laws and Congress to pass new legislation to replace parts of the Voting Rights Act. Clinton also hinted at future speeches on national security transparency and global issues, setting the stage for a potential presidential campaign.

Jamaican lawmakers have passed legislation decriminalizing small amounts of marijuana possession and establishing a licensing agency to regulate a lawful medical cannabis industry. The act makes possession of up to 2 ounces of marijuana a petty offense, avoiding criminal records. Cultivation of five or fewer plants is permitted. The law also allows Rastafarians to use marijuana for religious purposes for the first time. Tourists prescribed medical marijuana abroad can apply for permits to legally purchase small amounts. National Security Minister Peter Bunting emphasized that the new law does not undermine efforts to combat drug trafficking. The move aligns with global trends of easing marijuana restrictions, with other countries like Uruguay, Argentina, and some U.S. states also legalizing or decriminalizing the drug for medical or recreational use.

The Houston Rockets have been sold to local billionaire Tilman Fertitta for a record $2.2 billion, pending approval by the NBA's Board of Governors. Fertitta, a native of Galveston, Texas, expressed that the purchase is a "dream come true." The sale occurs as Houston recovers from Hurricane Harvey. Fertitta, who owns Landry's, Inc., and Golden Nugget Casinos and Hotels, plans to keep the Rockets in Houston. The transaction also includes the operation of the Toyota Center in Houston. Current owner Leslie Alexander, who bought the team for $85 million in 1993, will step down. Fertitta is the latest in a series of high-profile buyers for the Rockets franchise, following Beyoncé's rumored interest in the team through an investment group.

A woman named Michele Leonard, 47, of Somerset, Pennsylvania, was arrested twice in one day for drunken driving. After being released from state police following a crash, she offered a stranger $3 for a ride back to her vehicle. Leonard then crashed into another car and a shed, damaging both. She was arrested again for driving under the influence. Charges are pending once blood-alcohol test results are available. The shed owner, Stanley Fisher, had costly tools destroyed and will need to build a new shed, incurring additional expenses.

Democrats face a wage stagnation issue during the Obama presidency, which could be a significant vulnerability for their candidates, especially Hillary Clinton. Median household income in 2014 was $1,656 lower than in 2009, and it took until this year for it to surpass its June 2009 level. While Republicans criticize Obama for failing to boost incomes, they struggle to articulate specific solutions without alienating their base. Only Rick Santorum supports a minimum wage increase, while most candidates oppose it. The minimum wage debate highlights the Republicans' challenge in addressing wage growth without proposing policies that might not resonate with voters.

Thousands of Native Americans protested the Washington Redskins' name outside TCF Bank Stadium in Minneapolis before the team's game against the Minnesota Vikings. Organizers estimated the protest, which included chants and banners, as the largest ever against the team's name, with up to 5,000 participants. Despite the large turnout, Redskins fans, some of whom initially wore the team's gear, mostly avoided confrontation. The protest highlighted the ongoing debate over the name's offensive nature, with Native American leaders and activists calling for a change, while team owner Daniel Snyder maintains it honors Native Americans. The University of Minnesota, which hosts the game, requested the team avoid using the name and logo inside the stadium, reflecting the institution's commitment to diversity and Native American respect.

I've never heard anything as ridiculous as Phil Schiller's explanation for removing the headphone jack from the iPhone 7 at an Apple keynote since 1998. Schiller claimed it was "courage" to move on and do something better, but that definition of courage is misplaced. Eradicating the most successful, widespread, and best-sounding audio standard in favor of a proprietary system is more hubris or greed than courage. Users can't charge and use headphones simultaneously, and there's no technological justification for it. Wired audio almost always sounds better than wireless, yet Apple's AirPods offer inferior alternatives. Schiller's claim about space inside the iPhone is also questionable, as the headphone jack's removal doesn't significantly impact space. Apple is building a higher wall around its ecosystem, making it harder for users to connect third-party accessories. That's not courage, but it may provoke pure rage.

A San Francisco judge has ordered Wells Fargo to pay $203 million to its California customers due to the bank's manipulation of debit transactions to maximize overdraft fees. The judge's 90-page opinion accused Wells Fargo of profiteering by processing transactions from highest to lowest amount, which depleted accounts faster and increased the number of overdrafts. This practice is also being challenged in a separate class-action lawsuit in Florida, which includes similar claims against 30 other lending institutions. Wells Fargo plans to appeal the decision. The ruling could have implications for the Florida case, as the judge's findings may influence the outcome. New federal regulations will require banks to obtain customers' permission for overdraft protection, which could impact how such practices are handled in the future.

President Donald Trump criticized the FBI before attending a graduation ceremony at the FBI's National Academy, calling the bureau's handling of the Hillary Clinton email investigation "really disgraceful" and stating, "It's a shame what's happened" with the FBI. Trump said, "We're going to rebuild the FBI," and praised law enforcement, declaring, "I am more loyal than anyone else could be" to police. He warned MS-13 gang members, "We will find you; we will arrest you; we will jail you; we will throw you the hell out of the country." Trump also questioned rising violence in Chicago, saying, "What the hell is going on in Chicago? What the hell is happening there?" His comments followed a barrage of criticism directed at the FBI, including a tweet that the bureau's reputation was "in Tatters — worst in History!" Trump's remarks came as special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into possible coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia continued to yield indict

President-elect Donald Trump met with Martin Luther King III, son of the late civil rights leader, at Trump Tower in New York on January 16, 2017. The meeting was seen as a gesture towards unity and inclusivity, coming days after Trump had criticized civil rights leader John Lewis on Twitter.

A woman named Avital was told she couldn't board a Southwest flight from Las Vegas to New York because her cleavage was "inappropriate." Despite being instructed to cover up, she boarded the plane in a cotton dress, flannel shirt, and scarf, and made it to her destination without incident. Southwest offered Avital an apology and a refund. A man on the same flight, wearing a shirt with a condom, was not stopped. This incident highlights Southwest's inconsistent enforcement of its dress code and the discomfort it causes passengers.

Rapper Andre Johnson, who performs under the stage name Christ Bearer with the Wu-Tang affiliated group Northstar, spoke to E! News about cutting off his own penis and jumping from a second-story balcony in April. Johnson, 41, says he was using drugs and had a drug-induced delirium when he made the decision. He believes sex is for mortals, while he considers himself a god, stating that the incident was a blessing. Johnson says doctors did not reattach his penis and that he still experiences sexual arousal. He also mentioned that he recently welcomed a new daughter into his life and expressed optimism about his future, including plans to pursue stand-up comedy.

Saturn's Phoebe ring, previously thought to be over 200 times the radius of the planet, has been found to be even larger, extending from about 3.75 million to 10.1 million miles from Saturn. This ring, composed mostly of tiny particles, challenges the conventional understanding that rings beyond a certain distance would collapse and form new moons. The ring's immense size and composition could provide insights into the evolution of Saturn's ring system and the history of the solar system. The discovery, made using data from NASA's WISE spacecraft, suggests that material from Saturn's distant moon Phoebe continually coats Saturn's moon Iapetus, explaining its two-toned appearance. This finding hints at the possibility of similar rings around other planets and even around stars, potentially revealing new insights into the formation and dynamics of planetary systems.

In an election year marked by unpredictability, the Tea Party has emerged as a powerful force, reshaping political debates and toppling established lawmakers. Yet, a Washington Post survey of hundreds of local Tea Party groups reveals a disparate and loosely organized network, with many groups showing little engagement in political campaigning or candidate support. Most groups lack formal platforms, financial resources, and clear goals, suggesting the movement's breadth might be overstated. Despite their diverse views, these groups share a common frustration with government and a desire for reform, but their lack of cohesion poses a challenge for both political opponents and potential allies.

McDonald's faced a unique challenge in Bolivia, where the fast-food giant struggled to gain acceptance despite its global dominance. For over a decade, McDonald's attempted to establish itself in Bolivia but consistently lost money. In 2002, the company was forced to close all eight of its Bolivian restaurants, making Bolivia the only country in the Americas without a McDonald's. The documentary "Why Did McDonald's Bolivia Go Bankrupt?" explores the reasons behind this failure. Interviews with cooks, sociologists, nutritionists, and educators reveal that Bolivians reject the concept of 'fast food,' valuing meals prepared with love, dedication, and proper hygiene. This cultural preference for traditional, home-cooked meals over processed fast food led to the closure of McDonald's in Bolivia, highlighting a unique rejection of the brand's global presence.

Since 1955, the Tully monster, a mysterious creature discovered in Illinois, has puzzled paleontologists due to its unusual features, resembling traits of worms, mollusks, arthropods, and even fish. Recently, a team from Yale University and the Field Museum, using advanced imaging techniques from Argonne National Laboratory, has resolved the mystery, classifying the Tully monster as a vertebrate closely related to lampreys. The key to this discovery was identifying the creature's notochord, a primitive backbone, which was previously mistaken for a gut. This finding not only resolves the long-standing debate but also places the Tully monster on the evolutionary lineage leading to lampreys, a significant breakthrough in understanding the evolution of vertebrates.

At the University of California's Board of Regents meeting, a 32% increase in undergraduate fees was approved, leading to student protests outside the meeting. Students, including Isaac Miller and Irene Van from Berkeley, expressed concerns about the impact on illegal immigrant and minority students. The fee hike, equivalent to $2,500, will be implemented in two steps, bringing the total cost of a UC education to about $10,300, plus additional campus-based charges. Amid loud protests, only one student regent voted against the fee increase. Students from various campuses rallied at UCLA, with some occupying a classroom building. UCLA officials declared the building closed, but no arrests were made.

A report from the Australian Crime Commission finds that doping is widespread in Australian sports, facilitated by sports scientists, high-performance coaches, and sports staff. The commission, which did not name specific individuals, says that peptides and hormones are being used by professional athletes across various sports disciplines, with some instances involving organized-crime groups. The Australian Football League and the National Rugby League are under the most scrutiny. The report draws parallels to the Lance Armstrong case, stating that the Australian threat is current, crosses sporting codes, and is evolving.

Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi, the reality star from Jersey Shore, is reportedly pregnant with her first child, despite her earlier denials. Sources say she is three months along, and the father is her boyfriend, Jionni LaValle. This pregnancy could complicate her career, as Snooki has built her public persona around her wild antics and frequent alcohol consumption. However, pregnancy may also present an opportunity for Snooki to rebrand herself, as she has reportedly brokered a deal to announce her pregnancy on the cover of Us Weekly. Her upcoming spinoff series with Jenni "JWoww" Farley may face delays due to this unexpected development. Snooki has admitted to frequently overindulging in alcohol, which could pose challenges for her new role as a mother.

The inspector general for the intelligence community informed Congress that some of Hillary Clinton’s emails from her private server contained classified information, though it was not marked as such. A review of 40 emails found four that contained classified information, which should have been marked and transmitted via a secure network. Clinton has criticized reports, stating she has released 500 pages of emails and will answer questions from a congressional panel. She maintains she did not send any classified material and was unaware of potentially compromising classified information. The State Department Freedom of Information Act officials stated there are potentially hundreds of classified emails within the approximately 30,000 provided by Clinton. The Justice Department is considering whether to launch a criminal investigation into Clinton’s possible mishandling of classified emails, though there has not yet been a decision.

Pete Kostelnick, a 29-year-old from Nebraska, broke the record for running across the United States, completing the 3,100-mile journey from San Francisco to New York City in 42 days, 6 hours, and 34 minutes. Kostelnick, who had previously won the Badwater Ultramarathon twice, averaged 72 miles per day and was accompanied by a small group of supporters during his run. Upon reaching City Hall, Kostelnick expressed his desire for a beer and time with his wife. Frank Giannino, the previous record holder, was present to congratulate Kostelnick, calling it a testament to the spirit of running. Kostelnick's rigorous training regimen and meticulous planning ensured he maintained his pace and completed the historic feat.

Paralyzed rats have regained some bladder control after a new treatment that encourages severed nerves to grow, researchers report. Scientists from Case Western Reserve University and the Cleveland Clinic successfully restored urinary function in rats with severe spinal cord injuries by transplanting healthy nerve bundles and using a combination of enzymes and growth factors to overcome scar tissue. The rats could now control their bladder function to a degree not seen before in such severely injured animals. This breakthrough could potentially lead to treatments for humans with spinal cord injuries, offering hope for improved quality of life and reduced risk of kidney damage. However, further research is needed before human trials can be considered.

A Shorewood man, Robert D. Monroe, has been charged with over a dozen counts of illegal voting, accused of casting multiple ballots in four elections between 2011 and 2012. Monroe, a health insurance executive, used addresses in Shorewood, Milwaukee, and Indiana to vote, and even cast ballots in the names of his son and his girlfriend's son. He voted illegally at least a dozen times, including in the 2012 gubernatorial recall election and the 2012 presidential election, where he cast ballots both in person and using a rental car to vote in Indiana. The investigation, which began in Waukesha County, uncovered DNA evidence linking Monroe to the illegal votes and included text messages urging family members to vote. Monroe faces 13 felony charges, each carrying a maximum penalty of up to 18 months in prison. His initial court appearance is scheduled for July 17.

For the first time since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) will allow passengers to carry small knives, golf clubs, and other sporting equipment onto planes. The policy change, effective April 25, aims to align U.S. regulations with international standards and reduce the time passengers spend in security lines. However, the TSA will still prohibit knives with locking blades or molded handles, as well as box cutters and razor blades, due to the emotional sensitivity surrounding these items. The move has been criticized by flight attendants, who argue that small knives and sporting equipment pose real threats to passengers and flight attendants in the cabin. The TSA maintains that these changes will help focus security efforts on more significant threats, such as small, non-metallic bombs.

Florence's mayor, Dario Nardella, is using high-pressure hoses to discourage tourists from eating on church steps, aiming to maintain decorum in the historic city. The first steps to be treated are those of the Basilica of Santa Croce and Chiesa di Santo Spirito. Nardella claims the move is not anti-tourism but aims to keep visitors respectful of the city's cultural heritage. The measure is part of a broader campaign by Nardella to address issues caused by mass tourism, including restrictions on new fast-food outlets and the promotion of lesser-known areas. While some locals criticize the approach as elitist, Nardella insists it is a more elegant solution than fines.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's defiant speech on Sunday, delivered to the newly elected People's Assembly in Damascus, did little to advance the prospects of a political transition or dialogue with the opposition. Al-Assad's speech, which came after days of hints that he might be ready to negotiate, instead reinforced his stance that the uprising against him is driven by "murderous criminals" and "terrorists" with foreign backing. This stance has dashed hopes for a diplomatic solution and may prompt the United States and its allies to consider more aggressive intervention. The speech was met with skepticism from both pro-opposition and pro-government Syrians, who see no sign of peace or change. The United Nations estimates that over 60,000 people have died in the civil war, which has now entered its 21st month. Despite the rhetoric, neither side appears close to achieving a military victory, and the conflict shows no signs of abating.

On Wednesday, the Kansas House of Representatives passed House Bill No. 2453, a controversial "religious freedom" bill that allows businesses and government employees to deny service to same-sex couples based on religious beliefs. The bill, approved by a vote of 72 to 49, could have wide-ranging impacts, potentially allowing owners of public accommodations to refuse service to gay couples. Critics argue the bill could be used to legalize discrimination, with opponents pointing to similar cases in other states where businesses were forced to serve same-sex couples. The bill also authorizes state employees to refuse service, raising concerns about potential violations of civil rights. Despite Republican control of the statehouse and governorship, the bill faces challenges in the Senate, where a majority of Republicans do not support it. Legislative leaders have indicated the bill will be reworked to address concerns about discrimination.

A 68-year-old grandfather from England died after doctors accidentally pumped cleaning detergent into his lungs during a saline flush procedure at Salford Royal Hospital in 2017. The hospital's internal investigation found multiple factors contributed to the mistake, including an un-stocked equipment trolley, distractions, lack of clear communication, and inadequate staff training. The patient's family is suing the hospital and plans to hold a hearing in February 2019. The hospital apologized and implemented new measures to prevent similar incidents.

An 15-month-old girl named Sania Cunningham was killed by a stray bullet inside her home in Irvington, New Jersey, as she played with her parents on Saturday afternoon. The chaotic gun battle left multiple bullet holes in the neighborhood, including in the family's apartment, a nearby SUV, and a neighbor’s air conditioner. Neighbors described the area as frequently plagued by violence, with drug activity and gang involvement. The Essex County Prosecutor's Office is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. Minister Thomas Ellis arrived to comfort residents and urged the shooter to turn themselves in. The incident has drawn attention to the ongoing safety concerns in the neighborhood.

Iranian hackers infiltrated a small New York dam in 2013, according to The Wall Street Journal. The breach, which did not allow the hackers to take control of the system, raised concerns that reached the White House. This incident occurred amid a wave of Iranian hacks on U.S. banks and just three years after the Stuxnet worm damaged Iranian nuclear infrastructure. The intrusion fits a pattern of hackers from Russia, Iran, and China testing U.S. critical infrastructure networks for vulnerabilities. National Security Agency Director Michael Rogers warned that China and "one or two" other countries could potentially disrupt portions of U.S. infrastructure with a cyberattack. In 2015, the Department of Homeland Security responded to 295 hacking incidents related to industrial controls, up from 245 the year before. Critics hail "War for the Planet of the Apes" as a powerful and emotionally resonant conclusion to the critically acclaimed "Planet of the Apes" franchise, offering a sophisticated and morally complex narrative that surpasses its predecessors. Directed by Matt Reeves and co-written with Mark Bomback, the film seamlessly blends homage to the original series with innovative storytelling and character development. Andy Serkis reprises his role as Caesar, the intelligent and compassionate chimp leader, who faces a brutal conflict with a human military led by the ruthless Colonel (Woody Harrelson). The film's intense action sequences and poignant moments, such as Caesar's emotional journey and the plight of the captured apes, create a profound and thought-provoking experience. While some critics find the Colonel's character a bit one-dimensional, the overall film is praised for its intelligent script, compelling performances, and its unflinching exploration of themes such as war, morality, and the treatment of non-human species.

People with motion sickness are experiencing discomfort and even nausea due to the dynamic and aggressive animations in Apple's iOS 7 update. Features like screen zooms, parallax effects, and sliding transitions can trigger symptoms in those with vestibular disorders, causing headaches and dizziness. The introduction of these effects has made some iOS users with motion sickness feel as if the entire screen is moving, leading to feelings of nausea. While Apple provides a "Reduce Motion" option, it only disables the parallax effect and does not address other triggers. Developers and users are calling for more comprehensive options to disable these animations, as they can be particularly distressing for those with vestibular dysfunction.

Former teen tennis star Jennifer Capriati was rushed to the hospital early this morning after paramedics responded to a call for a possible overdose at a hotel in Riviera Beach, FL. Her father told TMZ she is recovering well. Capriati, who won 14 career titles including three Grand Slams and a gold medal at the 1992 Olympics, has struggled with drug issues in the past.

At least 16 Americans have been affected by "incidents" targeting U.S. staff and officials in Cuba, according to U.S. officials. The situation, described as unprecedented, has caused a variety of physical symptoms, and the U.S. government is working to provide the best medical attention possible. The source of the incidents remains unknown, and no device or piece of equipment has been discovered. The Cuban government denies any involvement and is cooperating with the ongoing U.S. investigation, but the two governments are not working together on the matter. The State Department has not ruled out the possibility of a covert device or other unknown factors. The incidents began in late December 2016, and some U.S. officials believe the attacks may have been carried out using a sonic device. Medical records reviewed by CBS News indicate that some diplomats were diagnosed with conditions as serious as mild traumatic brain injury. In the fall of 1981, Linda Hooper, a teacher at Brown Elementary School in Lubbock, Texas, was warned about a "holy terror" student named Cruz Riojas. Hooper, a veteran teacher, initially planned to quit if assigned Cruz, but instead took him in, seeing his potential beyond his disruptive behavior. Cruz's home life was fraught with physical abuse, leading him to run 7.5 miles to the Hoopers' home for safety. As Cruz grew closer to the Hoopers, he began working odd jobs and improving academically. At 12, Cruz moved in with the Hoopers permanently after a fight with his stepfather. By his 30th birthday, Cruz asked to be legally adopted, which the Hoopers agreed to. The adoption in 1998 made Cruz Hooper, and he and his wife, Anel, now live in San Antonio with their two children. Actress Melissa Gilbert, known for her role in "Little House on the Prairie," is facing a significant tax debt of over $360,000. The Internal Revenue Service accused her of failing to pay federal income taxes from 2011 to 2013. Gilbert attributed the debt to a stalled acting career, the economy, and divorce. She and her husband, actor Timothy Busfield, are moving to a log house in Livingston County, Michigan. Gilbert has set up an installment plan to pay off the debt. The couple recently signed a new cookbook, "My Prairie Cookbook," and continues to pursue acting and directing careers.

A North Carolina woman's 911 call led to the arrest of Dylann Roof, the alleged gunman responsible for killing nine people in a Charleston, South Carolina, church. Debbie Dills, a bookkeeper, recognized Roof from surveillance footage and alerted authorities, resulting in his apprehension during a traffic stop in Shelby, North Carolina. Roof cooperated with the officer who stopped him. His arrest comes after a manhunt and the release of surveillance images and car details. Roof's Facebook profile showed racist views and symbols, and he had recent run-ins with the law.

U.S. Antarctic Program researcher Dr. Gordon Hamilton, 50, died in a snowmobile accident in the Shear Zone, a dangerous ice region near McMurdo Station. Hamilton's team was working to map crevasses for safe passage of supply vehicles. Despite safety training and support from experienced mountaineers, Hamilton fell 100 feet into a crevasse. The NSF is investigating the accident, which highlights the risks of polar research.

A Pembroke Pines police officer was allegedly denied service at an Arby's restaurant because she is a cop, sparking controversy and calls for a national boycott. The incident reportedly occurred when a manager told the officer, "He doesn't want to serve you because you are a police officer," after the officer tried to order a meal. Despite Arby's CEO apologizing and stating the behavior was unacceptable, the police union is demanding firings and a public apology. Protesters, including police officers' wives, staged a demonstration outside the restaurant, expressing disappointment and calling the behavior disrespectful. The Pembroke Pines Police Department chief called the incident "offensive and appalled," emphasizing the importance of respect for law enforcement.

Jeffrey Zaslow, a best-selling author known for works such as "The Last Lecture" and "Gabby: A Story of Courage and Hope," was tragically killed in a car accident in northern Michigan. A Wall Street Journal reporter and former advice columnist, Zaslow authored books that inspired millions, including "The Girls from Ames" and "Highest Duty." His latest, "The Magic Room," chronicled stories from a Michigan bridal store. Zaslow was married to Fox 2 Detroit news anchor Sherry Margolis and had three daughters. His work was celebrated for its depth and emotional resonance, touching on themes of love, loss, and personal growth.

A woman from Commack claims her 29-year-old son died in a drunken driving crash because police did not arrest him earlier that night for driving while intoxicated, according to a federal wrongful death lawsuit filed in federal court. Kathi Fedden is seeking $30 million in damages. The lawsuit alleges that when Peter Fedden was in a car crash, officers drove him home even though he was "severely intoxicated" and visibly injured. After being dropped off, Fedden, who owned a local deli frequented by police, drove off and crashed into a Hauppauge marketing firm, causing $100,000 in damage. The lawsuit also names Ruby Tuesday's restaurant, where Fedden was drinking, as responsible for his intoxication, alleging the bartender served him too much alcohol.

Ken Mehlman, former chairman of the Republican National Committee and Bush's 2004 campaign manager, has come out as gay. His announcement, made in an interview with Marc Ambinder, is significant as Mehlman played a key role in anti-gay initiatives during his tenure. Despite his past, Mehlman plans to advocate for gay rights within the GOP, emphasizing that his political identity is not defined by any single issue. His coming out may normalize homosexuality within the party and influence public opinion. Reactions from colleagues like RNC Chairman Michael Steele and former chairman Ed Gillespie reflect the evolving attitudes among Republicans. Mehlman's advocacy for gay marriage could potentially bridge the gap between the party and the LGBTQ+ community.

In one week, the burning of Korans by U.S. troops in Afghanistan triggered a series of events that have raised doubts about the reliability of Afghan security forces to protect their Western partners. The killing of two high-ranking NATO officers by an Afghan security official, followed by the decision to recall NATO advisers from Afghan ministries, has highlighted potential weaknesses in the U.S. strategy to transition from combat to advisory roles. Former U.S. officials and analysts warn that an erosion of trust could severely impact the endgame of the war. The incident has led to ongoing protests and violence, with 25 Afghan lives lost. While U.S. officials remain committed to a partnership with Afghanistan, the temporary withdrawal of advisers may hinder cooperation and make U.S. troops more vulnerable to attacks. The U.S. force is expected to reduce from 100,000 troops to about 68,000 by the summer, with all NATO combat troops withdrawing by 2014.

A major draft federal report warns that climate change is already affecting U.S. residents through heat waves, droughts, and other changes, with temperatures projected to rise by 2-4 degrees Fahrenheit in most areas in the coming decades. The report, developed by a federal advisory panel, concludes that there is "unambiguous evidence" that Earth is warming, and climate change over the past 50 years is primarily driven by human activity, especially from burning fossil fuels. It highlights the impacts of climate change across the U.S., including water supplies stressed by declining runoff, increased risk of heat stress and waterborne disease, and infrastructure harmed by sea-level rise, storm surges, and heavy downpours. Environmentalists are calling for more aggressive steps to reduce emissions, while some Republicans dispute the conclusion that human activities are the primary driver of climate change. The Roswell Park Cancer Institute and Infor have signed agreements with Cuban counterparts to advance a lung cancer vaccine and introduce healthcare software, respectively, marking steps towards normalizing U.S.-Cuba relations. The vaccine, known as Cimavax, has shown promise in extending survival for lung cancer patients in Cuba, where it is provided free of charge. The deal allows Roswell Park to conduct clinical trials in the U.S., potentially bringing the vaccine to a broader market. Cuban researchers have developed other innovative treatments, constrained by economic sanctions, and now seek to collaborate more openly with U.S. partners to enhance medical advancements.

Russian President Vladimir Putin showcased his hockey skills at the All-Russia Festival of Night Hockey League in Sochi, wearing jersey number 11. Despite missing several goals, he eventually scored, much to the delight of the crowd. This event, part of Putin's tradition of macho publicity stunts, included playing alongside retired Soviet hockey legends. Putin, known for his various publicity stunts, has previously shot a whale, hugged a polar bear, and scuba-dived for fake ancient Greek vases. His latest hockey game, while successful, highlights his penchant for such events to boost his image and engage with the public.

Snap Inc. is now selling its video-recording sunglasses, Spectacles, directly online for $129.99 in the U.S. on Spectacles.com. Previously, the glasses were available through surprise-location vending machines and a pop-up store in Manhattan. With the online launch, Snap aims to make Spectacles more accessible and generate revenue, as the previous limited release strategy did not significantly contribute to the company's income. Users can also purchase charging cases and cords for an additional fee. The move to open online sales reflects Snap's strategy to integrate Spectacles more deeply into its business model and potentially boost investor confidence ahead of its upcoming IPO.

Facebook is set to launch a music service next month, partnering with Spotify, MOG, and Rdio, according to sources. The service will allow users to listen to music directly from within Facebook.com, integrating with existing music services. Unlike Apple, Google, and Amazon, which host music content on their servers, Facebook plans to rely on partners to provide the content, positioning itself as a platform for media content similar to its app and game platforms. The launch is expected at Facebook's f8 developer conference on September 22. While the initial focus is on music, there are whispers that the platform could expand to include other media content, such as movies. However, Facebook has not confirmed any plans beyond the music service announcement.

Russian hackers breached the White House's unclassified computer system, gaining access to sensitive information about President Obama's schedule, according to U.S. officials. The intrusion was linked to the same sophisticated cyberattack that compromised the State Department's network. The hackers likely entered the White House system through the State Department, using a phishing email to infect a White House computer with malware. The White House unclassified system was shut down for several days to address the breach, but officials stated that no classified information was compromised. The incident highlights the ongoing threat of Russian cyberattacks and the difficulty in fully eradicating hackers from government networks.

The solar-powered MS Turanor PlanetSolar completes an 115-foot, 37,294-mile journey around the world, pulling into Monaco's Hercule Harbor after 584 days. Swiss engineer Raphael Domjan and German entrepreneur Immo Stroeher's project proves that solar energy can power sea travel, aiming to promote sustainable alternatives to fossil fuels and wind. The catamaran, designed by Craig Loomes, uses 38,000 solar cells to charge six blocks of lithium-ion batteries. After the mission, the team considers renting or selling the vessel for scientific, commercial, or luxury uses.

President Donald Trump embarks on his first foreign trip as commander-in-chief, a nine-day journey to Saudi Arabia, Israel, Belgium, Italy, and the Vatican, aimed at projecting American power, rebuilding relationships, and addressing domestic controversies. The itinerary includes visits to the birthplace of Islam, the Jewish homeland, and the Vatican, with a focus on religious symbolism and unity. Trump seeks to strengthen alliances and assert American leadership, despite initial reluctance. His visit to Saudi Arabia will involve discussions on security and economic cooperation, while in Israel, he will meet with leaders and reaffirm the U.S.-Israel alliance. The Vatican visit, despite past tensions, aims for diplomatic engagement and common ground. In Belgium, Trump will address NATO and reaffirm America’s commitment. The trip also sees First Lady Melania Trump participating in various events, highlighting the family’s involvement.

When Jeb Bush's presidential campaign began to face challenges, many of his supporters pointed to Dallas as a pivotal moment. Bush's team held regular staff meetings at a Hyatt hotel inside a Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport terminal, aiming for a central and cost-effective location for a team spread across multiple cities. However, this setup quickly became awkward, with donors and other Republicans finding it ungainly for a campaign-in-waiting. Internal disputes over money and resource allocation between Bush's allied super PAC and his official campaign also emerged. Bush's candidacy, which initially relied on a fast start to scare off rivals, has faced a series of miscalculations, leading to diminished standing in polls. His campaign's ability to raise large sums of money fueled inflated expectations, but an allied super PAC may fall short of predictions. Bush's middle-of-the-road positions on issues like immigration and education have been seen as out of step with the Republican base. His campaign has been criticized for its approach and for

European counter-terror raids led to the arrest of 15 suspected jihadis in Belgium and France, foiling an alleged plot to kill police officers. Two suspects were shot dead in Verviers, near the German border, while nine were arrested in Molenbeek, two in Brussels, one in Berchem, and two in France. The operation aimed to dismantle a terror cell with intentions to attack police stations and officers. Belgian authorities closed several Jewish schools amid heightened security concerns, with cities across the country on high alert. European intelligence agencies identified up to 20 sleeper cells of between 120 to 180 people potentially ready to strike in France, Germany, Belgium, and the Netherlands. The threat is seen as evolving, with thousands of independent actors or semi-independent terrorist suspects making it difficult for law enforcement to prevent every attack.

At least 19 people have died and dozens remain missing after a hydropower dam under construction in southeastern Laos collapsed, releasing a massive volume of water that has displaced over 6,000 people. Rescue efforts are underway as government officials and aid organizations respond to the disaster. The Xepian-Xe Nam Noy dam, a joint venture project involving South Korean and Thai companies, was still under construction when the collapse occurred. The accident has raised concerns about the safety and environmental impact of hydropower projects in Laos, a country known for its ambitious dam-building plans.

This year's Golden Globe nominations included some surprising snubs and surprises, particularly on the TV side. NBC’s The Good Place finally received a best comedy series nomination, while Sacha Baron Cohen and Showtime’s Bodyguard unexpectedly landed nods. However, Hulu’s The Handmaid’s Tale and HBO’s Westworld were notably omitted from the best drama series category, despite strong performances from stars like Elisabeth Moss and Yvonne Strahovski. Other notable snubs include Sterling K. Brown, John Krasinski, and Liev Schreiber for their roles in This Is Us, and Jodie Comer for her performance in Killing Eve. The H.F.P.A. also overlooked Ethan Hawke for his role in First Reformed and Patrick Melrose for its second season. In the movies, Sam Elliott’s performance in A Star Is Born was notably absent from the supporting actor category, while Mary Poppins Returns missed a nomination for best original song. A 29-year-old Baltimore County police officer was killed during a confrontation with a 16-year-old suspect in Perry Hall, Maryland, on May 21, 2018. The officer, identified as Amy Caprio, was responding to a call about a suspicious vehicle when she encountered the suspect, who was later arrested. The incident prompted a large manhunt and left several schools on alert. Officer Caprio, a four-year veteran, was a dedicated officer who had helped solve a significant package theft case. Her death was mourned by the community and police department.

President Donald Trump held a lengthy and combative press conference on Thursday, defending his administration and its accomplishments while repeatedly criticizing the media as "fake news." Trump dismissed the notion that his White House is in chaos, asserting it is "running like a fine-tuned machine." He attacked reports about his campaign’s alleged contacts with Russian officials, calling them "fake news" and suggesting they were fabricated to explain Clinton’s loss. The president also downplayed the significance of his Electoral College victory, claiming it was the largest since Ronald Reagan, despite evidence to the contrary. Throughout the session, Trump engaged in tense exchanges with reporters, often interrupting and dismissing their questions, and maintained that the public does not trust the media. His performance was seen as a bid to regain control and re-energize his supporters, though it also highlighted ongoing challenges and controversies within his administration.

Scientists have uncovered how animals link the change in seasons to their fertility, revealing a link between breeding season and the hormone melatonin produced in the pineal gland during long winter nights. In sheep, melatonin controls the production of two different types of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) within a specific region of the pituitary gland, away from the area where sex hormones are made. In winter, VEGF forms that prevent blood vessel growth are produced, while in summer, forms that stimulate vessel growth are made. This allows VEGF to act as a messenger to control sex hormone-producing cells and fertility. The findings could help farmers adjust the timing of the lambing season and have wider implications for understanding seasonal changes in human health and disease.

JC Penney's social media account posted a series of confusing and grammatically incorrect tweets, sparking speculation about who might be behind the "drunk tweeting." Sample tweets included "Who kkmew theis was ghiong tob e a baweball ghamle. #lowsscorinh 5_0" and "Toughdown Seadawks!! Is sSeattle going toa runaway wit h this????" The tweets drew humorous responses from users, with some suggesting the tweets were written by an intoxicated intern or even that the account was hacked. JC Penney later apologized with a tweet about the Super Bowl, which many saw as a cover-up. The incident comes after reports of the company planning to raise prices temporarily before lowering them again for Valentine's Day, further highlighting JC Penney's struggles in the retail market.

The Bank of England has confirmed Jane Austen as the new face of the £10 note, reversing a previous plan that sparked public outrage by excluding women from British currency. Austen, known for classics like "Pride and Prejudice," will replace Charles Darwin on the note, likely starting in 2017. The decision comes after a campaign by Caroline Criado-Perez and widespread public pressure, including an online petition with over 30,000 signatures. Chancellor George Osborne praised the move as showing "sense and sensibility." Mark Carney, the new governor of the Bank of England, also announced a review of the selection process for future banknotes to ensure greater diversity.

Obama's public approval rating has dropped back to 50%, reflecting growing economic concerns and political disillusionment among Americans, according to a recent Washington Post-ABC News poll. The poll shows a more even split between trust in Obama and congressional Republicans on economic matters, with a significant number expressing distrust in both sides. Majorities expect the sequester to harm the economy, military, and government services, but also desire cooperation to address the issue. Obama's support has eroded, particularly among political independents, with a 12-point decline among women. His standing is lower than that of other second-term presidents at this stage. Congress remains highly unpopular, with only 16% approving of its performance. The poll highlights the ongoing economic challenges and political polarization, with limited support for cutting popular social programs to reduce deficits.

Stanford University student Josh Browder, 19, discusses his innovative use of blockchain for HIV disclosure and his app DoNotPay, which fights parking tickets. Browder explains how his app, using blockchain for secure and permanent records, helps HIV-positive individuals prove disclosure. He also shares the success of his DoNotPay app, which has appealed over $4 million in parking fines for free. Browder highlights the potential of blockchain and AI in legal services, aiming to make legal assistance more accessible and efficient. He discusses his plans to expand DoNotPay and explore a developer platform for legal advice.

President Barack Obama will not attend Justice Antonin Scalia’s funeral on Saturday, the White House confirmed, instead paying his respects on Friday during the justice's repose at the Supreme Court building. Vice President Joe Biden and his wife Jill will attend Scalia’s funeral at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception. The White House defended Obama’s decision, emphasizing the importance of honoring Scalia’s service. Despite criticism from some Republicans, the White House reiterated the president’s constitutional right to nominate a successor. The decision to skip the funeral has been seen as a political move, with some calling it a snub. The article also discusses the precedent of presidential attendance at Supreme Court funerals and reactions from political figures and Scalia’s family.

Katie Holmes has reportedly received an "emotional letter" from ex-husband Tom Cruise, who is reportedly trying to rekindle their friendship after their July 2012 divorce. Sources say Cruise wrote the letter because he knew Katie Holmes would be unreceptive over the phone and that it wouldn't be an over-the-top message. The letter is said to express Cruise's continued feelings for Holmes and his hope that she is doing well. While Holmes has reportedly been "genuinely touched" by the letter, insiders suggest she is not interested in rekindling their relationship. Holmes has settled in New York City with their daughter Suri and is building a new life.

The funeral director who prepared Trayvon Martin's body for burial found no signs of a fight, CBS News reports. George Zimmerman, a neighborhood watch volunteer, claims he shot Martin in self-defense after a violent confrontation. However, video footage shows Zimmerman leaving the scene with no apparent injuries. Trayvon's family argues this proves police never intended to charge Zimmerman. Detective Chris Serino, who questioned witnesses, stated they did not believe it was self-defense. A special prosecutor will now decide whether to press charges against Zimmerman.

Scientists have found that Neanderthal DNA influences a wide range of human traits and diseases, including nicotine addiction, skin biology, and psychiatric conditions. A study by John Capra and colleagues, published in Science, analyzed the genomes of 28,000 people of European ancestry and linked them to their medical records. The research confirmed previous hypotheses, such as Neanderthal DNA affecting skin biology and risk of sun-induced skin lesions, and revealed new associations, including a specific Neanderthal DNA variant that significantly increases the risk of nicotine addiction. The study also found that many Neanderthal DNA snippets are linked to psychiatric and neurological effects. According to Capra, these findings suggest that Neanderthal DNA may have provided modern humans with adaptive advantages when migrating into new environments, but many of these traits may no longer be advantageous in today’s environment.

The Philae lander, which successfully touched down on Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko, is now facing a critical challenge as its batteries run out of power. After a last-ditch attempt to rotate into a slightly sunnier position, Philae may not have enough energy to continue its mission. Mission controllers are hopeful that the lander's batteries might be recharged as the comet approaches the sun in August 2015, potentially allowing Philae to wake up and resume communication. Meanwhile, Philae has already achieved significant success, with 80% of the primary mission objectives reportedly met. Engineers are exploring various strategies, such as deploying the drill to capture samples, to maximize the scientific data collected before the batteries expire. The lander's primary mission was designed to last around 60 hours, but the extended use of solar panels could extend the mission for months.
