The Officer Down Memorial Page (ODMP) has launched a new program, ODMP K9, to honor police canines that have died in the line of duty. Since 2007, over two dozen police K-9s have died from heat-related symptoms after being left in vehicles. These dogs, often Belgian Malinois or German Shepherds, are susceptible to heat stroke due to their thick coats and lack of sweat glands. In 2009, Officer Jason Lewis of the New Orleans Police Department left his K-9, Primo, in his police SUV, leading to Primo's death from heat stress. Similar cases have occurred in various states, with some departments installing heat alert systems to prevent such incidents. Despite the high cost of K-9s and their training, these systems are seen as a necessary measure to protect the dogs. The deaths of these police dogs are not only tragic but also preventable with proper equipment and procedures.

CVS Caremark, the largest pharmacy chain in the US, will stop selling cigarettes and tobacco products in all 7,600 of its stores by October 1, a move praised by health organizations. CEO Larry Merlo stated that the sale of tobacco products is inconsistent with the company's purpose of improving health outcomes. This decision is part of CVS's broader strategy to position itself as a key player in the healthcare system, offering services like flu shots and chronic disease management. The company expects to lose $2 billion in annual revenue but believes this will enhance its credibility with healthcare providers and improve patient trust. The move is seen as a significant step in reducing smoking rates, with potential long-term health benefits.

Yo, an app that lets you send the word "Yo" to your contacts, has gained unexpected popularity and $1 million in funding. Co-founder Or Arbel, after initially dismissing the idea, spent eight hours building the app. Now, Arbel has quit his job and moved to San Francisco to focus on Yo full-time. The app sends push notifications with the word "Yo," allowing users to communicate in a simple, non-intrusive way. Arbel sees potential in integrating Yo with various services, such as sending Yos from brands when customers make purchases or when their orders are ready. While some find the concept amusing, Arbel believes Yo can significantly impact users' lives. The app has attracted over 50,000 users and 4 million Yos, making it popular among tech-savvy individuals. However, the app's simplicity and the recent surge in tech investments raise questions about its sustainability and whether it represents a new tech bubble.

Incumbent Democratic state Representative Roger Freeman, who died from cancer shortly before the election, is leading in a Washington state House race. Early results show he has a 53% to 47% advantage over his Republican opponent, Jack Dovey. Freeman's death has left his 30th legislative district in a unique situation, as local Democrats will select a temporary replacement from three nominees, with a special election planned for next year to fill the remainder of Freeman's term. Freeman's campaign encourages voters to support him in memory of his contributions, despite his passing.

The $39,000 backpack from The Row, the luxury fashion line by Olsen twins Ashley and Mary-Kate, is selling out at Barneys New York. Ashley told Women's Wear Daily that the bags were the first item to sell out. The high-end accessory, made from crocodile skin, is designed to appeal to a younger crowd willing to spend a lot on a long-lasting, classic bag. While the price tag may seem excessive, Barneys New York's fashion director sees it as a way to compete with other luxury brands.

On Valentine's Day, Freestyle Releasing aims to challenge Fifty Shades of Grey with their faith-based romance film "Old Fashioned," which stars Rik Swartzwelder as a former frat boy and Elizabeth Ann Roberts as a free-spirited woman. The movie, with its tagline "Chivalry makes a comeback," seeks to offer an alternative to the anticipated Fifty Shades, focusing on a higher standard in relationships without objectification or domination. Freestyle, known for hits like "God's Not Dead," hopes to appeal to the Christian singles audience and differentiate itself from the explicit content of Fifty Shades.

In a disturbing video from 2010, a MoveOn.org activist named Lauren Valle is seen being pushed to the ground by a Rand Paul supporter and then stomped on by another. The incident occurred in Lexington before Paul debated his Democratic rival, Jack Conway. Tim Profitt, a Bourbon County coordinator for Paul, admitted to stepping on Valle's head. Lexington police identified Profitt as the suspect and served him with a criminal summons. The Paul campaign distanced themselves from the violent volunteer, stating that any level of aggression or violence is deplorable and not tolerated by their campaign.

A plastic skull painted with "household gloss" is part of a gift shop in Damien Hirst's major exhibition at the Tate Modern, priced at £36,800. Other items include a set of 12 china plates for £10,500, a spotted skateboard for £480, a deckchair for £310, and a butterfly-print umbrella for £195. The butterfly-print wallpaper costs £700 a roll. The gift shop is the final room in Hirst's first major UK exhibition, which features his famous works like a shark suspended in formaldehyde and a human skull covered in 8,601 diamonds. Hirst defended the price of his work, saying it's about demand, not the materials.

The Pentagon's Excess Property Program, which sends surplus military equipment to police departments, has faced scrutiny following civil unrest in Ferguson, Missouri. The Defense Department has released detailed data on the program for the first time, showing that over $4.3 billion in gear has been supplied since 1997, including $449 million in 2013. The data reveals a wide range of equipment, from mundane items like battery chargers to powerful armored vehicles and even unexpected items such as snowshoes and televisions. Small police departments, including those in rural areas, have received significant amounts of military-grade equipment, raising questions about its necessity and potential misuse.

Investigators are reviewing surveillance video from a nearby gas station after two escaped murderers, David Sweat and Richard Matt, left clues that led police to follow their scent east toward Cadyville. A Subway restaurant at the gas station suggests the men might have been looking for food in the trash. In Cadyville, authorities are using infrared technology to search for the fugitives, who are believed to be in the area. The search has expanded to nearby Vermont, with state police vessels and troopers looking for the men on Lake Champlain. Despite the extensive manhunt, authorities have not ruled out the possibility that the men have left the state. The escape timeline includes the discovery of an imprint from a shoe or boot, as well as a food wrapper, which may indicate where the men bedded down. Residents have been advised to stay indoors, and schools have been closed. The article also mentions a history of escapes from the Clinton Correctional Facility, highlighting the meticulous planning involved in previous attempts.

"Bitch Slap" aims to be a tribute to hot-women-in-peril movies but falls short with scant humor, interminable girl-fighting, and a plot that borrows from "Memento." The film's primary focus is on the assets of its actresses, with moments of enjoyment overshadowed by a surfeit of fistfights. Despite its obsession with décolletage, "Bitch Slap" is surprisingly puritanical, substituting violence and a predictable "shock" ending for the payoff it promises. The film's target audience is likely those who enjoy women punching each other, but the overall experience is disappointing.

After years of restoration, the ninth-century Qarawiyyin library in north-eastern Morocco is set to reopen, with strict security and a new underground canal system to protect its manuscripts. The library, believed to be the oldest in the world, will house a collection of ancient texts, including a ninth-century copy of the Qur’an. The restoration, led by architect Aziza Chaouni, aims to preserve the library’s historical significance while integrating modern preservation technologies. The reopening is seen as part of Morocco’s plan to restore Fez as a cultural and spiritual capital.

A survey by Transparency International found that more than a quarter of people worldwide paid a bribe in the last year. The 2013 Global Corruption Barometer, based on responses from over 114,000 people in 107 countries, revealed that police and the judiciary are the most prone to bribery, with nearly one-third of respondents reporting paying bribes to police and 24% to the judicial system. In countries where corruption in these institutions is perceived as a major issue, the rates are even higher. Over half of those surveyed believe corruption has increased in the past two years, with an average score of 4.1 on a five-point scale, where 5 indicates a very serious problem. Political parties are seen as the most corrupt institution in more than 50 countries, and trust in government efforts to combat corruption has declined from 31% in 2008 to 22% currently.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, battling a rare cancer, announced he has a "50-50" chance of survival and is considering running for his old council seat in Ward 2 despite undergoing chemotherapy. Ford defended his decision, stating that many residents support his candidacy. His opponents, however, criticized his lack of engagement, such as skipping debates. Ford's brother, Doug, is now running for mayor, unveiling a transit plan that includes a $9-billion, 32-kilometre subway project, with a downtown relief line as the top priority. Ford's health struggles have deeply affected his family, particularly his children, who are growing up with the uncertainty of his future.

A University of Utah student, Lauren McCluskey, was shot and killed on campus by her ex-boyfriend, Melvin Rowland, who had a history of sexual offenses and was on parole. Rowland, 37, had been stalking McCluskey, a 21-year-old member of the track and field team, for days before the fatal shooting. McCluskey had broken off their relationship after learning of Rowland's criminal background. Rowland confronted McCluskey in a parking lot, dragged her into a car, and shot her multiple times. After the shooting, Rowland killed himself in a church. University police chief Dale Brophy said McCluskey had wired $1,000 to an account to prevent the release of compromising photos. The case highlights issues in campus security and the handling of sexual extortion complaints.

A Guardian investigation reveals that sex traffickers are targeting women in prisons and jails across the United States, using government websites and personal data to identify potential victims. Predators exploit the vulnerability of incarcerated women, often luring them with promises of money, housing, and support upon release. Once released, these women are forced into prostitution to repay debts or face further incarceration. The issue is widespread, with cases reported in Florida, Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, and Mississippi. Survivors and experts highlight the systemic failures in the criminal justice system, which fail to protect inmates and instead contribute to the cycle of exploitation. Advocates call for increased training and interventions to support women and prevent trafficking, but many remain trapped in a cycle of abuse and exploitation.

NOAA Fisheries has declared the deaths of 30 large whales in the western Gulf of Alaska since May an "unusual mortality event," triggering a focused investigation. This number is about three times the historical average for the region. The deaths include 11 fin whales, 14 humpback whales, one gray whale, and four unidentified cetaceans. A federal agency announced plans for a more intense investigation into the cause, with a leading hypothesis being harmful algal bloom toxins, though no conclusive evidence has been found yet. Scientists can only conduct limited examinations due to the difficulty of accessing the carcasses, especially in areas where bears pose safety concerns. The public is urged to report any sightings of dead whales or distressed animals. Six additional large whales have been reported dead off the coast of British Columbia, Canada, with necropsies conducted on two of the more recent carcasses. The situation is concerning, but a coast-wide event does not appear to be occurring.

California State University at Chico's Pi Kappa Alpha fraternity faces criminal charges for allegedly hacking down more than 32 trees and firing guns during a tree-cutting initiation ceremony in Lassen National Forest. A campground visitor's photos revealed the mess left behind. Each member now faces vandalism, illegal firearms, and degrading U.S. territory charges. The fraternity denies some allegations and faces community threats. Their case is set for court on June 26, 2017.

A 14-year-old girl, Ayvani Perez, who was abducted from her home in Clayton County early Tuesday, has been found safe and returned to her family. A neighbor reported seeing Ayvani return to her home in Ellenwood early Wednesday night. However, Ayvani did not spend the night at the home where she was abducted. Clayton County police arrested Wildrego Jackson, 29, and Juan Alberto Rodriguez, 40, in connection with the abduction. The two arrested men are not the same as those depicted in the sketches released earlier. Federal agents found Ayvani at a home in Conyers, but did not disclose how they located her. Both suspects are facing charges, with Rodriguez facing immigration-related charges and Jackson facing conspiracy to commit kidnapping charges. Neighbors expressed relief and gratitude for Ayvani's safe return.

Actress Sienna Miller is expected to join legal action against Scotland Yard and the News of the World over phone-hacking, following revelations that the paper's private investigator had obtained her mobile phone details. Miller, who had previously sued the News of the World for privacy invasion, plans to join a legal review of Scotland Yard's handling of the case. Meanwhile, former News of the World staff Sean Hoare has been interviewed by police under caution, raising questions about his claims of involvement in hacking. MPs are also set to investigate whether parliamentary privileges were breached by the private investigator.

California is experiencing its driest year on record, with 100% of the state under some level of drought for the first time in 15 years. Governor Jerry Brown declared a drought emergency, emphasizing the need for water conservation. The state's reservoirs are at critically low levels, with Santa Clara County reservoirs at 3% capacity or less. Brown's executive order aims to reduce urban water usage by 25% in 2013, focusing on measures like removing grass, replacing water-guzzling appliances, and discouraging water waste. While Southern California agencies are already implementing some of these measures, the order may be more challenging for other areas. The Sierra Nevada snowpack, which supplies about 30% of the state's water, is at its lowest level in over 60 years, highlighting the severity of the drought.

A rare blue moon appeared in the sky on Tuesday night, prompting many to take photos and share them on social media. The term "blue moon" typically refers to the second full moon in a calendar month, although it has different definitions. The next blue moon will not occur until 2015. While the moon does not actually turn blue, there have been instances in history where the moon appeared blue due to atmospheric conditions, such as after volcanic eruptions. The blue moon is also known by other names, such as the Full Sturgeon Moon, Green Corn Moon, or Grain Moon.

Fernando Colon, step-father to Ariel Castro's children and ex-husband of Castro's ex-wife, maintains that Castro orchestrated the disappearance of Gina DeJesus and Amanda Berry, accusing him of using the case to divert attention from his own crimes. Colon was convicted of molesting two of Castro's daughters in 2004. In 2004, Colon told the FBI that he was the last person to see DeJesus alive, and a friend of Berry's, Arlene Castro, also provided information to America's Most Wanted. A private investigator, Chris Giannini, supports Colon's claims, suggesting that authorities should have investigated Castro more closely. Colon now plans to appeal his molestation conviction based on the new evidence.

A 20-year-old American University student, Maria Rose Belding, co-founded MEANS Database, a platform that connects food pantries, donors, and businesses to reduce food waste and hunger. In its first year, the system rescued about 4,000 pounds of food, won a $10,000 prize from L'Oreal Paris, and aims to become self-sufficient. MEANS operates through a website and app, allowing donors to list available food, and nearby food banks or pantries to claim it. Belding, inspired by witnessing food waste at a local pantry, met her co-founder Grant Nelson, who developed the technology. The platform addresses inefficiencies in emergency food provision, such as incorrect contact information for food pantries. By using data science and meticulous record-keeping, MEANS has identified significant issues and worked on solutions, such as a searchable directory of food pantries. Nicky Hilton Rothschild and her husband, James Rothschild, are expecting their first child together due this summer, a source confirms. The newlyweds, who married in July 2015 at Kensington Palace, are over the moon. "I highly recommend it," Nicky told E! News, "If you find the right person, absolutely. It's so much fun." Paris Hilton, Nicky's older sister, also expressed her desire to have children in the future.

District Attorney Jill Ravitch announced no criminal charges will be filed against Sonoma County sheriff's deputy Erick Gelhaus for shooting and killing 13-year-old Andy Lopez last year. The shooting occurred when Lopez was carrying an airsoft BB gun resembling an AK-47. Ravitch's 52-page report revealed Lopez was likely under the influence of marijuana at the time. The deputy feared for his life and fired eight shots, striking Lopez seven times. Protests and a federal civil rights lawsuit against Gelhaus and the county followed the decision. The community remains divided, with some calling it an injustice and others defending the deputy's actions.

Looking for a safer state? Consider moving to Maine, the most peaceful state in the U.S., according to 24/7 Wall St. Maine has the second-lowest violent crime rate and the fourth-lowest murder rate. The state's lower poverty rate and higher median household income contribute to its peacefulness. Other top peaceful states include Vermont and New Hampshire, which also have lower poverty rates and higher incomes. Arizona, South Carolina, Florida, Missouri, and Arkansas rank among the least peaceful states, with higher violent crime rates and poverty levels. These states also have larger law enforcement operations and higher gun ownership rates.

With the federal government shutdown entering its third week, Senate Democrats and Republicans are closing in on a deal to reopen the government and extend the debt ceiling, though significant hurdles remain as a Thursday deadline looms. Senate Democratic Leader Harry Reid expressed optimism that an agreement could be reached soon, while Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell echoed similar sentiments. The proposed plan would raise the debt ceiling by enough to cover borrowing needs at least through mid-February 2014 and fund government operations through January, maintaining sequester cuts but giving agencies more flexibility to ease their impact. However, the deal would not resolve long-term spending and healthcare disagreements, representing a clear retreat for Republicans who sought to tie continued funding to measures undercutting President Obama's Affordable Care Act. The agreement must still win approval in the House, where conservative Republicans have insisted on measures to undermine the health law. President Obama will convene a meeting with congressional Democrats on Wednesday to strategize on protecting the Affordable Care Act from Republican efforts to repeal it, reports POLITICO. The meeting, set for 9 a.m. in the Congressional Visitors Center auditorium, will include both House and Senate Democrats. With Republicans planning a swift repeal of the law early next year, Democrats are divided on how to proceed, with some willing to work with Republicans on a replacement, but almost all opposing any repeal. Incoming Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has vowed to block Republican repeal efforts and a conservative replacement. More than 20 million people benefit from the Affordable Care Act, including those under 26 who can stay on their parents' plans and those with preexisting conditions. Democrats are also planning a broader health care offensive, including a “day of action” on January 15, to defend social safety net programs. Republicans can use reconciliation to dismantle Obamacare with a simple majority, but a lengthy transition period may be considered.

A Colorado man, Jack McAtee, went missing after a car accident in 2014, leaving behind only a skull found on Peak 1 in 2015. His father, Steve McAtee, and family members searched extensively, following clues from Jack's favorite book and his history of going missing before. They traveled to potential locations like Alaska, Moab, and various shelters, posting his picture and information. Despite their efforts, the cause and exact circumstances of Jack's death remain unclear, bringing both hope and despair to his family.

A Canadian man and his American wife, kidnapped by the Taliban in Afghanistan in 2012, have appeared in a new video, warning that their captors will kill them and their children unless the Afghan government stops executing Taliban prisoners. The video, uploaded to YouTube, shows Canadian Joshua Boyle and American Caitlan Coleman, who have been held captive for four years, pleading for their release. Caitlan, now 31, has given birth to two children in captivity. The U.S. State Department is evaluating the video, which has not been independently verified, and continues to urge for their immediate release on humanitarian grounds. Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid confirmed the couple is still in captivity but in good health. Canada's Global Affairs spokesman, Michael O'Shaughnessy, called for their unconditional release. The couple's last known video was in 2013, and their case has garnered little public attention despite their four-year ordeal.

An 89-year-old former SS guard from Philadelphia died the night before a judge ruled he should be extradited to Germany to face charges of aiding and abetting the murder of 216,000 Jewish men, women, and children at Auschwitz. Johann Breyer, who had been held without bail, passed away at a Philadelphia hospital, according to his lawyer. U.S. Magistrate Timothy Rice approved the extradition request, stating there was probable cause that Breyer was the same person sought for aiding and abetting murder in Germany. Breyer, a retired tool-and-die maker, was accused of serving as an SS guard at Auschwitz during World War II and claimed he was unaware of the massive slaughter. German authorities issued a warrant for his arrest in 2013, charging him with 158 counts of accessory to murder, one for each trainload of victims brought to the camp from May to October 1944.

The European Commission is investigating claims that software in some TVs may skew their energy efficiency ratings. Samsung acknowledged using software that alters its TVs' performance during tests but denied any wrongdoing. An unnamed manufacturer is accused of adjusting brightness when recognizing test films. These allegations parallel the Volkswagen emissions scandal. Independent tests found Samsung TVs' power consumption dropped significantly during standardized tests. The European Commission will verify the findings and consider tightening energy efficiency regulations to ban "defeat devices" in TVs and other products.

Perez Hilton, the openly gay blogger, has become a father to a baby boy. In a post titled "A Very Important Message from Perez," Hilton shared the news on his blog, expressing gratitude to his fans for welcoming his website into their lives. The 34-year-old blogger, who previously made a name for himself with snarky comments and celebrity photos, now humbly acknowledges the challenge of parenthood. "Thank YOU for welcoming PerezHilton.com into your homes, offices, classrooms, cell phones and wherever else you may read my five websites. And thank you for welcoming ME into your lives! I am so humbled to welcome this little man into my life. And I am honored and ready for the challenge of guiding him through his."

A Delaware man, William Jacob Raak, survived a New Year's Eve attack at an Istanbul nightclub by playing dead, NBC News reports. Raak, 35, was shot in the hip but remained silent and motionless during the attack. He was one of about 60 people injured in the shooting at the Reina nightclub, where 39 people, mostly foreigners, were killed. Istanbul authorities are hunting for the gunman, who fled the scene. The Islamic State group claimed responsibility for the attack.

President Trump issued his first pardon, for former Arizona sheriff Joe Arpaio, on the eve of Hurricane Harvey, drawing widespread criticism. Trump had privately considered pardoning Arpaio for months, seeing him as a law-and-order ally. The pardon, announced without Justice Department consultation, was seen as politicizing the judicial process. Arpaio, convicted of criminal contempt for defying a court order to stop detaining undocumented immigrants, faced up to six months in prison. Trump’s decision, made after Arpaio’s conviction but before sentencing, raised questions about the separation of powers and the rule of law. The pardon was met with condemnation from both Democrats and some Republicans, who criticized it as undermining law enforcement and deepening national divisions.

Astronomers have directly imaged a part of the cosmic web, a vast network of dark matter and gas that underlies the visible universe, for the first time. Using the 10-meter Keck I Telescope in Hawaii, researchers from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy detected a large, bright nebula of gas illuminated by the intense radiation from a distant quasar. This quasar, UM287, located 10 billion light-years away, acts like a cosmic flashlight, highlighting a filament of gas stretching approximately 2 million light-years across intergalactic space. The discovery supports the standard model of cosmology, which predicts that galaxies are embedded in a cosmic web of dark matter and gas. While the observed gas extends beyond the quasar's galactic environment, the team notes that only the illuminated portion of the filament is visible. This finding provides a new way to study the structure and evolution of the universe, potentially revealing

Archaeologists have uncovered a large ancient tomb in northern Greece, dating to around 325-300 B.C., near the city of Amphipolis. The tomb, believed to be the largest ever found in Greece, features two sphinxes guarding its entrance and a 497-meter-long marble wall. Prime Minister Antonis Samaras called the discovery "extremely important." The tomb, which may have belonged to a prominent Macedonian official, is expected to be opened in the next two weeks, revealing more about its contents. So far, archaeologists have uncovered a flight of 13 steps leading to a broad path flanked by masonry walls and an arch covering two headless, wingless sphinxes.

Violence escalated in Gaza and Israel on Monday, with 18 Palestinians killed in air strikes and at least five Israeli soldiers dying in a militant tunnel attack, according to the IDF. Despite calls for a cease-fire, rockets and mortars hit a Gaza refugee camp, a hospital, and Gaza City center, killing 10 people, including eight children. Hamas and Israel blamed each other for the attacks. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned of a "protracted campaign" in Gaza, while Palestinian officials called for Israel to withdraw its forces. The conflict has left 1,101 Palestinians and 53 Israeli soldiers dead, with 6,500 Palestinians wounded. Israel aims to destroy Hamas tunnels used for attacks, while Hamas demands an end to the Gaza blockade. International pressure for a cease-fire intensified, with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and world leaders urging a halt to the violence.

Whale sharks, the largest living fish, are increasingly using volcanic islands off the western coast of Europe as new homes due to rising sea surface temperatures, according to a new study. This finding could shed light on how climate change might alter fish behavior globally. Whale sharks prefer warm waters between 79 to 86 degrees Fahrenheit, but sightings around the Azores Islands, nine volcanic isles in the central North Atlantic west of Portugal, have increased sharply, particularly in 2008. Researchers analyzed 16 years of data from tuna fishing boats and found that higher water temperatures and seafloor features rich in chlorophyll—a potential food source—correlated with more whale shark sightings. The study, published in PLOS ONE, suggests that as climate change continues, the Azores region may become more important as an oceanic habitat for whale sharks, potentially leading to shifts in their distribution across the Atlantic Ocean.

President Trump tweeted on Thanksgiving Day that Republicans and Democrats must come together to pass a major Border Security package, including funding for the wall, emphasizing the need for action after 40 years of discussion. He also called for criminal justice reform, noting that Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Democratic leader Chuck Schumer have a chance to address a needed issue in the country. However, Trump's tweet mistakenly tagged a fan of Senator Chuck Schumer instead of the senator himself. Trump spent Thanksgiving by calling troops, answering reporters' questions, visiting a Coast Guard station, and having dinner at his Mar-a-Lago club. Despite the recent loss of the House to Democrats, Trump remains firm on border security funding and criminal justice reform.

Dunkin' Donuts plans to launch a croissant-doughnut hybrid, dubbed the "Croissant Donut," in the U.S. next week, aiming to capitalize on the popularity of the Cronut without directly copying it. The Cronut, created by Dominique Ansel in New York City, became a viral sensation and spawned numerous imitations. Dunkin', based in Massachusetts, has been tracking consumer and bakery trends for several years, noting that bakers have been mixing doughnuts and croissants for at least 20 years. The Croissant Donut will be sold nationally for a limited time starting November 3, 2014, priced at $2.49, making it more profitable for the company compared to other doughnuts. Unlike the Cronut, which features a cream filling, the Croissant Donut will be covered with the same glaze used for Dunkin's Glazed Donut. Dunkin' is considering various fillings and

Syrian government official Bouthaina Shaaban suggested that talks could be opened with certain Syrian religious and community leaders who have influence over some rebel fighters, marking a subtle shift in the government's stance. However, identifying acceptable negotiating partners among the diffuse opposition remains challenging, as the conflict has killed over 100,000 people and displaced millions. Despite this, the government expressed confidence in its military and diplomatic victories, including achieving a deal to give up chemical weapons to avoid a U.S. airstrike. Bashar al-Assad’s regime also accused rebel forces of using chemical weapons in the Damascus suburbs, a claim dismissed by U.S. officials.

An Ohio mother and her 21-month-old daughter were killed when a teen allegedly racing another car struck them with a Ford Mustang in Florida. Jessica Raubenolt, 24, was pushing her daughter Lillia in a stroller across Bayshore Boulevard in Tampa when the crash occurred. The teen driver, Cameron Herrin, 18, and his 17-year-old passenger were arrested for street racing, vehicular homicide, and reckless driving. Raubenolt was visiting family while her husband awaited his airplane pilot certification. Her uncle, John Reisinger, offered forgiveness to the teens and their families. Raubenolt was described as a health and fitness advocate who left a lasting impact on those who knew her.

In Argentina, the widespread use of agrochemicals, particularly glyphosate, has raised health concerns amid a boom in genetically modified crops. Farmers often spray without proper caution, leading to drift into schools, homes, and water sources. Doctors report higher cancer rates and birth defects in areas with intensive farming. Despite regulations, enforcement is lax, and studies suggest interactions between chemicals may pose risks not fully assessed. The government's health commission has not met since 2010, and complaints of spraying violations go unaddressed.

Up to 25 teaspoons of sugar per serving, equivalent to about 3 cans of Coca Cola, have been found in many hot flavoured drinks, warns Action on Sugar. Of the 131 hot flavoured drinks analyzed, 98% would receive a 'red' label for high sugar content, with 35% containing as much sugar as a can of Coca Cola. The worst offender is Starbucks' Hot Mulled Fruit - Grape with Chai, Orange and Cinnamon Venti, containing 25 teaspoons of sugar, more than three times the maximum adult daily intake of free sugars. Action on Sugar calls for stricter product reformulation, a ban on unhealthy product promotions, and a 20% tax on sugar-sweetened drinks as part of the government's Childhood Obesity Strategy.

The individual mandate at the heart of President Obama’s healthcare law faces a significant challenge, with early reports from the second day of Supreme Court arguments indicating a skeptical stance from key justices. Journalists present observed that the Obama administration’s solicitor general, Donald Verrilli, struggled to defend the law, facing pointed questions from conservative justices like Anthony Kennedy, Antonin Scalia, Samuel Alito, and Chief Justice John Roberts. Kennedy, seen as a potential swing vote, appeared particularly critical, raising doubts about the mandate’s constitutionality. While the outcome remains uncertain, the administration’s performance during the arguments suggests a difficult path ahead for the healthcare law.

At least 21 people, including two teenage boys, were killed in a gunfight that erupted at a wedding party in northern Afghanistan's Baghlan province, officials said. The conflict between two armed groups attending the wedding in Deh Salah district led to crossfire that also injured eight others. Police chief Gulistan Qusani reported a higher death toll of 21, while provincial police spokesman Jawed Basharat gave a lower count of 20. The cause of the dispute remains unclear. The incident highlights ongoing security challenges in Afghanistan, where wedding celebrations can turn deadly due to disputes or criminal activity.

The Backstreet Boys have announced new Vegas residency dates and hinted at upcoming new music. They unveiled 21 additional shows from July 25 to Nov. 17, and during a Twitter Q&A, revealed they have a new single "Coming Soon." Kevin Richardson said it's "coming out real soon," but didn't specify a release date. The band is working on their 10th studio album to coincide with their 25th anniversary later this year. They plan to add the new song to their Vegas set list starting in July or August.

A 30-year-old Baton Rouge mother, Schaquana Evita Spears, was arrested for allegedly beating her three sons after they broke into a neighbor's home. Spears admitted to using an RCA cord to discipline the boys, resulting in cuts and bleeding. The boys' injuries sparked debate over the line between appropriate discipline and child abuse. District Attorney Hillar Moore III is reviewing the case, considering the severity of the injuries. Spears, who runs a catering business, is currently out of jail on reduced bail. Defenders argue that her actions were necessary to prevent her children from stealing and potentially facing more severe consequences.

An 8-year-old girl named Sa’fyre Terry received a Christmas miracle when she was flooded with thousands of cards and gifts after asking for them as her only wish. Sa’fyre, who lost her father and three younger siblings in a fire three years ago and now has burns over 75% of her body, was simply hoping to fill a thrift store Christmas tree stand with cards. However, her wish turned into a global outpouring of love. Her aunt, Liz Dolder, shared Sa’fyre’s story on social media, and in just a few days, the family received more than 300,000 letters and packages. Sa’fyre’s story inspired a charity, Baking Memories 4 Kids, to offer the Terry family a trip to Walt Disney World, which will take place in February. The family is overwhelmed by the support and Sa’fyre is still in disbelief at the number of cards she receives daily.

IBM and the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) are partnering to bring Watson for Genomics technology into VA hospitals and doctors' offices, aiming to expand access to precision medicine for 10,000 American veterans with cancer over the next two years. This initiative, part of Vice President Joe Biden’s Cancer Moonshot program, uses Watson’s ability to analyze genomic data and provide treatment options ranked by evidence levels, significantly speeding up the process compared to current methods. The VA's Michael Kelley notes that this will help scale precision medicine, which is currently limited by the number of patients that can be reviewed by Molecular Tumor Boards. The partnership is expected to democratize access to advanced cancer treatments, benefiting veterans and potentially setting a precedent for broader healthcare applications.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg fractured three ribs after falling in her office. The 85-year-old liberal justice was admitted to George Washington University Hospital for observation and treatment. This incident has renewed speculation about Ginsburg's health, given her history of surviving multiple bouts with cancer and other medical issues. Ginsburg, one of four liberal justices on the nine-member court, has stated her intention to serve until she is 90. Her approach to the law is described as cautious, yet she has been influential in cases involving gender discrimination, women's reproductive health, and international law. The fall occurred on the same day as the formal investiture ceremony for Justice Brett Kavanaugh, President Donald Trump's second Supreme Court nominee. Many supporters have offered well-wishes on social media, with some expressing concern about potential changes to the court's composition if Ginsburg were to retire soon.

Breitbart News's application for press credentials to cover Congress has been denied, and their temporary credentials will not be renewed. The Standing Committee of Correspondents cited concerns about Breitbart's editorial independence, particularly regarding its ties to Steve Bannon and Rebekah Mercer. Breitbart had hoped to gain access to the Capitol and participate in White House "pools," but the committee expressed doubts about the organization's ability to meet the criteria for press credentials. Breitbart CEO Larry Solov argued that the site is editorially independent and should be granted permanent credentials, but the committee remained unconvinced. They stated that Breitbart could reapply if it addresses the concerns, but for now, three staff members with current temporary credentials will lose access after May 31.

A Manhattan Criminal Court judge ruled that Twitter must hand over messages sent by a Brooklyn writer during the Occupy Wall Street protests to prosecutors. The judge stated that while private speech is protected, public comments on Twitter are not. The case raises significant issues in the evolving area of social media and privacy. American law enforcement made up 80% of the 849 law enforcement requests Twitter received from Jan. 1 to June for user information, with 63% of those requests granted. Twitter's openness contrasts with Facebook's more secretive policies, and the company's data shows a growing trend of government requests for user information.

Mike Huckabee, former Arkansas governor and 2008 Republican presidential candidate, is reportedly launching a new website called the Huckabee Post. Multiple reports indicate Huckabee is seeking reporters for the new venture, which will cover politics, U.S. and international news, media, sports, and other general news. Huckabee has previously flirted with another presidential run in 2016 and has been actively discussing his potential candidacy in various interviews. His Fox News show and radio commentaries could potentially support his media presence, though he would need to consider the financial implications of leaving his lucrative Fox position.

An early warning system that could have prevented some deaths during the recent tsunami in Indonesia has been stalled in the testing phase for years. The high-tech system, involving seafloor sensors, data-laden sound waves, and fiber-optic cable, was meant to replace an older system set up after the 2004 tsunami that killed nearly 250,000 people. However, inter-agency wrangling and delays in securing just $69,000 to complete the project mean the system hasn't moved beyond a prototype developed with $3 million from the U.S. National Science Foundation. The system is too late for central Sulawesi, where a magnitude 7.5 earthquake and tsunami killed at least 832 people in the cities of Palu and Donggala, highlighting the weaknesses of the existing warning system and low public awareness. The latest edition of Merriam Webster's "Official Scrabble Players Dictionary" introduces 300 new words, including "OK" and "ew," enhancing the game's vocabulary. Notable additions like "bizjet" and "arancini" offer high-scoring opportunities. Lexicographer Peter Sokolowski highlights the inclusion of "macaron" for its cultural significance. The dictionary, updated every four to eight years since 1976, now contains over 100,000 words, with new entries such as "schneid," "bibimbap," and "emoji." These updates reflect the evolving nature of language, particularly from digital communication.

An elderly woman in her 80s, limited to the first floor due to mobility issues, discovered a man living in an upstairs closet of her home in central Pennsylvania. The unidentified homeowner and her daughter heard noises upstairs and found the man, who had been living there for several weeks. Police say the man, Mark Potts, was the boyfriend of the woman's caretaker. They found several suitcases and a small handgun in the closet. Potts faces criminal trespassing charges, and the caretaker could face additional charges for aiding him.

The situation at Japan's Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant remains critical, with radiation leaks and explosions raising concerns about the safety of the reactor fuel. The Japanese government and Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) have reported that an explosion at reactor No. 1 may have been caused by a buildup of hydrogen, though the extent of damage to the reactor core remains unclear. Radiation levels outside the plant have increased, with up to 160 people potentially exposed. TEPCO has begun flooding the reactor core with seawater to prevent a meltdown. The exact cause of the explosion and the status of the fuel inside the reactor are still under investigation. While officials reassure the public that the reactor container was not damaged, experts caution that the potential for a significant release of radiation remains, especially if the fuel is significantly damaged.

Researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology have created a miniature replica of the Mona Lisa, measuring just 30 millionths of a meter wide—roughly one-third the width of a human hair. This "Mini Lisa" showcases a new nanolithography technique called ThermoChemical NanoLithography (TCNL). Using an atomic force microscope, the team heated a microscopic cantilever to trigger chemical reactions on a plastic surface, varying the surface concentration of molecules to create the grayscale image. Each pixel, measuring 125 billionths of a meter, was carefully crafted to replicate the original painting's details. This technique not only demonstrates artistic precision at the nanoscale but also opens possibilities for nanomanufacturing and advanced applications in fields like nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, and bioengineering.

Astronaut Scott Kelly, after spending nearly a year aboard the International Space Station, is about two inches taller than when he left Earth. This is a common and temporary side effect of spaceflight, where the spine elongates due to the lack of gravity. Upon returning to Houston, Kelly reunited with his identical twin brother, retired astronaut Mark Kelly, who remained on Earth as a control subject. NASA's "Twins Study" aims to compare the brothers to determine the effects of long-term space travel on the human body. Kelly's mission, lasting 342 days, is a record for the United States and the International Space Station. Scientists will analyze data from blood samples, psychological tests, and other experiments to understand the physiological and psychological impacts of extended space travel, crucial for future missions to Mars.

The murder of 9-year-old Tyshawn Lee, allegedly carried out by Dwright Boone-Doty, shocked Chicago and drew national attention. Boone-Doty, a 22-year-old gang member, lured Tyshawn from a park with a basketball, then shot him execution-style, hitting him in the head and other parts of the body. Boone-Doty also bragged about the killing in jail, saying he "couldn't take it no more." Prosecutors allege Boone-Doty and his accomplices, including Corey Morgan and Kevin Edwards, targeted Tyshawn because of his father's gang ties. The shooting was part of a gang feud between the Bang Bang Gang/Terror Dome faction of the Black P Stones and the Killa Ward faction of the Gangster Disciples. Boone-Doty was already in jail on a separate gun charge when he allegedly committed the murder. He was charged with first-degree murder and faces a hearing where he was ordered held without

Actress Joan Fontaine, known for her roles in Alfred Hitchcock's "Suspicion" and "Rebecca," died at her home in Carmel, California, at the age of 96. Her rivalry with her older sister, Academy Award-winning actress Olivia de Havilland, was legendary, with the two sisters famously not speaking for decades. Fontaine's career spanned from the 1930s to the 1960s, with notable performances in "The Women," "Rebecca," and "Suspicion," where she won an Oscar over her sister. Despite her success, she faced criticism for being over-dressed in a photograph, and her later career included television appearances and work as an interior decorator.

Americans are feeling less safe, with 47% now believing the country is less safe than at any point since 9/11, according to a new NBC News/Wall Street Journal Poll. The backdrop is President Obama's upcoming speech on Wednesday to outline his plan to combat ISIS, a group that has beheaded two American journalists and launched a social media campaign. More than six in 10 respondents believe military action against ISIS is in the nation's interest, and 94% have heard about the beheadings. The poll highlights a generation that has grown up amid continuous conflict, with no end in sight. President Obama's plans for expanded operations against ISIS are expected to include intensified airstrikes but no major deployment of ground troops, with a heavy reliance on allies.

This summer, the author finds herself surrounded by alcohol in various forms—rosé, wine, and cocktails, often served in excessive quantities. She reflects on how drinking has become a ubiquitous part of social and professional life, with alcohol being offered at work events, in stores, and even at farmer's markets. The author wonders if women drink more to cope with the pressures of a sexist society or if it's a universal human behavior. She recalls a recent essay by Kristi Coulter, which argues that women drink to escape the realities of living in a sexist world, but also considers that men may drink for similar reasons. The author questions the relationship between drinking and other societal pressures, such as the need to look perfect or be successful. She shares her experiences of being sober for the first time and how it makes her more aware of the constant availability of alcohol and the expectations to consume it. The author concludes that while drinking may be a coping mechanism, it's also a way to bond and express

The Trump administration announced that Salvadoran immigrants with temporary protected status (TPS) will lose their right to remain in the United States in 2019, affecting approximately 200,000 individuals. This decision, part of broader immigration enforcement efforts, will give Salvadorans 18 months to either leave or seek lawful residency. The program, initially granted after devastating earthquakes in 2001, is criticized for potentially separating families and ignoring ongoing violence in El Salvador. Critics argue that the move undermines the temporary nature of TPS and could lead to increased instability in Central America. Salvadorans, who have been living and working in the U.S. for nearly two decades, face the prospect of being deported or remaining illegally. The decision impacts not only Salvadorans but also Haitians and Nicaraguans, with similar measures potentially affecting Hondurans.

A team of scientists and legal experts proposes founding a space nation called Asgardia, aiming to open access to space technologies, protect Earth from cosmic threats, and foster peace. Named after the city in the skies from Norse mythology, Asgardia would initially consist of a single satellite launched in 2017, with its citizens remaining on Earth. To gain recognition, the project needs 100,000 citizens, after which it can apply for UN status. The plan faces legal challenges, as existing international space law may not accommodate a stateless space nation.

A $6.3 million grant from The Leona M. and Harry B. Helmsley Charitable Trust will help save lives in Iowa by funding the purchase of LUCAS 2 Chest Compression System devices and providing training for their use in ambulances and hospitals. Each device costs $10,000 and can improve CPR outcomes by 5-50 percent. The grant aims to enhance the delivery of consistent chest compressions during cardiac arrests.

The 111th Congress, despite being the most productive in decades, will be remembered for its historic legislation and unprecedented unpopularity. Lawmakers passed landmark bills including the Affordable Care Act, Wall Street reform, and the repeal of "Don't Ask, Don't Tell." However, the session was marked by partisan gridlock, with the Tea Party's rise contributing to a Democratic loss of 63 House seats and a Senate majority reduction. Despite challenges, President Obama signed the "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" repeal, and Congress approved a nuclear arms treaty with Russia. The session concluded with a $858 billion tax cut extension and other measures, but the 9.6% unemployment rate and voter backlash highlighted the gap between legislative achievements and public satisfaction.

XPRIZE has launched a new ocean mapping challenge, offering a $7 million prize to teams developing advanced robotic exploration platforms. The competition, part of the foundation’s “Ocean Initiative,” aims to map and explore the deep ocean, an area that remains largely unexplored despite covering two-thirds of the planet’s surface. Teams must create devices capable of operating at depths up to 4,000 meters, tasked with creating high-resolution maps, taking high-definition images, and identifying key features. The competition, open to anyone, runs for three years, with registration now open. The top prize is $4 million, with additional bonuses for specific tasks.

NORAD has switched to Microsoft Bing for tracking Santa's journey this Christmas Eve, after five years of using Google. Both Google and NORAD will continue to monitor Santa's sleigh ride, with Google launching its own Santa Tracker website and apps. NORAD will use four high-tech systems—radar, satellites, Santa Cams, and fighter jets—to track Santa for 62 years, running its Santa-tracking site on Microsoft's Windows Azure cloud-computing platform and Bing Maps. The switch was a mutual decision, with Google still offering services like personalized calls from Santa through its YouTube channel. Updates will be available via NORAD's website, apps, and phone line, as well as on social media platforms.

A Bronx woman, Liana Barrientos, 39, was arrested after failing to appear in court on felony fraud charges related to her alleged marriage scam. Barrientos is accused of marrying 10 men between 1999 and 2010 without divorcing any of them, with seven of the men allegedly from "red-flagged" countries. She is charged with filing false marriage license applications and faces up to four years in prison if convicted. Barrientos is also reported to have two children with different men.

Texas native Peggy Sue Gerron, who inspired Buddy Holly's 1958 hit "Peggy Sue," passed away at a Lubbock hospital at the age of 78. Gerron, who released her autobiography "Whatever Happened to Peggy Sue?: A Memoir by Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue" in 2008, had been a close friend of Holly. She married drummer Jerry Allison from Holly's band The Crickets but later divorced. Gerron's story is part of the enduring legacy of Buddy Holly, who tragically died in a plane crash in 1959.

A historic 19th-century mining town called Cerro Gordo, nestled in the Inyo Mountains near Death Valley, has been sold for $1.4 million. The town, which once averaged a murder a week and was the largest producer of silver and lead in California, was listed for $925,000. Brent Underwood and Jon Bier, along with a group of Los Angeles investors, purchased the town on Friday the 13th. They plan to preserve the town's history and open it to the public, potentially adding overnight accommodations and events like writing retreats and concerts. The town features 22 buildings, including a saloon, a hotel, and a church, and spans over 300 acres with mineral rights. The new owners hope to maintain the town's historical integrity while enhancing its appeal to visitors.

A young African-American man visits his white girlfriend's family estate, only to find himself ensnared in a sinister truth. Jordan Peele's "Get Out" combines horror tropes with a sharp critique of racism, creating a film that is both terrifying and thought-provoking. The story follows Chris, played by Daniel Kaluuya, as he meets the parents of his girlfriend, Rose, played by Allison Williams. Peele masterfully weaves a narrative that is both unsettling and humorous, drawing from classics like "Rosemary's Baby" and "The Stepford Wives." The film's strength lies in its ability to explore the anxieties of existing as a black person in America while maintaining a tight, suspenseful plot. With a debut feature that is both a genre triumph and a social commentary, Peele has crafted a film that is both entertaining and deeply relevant.

Support LGBT youth by donating to the It Gets Better Project, which raises awareness and funds suicide prevention and anti-bullying programs. Share your story or create an It Gets Better video. Take the pledge to spread hope to LGBT youth. Purchase items from the store or buy the book to help the project. For $25, you can also order a copy of the book for your local library or school.

Airbus's A350 XWB aims to make long-haul flights more comfortable by addressing common complaints such as jet lag and cramped seating. With a 30% improvement in fuel efficiency compared to similar aircraft, the A350 features a larger and wider fuselage, allowing for more spacious economy seats and easier movement down the aisles. LED lights in the cabin adjust to mimic natural sunlight, helping to regulate passengers' circadian rhythms. The air is refreshed every two to three minutes, and the cabin is pressurized to 6,000 feet, enhancing passenger comfort. The aircraft's carbon fiber structure reduces weight, contributing to better fuel economy. Airbus emphasizes an adaptable interior design to meet various airline needs, ensuring the A350 remains relevant for the next 30 years. Qatar Airways was the first to introduce the A350 to its fleet, with other airlines following suit.

Britain plans to ban the sale of new gasoline and diesel cars by 2040, aligning with similar commitments from France and India, as part of efforts to combat air pollution. The move aims to accelerate the adoption of cleaner technologies, though experts question the feasibility and timeline. The government will invest £1.4 billion to support the transition to zero-emission vehicles, focusing on infrastructure and local air quality improvement measures. However, the auto industry remains cautious, citing the need for extensive planning and infrastructure development. The ban will also affect hybrid vehicles, signaling a significant shift in the automotive landscape.

A Jewish professor at Columbia University's Teachers College, Elizabeth Midlarsky, found her office vandalized with swastikas and anti-Semitic slurs on Wednesday. Midlarsky, who has studied the Holocaust, was shocked to discover the graffiti in her office entryway. The NYPD Hate Crimes Task Force is investigating the incident, treating it as aggravated harassment. Midlarsky's office had been previously vandalized in 2007, with a swastika spray-painted on her door. Both the Office of University Life and Barnard College issued statements denouncing the act and supporting Jewish students. Columbia University's President Thomas Bailey condemned the hate crime and reaffirmed the College's commitment to a respectful and welcoming environment.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has stated he believes the allegations against Alabama Republican Senate nominee Roy Moore and that Moore should leave the race. Moore's tweet in response called for McConnell to step aside, saying he has "failed conservatives and must be replaced." The Washington Post's report on Moore's alleged sexual misconduct with teenage women has increased pressure on Republicans to distance themselves from the candidate. The National Republican Senatorial Committee has cut its fundraising ties with Moore.

President-elect Donald Trump called for jailing or stripping citizenship from those who burn the American flag, tweeting, "Nobody should be allowed to burn the American flag - if they do, there must be consequences - perhaps loss of citizenship or year in jail!" This stance contradicts Supreme Court rulings that have upheld flag burning as a form of protected free speech. Trump's tweet sparked debate, with some Republicans like Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and late Justice Antonin Scalia supporting the right to burn the flag. Trump's proposal also aligns with his broader pattern of questioning democratic norms and free speech protections.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet began donating their daily crawl data to the Internet Archive. These data, added to the Wayback Machine with an embargo period, provide a continuous record of web content. The data also include examples of failed celebrity businesses, such as Hulk Hogan's Pasta Joint, Vince McMahon's XFL, and Kiss's various merchandise ventures. Despite their fame, celebrities often struggle to succeed in business, as evidenced by these and other failed endeavors.

President Donald Trump defended his record at a raucous rally in Iowa, where he attacked the Russia investigation as a "witch hunt" and touted job gains and an improving stock market as evidence of his economic policies. Trump, under siege in Washington with no major legislative achievements, focused on his supporters' loyalty and recent Republican victories in special congressional elections. He vowed to eventually fund a border wall with solar panels and criticized Democrats as "obstructionists." Trump also mocked Democratic candidates and praised his wealthy appointees, appearing more at ease in a campaign setting than in the White House. His visit to Iowa highlighted the challenges he faces in advancing his agenda and maintaining support beyond his base.

Newcomers "Project Almanac" and "Black or White" had quiet openings over the football-focused weekend. Clint Eastwood's "American Sniper" earned a strong $30.7 million over Super Bowl weekend, just missing the record for the biggest Super Bowl weekend gross of all time. The war drama, now in its third weekend, has become the biggest war-themed film of all time with a domestic tally of $247.98 million. Despite the NFL championship game, "American Sniper" easily outperformed three new films: "Project Almanac," "Black or White," and "The Loft." "Project Almanac," a found-footage thriller, opened to an estimated $8.5 million, while "Black or White," a racially charged drama starring Kevin Costner and Octavia Spencer, debuted with $6.5 million. "The Loft," an English-language remake, struggled with a soft $2.9 million opening.

Federal prosecutors have recommended felony charges against David Petraeus for mishandling classified information, according to federal officials. Attorney General Eric Holder must decide whether to file charges based on evidence assembled by the FBI and a case built by prosecutors. The recommendation stems from an affair between Petraeus and biographer Paula Broadwell, which began in 2011 while Petraeus was CIA director. Neither the Justice Department nor Petraeus' lawyer immediately commented. The case aims to put pressure on Holder to bring charges, especially considering lower-level officials have been prosecuted for similar offenses.

Ford has introduced the new F-Series Super Duty Limited, positioning it as the pinnacle of luxury and capability in heavy-duty pickup trucks. Starting at $80,835 for the F-250, the Limited series can reach up to $94,455 for the F-450, which is nearly the price of a Mercedes-Benz S-Class. The truck features two-tone leather seats, hand-finished dark ash wood trim, and a panoramic moonroof. Standard tech includes a 360-degree camera, adaptive cruise control, and lane-keeping alerts. Capable of towing up to 30,000 pounds, the F-450 Limited is designed for high-end customers like boat captains and contractors. Ford aims to offer a range of Super Duty models to cater to various customer needs, from the work-ready F-250 XL starting at $32,890 to the luxury-focused Limited.

Former Trump adviser Sebastian Gorka, who served as a deputy assistant to the president, had an active arrest warrant in Hungary for "firearm or ammunition abuse" during his entire White House tenure, according to a Hungarian police website. The warrant, first reported by 444 and BuzzFeed News, was issued in September 2016 and could have resulted from an incident as far back as 2009. Gorka, a former Breitbart writer and editor, declined to comment on the charges, stating on Twitter that he moved to the U.S. in 2008. He has faced questions about his credentials and connections to the "alt-right" movement. In 2016, Gorka was also charged with carrying a gun at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

Target was aware of a potential security breach nearly two weeks before it publicly disclosed the issue, according to a Bloomberg Businessweek report. In November 2013, Target installed a $1.6 million malware detection tool from FireEye and had a team in Bangalore monitor the system. On November 30, FireEye detected malware but Target's security team in Minneapolis did not act on the alert. The report suggests Target's security team disabled an automatic malware deletion feature, which could have prevented the breach. Target's CEO and CIO have faced criticism, with the CIO resigning. The article also speculates that a 22-year-old Ukrainian hacker named Rescator may have been behind the attack, though no definitive proof exists.

Samantha Anderson's life became a living nightmare when she suddenly lost the ability to swallow, a condition known as dysphagia. Diagnosed after months of struggling, her case turned out to be caused by shingles that had damaged four of her cranial nerves. After a series of treatments, including a high dose of the Alzheimer’s drug donepezil, she slowly regained her strength. Today, she can eat some foods with water until they become liquid, but still cannot eat alone due to the risk of choking. Her journey has taught her to appreciate the simple pleasures of life and has made her more resilient.

The Pentagon announced a six-month delay in lifting the ban on openly transgender troops joining the military, effective until January 1, 2018. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis approved the recommendation from the armed services to defer the implementation, citing the need to review the impact on military readiness and lethality. This decision affects only new recruits, not the estimated 15,500 transgender troops already serving. The delay follows requests from the Army and Marine Corps for additional time to prepare. While the move faces criticism from gay-rights advocates, who argue it undermines efforts to create a more inclusive military, it is seen as a pragmatic approach by some to ensure the military's readiness remains unaffected.

Since 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive, adding to the Wayback Machine. A long-awaited article in the Harvard Theological Review supports the argument that the "Gospel of Jesus’s Wife" is an authentic document, written on ancient Egyptian papyrus and referring to Jesus as being married. Harvard professor Karen L. King introduced this controversial text at a conference 18 months ago, sparking worldwide headlines and skepticism from many academic peers and the Vatican. New scientific tests, including carbon dating and ink analysis, found no evidence of modern forgery. The papyrus, likely cut from a larger document, contains eight partial lines, one of which says, "And Jesus said to them, ‘My wife.’" King believes the document may have been copied from a second-century Greek text and is significant for understanding early Christian debates about discipleship, celibacy, and the role of women. Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg plans to sell 41.35 million 'B' shares, worth approximately $2.3 billion, to cover taxes from exercising an option to buy 60 million additional 'B' shares. These shares carry 10 voting rights each, allowing Zuckerberg to retain significant control over Facebook. The sale will also benefit the Silicon Valley Community Foundation, with Zuckerberg donating $1 billion worth of stock. Zuckerberg's reduced stake will still give him about 62.8% of voting power. Zuckerberg has pledged to give away more than half his wealth to philanthropy as part of the Giving Pledge campaign. Facebook will use the $1.5 billion raised from selling 27 million new shares for unspecified purposes, while the company's stock price has surged, making Zuckerberg one of the world's wealthiest individuals.

Sen. Ted Cruz leads Rep. Beto O’Rourke by just 1 point in a new Emerson College poll, with Cruz at 38% and O’Rourke at 37%. The race remains tight, with 4% favoring other candidates and 21% undecided. O’Rourke continues to gain momentum, despite Texas not having elected a Democrat to the Senate in three decades. The poll shows O'Rourke leading among younger voters, while Cruz has an edge among older voters.

The sale of the highest-priced home in the U.S. is nearing completion, with 22-year-old heiress Petra Ecclestone set to purchase Candy Spelling's 57,000-square-foot Los Angeles mansion for an undisclosed price. The French chateau-style property, built in 1991, spans five acres and features amenities like a bowling alley, beauty salon, and parking for 100 cars. Spelling, widow of TV producer Aaron Spelling, plans to downsize after selling her previous home for $35 million in 2010. The buyer, Petra Ecclestone, will split her time between London and Los Angeles following her wedding to entrepreneur James Stunt in August. The sale highlights the role of foreign buyers in the U.S. real-estate market, with other high-profile purchases including a $100 million Silicon Valley home and a $90.9 million New York apartment.
