Relin had previously worked on humanitarian stories and had completed a new book on curing cataract-related blindness in the developing world, which was scheduled for publication in spring 2013. He is survived by his wife, stepfather, and sisters.

Austin voters backed a measure requiring fingerprint background checks for ridesharing company drivers, despite the companies' significant spending to repeal the city ordinance. Uber and Lyft, which spent over $8 million, are suspending operations in Austin. The companies argue their background checks are already rigorous. The election outcome could encourage other cities to impose similar regulations. The Austin vote was the first time a major U.S. city put such regulations to a vote, with the measure passing by a 56 to 44 percent margin.

For years, would-be thieves have targeted ATMs with ease, but a new design inspired by the bombardier beetle aims to change that. Researchers at ETH Zurich University have developed ATMs that emit hot, foamy dye when tampered with, marking both the cash and the perpetrator. This defense mechanism, which uses chemical reactions to produce a non-face-melting foam, could make ATM theft far less profitable. The technology, which includes DNA nanoparticles for tracing the source of the cash, represents a significant step in protecting financial assets from vandalism. While still in testing, this innovative approach could soon provide a robust barrier against theft.

A couple from Minnesota, Briggs Fussy and Brittney Husbyn, walked down the aisle for the second time 20 years after their first encounter as a ring bearer and flower girl, respectively. The pair first met in high school when Brittney sat in front of Briggs in government class and later discovered they had walked together in a wedding decades ago. They began dating in 2009 and got married on January 10, 2015, surrounded by 310 family and friends. The couple's unique story has garnered significant attention, with their godmother taking credit for bringing them together. They are enjoying the positive publicity and plan to keep articles about their wedding as a keepsake.

Actress Mira Sorvino has publicly apologized to Dylan Farrow, the adopted daughter of director Woody Allen, and expressed regret for working with Allen. Sorvino, who starred in Allen's 1995 film Mighty Aphrodite, wrote an open letter to Farrow, acknowledging that she initially dismissed Farrow's allegations of abuse due to the media's portrayal of the situation as stemming from a custody dispute. Sorvino stated that she was "naïve" at the time and did not thoroughly investigate the claims, adding that her support for Allen was "naively influenced" by his talent and the positive impact his films had on her career. She now believes the evidence strongly supports Farrow's story and expresses regret for not speaking out sooner. Sorvino also highlighted the support of other actresses, such as Ellen Page and Greta Gerwig, who have also distanced themselves from working with Allen.

During National Rifle Association (NRA) conventions, gun-related injuries and deaths in the U.S. drop by 20%, with a more significant 63% decrease in the hosting state, according to a new study in the New England Journal of Medicine. The analysis, based on nearly 76 million insurance claims from 2007 to 2015, shows that firearm injuries decrease during the conventions, particularly among men and in states with higher gun ownership. The findings suggest that experienced gun owners may still be at risk of accidents, challenging the notion that training and practice can eliminate safety concerns. The NRA disputes the study, calling the results "absurd" and questioning the sample size's impact on injury rates. The research highlights the ongoing debate on gun safety and the role of experienced users in reducing firearm-related incidents.

A man opened fire inside a ticketing area at Houston's Bush Intercontinental Airport, sending passengers scrambling and screaming. Carnell Moore, 29, entered Terminal B and fired two shots into the ceiling, causing panic. A Homeland Security Investigations agent confronted Moore, who was killed when he turned toward the agent and shot himself. Moore had posted on social media earlier that day about his intention to commit a mass shooting. The terminal was closed, but parts were later reopened. The incident disrupted flights, with some passengers rerouted to other terminals. Moore's home in Beaumont was later searched by authorities.

Starbucks has updated its dress code, allowing employees to wear a wider range of clothing and hair colors. The new policy permits shirt colors beyond solid black or white, including gray, navy, and dark denim, as well as patterns. Employees can now wear shorts, skirts, dresses, and dark wash jeans. Most notably, the company has removed restrictions on hair color, allowing employees to dye their hair any color as long as it is permanent or semi-permanent and meets food safety standards. The changes are intended to reflect the personal style of Starbucks employees and boost their morale.

Two men from south Georgia, Michael Mancil and James Dryden Jr., are accused of planning to attack a research facility in Alaska linked to conspiracy theories of mind and weather control. Authorities seized nine firearms, thousands of rounds of ammunition, and other items from their home. The suspects confessed to planning to destroy the facility, believing it trapped souls. The High Frequency Active Auroral Research Facility, now owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks, studies the Earth's ionosphere and has faced threats before. No specific charges beyond those related to drug offenses have been confirmed.

A Scottish mountaineer, Steve Aisthorpe, has found closure after the remains of his two friends, Kristinn Rúnarsson and Þorsteinn Guðjónsson, who disappeared in the Himalayas 30 years ago, were discovered. Aisthorpe, who was part of an expedition to Pumori in 1988, fell ill and sent his friends on ahead, never to see them again. The bodies were found last month by an American mountaineer at the base of a glacier. Aisthorpe, now 55, says the discovery brought a mix of emotions and has helped bring the group together. The remains were returned to Kathmandu, Nepal, for a cremation, and the ashes were sent back to Iceland. Aisthorpe plans to visit Iceland to meet the families of his friends. His faith played a significant role in helping him cope during the search and aftermath.

Alec Baldwin will return to "Saturday Night Live" this fall to impersonate President Donald Trump, despite his busy schedule, according to CNN. The actor's impression has become one of his most memorable sketches on the show. While he plans to limit the number of Trump impersonations, treating fans to "a couple celery sticks" rather than a "whole meal," Baldwin's return is anticipated by many. His previous hosting appearances on "SNL" total 17, a record, and his Trump impersonation has been a highlight of his career.

The family of Walter Scott, an unarmed African-American man fatally shot by a white police officer in North Charleston, South Carolina, has reached a $6.5 million settlement with the city. The settlement, approved by the North Charleston City Council, precludes the family from bringing civil claims over Scott's death. Scott's shooting, captured on video by a passerby, sparked national discussions on police use of force against black individuals. The police officer involved, Michael Slager, was fired and is facing murder charges. The city's decision to settle without a lawsuit is seen as setting a precedent for handling similar cases. Mayor Keith Summey emphasized the city's commitment to addressing the issue, stating that it was important to acknowledge the harm done to Scott and his family. The settlement also includes provisions for donating a portion of the money to flood victims and protecting city employees from being sued.

A Pittsburgh man claims he contracted a harmful parasite that eats away at the cornea of the eye after being splashed with water during a ride on the Raging Rapids at Kennywood Park. The lawsuit filed by Robert and Krystsina Trostle alleges negligence against Kennywood Entertainment. On July 2, the Trostles noticed the water around the ride was dirty and the waterfall was not operating. Robert was splashed with water in his left eye, leading to a series of severe eye issues including acute conjunctivitis and microsporidia keratitis. He had to undergo surgery to remove the parasite, which still causes ongoing vision problems. The lawsuit claims Kennywood failed to maintain adequate water safety protocols. Kennywood declined to comment on the pending litigation.

Hurricane Irma, currently a Category 3 storm in the Atlantic, has the potential to rapidly intensify and become a Category 4 hurricane before reaching the Lesser Antilles. Rapid intensification, defined as a 30-knot increase in wind speed in 24 hours, is a key factor in Irma's potential to strengthen. Irma's path and eventual impact on the United States remain uncertain, with forecasts ranging from a direct hit on the East Coast to a harmlessly offshore encounter. The European and American weather models diverge significantly, with the ECMWF suggesting a more westward track towards the Caribbean and the GFS predicting a more northerly path. Regardless of its exact path, Irma's strength and potential impact highlight the ongoing hurricane season's unpredictability and the need for preparedness in hurricane-prone areas.

A rare European bison, recently spotted in Germany after a 250-year absence, was shot and killed by local authorities, sparking controversy. Conservationists argue that the decision to shoot the bison, a protected species, was inappropriate and criminal, especially given the bison's non-threatening nature. The bison, likely a bull, had been wandering in the Ujście Warty National Park, straddling the German-Polish border. Brandenburg's Environment Minister noted that the bison are not considered dangerous and suggested tranquilization as an alternative. Critics blame a lack of trained wildlife professionals and question the state's handling of similar situations involving wolves and elk. The incident highlights the ongoing challenges in managing wildlife populations and balancing conservation efforts with public safety concerns.

Facebook is acquiring a significant number of patents from Microsoft, which it recently purchased from AOL. This move is seen as a strategic effort to strengthen Facebook's intellectual property portfolio, particularly in light of ongoing patent disputes, especially with Yahoo. The deal involves Facebook paying $550 million for 650 patents, while retaining a license to 275 AOL patents Microsoft plans to keep. Analysts view this as a move against Google and to create a more balanced power dynamic on the internet. The acquisition is part of Facebook's broader strategy to protect its interests and counter potential legal challenges, particularly from companies like Yahoo, which have already sued Facebook for patent infringement.

The brony community, adult male fans of the animated series My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic, faced a major setback when Hasbro, the franchise's owner, demanded the shutdown of the popular fan site PonyArchive.org, which offered free full episodes of the show. The site's defiant response, including a cheeky "Fuck you, Hasbro" message, sparked a controversy within the brony community. Despite the legal threats, the site's closure left fans, especially those in other countries, seeking alternative pirated sources. The incident highlighted the tension between corporate copyright enforcement and the passionate fanbase, with some bronies defending the site's stance while others criticized its aggressive response.

A former Royal Canadian Mint employee, Leston Lawrence, 35, was found guilty of stealing 22 gold "pucks" worth about $190,000. His job involved testing molten gold samples, and he managed to sell 17 of the pucks for a total of $130,000 before being caught by a bank employee who flagged his suspicious cheque deposits. Lawrence used his rectum to smuggle the pucks out, and evidence included Vaseline and latex gloves in his locker. He was sentenced to 30 months in jail and fined $190,000, which he must pay within three years or face another 30 months in prison. The mint has since improved its security measures.

A group of young men in their 20s in Washington state are seeking a "generic dad" to grill burgers and hotdogs for a Father's Day gathering. The event is set for the Saturday of Father's Day weekend in mid-June. Qualifications include at least 18 years of fatherhood experience and 10 years of grilling. The successful candidate must bring their own grill, with food and beer provided. Additional requirements involve discussing typical dad topics like lawnmowers, building decks, and musician Jimmy Buffett. Several potential grilling dads have already responded to the Craigslist ad.

Ford is shifting its focus to trucks, SUVs, and utility vehicles, announcing it will phase out most of its car lineup in North America by 2020, retaining only the Mustang and a new Focus Active crossover. The company aims to increase its investment in hybrid and electric powertrains for SUVs, aiming to become the leader in U.S. hybrid vehicle sales by 2021. Ford's first-quarter profit of $1.7 billion was driven by a lower tax rate, and the company plans further cost reductions and capital expenditure cuts. This move reflects broader industry trends towards larger, more profitable vehicles as car sales decline.

President Donald Trump's administration is preparing for potential conflicts with unregulated militia groups and transnational criminal organizations along the U.S.-Mexico border as thousands of Central American migrants approach. According to intelligence assessments, up to 200 unregulated militia members may be operating along the southwest border, potentially posing a threat to law enforcement and civilians. The Minuteman Project, a civilian border patrol group, has called for volunteers to converge on the border to support U.S. law enforcement and military. While some border communities are wary of these militia groups, others see them as necessary for border security. As the migrant caravan nears, tensions rise, and the U.S. military deploys additional troops to the southern border to handle the influx of migrants.

Manuel Uribe, once listed as the world's heaviest human being with a peak weight of 1,230 pounds (560 kilograms), has died at the age of 48. Uribe had been confined to his bed for years, relying on his mother and friends for daily care. His weight had significantly decreased to about 867 pounds (394 kilograms) before his death. Uribe was admitted to a hospital in Nuevo Leon, Mexico, due to cardiac issues, and had to be transported there using a crane. His first marriage and illegal immigration to the United States were mentioned, but his second marriage to Claudia Solis was one of the few times he left his home in recent years. Doctors have not yet determined the exact cause of death, which was believed to include liver problems and cardiac arrythmia.

Paul Ryan released a video promoting his unity strategy for the House GOP, but it plays like a campaign ad, fueling speculation that he could run for the Republican presidential nomination at a contested convention. Ryan has repeatedly denied interest in running for president, calling such speculation "fake unity." However, his office released a "Shermanesque" statement from his spokeswoman, AshLee Strong, definitively stating he is not interested in a nomination. The video, titled "Politics These Days," highlights Ryan's concerns about divisive politics and suggests he wants to inspire unity. Despite his denials, Ryan's popularity and the GOP's need for a unifying figure make him a potential candidate, especially if the party faces a contested convention.

A dog named Soshe was rescued from a flooded home in Pender County, North Carolina, thanks to the Humane Society of Missouri’s Disaster Response Team. The dog’s owner, who had evacuated about a week ago, was stranded in Wilmington, North Carolina, and unable to reach her dog. The rescue team made three trips by boat, facing deep floodwater that obscured house identification. After reaching the correct house, rescuers heard barking and found Soshe on a floating couch. The team carefully removed the dog and reunited her with her owner. The Humane Society of Missouri’s team also rescued other animals, including cats, chickens, goats, and horses, during their 10-day deployment following Hurricane Florence.

U.S. Army Staff Sgt. Robert Bales, suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and a traumatic brain injury, is set to plead guilty to avoid the death penalty in the killing of 16 Afghan villagers. His lawyer, John Henry Browne, revealed that Bales will recount the horrific attack for the first time during a plea hearing on June 5. The plea deal, which requires approval from a judge and a commanding general, aims to spare Bales the death penalty. Bales, who was on his fourth combat deployment, allegedly attacked two villages in southern Afghanistan after slipping away from his remote outpost. His mental state did not meet the criteria for an insanity defense, but his state of mind will be a key factor in the sentencing trial set for September. The case has strained U.S.-Afghan relations and intensified debates about the war's future.

A new bridge in Vietnam, known as the Golden Bridge, has opened at the Bà Nà Hills mountain resort near Da Nang. Suspended almost 4,600 feet above sea level, the nearly 500-foot-long bridge appears to be held up by a pair of giant stone-colored hands, creating a unique and visually striking structure. The bridge, part of the Thien Thai Garden development, offers visitors a 1.5 million-strong flock a chance to walk on a bridge seemingly suspended in the air. It is one of several unusual bridges around the world, including the Fan Bridge in London and the Lucky Knot bridge in China, each designed to be a statement in itself rather than just a functional walkway.

A new study from the University of Rochester suggests that emotions can influence our ability to perceive color. In two experiments, participants who felt sad performed worse on a color accuracy test than those who felt amused or neutral, specifically in distinguishing colors along the blue-yellow axis. Sadness did not affect their ability to perceive colors in the red-green spectrum. The researchers believe this may be linked to dopamine, as perception along the blue-yellow axis is associated with this neurotransmitter. This study supports the idea that our emotions can shape how we see the world around us.

Efforts to cool overheated reactors at Japan's Fukushima Dai-ichi nuclear plant faced a critical moment when officials decided to vent radioactive steam to relieve pressure, risking a hydrogen explosion. This decision, aimed at preventing a full meltdown, came amid a series of escalating crises. Without proper backup power, workers resorted to using seawater, a desperate measure that required continuous application. The potential for a catastrophic meltdown loomed as temperatures rose, leading to the venting of hydrogen-laden steam. If the reactor core were exposed, officials might resort to sealing the facility with cement, a process that could render the surrounding area uninhabitable for years. The situation at Fukushima Dai-ichi was part of a broader disaster, with the earthquake and tsunami causing widespread destruction and loss of life, leaving hundreds of thousands of people in urgent need of aid and supplies.

Fitch has placed the U.S. AAA credit rating on negative watch, citing prolonged congressional negotiations over raising the debt ceiling. The agency warns that the negotiations risk undermining the U.S. dollar's role as the global reserve currency and casting doubt on the country's full faith and credit. While Fitch still expects an agreement to be reached, the political brinkmanship could increase the risk of a default. The U.S. Treasury Secretary has said that extraordinary measures will be exhausted by October 17, leaving cash reserves of just $30 billion. Fitch expects to resolve the negative watch by the end of Q1 2014, contingent on the outcome of the negotiations and the perceived risk of similar episodes in the future.

Chelsea Handler is excited about her new studio at Universal Studios, which includes a private shower in her office. She jokes about no longer having to walk past guests semi-nude and mentions plans to use the space for creative audience interactions. The new set, formerly used by Jack Benny and Conan O'Brien, can accommodate a larger audience, and Handler hopes to maintain an intimate feel for her show. Her first guests in the new studio include Jennifer Aniston, Fergie, Miley Cyrus, and Christina Aguilera. The improved facilities will allow for better sound and lighting, and Handler is confident about staying with the show.

UK police have contacted Australian authorities about the discovery of a child's remains in a suitcase, which has led to speculation that the remains could be those of Madeleine McCann. The body, believed to be of a fair-haired girl aged between 2 ½ and 4, was found in a suitcase near Adelaide. Australian police have ruled out the possibility that the victim is Madeleine, stating there is no evidence linking the case. The remains were found alongside items of clothing and a quilt, and police are focusing their inquiries within Australia while considering any potential missing child.

An 86-year-old man in Port St. Lucie, Florida, is charged with first-degree premeditated murder for allegedly killing his 78-year-old wife because he could no longer afford her medications. William J. Hager told police he had been contemplating the act for several days due to his wife's chronic pain. After shooting his wife, Hager consumed coffee, contacted his daughters, and called 911. Neighbors describe the couple as kind and down-to-earth, though one neighbor noted the wife's physical suffering. Hager's wife had been ill for about 15 years, suffering from severe arthritis and other health issues. The couple had filed for bankruptcy in 2011. Hager's daughters live out of state and will be in Florida later that week. The sheriff's office suggests there are always options for people in similar situations, such as calling 2-1-1 for community resources.

Scientists have discovered a vast underground reservoir of liquid water beneath the Greenland ice sheet, stored in the air spaces between ice particles. This water, covering an area the size of Ireland, could provide crucial insights into sea level rise. The aquifer, estimated to hold about 140 billion tons of water, could contribute to sea level rise by 0.4 millimeters per year. Researchers found liquid water flowing back to the surface even when air temperatures were below freezing, suggesting the water remains liquid throughout the winter. The water is insulated by the large amounts of snow that fall on the ice sheet in the summer, preventing it from freezing. This discovery complicates the understanding of how meltwater from the ice sheet is stored and eventually reaches the ocean, potentially affecting predictions of sea level rise.

Democratic strategist Hilary Rosen sparked controversy by stating that Ann Romney "never worked a day in her life," a comment that drew widespread criticism. Rosen's statement was tweeted and retweeted, with many defending Ann Romney, who has raised five boys and battled MS and breast cancer. Ann Romney responded by tweeting, "I made a choice to stay home and raise five boys. Believe me, it was hard work." President Obama's campaign manager Jim Messina and top adviser David Axelrod tweeted disapproving statements, distancing the campaign from the remarks. Rosen doubled down, tweeting that she meant Ann Romney never had to care for her kids and earn a paycheck like most American women. Her comments are likely to be used by Democrats to highlight Ann Romney's privileged background compared to the struggles of many working women.

A 14-year-old boy from Cuba, Emanuel Zayas, died after undergoing surgery to remove a 10-pound tumor from his face at Holtz Children's Hospital in Miami. The tumor, which initially appeared as a pimple and grew larger than a basketball, was benign but posed risks of suffocation or neck breakage. Dr. Robert Marx, chief of oral and maxillofacial surgery for the University of Miami Health System, expressed that the physiological stress of the surgery was too much for Zayas, who had polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, a condition causing scar-like tissue instead of bone. Zayas' family plans to donate his body to science to aid in understanding polyostotic fibrous dysplasia.

A Minnesota couple dropped a $500,000 personal check into a Salvation Army kettle at a Cub Foods store in Rosemount over the weekend, making it the largest single donation the organization has ever received in the Twin Cities. The couple, who asked to remain anonymous, said they wanted to encourage others to give generously and honor their father, who served in World War I and was grateful for Salvation Army doughnut and coffee deliveries. They also mentioned relying on discarded food from a local grocery store when they first got married. The donation came a day after the Salvation Army's annual mystery benefactor or benefactors, "Saint Grand," left $1,100 in cash in two Roseville kettles. The Salvation Army is trying to raise $11.6 million this year and is seeking bell-ringer volunteers.

A manhunt continues for suspected killers William Boyette Jr. and Mary Rice, who are accused of a multi-state killing spree. Boyette, 44, and Rice, 38, are believed to be responsible for the deaths of three women and a home invasion. The pair allegedly killed Alicia Greer and Jacqueline Moore at a Florida hotel on January 31, then killed Peggy Broz in Alabama on February 3. On February 6, Rice was named as a suspect in the shooting of Kayla Crocker, 28, in Florida. Boyette and Rice are considered armed and extremely dangerous. Authorities have released images of the suspects and are urging the public to be cautious. The Escambia County Sheriff’s Office has doubled the number of deputies searching for the pair, who are believed to have changed their appearance. A $10,000 reward has been offered for information leading to their arrest.

Ellen DeGeneres will host the 86th Academy Awards for the second time, announced on Twitter. The decision comes after Seth MacFarlane's controversial hosting of the 85th Oscars, with MacFarlane's opening monologue criticized for its offensive content. DeGeneres, known for her kinder, gentler humor, is expected to bring a different tone to the show. The Academy rehired producers Craig Zadan and Neil Meron for the 2014 ceremony, which will air on March 2.

At least 132 children and nine staff members were killed in a Taliban attack on a military-run school in Peshawar, Pakistan, where 60 pupils were taking an exam when the gunmen entered. The attack, the deadliest in Pakistan, left 125 people injured, including seven army rescuers. Seven Taliban gunmen, wearing suicide bomb vests, entered the school through an undefended back wall, starting a siege that lasted eight hours. Students hid under tables as the gunmen shot at them, and one teacher was burned alive. Army commandos eventually killed all the attackers. The school, educating boys and girls from military and civilian backgrounds, is in an area where many army families live. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif declared three days of mourning and lifted the death penalty moratorium. World leaders condemned the attack, with even the Afghan Taliban criticizing it as un-Islamic.

President Obama, now tobacco-free with occasional use of nicotine gum, has been caught chewing gum during international meetings, drawing criticism from some. His gum-chewing is seen as a lifelong struggle, stemming from teenage years. Despite occasional lapses, Obama has been a vocal advocate for smoking cessation efforts. The practice has sparked controversy, with some viewing it as disrespectful, while others see it as a common habit. The White House physician noted that Obama should continue with smoking cessation efforts and maintain a healthy diet. His cholesterol levels have slightly increased, and he was advised to modify his diet to lower LDL cholesterol.

Pope Benedict XVI's visit to Mexico faces cyber attacks from the hacker group Anonymous, which claims the papal visit is a political move to support the conservative National Action Party. The Mexican Episcopal Conference's website on the papal visit was blocked, affecting logistics. Anonymous argues the visit will cost Mexicans money that could be better spent on the poor and is meant to support the PAN in the upcoming July 1 presidential election. The visit to Guanajuato, governed by the National Action Party, is seen as politically strategic. Pope Benedict is expected to address drug violence in Mexico, a sensitive issue that has claimed 50,000 lives over the past five years. Security measures are in place, and the local archbishop calls on people not to be afraid. The visit aims to reinforce faith and hope in a country grappling with violence and corruption.

The Dougherty siblings, accused in a cross-country crime spree, faced charges of attempted first-degree murder of a peace officer after a high-speed chase and shootout in southern Colorado. Lee Grace Dougherty, 29, was shot in the leg by Walsenburg Police Chief James Chamberlain after she pointed a machine pistol at him. The siblings, Ryan Dougherty, 21, and Dylan Dougherty Stanley, 26, were captured after a 20-mile pursuit along Interstate 25. They were found with two AK-47 assault rifles, a submachine gun, and a handgun. The chase began after they were spotted in Colorado Springs and ended near Walsenburg. The trio had been on the run since August 2, having fired at a Florida police officer and robbing a bank in Georgia. They were listed on the FBI's Most Wanted List and were being held on $1.25 million bond.

Illinois health officials are warning about a synthetic cannabis product linked to severe bleeding in at least 32 people across the state, including in the Chicago area. Since March 10, 17 cases of severe bleeding have been reported, with symptoms including coughing up blood, blood in the urine, bloody nose, and bleeding gums. The Illinois Department of Public Health reports 32 cases as of Friday, up from 22 the previous day. Symptoms vary but include heavy menstrual bleeding. Health officials are investigating to identify a common product and source. The synthetic cannabinoids, often called "fake weed," "K2," or "spice," are made up of hundreds of chemicals and can cause hallucinations and violent behavior. While there have been no deaths reported, health officials advise anyone experiencing unexplained bleeding or bruising to seek medical attention.

A federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the White House press credentials of CNN reporter Jim Acosta. U.S. District Court Judge Timothy Kelly, an appointee of President Donald Trump, granted CNN's request for a temporary restraining order, finding that Acosta suffered "irreparable harm" and dismissing the government's argument that CNN could send another reporter in Acosta's place. The judge's ruling comes after a contentious press conference where Acosta clashed with Trump and a White House intern. The White House initially cited physical contact between Acosta and the intern as the reason for revoking Acosta's credentials, but witnesses and a doctored video later suggested Acosta was not as aggressive as portrayed. Acosta's return to the White House is seen as a victory for press access and a challenge to the administration's treatment of journalists.

Over 50 ancient geoglyphs, including a swastika, have been discovered in northern Kazakhstan. Archaeologists found these man-made ground patterns using Google Earth, featuring various shapes like squares, rings, and crosses. The largest geoglyph measures 1,312 feet in diameter, suggesting construction by a large, well-established culture. While the purpose remains unknown, archaeologists have found evidence of rituals and land ownership markers. These geoglyphs join a global network of ancient enigmatic structures, similar to the famous Nazca Lines in Peru, adding to the mystery of prehistoric art and culture.

A new study using satellite technology has revealed that understory fires in the Amazon rainforest, previously hidden beneath the canopy, are destroying more forest than deforestation. These fires, which can last for weeks and damage up to 50% of the trees in affected areas, cover an area several times larger than that lost to deforestation annually. Climate conditions, not deforestation, are the primary factor in determining the frequency and extent of these fires. NASA scientists found that between 1999 and 2010, understory fires burned over 33,000 square miles of the Amazon, an area larger than South Carolina. These fires, often ignited by human activities like cooking or camping, pose a significant threat to the rainforest's health and carbon storage capabilities.

Michael Douglas sparked controversy by suggesting his throat cancer was caused by HPV, which he linked to cunnilingus in an interview with The Guardian. His publicist, Allen Burry, quickly clarified that Douglas did not claim oral sex was the specific cause of his cancer, but rather one of many factors. Douglas stated during an appearance at the American Cancer Society's 100th birthday celebration that HPV, a sexually transmitted disease linked to oral cancer, was a cause of his cancer. Burry denied that Douglas' comments might have led people to believe he contracted cancer from sex and refused to confirm if Douglas tested positive for HPV. Catherine Zeta-Jones, Douglas' wife, did not comment on the situation.

People bereaved by the sudden death of a friend or family member are 65% more likely to attempt suicide if the deceased died by suicide than if they died by natural causes, according to new UCL research. The study, involving 3,432 UK university staff and students aged 18-40 who had been bereaved, found that those bereaved by suicide were also 80% more likely to drop out of education or work, with 8% of the people bereaved by suicide having dropped out of an educational course or a job since the death. The findings highlight the profound impact that suicide might have on friends and family members, though these outcomes are not inevitable. Support is available, and people bereaved by suicide should not be made to feel responsible. Addressing the social stigma attached to suicide bereavement might help to limit its impact on people's lives. Previous studies have shown family history of suicide to be a risk factor for suicide attempt,

The British Library has revealed that three pairs of spectacles found in Jane Austen's writing desk may hold clues to the mystery of her early death. The spectacles, believed to have belonged to Austen, were tested and found to be convex lenses, indicating a need for glasses for close-up tasks. One pair was notably stronger than the others. The British Library suggests that Austen's increasing need for stronger glasses could point to an underlying health issue, possibly arsenic poisoning. Arsenic, common in medicines and water supplies during Austen's time, could have caused cataracts, requiring stronger lenses. However, the library acknowledges that the glasses may not have been prescribed by a physician and that Austen may not have worn them consistently. The findings have sparked debate among scholars and experts, who continue to explore various theories about Austen's death, including Addison's disease, cancer, and Hodgkin's lymphoma.

The Netherlands received the first victims' bodies from the downed Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 in a solemn ceremony at Eindhoven air base, with 40 coffins arriving from the crash site in eastern Ukraine. Flags were at half-mast, and a national day of mourning was observed in the Netherlands for the 298 victims, most of whom were Dutch. Forty hearses left for Hilversum, where identification will begin using DNA, dental records, and fingerprints. Two more planes carrying victims are due to arrive on Thursday. International anger over delays in recovering bodies has grown, with accusations against pro-Russian separatists. The Dutch air safety board reported valid data from the cockpit voice recorder, while UK investigators are examining the flight-data recorders. Meanwhile, fighting in eastern Ukraine has reportedly left 16 people dead.

At the 2015 Met Gala, Solange Knowles made a bold fashion statement in a Giles mini-dress with teeny pleats, writing on Instagram, "When @cartier is your date, and Giles is your dress." Her appearance, sans regal cape or bold, monochrome look, sparked curiosity and questions about whether she might upstage her sister Beyoncé, who usually arrives late. Will Solange's 3-D dress design be a hit or miss? Only time will tell.

Gary McKinnon, 43, with Asperger's syndrome, faces extradition to the U.S. despite medical concerns, including a "fixed-psychological conviction" of suicide if extradited. A report by Professor Jeremy Turk of St George's Hospital stated that suicide is "almost certain" for McKinnon. The Home Secretary, Alan Johnson, decided not to block the extradition, citing no breach of human rights. McKinnon's lawyer plans to seek a judicial review. McKinnon's mother criticized the decision, calling it "cruel and miserable." Opposition MPs and campaigners strongly oppose the extradition, arguing it disregards McKinnon's medical condition. McKinnon, accused of hacking Pentagon and NASA computers, could face up to 60 years in U.S. prison.

The TF-2 aims to revolutionize daily travel by combining air and ground transportation into a single system. This three-part design features a passenger cabin that transitions between a road vehicle and an air vehicle, allowing passengers to complete their journey without switching vehicles. The TF-2 takes off like a helicopter, flies like an airplane, and drives on roads using advanced electric propulsion, materials, and manufacturing techniques for safety and reliability. Classified as a "light sport" aircraft by the FAA, despite being 120 pounds over the weight limit, it can use front-wheel drive on roads at highway speeds, with wings folded for 30 miles per gallon efficiency. Once at a suitable take-off spot, wings fold down, and a rear-facing propeller engages for flight. Cruising at 115 mph with a 460-mile range, it requires a 1,700-foot runway and fits in a standard garage. One of its key safety features is the ability to drive

Iran plans to boost its naval presence in the Gulf to secure three disputed islands near the Strait of Hormuz, according to IRGC Commander Mohammad Ali Jafari. The islands, claimed by both Iran and the UAE, are part of a new naval defense zone inaugurated at Bandar Lengeh. Iran's media reports also mention a domestically-made advanced drone set to be displayed in February, capable of silent vertical take-off and landing. This comes amid ongoing tensions over the islands and Iran's claims of Israeli drone incursions.

Portland officials decided to drain and clean 38 million gallons of water from the Mt. Tabor Reservoir after video footage showed a teenager urinating near the reservoir. Despite the urine being diluted, city leaders chose to flush the water to avoid any public health concerns. The decision, which drew criticism from some, was made to ensure safety, even though the risk was minimal. The reservoir can hold up to 50 million gallons, and city officials say the risk of illness from the incident is very low. The teenager, Dallas Swonger, denies urinating in the water and claims he only urinated on a wall nearby. Swonger faces citations for trespassing and public urination, and the city is considering additional charges. The incident highlights the ongoing debate over the use of open-air reservoirs in Portland, which must be phased out by 2015 due to federal mandates.

British police have halted sharing information with the U.S. over leaks about the Manchester bombing, angering authorities and prompting a review by the U.S. Department of Justice. Prime Minister Theresa May expressed concern to President Donald Trump at a NATO summit, emphasizing the need for secure intelligence sharing. The leaks, including photos of bomb remnants published by the New York Times, have strained the "special relationship" between the U.K. and U.S. security services. Eight men are in custody, and searches have yielded crucial evidence. The attack, which killed 22 people and injured 116, has raised the threat level to critical, with troops deployed to key locations.

During a Sunday morning show, Republicans who attended the immigration meeting where President Donald Trump reportedly called immigrants from Haiti and African nations "shithole countries" defended his comments, stating they were misrepresented or that they couldn't recall him saying those exact words. Conservative commentator Rich Lowry suggests that Trump might have actually said "shithouse countries" instead of "shithole," noting that the general tenor of the discussion has been reported accurately.

Jesse James' alleged mistresses continue to surface. Brigitte Daguerre, a photographer, claims to be his third known mistress, stating their relationship was brief compared to the others. She has 195 text messages with James, detailing their interactions. Meanwhile, Melissa Smith, a stripper, reveals a two-year affair with James during his marriage to Sandra Bullock, involving multiple encounters and no mention of Bullock. Smith, who has a history of legal troubles, recently sold her story to a tabloid. Both women highlight James' pattern of infidelity, with one suggesting he is "once a cheater, always a cheater."

Chelsea Manning believes she had a "responsibility to the public" when she leaked a trove of classified documents, saying she didn't think she was risking national security. Manning, who was formerly known as Bradley Manning, told ABC's "Good Morning America" that she leaked the 700,000 military and State Department documents because of the human toll of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. She has accepted responsibility for her actions but says no one directed her to do so. Manning was released from a military prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, after serving seven years of a 35-year sentence, which was commuted by former President Barack Obama. She remains in the Army but is off duty while appealing her court-martial conviction. Manning also discussed her struggles with gender transition while in prison, noting that she tried to kill herself twice and fought for hormone treatments that she says are crucial for her well-being.

Swiss voters will decide next month whether to guarantee every citizen and legal resident a generous monthly income, a unique proposal that could set a global precedent. On June 5, Swiss citizens will vote on a plan to provide $2,600 tax-free to every adult and $650 to each child. The initiative, spearheaded by a group of artists, writers, and intellectuals, aims to offer people an option of reducing their working hours while maintaining a decent standard of living. While supporters argue it would lead to a more motivated workforce and a more stable economy, critics contend it could destroy work motivation and strain the government’s budget. The plan, estimated to cost about $200 billion a year, would be funded by increasing the value-added tax. The vote is a notable step for the basic income movement, potentially legitimizing the idea on a national scale.

The nation's top military officer, Admiral Mike Mullen, expects a significant increase in family crises and suicides among service members as troops return from multiple deployments. With the drawdown in Iraq, bases like Lewis-McChord in Washington state will see a large influx of soldiers, presenting challenges for commanders. Mullen is particularly concerned about rising suicide rates, which have hit record highs in the Army. Fort Hood, a major Army post, has seen 14 confirmed and six suspected suicides since the beginning of the year, on pace to shatter its annual record. Despite efforts to reduce stigma and increase mental health resources, Fort Hood officials are struggling to explain the surge in suicides, attributing them to stressors like family issues, financial problems, and substance abuse.

President Donald Trump in a wide-ranging interview with CBS's "60 Minutes" expressed uncertainty about climate change, suggesting it might "change back again" and that he doesn't want to "give trillions and trillions of dollars" to address it. He also vowed "severe punishment" if evidence emerges that Saudi Arabia was behind the disappearance of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, though he noted he wouldn't want to harm U.S. defense industry jobs. Trump defended his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, calling him a "good guy" despite human rights concerns. On trade, he insisted he's not trying to "crush" China's economy but wants fair negotiations. He criticized the European Union, claiming it takes advantage of the U.S. in trade. Trump disputed claims that NATO has kept the peace for 70 years and said he has a good relationship with China's President Xi Jinping. He denied any involvement of Russia in the 2016 election,

Kanye West was not placed on a 51-50 psychiatric hold before voluntarily being hospitalized for exhaustion, a source confirms to PEOPLE. West, 39, canceled the remaining 21 dates of his Saint Pablo tour due to exhaustion and sleep deprivation, according to a source. Kim Kardashian West supported her husband during his hospitalization and canceled her scheduled appearance at the Angel Ball in New York to visit him. West's insurance policy may cover the costs related to the tour cancellation, but specifics remain unclear.

Research by San Diego State University suggests the San Jacinto fault, which runs through East County, could produce earthquakes as powerful as magnitude 7.6 to 7.7, potentially rivaling the San Andreas fault. Led by seismologist Tom Rockwell, the study, published in Pure and Applied Geophysics, examines 21 seismic events over the past 4,000 years and indicates that if the San Jacinto fault ruptures onto the San Andreas, it could approach a magnitude 8.0. This finding highlights the significant earthquake risk posed by the San Jacinto fault, which is part of the larger San Andreas system.

A French serial killer, Michel Fourniret, known as the "Ogre of the Ardennes," has confessed to the murder of British student Joanna Parrish, 20, in 1990, according to her family's lawyer. Fourniret, already serving a life sentence for the rape and murder of seven other young women, admitted to killing Parrish and another teenager, Marie-Angele Domece, during interviews with magistrates in Paris. Lawyer Didier Seban stated that Fourniret made detailed and repeated confessions, acknowledging his involvement in both cases. This development brings closure to Parrish's family after years of denials and unresolved investigations. Fourniret's wife, Monique Olivier, who had twice accused him of the unsolved murders, will also be questioned. The case of Parrish, who worked as a language assistant in Auxerre, has haunted her family for decades.

Manchester police confirmed 19 fatalities and around 50 injuries after an explosion at Ariana Grande's concert on May 22, 2017. The incident, treated as a possible terrorist attack, left children among the victims. Emergency services rushed to the scene, and witnesses described chaos as concertgoers fled. Grande, who was not injured, expressed deep sorrow on Twitter, writing, "broken. from the bottom of my heart, i am so so sorry. i don't have words." The attack, the deadliest in the UK since 2005, prompted increased security measures across the country and international condolences.

Charlie Sheen has not yet commented on the death of his former assistant and close friend, Rick Calamaro, who was found deceased in his Los Angeles apartment. Calamaro, 46, had reportedly been dead for a few days before police discovered him, with numerous pain medications and an open bottle of alcohol in the apartment, according to TMZ. Calamaro was known for his close relationship with Sheen, having been present during Sheen's infamous 36-hour drug binge in October 2010. While Calamaro's cause of death has not been determined, many have speculated that he may have been a bad influence on Sheen and possibly supplied him with drugs over the years.

Iranian protesters stormed British diplomatic compounds in Tehran, smashing windows, burning the British flag, and setting a car ablaze in response to new sanctions imposed by London over Iran's nuclear program. The British Foreign Office condemned the attacks, stating they were "outrageous and indefensible." The U.N. Security Council and U.S. President Barack Obama also expressed strong disapproval. The storming of the embassy is seen as a sign of deepening political infighting within Iran's ruling hardline elites, with conservatives attempting to force the government to expel the British ambassador. British Prime Minister David Cameron warned of "serious consequences" for failing to protect British staff. British embassy personnel were accounted for and safe. The attacks were reminiscent of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. embassy in Tehran and the hostage crisis that followed.

Heather Locklear's daughter Ava celebrated her 21st birthday, and Heather shared a touching video tribute on Instagram. The actress, currently in rehab for substance abuse and mental health issues, showcased photos of Ava throughout the years, expressing her love and pride. Locklear praised Ava as "the kindest, funniest, smartest, most beautiful child in the world." A source notes that Heather is doing well in rehab and is scheduled to remain there until September. Heather was previously arrested in June for allegedly attacking a police officer and an EMT during a disturbance at her home, and is now facing a lawsuit from the paramedic who claims to have suffered injuries during the incident.

This is the first serious biography of Julius Rosenwald, who transformed Sears, Roebuck into America's most important retailer and became one of the early 20th century's notable philanthropists. Born to German Jewish immigrants, Rosenwald apprenticed in New York before joining Sears, where he eventually became its most powerful executive. He founded Chicago's Museum of Science and Industry and supported the construction of over 5,300 schools named after him in the American South. Rosenwald's philanthropy extended to funding the development of black artists and improving living conditions for African Americans. His life and work highlight his commitment to family, community, and giving back, making him a significant figure in American business and philanthropy.

In India, a 16-year-old girl died after being set on fire by her attacker in Sagar district, Madhya Pradesh, the third such case reported this month. The girl was allegedly raped and burned alive after her cousin informed the accused she was home alone. Police arrested the girl's cousin and the 28-year-old suspect. In a separate incident, a 17-year-old girl remains in critical condition after being set on fire by a man who allegedly wanted to marry her but was rejected. Widespread outrage over sexual violence in India has surged following high-profile cases, including the 2012 gang rape and murder of a student in Delhi, which led to new anti-rape laws.

Astronomers have identified the first comet with water similar to Earth's oceans, significantly boosting the theory that comets played a major role in delivering water to a young Earth. The comet, 103P/Hartley 2, analyzed using the Herschel Space Observatory, exhibits a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio nearly identical to that of Earth's oceans. This finding suggests that comets may have contributed more extensively to Earth's water supply than previously thought. Previously, comets from the Oort Cloud were found to have higher deuterium ratios, making their contribution to Earth's water less likely. However, Hartley 2, originating from the Kuiper Belt, shows a deuterium fraction closer to Earth's, opening the possibility that many Kuiper Belt objects could have similarly contributed to Earth's water. This discovery challenges existing models of early Earth and the origins of its water, prompting a reevaluation of the role comets played in its formation.

People have been warned not to take selfies in the bad weather as Storm Barney sweeps across the UK. The storm, currently moving across central Ireland with gusts of 78mph, has caused power cuts, fallen trees, and diverted flights. With winds expected to pick up further over Wales and southern England, the Environment Agency and the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) have warned against taking "storm selfies," citing numerous past incidents where people have died or been injured while attempting to capture extreme moments. Storm Barney is the second named storm after Abigail hit last week, caused by a series of low pressure systems from the Atlantic.

A 23-year-old woman named Ruth Correa and her 26-year-old brother Sergio Correa are charged with the brutal murder of a Griswold couple and their 21-year-old son. Court documents reveal that Ruth Correa and her brother had conspired with the son to exchange drugs for guns kept in the couple’s home. Matthew Lindquist, the son, had texted about the planned drug-for-guns exchange, but backed out when it turned violent. Ruth Correa told investigators that the incident began when Matthew Lindquist panicked and ran, leading to a chase where her brother used a machete to hit him. The couple and their son were later found dead in their burned-out home. Ruth Correa admitted to stabbing Matthew Lindquist multiple times, and Sergio Correa is said to have used a bat to beat the parents. The couple’s dog was also reportedly injured. Ruth Correa and her brother stole items from the home before setting it on fire.

An affluent Connecticut couple, Jeffrey and Jeanette Navin, disappeared a week after losing an appeal over over $2.2 million in debt, according to court records. The couple, last seen on August 4 at their refuse company in Westport, were reported missing by relatives on August 7. Their car was found in a commuter parking lot off the Merritt Parkway in Westport on August 9. The couple's financial troubles, including a long-running foreclosure battle over a $1.4 million home in Guilford, have been detailed, but their family maintains the debt issues are unrelated to their disappearance. The investigation has been turned over to state police, who are searching the couple's son's home in Bridgeport. Detectives are reviewing bank records, credit card purchases, and cellphone records, and interviewing friends and coworkers. The couple's disappearance remains unsolved.

Two FBI agents who worked on the Russia probe exchanged texts critical of President Donald Trump, including calling him an "idiot," according to messages turned over to Congress. Special Counsel Robert Mueller removed one of the agents, Peter Strzok, from the investigation "immediately" after learning of the texts in late July. The messages, which span from mid-2015 to December 2016, also show the agents holding negative views of other political figures, including Chelsea Clinton and former Attorney General Eric Holder. The texts are fueling Republican calls for a second special counsel to investigate Mueller's operation.

Susan Olsen, the former actress who played Cindy Brady on "The Brady Bunch," was fired from her role as a co-host on LA Talk Radio's "Two Chicks Talkin' Politics" segment after posting a homophobic rant on Facebook. The openly gay co-host, Leon Acord-Whiting, accused Olsen of spreading "outrageous misinformation" and called for her dismissal from the show. In response, Olsen engaged in a heated exchange, sending Acord-Whiting an expletive-laden private message. LA Talk Radio subsequently announced Olsen's termination, emphasizing their commitment to a positive and inclusive environment for their listeners.

The Department of Homeland Security announced heightened security measures at federal buildings nationwide on Tuesday, citing recent shootings at the Canadian Parliament and ongoing U.S. military operations as reasons for increased vigilance. These precautionary steps, not based on specific intelligence, will be implemented at federal facilities in the District of Columbia and other major cities, with details remaining undisclosed. Secretary Jeh Johnson emphasized the need for enhanced protection amid public calls for attacks on the homeland and government personnel.

As U.S. combat troops prepare to leave Iraq by the end of 2011, the Obama administration is planning a significant civilian effort, including doubling the number of private security guards to up to 7,000, to fill the void. The State Department will take over training the Iraqi police, largely through contractors. American diplomats will operate in two new $100 million outposts to manage potential conflicts between the Iraqi Army and Kurdish forces. The State Department aims to protect civilians in a country still facing threats from Al Qaeda-linked insurgents and Iranian-backed militias. While the U.S. military presence will be reduced to around 50,000 troops by August 31, the civilian mission will focus on training, economic development, and maintaining influence in Iraq.

Paramount has made changes to its promotional materials for "Jack Reacher," the upcoming Tom Cruise action film, in light of the Newtown school shooting. The studio has decided to cut a scene featuring Cruise's character using a semi-automatic weapon from some of the marketing spots. Meanwhile, Quentin Tarantino's "Django Unchained," also rated R and set to open on Christmas Day, has had its Los Angeles premiere canceled by The Weinstein Company. The company stated, "Our thoughts and prayers go out to the families of the tragedy in Newtown, Conn., and in this time of national mourning we have decided to forgo our scheduled event." Other Hollywood events have also been postponed or canceled, including the planned premiere of "Jack Reacher" in Pittsburgh.

Six members of the Harvard Women’s Soccer recruiting class of 2012 publicly denounce a “scouting report” written by members of the 2012 men’s soccer team, detailing inappropriate comments about their physical appearances. The women express frustration that such behavior is not only common but also normalized, affecting female athletes across various sports. They emphasize the importance of mutual respect and the need for men to take responsibility for their actions. Additionally, the article reveals that the men’s cross country team also produced yearly spreadsheets containing explicit comments about the women’s team, highlighting the broader issue of objectifying female athletes. The men’s soccer team subsequently apologized and committed to addressing the cultural issues within their team and across Harvard Athletics to promote gender equality and respect.

Five years after Casey Anthony's acquittal in the death of her daughter Caylee, new allegations resurface in her bankruptcy case, with her former private investigator, Dominic Casey, claiming Anthony had a sexual relationship with her lawyer, Jose Baez. Baez strongly denies these claims, stating he has always adhered to high ethical standards. This isn't the first time Dominic Casey has made controversial claims, as he previously suggested Anthony and others were involved in Caylee's disappearance. Baez's firm is threatening legal action against Dominic Casey.

Scientists have discovered that the hormone kisspeptin, which plays a crucial role in triggering puberty and regulating sexual fertility, can also enhance brain activity related to sexual arousal and romantic love. A study from Imperial College London found that an injection of kisspeptin increased activity in brain regions associated with sexual and emotional processing in healthy young men. This suggests kisspeptin could potentially be used to treat psychosexual disorders and depression, as well as aiding in infertility treatments. The hormone's ability to modulate sexual and bonding stimuli could have significant implications for understanding and treating sexual and emotional processing issues.

Juneau Mayor Stephen "Greg" Fisk was found deceased at his residence, with the cause of death pending an autopsy. His adult son discovered the body and called 911. Juneau Police are investigating and have ruled out immediate speculation of foul play. The City and Borough of Juneau canceled scheduled Assembly meetings. Deputy Mayor Mary Becker will temporarily assume the role of acting mayor. The investigation is ongoing, with autopsy results expected within days. (KTUU)

Lady Gaga is set to launch a residency at the Park Theater in Las Vegas in late 2018, with plans for 36 shows that could extend into 2020. The deal, reportedly worth nearly $100 million, allows Gaga to earn about $400,000 per performance. She is currently starring in the film "A Star is Born" and has been in good form since recovering from health issues. The residency will feature a new show and marks Gaga's lifelong dream of performing in Las Vegas.

President Donald Trump has released the final batch of documents related to the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, as mandated by a 1992 law. The National Archives released 19,045 documents, the largest batch to date, on Thursday. Trump had previously allowed the release of some documents but blocked others at the request of the FBI and CIA, citing national security concerns. These documents, which include 15,884 partially released records with heavy redactions, will undergo further review over the next three years. The remaining documents, including 3,161 that were fully withheld, may never be released. The release is part of an ongoing effort to fulfill a 25-year deadline set by Congress to make most Kennedy assassination records public.

A rock festival in Germany, Rock am Ring, was evacuated on Friday due to a suspected terrorist threat, with thousands of people temporarily displaced. The festival, scheduled to run for three days near Koblenz, faced this disruption following "concrete indications" that could not be dismissed. Organisers halted the event after police requested it "due to a terrorist threat." This closure occurred just a few weeks after a terrorist attack in Manchester claimed 22 lives. Despite the heightened security measures, including an increase in police presence to 1,200 officers, the festival's organisers and authorities prioritised safety, urging attendees to leave the site calmly. The German band Rammstein was set to perform that night, but their show was postponed. The incident highlights ongoing concerns about terrorism in Europe.

A Groupon Super Bowl commercial that pokes fun at the political situation in Tibet has sparked controversy, potentially jeopardizing the company's expansion plans in China. The ad, which aired during the Super Bowl, humorously portrays Tibetans in trouble and their culture in jeopardy, offering a Groupon deal for Tibetan food. This has angered both U.S. and Chinese viewers, with Chinese Internet users criticizing Groupon for mixing business with politics. If Groupon hopes to enter the Chinese market, it may face challenges given the sensitive nature of the Tibet issue. The ad may also impact Groupon's relationship with potential Chinese partners like Tencent, as it could be seen as an affront to Chinese national sentiment.

Cesar Millan, star of the Nat Geo WILD Channel's "Cesar 911," is under investigation for alleged animal cruelty after a complaint was made against his dog psychology center in Santa Clarita, California. The complaint, made by a single citizen, involves a dog attacking and injuring a pig during a training session. Millan's spokesperson defended his methods, stating that the dog, Simon, was on a long lead and that the pig was tended to immediately after the incident. A petition and call for support have been launched to demand the removal of Millan's shows from airtime, citing concerns over the use of animals as bait and the potential for public imitation of his methods.

President Donald Trump criticized NFL players for protesting during the national anthem at preseason games, tweeting that they should be "happy" and "cool" and suggesting they find another way to protest. Trump accused the players of not being able to define what they are protesting and said football games are not the place for such demonstrations. The protests, which began two seasons ago to address racial injustice and police brutality, have grown into an NFL-wide trend. Players like Malcolm Jenkins and Kenny Stills raised their fists or knelt during the anthem. The NFL Players Association did not immediately respond. Trump's attention to the issue has sparked significant controversy and led to a new league policy allowing fines for players who do not stand during the anthem, though enforcement has been on hold.

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has scaled the country's highest mountain, Mount Paektu, state media reports. Photos show him standing atop the 2,750-metre peak, with troops cheering. The climb is part of North Korea's propaganda efforts, linking the Kim family to the sacred mountain. Kim Jong-un, like his father before him, frequently makes "field guidance trips" to showcase his connection to the people. Despite the country's economic struggles and human rights issues, North Korea continues to focus on its nuclear weapons program and military development.

Josh Greenberg, co-founder of the once-popular music-streaming site Grooveshark, was found dead in his Gainesville, Florida, home on Sunday evening at the age of 28. His mother stated there was no evidence of injuries or drugs, and toxicology results are pending. Greenberg was relieved about the April settlement that shut down Grooveshark, as it ended a lawsuit from major record labels. He was known for mentoring young entrepreneurs and computer programmers through programs like Grooveshark University and the Founders Pad business incubator. Grooveshark had up to 40 million users and 145 employees at its peak. Friends and colleagues described Greenberg as a visionary and a mentor, noting his contributions to Gainesville's tech community. A memorial service is planned to honor his legacy.

A Thai man hanged his 11-month-old daughter on Facebook Live and then killed himself in an apparent dispute with his wife, Thai police said. The disturbing footage was posted Monday evening and made inaccessible by Facebook late Tuesday. The incident highlights the ongoing challenge Facebook faces in managing graphic content. Less than two weeks prior, a man in Cleveland, Ohio, streamed himself shooting a man to death. Facebook has been under scrutiny for its handling of such videos, with founder Mark Zuckerberg acknowledging the company has "a lot of work" to do. The company is exploring ways to speed up its review process and is considering using artificial intelligence to flag potentially problematic content.

Scientists have made progress in using stem cell therapy to repair heart damage caused by heart attacks. In a study published in Nature, researchers from Japan injected heart cells created from the skin of a genetically matched donor into the hearts of monkeys that had undergone induced heart attacks. These lab-made heart cells replaced about 16% of the damaged tissue and helped the monkeys' hearts pump more effectively. However, the procedure led to the development of unusual heart rhythms in the monkeys, which the researchers acknowledge requires further investigation. While the therapy shows promise, it is not yet ready for human trials due to the risk of arrhythmias. Experts suggest that a bank of pre-prepared, matched cells could be used to treat patients more quickly than the current method of reprogramming and differentiating the patient's own cells.

The White House corrected its official transcript of President Trump's Monday press conference, where he reportedly insulted ABC News reporter Cecilia Vega. In the corrected transcript, Trump is quoted as saying, "she’s shocked that I picked her. Like in a state of shock," to which Vega responded, "I’m not, thank you, Mr. President." Trump later said, "That’s okay. I know you’re not thinking, you never do," before refusing to answer a question about Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh. The incident drew criticism online, with Vega emphasizing the right to ask any question at a press conference.

Facebook users were caught off guard on Friday when a bug caused the social network to mistakenly label many accounts as deceased, displaying memorial banners on profile pages. The error, intended for memorialized profiles, appeared on the pages of people who were still alive, including Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Users posted status updates to reassure friends and family they were not dead. "We hope people who love [Facebook user] will find comfort in the things others share to remember and celebrate [his or her] life," the banner read. The issue was quickly addressed by Facebook, which issued a statement apologizing for the mistake and confirming the bug has been fixed.

North Korea has threatened to conduct a "new form of nuclear test," escalating rhetoric after the United Nations Security Council condemned its recent ballistic missile launches. The North Korean foreign ministry stated that upcoming drills by the Korean People's Army will involve "more diversified nuclear deterrence," potentially including a "new form of nuclear test" to bolster its nuclear arsenal. This follows North Korea's firing of two medium-range Rodong missiles into the sea off the Korean peninsula, in defiance of U.N. resolutions. The Security Council condemned the launches, expressing concern over a potential regional arms race. The article also discusses the possibility of North Korea preparing multiple test sites for more frequent nuclear tests, raising concerns about the frequency and scale of future tests.

Mitt Romney said it is "not a time to be talking about the politics associated with what happened in Aurora" during an interview, but stressed that legislation he signed as governor of Massachusetts to ban assault weapons was a "combination of efforts" from both sides of the debate. Romney believes new laws will not make a difference in tragedies like the Colorado shooting. Both presidential campaigns dialed down the rhetoric after the tragedy, but Romney admitted the pause was over. Obama and Romney both changed their tone, turning campaign events into speeches remembering the victims. However, Romney criticized Obama's campaign for negative ads.

Colombian authorities are investigating the crash of a chartered plane carrying the Brazilian soccer team Chapecoense, which killed 71 people, including 19 team members, leaving only six survivors. The British Aerospace 146 jetliner's cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder were found among the wreckage. Initially, officials suggested an electrical failure, but there were also reports of heavy rain and the plane disappearing from radar just before the crash. A surviving flight attendant reported the plane had run out of fuel. The team was on its way to play the first game in the Copa Sudamericana final against Atletico Nacional. The crash site is in La Union, Colombia, and the plane had a maximum range of about 2,965 kilometers, raising concerns about fuel management. The team had been having a breakout season, advancing to the Copa Sudamericana finals after defeating top teams like San Lorenzo and Independiente. The tragedy has affected the soccer world,

The Sudbury Police Department is reminding residents to transport their Christmas trees safely, sharing a photo of a car nearly hidden under a large conifer on their Facebook page. A single tree was found on a small sedan, and the family inside was given a holiday-themed warning by an officer, who helped secure the tree and marked it with caution tape. The department uses this example to encourage responsible vehicle loading during the holiday season.

Custom-fit condoms, now available in 60 sizes, aim to address the common complaints of poor fit and discomfort. ONE Condoms, based in Boston, has launched myONE Perfect Fit, offering a range of 60 different condom sizes to better suit a wider variety of penis sizes. This innovation addresses the issue that only 12% of men find their condoms properly fitted, leading to discomfort and potential health risks. The new condoms come in 10 different lengths and 9 widths, providing a more comfortable and pleasurable experience. However, the public health impact remains uncertain, as similar innovations have faced challenges in gaining market acceptance due to regulatory and manufacturing complexities. Despite these hurdles, ONE Condoms hopes to increase condom usage and reduce unintended pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections.

A study examining 45-year trends in women's time allocation and household management energy expenditure (HMEE) reveals a significant decrease in HM activities and associated EE. From 1965 to 2010, the time spent on HM by women decreased from 25.7 hours per week to 13.3 hours, with non-employed women experiencing a 42% reduction and employed women a 30% reduction. This shift was accompanied by an increase in screen-based media use, with women now spending more time watching TV than on HM activities combined. The study suggests that the decline in HMEE may contribute to the increasing prevalence of obesity, as the reallocation of time from active pursuits to sedentary pastimes has health consequences.

A 15-year-old girl from Mississauga, Ontario, called 911 last Tuesday to report that her parents "forced her" to go on vacation with them, but police determined there was no real emergency and cautioned her for misuse of the emergency number. Northumberland OPP Const. Stephen Bates said the call appeared to be "a case of a teenager being a teenager," as the girl perceived it as a serious issue but it was not an appropriate use of 911. Officers responded to a rental cottage in Trent Hills to ensure everyone was safe, and the girl has been cautioned for tying up police resources that could impact others in need of assistance.

A couple planning to get married inadvertently revealed the woman was already pregnant in a Facebook post meant to announce their engagement. The couple, Miranda Levy and her fiancé, shared a picture of themselves with a ring on Miranda's finger. However, her friends noticed a pregnancy test in the lower left corner of the photo. Miranda was initially confused by their questions about the test, but eventually admitted, "Hey we're having a baby, too." The incident serves as a reminder to always check and crop photos before posting on social media.

A man skinny-dipped in the shark tank at Ripley's Aquarium of Canada in Toronto, swimming among marine animals before security asked him to leave. Security footage shows the man entering the aquarium, buying a ticket, and immediately stripping before jumping into the Dangerous Lagoon, a 2.9-million-litre tank housing sharks and other marine life. The man was eventually escorted out by security but not before he was seen swimming with sharks and even performing a backward dive into the water. No marine animals were harmed, but the stunt was deemed extremely dangerous. The man, identified as David Weaver, 37, from Nelson, B.C., is wanted for assault and mischief. He is described as 35-40 years old, 5'10", 220 pounds, with a shaved head, dark goatee, and missing front tooth.

Troubled singer Amy Winehouse died from alcohol toxicity, a second inquest has confirmed. The coroner recorded a verdict of misadventure, identical to the first inquest in 2011, which had to be repeated due to the deputy coroner's lack of proper qualifications. Winehouse, 27, was found dead at her home in Camden, north London, with a blood alcohol level over five times the legal driving limit. Two empty vodka bottles were found beside her bed. The inquest heard she specifically said she did not want to die the night before. Winehouse struggled with an eating disorder and had no illicit drugs in her system. The court concluded she accidentally drank herself to death.

A 80-year-old woman used sodium azide, a toxic chemical found in car airbag systems, to commit suicide in her room at the Berkeley City Club, authorities said. The woman left a suicide note warning of the hazardous situation, leading to the evacuation of hotel guests and residents. Police, fire, and bomb squad technicians responded to the third-floor apartment at 2:00 p.m. and removed the suspicious material. The Berkeley City Club, a historic landmark, remains evacuated, and Durant Avenue was closed for several hours. No injuries were reported, and the investigation is ongoing.

At 17, Hayden Kennedy showed promise as a climber, ticking off difficult routes like El Niño with confidence. Now 27, Kennedy has climbed some of the world's most challenging peaks, including the first ascent of Carbondale Short Bus and a 10-hour free ascent of the Hallucinogen Wall. His career highlights include bold first ascents in Patagonia and the Karakoram. However, his life took a tragic turn when he and his girlfriend triggered an avalanche that killed her, leading Kennedy to take his own life. Despite his media shyness, Kennedy's climbing achievements have earned him respect and admiration in the climbing community.

A father and his twin one-year-old daughters narrowly escaped a carjacking at a gas station in northwest Atlanta on Saturday night. Lester Chaney says fear quickly set in when he was forced to watch someone driving off with his Toyota Camry, which contained his twin daughters, Nadia and McKenzie, in the backseat. Surveillance video shows the carjacker running toward the car and quickly slipping inside. Police found the girls a quarter of a mile away after the suspect ditched the car in an apartment complex parking lot. McKenzie was found in her car seat, while Nadia was removed from the car and dropped in a wooded area. Both girls slept through the entire incident.

Republican frontrunner Donald Trump maintained his strong lead in New York, with 54% support among likely Republican primary voters, compared to 25% for John Kasich and 16% for Ted Cruz. Trump's campaign rally in Buffalo drew enthusiastic support and highlighted his key campaign promises, including building a wall on the Mexican border and revamping trade agreements. Despite his recent gaffe of mistakenly referring to the 9/11 attacks as "7-11," Trump's message resonated with the crowd, who filled less than two-thirds of the arena. His campaign strategy emphasized job loss due to trade deals and promised to restore manufacturing jobs in New York. Trump also criticized his rivals, calling Cruz a "liar" and Kasich a supporter of NAFTA, which he deemed a "disaster."
