The rally underscored Trump's commanding lead in the state, with 64% of likely voters strongly supporting their chosen candidate.

A pet pig in Indianapolis might have scared off burglars during a recent home break-in, according to WXIN and CNN. The homeowner, a single mother with four children, says the intruders broke the back door glass and kicked their way inside but fled when they encountered the pig. The homeowner, who rescued the full-grown swine earlier this year, says the pig's presence likely deterred the burglars. Home break-ins are common in the neighborhood, and this incident occurred just a few weeks after the family bought their first home. The homeowner hopes the suspects are caught and wishes more people would adopt pet pigs.

A London man named Stephen Port, 41, was sentenced to life in prison for the murder of four young gay men he drugged and raped before dumping their bodies near his flat. Port, a chef and part-time male escort, lured his victims to his home using online dating sites, where he gave them lethal doses of the drug GHB to render them unconscious and sexually assault them. He then disposed of their bodies in a graveyard near his home. Port attempted to cover up two of the murders with fake suicide notes. A judge ruled that Port intended to cause serious harm rather than death but must have known there was a high risk of death. Port's family maintained his innocence, but his victims' families expressed satisfaction with the verdict. The Metropolitan Police Service admitted missing opportunities to catch Port sooner and is now investigating 58 other unexplained GHB-related deaths.

Miami Dolphins offensive line coach Jim Turner and head trainer Kevin O'Neill have been dismissed following the release of Ted Wells' independent investigation into locker room misconduct. Dolphins owner Stephen Ross stated, "The language and behavior as described in the Ted Wells report are against the core values of our organization." Coach Joe Philbin acknowledged the need for a "team-first culture of respect" and will address the media at the NFL Scouting Combine. Turner's involvement in harassing players and attempting to convince Jonathan Martin to defend Richie Incognito is detailed in the report. The Dolphins may replace Turner with former Houston Texans offensive line coach John Benton.

Facing fixed-mount solar panels west instead of south could produce more electricity during peak demand, according to a new study from Pecan Street Research. The research, conducted on 50 Austin homes, found that west-facing panels produced 2% more electricity daily and 49% more during peak demand hours of 3 to 7 pm, compared to south-facing panels. Homeowners with west-facing panels reduced their peak energy usage by 65%, compared to 54% for south-facing panels. This could open the solar market to more homeowners and reduce stress on utility grids during peak demand periods. However, the study was conducted during summer months, and its overall outcome during winter months is uncertain.

It’s been one year since Robert Mueller was appointed special counsel to investigate potential links between the Russian government and individuals associated with the Trump campaign. Mueller’s investigation has led to five guilty pleas and multiple indictments, despite facing criticism from Trump and his allies. The investigation’s endgame could involve complex legal questions about presidential immunity and the use of pardons. Mueller’s team, comprising mostly Democratic-affiliated attorneys, has remained tight-lipped about its activities, except for public announcements of indictments and plea deals. Legal experts debate whether Mueller can subpoena Trump, indict him, or be fired by Trump. Trump has considered using pardons to circumvent Mueller but faces uncertainty and potential legal challenges.

A 6-year-old boy with autism was found driving a toy ATV on the Bronx River Parkway in Mount Vernon over the weekend, prompting several good Samaritans to protect him from traffic. The boy, who had slipped away from his grandmother near a park, was discovered on the highway just after 7 p.m. Sunday. Good Samaritans slowed their vehicles to form a protective barrier around the child, who was riding in the far right lane. The boy, repeatedly calling for his mother, was safely removed from the road by the time police arrived. He was taken to a hospital for observation and found to be in good condition before being reunited with his family. The incident is under investigation.

For classic Ford Mustang enthusiasts, a new body shell option is now available for the 1967 convertible. This restoration part, produced by Dynacorn and licensed by Ford, ensures a fit, finish, and quality that match or exceed the original. The body panels are made from modern, slightly thicker automotive-grade steel and feature reinforcements in stress areas for added strength. At $15,995, it offers a new option for those looking to restore or build a 1967 Mustang, with over 90% of the necessary parts available as Ford-licensed reproduction components. This new body shell is the fourth in a series of classic Mustang restoration parts, joining the 1965 convertible, 1967 fastback, and 1969 fastback.

The Audubon Zoo in New Orleans closed after a jaguar named Valerio escaped and killed six animals, including five alpacas, one emu, and one fox, according to a zoo release. Despite efforts to resume normal operations, the incident cast a shadow over the zoo, with parents reminding children about the circle of life. The alpacas, acquired in March from farms in Alabama and Mississippi, were among those killed. The jaguar was captured and returned to its enclosure after being sedated. The zoo reopened on Sunday but faced questions about the safety of keeping such large predators. Staffers were offered grief counseling, and a young girl left a touching letter to the deceased animals.

China has suspended all coal imports from North Korea for the rest of 2017, applying pressure on its neighbor to abandon its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. This move aligns with UN Security Council sanctions imposed in November 2016 following North Korea's fifth nuclear test. Coal is North Korea's primary export and a significant source of foreign currency. Beijing, despite limited influence, has grown increasingly frustrated with North Korea's defiance of UN demands to halt missile tests and nuclear development.

Walmart, Amazon, and Sears pulled a home decoration poster featuring a photo of Nazi Germany's Dachau concentration camp sign over the holiday weekend. The sign bears the infamous phrase "Arbeit macht frei," meaning "work makes you free." Walmart apologized, stating the item was sold by a third-party seller on its marketplace and was quickly removed. Similar items, including ovens used for cremating prisoners, were still listed on Sears' website, prompting further criticism. The incident sparked outrage on social media and highlighted retailers' challenges in selling Nazi-related merchandise.

Sentiment in 2017 was mixed, with supporters of change pointing to growth expectations from tax reform and deregulation, while economists like Paul Krugman were skeptical. U.S. stocks rose over 20% in 2017, leading to optimism for 2018, with some analysts setting targets for the S&P 500. However, extrapolating recent trends into the future can be risky. Long-term predictions are particularly challenging, akin to predicting the New York Jets winning the Super Bowl in 2020. While it's reasonable to plan ahead, it's important to consider multiple perspectives. PMI data suggests global growth, benefiting U.S. multinationals. Corporate tax reform could boost earnings, but buybacks have slowed, potentially leading to increased capital expenditure. The article concludes with Fortune's predictions for 2018, including modest GDP growth, continued low unemployment, and a rebound in the U.S. IPO market.

Washington, D.C., dominated national English-language television ratings for World Cup matches, with the Ghana-USA game on ESPN earning an 11.8 overnight rating, the highest in the country. The D.C. area also led in ratings for other matches, including the Brazil-Croatia opener and the Spain-Netherlands game. Through 14 matches, D.C. had the highest average ratings on ESPN networks. The ratings did not include Spanish-language broadcasts. Comparatively, D.C.'s best-rated Capitals game earned an 8.63 rating, while the Wizards' best playoff game had an 8.51 rating. The U.S. vs. Ghana match also set viewership records for both ESPN and Univision, with a total of 15.9 million viewers.

This was the year Lady Gaga dominated the music scene, earning Billboard's top artist of the year honor, just a year after she was named top new artist. The last time an artist made such a rapid transition was in 2006 when Chris Brown achieved both titles. Since 1981, only seven women have won the top artist award, including Gaga. Her success is attributed to the chart performance of "The Fame" and "The Fame Monster," which rank 4th and 13th, respectively, on the year-end Top Billboard 200 Albums. Four singles from these albums appear on the Hot 100 Songs list, led by "Bad Romance" at No. 8. Taylor Swift, who was top artist in 2009, comes in second this year, marking the first time an act has been in the top two for consecutive years since Destiny's Child in 2000 and 2001.

Sean "Diddy" Combs shared a heartfelt tribute to his ex Kim Porter on social media three days after her death at the age of 47. Porter, the mother of three of his children, was found dead at her home in Toluca Lake, California. Diddy wrote, "For the last three days I've been trying to wake up out of this nightmare. But I haven't. I don't know what I'm going to do without you baby. I miss you so much." Diddy and Porter were together for over a decade and remained close after their breakup in 2007, sharing twin daughters and a son.

During a 1,700-mile road trip across Iran, Nicholas Kristof found a nation where pro-American sentiment is strong, especially in urban areas, but support for the government is also prevalent, particularly among less educated workers. Kristof's journey, which included interviews with random individuals along the way, revealed a complex landscape of opinions. While some Iranians blame their own leaders for economic hardships exacerbated by Western sanctions, others are wary of speaking freely, fearing repercussions from the authorities. Kristof notes that the Iranian government's media control is evident, as many interviewees cited state sources as their only news. Despite occasional "Death to America" signs, Kristof encountered numerous Iranians who warmly welcomed him and expressed love for America. Kristof suggests that the current system may be on the verge of collapse, but a potential conflict with the West could strengthen the regime.

The federal government plans to order emergency inspections of 80 older Boeing 737 aircraft similar to the Southwest Airlines jet that suffered a 5-foot tear in its roof, amid concerns about possibly dangerous cracks. The FAA's inspection order will cover 737-300s, 737-400s, and 737-500s built with a specific manufacturing process and with over 30,000 flights. Although the number of affected jets is small, the incident could change the conversation regarding the risk of aging aircraft, according to aviation safety experts. Southwest and other airlines have found similar cracks on some of their planes and have grounded the affected aircraft. The inspections will use eddy current technology to detect cracks invisible to the naked eye, with more sophisticated tools used if needed.

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit against North Carolina on Monday, alleging that the state’s new voter ID law violates the Voting Rights Act by disproportionately affecting African-American voters. Attorney General Eric Holder stated that the law’s provisions, including the elimination of early voting days and same-day registration, were intentionally designed to limit minority voter turnout. The lawsuit seeks to block the law and place the entire state under a requirement to preclear any changes to voting laws with the Justice Department or a federal court. North Carolina’s law is seen as the most sweeping voter ID requirement in the country. Critics argue it will disenfranchise African-American and elderly voters, while supporters claim it prevents voter fraud. The lawsuit follows similar actions against Texas, where the Justice Department also sought to reinstate preclearance requirements. North Carolina’s law, signed by Governor Pat McCrory, goes into effect for the 2016 elections.

A U.S. rock band, Bloodhound Gang, faced bans, beatings, and potential criminal charges after one of its members desecrated a Russian flag during a concert in Ukraine. The incident, caught on video and posted to YouTube, sparked outrage in Russia, leading to the band's cancellation of a performance at the Kubana rock festival near Anapa. Russian authorities opened a criminal case for flag desecration, which can result in up to a year in prison. The band left Russia after being attacked by a group of self-described Cossacks at Anapa airport. U.S. Ambassador Michael McFaul condemned the incident but noted that flag desecration is protected under the First Amendment. Russian and Ukrainian lawmakers proposed permanently banning the band from entering their countries.

The Supreme Court on Friday rejected the Trump administration's request to halt a lawsuit brought by youths who are seeking to hold the government accountable for failing to do enough to fight climate change. The administration argued the lawsuit was "misguided" and a "radical invasion of the separation of powers." However, the court did not release the vote total and suggested the government might seek relief from the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals at a later stage. Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch would have ruled in favor of the administration. The lawsuit, filed in 2015 by 21 young people, argues that the government's failure to combat climate change violates their constitutional rights to a clean environment. The plaintiffs are seeking a plan to reduce atmospheric CO2 levels to 350 parts per million by 2100. The case is set to proceed, with the plaintiffs hoping to move toward trial.

Rick and Morty fans bid $14,700 on eBay for a 19-year-old McDonald’s Szechuan dipping sauce, a stunt that began with the show’s April Fools’ Day episode featuring the sauce. The condiment, released in 1998 for Disney’s Mulan, has been a running gag in the series. To capitalize on the show’s popularity, Rick and Morty creators launched a Change.org petition and engaged with McDonald’s on social media, garnering over 20,000 signatures. McDonald’s responded with a vague statement, leaving fans hoping for a comeback. Meanwhile, eBay sellers continue to offer the sauce for exorbitant prices, with one packet fetching $1,000.

Federal prosecutors are investigating Anthony Weiner over alleged sexually explicit exchanges with a 15-year-old girl, according to law enforcement officials. The FBI and the New York Police Department have opened preliminary investigations. Weiner, a former New York Democratic congressman, is alleged to have sent the girl explicit photos and engaged in sexual conversations with her. Law enforcement officials have issued a subpoena for Weiner’s cell phone records. The girl claims the relationship went on for months, involving explicit messages and photos. Weiner’s wife, Huma Abedin, an aide to Hillary Clinton, recently announced their separation. Weiner has acknowledged the allegations, saying he likely was the subject of a hoax, and provided emails from the girl that he contends raise questions about her claims.

A planned endorsement event with 100 black religious leaders at Trump Tower turned into a tense closed-door meeting as many pastors demanded an apology from Donald Trump for his controversial comments. The meeting, initially promoted as an endorsement, became contentious with pastors asking for apologies to both the black community and Mexicans. While some left with hopes their message had been heard, Trump maintained he had no plans to change his approach. The event highlighted the challenges Trump faces in appealing to black voters, who overwhelmingly supported President Obama.

The Alberta government has condemned a controversial hunting practice after a U.S. hunter posted a YouTube video showing him killing a bear using a spear. The video, believed to have been shot in May northeast of Edmonton, has sparked outrage, with many calling the method "barbaric" and "unnecessary." The Alberta Ministry of Environment and Parks stated that the type of archaic hunting seen in the video is unacceptable and plans to introduce a ban on spear hunting this fall. Fish and wildlife officers are also investigating to see if charges are warranted under existing laws. Conservation groups and some hunters argue that spear hunting poses a risk of unnecessary suffering to the bear, as the injured animal could run off and suffer for an extended period. The government is updating its hunting regulations and promised to introduce a spear ban in the fall.

The Samsung Galaxy Note 7, once hailed as the best smartphone, has been discontinued due to safety concerns. After initial reports of battery fires, Samsung initiated a global recall and halted production. The device, praised for its large AMOLED screen, S Pen, and waterproof design, faced a second production halt due to replacement phones also catching fire. This led to a complete ban on the Note 7, with carriers stopping sales and urging users to power down and return the device. Despite its many features, the Note 7's battery issues severely impacted its reputation and market availability.

Tracy Fain, who survived a vicious dog attack on Christmas Eve that left her son Ethan with a missing ear, suffered a brain aneurysm and stroke while taking him to the hospital for stitches on August 7th. She is now declared brain dead, leaving her family devastated. Tracy's mother, Sandra Moore, is heartbroken and struggles to cope with the loss. Moore and the family have been praying for a miracle and have set up a GoFundMe page to support them during this difficult time.

A new progressive group, the Agenda Project, has launched "F*ck Tea," aimed at dismissing the tea party movement and promoting progressive causes. The project includes merchandise, polling statistics portraying tea party members as ignorant, and a mocking video. Co-founder Erica Payne, a veteran consultant to progressive groups, describes the initiative as a way to strengthen the progressive movement by countering the grass-roots conservative resurgence.

Emerson College is launching a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in Comedic Arts, set to begin in fall 2016. The program will cover comedy writing, production, and performance, with hands-on training and guest lectures from industry professionals. Alumni such as Jay Leno and Denis Leary have credited Emerson for their success in comedy. The school aims to combine academic rigor with practical experience, offering courses in comedy history and theory alongside performance opportunities.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, also known as the Mormon Church, has a complex history with plural marriage. The practice was introduced to early members through a revelation to Joseph Smith, who married multiple wives and authorized others to do the same. Plural marriage was seen as a way to honor ancient biblical principles and to increase the number of children born into the faith. It also played a significant role in shaping 19th-century Mormon society, providing economic and social benefits to participants. However, the practice faced significant legal and social opposition, leading to the 1890 Manifesto, which officially ended the practice. Despite the end of plural marriage, many modern Latter-day Saints descend from those who practiced it, and the Church now allows posthumous sealings for those who married multiple times in life.

The new Miss America, Kira Kazantsev, has a controversial past that includes allegations of hazing while she was a sorority leader at Hofstra University. Despite her impressive academic achievements and commitment to women's health, her involvement in hazing practices as the head of the recruitment committee for Alpha Phi sorority has come to light. Pageant officials have defended Kazantsev, stating that she was transparent with the organization about her termination from the sorority. However, the controversy has raised questions about the values of the Miss America organization and the candidates it chooses to represent. Kazantsev has denied the allegations, claiming they were taken out of context.

PETA criticizes Kim Kardashian for riding captive dolphins, calling her actions "intrusive," "dangerous," and "harmful." Kardashian posted a video of herself and a friend riding dolphins on Instagram, sparking backlash from the animal rights organization. PETA argues that such public interactions with captive dolphins are stressful and can lead to injuries for the animals. The organization highlights the suffering of dolphins in captivity, noting that they are confined to small tanks and denied natural behaviors. PETA also mentions the tragic consequences of keeping orcas and dolphins in captivity, including physical and psychological harm, and advocates for their release into the wild.

Nike has unveiled the HyperAdapt 1.0, a self-lacing shoe that brings the futuristic concept from Back to the Future II into reality. When you step into the shoe, sensors automatically tighten the laces, and you can adjust the fit with buttons on the side. Unlike the Air Mag from the movie, which was never intended for mass production, the HyperAdapt 1.0 is available to Nike+ members this holiday season in three color options. Nike envisions a future where shoes can adapt to your biometric data, but for now, the shoe will remember your preferred fit after a couple of wears. The self-lacing technology uses a battery that lasts about two weeks on a single charge, adding a tech dependency to the user experience.

Veteran race car driver David Steele, 42, died in a wreck during a sprint car race at Desoto Speedway in Bradenton, Florida. Steele, a multiple USAC national champion and two-time winner of the Little 500, was competing in the Southern Sprint Car Shootout Series. His death drew immediate tributes from fellow racers and drivers, including Alex Bowman and Tony Stewart Racing. The incident occurred when Steele’s car flipped and hit the wall after colliding with another vehicle. Desoto Speedway released a statement expressing condolences to Steele’s family.

The National Security Agency (NSA) collects millions of photos daily from electronic communications as part of a major facial recognition effort, according to leaked documents obtained by The New York Times. The NSA harvests about 55,000 "facial recognition quality" images per day, with current US privacy and surveillance laws not specifically protecting against the use of facial recognition technology to identify individuals. Although the NSA does not have access to US state databases of driver's licenses or passport photos, it can likely obtain that information from other sources like social media. The NSA's facial recognition program is separate from its bulk metadata collection program, which requires court approval to collect images from American citizens. The selfie phenomenon is making the NSA's job easier by producing a mountain of tagged online data to feed its facial recognition algorithms. While the NSA does not have access to US state databases, it can obtain similar information from social media platforms. The use of facial recognition technology raises concerns about privacy and civil rights, and experts

Queen Elizabeth II has surpassed her great-great-grandmother Queen Victoria as Britain's longest-reigning monarch, marking a historic milestone on September 9, 2015, at approximately 5:30 p.m. local time. The Queen, now 89, expressed gratitude for the "touching messages of kindness" she received from well-wishers both at home and abroad. In Scotland, she officially opened the new Scottish Borders Railway, while in London, a flotilla of historic vessels and a four-gun salute honored her achievement. Prime Minister David Cameron praised her "rock of stability" role during her reign, which has spanned three post-war generations. The Queen, who will celebrate her traditional summer break at Balmoral, maintains her usual routine, though Buckingham Palace released official photographs to commemorate the occasion.

Patton Oswalt and Meredith Salenger have tied the knot, marking a new chapter for the 48-year-old actor and the 47-year-old actress. The couple, who met through mutual friends, announced their engagement in July 2017. Salenger shared a series of sweet wedding photos on social media, including a picture of her walking down the aisle with Oswalt and their daughter, Alice. The nuptials took place at the Jim Henson Company lot in Los Angeles on November 4, 2017. Oswalt's first wife, Michelle McNamara, passed away unexpectedly in 2016, and the couple faced criticism for their decision to marry so soon after her death. Despite the backlash, Oswalt and Salenger remained committed to their relationship, focusing on the happiness of their daughter and their own love.

A New York man named John Caltabiano Jr., 49, pretended to be blind to collect workers' compensation and disability benefits, reports ABC News. He claimed a workplace accident in 2006 left him almost completely blind, but investigators caught him driving, shopping, and going to the gym. Caltabiano was sentenced to almost five years in prison after being found guilty of conspiracy to commit mail fraud, mail fraud, and theft of government property. His girlfriend, Colleen McCarten, received three years' probation for her role in the fraud. The case highlights the prevalence of disability fraud, with the U.S. Social Security Administration receiving 90,000 allegations to investigate annually.

Fuel removal operations began on the Costa Concordia, nearly a month after the cruise ship ran aground off Tuscany, with plans to pump out 500,000 gallons of fuel over 28 days. The process, overseen by Dutch salvage firm Smit, involves attaching valves to underwater fuel tanks and pumping the oil into a crane barge, then transferring it to an oil tanker. The operation aims to prevent environmental contamination in the protected waters off the island of Giglio. Seventeen people died in the accident, and 15 remain missing. The ship's captain, Francesco Schettino, faces charges of manslaughter and abandoning the ship.

Astronomers investigating a distant star system are re-examining a mysterious signal that could potentially be an extraterrestrial communication. The signal, detected in 2015 by the RATAN-600 radio telescope in Russia, appears to originate from the star HD 164595, located about 95 light-years away. HD 164595 is a sun-like star with an estimated age of 6.3 billion years and hosts at least one Neptune-sized planet. The signal's strength suggests it could be from a highly advanced civilization, either broadcasting in all directions or targeting Earth specifically. However, the signal has only been observed once, raising doubts about its extraterrestrial origin. The SETI Institute and other organizations are now using advanced telescopes to confirm the signal's nature, with preliminary results from the Allen Telescope Array in California showing no evidence of the signal. The possibility of terrestrial interference remains a significant factor, and further observations

Actress Amy Adams, 39, demonstrated exceptional class during a Delta flight from Detroit to Los Angeles by giving up her first-class seat to an American serviceman. Co-host of ESPN's "Numbers Never Lie," Jemele Hill, witnessed the gesture and shared the story on Twitter. Adams, a five-time Academy Award nominee, was initially seated in first class but vacated her seat before takeoff, allowing the serviceman to take her place. A flight attendant brought the soldier to Adams' original seat, and she took a seat in coach. Adams' act of kindness was captured in a selfie with Ernest Owens, another passenger who praised her actions. The actress stated her intention was to draw attention to the troops rather than for personal recognition.

A U.S.-Russia-brokered ceasefire began in Syria at sundown, amid mixed signals from rebel groups and with cautious support from President Bashar Assad's government. The deal, announced last week, aims to halt fighting between the U.S.-backed opposition and the Russian-supported Syrian government, allowing for humanitarian access to besieged areas. However, early reports indicated some reduction in violence, and it remains unclear how widely the truce will be observed. The cessation of hostilities is set to be renewed every 48 hours, with the U.S. and Russia planning to establish a joint center to combat jihadist groups. The conflict in Syria, which has lasted five years, has claimed over 250,000 lives and displaced millions.

A judge declared a mistrial in the second trial for the murder of Jessica Chambers, as the jury was unable to reach a verdict. Quinton Tellis, 29, faces a capital murder charge for Chambers' 2014 killing, where she was burned alive in her car. The first trial ended with a hung jury, and this is the second time a jury failed to reach a unanimous decision. Chambers was discovered burned in Courtland, Mississippi, and reportedly told first responders that "Eric did this to me." The case garnered national attention, leading to a $54,000 reward and involvement from federal agencies. Tellis is also facing charges in a separate murder case in Louisiana, where he is currently serving time. The next steps for the Chambers case are uncertain, with no indication if there will be a third trial.

Adele reportedly turned down an offer to perform at the 2017 Super Bowl halftime show, citing that the show is not about music and she cannot dance. During a concert in Los Angeles, she stated, "I’m not doing the Super Bowl. That show is not about music, and I don’t really -- I can’t dance or anything like that." The NFL and Pepsi Co. have not officially extended a formal offer to Adele, maintaining that they are still in the process of putting together a fantastic show for Houston.

Former President Barack Obama discussed the responsible use of social media and the challenges of leadership in a rare interview since leaving office. He warned against the distortion of complex issues and the spread of misinformation, emphasizing the need to find common ground and avoid a "Balkanisation" of society. Obama highlighted the importance of face-to-face interactions to counteract the simplification of complex issues online. Reflecting on his presidency, Obama expressed serenity despite unfinished work, citing Obamacare as a major achievement. Prince Harry, guest-editing BBC Radio 4's Today programme, interviewed Obama, asking about his personal preferences and future plans. The interview also touched on climate change and the prince’s upcoming wedding to Meghan Markle.

A top U.S. Navy admiral ordered a thorough investigation into the collision of the USS John S. McCain with an oil tanker near Singapore, marking the second deadly mishap in the Pacific in three months. Adm. John Richardson called for a worldwide operational pause and a review of the 7th Fleet’s maintenance, personnel, and equipment. The USS John S. McCain suffered significant damage, flooding nearby compartments including crew berths, machinery, and communications rooms. Ten sailors remain missing, and five were hospitalized. The collision occurred in a busy waterway, and some experts suggest the possibility of cyber intrusion or sabotage, though no evidence has been found. The USS Fitzgerald, also part of the 7th Fleet, had a similar collision earlier this year, raising questions about systemic issues.

A U.S. official confirmed the deaths of two more Americans in the hostage standoff at an Algerian gas complex, raising the U.S. death toll to three. Seven Americans survived. The Algerian prime minister accused a Canadian of coordinating the attack and praised the military's actions, which resulted in the deaths of 38 foreign hostages. Seven Americans among the dead, with others from Japan, the Philippines, and Britain unaccounted for. The Algerian government vowed to combat terrorism and prevent the establishment of an "Sahelistan" in the Sahara. The attack, claimed by an Algerian al Qaeda leader, was seen as retaliation for France's intervention in Mali. The incident raised questions about Algeria's security capabilities and strained relations with Western powers, who criticized the harsh response. The Algerian military's assault, which killed 29 militants, was defended as necessary to prevent hostage deaths and sabotage. The debate highlighted differing approaches to handling hostage situations in the post-9/11

Congress's 2012 legislative year stands as one of the least productive in post-World War II history, with only 61 bills signed into law out of 3,914 introduced, according to USA TODAY. This marks the lowest number of laws passed in a two-year period since records began in 1947. The 112th Congress, covering 2011-2012, is now the least productive in 65 years. Despite bipartisan efforts, key issues like the Super Committee's deficit reduction, Bush tax cuts, and farm bill extensions remain unresolved. Low approval ratings for Congress continue, hitting a historic low of 10% in a Gallup poll, with no significant improvement across party lines.

President Donald Trump said Tuesday he doesn't believe Oprah Winfrey will run for president in 2020, but if she did, he'd beat her. Trump addressed the speculation during a meeting with lawmakers on immigration, stating, "I'd beat Oprah. Oprah would be a lot of fun. I know her very well. I like Oprah. I don't think she's going to run." Winfrey's speech at the Golden Globes, focusing on the #MeToo movement, has reignited discussions about her potential presidential run. Best friend Gayle King said Winfrey is "intrigued by the idea" of running and is taking it seriously. Trump has previously praised Winfrey, appearing on her show with his family in one of its final episodes.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee has ruled that Ireland's strict abortion laws violated the human rights of a woman carrying a foetus with fatal abnormalities, ordering reforms to ensure women can terminate pregnancies safely. Amanda Mellet, who was denied an abortion in Ireland in 2011 when doctors found her foetus had fatal heart defects, faced the choice of continuing an unsustainable pregnancy or traveling abroad for a termination. The committee found her rights were violated, citing discrimination and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. Ireland must now provide compensation to Mellet and prevent similar violations, potentially requiring constitutional changes. The ruling could influence abortion laws in other restrictive countries.

In Vermont, the Rich Earth Institute collects human urine to test it as a natural fertilizer. Since 2012, volunteers have donated over 6,000 gallons of urine, enough to fill a third of an average swimming pool. Urine contains essential plant nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, which are usually mined or produced through the air. The project aims to divert these chemicals from waterways to farms, making a potentially harmful substance beneficial for crop production. The institute has faced public perception challenges but has developed methods to sanitize urine, such as solar pasteurization. They have received grants to expand trials and study the safety of using urine as fertilizer. Despite some skepticism, the approach could offer a sustainable alternative to chemical fertilizers, especially in regions where urine collection is culturally acceptable.

Sen. Al Franken's amendment to the FY 2010 Defense appropriations bill, which aimed to bar the government from contracting with companies that prevent their employees from bringing workplace sexual assault cases to court, has survived and includes "remarkably strong" language, according to an aide. The amendment, which passed 68 to 30, now prohibits the government from contracting with companies that restrict employees from suing over charges of assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress, or negligent hiring practices. Additionally, the amendment allows employees to sue not only the alleged perpetrator but also the perpetrator's employer. The amendment applies to all contracts totaling $1 million or more. However, a national security waiver is included, which would allow the Department of Defense to prevent a case from coming to court if it imperils safety measures, but the Secretary of Defense would have to explain the use of the waiver to Congress and make it public.

A gray two-piece ensemble worn by Vivien Leigh as Scarlett O'Hara in "Gone With the Wind" sold for $137,000 at an auction in Beverly Hills, California. The dress, part of a collection amassed by James Tumblin, who worked at Universal Studios, was among 150 items from the film up for auction. Tumblin discovered the dress decades ago when it was about to be thrown away, purchasing it for $20. Other notable items included a hat worn by Leigh and a suit worn by Clark Gable. The collection, numbering over 300,000 artifacts, is expected to raise up to $1 million.

A 58-year-old teacher at Broward Community Charter School in Coral Springs was arrested after police alleged she ordered a 10-year-old student to clean a clogged urinal with his bare hands. Jennifer Forshey, a third-grade teacher, was charged with battery of a child by exposure to urine. The boy told police that Forshey accused him of clogging the urinal and ordered him to remove paper towels from the drain. The bathroom had no soap, and the boy's hands were saturated with what smelled like urine. Forshey admitted to making the boy clean the urinal but claimed she only saw it as wrong because she faced legal trouble. She was released on $1,000 bond. The school's principal said the child came to his office seeking soap because his hands smelled of urine.

George Washington's name, once predominantly white, has become overwhelmingly associated with African-Americans, according to a 2000 U.S. Census. With 163,036 people bearing the surname, 90% of whom are black, it stands out as the "blackest name" in America. This phenomenon began with slavery and took a significant turn after the Civil War, when all blacks were allowed to choose surnames. Some historians suggest that post-Civil War blacks might have chosen the name Washington as a form of pride in the nation's history and to assert their freedom. Others argue that the connection is a coincidence. The name's current distribution highlights the complex relationship between George Washington and slavery, as he was a slaveowner but also expressed opposition to the institution in his will. Today, many black Washingtons view the name as a symbol of their history and progress, while some white Washingtons have experienced discrimination due to their name. The name's status as

At least 27 people have been killed and nearly 100 wounded in twin car bombs that struck intelligence and security buildings in Damascus on Saturday, according to state media. The blasts, which targeted a customs office and air force intelligence, are the latest in a series of attacks on regime installations, raising questions about who is behind the violence. The government blames "terrorists," while the opposition suggests the attacks may be staged by loyalists to discredit the uprising. U.S. intelligence points to al-Qaida in Iraq as a possible culprit. The attacks come amid ongoing violence and a year-long uprising against President Assad. The U.N. estimates over 8,000 people have died since the protests began. Diplomatic efforts have failed to resolve the crisis, with Russia and China blocking U.N. action against Assad's regime.

Facebook is blocking all mentions of the social media site Tsu.co across its platforms, including Facebook, Messenger, and Instagram. Tsu.co, with about 4.5 million users, shares its ad revenue with its users, a model Facebook does not follow. Facebook claims Tsu links are spam, but Tsu argues it's being targeted to eliminate competition. Facebook deleted over 1 million posts mentioning Tsu.co and blocks any new posts containing Tsu.co links. Tsu users feel this is unfair and believe Facebook is trying to protect its own business model.

Former professional wrestler Bret "The Hitman" Hart is battling prostate cancer, revealing his diagnosis on Instagram. The 58-year-old, who won world heavyweight titles with both WWE and WCW, will undergo surgery soon and vows to fight with determination. Hart, a member of the wrestling Hart family, previously survived a stroke in 2002.

A 33-year-old Marine died during a skydiving trip in Australia with his wife, who had won the trip on The Ellen DeGeneres Show. Brandon McGraw, an experienced skydiver, crashed into the ground after a flawless descent, reportedly due to unexplained complications. The couple, from North Carolina, had recently returned from military service. McGraw's wife Cherilyn, a special education teacher, paid tribute to her late husband, describing him as her "hero" and "angel." The Euroa Skydive school, which has not previously experienced a fatality, is now investigating the incident.

Newt Gingrich faces criticism from conservative quarters for his lack of true conservative credentials and his history of controversial behavior, including multiple divorces and alleged infidelities. Critics argue that Gingrich is more like Bill Clinton than a true conservative, citing his past criticisms of President Reagan and his role in the House impeachment process. Despite his current popularity among some Republican voters, his record and personal life raise questions about his suitability as a nominee. Mitt Romney, Rick Santorum, and Ron Paul are presented as more genuine conservative alternatives. Gingrich’s campaign has focused on attacking the media, portraying himself as an outsider, and emphasizing his ability to debate effectively against Obama. However, conservative media outlets and former colleagues have begun to challenge Gingrich’s leadership and character, suggesting that sticking with him could be risky. The debate highlights the tension between Gingrich’s populist appeal and his establishment background, as well as the importance of character and consistency in conservative politics.

Jennifer Aniston introduced her new boyfriend Justin Theroux to some of her closest friends, including Courteney Cox and Chelsea Handler, at a party last Friday night. The couple, which met while making the upcoming film 'Wanderlust,' are "doing great," according to a source. Meanwhile, there's tension in the friendship between Aniston and Cox, with Aniston reportedly hating watching Cox run around with other men while refusing to file for divorce from husband David Arquette. Cox's post-separation antics with costars Brian Van Holt and Josh Hopkins even reminded Aniston of her own marital heartache with ex-husband Brad Pitt. Despite the tension, Cox and Brad Pitt had a relaxed dinner together at a Hollywood hotspot, celebrating their manager's birthday.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Christine Lagarde emphasized the need for a balanced solution to avoid the fiscal cliff, advocating for both increased revenue and spending cuts. Former Sen. Alan Simpson predicted higher tax rates for the wealthy next year, aligning with Lagarde's call for a comprehensive fix rather than a quick one. Both Simpson and Erskine Bowles, co-chair of the Simpson-Bowles commission, agreed that raising taxes on the wealthy alone wouldn't solve the deficit, stressing the importance of cutting spending, particularly in entitlement programs. They warned that going over the fiscal cliff could lead to widespread economic uncertainty and job losses. Republicans like Bob Corker suggested ceding the tax fight to President Obama, focusing instead on spending and entitlements next year, leveraging the debt ceiling as a bargaining chip. Meanwhile, political discussions included speculation about Hillary Clinton's potential 2016 presidential run and the consideration of Newark Mayor Cory Booker for governor or Senate races in New Jersey. The victim of a vicious attack on the MacArthur Causeway in Miami has been identified as 65-year-old Ronald Poppo. Poppo remains in critical condition with severe facial injuries. His attacker, 31-year-old Rudy Eugene, who had a history of minor arrests, was killed by police during the incident. Eugene, who had recently been married and divorced, was reportedly seen as having a contentious attitude. The attack, which left 80% of Poppo's face missing, sparked theories about possible drug involvement, though police have not confirmed a specific cause. Poppo, a homeless man, is being treated at Jackson Memorial Hospital, while Eugene's ex-wife described him as feeling persecuted by society.

Nearly 20% of contact lens-related eye infections reported to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration over 10 years resulted in serious eye injuries, a new report finds. Improper wear and care of contact lenses can lead to eye infections that sometimes cause long-term damage, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The CDC analyzed nearly 1,100 cases of eye infections related to contact lens use reported to the FDA between 2005 and 2015. Nearly 1 in 5 patients experienced eye damage, including a scarred cornea or the need for a corneal transplant. More than 10% of patients required emergency treatment. The CDC recommends proper care, including not sleeping in contact lenses, not topping off lens solution, and replacing lenses as recommended.

In the small Ohio town of Chillicothe, at least six women have disappeared or turned up dead in less than a year, raising fears of a serial killer or sex traffickers. Family members and friends fear that a serial killer or sex traffickers are responsible for the disappearances. Charlotte Trego, Tameka Lynch, Wanda Lemons, and Tiffany Sayre have all vanished, while the bodies of Tameka Lynch and Tiffany Sayre have been found. The cases have left the town's police department and families questioning their ability to solve the crimes. The women shared commonalities, including drug addiction and involvement in the sex trade, which may link their cases. The investigation has expanded to include other missing women from nearby areas, and authorities are treating the cases as potentially linked. Despite the efforts of a task force, including the FBI, the families of the missing women remain unsatisfied with the progress and accuse the police of not taking the cases seriously.

A UK man has been infected with a highly resistant form of gonorrhea, the first global case reported to be completely resistant to the first-line treatment of azithromycin and ceftriaxone. Public Health England is investigating the case, which was contracted in Southeast Asia. The infection is spreading concerns about antibiotic-resistant strains of gonorrhea. Doctors are tracing the man’s sexual partners to contain the spread. The case highlights the growing threat of untreatable gonorrhea infections worldwide.

Sandra Bullock remained calm when Jesse James suddenly proposed to tattoo artist Kat Von D, sources close to her tell PopEater. Bullock, focused on her adopted son Louis, accepted that James is moving on. While not thrilled, she is determined to be the best mother she can be. Jesse, 41, and Kat, 28, have been dating since last summer following their separate divorces. James says 2010 was the best year of his life, falling in love with his best friend. He adds, "Growing old with her is going to be a f----n' blast!" Despite the engagement, Kat plans to keep her Los Angeles home, saying, "Home is where the heart is, and my heart's with him."

The Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) is experiencing an influx of hikers inspired by the movie "Wild" and the success of author Cheryl Strayed's memoir. The PCT, stretching 2,650 miles from the Mexican border to the Canadian border, has seen a significant increase in inquiries and permit requests, with website traffic up 300 percent since the film's release. While the trail offers a life-changing experience, the PCT Association warns that unprepared hikers can negatively impact the environment and other trail users. The association promotes responsible hiking practices and emphasizes the importance of proper planning, equipment, and financial preparedness. The article also notes that the PCT is becoming more popular among female hikers, with anecdotal evidence suggesting a rise from fewer than 10 percent to 30 percent in recent years.

Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia's body was transported to an El Paso funeral home after his death on a Texas ranch. Presidio County Judge Cinderela Guevara pronounced the cause of death as a heart attack, though an autopsy was not performed. Guevara discussed Scalia's health with his personal physician before making the determination. Scalia, 79, was found unresponsive in his bed at the Cibolo Creek Ranch, where he was on a hunting trip with a friend. The judge was initially called to the scene but later decided an autopsy was not necessary. President Obama stated his intention to nominate a successor to Scalia's seat.

A mother discovered a teacher's aide at Miramonte Elementary School was allegedly writing love letters to her 11-year-old son. The letters, penned by Areceli Luisjuan, contained disturbing passages expressing affection and desire. The mother first reported the matter to school officials and sheriff's deputies, but they failed to take it seriously. The incident is part of a wider investigation into misconduct at the school, which has seen the arrest of veteran teacher Mark Berndt and another teacher, Martin Bernard Springer, for alleged sexual abuse of students. The mother's experience highlights the challenges faced when parents report inappropriate behavior by school staff, especially when the accused is a teacher's aide.

A charismatic, ultra-wealthy New York businessman and celebrity, frequently criticized as a con man and "crypto-fascist clown," embarks on his first run for elected office. He captivates his conservative base with appeals to patriotism, family values, pride, and wealth, promising to restore America’s greatness. This narrative eerily mirrors Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign. Like Trump, Bob Roberts, the protagonist of the 1992 political mockumentary, is a masterful manipulator of the media, unapologetically boasting about his wealth and the importance of winning. His campaign bus and staff double as a mobile trading unit, and he sings “down-home fascist” folk anthems at massive rallies, promoting greed and attacking political correctness, Arabs, and “lazy complainers.” As Roberts’ fortunes rise, his aggressive campaign tactics and controversial persona alienate journalists and entertainers. A widow forgave the woman who caused a crash that killed her husband and his teenage son. Tamara Matthews pleaded guilty to misdemeanor counts of homicide by vehicle and failure to maintain lane, entering a plea nearly 2.5 years after the November 2011 accident. She was sentenced to 36 months' probation and 500 hours of community service. Sandra Walker, the widow, hugged Matthews during the court proceedings and expressed forgiveness. Matthews apologized to the Walker family in court. The crash occurred on Flat Shoals Road in south Fulton County, involving Matthews' out-of-control minivan and the Walker family's van. Glen Walker, 35, died days after the crash, while his wife suffered a life-altering brain injury. Their two children were not injured.

Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor granted a temporary exemption to a small group of Catholic nuns, shielding them from having to comply with a part of the Affordable Care Act that requires providing contraceptive coverage in their insurance plans. The exemption prevents the nuns from facing "draconian fines" if they fail to comply by New Year's Day. The Obama administration has exempted churches and religious groups from providing contraceptive coverage but has offered a more limited exemption for religiously affiliated charities, requiring their insurers to include the coverage. Several religious groups continue to challenge the Affordable Care Act in court. The Supreme Court is set to hear cases in March involving corporations and the contraceptive mandate, signaling a new phase in the political battle over the healthcare law.

The Arctic Ocean is undergoing a significant transformation, with warm Atlantic waters infiltrating from below, contributing to the rapid retreat of sea ice. This phenomenon, known as "Atlantification," is altering the Arctic's stratification and ice formation processes. Sensors installed since 2002 have revealed that warm currents from the Atlantic are creeping into the Arctic, particularly in the western Eurasian basin, where they reach depths of 200 to 250 meters. These warm waters, which are about 4°C warmer than the surface, mix with the cold surface waters during winter, creating a warmer, well-mixed ocean layer. In the eastern Eurasian basin, a barrier called the cold halocline layer (CHL) previously prevented the warm Atlantic waters from mixing with the surface. However, this barrier has weakened, allowing the warm waters to rise closer to the surface, leading to increased mixing and reduced ice formation. A former Canadian radio star, Jian Ghomeshi, has been fired from his popular Q radio show at CBC over allegations of sexual assault and harassment. Three women have come forward, alleging that Ghomeshi physically attacked them during dates without consent, including choking, hitting, and biting. Ghomeshi maintains that all his sexual encounters were consensual and blames an ex-girlfriend for orchestrating a campaign against him. He is now pursuing a $50 million lawsuit against CBC, claiming breach of confidence and bad faith. Ghomeshi's lawyers argue that the allegations are false, while the women who accused him fear public backlash if their names are revealed. Ghomeshi's firing sparked a broader debate on workplace safety and the treatment of sexual misconduct allegations.

Terry Wayne Ward's funeral service became a fitting sendoff for a man who "couldn't give a damn about most material things," according to his daughter's humorous and viral obituary. Jean Lahm, who works at Geisen Funeral Home, wrote the obituary, which detailed Ward's quirky life, including his 39-year career at AT&T where he accumulated 3,000 rolls of black electrical tape. The obituary went viral, and Ward's funeral service reflected his lighthearted spirit with plenty of laughs. His family read many online comments from strangers who expressed interest in attending the funeral for a man they never met. Ward passed away from a stroke, and in lieu of flowers, his family asked for donations to be made at a favorite watering hole.

Julian Assange, founder of WikiLeaks, claims more damaging information is yet to be revealed and warns against believing all media reports, as he spoke exclusively to RT. Assange argues that the recent Middle East uprisings are genuine but notes some countries, like Libya, show signs of outside influence. He criticizes Facebook as a tool for U.S. government surveillance, stating it is the "most appalling spying machine ever invented." Assange also criticizes media partners like The Guardian, saying they have over-redacted WikiLeaks cables, pushing the right of the public to know to the "very, very edge." He fears extradition to Sweden and the U.S., citing corruption in the Swedish process. Assange considers ignorance to be the world's biggest enemy, believing media often distort information, leading to wars and corrupt governments.

A family's boating trip off the coast of Noank, Connecticut, turned into a distressing search when their 8-month-old Shiba Inu puppy, Ryder, fell into the ocean. Despite extensive efforts, including the involvement of the Coast Guard and local residents, the family feared the worst. However, a Facebook post about the missing dog on the Groton Animals Lost and Found page led to a happy reunion. Boater Phil Q. Bigelow and his friends found Ryder in the water and rescued him, drying him off and giving him water. The family expressed deep gratitude for the safe return of their pet and the community's support.

American Amanda Knox and her Italian ex-boyfriend Raffaele Sollecito are set to learn their fate Wednesday when Italy's highest court hears their appeal in the 2007 murder of Knox's British roommate Meredith Kercher. Several outcomes are possible, including confirmation of the verdicts, a new appeals round, or even a ruling that amounts to an acquittal. The case, involving Knox, Sollecito, and a drifter from the Ivory Coast named Rudy Guede, has captivated audiences on both sides of the Atlantic. If the high court upholds the Florence convictions, Italy could seek Knox's extradition. A new trial could be ordered, or the court might acquit them, bringing the criminal proceedings to a close. The high court's decision will be based on specific directions regarding which elements of the case need re-examination.

Robert De Niro stars in Everybody's Fine, a remake of Giuseppe Tornatore's 1990 film Stanno Tutti Bene, which has been Americanized with a cast including Kate Beckinsale, Sam Rockwell, and Drew Barrymore. The plot follows widowed retiree Frank, played by De Niro, as he travels to visit his four adult children, each secretly unhappy and lying to their father. The film is criticized for its shallow characters, predictable plot, and false fronts. Directed by Kirk Jones, the movie fails to capitalize on De Niro's acting prowess and instead relies on a syrupy score and forced emotional moments. The production design and cinematography attempt to create an American landscape but fall short in providing depth to the story. Overall, Everybody's Fine is seen as a disappointing and inauthentic remake.

Twitter filed a lawsuit against the U.S. government to block a request for personal information about the user behind the @ALT_uscis account, which criticizes the Trump administration's immigration policies. The account, claiming to be run by a federal immigration employee, has over 40,000 followers. According to Twitter, the request is a threat to free speech, including the right to disseminate anonymous political speech. The lawsuit, filed in Northern California District Court, names the Department of Homeland Security and four individuals as defendants. Twitter argues that unmasking the account would have a "grave chilling effect" on speech and infringe on political speech protected by the First Amendment. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) is supporting Twitter in the case. This action comes amid a broader trend of the Trump administration aggressively responding to leaks and criticisms.

A British hacker, Lauri Love, won his appeal against extradition to the US, where he faced severe conditions in prison. The High Court ruled that his extradition would be "oppressive" due to his health conditions, including Asperger's syndrome and depression. Love, 33, from Suffolk, was accused of hacking into US government websites in 2012 and 2013. His supporters feared he would commit suicide if sent to the US. The court urged the Crown Prosecution Service to prosecute Love in England, where he would face less risk of suicide and be closer to his family. The US now has 14 days to appeal the decision. Love hopes his case sets a precedent for handling similar cases in the UK.

At the University of Texas, Professor Daniel S. Hamermesh has resigned due to concerns about the new campus carry law, which allows licensed gun owners to carry concealed weapons in classrooms. Hamermesh fears the presence of firearms could inhibit classroom discussions and compromise student safety. He is not the only faculty member opposed to the law; many others have expressed similar concerns. The University of Texas is gathering input on how to comply with the new state law while ensuring safety. The law, which takes effect in August 2016, has led to increased anxiety among students and faculty, with some considering the risk too high to continue teaching.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warns that Iran's pursuit of nuclear weapons poses an unprecedented threat to Israel's security, overshadowing other regional concerns. Reports in Haaretz and Israel Hayom cite a new U.S. National Intelligence Estimate suggesting significant progress by Iran in developing a nuclear warhead. The Israeli government is intensifying emergency preparedness, including home-front defense drills and crisis scenario exercises. The debate over potential military action against Iran continues, with some critics arguing the public discussion could compromise security.

Kevin Spacey is accused of creating a "toxic" work environment on the set of Netflix's "House of Cards," with eight current or former employees alleging sexual harassment and assault. One former production assistant claims Spacey sexually assaulted him during a drive to the set. Other crew members describe Spacey's inappropriate touching and crude comments, which reportedly targeted young and male staff. The allegations follow Anthony Rapp's accusation of sexual advances from Spacey in 1985. Production of the show's sixth season was suspended, and Netflix and the production company Media Rights Capital stated they are addressing concerns for the cast and crew. Spacey's publicist said he is seeking treatment.

TransCanada Corp. plans to sue the U.S. government for $15 billion in damages over the rejection of the Keystone XL pipeline, while also challenging the decision in a U.S. Federal Court, arguing it was unconstitutional. The rejection, made by President Obama in November, was based on the pipeline not significantly helping the U.S. economy or increasing energy security. TransCanada contends the decision was politically motivated and unfairly treated the company. The legal actions come as U.S. and Canadian officials work on a North American energy and climate agreement. Activists support the rejection, citing environmental concerns, while some politicians see the lawsuit as a desperate move by the oil industry.

Wyoming lawmakers are drafting a bill to allow firing-squad executions, despite the state having only one death-row inmate. The bill follows similar proposals in Utah and Tennessee, which have recently reintroduced the electric chair as a backup method. Tennessee's new law mandates electrocution if lethal injection drugs are unavailable, making it the first state to do so. The shortage of execution drugs, due to European manufacturers' boycotts, has prompted these states to consider alternative methods. Legal experts warn that such changes could face constitutional challenges.

In Lausanne, Switzerland, key issues remain unresolved as negotiators from Iran and six major world powers, including the United States, France, Germany, Britain, China, and Russia, work towards a permanent nuclear agreement. The deal, which requires Iran to reduce its stockpile of enriched uranium and limit its research into advanced centrifuges, faces criticism from both sides. Critics argue that Iran will continue research into next-generation centrifuges, potentially accelerating its path to a nuclear weapon. Meanwhile, Congress remains skeptical, with lawmakers like Bob Corker and Marco Rubio expressing concerns and demanding detailed reviews. President Obama urges Congress to give the administration time to finalize the deal, warning that any new sanctions could jeopardize diplomatic progress. The agreement's success hinges on addressing remaining issues, including Iran's past nuclear research and the fate of its advanced centrifuge program, while navigating potential opposition from Congress.

Sushi lovers may face higher prices due to the historic drought in California, which is expected to reduce specialty rice production by 25%. California, especially the Sacramento Valley, is the primary source for high-quality short- and medium-grain rice used in sushi. This year, farmers planted about 420,000 acres, a quarter less than usual, due to limited water allocations. The drought has also affected other crops, with about half a million acres of fruits and vegetables unplanted. While some rice growers may see increased prices, the real impact will be felt at sushi restaurants, which may have to pass on the higher costs or reduce profit margins. Overall, U.S. rice production is projected to increase by up to 21%, but sushi chefs prefer the California variety for its taste and texture.

Josh Groban couldn’t help but tease Mariah Carey after her disastrous New Year’s Eve performance. Groban initially tweeted, “Any time one of the greatest voices of my generation lip syncs, an angel loses its wings,” according to PEOPLE. However, he later deleted the tweet and explained, “Deleted my tweets about a certain performance because it was made in humor but taken way more meanly than intended. Not out to diss artists.” Carey, on the other hand, took the performance in stride, tweeting, “Shit happens. Have a happy and healthy new year everybody! Here’s to making more headlines in 2017.” Mariah Carey’s manager, Stella Bulochnikov, blamed Dick Clark Productions for the technical issues during the singer’s performance. Nations have fallen behind in efforts to combat climate change, according to a draft United Nations report. Delaying action could make solving the problem virtually impossible with current technologies, experts found. The report suggests that another 15 years of inaction could force future generations to develop methods to remove greenhouse gases from the atmosphere. However, it is uncertain whether such technologies will exist at the necessary scale or if they would be economically feasible. Meanwhile, governments continue to spend more on subsidizing fossil fuels than accelerating the shift to cleaner energy. Fast-growing countries like China are outpacing efforts to reduce emissions, and nuclear power is declining as a percentage of the global energy mix. The Obama administration is pushing for a new international treaty to replace the Kyoto Protocol, but it is unclear if the U.S. will gain enough political support, especially from China and the U.S. itself.
