A mysterious illness causing paralysis has claimed its first fatality in Washington state, with a 6-year-old boy named Daniel Ramirez passing away after contracting what doctors believe to be acute flaccid myelitis (AFM) at Seattle Children's Hospital. Eight children, including Daniel, have been treated for AFM symptoms, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) investigating a recent spike in cases across 24 states. AFM affects the nervous system, leading to sudden weakness or paralysis in one or more limbs. Symptoms can develop after a cold or respiratory illness and there is no specific treatment. In Oregon, three cases of AFM have been confirmed, with two children under 10 and an adult over 50 hospitalized. The exact cause of AFM remains unknown, though it has been linked to enteroviruses and other germs. The illness is rare, but health officials are monitoring cases to better understand and address the condition.

Italian scientists face jail over 2009 quake, accused of downplaying risks before a 6.3 magnitude earthquake that devastated L'Aquila and killed 309 people. Prosecutors claim the defendants, including six leading scientists and a government official, should have warned residents to evacuate their homes. The experts were part of a panel that met six days before the quake to assess risks after hundreds of tremors. They issued a reassuring statement, stating that a major earthquake was unlikely. The defendants argue that predicting earthquakes is impossible. The case has drawn attention from the scientific community, with over 5,000 scientists signing an open letter supporting the defendants. The trial, which opened in L'Aquila, could set a precedent for how science is treated in legal proceedings.

A Pennsylvania woman, Michele Kalina, was charged with criminal homicide after forensic tests linked her to the remains of five infants found in her home and a nearby landfill. Kalina, a 44-year-old nurse's aide, was in jail since her arrest on August 9 for the discovery of infants' remains in her Reading apartment. DNA evidence matched her to four of the five infants, with her boyfriend confirmed as the father for three. Kalina's teenage daughter first contacted authorities on July 29, unsure of what she had found in the living room closet. Detectives recovered the suspected remains of three infants and later found a fourth set and a bone believed to be from a fifth. Kalina's attorney declined to comment. The investigation revealed Kalina had hidden pregnancies for 14 years, concealing four infants' births from her husband and their daughter. The babies were born between 1996 and 2010.

At least 38 deaths have been reported as Tropical Storm Harvey continues to flood homes and sweep vehicles off roads in Texas and Louisiana. The death toll is expected to rise as authorities investigate several other deaths to determine if they are storm-related. The grim reality is setting in as floodwaters recede, with bodies potentially trapped in homes or cars. The number of fatalities may increase further during the recovery phase due to accidents or carbon monoxide poisoning. Officials warn that the death toll from Harvey might not reach the levels seen during Hurricane Katrina, thanks to improved emergency responses and community support.

"Lee Daniels' The Butler" continued its strong performance, earning $17 million in its second weekend and pushing its domestic total to $52.3 million, reports the LA Times. The film, starring Forest Whitaker and Oprah Winfrey, fell just 31% and surpassed the $47.6 million earned by Precious in 2009. It broadened its appeal, with 55% of the audience being Caucasian and 62% under 25. "We're the Millers" also performed well, grossing $13.5 million in its third weekend and reaching $91.7 million total. "Mortal Instruments: City of Bones" underperformed, opening with $9.3 million. Edgar Wright's "The World's End" opened to $8.9 million from 1,549 theaters, placing fourth.

Pressure mounts on House GOP to vote on China currency bill. House Republican leaders face criticism from Senate Democrats if they do not act on a currency measure. The bill, which could become a key issue in the 2012 elections, aims to address China's undervalued renminbi. Speaker John Boehner calls the bill "dangerous," but 99 House Republicans voted for a similar bill last year. Boehner and Majority Leader Eric Cantor have previously opposed such legislation. Democrats, including House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, urge action to level the playing field for American workers and businesses. The Senate bill, with GOP support, has cleared procedural hurdles. House Democrats are attempting to force a floor vote through a discharge petition, requiring 218 signatures. Boehner and Cantor face political pressure from their rank-and-file members, who may break with leadership if the bill is not passed. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz dismissed a New York Times report that he failed to properly disclose a loan from Goldman Sachs during his 2012 Senate campaign, calling it a "filing error." Cruz told reporters that the facts of the underlying matter have been disclosed for many years and that their finances are not complicated. The loan, worth just under $500,000, was taken out from his own assets and not borrowed money. Cruz's campaign also disclosed that he personally fronted $1.43 million of his campaign's financing from personal savings, sold stock, and this particular loan. Cruz has not specified how he ultimately repaid the loan in full. The omission was first reported by the New York Times, and the campaign plans to ask the FEC what to do regarding the filings.

In July 2016, Betsy Davis, a 41-year-old artist with ALS, organized a going-away party for her friends and family before ending her life legally under California's new doctor-assisted suicide law. Davis invited over 30 people to a home in Ojai, California, for a two-day event filled with laughter and joy, despite the impending end. She shared her plans with guests, including the precise time she would take the lethal dose. The party featured activities like a movie screening and a fashion show, with Davis interacting with her loved ones in her electric wheelchair. As the weekend drew to a close, friends and family said their goodbyes, and Davis took the prescribed medication at 6:45 p.m., passing away four hours later surrounded by her caretaker, doctor, and sister. The event was seen as a beautiful and meaningful way for Davis to end her life on her own terms.

Tom Hardy, the British actor known for his intense and often villainous roles, recently lost a bet with Leonardo DiCaprio. While filming The Revenant, DiCaprio wagered that Hardy would receive an Oscar nomination for his performance. Hardy, confident in his own abilities, bet a tattoo of DiCaprio's choosing. DiCaprio's design, written in "shitty handwriting," read "Leo knows everything." Hardy, despite his initial reluctance, eventually agreed to the tattoo, which now adorns his right bicep. Hardy, who is already covered in various tattoos, views this as a minor inconvenience, even joking that a more prominent design would have been a fairer outcome. This incident highlights Hardy's willingness to fulfill his end of the bargain, even when it involves a less-than-glamorous body modification.

Researchers from NYU Langone Medical Center found that long-term members of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) who recited AA prayers after viewing drinking-related images reported reduced cravings for alcohol compared to those who just read a newspaper. MRI scans showed increased activity in brain regions responsible for attention and emotion. These findings suggest that AA members develop an innate ability to use their experience—such as prayer—to minimize alcohol triggers' effect on craving. The study highlights the potential physiological changes associated with long-term AA involvement and supports the validity of AA's long-term experience in managing alcohol cravings.

One of Russia's most notorious criminal masterminds, Aslan Usoyan, also known as 'Grandpa Hassan,' was shot dead by a sniper in central Moscow. The 75-year-old was killed as he exited a restaurant in Povarskaya Street, near the Kremlin. Usoyan's bodyguards failed to protect him, and he died en route to the hospital. The assassin used a silenced Val 9mm assault rifle, making the location difficult to pinpoint. A woman walking with Usoyan was also wounded but remains in critical condition. The investigation suggests the killing was part of a turf war in the criminal underworld. Usoyan had survived previous assassination attempts and was known for his involvement in illegal activities such as gambling, arms and drug trafficking, and theft of natural resources.

A member of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, Jan Chamberlin, resigned over the choir's decision to perform at President-elect Donald Trump's inauguration, stating she could not look herself in the mirror again with self-respect. Chamberlin, who has been with the choir for five years, wrote in a Facebook post that the choir's participation would "severely damage" its image and networking, and that many good people would feel betrayed. The choir's participation is voluntary, with about 215 out of 360 singers expected to volunteer. The church's decision to perform at the inauguration has sparked a petition with nearly 19,000 signatures, with many expressing being "saddened and perplexed" by the decision. The church maintains that the performance is not a political statement but a demonstration of support for freedom, civility, and the peaceful transition of power.

Hollywood director Bryan Singer is under investigation by the New York Police Department for a forcible sexual assault allegedly committed in 2013 against a man in his twenties. Singer's lawyer denies any wrongdoing and accuses BuzzFeed of conducting a "witch hunt" against his client. The NYPD confirmed the investigation but provided limited details, citing the case as ongoing. Singer is known for directing X-Men films and has faced previous allegations of sexual abuse.

A collection of six personal letters written by Harper Lee to her close friend, architect Harold Caufield, failed to sell at auction for the expected $250,000. The letters, dating from 1956 to 1961, offer a glimpse into Lee's creative struggles, her strained relationship with her hometown, and her views on religion and Southern politics. The letters, which will be auctioned at Christie's, include one where Lee expresses her shock and delight at the success of "To Kill a Mockingbird." Lee's second book, "Go Set a Watchman," is set to be released in July, adding to the anticipation surrounding the sale of these intimate documents.

Angry protests against an anti-Islam film spread globally on Friday, with clashes and attacks on U.S. and Western embassies and consulates in multiple countries. In Tunisia, thousands of protesters battled police outside the U.S. embassy, setting part of it on fire. In Sudan, protesters stormed the German embassy, burning a car and setting trash cans ablaze. In Yemen, security forces fired tear gas and live rounds to disperse crowds near the U.S. embassy in Sanaa. In Egypt, President Morsi urged Muslims to protect foreign missions, denouncing the killing of the U.S. ambassador in Libya. Protests also erupted in Iraq, Lebanon, Malaysia, Pakistan, and Indonesia, with some burning U.S. flags and calling for retaliation against America. The film, "Innocence of Muslims," was condemned as "disgusting and reprehensible" by U.S. Secretary of State Clinton, who warned of further turmoil.

Rep. Michele Bachmann, a leading 2012 presidential hopeful, has faced criticism for advocating reduced federal spending while her family has benefited from government assistance. Her husband's counseling clinic has received nearly $30,000 in state funds over five years, partly from the federal government. Bachmann's father-in-law's family farm in Wisconsin received nearly $260,000 in federal farm subsidies. Despite publicly opposing such subsidies, Bachmann has sought stimulus funds for projects in her district. Her campaign faces the challenge of reconciling her fiscal conservatism with her family's receipt of government aid.

In response to controversy surrounding the character of Apu Nahasapeemapetilon, "The Simpsons" is reportedly planning to quietly write him off the show, according to Adi Shankar, producer of the "The Problem with Apu" documentary. Shankar, who launched a spec script contest to address the issue, says he heard from sources that the show is dropping Apu altogether to avoid controversy. This decision has sparked criticism, with some arguing that it's a cowardly move for a show known for cultural commentary. The winning script from Shankar's contest, written by Vishaal Buch, envisions Apu evolving into a thriving businessman in Springfield, incorporating other Indian-American characters. Shankar plans to produce the script through his Bootleg Universe site, despite "The Simpsons" not committing to it.

In Jamaican fruit bat colonies in Cuba, Cuban boas coordinate their hunting behavior, creating a deadly curtain that targets bats as they emerge from cave entrances. Researchers observed these snakes positioning themselves along the cave’s ceiling, ready to strike as bats flew past. Over eight days, Vladimir Dinets, a research assistant professor at the University of Tennessee, documented the snakes' hunting positions and success rates. His findings, published in Animal Behavior and Cognition, suggest that the snakes coordinate their hunting, significantly increasing their chances of capturing bats. While the snakes did not exhibit social behavior, they adjusted their positions to form a barrier, making it difficult for bats to avoid being caught. This coordinated hunting is rare among reptiles, challenging the long-held belief that reptiles are solitary and unintelligent hunters.

Amy Schumer is not appearing in any Super Bowl LIII commercials, choosing instead to support Colin Kaepernick's take-a-knee protest against racism and police brutality. She challenged white NFL players to kneel as well, stating, "Otherwise how are you not complicit?" The comedian explained her stance on Instagram, saying she personally told her representatives she wouldn't do a Super Bowl commercial this year. She also used the opportunity to promote her #NewsNotNoise campaign, encouraging followers to vote in the upcoming midterm elections. Schumer's pregnancy announcement was strategically tied to her political activism, with her Instagram page directing users to a list of recommended candidates.

Melania Trump discussed the #MeToo movement during an exclusive interview in Kenya, noting her support for women and the need for hard evidence in sexual assault cases. She addressed criticism over her "I really don't care" jacket worn during a visit to a child immigration center, stating it was a personal choice. Trump also defended her first-ever solo international trip to Africa, emphasizing her focus on children's welfare and conservation efforts rather than her attire. The interview, part of ABC's "Being Melania" series, promises to delve into her experiences as first lady, including her marriage and past fashion controversies.

After a nearly three-year delay, the state of Alaska is set to release over 24,000 pages of emails Sarah Palin sent and received during her tenure as governor, a move that has gained national attention as she remains a possible 2012 presidential contender. The emails, which span from December 2006 to September 2008, will be made available in paper form only, with reporters from various news organizations gathering in Juneau to review the documents. The release comes after a long and complex process, involving multiple requests and extensions, as well as the use of personal email accounts for state business. While the state has withheld some pages for reasons including attorney-client privilege, the release is expected to provide insight into Palin's governance and communications. The voluminous nature of the release and the logistical challenges of accessing the documents in Juneau have led to creative solutions for disseminating the information, including the creation of searchable databases by several news outlets. The contents

President Trump is set to announce his Supreme Court nominee to replace Justice Anthony Kennedy on Monday night, narrowing his choices to three federal appeals court judges: Brett Kavanaugh, Raymond Kethledge, and Amy Coney Barrett. Conservative activists are urging Trump to consider a number of picks that could push the court further to the right. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell reportedly favors Kethledge or Thomas Hardiman, citing their fewer obstacles to confirmation. Conservative figures like Hugh Hewitt, Matt Schlapp, Mark Levin, Laura Ingraham, Ben Shapiro, Jim DeMint, and Adam Brandon have publicly supported various candidates, with some pushing for Mike Lee. Trump has stated he will not ask candidates about their stance on Roe v. Wade.

Doctors on Long Island performed the first-ever operation on triplets born with a rare skull condition, craniosynostosis, at Stony Brook University Hospital. The Howard triplets—Hunter, Jackson, and Kaden—underwent surgery to repair improperly formed skulls. This condition, affecting about 1 in 2,000 births, is extraordinarily rare in triplets, with only a 1 in 500 trillion chance. The surgery, involving small incisions and the use of an endoscope, was successful, and the babies are recovering well. They will wear helmets for the next few months to ensure proper skull development. The triplets, conceived naturally, are now leading normal lives.

A veteran detective and the murder suspect he was interviewing were killed Thursday in a shooting inside the Jackson, Mississippi, police headquarters. Jackson police said Detective Eric Smith, 40, was talking with suspect Jeremy Powell, 23, when the shots were fired. Other law enforcement officers overheard the gunshots and rushed into the room, finding both individuals dead. The incident occurred around 6 p.m. The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation is leading the investigation. Jackson, with about 175,000 residents, is the capital of Mississippi. The entire city and the Jackson Police Department family are mourning this tragic event.

Actor Jon Bernthal says he had reservations about working with Kevin Spacey before the recent sexual misconduct allegations surfaced. Bernthal, who starred alongside Spacey in the film Baby Driver, recalled feeling uncomfortable around Spacey on set, noting, "I just remember losing a ton of respect for him." He described Spacey as rubbing him the wrong way and behaving in a bullying manner towards others. However, Bernthal did not witness any of the sexual misconduct allegations that have emerged. The article details a series of accusations against Spacey, including claims from Anthony Rapp, Roberto Cavazos, and Daniel Beal, spanning from 1983 to 2016. Spacey has faced multiple investigations and has been removed from his roles in House of Cards and All the Money in the World. His representatives have stated he is seeking evaluation and treatment.

A 24-year-old man arrested after fleeing an Anchorage home in boxer shorts has been charged with the brutal murders of an elderly couple and the sexual assault of their 2-year-old great-granddaughter, a case that has deeply shaken investigators, reports the Anchorage Daily News. The victims, Touch Chea, 71, and Sorn Sreap, 73, were found dead from significant blunt force injuries, with the toddler also sexually assaulted. Police say the suspect entered the apartment through an unlocked window and fled after a struggle with the family members who returned home to find the victims. The suspect, Jerry Andrew Active, was arrested a block away and charged with first and second-degree murder, sexual assault, and burglary. His criminal history includes previous sexual assault charges and probation violations. The case is considered unusual due to the apparent randomness of the attack and the suspect's history.

A customer at Saint Marc Pub-Cafe in Pacific City says she and her friends were asked to show proof of residency before being served, leading to an uncomfortable experience. The 24-year-old woman, Diana Carrillo, shared her story on social media, sparking attention. The restaurant apologized and fired the waiter involved, stating the behavior was not representative of their brand. Carrillo, whose parents are immigrants, fears such incidents may become more common. The restaurant offered a donation to a charity of her choice, which she accepted for Orange County Immigrant Youth United.

A security officer at two Manhattan hotels, Mariano Barbosa Jr., 30, was arrested and charged with setting eight fires over four years to make the hotels less popular and his job more manageable, authorities said. Barbosa, who worked at the Yotel and the SoHo Grand, allegedly set fires in hallways, stairwells, and near exit doors to maximize damage. He was on duty during the fires, which were quickly extinguished. Two firefighters sustained minor injuries. Barbosa's wife defended him, saying he worked hard for the company and often slept in complimentary rooms. The fire commissioner called his actions "disturbing."

A tiger and a goat at a Russian safari park had a falling out, with the goat receiving a lesson from the tiger. Timur the goat, initially placed in Amur the tiger's enclosure to potentially be eaten, instead became friends with the big cat. However, Timur's bold behavior, including scratching Amur's fur, eventually led to a fight. Amur mauls Timur, who lies in the snow, before the staff rescue him and take him to the vet. The park director says it's too early to determine if they will reunite the two, as Amur chose to give Timur a lesson rather than eat him.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s new ambassador to Germany, Richard Grenell, issued a warning to German companies to cease activities in Iran following the U.S. withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal. Grenell, a long-time critic of the deal, posted the warning on Twitter shortly after arriving in Berlin. His message to German companies highlighted the impending reimposition of U.S. sanctions and urged them to wind down operations immediately. German industry reacted nervously, concerned about potential U.S. fines for their Iranian business partners. The event marked Grenell’s official start in Berlin, nearly 16 months after his predecessor left. Known for his role as a Republican foreign policy writer and avid Twitter user, Grenell joined Trump at the White House for talks with Chancellor Angela Merkel, though no significant progress was made on trade disputes or the Iran accord. The ambassador’s confirmation faced opposition from key Democrats due to his history of making insulting statements, which he later claimed were meant to be humorous.

Thirty years after her iconic billboards and pink Corvette became Hollywood staples, the self-created sex symbol remains an object of fascination, curiosity, and a profound mystery: "I'm like heroin. I have to dole myself out carefully. I don't want people to overload." Angelyne, the legendary L.A. billboard queen, drives her hot pink Corvette around West Hollywood, passing beauty stores and reminiscing about encounters with celebrities like Paris Hilton. Her appeal spans generations and industries, with fans ranging from RuPaul to Fergie. Yet, she holds a special allure for the entertainment industry itself, where she is known as a cult figure. Angelyne avoids talking about her personal life, rejecting reality show offers and maintaining a veil of mystery. She claims to have rejected a sugar-daddy investor and instead credits Hugo Maisnik, a wealthy businessman, for her rise. Angelyne's self-branding began with the billboards and has evolved into a lifestyle that includes image licensing and appearances

A former surgeon and his business associate are accused of counterfeiting medical implants and paying doctors to use their products, leading to potential harm for patients. Richard Walker, owner of a surgical supply firm, discovered counterfeit screws from a distributor in 2009. Despite warnings, the distributor, Spinal Solutions LLC, continued selling implants to doctors nationwide. Patients received screws that may have been substandard, raising concerns about long-term health risks. Spinal Solutions' founder, Roger Williams, used private planes, expensive gifts, and cash to woo doctors, accumulating a lavish lifestyle. Williams allegedly paid kickbacks to surgeons, while patients faced financial and physical burdens. The FDA was informed of the counterfeiting in 2011 but did not immediately shut down the company. By 2013, Spinal Solutions was in debt and shut down, leaving thousands of patients with potential health risks.

In his first public account of the shooting, Cleveland police officer Timothy Loehmann told grand jurors he thought he was facing an active shooter situation and believed Tamir Rice was 18 years old. Loehmann stated he shot because Tamir pulled a gun from his waistband, which turned out to be a pellet gun. Loehmann and his partner, Frank Garmback, continuously yelled "show me your hands" before Loehmann fired two shots within two seconds of arriving at the scene. Surveillance video shows the officers driving their cruiser over a curb and across the lawn of a West Side recreation center, approaching Tamir, who was 12 years old. Loehmann's and Garmback's statements were released by prosecutors as part of the ongoing investigation, with both officers claiming Tamir was reaching for a weapon. The Cuyahoga County grand jury is considering whether to bring charges against the officers.

Indonesian searchers battled bad weather Wednesday, hampering efforts to find more remains from AirAsia Flight QZ8501. Conflicting reports emerged about whether any parts of the plane had been located underwater. Sonar equipment detected wreckage, but search and rescue chief Bambang Soelistyo stated the body of the aircraft hasn't been found, with only seven bodies recovered so far. The search zone covers 156,000 square kilometers, and multiple nations are assisting, including the U.S. Navy and Air Force. Families of the victims expressed anguish, with some fainted during a live news conference. The key to understanding the crash is likely the flight recorders, as heavy weather continues to complicate the recovery efforts.

Walt Disney Co. faced backlash for attempting to trademark "Dia de los Muertos," a centuries-old Mexican holiday honoring the dead. The company filed 10 trademark applications for the phrase, including for toys, cereals, and jewelry, in anticipation of an upcoming animated film about the holiday. However, Disney later withdrew the applications, stating the film's title would change. The move drew criticism from those who see the holiday as a sacred tradition, not for commercial exploitation. A petition on change.org garnered over 19,000 signatures.

Facebook's IPO roadshow is set to begin on May 7, with shares potentially debuting on May 18, according to a source. CEO Mark Zuckerberg will participate in the roadshow, reversing his absence during a March analysts' meeting. This marks a significant moment for Facebook, aiming for the largest Silicon Valley IPO ever. Despite slowing growth and margin pressures, strong investor interest persists. Facebook's decision to go public now raises questions about its current financial health and future prospects.

Pop star Justin Timberlake traveled to Tennessee to vote early in his hometown of Memphis, posting a selfie of himself about to cast his ballot on Instagram. "Hey! You! Yeah, YOU! I just flew from LA to Memphis to #rockthevote !!! No excuses, my good people!," he wrote. Fans were quick to react, expressing surprise and excitement at the unexpected appearance of a celebrity at their local polling place.

Rapper 50 Cent's latest album, "Before I Self Destruct," aims to revive his career by returning to the gritty, gangsta rap roots that once made him a star. The album, produced by Dr. Dre and others, features tough beats and 50's most ferocious delivery in years, boasting about shootings, drugs, and bloody 'hoods. While the album is packed with dense production and boasts of financial and physical success, it feels somewhat outdated in today's hip-hop market. The album's themes, while tough, are not as fresh as they once were, and the overall quality is inconsistent, with some tracks standing out more than others. Despite the album's attempts to re-establish 50 Cent as a kingpin of gangsta rap, the genre has receded from hip-hop's mainstream, and the album's quality is questionable.

Rupert Murdoch, 84, and Jerry Hall, 59, have announced their engagement in the births, marriages, and deaths section of The Times newspaper in London. The couple, introduced by Murdoch’s sister and niece in Australia, has been dating for four months. Their engagement was made public after attending the rugby World Cup final in London in October. The Times ran an announcement and a news story online. Murdoch’s family spokesperson stated they are "thrilled to be getting married and excited about their future." Former model Hall, who has four children with Mick Jagger, is Murdoch’s fourth wife, while 14-year marriage to Wendi Deng ended in 2013.

Since its launch in 2009, the Masters of Beef Advocacy (MBA) has trained nearly 3,000 students and farmers to combat critics like PETA and engage in social media "Food Fights." The program, funded by the Beef Checkoff program, trains advocates to address concerns about beef production and promote the industry's positive message. MBA graduates, like Carrin Flores, a veterinary student, are equipped to address environmental sustainability, beef nutrition, animal welfare, and beef safety. Despite concerns from critics like Michael Pollan, MBA aims to ensure the future of agriculture and beef production in a changing world.

More than 817,000 people lost power across five states as Hurricane Isaac brought heavy rain and flooding to the Gulf Coast. Isaac's maximum sustained winds dropped to 60 mph, but the storm's slow movement and large size worsened its impact. In Plaquemines Parish, officials considered breaching a levee to relieve pressure, with water overtopping the east bank and trapping people in attics. New Orleans Mayor Mitch Landrieu imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew, and residents reported flooding and looting incidents. Emergency crews rescued people stranded by floods, and the storm caused significant damage to homes and infrastructure.

Two children from the same family in the Charnwood area of Leicestershire have died after contracting a severe form of E. coli, Public Health England (PHE) has confirmed. The children, whose ages are not disclosed, were treated in the past two weeks. PHE is working with environmental health officers to investigate the cases, which were not being treated as an outbreak. The children died due to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a complication of E. coli that affects the kidneys. PHE states the cases are not linked and are investigating potential sources of infection, including contaminated food, contact with farm animals, or infected water. Young children and the elderly are more prone to complications from E. coli. Tests to determine the exact strain of E. coli are ongoing.

The new deputy commissioner of the NYPD, Michael Julian, is launching a campaign to curb the use of profanity by police officers and improve their use of force. Julian vows to train officers to control their language and behavior, aiming to reduce civilian complaints by 30%. He cites 30% of all Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) complaints involving curse words and plans to address this issue alongside teaching officers to manage their emotions and use of force. Julian emphasizes that NYPD officers are not brutal and aims to teach them techniques to control their actions during confrontations. The retraining is part of efforts to improve trust between police and the community following incidents like the death of Eric Garner.

San Francisco 49ers linebacker Aldon Smith was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport after allegedly making a false bomb report during secondary screening. Smith, who is facing multiple legal issues, was charged with a false bomb report and released on $20,000 bail. The incident occurred as he was going through Terminal 1 screening and became uncooperative with TSA agents. This arrest is the latest in a series of off-field troubles for Smith, including previous felony charges from an incident at his home in 2012 and missed games due to alcohol treatment.

Greenland's ice sheet is darkening, absorbing more solar radiation and increasing the risk of melting, according to a new study. This darkening, driven by two feedback loops, is reducing the ice sheet's albedo by about 2% per decade since 1996. As the ice melts, old impurities like dust and soot are exposed, while larger snow grains absorb more sunlight. These processes, invisible to the naked eye but detectable by satellites, are accelerating due to rising temperatures. By the end of the century, the ice sheet could be 10% darker, potentially increasing melting by 8%. This darkening is a concerning feedback loop, as it intensifies the melting process, leading to accelerated ice loss and contributing to sea-level rise.

George Zimmerman, who gained notoriety after the shooting death of Trayvon Martin, attended a firearms expo in Lake Mary, where he interacted with gun enthusiasts and posed for photos. Despite his celebrity status, Zimmerman described his life as constantly moving and fraught with financial difficulties and death threats. He carries a semi-automatic handgun for safety and has received numerous invitations to social events from strangers. Zimmerman launched a website to sell replicas of paintings honoring victims of the Benghazi attack, with proceeds going to wounded veterans' organizations. He emphasizes the importance of making the names of these victims known.

A new study suggests that pregnant women who frequently take acetaminophen, commonly found in Tylenol, may increase the risk of ADHD and similar disorders in their children. Researchers analyzed data from 64,000 children and their mothers in Denmark and found that women who took acetaminophen during pregnancy had a 29% higher risk of having a child diagnosed with ADHD and a 37% higher risk of having a child diagnosed with hyperkinetic syndrome. However, the study does not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, and experts advise pregnant women to avoid chronic or long-term use of the drug and consider alternatives for pain relief.

A meta-analysis of four studies found that swaddling infants for sleep may increase the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Of 760 SIDS cases, 17.5% were swaddled, compared to 10.8% of control infants. The risk was highest for infants sleeping on their stomachs (12.99 times higher) and side (3.16 times higher), with a 1.93 times higher risk for those sleeping on their backs. The risk increased with age, particularly for infants over 6 months old. The authors recommend avoiding swaddling before a child turns six months and always placing infants on their backs to sleep.

A legal dispute has erupted in Monroeville, Alabama, between Harper Lee, the author of the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel "To Kill a Mockingbird," and the Monroe County Heritage Museum, which celebrates the book and Lee's legacy. Lee, now 87 and in poor health, has filed a trademark infringement lawsuit against the museum, seeking to prevent it from using the book's name and characters. The museum denies the claims, stating that it has been honoring Lee's legacy for over 20 years and that the lawsuit is "false" and "meritless." The conflict highlights the complex relationship between Lee and her hometown, where the novel is deeply ingrained in local culture. The museum's lawyer, Matt Goforth, suggests that the lawsuit is the result of "handlers" who have gained influence over Lee's affairs. The dispute has divided the community, with some residents supporting the museum and others sympathizing with Lee.

Researchers have developed an origami robot that can unfold from a swallowed capsule and, guided by external magnetic fields, crawl across the stomach wall to remove a swallowed button battery or patch a wound. The robot, a collaboration between MIT, the University of Sheffield, and the Tokyo Institute of Technology, uses a "stick-slip" motion and a magnet to navigate and perform tasks inside the body. Made from dried pig intestine and other biocompatible materials, the robot can move both by sticking to surfaces and by propelling itself through stomach fluids. Tests in a synthetic stomach model showed the robot could locate and remove a battery. The researchers hope to add sensors and self-control capabilities to improve the robot's functionality for medical applications.

Ford Motor Company announced it will close its two Australian auto plants and cease production in the country by October 2016, resulting in 1,200 job losses. The decision, made by Ford Australia's Chief Executive Bob Graziano, comes due to unsustainably high business costs, with wages highlighted as a particular concern. Ford cited the business case not stacking up, noting that costs are double those in Europe and nearly four times higher in Australia.

In recent years, a new usage of "because" has emerged, where the word introduces a noun phrase rather than a clause or "of." This "because NOUN" construction, also called "because+noun" or "because NOUN" by linguists Laura Bailey and Mark Liberman, has gained popularity, especially among younger speakers. It often carries a casual, jocular tone and can imply that the referenced reason is weak or obvious. The construction is versatile, allowing for various grammatical classes, including nouns, verbs, adjectives, and interjections. Examples from Twitter illustrate its usage across different contexts, from expressing simple reasons to conveying complex emotions. While the exact origin of this usage is uncertain, it may have evolved from "because hey" type sentences or similar constructions in child-parent exchanges and insults. The spread of this linguistic trend highlights the adaptability of language and the appeal of syntactic economy.

Lindsay Lohan faces potential jail time as prosecutors aim to send her back to custody for violating probation terms in her 2007 DUI and 2012 necklace theft cases. Los Angeles City Attorney's spokesman Frank Mateljan said his office will seek jail time. Despite a favorable probation report, Lohan was terminated from the Downtown Women's Center for missing appointments and is now completing community service at the American Red Cross. Judge Stephanie Sautner will review Lohan's progress at a Wednesday hearing, where she could face a probation violation hearing. Lohan has completed only 21 of 360 required hours at the women's center and has not shown up at the coroner's office for 120 hours of service. Her publicist claims she has been working diligently to meet court-ordered obligations.

Donald Trump's Cabinet confirmation process is facing significant delays, with Republicans on track to take longer to fill out his team than any administration since George H.W. Bush in 1989. Despite control of both the White House and Senate, Trump's nominees are encountering ethics complications, Democratic opposition, and a congested legislative calendar. As of the article's writing, only a few of Trump's picks are expected to be confirmed on Inauguration Day, with confirmation hearings for key positions like Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and Education Secretary Betsy DeVos facing challenges. The process could take weeks or even months, with Democrats using parliamentary tactics to slow down confirmations and Republicans expressing confidence in eventually approving all nominees.

To protect privacy from the National Security Agency's surveillance, several methods can be employed. First, using Tor allows anonymous web browsing by routing traffic through multiple nodes, making it difficult to trace. Second, OTR (Off the Record) encryption can be used for instant messaging to ensure end-to-end privacy. Third, Silent Circle and Redphone offer secure, end-to-end encrypted phone calls, though they require open-source software and independent audits to ensure no backdoors. Fourth, removing the battery from a cellphone can prevent location tracking. Lastly, while encryption can protect the content of communications, it is harder to prevent the NSA from identifying the parties involved, as metadata can reveal significant information.

Joe Miller conceded the Alaska Senate race to incumbent Senator Lisa Murkowski, ending two months of legal battles. Miller, who won the Republican primary, lost the general election to Murkowski's write-in campaign. After a news conference where he stated he would not appeal the court's decision, Miller expressed his commitment to his ideological stance while acknowledging the outcome. Murkowski's campaign celebrated the certification of her victory, emphasizing her historic win as the first senator to win by write-in since 1954. Miller also revealed he does not have Murkowski's phone number and has not called to concede.

Scientists are on the verge of reviving an ancient species of super-cow, the auroch, which went extinct nearly 400 years ago. The auroch, a large, wild ancestor of today's cattle, was revered by Nazis as part of their Aryan mythology. Conservationists, aiming to restore the ecosystem's natural "gardening service" provided by the auroch, are breeding a "neo-auroch" through a process called back-breeding. The Tauros Project, led by ecologist Ronald Goderie, has released the fourth generation of these cattle into areas of Spain, Portugal, Croatia, the Czech Republic, and Romania, where they face challenges from predators like wolves. By 2025, the seventh generation of neo-aurochs is expected to closely resemble the original. The project, supported by Rewilding Europe, aims to reintroduce these cattle to restore natural landscapes and biodiversity, though critics raise concerns about potential unintended consequences.

Pope Benedict XVI faces criticism for his handling of sexual abuse cases within the Catholic Church, with a New York Times op-ed calling his latest apology inadequate. The Catholic League responded with an ad in the New York Times, blaming the scandal on homosexuality. Experts argue that pedophilia is more about attraction to youth and control rather than the gender of the victim or the molester's orientation. In a rare interview, Cardinal William J. Levada, head of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, defended Pope Benedict's handling of abuse cases and criticized The New York Times for unfair coverage. Levada praised Benedict for vigorously investigating and prosecuting abuse cases but also acknowledged that the Vatican's decision to suspend a canonical trial for a priest who abused deaf boys was not without controversy.

A South Carolina high school teacher, Leigh Anne Arthur, resigned after a nude photo of her was shared by a student who took her unlocked phone. The incident occurred when the student, who had access to the phone, took pictures of the photo and distributed them to classmates. Arthur claims she intended the photo for her husband and left her phone unattended while patrolling the halls. The student warned her that "your day of reckoning is coming." Arthur says she did not knowingly leave the phone unsecured. The Union County School District interim superintendent, David Eubanks, stated that Arthur could have contributed to the delinquency of a minor by leaving her phone unlocked. Arthur filed a lawsuit against the school district and the superintendent, alleging false accusations and a lack of proper due process. She has received support from students and parents through a petition.

Sherri Papini's husband, Keith, provided new details about his wife's condition after her alleged kidnapping. She was found on Thanksgiving with her face bruised, her nose broken, and her long blonde hair cut off. Keith expressed gratitude for the support from thousands of people during the ordeal. Sheriff Tom Bosenko confirmed that investigators are searching for two Hispanic women driving an SUV, matching Papini's description of her alleged captors. The case remains under investigation with no known motive.

Hurricane Sandy's approach is reshaping the final days of the 2012 presidential campaign, forcing Obama and Romney to adjust their schedules and potentially impacting early voting in affected areas. The storm may also influence voter psychology, with a 2011 study suggesting that electorates punish presidents and governors for severe weather damage but reward them for their responses. The study found that presidents receive a smaller electoral boost for disaster declarations compared to governors. Polling results could be affected, with an estimated 15 million voters potentially unable to participate due to the hurricane, which could shift the polls by a net one percentage point in favor of Romney. However, the storm's timing and inland impacts might mitigate these effects. The hurricane will also alter campaign plans and news coverage, highlighting the importance of cautious planning and safety.

A report commissioned by Nestle found that its Thailand seafood suppliers are engaged in abusive labor practices, including the use of forced and underage labor, in the country's fishing industry. Migrant workers, often from poorer neighboring countries, are lured to work under false pretenses and face hazardous, inhumane conditions. Workers are frequently charged excessive fees, leaving them in debt, and their pay is often withheld. Some laborers are subjected to verbal and physical abuse, and are even sold to boat captains needing crews. These issues are not unique to Nestle's supply chain, as virtually all companies sourcing seafood from Thailand face similar risks. Nestle has committed to improving the situation by setting up grievance channels, training boat captains, and conducting audits. The company aims to eliminate forced labor in its seafood supply chain, working alongside other stakeholders to address this complex issue.

Opinions on closing Guantanamo Bay have remained largely unchanged since 2009, with 66% of Americans opposing the idea of moving its prisoners to U.S. prisons. Despite recent controversy surrounding the release of five Taliban prisoners in exchange for U.S. Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl, support or opposition has not significantly shifted. President Obama has consistently aimed to close the facility, but public support remains low, especially among Republicans. The White House is exploring options to bypass congressional bans on bringing detainees to the U.S., potentially using executive power to close the prison.

每年六月，数百万中国高中生参加高考，这是决定他们能否进入顶尖大学的关键考试。如果成绩不理想，他们可能需要花费一年甚至更长时间才能找到另一条上大学的途径。如今，他们可能有了更快的选择。美国新罕布什尔大学宣布，将开始接受高考成绩，成为美国首个接受高考成绩的州立大学。此举旨在吸引更多优秀的中国高中生，尤其是在高考成绩公布后的六月，他们可以更快地申请入学，而通常这个过程需要等到秋季。中国是美国最大的留学生来源国，超过377,000名中国学生在美国大学就读。新罕布什尔大学还推出了一个针对高考成绩优异学生的早申请项目，学生需提交高考成绩、高中成绩单，并参加英语面试。该校认为，高考能测试学生是否掌握了特定的知识体系，以及他们是否具备刻苦学习和坚持到底的品质。

APOE gene variants, including e2, e3, and e4, influence various health conditions. Carrying one or two e4 variants significantly raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease, while e2 variants are linked to more brain plaques but potentially delayed dementia symptoms. These genetic factors also impact cardiovascular health, with e4 increasing the risk of atherosclerosis, and e2 associated with a rare condition called hyperlipoproteinemia type III. However, the role of APOE in age-related macular degeneration remains unclear, with mixed findings on its protective or harmful effects.

Scout Willis, daughter of Bruce and Demi Moore, took to the streets of New York City topless to protest Instagram's censorship policies. She tweeted photos of her stroll, captioning one "Legal in NYC but not on @instagram" and another "What @instagram won't let you see #FreeTheNipple." Willis even changed her Instagram handle to "Scout (Areola) Willis" before her account was disabled. This isn't the first time celebrities have pushed back against Instagram's rules; Rihanna's account was suspended for a topless magazine cover. Instagram's guidelines prohibit "nude, partially nude, or sexually suggestive photos," but Willis argues her comfort with her body shouldn't be dictated by social media policies.

A Houston family experienced a terrifying incident when a stranger hacked into their baby monitor and verbally abused their 2-year-old daughter. Marc Gilbert heard strange noises and an unfamiliar voice in his daughter's room while she was sleeping. The voice called the child a "slut" and directed harsh remarks at both parents. Fortunately, the child was deaf and did not hear the abusive comments. Upon realizing the situation, Gilbert disconnected the device. The incident highlights the potential security risks of internet-connected baby monitors. Experts advise changing default passwords, securing Wi-Fi networks, and limiting access to sensitive devices.

President Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser, Jared Kushner, has had his White House security clearance restored, ending months of uncertainty. Kushner met with special counsel Robert Mueller's investigators for seven hours in April, following a previous interview in November that focused on former national security adviser Michael Flynn. The Mueller investigation and other congressional inquiries have been ongoing, including those related to Kushner's role during the campaign and transition, particularly his contacts with Russians and events involving former FBI Director James Comey. While White House officials attribute the delay in Kushner's clearance to administrative backlogs and the complexity of his application, his security clearance has now been restored, allowing him to access sensitive information and continue his work.

A French MP faced outrage and had to interrupt her speech in the National Assembly when a conservative colleague began to mimic a hen's sound. Véronique Massonneau, from the green party Europe Ecology - The Greens, demanded the colleague to stop. The heckling continued, prompting the assembly president to intervene. The incident sparked calls for Le Ray to be officially reprimanded and was seen as sexist, especially in a country where "hen" is a derogatory term for women. An extraordinary meeting of party whips was called to address the issue.

In the Potomac River and other waterways in the Northeastern United States, male smallmouth bass are increasingly developing immature eggs in their testes, a phenomenon known as intersex. According to a study by the U.S. Geological Survey and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 85% of male smallmouth bass and 27% of male largemouth bass in 19 national wildlife refuges in the Northeast exhibit these characteristics. The exact cause remains unclear, but scientists suspect endocrine-disrupting chemicals, such as estrogenic compounds from agricultural runoff, pharmaceuticals, and pesticides, are responsible. These chemicals can interfere with the reproductive systems of fish, leading to the development of female characteristics in males. The issue is global, with similar cases reported worldwide. Efforts to address the problem include reducing runoff and managing chemicals more effectively.

Two adults and two children were found dead after a fire engulfed a large home in Colts Neck, N.J., on Tuesday. The fire, which continued into the evening, is being investigated as a possible arson. Officials are also investigating a fire that erupted at a relative's house earlier that day. The bodies of Keith Caneiro, 50, his wife Jennifer, and their two children were found inside the Colts Neck mansion. Keith Caneiro's brother, Paul Caneiro, 51, whose home was also the scene of a fire, is under investigation. The connection between the two fires remains unclear. Paul Caneiro's home was set ablaze around 5 a.m., with his wife and two daughters inside but unharmed. Neighbors reported seeing Paul Caneiro at his home until about noon, shortly before the Colts Neck fire broke out. The Caneiros were business partners, owning a technology firm and a pest control company together. The Colts

A newborn baby, with the umbilical cord still attached, was found barely breathing in a dumpster at an apartment complex in Houston, according to MyFoxHouston.com. Maintenance worker Carlos Michel discovered the baby upside down in a trash bag after hearing crying. The baby was taken to Hermann Hospital and is reported to be doing well. Authorities are trying to locate the baby's parents, suspecting the mother might be a teenage girl living on the property. Child Protective Services will also investigate. The incident highlights the importance of the "Baby Moses" law, which allows parents to leave newborns at places offering 24-hour medical care without fear of prosecution.

Taylor Swift, now living in New York and promoting her new album 1989, discusses her decision to fully embrace pop music and her reasons for not dating. She explains that being famous is like walking around with a cat on your head—sometimes you want privacy, but you can't be ungrateful for the attention. Swift's upcoming music video for "Shake It Off" required intense security, highlighting the challenges of maintaining privacy in the public eye. The article delves into Swift's new apartment, her friendships with Lena Dunham and Karlie Kloss, and her reflections on her career and personal life. She also shares her thoughts on feminism and sisterhood, and how her experiences have shaped her new album.

Baywatch won't make anyone think about anything, except maybe about where to plan their next vacation where they, too, can run in slo-mo on the sand. But, with everything else going on in the world these days, that may not be such a bad thing. The film discards any real connection to the cheesy television series that inspired it, with words you can’t say in prime time lobbed frequently and jokes based on male nether parts extended to excruciating effect. Director Seth Gordon seems to have decided to go full gonzo and the result is an ideal movie for immature, socially maladjusted males and their long-suffering girlfriends. The plot is equal parts slight and ludicrous, with head lifeguard Mitch Buchannon wanting to bust a drug ring operated by Victoria Leeds (Priyanka Chopra) to save the unspecified “bay” he keeps watch over. A 43-year-old man in Italy who had been in a minimally conscious state for nearly two years unexpectedly regained full consciousness and the ability to talk after being given a sedative typically used before surgery. The man, admitted to a hospital following a car accident, initially awoke from a coma but remained largely unable to communicate or move. Over the next year, his cognitive abilities declined, and he exhibited repetitive behaviors. About two years after the accident, he was given midazolam, a sedative, during a CT scan. Minutes later, he began talking and interacting with others, recognizing his family and performing simple tasks. The drug's effect was temporary, but it provided a brief window of improved cognitive function. Researchers identified brain regions affected by midazolam, which were previously linked to catatonia symptoms. Although midazolam was effective, it could only be administered in intensive care settings. The man's doctors then switched to carbamazepine, an epilepsy

After weeks of tension and conservative efforts to derail his nomination, Donald J. Trump was officially declared the Republican nominee at the 2016 Republican National Convention in Cleveland. Despite the anti-Trump conservatives' attempts to ignore state party rules and back their preferred candidates, the delegates overwhelmingly supported Trump, leaving no doubt that he would face Hillary Clinton in the general election. The convention focused on themes of job creation and family values, with speeches from Trump's children aiming to humanize the candidate. However, the proceedings also highlighted the divisions within the Republican Party, as seen in the dramatic speeches from Chris Christie and the continued emphasis on Clinton's Benghazi scandal. The nomination, while expected, marked a significant victory for Trump and set the stage for a contentious general election campaign.

Admiral John Sidney McCain, Sr. (1884-1945) was a commander of the Fast Carrier Task Force during World War II and a naval aviator. His son, John S. McCain, Jr., and grandson, John McCain III, also served in the Navy and became admirals and a U.S. Senator, respectively. All three attended the United States Naval Academy, and his great-grandson, John S. (Jack) McCain IV, is currently enrolled. McCain graduated from the Naval Academy in 1906 and served in various ships and commands, including the aircraft carrier Ranger, where he contributed to carrier tactics. He was involved in significant naval battles, including the Battle of Savo Island, where his failure to order reconnaissance missions contributed to an Allied defeat. In 1944, he commanded the Fast Carrier Task Force, earning the Navy Cross for his tactics. He died shortly after returning to the U.S. and was buried

Zimbabwean first lady Grace Mugabe, 52, faces an assault case in South Africa after a 20-year-old woman claims she was beaten with an extension cord by Mugabe at a hotel in Johannesburg. The alleged incident occurred when the woman visited Mugabe's sons in a hotel room. Mugabe's bodyguards reportedly did not intervene. The woman, Gabriella Engels, suffered a head injury and posted photos of her wound online. South African police confirmed an assault case was registered but have not named Mugabe as the suspect. Mugabe was reportedly in South Africa to have her ankle examined after an accident. She is due to appear in court, though she is not under arrest. The incident has drawn attention to Mugabe's controversial public image and her role as a powerful figure in Zimbabwe's ruling party.

The family of a 23-year-old physiotherapy student, who died after a brutal gang rape in Delhi, remember her as a brave and determined girl who dreamed of helping people and building a hospital in her ancestral village. Her father, proud of her academic achievements, sold family land to fund her education. The attack, which sparked nationwide protests and debates about violence against women in India, left her family devastated. The accused, five men, were formally charged in court, with the death penalty being widely demanded. The case has fueled calls for stricter laws and faster trials, but also sparked concerns about the potential for rushed legislation. The family's grief is palpable, with the victim's brother recalling their sister's determination and the last time he spoke to her. The incident has reignited discussions on women's safety and the need for more stringent legal measures.

Women can expect to live longer than men globally, with significant differences in life expectancies first emerging around the turn of the 20th century, according to a new study. Researchers from the University of Southern California found that female death rates decreased 70% faster than those of males in individuals born after 1880, with heart disease identified as the primary cause of excess deaths in adult men. The study, which examined data from 13 developed nations, suggests that sex hormones and biological factors may play a role in the varying aging processes of men and women.

Some everyday items, like wine bottles, have remained unchanged for centuries, seemingly immune to improvement. However, an innovative biophysicist, Daniel Perlman, has devised a solution to a long-accepted issue: wine dripping down the bottle's neck when poured. By adding a tiny groove just two millimeters wide around the bottle's opening, Perlman has altered the wine's behavior, preventing it from clinging to the bottle and dripping. This simple yet effective design change could potentially eliminate the need for napkin bandanas or other accessories used to address the problem. Currently, Perlman is in discussions with wine bottle manufacturers to potentially implement his design, which could bring an end to 200 years of wine drips.

This month has been tough for the Obama administration and the Affordable Care Act (ACA), with negative news dominating public perception. Polls show declining approval for President Obama, and the rollout of the health care exchanges has been plagued by technical issues and cancellations of existing insurance plans. While many people will qualify for subsidies or better coverage, the overall narrative has been one of disruption and dissatisfaction. The administration's promise that people could keep their existing plans if they liked them has proven misleading, and the website issues are likely to persist, overshadowing the law's benefits for months. The ACA's design, which forces people to switch to more comprehensive plans, has created a backlash, highlighting the flaws in a market-based approach. Democrats, who pushed for the law, now face the consequences of their decisions, while Republicans continue to criticize without offering solutions. The law's success hinges on addressing these issues, but the current narrative is one of failure and frustration.

Selena Gomez underwent a kidney transplant this summer due to her lupus, with her best friend Francia Raisa serving as the donor. Gomez revealed this on Instagram, thanking Raisa for the "ultimate gift and sacrifice." She had been quiet during part of the summer, recovering from the procedure. Gomez previously shared that she was diagnosed with lupus and underwent chemotherapy. She took a break from her career in August 2016 to address anxiety, panic attacks, and depression related to her lupus diagnosis.

Google has invited 34 cities in nine metropolitan areas to explore the possibility of bringing its ultra-fast fiber internet service, known as Google Fiber, to their communities. The company aims to provide updates by the end of the year on which cities will officially join the list of potential Fiber cities. Google Fiber offers 1-gigabit-per-second uploads and downloads, a speed that is significantly faster than what most consumers currently experience. The cities will be asked to complete a checklist of items to help Google understand what it would take to build a network in their area. Google Fiber currently has a presence in Kansas City and Provo, Utah, with rollouts also planned for Austin, Texas, and Shawnee, Kansas. This move could potentially expand Google's customer base and provide it with greater negotiation leverage with entertainment companies for its TV lineup. However, it is unclear which of the 34 cities will ultimately be selected, and Google has stated that it might not work out for everyone.

Former President George H.W. Bush, 91, has been discharged from Maine Medical Center after falling at his summer home and breaking a bone in his neck. Bush, who uses a motorized scooter or wheelchair due to Parkinson's disease, was treated for four days. Doctors say he will recover fully in three to four months and will not need surgery, though he will wear a neck brace for at least a couple of months. Bush was in good spirits during his hospital stay, according to a family spokesman.

North Korea claimed it successfully tested a powerful hydrogen bomb, drawing international condemnation and prompting calls for new sanctions. The underground explosion registered as a seismic event, causing concern among experts who doubted the claim of a hydrogen bomb. The United Nations Security Council planned an emergency meeting to discuss potential new measures. The U.S. and South Korea vowed to bolster their defenses, while China, North Korea’s main ally, expressed resolute opposition and threatened to lodge a protest. Analysts debated whether the test was a hydrogen bomb or a conventional atomic bomb, with some suggesting it might have been a "boosted" device. The test came as a surprise, given North Korea’s lack of activity in this area for some time. The international community faced challenges in addressing North Korea’s nuclear program, with ongoing efforts to find effective ways to curb its nuclear ambitions.

In 2009, the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, opened an exhibition featuring a mummified human head discovered in 1915 at the necropolis of Deir el-Bersha, Egypt. The head, found atop a governor's coffin, was part of Tomb 10A, which contained the remains of Djehutynakht and his wife. After the tomb was looted, the mummies were damaged, leaving a head and a torso. In 2005, CT scans suggested the head belonged to a man due to its robust features, but definitive sex determination required DNA analysis. Despite earlier failures to extract usable DNA from ancient Egyptian remains, forensic scientists from the FBI successfully sequenced DNA from the head, confirming it belonged to a male. This breakthrough demonstrates the potential of high-throughput sequencing for analyzing ancient DNA and resolving long-standing mysteries.

The Paterno family argues that the Freeh report, while accepted as definitive, is flawed and incomplete, and does not provide a fair hearing for Joe Paterno. They contend that uncovering the full truth requires a more thorough examination, including the opportunity to interview key witnesses and review critical evidence. The NCAA is set to impose corrective and punitive measures against Penn State in response to the child sex-abuse scandal involving Jerry Sandusky, based on the Freeh report. The family believes the University should have taken a stronger stand for due process to ensure the complete truth is uncovered, rather than accepting the report as conclusive.

A judge found two Ohio high school football players, Trent Mays and Ma'Lik Richmond, guilty of raping a 16-year-old girl after an alcohol-fueled party in August. The girl testified that she woke up naked in a strange house the next morning, unable to remember what happened. She pieced together the events from a video and photo that circulated online. Defense attorneys argued that the girl had a history of heavy drinking and lying, and suggested she might have consented to the sex. The case divided the community, with some residents complaining about a culture that protects the team, while others believe the girl and her supporters have blown the incident out of proportion.

The Russian ambassador to the U.S., Sergey Kislyak, has become a central figure in the Trump administration's Russia-related controversies. His meetings with key Trump officials, including former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn and Attorney General Jeff Sessions, have led to Flynn's resignation and calls for Sessions to recuse himself from investigations into Russia's alleged interference in the 2016 election. Kislyak, a 66-year-old diplomat with extensive experience, has a reputation for being a shrewd and loyal representative of Russian interests. Despite his low public profile, he has hosted cultural events and maintained a network of contacts in Washington. His role in the Trump administration's Russia saga has raised questions about his potential involvement in espionage and his interactions with U.S. officials.

JetBlue is offering a free round-trip flight to 50 lucky winners and their guests as part of their "For Good Month" initiative. The catch? The destination remains a mystery until the morning of the trip, which takes off from JFK International Airport on November 27. Participants will engage in three days of volunteer work focusing on JetBlue's three main pillars: youth and education, community, and the environment. Contestants must be U.S. residents over 18 and can enter by answering philanthropic questions on the JetBlueCheckInForGood website by October 26. Winners will be notified by November 20. The airline aims to make a significant impact in a city they serve, where participants will work alongside JetBlue crew members and non-profit partners.

A genetic study of Burmese pythons in the Florida Everglades has revealed that some snakes carry genetic markers from Indian pythons, raising concerns about the potential for hybrid super-predators. This discovery, made during a study to understand the invasive species better, indicates that crossbreeding may have occurred before the pythons established themselves in Florida. While the number of hybrid snakes is small, the findings suggest that the offspring might be better adapted to the local environment, potentially expanding their range more rapidly. The Burmese python, already a significant threat to native wildlife, could become even more formidable if these hybrid snakes become more common. Efforts to control the python population, including hunting programs and genetic studies, continue to face challenges in managing the invasive species.

The Duke of York has joined Twitter, becoming the first member of the Royal Family to do so. He launched his account with a simple "Welcome to my Twitter account - AY," prompting mixed reactions from other users. Some questioned his friendship with Jeffrey Epstein, while others joked about his name. The Duke, known for his work in free speech and technical education, aims to use the platform to share his activities. Within hours, his account gained over 3,000 followers.

Star Wars mania continues with a packed schedule of upcoming films, including spin-offs and anthology movies. "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story" is set for release on December 16, 2016, focusing on a group of Rebel fighters stealing plans for the Death Star. Felicity Jones stars alongside Mads Mikkelsen, Diego Luna, and Ben Mendelsohn. "Star Wars Episode VIII" follows in 2017, directed by Rian Johnson and featuring many from "The Force Awakens." The "Star Wars Anthology: Han Solo" is planned for 2018, with Phil Lord and Chris Miller directing and Lawrence Kasdan writing. "Star Wars Episode IX" is set for 2019, with Colin Trevorrow at the helm. A "Boba Fett" anthology is scheduled for 2020.
