Shorter mothers are more likely to have shorter pregnancies, smaller babies, and a higher risk of preterm birth, according to new research from the March of Dimes Prematurity Research Center Ohio Collaborative. Analyzing data from 3,485 Nordic women and their babies, the study found that maternal height, determined by genetic factors, influences the length of pregnancy and the frequency of preterm birth. Birth length and birth weight are mainly influenced by fetal genetics. The research highlights the importance of understanding genetic factors in fetal growth and gestational length, with the goal of preventing preterm birth. The March of Dimes is supporting this research through its nationwide network of prematurity research centers, bringing together experts from various disciplines to identify genetic contributions to fetal growth and pregnancy duration.

The 2013 Nathan's Fourth of July hot dog eating contest saw Joey Chestnut defend his title by consuming 69 hot dogs in 10 minutes, breaking his own record. Chestnut's victory marked his seventh consecutive win, while Matt Stonie finished second with 51 hot dogs. Sonya "The Black Widow" Thomas won the women's competition with 36.75 hot dogs, narrowly beating Juliet Lee. The event, in its 98th year, drew thousands of spectators to witness the competitive eating spectacle.

Kim Kardashian's ex-girlfriend Amber Rose claims the reality star is a "homewrecker" who initiated an affair with Kanye West when both were dating other people. According to Rose, she was dating Kanye while Kim and NFL player Reggie Bush were cheating on each other. Rose says Kim sent Kanye racy photos and texts, but Kim did not respond when Rose confronted her about it. Despite their past, Rose now credits Kim for helping her find true love with rapper Wiz Khalifa.

Hurricane Sandy's impact on Halloween celebrations is uncertain, with many East Coast businesses and pumpkin patches closing due to the storm. Small businesses relying on last-minute Halloween shopping are expected to face significant financial losses. The New York Greenwich Village Halloween Parade, originally scheduled for Wednesday, may be reduced in size due to the weather. Some stores and pumpkin patches are closing early or indefinitely. The storm's effects on takeout food and pumpkin patches are also anticipated to be substantial. Fundraisers and events, like the Goodwill Gridiron Halloween Party, have been postponed. New Jersey Governor Chris Christie has officially postponed Halloween celebrations until November 5 to ensure public safety. Many communities are also pushing back their Halloween festivities to the weekend or next week. Despite the disruptions, some parents are finding ways to celebrate Halloween indoors or in alternative settings.

A 20-year-old Burbank man died in a rollover crash on the southbound 5 Freeway near Griffith Park. The man, identified as Richard Pananian, was not wearing a seatbelt and was driving his 2004 Ford Fiesta at a high speed on the right shoulder of the freeway. He veered left, hit a 2004 Ford F-150, and lost control, overturning multiple times. Pananian was ejected and landed 20 to 30 feet onto a freeway sign, coming to rest on its ledge. His body remained there for several hours before being removed. The freeway was closed for about 20 minutes while firefighters extracted the body. No other injuries were reported.

The original illustrated map of The Hundred Acre Wood from A.A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh books is set to be auctioned, with an estimated price of up to $200,000. Created by E.H. Shepard in 1926, the map features characters like Winnie-the-Pooh, Christopher Robin, Piglet, and Eeyore. It will be sold at Sotheby's along with four other Shepard illustrations, including one of Christopher Robin and Pooh saying goodbye. The map, which also appears in the 1966 Disney film, is considered a valuable piece due to its significance in introducing readers to the Winnie-the-Pooh world.

A Vancouver police officer recently commended for a water rescue went beyond the call of duty by jumping into frigid waters to save a stranded dog at Lost Lagoon in Stanley Park. On Friday afternoon, the large pup chased a ball out onto the frozen lagoon and crashed through the thin ice. Officers arrived to find the tired dog struggling to stay above the water. Constable Peter Colenutt, known for his water rescues, stripped off part of his uniform and leapt into action. With the help of his co-workers holding a rescue rope, he made his way to the dog. Both the dog and the officer made it back to shore, cold but uninjured. The officer's heroic act earned him praise on social media, with users commending his "act of kindness" and "over and above" efforts.

Cardinal Donald Wuerl, the embattled archbishop of Washington, plans to travel to Rome to discuss his resignation with Pope Francis, as the U.S. Catholic Church continues to grapple with a growing sexual-abuse scandal. Wuerl, who previously served as the archbishop of Pittsburgh, faces calls for his resignation due to his handling of past cases of clerical sexual abuse, as highlighted in a recent grand jury report in Pennsylvania. The report alleged that Wuerl allowed several priests accused of abusing children to remain in ministry, relying on psychological assessments that were later criticized. Wuerl's decision to resign comes as the Church seeks to address new revelations of the extent of clergy abuse and failures in episcopal oversight.

Democrats hailed President Obama's move to halt deportations for millions of immigrants, but emphasized it as a temporary step, urging Congress to pass comprehensive reform. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi said it was "not a permanent solution" and called for Congress to act. Republicans, however, accused Obama of overstepping his authority and warned that his actions would make it harder for Congress to pass immigration reform. Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell struggled to contain a conservative backlash, with some tea party lawmakers calling for immediate and hard-line responses. Despite the political tension, both parties acknowledged the need for reform, with some moderate Republicans urging a measured approach. The debate highlighted the challenge for Republicans to balance their desire for action with the risk of alienating Hispanic voters and damaging their political brand.

This "Simpsons" episode from 1995 predicted several future technologies and trends, including soy snacks, widespread home satellite dishes, and motion-controlled video games. It also foresaw a future where classrooms were overcrowded, credit cards were used at vending machines, and the Rolling Stones were still performing. However, some predictions like ubiquitous video phones and robot servants fell flat. Overall, the episode offered a mix of accurate and inaccurate visions of the future.

House Speaker John Boehner signaled a clash with the White House and the Democratic-led Senate over raising the U.S. borrowing authority later this year, insisting that "we're not going to raise the debt ceiling without real cuts in spending." Boehner's comments come as President Obama prepares a series of economic speeches, which he is accused of using as a "big set-up" for a push for higher taxes. Republican leaders mocked Obama for giving more economic speeches while ignoring House-passed legislation aimed at boosting job growth. Any discussion about raising the debt ceiling must start with the premise that "we are the United States; we do not default," according to White House press secretary Jay Carney. Congressional Republicans are staking their ground in fiscal negotiations that could again pose the threat of default or a government shutdown.

Pentagon investigators concluded that Undersecretary of Defense for Intelligence Michael Vickers, a possible future CIA director, leaked restricted information to the makers of the film "Zero Dark Thirty," and referred the case to the Justice Department. Vickers provided the restricted name of a U.S. Special Operations Command officer who helped plan the Osama bin Laden raid. The Justice Department has not launched a criminal prosecution. The case highlights the ongoing debate over classified information and leaks, with the Obama administration facing criticism for potentially withholding the report to avoid political embarrassment. Vickers, a respected intelligence professional, is not expected to face serious consequences.

A Colorado busboy named Johnny "Thumper" Duckworth found $3,000 on the floor at Randy's Southside Diner and turned it in. Duckworth, who has worked at the diner for 9 years, insists the money is not his and should be returned to its rightful owner. The story gained attention, and a GoFundMe page was created to help Duckworth, who lives house to house and faces medical bills garnishing his paycheck. As of the update, the page has exceeded its $3,000 goal, raising over $3,800. Duckworth's honesty and willingness to return the money have touched many, highlighting the positive impact of integrity in the workplace.

After evading 1,200 police for 22 days in rugged northern Adirondack terrain, cop killer David Sweat was captured near the Canadian border. The search for Sweat intensified as authorities pieced together the last days of his fellow escapee, Richard Matt. Matt, who had grown up in Tonawanda, was found dead in a camp near Malone, NY, shot by a U.S. Customs and Border Protection tactical team. Matt, 49, had been sick and drunk, and his camp showed signs of prolonged outdoor living. The search for Sweat continued, with investigators finding no concrete evidence that the two had stayed together. Despite the massive manhunt, Sweat remained elusive, and his capture came after a state trooper shot him twice in the torso. Governor Cuomo expressed relief, stating, "The nightmare is finally over." Law enforcement officials hope to use Sweat's survival to uncover details of the escape and identify any accomplices.

A Colorado meatpacker, Cargill Meat Solutions, is recalling approximately 132,606 pounds of ground beef products that may be contaminated with E. coli O26, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service announced. The ground beef was produced and packaged on June 21, 2018, and distributed nationwide. The recall includes products from various brands including Our Certified, Excel, Sterling Silver, Certified, and Fire River Farms with use or freeze by dates of July 11, 2018. Consumers are advised to check their freezers for potentially affected products and discard or return them. The recall follows an investigation linking the ground beef to 17 illnesses and one death, with symptoms starting from July 5 to July 25, 2018. Cargill stated that all affected products have been removed from supermarkets and that food safety teams are reviewing facilities to ensure safe food delivery.

In November 2015, an email from Yale lecturer Erika Christakis about Halloween costumes sparked controversy and protests over racial sensitivity, leading to her decision to resign from her teaching position. The email, which encouraged students to wear any costume they wanted, was seen as insensitive by many students and faculty. Despite support from nearly 70 faculty members, Christakis decided the current climate at Yale was not conducive to open dialogue, and she stepped down from teaching. Her husband, Nicholas Christakis, also took a sabbatical to focus on his research and student needs. While Yale unveiled initiatives to improve its racial climate, the incident highlighted ongoing tensions between free speech and cultural sensitivity on college campuses.

A Michigan woman, Elizabeth Rathburn, pleaded guilty to selling infected human remains to medical and dental students, reports Reuters. Rathburn and her husband, Arthur Rathburn, ran a business called International Biological, Inc., selling or renting diseased cadavers to maximize profit. Prosecutors allege the couple purchased infected specimens at a discount, misrepresented them, and exposed customers to infection. Elizabeth Rathburn faces up to 10 months in prison and $55,225 in restitution. Her husband, Arthur Rathburn, is charged with transporting hazardous materials and making false statements, with a trial set for April 5. The Rathburns' business involved dismembering bodies with chainsaws and storing over 1,000 body parts in a Detroit warehouse. The case highlights the ethical and legal issues surrounding the sale of human remains for educational purposes.

With the first debate approaching, Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton are in a tight race nationally, with Clinton holding a 2-point edge in a two-way matchup among likely voters. The race is tied when third-party candidates are included. Among registered voters, Clinton leads Trump by five points. However, Clinton's voter enthusiasm has diminished, with Democrats less enthusiastic now than in August. About 40% of voters think each candidate should release more medical records. This is the first national poll measuring the race among likely voters, which considers voting intent and enthusiasm. When third-party candidates Gary Johnson and Jill Stein are factored in, the race is tied, with both receiving 42% support. Trump and Clinton retain most of their support, but slightly more of Clinton’s supporters are moving to Johnson or Stein. The gender gap remains, with Trump leading among men and Clinton among women. Clinton is ahead among non-white voters but not getting the same level of support as Obama did in 201

A year after a brutal gang rape on a bus in New Delhi shocked India and the world, public protests and new laws aimed at protecting women have been held across the country. The victim, a 23-year-old physiotherapy student, was attacked by six men who beat her and her male friend, then dumped them on the roadside. She died 13 days later. The case led to nationwide protests, prompting the government to pass stricter laws, including doubling the minimum sentence for rape to 20 years and criminalizing stalking and voyeurism. Fast-track courts were established for rape cases, and the attackers were tried relatively quickly. However, while the number of reported rapes has increased, some argue that social attitudes toward women need to change. The victim's father stated, "Social mindsets have to change. Only then can we say a difference has been made."

The decision not to release post-mortem photos of Osama bin Laden is seen as a pragmatic choice, despite arguments for their publication. President Obama and others argue that releasing the photos could inflame anti-American sentiment and endanger troops. Critics contend that withholding such images undermines transparency and could fuel conspiracy theories. The photos, described as gruesome, show bin Laden with a gunshot wound to the head. Opponents argue that not releasing them infantilizes the nation and sets a dangerous precedent. Proponents believe the photos are essential to the war on al-Qaeda and that the public can handle viewing such images. The debate highlights the tension between national security concerns and the public's right to know.

Former child actor Jason Michael Handy, who once described himself as a "pedophile," secretly took over 1,000 photos of young girls using a telephoto lens and worked with children in the entertainment industry, exploiting their dreams of stardom. After pleading no contest to charges of lewd acts on a child and distributing sexually explicit material by email, Handy was sentenced to six years in prison. His case, along with recent arrests of other industry professionals, is prompting calls for stricter background checks and licensing for those working with young actors. The entertainment industry has historically lacked stringent standards for employees with unsupervised access to children, making it easier for predators to gain such positions.

Martin Shkreli, the notorious "pharma bro" convicted on three counts of fraud, faces the possibility of being sent back to jail despite his recent conviction. Federal prosecutors moved to revoke his $5 million bail after he posted on Facebook an offer of $5,000 for a strand of Hillary Clinton’s hair during her book tour. The government argues this "threat" poses a danger to society, as it required Secret Service resources and could lead others to act on his words. Shkreli's lawyers have until Tuesday to respond, with a hearing scheduled for Thursday. His behavior since his arrest, including harassment of journalists and social media outbursts, has further complicated his case. Shkreli could face up to 20 years in prison, but his defense plans to appeal the convictions.

A federal judge is set to hear arguments on whether Louisiana prison officials are adequately protecting death-row inmates from dangerous heat and humidity at Angola State Penitentiary. The state refuses to install air conditioning, despite a 2014 ruling by U.S. District Judge Brian Jackson that such conditions impose unconstitutionally cruel and unusual punishment when the heat index exceeds 88 degrees. The state argues that current measures, including cold showers and fans, are sufficient. Inmates, represented by attorneys from The Promise of Justice Initiative, argue for air conditioning as a necessary remedy. The case has already cost taxpayers over $1 million in legal fees, with private attorneys from a law firm with ties to the state's former Attorney General billing the state more than $424,000. The judge has scheduled a hearing to determine if the state's current measures are adequate or if air conditioning must be installed.

Footage from the Grandview Aquarium in Guangzhou, China, reveals animals like bears, wolves, beluga whales, and walruses trapped in small, dim enclosures, with visitors banging on the glass to get their attention. The aquarium, located inside a mall, has faced criticism for neglect and poor animal care, with videos and photos showing stressed animals pacing and swimming in confined spaces. Animal welfare groups, including Animals Asia, have launched a petition with over 270,000 signatures calling for the facility's closure. Despite public pressure, the aquarium remains open, but management has taken some steps to improve conditions, such as providing snow for polar bear hybrids. Animal welfare advocates continue to push for better treatment and more natural living conditions for the animals.

The U.S. Department of Justice has withdrawn its legal action compelling Apple's assistance in unlocking an iPhone linked to the San Bernardino shootings, stating it successfully accessed the device's data. In a court filing, prosecutors announced they no longer need Apple's help and have asked a federal judge to vacate the previous order. This move ends the legal battle between Apple and the FBI over a single iPhone but leaves unresolved broader concerns about privacy and security. Apple had argued that creating a workaround would weaken the security of millions of iOS devices and infringe on privacy rights. The government's success raises questions about the security of Apple's devices and potential future methods for law enforcement to access data. Apple reiterated its stance that the case should never have been brought and stressed the importance of data protection and privacy.

"Clash of the Titans" is a loud, over-the-top remake that fails to engage despite its 3D effects and star-studded cast. The plot, based loosely on the 1981 version, is filled with clichés and poorly executed action sequences. Sam Worthington's Perseus is an ineffective hero who does little until the final act, while Ralph Fiennes and Liam Neeson provide some of the only moments of interest. The dialogue is weak, and the characters are underdeveloped. Director Louis Leterrier's handling of the material is uninspired, resulting in a film that feels like a series of disconnected set pieces. The 3D effects are minimal and poorly executed, adding little to the overall experience. Overall, "Clash of the Titans" is a forgettable entry in the summer blockbuster lineup.

A New Hampshire high school senior, Stiles Zuschlag, was told he was no longer welcome at the private Christian school he had attended since kindergarten due to his gender identity. The school's administrator suggested he get counseling and told him he could not return to the campus. Zuschlag, who was on track to be valedictorian, transferred to a public school where he feels accepted. The school administration declined to comment, citing privacy. Zuschlag's mother supported his transition, and his sister adjusted to the change. Despite bullying, Zuschlag is now nominated for "Prince of Homecoming" at his new school.

Mariner Energy has a history of accidents and pollution incidents in the Gulf of Mexico, according to federal regulators. The company was involved in at least a dozen offshore accidents or pollution spills, including fires, blowouts, and worker injuries. These incidents occurred between 2006 and 2009 and resulted in fines and violations. The latest accident, a fire on a Mariner Energy platform, highlights ongoing safety concerns in the offshore drilling industry, complicating efforts to resume drilling after a moratorium.

Jon Gosselin, 39, and father of eight, will strip for a one-night-only event at Caesars Atlantic City’s Untamed Male Revue on April 1, his 40th birthday. Gosselin, who previously worked as a DJ at the club, now promotes events and says he feels part of a "brotherhood." The performance, described as "Vegas style" with choreography from a former Vegas showgirl, will feature Gosselin in a non-cheesy, non-sleazy act. He confirmed the news to Entertainment Tonight, stating he never imagined himself in such a role.

A Grand Rapids, Michigan, woman was asked to leave Woodland Mall on a 90-degree day for wearing denim cutoff shorts and a tank top, sparking outrage online. Hannah Pewee shared her experience, stating she was surrounded by other similarly dressed shoppers. The mall's code of conduct only requires appropriate attire and shoes, with no mention of shorts length. Pewee received an apology from mall management, who plan to revise their website's dress code policy for clarity. The incident highlights the need for clear and inclusive dress codes, especially in warmer weather.

A 3-year-old girl named Aubri Degeffered was found safe in Jefferson County with a suspect after being abducted in a carjacking. The incident occurred when Aubri was inside a red 2014 Volvo SUV, which was stolen in Milwaukee. Later, the same red Volvo was involved in an attempted strong-arm robbery in Brookfield. Aubri was found safe and a 32-year-old suspect was in custody, though details of the discovery were not provided. The Amber Alert for Aubri was cancelled shortly after her safe recovery.

A Mormon missionary from Utah, Gavin Paul Zimmerman, 19, died after falling from a cliff at Cape Solander in Kurnell, Sydney. The incident occurred as he was taking selfies with friends. Local authorities recovered his phone with photos taken moments before the fall. Zimmerman, who had been serving his mission in Australia for nearly a year, was described by his parents as a bright light who loved his mission. The area is popular for whale-watching but lacks proper fencing, leading to repeated incidents of visitors falling.

A 26-year-old mother, Lacey Spears, has been charged with second-degree depraved murder and first-degree manslaughter in the death of her 5-year-old son, Garnett, who died from sodium poisoning at Westchester Medical Center. Spears, who had been living at the Fellowship Community in Chestnut Ridge, New York, with her son, pleaded not guilty and was ordered held without bail. Prosecutors believe she systematically poisoned her son, possibly suffering from Munchausen syndrome by proxy, a psychiatric disorder where a parent sickens a child to gain attention and sympathy. The case is thought to be one of the first involving such a disorder in the social media era. Spears documented Garnett's medical struggles on social media, and investigators found evidence she had researched the effects of salt poisoning online. Garnett's death came after he was admitted to Nyack Hospital with seizure-like symptoms and later transferred to Westchester Medical Center. The investigation involved extensive interviews and medical record analysis, and

New York Times reporter James Risen defended his recent story on Afghanistan's mineral deposits, dismissing critics as ignorant bloggers. Risen, who previously won a Pulitzer Prize for uncovering the NSA's secret wiretapping program, accused online critics of sitting in pajamas and questioning his reporting chops. He insisted the story was based on Pentagon research and not a PR campaign. Risen acknowledged some of the information was not new, but argued it was the comprehensive nature of the Pentagon's findings that made the story significant. Despite potential risks and challenges, officials believe the mineral wealth could transform Afghanistan's economy and provide jobs. However, concerns remain about corruption, environmental impact, and foreign influence, especially from China.

President Donald Trump is narrowing his search for a Supreme Court nominee to about five finalists, including two women, and plans to announce his pick on July 9. Trump is studying the backgrounds, judicial philosophies, and temperaments of his shortlist at his Bedminster, New Jersey, golf club. He had extensive conversations with White House Counsel Don McGahn to seek additional insights on potential candidates. While Trump may interview one or two candidates over the weekend, no interviews have taken place as of Saturday evening. The finalists include Brett Kavanaugh, Amy Coney Barrett, Thomas Hardiman, Raymond Kethledge, and Amul Thapar. Trump stated he won’t ask candidates about the 1973 Roe v. Wade abortion-rights decision during interviews. Confirmation of the nominee is expected to be a partisan process, with Republican control of the Senate providing the majority needed for confirmation.

A schoolgirl's message in a bottle, thrown into the North Sea over 20 years ago, has been discovered and responded to in the Netherlands. Zoe Averianov, now 33 and living in Salford, tossed the letter into the sea when she was 10 years old during a family holiday from Hull to Germany. Her parents received a letter addressed to her maiden name, containing both her original message and a reply from Piet and Jacqueline Lateur, who found the bottle while walking their dog near Rotterdam.

Former Florida Governor Jeb Bush tells WHAS11 News he is "not running for President," despite speculation about a potential 2016 candidacy that could continue the Bush political dynasty. Bush is in Louisville to speak about education reform at the National Conference of State Legislatures, highlighting Florida's success in improving students' educational performance, particularly for Latino students. He hosted a fundraiser for Republican U.S. Senate candidate Rand Paul, a critic of federal education policy, while praising President Obama's contributions to education. Bush emphasizes that all kids can learn and that education is key to solving social problems.

Three French workers, while leveling land at a house in Normandy, discovered a hidden treasure trove worth over €900,000 ($1.2 million) in gold bars and coins. Rather than informing the property owner, they decided to keep the find, selling some of the gold to a local coin collector. Tax officials became aware of the theft when one of the workers deposited high-value checks. The workers, aged 20, 33, and 40, confessed to their crime when caught. They used the gold to buy vehicles and motorcycles, and even invested in life insurance and home improvements. The three will appear in court in Evreux, northwest of Paris, while the coin collector faces charges for handling stolen goods. The property owners, who wish to remain anonymous, had jokingly told the workers to inform them if they found any treasure.

Scientists have discovered that up to half of Earth's water is older than the sun, potentially originating from a cloud of dust before the sun's formation. This finding, published in Science, suggests that water might be a common ingredient in the formation of other planets. By measuring the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio, researchers found that Earth's water contains more heavy hydrogen than the protoplanetary disk from which the solar system formed, indicating that some water predates the sun. This discovery implies that water-rich environments and potentially life-supporting conditions may be more common in the universe.

In 1933, Jack Yufe and Oskar Stohr, identical twins separated at six months, grew up in vastly different environments: Yufe in Trinidad as a Jew, Stohr in Nazi Germany as a member of the Hitler Youth. Their unique bond, explored through the Minnesota Twin Study, revealed striking similarities in habits and temperaments despite their contrasting upbringings. Both wore the same outfit, shared nervous habits, and had competitive drives. Their relationship, marked by both love and rivalry, was deeply affected by their shared past and the stark differences in their experiences. Yufe, who died of cancer in 2019, and Stohr, who passed away in 1997, remained fascinated by each other's similarities and differences throughout their lives.

After nearly six months in a coma, Bobbi Kristina Brown, 22, passed away on July 26, 2015, at Peachtree Christian Hospice in Georgia. She was found unresponsive in a bathtub at her home in January and was initially placed in a medically induced coma. Her condition worsened in June, leading her family to transfer her to hospice care. The Houston family released a statement confirming her death and expressing gratitude for the support she received. Celebrities and friends shared messages of condolences on social media, offering their sympathies to Bobby Brown and the family. An autopsy will be conducted to determine the cause of her death.

A 57-year-old Indian citizen, Sureshbhai Patel, arrived in the U.S. to help care for his grandson. Less than a week later, he was approached by Madison Police in response to a suspicious person call. Despite not speaking English, Patel struggled to communicate. In an attempt to search him, an officer forced Patel to the ground, causing severe injuries that left him partially paralyzed. Patel underwent cervical fusion surgery and faces a long recovery. The family has hired a local attorney to sue the Madison Police Department. Chief Larry Muncey recommended Officer Eric Parker be terminated for his actions, which did not meet department standards. Parker has been charged with third-degree assault and turned himself in. The FBI is conducting a civil rights inquiry. Members of the local Indian community attended a press conference to support Patel and called for better communication between police and the community.

The Jackie Robinson biopic 42, directed by Brian Helgeland, faces criticism for its overly reverent approach, which leaves little room for Robinson's naturalism and idiosyncrasy. The film focuses on Robinson's first season with the Brooklyn Dodgers, where he faces relentless racial slurs from Philadelphia manager Ben Chapman. While the movie aims to highlight Robinson's noble character, it often feels like a commencement speech rather than a compelling drama. Chadwick Boseman's performance is praised for capturing Robinson's dignity and barely contained rage, but the overall narrative is seen as obvious and lunkily plotted. Danny Boyle's Trance, on the other hand, offers a high-order, film noir experience with a complex plot involving an auction-house art heist and hypnosis. The movie's visual style and editing create an exhilarating, attention-deficit disorienting effect, making it a thrilling watch despite its moral ambiguity.

HMD Global, the Finnish company behind the Nokia brand, has unveiled the Nokia 8, its first flagship Android smartphone. The device features a 5.3-inch 2560x1440 display, a Qualcomm Snapdragon 835 processor, 4GB of RAM, and 64GB of storage. Its standout feature is the "bothie" mode, which simultaneously activates the front and rear cameras to capture dual perspectives, ideal for live streaming or social media content. The Nokia 8 also boasts a dual-camera setup with Zeiss optics and Ozo audio, enabling 360-degree sound capture. Despite these innovative features, the phone's design and specifications are largely standard for a top-tier device, placing it in the same price range as competitors like the Samsung Galaxy S8. The Nokia 8 will be available in Europe for €599 in September, hoping to capitalize on the nostalgia of the Nokia brand while competing with established players in the

A feminist group at the University of Mary Washington filed a Title IX complaint with the U.S. Department of Education, alleging that the school failed to protect its members from harassment on the anonymous app Yik Yak. More than 700 threatening and sexist messages were posted about the group and its members, including explicit threats of violence. Despite multiple complaints, the university did not take action, citing First Amendment concerns. The group's president, Paige McKinsey, said the threats left members feeling unsafe and forced to walk in groups. Grace Rebecca Mann, a member of the group, was killed in April, though it's unclear if the harassment was related. The University of Mary Washington stated it acted on all threats of violence but faced limitations in blocking the app due to free speech concerns. Yik Yak has implemented measures to combat abuse but faces criticism for its handling of the situation.

Weight Watchers International Inc. reported a loss in the holiday quarter and expects its turnaround strategy to take longer than anticipated due to a challenging start to 2015. The company plans to cut $100 million more in costs this year and forecast lower profits. Weight Watchers has faced declining subscriptions and revenue as consumers increasingly use apps and other gadgets to track calories and maintain fitness. The stock dropped 35% in a single day, its biggest decline since the company's initial public offering in 2001. Fitness trackers are expected to triple in usage by 2018, with smartwatches gaining popularity. Juniper Research predicts that by 2018, smartwatches will surpass fitness trackers in usage. Weight Watchers has embraced activity trackers but faces challenges in keeping pace with digital trends.

Mexico's northeastern border region will receive an increase in troops and federal police as part of "Coordinated Operation Northeast" to regain control from two rival drug cartels. The operation aims to reinforce government authority in Tamaulipas and Nuevo Leon, areas heavily affected by the split between the Gulf cartel and the Zetas. Details on the operation's scale and specific actions are limited due to security concerns. The region has seen intense violence, including the killing of local politicians and the closure of schools. Despite recent arrests of key cartel leaders, the drug war has claimed 28,000 lives since 2006, and 49% of Mexicans believe the government's efforts have been unsuccessful.

At the 2017 Golden Globes, Amy Schumer and Goldie Hawn brought some laughs while presenting the Best Motion Picture Comedy or Musical award. They joked about their roles in "Snatched," Amy playing the daughter and Goldie the mother, though Goldie's glasses kept getting in the way. The evening also saw Meryl Streep's emotional acceptance of the Cecil B. DeMille Award, where she criticized President Trump and called on the press to stay vigilant. Viola Davis's speech honored Streep, praising her talent and impact. Other highlights included Jimmy Fallon's jokes about Mariah Carey's New Year's Eve performance and his opening number with a guest verse from Millie Bobby Brown. The big winner was "La La Land," sweeping all its categories and breaking Golden Globe records.

A close friend, Dr. Prabhjot Singh, a Sikh American professor at Columbia University, was brutally attacked on a public street, the victim of a violent hate crime. His assailants taunted him, calling him "Osama" and "terrorist," and he described being punched repeatedly until falling to the ground, with head punches continuing as he lay on the sidewalk. Dr. Singh has dedicated his life to serving the underserved, working as the Director of Systems Management at the Earth Institute and a resident physician at Mt. Sinai Hospital. This incident, along with others targeting Sikh Americans, highlights the need for building bridges and combating hate and violence.

The TSA's invasive security measures, including full-body pat-downs and privacy-invading scanners, have become a source of public outrage. Critics argue that these measures have not significantly enhanced airport security and have instead turned into "security theater," a term coined by security expert Bruce Schneier. The full-body pat-downs, in particular, have sparked a revolt, with one traveler famously declaring, "If you touch my junk, I’ll have you arrested." The article suggests that the current system of treating all passengers as equally likely to be a threat is flawed and calls for a shift to a risk-based screening system. This would involve dividing passengers into three risk groups: low-risk, high-risk, and medium-risk. Low-risk travelers, such as frequent flyers and those with government security clearances, would face minimal screening. High-risk travelers, based on watch lists, would undergo more rigorous checks. Medium-risk travelers would face standard checkpoint screening. The article argues that this approach would be more efficient and

Singer Etta James, known for hits like "At Last" and "All I Can Do Was Cry," is suffering from leukemia and dementia, according to court documents. Her husband of 41 years, Artis Mills, is seeking control of over $1 million intended for her health care, while her son Donto James wants a third party to manage the funds to avoid family conflict. James, who hasn't performed since 2010, has been receiving round-the-clock care at her home. Mills previously filed for divorce in 2008 but withdrew the petition.

The Simpsons episode "Fraudcast News" on Sky 1 sparked a Twitter frenzy with viewers tweeting about the show's apparent dig at Rupert Murdoch. The episode depicts power plant tycoon Montgomery Burns buying up Springfield's media outlets, leading to Lisa Simpson's newspaper and a public response. Viewers praised the episode, seeing it as a commentary on Murdoch's media empire. Sky insisted the timing was coincidental. Meanwhile, Rupert and James Murdoch face calls to appear before British Parliament to answer questions about phone hacking, while a parliamentary committee investigates potential conflicts of interest among police officers involved in the initial phone-hacking inquiry.

Fiat Chrysler is recalling 1.4 million vehicles due to software security concerns, following a demonstration by hackers who remotely took control of a Jeep driving at 70 mph. The vulnerability affects cars with 8.4-inch touch displays, including Dodge Viper, Ram pickups, Jeep Grand Cherokee, Dodge Durango, Chrysler 200, 300, and Dodge Charger models from 2013 to 2015. Affected owners will receive USB devices for additional security upgrades. FCA is applying network-level security measures to prevent similar hacks and notes no related injuries or accidents have been reported. The hackers, Charlie Miller and Chris Valasek, plan to present their findings at the Black Hat security conference in August.

Apparel retailer Gap Inc. announced it will raise hourly pay for its U.S. employees to $9 in June 2014 and $10 in June 2015, following the White House's decision to raise the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $10.10 an hour starting in 2015. Gap, owner of Old Navy, Banana Republic, and Gap apparel chains, said the increased pay will benefit about 65,000 store employees. President Obama applauded Gap's decision, while Wal-Mart remained neutral on the federal minimum wage increase, stating it already pays most full-time employees above the proposed level.

Salt Lake City's District Attorney Sim Gill announced a criminal investigation into the arrest of Alex Wubbels, a nurse at University Hospital, after she refused to draw blood from an unconscious patient. The arrest, which was recorded on police body camera footage, drew widespread backlash and calls for accountability. Mayor Jackie Biskupski and Police Chief Mike Brown apologized to Wubbels and pledged changes to blood draw policies and officer training. Detective Jeff Payne, who arrested Wubbels, was placed on administrative leave. An internal affairs investigation is ongoing, and the Unified Police Department will conduct the criminal probe. The incident has sparked discussions about police-nurse relations and the handling of medical emergencies.
Jennifer Aniston and Justin Theroux have officially moved in together, according to a source for People.com. They are renting a house while continuing to search for their ideal home to purchase.

The FDNY mourned the death of Firefighter Michael R. Davidson, a 37-year-old 15-year veteran who died battling a 5-alarm fire at a Harlem movie set. Davidson, assigned to Engine Company 69, was critically injured and later succumbed to his injuries at Harlem Hospital. He leaves behind his wife and four young children. Two other firefighters suffered serious burns. The fire broke out during the filming of "Motherless Brooklyn," directed by Edward Norton. Davidson was cited for bravery four times during his career. His death comes a week after two FDNY firefighters died in a helicopter crash in Iraq. Mayor de Blasio toured the scene, expressing condolences to Davidson's family.

Astros first baseman Yuli Gurriel faced potential discipline from Major League Baseball after making a racially insensitive gesture during Game 3 of the World Series. Gurriel used his fingers to mock his own eyes and mouthed a derogatory term in Spanish after hitting a home run off Dodgers pitcher Yu Darvish. Gurriel said the gesture was meant to mock Japanese pitchers, as he had struggled against Darvish. Darvish called the gesture and the word "disrespectful" but said everyone is human and needs to learn from the incident. MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred intends to speak with Gurriel. Darvish and Astros manager A.J. Hinch expressed forgiveness, while Dodgers outfielder Enrique Hernandez found the situation disappointing.

Japanese authorities are attempting to identify eight decomposed bodies found on a wooden boat that washed up on a beach in northern Akita prefecture. The boat, about 7 meters long, was missing navigational devices and a rotor blade, leading officials to suspect it may have come from North Korea. This discovery follows a series of similar incidents, including the recent washing ashore of eight North Korean fishermen in good health. Over the weekend, two decomposed male bodies were also found on Sado island, with North Korean cigarettes and life jackets with Korean lettering nearby. Forty-four wooden ships from the Korean peninsula have drifted to Japanese shores or off its coast so far this year, with crew often already deceased, earning them the local moniker "ghost ships." Experts attribute these incidents to North Korea's efforts to satisfy food shortages by demanding large seafood quotas, forcing fishermen to use aging, ill-equipped vessels.

Mitt Romney faced hecklers during a Q&A session at the Iowa State Fair, leading to a shouting match. Romney defended low corporate taxes, stating "Corporations are people," a comment quickly seized upon by Democrats. The exchange occurred as Romney was stumping two days before the Ames Straw poll in Iowa. Romney also rebuffed questions about raising the cap on Social Security taxes and cutting Medicare benefits, emphasizing that he would not raise taxes. Democrats criticized Romney for seeming out of touch, while his campaign defended his remarks as accurate. This incident comes ahead of a Republican presidential primary debate in Iowa and a test of conservative strength before next year's Iowa caucuses.

President Trump is criticizing Sen. Dianne Feinstein for releasing a transcript from an interview with Glenn Simpson, co-founder of Fusion GPS, on Twitter. Trump calls Feinstein "Sneaky Dianne" and questions the authorization for the release. He also reiterates that the Russia investigation is a "Witch Hunt" and urges Republicans to take control.

Republican Senator Bob Corker, who recently announced his retirement, has engaged in a public feud with President Trump over the latter's handling of foreign policy and overall competence. Corker, who previously supported Trump, now criticizes him as "treating his office like a reality show" and potentially putting the nation "on the path to World War III." Trump, in turn, has called Corker "liddle" and accused him of not having the "guts" to run for re-election. The ongoing Twitter spat highlights tensions between Trump and key Republican lawmakers as the President struggles to achieve legislative success. Corker's comments have drawn criticism from the White House, which maintains that the President is "very successful" and "certainly entitled to his own opinion." The dispute underscores the challenges Republicans face in navigating Trump's presidency and maintaining their legislative agenda.

Researchers have discovered that chestnut-crowned babbler birds, a highly social species from the Australian Outback, can rearrange meaningless sounds in their calls to create new meanings, a process similar to how humans form words. This finding, published in PLOS Biology, suggests a potential early step in the evolution of complex language systems. Scientists at the Universities of Exeter and Zurich observed that the babbler birds use two sounds, "A" and "B," in different combinations during specific behaviors. For instance, a flight call "AB" is used differently from a "B-A-B" call made while feeding chicks. The birds can distinguish between these calls, looking at nests when hearing feeding calls and watching the sky when hearing flight calls. This rearrangement of sounds to generate new meanings is a significant discovery, as it was previously thought that this ability was unique to humans. Co-author Dr. Andy Russell suggests that rearranging sounds might be a quicker way to create new meanings than evolving entirely

This week, Hillary Clinton's image as a powerful and in-charge figure has gained renewed attention through the "Texts From Hillary" meme, which features a photo of Clinton on a C-17 military jet paired with bossy quotes. The meme, created by D.C.-based communications professionals Stacy Lambe and Adam Smith, has gone viral, garnering thousands of shares and generating national media coverage. It highlights Clinton's popularity and resurgence, especially in contrast to her 2008 campaign where she was often portrayed as overly calculated. Despite her lower visibility as Secretary of State, Clinton's approval ratings have reached new highs, including among Republicans. The meme captures the public's appreciation for her tough and competent leadership style, reinforcing her image as the "head bitch in charge." As speculation about a potential 2016 presidential run intensifies, Clinton's current position as Secretary of State has bolstered her reputation, making her a formidable candidate.

Bruno Mars dominated the 60th annual Grammy Awards, winning all six categories he was nominated for, including album of the year for "24K Magic," record of the year for "That's What I Like," and song of the year for the same track. Jay-Z, the leading nominee with eight, went home empty-handed, sparking criticism for the Recording Academy's perceived bias against hip-hop. Kendrick Lamar won five awards but missed out on the top categories, highlighting the ongoing challenge for rappers to secure broader recognition. Kesha's powerful performance of "Praying" with the Resistance Revival Chorus and other female artists drew attention to the #MeToo and Time's Up movements. The show featured emotional tributes, such as a rendition of "Tears In Heaven" to honor victims of the Route 91 Harvest Festival tragedy. Other highlights included Lady Gaga, Sam Smith, and Pink delivering standout performances. The ceremony also included a comedic skit involving Hillary Clinton,

In the ongoing investigation into actress Natalie Wood's 1981 drowning, officials have reopened the case, primarily due to new information from the boat's captain, Dennis Davern, and a book co-authored by Marti Rulli. The death was initially ruled an accident, but recent developments have sparked renewed interest. The book suggests foul play, with claims of an argument between Wood and her husband, Robert Wagner, and allegations that Wagner impeded a search for Wood. The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department has assigned full-time homicide detectives to the case and is interviewing key witnesses. While no one has been officially labeled a suspect, the investigation remains open, with the potential for significant new developments.

A Laysan albatross named Wisdom, estimated to be over 60 years old and the oldest known wild bird in the United States, has survived a devastating tsunami generated by Japan's 9.0 magnitude earthquake and recently hatched a chick on Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge. Wisdom, first banded in 1956, has likely raised at least 30 to 35 chicks during her breeding life. The albatross, known for its long-distance flying abilities, spends half the year at sea and returns to land only to breed. Wisdom's survival and continued ability to raise chicks despite the challenges highlight the resilience of these seabirds. The Midway Atoll, a breeding ground for thousands of Laysan albatrosses, faces threats from marine debris, habitat loss due to rising sea levels, and invasive species. Conservation efforts aim to protect these birds and their habitat, emphasizing the importance of preserving their unique lifestyle and the ecosystems they inhabit

A Minnesota woman charged with second-degree manslaughter after fatally shooting her boyfriend during a YouTube stunt foreshadowed the incident with a tweet. Monalisa Perez, 19, and Pedro Ruiz III, 22, were making a video where Perez shot a book Ruiz was holding against his chest. Perez shot from about a foot away, using a .50-caliber Desert Eagle pistol. Hours before, Perez tweeted, "Me and Pedro are probably going to shoot one of the most dangerous videos ever. HIS idea not MINE." Ruiz's aunt described him as a daredevil who enjoyed dangerous stunts. The incident occurred outside their home, and Ruiz's aunt said their 3-year-old daughter witnessed the shooting. Perez is currently pregnant and has a YouTube channel with prank and stunt videos.

A Dallas priest accused of molesting teens and stealing from his parish for 27 years is now missing, prompting concern among parishioners. Bishop Edward Burns of the Dallas Diocese said two private investigators are being hired to track down the Rev. Edmundo Paredes, who has been accused of sexually abusing three teenage boys over a decade ago and embezzling between $60,000 and $80,000 from St. Cecilia Catholic Church. The diocese first began investigating Paredes in May 2017 for financial misconduct, suspending him and removing him from the church. After receiving credible sexual assault allegations in February, the diocese reported them to law enforcement. Bishop Burns disclosed the allegations to parishioners after consulting with a review board, stating the delay was to avoid hindering the police investigation. However, the diocese faced criticism for not disclosing the information sooner, especially in light of a Pennsylvania grand jury report detailing

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor's stunning primary defeat has triggered a leadership scramble among Republicans. House Rules Committee Chairman Pete Sessions is aggressively seeking support for a potential bid to replace Cantor. House Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy, the No. 3 Republican, is also making calls but will not formally campaign until Cantor decides his future. Reps. Jim Jordan, Cathy McMorris Rodgers, and Jeb Hensarling are considered potential contenders for the majority leader position. Cantor's fate will dominate discussions and actions in the coming days and weeks. House Republicans are meeting to address the situation, with several lawmakers expressing interest in stepping up. If leadership races occur, McCarthy and Roskam, who already have whip teams, could benefit.

Scarlett Johansson, a busy actress with a packed schedule, agrees to write a passage for a magazine article, demonstrating her willingness to engage in playful and unconventional activities. The article explores Johansson's handwriting and her thoughts on the writing process, revealing her as a multifaceted individual who is both politically astute and generous. Despite her success, she expresses a desire for a more relaxed lifestyle, emphasizing the weariness of her current career. The piece also touches on her recent role as a mother, highlighting her approach to parenthood and her focus on privacy for her family.

Craft beer enthusiasts are facing a dilemma after ABInBev acquired Wicked Weed, a craft brewery. Black Project, another craft brewery, decided to sever ties with Wicked Weed due to ABInBev's business strategies and ethics. They will not collaborate on a beer with Wicked Weed or attend the Wicked Weed Funkatorium Invitational. Despite wishing Wicked Weed well, Black Project believes maintaining their mission and values requires cutting ties with ABInBev. This decision reflects broader tensions between craft and macro breweries, as evidenced by Budweiser's controversial Super Bowl ads that mock craft beer, despite ABInBev's recent acquisitions and craft beer offerings.

The chief prosecutor in Oscar Pistorius' murder trial accused his defense team of presenting conflicting and dishonest theories to defend against a murder charge for killing his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp. Prosecutor Gerrie Nel argued during final arguments that Pistorius' lawyers have suggested both self-defense and accidental discharge scenarios, which Nel believes are irreconcilable. The defense has maintained Pistorius shot Steenkamp by mistake, believing an intruder was in the bathroom, while the prosecution contends he intentionally killed her after a quarrel. Pistorius also faces gun-related charges stemming from an incident in a Johannesburg restaurant. Judge Thokozile Masipa will decide Pistorius' fate without a jury, considering whether he committed murder, negligent killing, or made a tragic error. Pistorius could face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of premeditated murder.

A man mistakenly pocket-dialed 911 while planning to kill his ex-friend, enabling authorities to record his conversation and link him to the murder. Scott Simon, 24, is charged with first-degree murder in the killing of Nicholas Walker, 33, after Simon followed Walker home and shot him multiple times near Interstate 95 in Oakland Park. Simon had previously gotten into a fight with Walker at a Waffle House, and surveillance video shows them arguing before the shooting. Simon is in Broward County jail awaiting trial, with detectives seeking the shooter and another man seen in the vehicle.

Australian DJs behind the prank call to the hospital where the Duchess of Cambridge was being treated for morning sickness have been taken off air and are receiving counseling. Jacintha Saldanha, 46, died days after answering the call, leading to an inquest. The radio station, 2Day FM, has suspended all advertising and put the DJs on indefinite leave. The Duke of Cambridge canceled his appearance at a military tournament to spend time with Kate. Police in London have contacted Australian authorities, but no criminal charges are expected. The DJs may have violated the Surveillance Devices Act in New South Wales. The hospital where Saldanha worked has criticized the radio station for the "truly appalling" stunt.

Michelle Obama's final appearance on "The Tonight Show" with Jimmy Fallon was filled with emotion and gratitude. The first lady expressed her concern for children's futures, emphasizing the importance of strength and hope. She pledged to continue her initiatives, particularly the school lunch program, beyond her time in the White House. Fallon's show featured a surprise video from regular viewers thanking Michelle Obama, and the pair played a game of Catchphrase. The evening concluded with a touching performance by Stevie Wonder, who sang "Isn't She Lovely" and "My Cherie Amour" in honor of the first lady. Obama also wrote a thank you note to her husband, calling it her greatest honor.

The U.S. has imposed visa bans and cut aid to Uganda in response to the country's new anti-homosexual law, which imposes harsh penalties on homosexuality. The Obama administration canceled a regional military exercise and halted $2.4 million in funding for a Ugandan community policing program. The U.S. also shifted funding for Ugandan health ministry employees to non-governmental agencies and reallocated funds for a planned national public health institute to another country. Uganda's President Yoweri Museveni signed the bill into law in February, despite previous statements that he would not do so. Uganda is a key ally in the fight against Islamic extremism in Somalia, but the U.S. stated it will continue to support Uganda's efforts even as it opposes discriminatory practices.

US President Donald Trump changed his Twitter header to include a tweet denying collusion with Russia, prompting ridicule from social media users. Trump’s tweet, which referenced Director Clapper’s statement about no evidence of collusion, replaced his usual profile picture. Critics noted it would have been simpler to pin the tweet rather than altering the header. Democrats seized on the change as evidence of Trump’s dismissive attitude toward the Russia investigation. Trump also tweeted questioning how classified information ended up in the media, suggesting Yates may have leaked it. The hearing highlighted tensions between Trump and his former acting attorney general, with Yates testifying about her warnings to the White House about Michael Flynn’s potential vulnerability to Russian blackmail. Trump’s actions and tweets continued to fuel speculation about his motivations and handling of sensitive information.

A 12-year-old boy attempted a solo drive across Australia, covering 1,300 kilometers from Kendall near Port Macquarie to Broken Hill in New South Wales, before being stopped by police for a dragging bumper. The boy, who was heading towards Perth, was arrested and taken to Broken Hill police station. His journey, spanning 4,300 kilometers, is equivalent to driving from New York to Los Angeles or from Paris to Prague. The Nullarbor Plain, a challenging 800-kilometer stretch, poses risks due to sparse services and wildlife. Authorities are investigating how the boy managed the journey and the safety measures in place for such a young driver.

A 2-year-old girl died after being left in a hot car for over 16 hours in Baltimore's Belair-Edison neighborhood, police said. The girl, Leasia Carter, was found unresponsive in a locked car around 5:30 p.m. on Monday. Her father, Wilbert Carter, 31, was arrested and charged with second-degree murder and child abuse. He reportedly left his daughter in the car after drinking heavily on Sunday. By the time he discovered her, she had suffered second-degree burns. The temperature outside reached 89 degrees during her time in the car. Authorities warn that leaving children unattended in vehicles can be deadly, especially in hot weather.

Archaeologists in Bulgaria have discovered a lead tube reliquary containing ashes from the alleged grave of John the Apostle, one of Jesus' apostles, during excavations of the ancient and medieval fortress of Burgos (Poros) on Cape Foros in the Black Sea city of Burgas. The reliquary, dating to the 6th century, is one of only 43 known from that period and is decorated with crosses. It was likely brought to Burgos by a pilgrim who traveled to Ephesus, Turkey, a common pilgrimage site for early Christians seeking healing. The discovery, made in 2014, is considered one of the most important finds in the history of the Burgas Regional Museum of History. Additionally, archaeologists uncovered a 10th-century Bulgarian royal seal at the site.

In 2006, rescue excavations during construction of a shopping center in Tulln, Austria, uncovered a complete camel skeleton, unique for Central Europe. Archaeozoologist Alfred Galik identified it as a camel based on cervical vertebrae, lower jaw, and metacarpal bones. The camel, a hybrid of a dromedary and a Bactrian camel, was male, around seven years old, and likely castrated. Found in a large refuse pit, the camel skeleton suggests it was not killed and butchered but possibly acquired as an exotic animal during the late 17th century. The complete skeleton, along with ceramic plates and a medicinal bottle, dates the find to between 1643 and 1715. Hybrids were used by the Ottoman army for transportation and as riding animals, and the Tulln camel likely served a similar purpose.

Pope Benedict accepted the resignation of Gabino Zavala, an auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, due to his fathering two children, a violation of priestly celibacy. Zavala, known for his work with the Hispanic community and social justice advocacy, resigned in December after informing the Vatican of his children. Archbishop Jose Gomez, in a letter to worshippers, announced Zavala's resignation and the offer of spiritual care and financial assistance for the children's college education. The archdiocese described the news as "sad and difficult." Zavala, 60 and born in Mexico, had overseen the San Gabriel region and was a vocal advocate for issues like immigration reform and an end to capital punishment. His resignation may spark renewed debate on the ecclesiastical laws of celibacy.

Weld County voters rejected the 51st State Initiative in a November 2013 election, with 58% voting against secession. However, in five of the 11 counties that considered the issue, residents supported the idea. Commissioners in some counties, like Kit Carson, Washington, Phillips, Sedgwick, and Cheyenne, pushed for further exploration of secession due to frustrations with state legislation. Despite the failure, proponents argue the campaign brought attention to rural concerns and may lead to new initiatives, such as equal county representation in the state senate.

A non-Spanish-speaking teacher in Miami-Dade County has filed a federal lawsuit against the school board, alleging employment discrimination. Tracy Rosner, a third-grade teacher at Coral Reef Elementary, claims she was denied a position teaching an hour of Spanish per day because she does not speak the language. Rosner says the school's principal had a policy requiring foreign language teachers to actually speak the language they were teaching, despite Rosner being otherwise qualified. After being denied the job, Rosner says the principal retaliated by doubling her workload. The lawsuit argues that seeking employment solely from Spanish speakers disproportionately affects non-Spanish speakers like Rosner. Rosner is seeking damages for emotional pain and suffering.

The 40-piece Chicken McNugget is the most calorie-dense menu item at McDonald's, containing 1,880 calories—nearly the daily recommended intake for an individual. The Big Breakfast with Hotcakes and a large biscuit comes in second with 1,310 calories. 24/7 Wall St. analyzed over 500 McDonald's menu items, revealing that high-calorie options often result from both portion size and additional ingredients like sauces and toppings. An entire meal consisting of a chicken sandwich, medium fries, and a McFlurry exceeds 2,000 calories. While McDonald's meals generally contain more calories than home-cooked or non-fast-food restaurant meals, no direct link has been established between McDonald's and adverse health outcomes, though high concentrations of fast food are associated with obesity and other negative health effects.

A Florida woman named Alana Annette Savell, 32, was arrested for aggravated battery with a firearm after shooting her house guests who she believed had overstayed their welcome, reports the Bay County Sheriff's Office. Savell armed herself with a .22 caliber handgun and shot at the guests' feet from the doorway of her home, hitting one of them in the leg. Savell's boyfriend was also hit in the leg. He had previously instructed her to use the gun in such situations, saying to shoot at the ground if the guests don't leave after three warnings, and to shoot them in the leg if that doesn't work. Savell is charged with aggravated battery with a firearm and was taken to the Bay County Jail.

A 12-year-old jaguar named Salman, borrowed for breeding from a zoo in Kerala, is being sent back due to his lack of interest in mating and his obesity, zoo officials say. Salman, who has shown no interest in his female partner Kalpana, has been on a strict diet and given more exercise, but to no avail. He is described as lazy, a glutton, and more interested in eating than mating. His weight, over 100kg, is believed to be the cause of his disinterest. While other jaguars in the Delhi zoo have also failed to breed, officials believe it may be due to the stress of relocation. The jaguar will be returned to Kerala as he is "too fat to breed."

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) expressed deep concern over Donald Trump's harsh immigration rhetoric, warning that it threatens to undermine the Republican Party's moral authority and electoral prospects. Graham, a former presidential contender, emphasized the need to reject Trump's characterization of most immigrants as criminals and rapists, especially in light of the potential impact on Latino voters. He stressed that embracing such views risks alienating the Hispanic community and eroding the party's ability to govern effectively. Former Sen. Jim Webb (D-Va.) also criticized Trump's divisive campaign tactics, comparing them to recent efforts to erase Confederate symbols, and highlighted the need for a more inclusive tone in the 2016 race.

The founder of ShipYourEnemiesGlitter.com, a site that allowed users to anonymously send glitter to their enemies for $9.99, sold his business for $85,000 just two weeks after launching it. Mathew Carpenter, a 22-year-old Australian, saw the site become a viral sensation, racking up over 2.5 million visitors and generating $20,000 in sales. Despite the success, Carpenter decided to shut down the site and sell it, citing stress from media attention. Competitors quickly emerged, but the original site's unique copy and viral marketing made it stand out. The new owner will find a profitable business with potential for expansion.

O.J. Simpson's parole hearing on Thursday could grant him release from prison as soon as October 1. The former NFL star and actor, now 70, has been serving a nine-to-33-year sentence for armed robbery and kidnapping charges stemming from a 2007 incident in Las Vegas. With no one registered to testify against him and a good chance of being granted parole based on his behavior in prison, Simpson's release would be a significant event, given his long history of public interest and controversy. If paroled, he would likely disappear from the public eye to avoid the spotlight, as his past experiences have shown that public attention can be detrimental.

The recent Category 4 hurricanes, including Harvey and Irma, have reignited discussions about the link between extreme storms and climate change. While these storms are primarily about immediate human suffering and response, climate change cannot be ignored. It exacerbates several characteristics of these storms, making them more intense and damaging. Sea level rise and warmer sea surface temperatures contribute to higher storm surges and increased rainfall. However, attributing specific storms to climate change is complex. Climate change does not cause individual storms but makes them more severe. It also raises questions about whether climate change is increasing hurricane frequency, a topic with mixed scientific evidence. Climate change is making severe downpours more likely, a trend that will become more evident in the future. Adaptation to climate change is crucial, but it is not a substitute for mitigation efforts. Without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, adaptation will become increasingly difficult and inequitable.
