Scientists have discovered 2.7-million-year-old soil buried beneath Summit, the highest point on Greenland's ice sheet. This soil, a remnant of a tundra landscape that existed before Greenland was covered in ice, suggests the ice sheet has persisted for millions of years, surviving periods of global warming. Researchers used beryllium-10 dating to determine the age of the soil, finding it had been exposed for 200,000 to 1 million years before being covered by ice. This discovery indicates the Greenland Ice Sheet has remained largely unchanged for at least 2.7 million years, providing insights into its resilience to climate change. The findings, published in Science, highlight the potential of ice cores to reveal ancient landscapes and the history of Earth's climate.

A newlywed couple from Pennsylvania is accused of attempting to steal over $1,000 worth of merchandise from a Wegmans supermarket, intending to use the items for their wedding reception. Brittany Lurch, 22, and Arthur Phillips, 32, were arrested after putting the goods, including seafood, hams, and dinnerware, into their shopping carts and leaving the store without paying. The couple, who got married a day earlier, were found to have a glass smoking pipe with marijuana residue in their car. Both were charged with misdemeanor retail theft and possession of drug paraphernalia.

New York state's Attorney General Eric Schneiderman has launched a civil rights investigation into The Weinstein Co. following sexual assault allegations against Harvey Weinstein, who was fired by the company he co-founded in October. More than 30 women have accused Weinstein of sexual assault and harassment. The investigation aims to determine if any New York employees faced pervasive harassment or discrimination. Meanwhile, Chris Savino, a Nickelodeon producer, has apologized for his behavior, which has been accused by up to 12 women of sexual harassment. Nickelodeon has confirmed Savino is no longer involved with the production of The Loud House, a show that has been a major ratings success for the network. Savino's behavior, dating back at least a decade, has been detailed by several women, including Anne Walker Farrell, who shared explicit text messages and offers of work in exchange for sexual favors. Nickelodeon stated it takes all allegations of harassment seriously and is committed to a safe workplace.

President Donald Trump announced Friday that the United States, along with France and Britain, launched military strikes on Syria in response to a suspected chemical weapon attack that killed civilians. Trump stated the aim is to establish a strong deterrent against future chemical weapons use and to pressure President Bashar Assad to end the pattern of killing his own people. The strikes, involving cruise missiles, targeted Syrian military assets. Trump criticized Russia and Iran for supporting Assad, calling for a change in their stance. The White House press secretary, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, emphasized the U.S. intention to sustain pressure on Assad until he ceases using chemical weapons. Trump also expressed a desire to reduce the U.S. military presence in Syria once the Islamic State is defeated.

Girls aged 5 to 14 spend 40% more time on unpaid household chores than boys, according to a UNICEF report. This amounts to 160 million additional hours daily globally. The disparity starts early, with 5-9 year-old girls spending 30% more time on chores than boys. By ages 10 to 14, the gap widens to 50%. Girls in South Asia and the Middle East and North Africa spend nearly double the time on chores compared to boys. In Somalia, 10 to 14-year-old girls spend 26 hours weekly on household tasks, the highest among surveyed countries. This extra workload limits girls' time for play, study, and childhood activities, and can expose them to risks like sexual violence. UNICEF's Anju Malhotra emphasizes that this unequal distribution of labor reinforces gender stereotypes and burdens women and girls across generations.

The genetic analysis of nearly 2000 microbial genomes reveals insights into the last universal common ancestor (LUCA), suggesting it was a heat-loving, anaerobic microbe that fed on hydrogen gas, likely living in hydrothermal vents. This study, led by William Martin from Heinrich Heine University, identified 355 gene families that trace back to LUCA, indicating an environment rich in CO2, hydrogen, and iron. These genes reveal LUCA's reliance on iron-sulfur clusters, radical reactions, and specific cofactors, supporting the theory of life's origin in a geochemically active environment, possibly near hydrothermal vents. This genetic portrait supports the hypothesis that life began in extreme conditions, such as deep-sea vents or volcanic areas, rather than in more conventional settings like Darwin's "warm little pond."

A five-year cyber espionage campaign, dubbed "Sandworm Team" by the cyber intelligence firm iSight Partners, has been targeting NATO, the European Union, Ukraine, and companies in the energy and telecommunications sectors, according to iSight. The operation, which is still ongoing, exploited a previously unknown bug in Microsoft Windows and other software to spy on targeted computers. iSight suspects the hackers are Russian due to language clues in the software code and the choice of targets, though technical indicators do not confirm a direct link to the Russian government. The firm plans to release a detailed report on the operation to its clients. Microsoft has released a patch for the vulnerability.

Fox News host Laura Ingraham mocked Taylor Swift after the candidate Swift backed in Tennessee lost. "Hey @taylorswift13, haters gonna hate. #shakeitoff," Ingraham tweeted, referencing Swift's hit song. Swift endorsed Phil Bredesen and Jim Cooper, but Rep. Marsha Blackburn beat out Bredesen for Bob Corker's Senate seat.

A Massachusetts judge approved the release of Mitt Romney's 1991 testimony in a Staples founder's divorce case, with no objections from Romney, Staples, or the founder's ex-wife's lawyer. The testimony, related to a new class of shares issued to facilitate the divorce, showed Romney described Staples as a high-risk, high-reward venture. The Boston Globe sought to release the documents, while Gloria Allred aimed to lift a gag order on the ex-wife's comments. Romney's lawyer deemed the release "absolutely false" and politically motivated, while Staples raised no objections. The case highlights Romney's role in Staples' early days, with the company's value increasing significantly after his testimony.

Bob Dylan's Nobel Prize in Literature has sparked debate, with some questioning his right to the award. Critics argue that popular song lyrics are not literature, yet Dylan's poetic expressions within the American song tradition have earned him this honor. His work, spanning decades, challenges and transforms our understanding of reality, influencing generations. Dylan's distinctive readings of classic songs and evolving performances, despite his advancing age, continue to captivate audiences. Despite his reclusive nature, his impact on American popular culture is undeniable, making him a unique and enduring figure in the literary world.

A 32-year-old woman, Ana-Alecia Ayala, who gained attention for her "bad dance moves" during chemotherapy, has passed away after a year-long battle with uterine sarcoma. Ayala, who was diagnosed in December 2015, had the tumor spread to her ovaries and stomach lining. She and her "chemo buddy," Danielle Andrus, posted a video of themselves dancing to "Juju On That Beat" in her hospital room, which went viral with over 25,000 views in 19 hours. Despite the rough in-patient treatment, Ayala encouraged others to not view cancer as a death sentence and to make the most of their situations. Her family and friends are continuing to support her GoFundMe page.

A Georgia couple, Elrey "Bud" Runion and June E. Runion, who were in their 60s, were found dead after going missing while on a car-buying trip. Their bodies, each shot in the head, were discovered in Telfair County, Georgia, near McRae. Ronnie Adrian "Jay" Towns, 28, who initially faced false statement charges, was arrested and now faces murder and armed robbery charges. The Runions were known for their charitable work, often helping those in need with bicycles, food, and other supplies. Towns, described as a good kid by his family, was found to have answered a Craigslist ad from the Runions, potentially luring them to the area. The case has shocked the community, with many expressing disbelief in Towns' guilt.

Rep. Elizabeth Esty, a vocal advocate for the #MeToo movement, is facing criticism for not adequately addressing sexual harassment allegations in her Washington office. Esty apologized for not suspending or firing her former chief of staff, Tony Baker, until three months after learning about the allegations in 2016. The allegations include harassment, death threats, and physical assault by Baker against female staffers. Esty has asked the House Ethics Committee to investigate whether she committed any wrongdoing in handling the dismissal. Calls for her resignation have come from fellow Democrats and state politicians. Despite her public apologies and efforts to improve workplace protections, Esty announced she will not seek re-election, citing the best interest of her constituents and family.

Black rats may not have been the primary carriers of the bubonic plague across Europe during repeated outbreaks in the 14th to 18th centuries, according to a new study. Scientists from the University of Oslo suggest that giant gerbils from Asia might have been responsible for the spread of the plague, which arrived in Europe from Asia via the Silk Road. Favorable weather conditions in Asia, such as a wet spring followed by a warm summer, could have led to a boom in gerbil populations, allowing the plague to spread to Europe. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, indicates that plague bacteria showed up in harbor cities in Europe some years after favorable conditions in central Asia. This theory challenges the long-held belief that black rats were the main culprits in plague transmission. Further research, including analysis of plague bacteria DNA from ancient skeletons across Europe, is needed to confirm this hypothesis.

Adult children who felt emotionally closer to their mothers than their siblings were more likely to show signs of depression, according to a new study from Purdue University. The research, involving 725 adult children from 309 families, found that those who perceived themselves as their mothers' favorites or disappointments reported higher depressive symptoms. The study suggests that perceived favoritism or disfavoritism from mothers can lead to increased depressive symptoms among adult children, regardless of race or gender. The findings highlight the ongoing impact of sibling rivalry and parental favoritism into adulthood.

Google's response to Apple removing Google Maps from iOS 6 involves using the web version or third-party apps, though Google aims to make its maps available across all devices. Meanwhile, a Tumblr has emerged to mock iOS 6's map failures, and various tech gadgets and deals are catching attention, including carabiners with built-in USB cables and a Pandora One subscription offer.

Florida prisoners are planning a statewide strike on Martin Luther King Jr. Day to protest unpaid labor and price gouging in prison commissaries, among other issues. The strike, dubbed Operation Push, aims to make the governor realize the financial impact of using inmates as unpaid labor, potentially costing the state millions. Inmates will refuse work assignments and avoid purchasing overpriced items. They demand a reasonable wage for their labor, the restoration of parole, and fair pricing in prison commissaries. The strike is part of a series of mass actions in Florida prisons, highlighting inhumane conditions and advocating for broader criminal justice reform.

Robin Williams, the beloved actor and comedian, was found dead in his home on August 11, 2014, after hanging himself with a belt. In the days leading up to his death, Williams was reportedly experiencing severe depression, sleeping up to 18 hours a day, and had no appetite. His wife, Susan Schneider, was in a different bedroom when he passed away, raising questions about their sleeping arrangements. Williams' longtime publicist, Mara Buxbaum, stated that he had no financial problems and that his family is amply taken care of. Williams had been battling depression for most of his adult life, and his comedic talent was often a coping mechanism for personal sadness. The last known photos of Williams show him at an art gallery reception in Marin County, California, a day or so before his death, where he seemed in good spirits and laughing frequently.

Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine confirmed that Facebook threats against members of the Rhoden family are among the evidence being examined in the investigation of the mass shootings of eight family members in Pike County. The killings, described as a "sophisticated operation," remain under investigation with no suspects identified. Marijuana grow operations were found at three of the four crime scene locations, though it is unclear if they are connected to the murders. Pike County Sheriff Charles Reader warned the Rhoden family to be prepared and armed, emphasizing the targeted nature of the attack. The investigation involves over 100 personnel, and a memorial fund has been established for the family. Seven adults and a teenage boy were found fatally shot at four different properties near Piketon. Authorities have released 911 calls from family members discovering the bodies, and are seeking leads through a tip line and a $25,000 reward offered by a local businessman.

Actor Ron Livingston defended his sister Jennifer, a news anchor whose emotional response to an insulting viewer's email went viral. Jennifer, 37 and a mother of three, received backlash from Kenneth Krause, who told her her "physical condition hasn't improved for many years" and suggested she should "transform herself" for her viewers. In response, Ron Livingston praised his sister as a dedicated role model. Jennifer did not publicly name Krause but received support from her news director and family, including fellow actor Ron Livingston. Krause later offered to provide advice for Jennifer's transformation.

A 10-year-old girl with cerebral palsy, Rosamaria Hernandez, faced deportation after crossing a Customs and Border Protection checkpoint to undergo gall bladder surgery at Driscoll Children’s Hospital in Corpus Christi. Her mother, Felipa Delacruz, an undocumented immigrant, brought her to the U.S. illegally when she was three months old. Despite a notarized letter to notify Border Patrol, the girl was detained by agents who followed her to the hospital and waited outside her room. Upon release, she was taken to a detention center in San Antonio, Texas, by Border Patrol, despite her parents living nearby. This case highlights the increased enforcement actions at sensitive locations, including hospitals, and the potential separation of children from their families due to their undocumented status.

On Christmas Eve 2017, the author was seated at a West Village restaurant when she noticed a familiar figure, Ken Starr, the independent prosecutor who had investigated her in 1998. Despite the awkwardness of the encounter, she chose to confront him, expressing her lingering resentment and the trauma of the investigation. Starr's response was non-apologetic, acknowledging the unfortunate nature of the events. Reflecting on the 20-year anniversary of the scandal, the author discusses the lasting impact on her life and society, drawing parallels to the #MeToo movement and the changing landscape of media and technology. She shares insights from cognitive linguist George Lakoff and psychologist Jack Saul, exploring the concept of collective trauma and the ongoing challenges of integrating and transforming the past.

Rep. Robert E. Andrews (D-N.J.), who served in Congress for 23 years and introduced over 600 bills, has resigned to take a position at the law firm Dilworth Paxson. Andrews claims his legislative record, characterized by a low success rate in passing bills, reflects his effectiveness in the current political system. His bills often failed to pass the Senate, and even when companion bills were enacted, Andrews argues he deserves credit for the ideas. Andrews' legislative strategy involved creating detailed bills for specific issues, which he then inserted into larger, more likely-to-pass legislation. His efforts led to changes in military health-care programs and insurance coverage rules, though many of his standalone bills did not become law.

Archaeologists have uncovered evidence of cannibalism among the starving colonists at Jamestown, Virginia, during the "starving time" winter of 1609-1610. Forensic analysis of a 14-year-old girl's remains, named "Jane," shows signs of butchery, including four shallow chops to her forehead and a final blow that split her skull open. The cuts are similar to those used in animal butchery, suggesting multiple individuals were involved. Jane's bones were found in a cellar at the site of the fort, which housed about 300 colonists, of whom only 60 survived. The discovery confirms accounts by colonists who described occasional acts of cannibalism during that period. The girl's remains provide the first physical evidence of cannibalism among European settlers in any New World colony, offering a grim insight into the desperate conditions faced by the Jamestown settlers.

Robin Williams' death, ruled a suicide, was triggered by a combination of severe depression, anxiety, and early-stage Parkinson's disease, according to the coroner's report. Williams, 63, was found hanging in his home in Tiburon, California, with antidepressants, caffeine, and Parkinson's medication in his system. His wife, Susan, revealed he had experienced an increase in paranoia. The night before his death, Williams placed several wristwatches in a sock and gave them to someone for safekeeping, indicating his concerns. Williams' body was discovered by his assistant, who found him hanging from a closet door with a belt. No alcohol or illegal drugs were present in his system. Williams had been struggling with depression and anxiety for years and was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease in 2013. His wife stated he was in the early stages of the disease, experiencing tremors and slowed movement. Williams was known for his philanthropy and had been entertaining troops through USO

Throughout World War II, Allied bombers struggled to sink the German battleship Tirpitz, a target of particular hatred for British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, who nicknamed it "the beast." In 2016, researchers studying tree rings in forests near Kafjord, Norway, discovered evidence of the ship's presence and the Allied attacks. The trees, particularly pines, showed a significant lack of growth in 1945, indicating severe damage from the chemical fog used by the Germans to hide the ship. The artificial fog, likely made from chlorosulphuric acid, caused extensive damage to the trees, with some showing no growth for up to nine years. The effects of the battleship's presence and the Allied bombing campaign are still visible in the forests of northern Norway, with tree rings providing a unique historical record of the conflict.

Smoke was detected in multiple places on EgyptAir flight 804 moments before it plummeted into the Mediterranean, but the cause of the crash that killed all 66 on board remains unclear, the French air accident investigation agency said. The plane's automatic detection system sent messages indicating smoke a few minutes before the plane disappeared from radar while flying over the east Mediterranean early Thursday morning. Search crews are continuing to look for further wreckage of the aircraft. Planes and vessels from Egypt and five other countries—Greece, Britain, France, the United States, and Cyprus—continued searching a wide area of the eastern Mediterranean on Saturday, a day after the Egyptian military found debris from the passenger jet in the sea 180 miles north of the Egyptian port city of Alexandria. The Egyptian military released photographs of the debris, showing heavily-damaged plane seats, life jackets, and other items. Egyptian authorities believe terrorism is a more likely explanation than equipment failure, but no hard evidence has emerged. French

Emma Watson's participation in a Disney movie and recent photo shoot for Vanity Fair has sparked criticism from some who see it as contradictory to her feminist stance. Watson, a UN Women Goodwill Ambassador and advocate for gender equality, has been vocal about women's rights and launched the HeForShe campaign. However, her appearance in a topless photo for the magazine and her role as a Disney princess have led to accusations that she is not practicing what she preaches. Critics argue that Disney's portrayal of women, despite recent attempts to modernize, still reinforces traditional gender roles. Watson defends her choices, stating that feminism is about giving women free choice and that her actions do not distract from her advocacy work. She emphasizes the importance of privacy and consistency in her public persona.

Two months before a 2-year-old boy was killed by an alligator at Walt Disney World, firefighters were warned to stop feeding the reptiles at a nearby fire station. Reedy Creek Emergency Services, which provides government services to the theme parks, received emails from employees about the feeding of at least one alligator, estimated to be between 4 and 5 feet long, and a smaller juvenile. Feeding alligators is illegal as it can cause them to lose their natural fear of humans. Despite the warnings, it is unclear if the alligator responsible for the fatal attack was ever removed. Disney installed warning signs about alligators and snakes after the incident.

A 25-year-old Maryland man, Ian Hawes, ran a fraudulent PAC that collected over $1 million from 20,000 donors, claiming to offer "Dinner with Donald Trump." The legitimate campaign's site and Hawes' look nearly identical, and the PAC spent $108,000 on Facebook ads. Despite collecting substantial funds, the PAC spent none on Trump's campaign. Donors, including those from the Trump campaign, were misled, believing they supported Trump. After POLITICO's exposure, Trump's campaign accused Hawes of fraud. Hawes also launched other fraudulent sites, raising concerns about online political scams.

A 19-year-old Washington State man, Allen Ivanov, is accused of killing three people at a party with his AR-15 rifle, court records show. Ivanov told detectives he bought the semi-automatic rifle a week before the incident for target practice and had planned to attend a safety class. However, he brought the gun to a party where his ex-girlfriend was attending. After seeing her with another man, he returned to his car, read the rifle's instruction manual, and loaded it. Ivanov then returned to the party and shot his ex-girlfriend Anna Bui and another man, killing them. He also wounded a third man. Ivanov claims the rifle symbolized power to him and that the incident was about his "dream girl." He is charged with three counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder. His lawyers say he viewed the rifle as a symbol of power and that he was distraught over his ex-girlfriend moving on.

On Facebook's 10th anniversary, users will receive a "Look Back" video compiling their most-liked moments from the past year. This feature, which required significant engineering effort, aims to remind users of the personal nature of their Facebook presence. Mark Zuckerberg's influence on the social network remains evident, with the company's ability to handle such a large-scale project highlighting its capabilities.

A harrowing and controversial film, "Detroit," directed by Kathryn Bigelow, reenacts the 1967 Algiers Motel incident, where three young black men were killed by police officers during the Detroit riots. Bigelow and screenwriter Mark Boal blend factual events with fictional characters, creating a tense and disturbing narrative. The film opens with a rapid historical overview of racial tensions leading up to the riots and the initial police raid on an after-hours club. It then focuses on the Algiers Motel, where the fatal events unfold amid chaos and racial hostility. The central antagonist, Philip Krauss, played by Will Poulter, leads a brutal interrogation of motel guests, resulting in the deaths of three men. Bigelow's immersive style and James Newton Howard's minimalistic score heighten the film's intensity. While the movie aims to expose systemic racism, some critics find it overly brutal and lacking in nuance, questioning the balance between historical accuracy and artistic license.

Dennis Rodman sang "Happy Birthday" to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during a 2014 basketball game, but this year Kim's birthday on January 8 remains relatively low-key, lacking the usual national holiday status. Kim's exact birth year—1982, 1983, or 1984—is uncertain, adding to the secrecy of his reclusive regime. Despite his age, Kim has consolidated power, marking the real beginning of his era in 2015. His birthday celebrations, while not a national holiday, include distributing sweets to children, a tradition from his grandfather and father. Analysts suggest Kim's birthday might be used to reinforce his image as a humble leader, while his age raises questions about his experience and the stability of his rule.

A new study challenges the long-standing practice of removing cancerous lymph nodes from the armpits of women with early-stage breast cancer, finding that for many patients, this procedure may be unnecessary. The study, published in The Journal of the American Medical Association, involved 891 women with clinical stage T1 or T2 breast cancer, where biopsies of one or two armpit nodes had detected cancer but the nodes were not visibly enlarged. These women underwent lumpectomies, followed by radiation and chemotherapy or hormone-blocking drugs. Half of the participants had 10 or more additional nodes removed, while the other half did not. Over a median follow-up period of 6.3 years, there was no significant difference in survival or recurrence rates between the two groups. The findings suggest that the addition of axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) does not improve outcomes for women who meet specific criteria, including those who receive chemotherapy and radiation. Concern is growing over the disappearance of a nine-year-old girl, Maëlys De Araujo, who vanished during a wedding in eastern France. Last seen in a children's room at about 3:00 AM on Sunday, extensive searches using a helicopter, police dogs, and divers have failed to find her. A kidnapping investigation has opened, and police are appealing for witnesses. The girl attended the wedding with her parents, older sister, and relatives from the nearby department of Jura. Guests searched for her for about an hour before alerting the police. Police have interviewed 180 wedding attendees and are also speaking to 70 people at nearby social events. Maëlys is described as 130 cm tall, weighing 28 kg, with dark skin, brown eyes, and chestnut hair, wearing a white sleeveless dress. Divers continued to search the nearby Guiers river on Tuesday. Actress Alyssa Milano criticized actor Matt Damon's comments on sexual harassment, tweeting that his remarks about a "spectrum of behavior" and a "culture of outrage" were "Orwellian." Milano argued that the outrage is justified because women were made to feel abuse was normal and were silenced for years. Damon's defense of comedian Louis C.K. also drew criticism from Milano and others, who questioned his ability to understand the severity of sexual misconduct. Driver, Damon's ex-co-star, echoed Milano's sentiments, stating that men cannot understand the daily experience of abuse and should not differentiate or explain sexual misconduct. Both women emphasized the need for men to listen and support women without offering opinions on the severity of abuse.

The parents of missing toddler DeOrr Kunz Jr. have been named suspects in his disappearance by Lemhi County Sheriff Lynn Bowerman. Bowerman said the couple, Jessica Mitchell and DeOrr Kunz Sr., have been "less than truthful" with investigators and have changed their stories multiple times. The toddler went missing on July 10, 2015, during a family camping trip near Leadore. Search teams have found no trace of the boy. The sheriff believes the parents know where DeOrr is but are not providing full information. They have not been arrested, and no warrants have been issued. Bowerman plans to take his time to ensure the case is solid before bringing charges. The family has hired private investigators and raised $15,000, which will now go toward other missing children's cases. The sheriff encourages the public to come forward with any information.

A father, Randall Margraves, rushed and was held in contempt of court after attempting to attack Larry Nassar during his sentencing. Margraves, whose three daughters were sexually abused by Nassar, expressed remorse but hoped Nassar faces severe punishment. Judge Janice Cunningham did not fine or jail Margraves, acknowledging his emotional state but stressing the need to use the legal system. Margraves apologized and said he came to support his daughters, unaware of the full details of their victim impact statements. The incident highlights the emotional toll on victims' families and the challenges of dealing with such cases in court.

Serena Williams, a 13-time Grand Slam champion, has resumed training after a break due to injury and illness, sharing a photo of herself serving in a hot pink full-length bodysuit on Twitter. Williams, who hasn't played since July, remains on blood thinners and is not taking long flights. Her return to the WTA Tour is uncertain, with her agent stating she is progressing well but not setting a timeline. Meanwhile, world No. 2 Kim Clijsters is out of the French Open due to a severe ankle injury sustained at her cousin's wedding. Young player Ryan Sweeting won his first ATP title, moving up to No. 71 in the rankings. The U.S. Fed Cup team will rely on teenagers Christina McHale and Melanie Oudin in a world group playoff.

A few lucky folks across the country will wake up Wednesday a whole lot richer after hitting Tuesday night's $636 million Mega Millions jackpot. If you matched all the winning numbers—8, 20, 14, 17, and 39, with a Megaball of 7—you should take a few important steps before celebrating. First, sign the ticket and take a selfie with it. Then, find a safe place to hide it, like a safe deposit box or portable home safe. Next, contact financial experts like lawyers and financial planners to help you decide between a lump-sum cash option or an annuity. If you can stay anonymous, do so; otherwise, hire a media consultant and lie low for a while. Finally, plan a trip to South America or the U.S. Virgin Islands to avoid unwanted attention. Kesha has transformed from the glitter-obsessed party girl of her early hits to a more natural look, revealing in a Vogue interview her struggles with an eating disorder that led her to enter rehab last January. She now focuses on staying healthy and loving herself, though she doesn't regret her past extravagant outfits. Kesha is also embroiled in a legal battle with music producer Dr. Luke, who denies allegations of sexual, physical, verbal, and emotional abuse. Despite a judge denying her request to no longer work with Dr. Luke, artists like Jack Antonoff and DJ Zedd have offered to produce new music for her, showing support in the wake of her court defeat.

In New York's 9th Congressional District, the special election to replace Anthony Weiner has become a referendum on President Obama, with Republican Bob Turner leading in polls. A kitchen-sink mailer from the GOP depicts a mosque over Ground Zero and Weprin alongside Obama, supporting the mosque. The race is seen as an Obama referendum, with low approval ratings hurting Democrats. The district is trending Republican due to its large Orthodox Jewish and conservative Catholic populations. Weprin, a last-standing candidate, faces challenges due to his campaign gaffes and ties to Albany. Democrats have spent nearly $500,000 on TV ads to save the seat. A loss could chill support for Obama's agenda in vulnerable districts.

Could you be held liable for texting someone who then gets into a car accident? Recent legal rulings suggest yes. In Pennsylvania, two men are now defendants in a lawsuit over a fatal crash, as they allegedly sent texts to the driver who was involved. The court ruled that if you know someone is driving and you send them a text, you could be liable for any accidents that result. However, proving that you knew the driver was texting at the time of the accident can be difficult. In New Jersey, a similar case set a precedent, but the defendant was not found liable due to insufficient evidence. These rulings could make people more cautious about texting while someone they know is driving.

Hundreds have died and many more are infected in the largest Ebola outbreak in history, prompting heads of state to cancel travel plans to focus on the crisis. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak an international emergency, urging affected nations to declare states of emergency and rigorously screen travelers. Aid groups like Samaritan's Purse and the Peace Corps are evacuating non-essential personnel due to safety concerns. In Liberia, President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf ordered schools closed and non-essential government workers sent home, deploying the army to enforce new precautions. The outbreak has killed over 650 people, with fears it could spread further. Ebola spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids and has no vaccine or specific treatment, with a fatality rate of at least 60%. The disease's symptoms include high fever, bleeding, and central nervous system damage.

The Johnson County Sheriff’s Department arrested Marvin E. “Buddy” Potter Jr., 60, and Jamie Lynn Curd, 38, on first-degree murder charges after a weeklong investigation into the deaths of Billy Clay Payne Jr., 36, and his girlfriend Billie Jean Hayworth, 23. The motive, Sheriff Mike Reece said, was “senseless and stupid,” stemming from Potter’s anger over Internet and telephone communications between the couple and his daughter. The arrests came after interviewing 150 to 170 people, with Potter and Curd remaining suspects. Curd cooperated after a polygraph test. The couple was found dead in their home with no signs of forced entry or struggle. Their 6-month-old child was left unharmed.

Arizona's Legislature has passed a controversial bill that would allow business owners, as long as they assert their religious beliefs, to deny service to gay and lesbian customers. The bill, which the state House of Representatives passed by a 33-27 vote, now goes to Governor Jan Brewer, who vetoed similar legislation last year. Critics argue the measure sanctions discrimination and could harm the state's economy, while proponents say it protects people against activist federal courts. The bill is similar to proposals in other states as they grapple with same-sex marriage laws. Governor Brewer, a Republican, expressed uncertainty about the need for such a law, stating, "I don't know that it needs to be statutory." The legislation faces opposition from Democrats and business groups, who fear it could lead to damaging litigation and boycotts.

At least 33 children and three adults from a 4-H summer camp in Lake Placid, Florida, are being examined after falling ill. The cause remains unknown, and the incident occurred at Camp Cloverleaf, which offers various facilities and activities year-round. Camp Cloverleaf, located on the banks of Lake Francis, provides accommodations, dining, and recreational spaces for diverse groups including school field trips, church retreats, and family reunions. The camp also supports environmental education and can host up to 150 people overnight.

Tony Dungy, a respected former NFL coach and analyst, faced criticism for stating he wouldn't have drafted Michael Sam, the NFL's first openly gay player, due to potential difficulties handling the situation. Dungy's comments were seen as a cop-out, lacking in courage and failing to address the broader issue of equality and opportunity. Dungy's stance raises questions about the intersection of personal beliefs and professional responsibilities, particularly in a league that has made significant strides in diversity and inclusion.

Greece will not pay a 1.6 billion euro loan installment due to the International Monetary Fund on Tuesday, a Greek government official confirmed, highlighting the depth of the financial crisis. The missed payment, expected after talks broke down and capital controls were imposed on Greek banks, brings Greece closer to potential exit from the euro zone. Despite the shock, Greece's fate is likely to remain unchanged until after a snap referendum on July 5, where Greeks will vote on bailout terms presented by creditors. European leaders urged a "yes" vote, warning of the risk of Greece's exit from the euro.

A new ISIS propaganda video threatens attacks in France, Italy, the United States, and beyond, including New York City. The video features two suspected ISIS fighters threatening to blow up the White House and launch more attacks on Paris, with one fighter mentioning a "conquest of Rome." In response, Italy has increased security in Rome and the Vatican, with 1,000 army members deployed. The U.S. Embassy in Rome advises Americans visiting Italy to remain vigilant, warning that St. Peter's Basilica, Milan's Duomo, and La Scala could be targets. New York City officials reassure residents, stating that there is no specific threat, but the NYPD remains on high alert. Mayor de Blasio encourages New Yorkers to continue their normal activities, emphasizing that the city will not be intimidated by terrorist threats.

Kurt Cobain: Montage of Heck, a documentary by Brett Morgen, offers a comprehensive and revealing look at the life of Nirvana's frontman, challenging the familiar narrative of his rise to fame and tragic end. The film, which premiered on HBO in May 2015, draws from extensive personal archives, including home movies, journals, and audio recordings, providing a raw and intimate portrait of Cobain. Morgen's approach, approved by Cobain's family, includes a mix of animated sequences and archival footage set to Nirvana's music, creating a dynamic and engaging narrative. The documentary delves into Cobain's early life, his struggles with addiction, and his relationships, including with his wife Courtney Love. It also explores the artist's creative process and his complex emotions, offering a more nuanced understanding of his legacy.

A new study in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics suggests that eating apples may improve sexual function in women. Researchers analyzed 731 sexually active Italian women aged 18 to 43, dividing them into two groups based on apple consumption: those who ate one to two apples daily and those who ate none. The women completed the Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI), which measures aspects of sexual function. Women who ate apples regularly scored higher on the FSFI, indicating better lubrication and overall sexual function. The study attributes these benefits to the polyphenols and antioxidants in apples, which can enhance blood flow and stimulate arousal. While the sample size is relatively small, the researchers find the results intriguing and suggest that apples might be beneficial for women's sexual health.

Casual journalist Natasha Exelby was taken off air by ABC24 after a live TV blooper went viral, but was not fired. Exelby, who recently returned from Turkish broadcaster TRT World, was caught off guard during a live news shift and reacted dramatically when the cameras returned to her after a prerecorded segment. Despite calls for her reinstatement, ABC24 management denied she was banned or sacked, stating she is a casual contributor and not a staff member. The ABC director of news, Gaven Morris, assured Exelby that she can continue working occasional shifts, emphasizing that live television is demanding and slip-ups are expected. Exelby's incident sparked support from other journalists who shared their own embarrassing moments on social media.

Former New York Governor George Pataki suspended his Republican presidential bid on Tuesday, citing the need to elect a president who can confront radical Islam, shrink Washington, and unite the country. Pataki, who previously flirted with presidential runs in 2000, 2008, and 2012, struggled to gain traction in a race dominated by political outsiders. His campaign, heavily focused on New Hampshire, raised minimal funds and failed to secure a spot on the main debate stage. Pataki's candidacy, which once upset Democratic Governor Mario Cuomo in 1994, ultimately failed to resonate with voters in a GOP field turning increasingly to the right.

The Senate Intelligence Committee recommended Gina Haspel as the next CIA director, clearing the path for her confirmation by the full Senate. The committee voted 10-5 to advance Haspel’s nomination, which is expected to be confirmed this week. Haspel, currently the CIA’s deputy director, has the support of at least six Democrats, ensuring her confirmation. Chairman Richard Burr of North Carolina praised Haspel, calling her the most qualified person to lead the CIA. In a letter to Senator Mark Warner, Haspel acknowledged that the CIA’s enhanced interrogation program, which included waterboarding, was a mistake and should not have been undertaken. However, she maintained that torture does not work. Despite her support, many Democrats expressed concerns about her nomination, citing her involvement with the controversial CIA program. Republican Sens. Rand Paul and John McCain remain opposed to her confirmation.

Seattle's city council voted 7-2 to repeal a tax on large companies such as Amazon and Starbucks, intended to combat a growing homelessness crisis. The repeal came after a raucous meeting with supporters and opponents facing off, and despite the tax being passed unanimously just a month prior. The tax, which would have raised about $47 million annually, targeted nearly 600 businesses making at least $20 million in gross revenue, charging them $275 per full-time worker. Amazon, Starbucks, and other companies funded a campaign against the tax, raising over $280,000 in just weeks. Council members cited the lack of resources and time to fight a potential referendum and the need for a more unified approach to addressing homelessness. The move was seen as a significant setback for those advocating for the tax as a step toward building affordable housing.

A 77-year-old retired nurse named David Knowles suffered a heart attack during a CPR training class at his local church in Exeter. Thinking he was demonstrating, his trainees continued the lesson until he passed out. Realizing the severity, Knowles instructed them to call 999 and perform CPR. His trainees successfully revived him until paramedics arrived. Knowles was hospitalized for five weeks, during which he suffered a second cardiac arrest and a pulmonary embolism. He awoke two and a half weeks later, having been in a medically induced coma. Doctors feared potential brain damage but noted his excellent recovery. Knowles, a St John Ambulance volunteer, continues to improve and is celebrating the organization's 140th anniversary.

An escape artist narrowly survived a near-fatal "buried alive" stunt during a fundraising event in West Yorkshire. Antony Britton, attempting to outdo Harry Houdini, was buried in a grave with handcuffed hands for nearly nine minutes before being pulled unconscious by his team. He suffered a cracked rib and minor injuries but credits the crew for his survival. Britton, who has staged similar daring escapes, says he may not attempt this stunt again. The event, part of the Escape for Life festival, aimed to raise funds for Bloodwise.

A Chinese tourist who tried to report a stolen wallet during a visit to Germany inadvertently signed an asylum application, getting stranded as a refugee for two weeks in the country's complex asylum system. The 31-year-old, known as Mr. L., spoke only Mandarin, and German authorities only realized their mistake after seeking help from a local Chinese restaurant for translation. He was fingerprinted, given a medical exam, and treated like other refugees, despite his well-dressed appearance and attempts to communicate his desire to return to his tour. It took 12 days for officials to understand the situation and release him. More than one million refugees have arrived in Germany in the past year, with only a few Chinese asylum seekers. The incident highlighted the challenges and bureaucracy in Germany's refugee process.

Nazi hunter Eli Rosenbaum has dedicated his career to pursuing justice for victims of the Holocaust. Since 1979, Rosenbaum and his team at the Justice Department's Office of Human Rights and Special Prosecutions have successfully stripped citizenship and deported 107 former Nazis, including John Demjanjuk, convicted of being an accessory to 28,000 murders. Rosenbaum, who joined the office as an intern, has become known as the Justice Department's leading Nazi hunter, working on 137 cases. Despite facing challenges such as limited documentation and witnesses, Rosenbaum remains committed to pursuing every last Nazi, emphasizing the importance of justice for the victims. The case of Jakiw Palij, a 92-year-old former guard at Trawniki concentration camp, highlights the ongoing efforts despite the race against time as many perpetrators age and die.

A man named David Welch mysteriously left his home in Kansas on September 2, driving his maroon Pontiac van without a word to anyone. For nearly seven weeks, his family searched for him with no clues. On October 18, a hitchhiker found Welch injured and trapped in a deep ravine in Utah, nearly 900 miles from his home. In his final days, Welch wrote love letters to his family. Authorities believe he veered off the road and crashed, becoming trapped for days or weeks. His death left many questions unanswered, including why he drove so far and how long he survived.

A 39-year-old Uzbek man, known to Swedish security services but not recently under investigation, is suspected of driving a hijacked beer delivery truck into a crowd in central Stockholm on Friday, killing four people and injuring 15. Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Lofven declared Monday a national day of mourning, urging citizens to "get through this" and emphasizing Sweden's determination to remain an open society. Police found a suspicious device in the truck but could not confirm if it was a bomb. The attack, which occurred near the site of a failed suicide bombing in 2010, has raised questions about Sweden's open immigration policies and its ability to prevent such incidents. Flags flew at half-mast, and a minute's silence was observed on Monday to commemorate the victims.

Papa John's released a new advertisement addressing customer outrage following founder John Schnatter's controversial remarks and his use of a racial slur. The video, posted on social media, features customer tweets criticizing the company and demands for policy changes. Papa John's responded by stating, "You expected better from Papa John's. So did we," and committed to earning back customer trust through action. The company is also implementing mandatory bias training for its workers and conducting an internal audit on diversity and inclusion practices.

Former Massachusetts Senator Scott Brown, known for his cycling passion and earlier political career, has been nominated by President Trump to serve as the ambassador to New Zealand. Brown, who endorsed Trump early in his campaign and has since worked as a Fox News contributor, lost his Senate seat in 2012 and another bid in 2014. His nomination requires Senate confirmation. Brown's cycling background includes racing in Europe and touring in Spain, where he describes exhilarating experiences. He now volunteers as a bike mechanic at Gus' Bike Shop in New Hampshire, sharing his expertise and passion.

Jennifer Love Hewitt and her husband Brian Hallisay are thrilled to announce the birth of their daughter Autumn James Hallisay, born on November 26. Hewitt's rep confirms the news exclusively to Us Weekly. The couple, who met on the Lifetime show The Client List, secretly tied the knot recently. Hewitt previously revealed she and Hallisay were keeping the baby's gender a surprise, celebrating with a gender-neutral baby shower in October. Hewitt, 34, has been vocal about her desire to be a mother, attributing her decision to have a child partly to the loss of her own mother to cancer.

India faces significant challenges in protecting its 430 million children, with 1.7 million dying before five years of age annually. Malnutrition and lack of education are prevalent, and many children are at risk of abuse, exploitation, and trafficking. In 2007, the government acknowledged child sexual abuse through a survey, revealing that 53% of children had experienced some form of abuse, with 20% facing severe cases. However, the survey's methodology limited its generalizability. Child abuse cases are rarely reported, with most victims not informing anyone, including the police. The government has enacted laws, such as the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, but implementation remains challenging. The National Commission for the Protection of Child Rights has made some progress but is understaffed. Despite efforts, the social services network is inadequate, as evidenced by the case of Falak, a two-year-old girl who died due to neglect.

Congressman Dennis Kucinich sued the Longworth House Office Building cafeteria for $150,000 after biting into an olive pit in a sandwich wrap in 2008, causing dental issues that required multiple surgeries, though he didn't specify the costs or the exact nature of the "enjoyment" lost. The complaint against Restaurant Associates and others involved in running the cafeteria claims negligence and breach of implied warranty. Kucinich's appearance on the House floor five days post-incident showed no signs of dental distress.

The husband of a Pakistani woman who was stoned to death by her family for refusing an arranged marriage admits to killing his first wife so he could marry his second wife, Farzana Parveen. Muhammad Iqbal, 45, told CNN he strangled his first wife six years ago to marry Parveen, though he was later released on his family's forgiveness. Parveen, who was three months pregnant, was beaten to death by about 20 family members, including her father, brothers, and cousins, in a public area of Lahore. Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif ordered a full report on the incident. The United Nations estimates 5,000 women are murdered annually in "honor killings," though advocacy groups believe the number could be closer to 20,000. The crime is often underreported, and victims' families can sometimes avoid prosecution through the law of Diyat, which allows for financial settlements instead of imprisonment.

Doubts and disputes surround a mummified head believed to be that of King Henry IV of France, with new genetic evidence suggesting it does not belong to the Bourbon monarch. Found in 1919 in the Royal Basilica of St. Denis, the head, along with several vertebrae, was initially identified as Henry's by a multidisciplinary team in 2010, based on facial reconstruction and CT imaging. However, a study by researchers from the University of Leuven compared the head's DNA with that of three male descendants of the House of Bourbon and found no match. Similarly, a blood sample purportedly from King Louis XVI also failed to match the Bourbon lineage. The original identification was based on injuries consistent with Henry's known history and a mushroom-like growth on the nose. Will Smith and his 14-year-old son Jaden discuss their approach to life and acting in the film "After Earth." Will, a self-described student of patterns and former physicist, sees the world through a lens of mathematical and scientific principles. Jaden, while agreeing with his father, suggests that the mathematics needed to fully understand the universe may not yet exist. The pair also delve into their family dynamics, with Jaden noting that his mother, Jada Pinkett Smith, is more assertive than he is. The father-son duo shares insights on their collaborative process, with Jaden describing their working relationship as a partnership rather than a traditional father-son dynamic. They discuss their family's transparency and the challenges of fame, emphasizing that their children make choices based on their own desires rather than external pressures. The conversation touches on their educational philosophy, financial management, and the influence of TED Talks on their thinking.

Police searched neighborhoods in Watertown, Mass., as Boston residents were ordered to stay indoors following the Boston Marathon bombings. After a chaotic night that left one suspect dead and another critically wounded, authorities apprehended Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the surviving suspect, in a boat in Watertown. The daylong search, which shut down much of Boston, culminated in the capture of Tsarnaev, who had escaped a shootout with police earlier in the day. The brothers, Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, were of Chechen heritage and had emigrated to the U.S., where they had lived for years. Tamerlan, 26, was killed in a shootout with police, while Dzhokhar, 19, was found hiding in a boat. The investigation into the brothers' alleged motives and potential help from others is ongoing.

North Koreans voted in local elections on Sunday, with a 99.97% turnout, casting ballots for pre-approved candidates in a process that is more show than substance. The elections, held every four years, are a means for the government to monitor the population and maintain control. Only one candidate appears on each ballot, chosen by the ruling Workers' Party, and dissenting votes are considered acts of treason. These elections serve as a form of census, allowing the government to check on citizens' whereabouts and identify defectors. The results are expected to be announced early next week.

In a murder case from 2015, police sought access to voice recordings from an Amazon Echo to investigate James Andrew Bates, accused of killing Victor Parris Collins. Amazon declined to give any information from the Echo's servers but handed over Bates' account details and purchase history. Police are interested in any audio the Echo may have picked up, despite the device's "always on" nature. The case raises questions about privacy in the age of smart home devices. Bates' defense argues that using such technology against him is unfair. The investigation also involved water meter data, which showed unusual water usage around the time of the murder, suggesting a cover-up.

A 64-year-old serviceman, Jeffrey Michels, who disappeared from an Air Force Base in North Dakota in 1977, has been arrested and charged with desertion after living a double life in Florida. Michels, originally from East Liverpool, Ohio, was found using the alias "Jeffrey Lantz" and operating a construction business. He will face trial in a military court, where sentencing for desertion can range from a dishonorable discharge to a prison term of two to three years. The case comes days after Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl pleaded guilty to desertion charges, highlighting the ongoing issue of desertion in the military.

Two bald eagles were spotted in a tree along the Neponset River in Milton, Massachusetts, marking the second sighting in less than a week of the birds in the area. Tom Palmer, a bird enthusiast, captured photos of the eagles, which have a seven-foot wingspan and are considered American icons. The Massachusetts Division of Fisheries and Wildlife reports around 46 eagle territories in the state, with numbers expected to have grown since the species was reintroduced in 1982. Eagles are often seen scavenging along roadsides, posing a risk of being hit by vehicles. The birds have made a significant comeback, with federal figures showing about 10,000 breeding pairs in the lower 48 states by 2007. In Boston, sightings of bald eagles have increased, with confirmed breeding pairs in towns like Milton, Waltham, Lynnfield, and Framingham.

A local women’s clinic, Isis Women’s Health Care, is changing its name due to confusion with a terrorist group. Dr. Hughan Frederick explains that the clinic has received numerous death threats from callers mistakenly associating the practice with the group known for torture, suicide bombings, and executions. To ensure the safety of employees and patients, Frederick decided to rename the clinic, marking the 10th anniversary of its founding. The new name will be unveiled on March 31 at the 1015 Mansell Road office. Despite the challenges of altering the clinic’s brand, Frederick hopes to turn this into a positive opportunity, inviting the community to contribute ideas for the new name.

Mixing alcohol types may not inherently worsen hangovers, but drinking darker, congener-rich beverages can increase hangover severity. A study found that consuming bourbon and cola resulted in more severe hangovers compared to vodka and cola or a placebo. Congeners, substances produced during fermentation, may contribute to hangover symptoms. Clear spirits like white rum, vodka, and gin, with lower congener content, generally cause fewer and less severe hangovers. Hangovers are primarily linked to dehydration, hormonal changes, and alcohol toxicity, rather than the order of drink types. Mixing drinks doesn't necessarily increase overall alcohol consumption but may lead to higher congener intake. Hangover severity can also be influenced by the rate of alcohol consumption and individual tolerance.

The Army psychiatrist charged with the 2009 Fort Hood shooting rampage did not give a closing argument on Thursday, despite prosecutors laying out a detailed case and asking for a verdict that could lead to the death penalty. Maj. Nidal Hasan, acting as his own attorney, declined to address the jury after prosecutors finished their closing argument. Prosecutors emphasized premeditation and presented evidence showing Hasan's preparation and targeting of soldiers preparing for deployment. The jury of 13 military officers began deliberations, with the possibility of a death sentence if they find him guilty of premeditated murder. Hasan's lack of defense and his previous statements about the attack being justified have raised questions about his strategy.

A San Jose man, Robert Farmer, was sentenced to 16 years in jail for killing up to 16 cats and sexually abusing one. Farmer, 26, pleaded guilty to 21 felony counts of animal cruelty. He will not have to register as a sex offender, a decision that disappointed some victims. The judge credited Farmer for time already served, allowing him to potentially be released in 4½ years. Farmer will be on probation for 10 years and must stay away from Cambrian Park. His attorney argued that Farmer's methamphetamine addiction and mental health issues contributed to his actions. The case shocked the Cambrian Park community, where cats began disappearing almost two years before Farmer's arrest. Video footage and forensic evidence linked Farmer to the killings. Farmer's letter to the judge admitted his guilt but expressed remorse. The sentencing brought relief to cat owners but raised questions about the need for a sex offender registry for animal abusers.

Some of Hillary Clinton's emails as secretary of state may contain classified information, according to a review by the State Department's inspector general. The inspector general found that four emails from Clinton's private server contained material from the intelligence community that should have been classified "secret" at the time they were sent. Clinton's aides say she did not knowingly handle classified information on her personal email and that any classified material found was not marked as such at the time. The State Department plans to release about 900 pages of Benghazi-related emails from Clinton's private account, though the full set of 55,000 pages is expected to take several months to review. Clinton maintains she did not send any classified information through her personal email.

Vice-presidential picks rarely have a decisive impact on elections, but Paul Ryan's selection could be significant. His Medicare plan, if not successfully countered, could cost Republicans Florida. Republicans counter with two arguments: the plan affects no one over 55, and President Obama cuts Medicare by $700 billion to finance Obamacare. This "judo throw" forces Democrats to debate their own weaknesses. If Mitt Romney and Ryan can counterattack effectively, Ryan's selection could make the election ideological, forcing Obama to confront his economic record and failure of vision. Ryan's youth and energy could also enhance the Republican image. His role as the party's intellectual and political leader, along with his identity as a movement conservative, could make him a dominant national force for decades, representing a new kind of conservatism focused on limited government and individual opportunity.

Most Holy Redeemer, a Catholic church in San Francisco with a membership that is 80% gay and lesbian, is facing leadership challenges under the incoming Archbishop Salvatore Cordileone, an outspoken opponent of same-sex marriage. The church is at a crossroads, with members worried about potential policy changes and even the possibility of the church being closed. Cordileone's decisions, such as banning drag queens from community events, have fueled paranoia among parishioners about an antigay agenda. Despite these issues, the church continues to thrive with a robust congregation and renowned music services. The appointment of Cordileone has raised concerns among gay Catholics about potential marginalization, while supporters view him as a defender of traditional values. Cordileone emphasizes the importance of adhering to the church's teachings and reaching out to those who may disagree, but his arrival has put the church in a difficult position.

NBA star Dwyane Wade's cousin, Nykea Aldridge, was shot and killed in Chicago while walking with her baby in a stroller. Donald Trump initially tweeted, "Dwayne Wade's cousin was just shot and killed walking her baby in Chicago. Just what I have been saying. African-Americans will VOTE TRUMP!" without offering condolences. Later, Trump posted a message expressing sympathy for the family. Trump has been trying to win support from African-American voters by highlighting issues in minority communities, such as poverty, violence, and dysfunction, especially in "inner cities."

Lawrence O’Donnell suggested that Mitt Romney’s campaign deliberately sought to get booed by an audience of African-Americans to appeal to racist voters. Guest Goldie Taylor agreed, arguing that Romney’s NAACP visit was more about appealing to a small part of the GOP base than engaging the black community. Pelosi hinted that Romney’s NAACP boos were intentional, while Cleaver gave Romney an “A” for effort but criticized his opposition to Obamacare. Rush Limbaugh questioned the NAACP’s standards, noting that Romney got a standing ovation despite the boos, and suggested that Obama’s absence from the NAACP convention was an insult. Limbaugh also highlighted Romney’s success in the private sector and criticized the left’s perception of his message to African-Americans.

The upcoming film “Blind,” starring Alec Baldwin as a blind novelist who loses his sight in a car crash, has faced criticism for casting an able-bodied actor in the lead role. The Ruderman Family Foundation, an organization advocating for disability rights, has accused the film of “crip-face” by having Baldwin portray the main character. The foundation, known for pushing for the casting of disabled actors, argues that it is unacceptable for white actors to play disabled roles, comparing it to the use of blackface. The foundation’s president, Jay Ruderman, stated that disability should not be treated as a costume. This criticism comes after the foundation previously criticized the 2016 romantic drama “Me Before You” for casting Sam Claflin as a young banker who was left paralyzed from an accident. The film, directed by Michael Mailer, premiered at the Woodstock Film Festival on October 13 and is set for a worldwide release on July 14 by Vertical Entertainment.

Ferguson, Missouri, is once again in turmoil following the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown by a police officer on Saturday afternoon. The incident has sparked intense debate and protests, with conflicting accounts from witnesses and authorities. Brown's mother, Lesley McSpadden, described her son as a "gentle giant" and pleaded for nonviolent demonstrations. The police chief, Tom Jackson, stated that Brown physically assaulted the officer and tried to take his gun, while witnesses claim Brown had his hands in the air and was unarmed. The officer involved is on administrative leave and will undergo psychological evaluations. The case has drawn national attention, with federal investigators and the FBI conducting their own inquiries. Attorney Benjamin Crump, who represented Trayvon Martin's family, is now working with Brown's family and calling for a thorough investigation. The situation in Ferguson remains tense, with calls for calm and justice from community leaders and activists.

Mitch Daniels, the former conservative favorite for the 2012 Republican presidential nomination, surprised his audience at a conservative think tank by praising President Obama’s education policies. "Most of what I’ve talked about so far, and much of what I will, is strongly supported by the Obama administration," Daniels said, saluting the president and Secretary Duncan. This unexpected turn from a typical Republican critic has positioned Daniels as a grown-up alternative to the current field of candidates, focusing on education and social issues in a more moderate tone. His approach, while well-received by the conservative elite, faces challenges in distinguishing him from other Republican candidates and maintaining his image as a non-threatening choice. Daniels’ strategy includes advocating for national standards, supporting collective bargaining, and promoting social justice, all while maintaining a folksy and humorous demeanor to appeal to a broader audience.

Former Alabama Senate candidate Roy Moore was the latest victim of Sacha Baron Cohen’s satirical show "Who Is America?" In the segment, Moore appeared to be duped by Cohen, who posed as an Israeli anti-terrorism expert named Col. Erran Morad. During the interview, Morad claimed to have a device that could detect pedophiles. When the device beeped when waved in front of Moore, the former judge walked off the set, stating he did not support such pranks. Moore had previously lost a Senate race to Democrat Doug Jones and faced allegations of inappropriate behavior towards teenage girls. He threatened legal action against Cohen and criticized the show’s portrayal of American values.

A Tumblr page dedicated to selfies taken at funerals has sparked controversy. The creator of the page, while seemingly unbothered, warns that he might stop updating it if offered enough money. He challenges readers to either follow him on Twitter or take a selfie at a funeral and face global mockery. The article highlights the growing trend of inappropriate social media behavior during solemn occasions.

Alexander "Sasha" Shulgin, a visionary chemist and prolific inventor of psychoactive substances, passed away at 88, leaving behind a legacy of groundbreaking research and a profound impact on the understanding of the human mind. Known for popularizing MDMA (Ecstasy) and detailing his work in the seminal books PIHKAL and TIHKAL, Shulgin synthesized over 200 unique psychoactive compounds, often testing them personally. His work, driven by a belief in the potential of these substances for therapeutic and spiritual exploration, has influenced countless researchers and enthusiasts. Shulgin's approach to drug research, emphasizing personal experience and open dissemination of knowledge, challenges conventional drug policies and advocates for the decriminalization of substances. His dedication to exploring the nature of the human soul through chemical means has inspired a community of scientists and individuals seeking alternative paths to self-discovery.

Iran has executed a currency trader known as the "Sultan of Coins" for accumulating approximately two tonnes of gold coins. Vahid Mazloumin and another member of his network were sentenced to death for "spreading corruption on earth," accused of hoarding coins to manipulate local market prices. Rights group Amnesty International condemned the executions as "horrific" and a violation of international law, stating that the death penalty is inappropriate for financial corruption. Mazloumin was arrested in July for operating as a speculator, and since August, special courts set up by Iran's Supreme Leader to handle financial crimes have sentenced several individuals to death, often broadcasting trials live on state television. The executions highlight the rising demand for gold coins in Iran, driven by the depreciation of the rial due to US sanctions, leading to a cost of living crisis and protests against perceived corruption.

A Georgia mother lost custody of her five children after hosting a party for her 16-year-old daughter, which included alcohol, drugs, a hot tub, and naked Twister. Rachel Lehnardt, 35, was arrested for two counts of contributing to the delinquency of a minor. Her Alcoholics Anonymous sponsor alerted the Columbia County Sheriff's Office after Lehnardt revealed the details of the party, which involved Lehnardt playing naked Twister, having sex with an 18-year-old, and using sex toys in front of the group. The 16-year-old daughter's boyfriend was also present, and Lehnardt woke up to find him having sex with her. Lehnardt was released on $3,200 bond and faces no sexual crime charges due to the legal age of consent.

Lawmakers unveiled a $1.1 trillion omnibus spending bill Monday night, covering federal agencies through the end of the fiscal year. The bill eases sequester cuts, fully restores Head Start funding, and provides a 1 percent raise for federal workers. It faces a tight deadline to avoid a government shutdown. Congressional leaders praised the compromise, which includes funding increases for military and domestic programs, as well as controversial riders on issues like gun control and veterans’ benefits. The bill is set for a House vote on Wednesday and a Senate vote by the weekend.

Police have released new surveillance video showing Karina Vetrano's final moments before she was found sexually assaulted and killed near her home in Queens on August 2. The video, captured in Howard Beach, shows Vetrano jogging carefree down a street bordering Spring Creek Park. NYPD Commissioner Bill Bratton said the release aims to keep the case fresh in the public's mind, as it remains one of the unsolved, high-profile murders. Vetrano's body was discovered in a marshy area of the park hours after she went missing. A reward of nearly $300,000 is being offered for information leading to an arrest. The NYPD has DNA from three investigative points, with the strongest sample from Vetrano's fingernails, but no matches have been found yet. The family hopes the video will inspire someone to come forward with information.

Japanese officials raised the severity level of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear crisis to 7, matching the scale of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, citing significant radiation releases. The decision, based on cumulative radiation data, reflects the "major accident" category with widespread environmental and health impacts. However, officials emphasized that the current situation does not match Chernobyl's severity, citing lower radiation levels and intact containment structures. The upgrade comes as a broader evacuation zone was announced, including areas with detected high radiation levels. Despite the severity, no direct health damage has been reported, and experts suggest the total radiation release could eventually exceed Chernobyl's, though this remains unlikely. The ongoing challenges at the plant, including aftershocks and radioactive water management, underscore the complexity of the situation.

Keith Olbermann's departure from MSNBC includes a generous exit package, sources tell Mediaite, with Olbermann set to pocket "well in excess" of $7 million. The deal also includes a relatively short benching period of less than 4 1/2 months, compared to the 9 months he was originally required to sit out. Olbermann's agent and attorney, Patty Glaser, handled the negotiations, similar to her work with Conan O'Brien's exit. Speculation suggests Olbermann might seek a role in Aaron Sorkin's upcoming TV project, a behind-the-scenes look at a cable news show, where he could contribute rants. Meanwhile, Olbermann's Twitter activity has slowed since his MSNBC departure, with his profile update hinting at a potential return to sports content, though this remains unconfirmed.

In 2014, Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, dramatically expanded Russia’s territory by annexing Crimea from Ukraine, marking the first territorial growth since the Soviet Union's collapse. This move significantly boosted Putin's popularity at home, with his approval ratings reaching 88%. The annexation of Crimea, seen as a restoration of Russia's great-power status, brought a sense of national revival and pride among Russians, who had long felt humiliated by the dissolution of the Soviet Union. Despite international condemnation and sanctions, Putin's actions bolstered his image as a strong leader willing to challenge Western dominance. However, the annexation came at a cost, including economic challenges and geopolitical isolation, as Russia faced economic sanctions and a drop in oil prices, leading to inflation and a weakened ruble.

Bill Gates disclosed at a foundation meeting that Donald Trump had twice inquired about his daughter Jennifer’s appearance and knew "scary" details about her, while also asking about medical differences like HIV and HPV. The remarks were made during a recent question-and-answer session at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, where Gates recounted how Trump had flown to a horse show to see Jennifer after meeting her there earlier. Trump’s extensive knowledge of Gates’ daughter’s personal life and his questions about vaccines and health issues during meetings with Gates have raised concerns about his priorities and competence.

Australian TV host Karl Stefanovic wore the same cheap Burberry suit for a year to test how his female colleagues are judged more harshly for their appearance. His co-host Lisa Wilkinson and other Today Show members knew about the experiment. Stefanovic found no complaints about his suit, highlighting the double standard women face. The prank gained global attention and support from the feminist community, illustrating the ongoing issue of gender bias in media.

Sen. Cory Booker testified against his Senate colleague, Jeff Sessions, for the Trump administration's nomination as attorney general, breaking with Senate tradition. Booker stated his "conscience" and "country" motivated his unprecedented action, emphasizing Sessions' "hostility" towards civil rights and justice. He highlighted Sessions' past record and criticized his potential to uphold equal rights and defend marginalized groups. Booker's testimony was part of two-day hearings that focused on civil rights and the "law and order" approach. Other civil rights leaders, including Rep. John Lewis, also testified against Sessions. Sessions' supporters defended his record, with his former staffer arguing he has a history of fighting for civil rights. The confirmation process is expected to continue with the Republican-controlled Senate likely to confirm Sessions.

Vice reporter Simon Ostrovsky has been freed from captivity in Ukraine, according to a statement from Vice. The reporter is in good health and is on his way to Donetsk. The news organization thanks everyone for their support during this difficult time, respecting the privacy of Ostrovsky and his family.

Scientists have discovered a vast subglacial aquatic system beneath the Antarctic ice sheets, consisting of hundreds of lakes and interconnected water channels. This system, maintained by geothermal heat and pressure, supports microbial life in some of the Earth's most extreme environments. The Whillans Ice Stream Subglacial Access Research Drilling (WISSARD) project aims to explore Subglacial Lake Whillans and the grounding zone, where the West Antarctic Ice Sheet meets the Ross Sea. Using advanced tools like radar and GPS, researchers have found evidence of active microbial ecosystems half a mile below the ice surface, raising questions about the potential for life in similar environments on other planets. This discovery highlights the importance of studying subglacial environments and could inform future missions to explore icy moons in our solar system.

Scientists are exploring selective breeding to reduce methane production in cows, goats, deer, and sheep, aiming to curb a major greenhouse gas and increase the efficiency of these animals. Preliminary findings suggest that methane production, primarily through belching, is consistent among these animals, allowing for the breeding of lower-emitting individuals. This could benefit the environment and lower feed costs. The RuminOmics project, a €7.7 million EU-funded initiative, is investigating the genetic factors influencing methane production and aims to develop tools for selecting cattle with reduced environmental impact and improved feed efficiency.

A woman accused of abusing a 2-year-old girl to the point of causing her death and then failing to appear for her trial was arrested in Portland, Oregon. Janet Killough Barreto, 43, and her husband Ramon Barreto are wanted in Mississippi for charges including manslaughter, child abuse, and child neglect. The couple allegedly abused multiple adopted children, forcing them to live in deplorable conditions and causing one child's death in 2008. Janet Barreto, who used aliases and changed her appearance to evade capture, was arrested at a Portland shopping mall after a tip led authorities to her. She and her husband are currently held in Multnomah County jail, awaiting extradition to Mississippi.

Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker says he believes governors make better presidents than members of Congress, citing their "fresh approach" and "executive experience from outside of Washington." Walker argues that potential Republican presidential candidates should run on the record of GOP governors, though he expresses support for Rep. Paul Ryan.
