President Trump added former White House aide Omarosa Manigault Newman to his Twitter attacks, calling her a "crazed, crying lowlife" after she alleged he is a racist. In an MSNBC interview, Manigault Newman accused Trump of having no respect for women and African-Americans. The White House could not guarantee there are no recordings of Trump using the "N-word," with press secretary Sarah Sanders acknowledging the president's tweets denying its use. Manigault Newman, promoting her memoir "Unhinged," also confirmed she was interviewed by special counsel Robert Mueller. The Trump campaign filed arbitration against her for alleged breach of a 2016 non-disclosure agreement.

A Tennessee middle schooler named Keaton, bullied for being "different," gained widespread support after his emotional video went viral. His mother, Kimberly Jones, posted the video on Facebook, showing Keaton's struggles with verbal and physical bullying at Gibbs Elementary School. The video, viewed over 21 million times, prompted numerous celebrities and athletes, including Tennessee Titans tight end Delanie Walker, University of Tennessee wide receiver Tyler Byrd, and country music star Kelsea Ballerini, to offer support and visit his school. Avengers actor Chris Evans invited Keaton to the next Avengers movie premiere, while Mark Ruffalo praised him as "one of the coolest kids I have ever seen." The incident highlights the impact of social media in addressing and combating bullying.

Ten years ago, National Weather Service meteorologist Robert Ricks issued a dire forecast for Hurricane Katrina, predicting unprecedented destruction and water shortages. His warnings, including statements like "MOST OF THE AREA WILL BE UNINHABITABLE FOR WEEKS," are now part of the Smithsonian Museum of American History. Ricks, who grew up in the Lower Ninth Ward, validated each prediction before issuing the statement. Despite his warnings, the devastation was beyond what he and his colleagues could have imagined. Ricks, now back at work alongside colleagues who lost their homes, reflects on the impact of the storm and the effectiveness of his warnings.

The film "Water for Elephants," based on Sara Gruen's novel, aims for a nostalgic and engaging Depression-era circus tale but falls short in delivering the emotional depth and grit expected from its source material. Director Francis Lawrence and screenwriter Richard LaGravenese streamline the story, focusing on the love triangle between Marlena (Reese Witherspoon), August (Christoph Waltz), and Jacob (Robert Pattinson). While the performances are strong, particularly from Waltz, the film lacks the rawness and complexity of the original. The circus setting and historical backdrop are well-realized, with impressive cinematography and production design. However, the climax feels rushed and underdeveloped. The film is a respectable adaptation but misses the spark that would make it truly compelling on screen.

A man named Richard Dunn spent his overnight wait at Las Vegas' McCarran Airport making a solo music video for Celine Dion's "All By Myself." Using his iPhone, a wheelchair, and a water bottle, Dunn recreated iconic scenes from Flashdance, capturing nearly 500,000 views on Vimeo. The video showcases Dunn's creativity and resourcefulness, turning a mundane airport experience into a viral sensation.

One person died and 19 were injured after a car plowed into a crowd of protesters in Charlottesville during a white nationalist rally. The suspect, James Alex Fields Jr., a 20-year-old from Ohio, was arrested and charged with second-degree murder and other counts. Multiple men were also arrested in connection with violent clashes between white supremacists and counter-protesters. A helicopter crash outside the city killed two troopers, occurring shortly after the car incident. The organizer of the rally, Jason Kessler, disavowed the violence. President Trump condemned the violence but faced criticism for his comments.

Alex Jones, host of Infowars and a well-known conspiracy theorist, made a surprise appearance at a Senate Intelligence Committee hearing on social media issues, disrupting proceedings by heckling Republican Senator Marco Rubio. The exchange escalated when Rubio warned Jones not to touch him, to which Jones mockingly called Rubio a "little gangster thug" and "frat boy." Jones livestreamed his entrance and sat near tech executives Jack Dorsey and Sheryl Sandberg, who were testifying about content moderation and misinformation. The incident occurred as many conservatives accuse social media platforms of bias against their views.

President Donald Trump is positioning himself to distance himself from potential Republican electoral losses in the 2018 midterm elections. In public, he emphasizes the elections are about him, but privately, he reportedly tells confidants that House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell are responsible for protecting their majorities. Trump reportedly believes he has done everything possible to assist Republican candidates and credits McConnell for motivating GOP voters. However, in the event of a Democratic wave, Trump is expected to blame congressional Republicans, particularly Ryan and McConnell, for any losses. His aides acknowledge the White House lacks clear plans for post-election messaging. Democrats, meanwhile, are tamping down expectations for a "blue wave," with key House races tightening and winning back the Senate looking increasingly difficult. Early voting data shows Republican-affiliated voters outpacing Democratic-affiliated ones in seven closely watched states, potentially dampening Democratic hopes. A shooting at Santa Fe High School in Texas left 10 people dead and 10 more injured, mostly students, on a day that began with a normal school start. The 17-year-old suspect, Dimitrios Pagourtzis, entered the school armed with a shotgun and a .38 revolver, both legally obtained from his father. Law enforcement officials found two homemade explosive devices at the scene. Pagourtzis, described as an introverted student with few warning signs, surrendered after the shooting. The incident, the worst in Texas since the Parkland shooting, shocked the small town and the nation. Students and teachers shared their experiences, with some noting the fear and disbelief that such an event could occur. The suspect had a history of interest in white supremacist groups, though his motivations remain unclear. The shooting left families and the community in mourning, with the victims including a teacher and an exchange student from Pakistan. The event reignited discussions on gun control and school safety,

Cynk Technology Corp., a social network with no assets, revenue, and only one employee, saw its stock surge 25,000% since mid-June, catching the attention of the SEC, which suspended trading. The company faces scrutiny over the accuracy and adequacy of information in the marketplace, with concerns about potentially manipulative transactions. Cynk's surge may be due to difficulty in shorting the stock and brokerage compliance systems preventing owners from selling after the suspicious price jump. The SEC is investigating how the company reached a $6 billion valuation, raising questions about the legitimacy of its operations and the accuracy of its financial disclosures.

Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner criticized Mitt Romney's argument that most jobs lost under Obama's administration were among women, calling it a "ridiculous way" to view the economy. Geithner stated that the crisis affected everyone and began in early 2008, with initial job losses hitting men due to construction and manufacturing sectors. Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus dismissed the Buffett Rule as a minor tax code change unlikely to impact the budget deficit. He argued it was merely a distraction from Obama's economic record. Rep. Darrell Issa predicted the Secret Service scandal involving Obama's trip to Colombia might be part of a larger issue, suggesting the entire organization needed scrutiny. Rep. Michele Bachmann defended Mitt Romney against attacks, criticizing Hilary Rosen's comments about Ann Romney's work history as "shocking and insulting." Bachmann expressed interest in endorsing Romney and aimed to unite the party.

A 44-year-old experienced outdoorsman, Marco Lavoie, was rescued after spending three months in the wilderness near Waskaganish, Quebec, following a bear attack that left him without food and survival gear. Lavoie, who had set out on a two-month canoe trek, was attacked by a bear in mid-August, which destroyed his equipment and ate his supplies but did not injure him. His German shepherd, however, protected him during the attack. Lavoie's family reported him missing on October 21, and a search began, hampered by harsh weather conditions. After nearly a month, Lavoie was spotted by a helicopter on October 30 and was carried for nearly two miles to safety. He was in critical condition, suffering from hypothermia, dehydration, and starvation, and was expected to survive but would need several weeks of medical care.

Susan Schneider Williams, an artist and advocate, shares her husband Robin Williams' battle with Lewy body disease (LBD), a condition that affected nearly 1.5 million Americans. Williams recounts the early signs, including gastrointestinal issues and anxiety, which escalated into paranoia, delusions, and memory loss. Despite extensive medical evaluations and treatments, Williams felt helpless as her husband's condition deteriorated. The diagnosis of LBD came only after Robin's death, revealing a severe pathology with high Lewy body concentration. Williams' journey includes her advocacy for LBD awareness and her support of research efforts, inspired by the hope that her husband's suffering might contribute to future breakthroughs.

The concept of "digital natives" and "digital immigrants" has been widely discussed, with many assuming that younger generations are inherently more adept at technology. However, a recent editorial in Nature challenges this notion, citing a review paper from Teaching and Teacher Education that found no evidence supporting the idea of digital natives possessing unique technological skills or superior multitasking abilities. The term was coined by educator Marc Prensky in 2001, but the authors argue that this distinction is a myth, similar to the idea of a "yeti with a smartphone." This misperception has influenced various aspects of education and workplace policies, potentially leading to ineffective strategies. The editorial suggests a more nuanced approach, focusing on the unique habits and worldviews of different generations rather than assuming inherent technological superiority.

The Tomah VA Medical Center has notified 592 veterans that they may have been infected with Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, or HIV due to improper sterilization practices by a dentist who used his own equipment and cleaned it between patients for a year. The acting medical center director stated that the dentist purposefully violated VA regulations. The VA is offering free screenings and treatment to those who test positive. The dentist has been removed from patient care and is now in an administrative role, with the inspector general investigating potential criminal charges.

The British tabloid News of the World is accused of hacking the voicemails of Kate Middleton and Prince Harry, a court in London heard. Prosecutors allege that the newspaper, owned by Rupert Murdoch, accessed the private messages of the future King and Queen to gather embarrassing personal details. The court was shown transcripts of messages between Prince William and Kate Middleton, including one where William called her "Babykins." The revelations are part of the ongoing trial of former News of the World editors Rebekah Brooks, Andy Coulson, and Stuart Kuttner, who are accused of conspiring to intercept communications without lawful authority. The trial has also uncovered evidence of the newspaper's extensive efforts to hack the phones of royal aides, including Prince Charles, William, and Harry.

A small study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests that oxytocin, often called the "cuddle chemical," may help individuals with autism spectrum disorders improve their social interactions. By using nasal inhalers to administer oxytocin to 13 adults with high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome, researchers observed significant improvements in the participants' social behaviors. These improvements included increased eye contact and better performance in social games. If confirmed, these findings could lead to potential therapeutic uses of oxytocin for autism, particularly for early intervention in young children. Lead author Angela Sirigu notes that administering oxytocin early in childhood might help change social interaction patterns from a young age. While more research is needed, the results are promising and could offer new treatment options for autism.

Target is launching a new $5 wine line called California Roots, offering five blends made from California grapes. The wines include chardonnay, pinot grigio, moscato, cabernet sauvignon, and a red blend. Each bottle is designed to provide a specific taste experience, such as tropical fruit flavors in the chardonnay or hints of oak in the cabernet sauvignon. Target aims to expand its alcohol selection in 300 stores, including seven in Southern California, to capitalize on growing demand for affordable wines.

One of the Secret Service supervisors ousted in the agency's ongoing prostitution scandal joked on Facebook that he was checking out former Republican vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin as he protected her during the 2008 campaign. David Chaney, 48, posted the comment after a friend had marveled at a picture of him standing behind Palin. Chaney is one of two supervisors accused in the scandal, which involved 11 Secret Service employees and 10 military personnel bringing prostitutes back to their hotel in Cartagena, Colombia, before President Obama's visit. The incident has raised questions about accountability and conduct within the Secret Service, with lawmakers predicting more firings and resignations. Chaney and another supervisor, Greg Stokes, have been accused of misconduct, though their involvement is still under investigation.

A Philadelphia man was caught using a cell phone jammer on a SEPTA bus, disrupting calls for those who needed to use their phones. NBC10 Investigator Harry Hairston uncovered the story, revealing that the man, who calls himself Eric, jams cell phones to avoid public conversations. Eric admits to the practice, stating he takes the law into his own hands and is proud of it. An NBC10 employee, "Marie," witnessed Eric's actions and reported him. The cell phone jamming device is illegal, potentially disrupting emergency communications and public safety. Eric was informed of the illegality but continued to use the device. SEPTA officials received complaints about lost calls but assured safety, stating their system is robust. The incident sparked debate on personal versus public space and the ethics of jamming cell phones.

A few years ago, a Yale Law School student preparing for a judicial clerkship received advice from professors Amy Chua and Jed Rubenfeld about federal judge Brett Kavanaugh. Chua advised the student to dress "outgoing" and send her pictures of outfits for interviews, while Rubenfeld warned about Kavanaugh's preference for female clerks with a "certain look." The student found the advice off-putting but still interviewed with Kavanaugh. The controversy surrounding Kavanaugh's nomination to the Supreme Court has resurfaced with allegations of sexual misconduct from Christine Blasey Ford. Chua and Rubenfeld's influence in vetting clerks for Kavanaugh has raised questions about their methods and the potential impact on female students. Chua denied coaching students on their physical appearance but praised Kavanaugh as a "mentor to women." The internal investigation into Rubenfeld's conduct at Yale Law School continues.

The doctor wasn't alarmed, suggesting that such side businesses are becoming more common as doctors face financial pressures. The IV hangover cure service, offered by New York urologist Dr. Elliot Nadelson and his son Adam, provides intravenous hydration and other medications to help alleviate hangovers. Clients can receive treatment at a clinic or have a nurse visit them at home. The service caters to a range of clients, including finance professionals and athletes, and is seen as a convenient and cost-effective alternative to emergency room visits. While it may not completely cure a hangover, it significantly reduces discomfort. The Nadelsons are expanding their service to new cities and using social media to attract clients.

A team of divers has connected two underwater caverns in eastern Mexico, revealing what is believed to be the world's largest flooded cave. The discovery, made near the beach resort of Tulum, links the Sac Actun system, previously measured at 263 km, with the 83-km Dos Ojos system, making the combined cave system 347 km long. This extensive network of submerged passages, known as the Gran Acuifero Maya (GAM), could provide new insights into the ancient Maya civilization. The interconnected cave system, named Sac Actun, contains more than 100 archaeological elements, including evidence of early human settlements, extinct fauna, and Mayan artifacts. The discovery highlights the importance of the Yucatan Peninsula's subterranean water systems and their role in supporting biodiversity and ancient human activity.

Saudi Arabia will shift its weekend to Friday and Saturday starting next week, bringing the country a step closer to opening its $400 billion stock market to foreign investors. The decision, based on "the economic position of the kingdom and its international and regional obligations," will align Saudi Arabia with other Gulf Cooperation Council countries. This move is seen as a step towards foreign market access, potentially attracting up to $30 billion in inflows. Global banks have already set up offices in Riyadh as a hub for brokers covering the GCC region, anticipating the market's opening. The change aims to reduce lost economic opportunities and better align with global markets, with similar changes for schools and educational institutions to begin in the next academic year.

An 11-year-old girl died after falling from a water ride at Drayton Manor theme park in Staffordshire. Evha Jannath, a student from Leicester, was on a school trip when she fell into the water on the Splash Canyon attraction. Park staff attempted to help her, but she was airlifted to a nearby hospital and later pronounced dead. The park, which has a similar ride that was involved in a fatal incident in Australia in 2016, has temporarily closed the Splash Canyon ride for an investigation. The incident has sparked concerns about the safety of water rides, with a mother recalling a near-miss her son experienced on the same ride in 2013. The Health and Safety Executive has begun an investigation, and the park has closed another rapids ride as a precaution.

Barnes & Noble is reconsidering its Nook tablet strategy after a 34% drop in sales during the fiscal fourth quarter. The company plans to continue selling its e-readers but will partner with a third-party manufacturer for future Nook HD tablets, potentially co-branding the devices. CEO William Lynch emphasized that Barnes & Noble is not exiting the device business. The move comes amid industry rumors suggesting Microsoft might purchase the Nook brand. Barnes & Noble's stock fell 18% following the earnings report. The company reported a net loss of $118.6 million, nearly double the loss from the previous year, while revenue decreased by 7.4% to $1.3 billion. Lynch expects the company to open five new stores and close 15 to 20 stores in the coming year.

A Twitter user named Stefanie Gordon captured photos and a video of the space shuttle Endeavour's final launch from her plane and shared them on Twitter, gaining widespread attention and hundreds of new followers. The unique perspective from the air drew interest from major news outlets, turning a casual tweet into a viral moment.

A man who communicated with former Trump campaign adviser Richard Gates has pleaded guilty to making false statements to the FBI in special counsel Robert Mueller's probe into Russian election interference. Alex Van Der Zwaan was charged with making "materially false, fictitious, and fraudulent statements and representations" to the special counsel's office and FBI agents, according to a court filing. He entered a guilty plea, allegedly lying about his last communications with Gates and deleting emails requested by the special counsel’s office. The new charges come as Gates is reportedly nearing a plea deal with Mueller that could lead to his testimony against Paul Manafort, Trump's former campaign chairman. Van Der Zwaan is accused of making false statements about a report he helped the Ukrainian Ministry of Justice prepare in 2012 on the trial of Yulia Tymoshenko, a former Ukrainian prime minister. The charges are related to a report produced by the law firm Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom that helped

White House counsel Kathryn Ruemmler faced a dilemma when she learned about an upcoming inspector general’s report on the Internal Revenue Service’s improper targeting of conservative groups. She shared the news with White House officials but advised against informing President Obama until the audit was completed and public. This approach aimed to shield Obama from any appearance of trying to influence the investigation. However, the situation was complicated by the sudden public disclosure of the IRS findings by Lois Lerner, creating a communications crisis. Ruemmler’s role as a lawyer focused on legal advice and protecting the presidency, often at the expense of political considerations, became central to the White House’s handling of the scandal. Despite her legal acumen, Ruemmler’s methods were criticized for potentially undermining the president’s knowledge and control. The episode highlighted the challenges of managing a White House with reduced political and media experience and underscored the tension between legal and political imperatives in crisis management.

A Danish inventor charged with the death of Swedish journalist Kim Wall has admitted to dumping her body into the ocean after an accident on his submarine. Peter Madsen, 46, initially claimed to have dropped Wall off at an island near Copenhagen but later told police and the court that she died on the submarine and he "buried" her at sea. The search for Wall's body continues, with divers, helicopters, and ships searching along the identified route in Koge Bay. Madsen has been charged with negligent manslaughter, and his lawyer maintains he has not admitted to any wrongdoing. The Danish inventor's 40-tonne submarine, the UC3 Nautilus, was deliberately sunk, and Wall's body was not found when the vessel was raised.

A 55-year-old man from Pendleton, Oregon, pleaded guilty in federal court to four charges of misconduct in national parks, including provoking a bison in Yellowstone National Park. Raymond Reinke was arrested in early August after video surfaced showing him running toward and waving his arms at a bison. He had previously been cited for drunk and disorderly behavior in Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks. Reinke initially pleaded not guilty but changed his plea to guilty during the hearing. Judge Mark Carman sentenced him to 130 days in jail, with 5 years of unsupervised probation and a ban from Yellowstone, Glacier, and Grand Teton parks. Reinke also faces alcohol restrictions and substance abuse treatment. He apologized to the bison, acknowledging his actions were wrong.

Police in El Cerrito are seeking the public's assistance to identify a woman who may have inadvertently captured evidence of her own crime through selfies taken with a stolen phone. The incident involved a teenage girl who was walking to school when a woman approached, demanded her iPhone and backpack, and assaulted her, causing minor head injuries. The victim later noticed the selfies on her iCloud account and recognized the attacker. Authorities believe the suspect did not realize the photos would upload to the cloud. Students suggest being more cautious with phone displays to avoid such situations.

A restaurant owner in Sedro-Woolley, Washington, has asked local law enforcement to no longer dine at their teriyaki establishment, after a misunderstanding led to a request that law enforcement no longer eat there. Through an interpreter, the owner explained that a language barrier may have caused a misunderstanding when an employee noticed customers at another table getting upset and asked the deputies if they were about to leave. The owner, feeling terrible about the situation, invited law enforcement to eat at the restaurant for free on July 18. The Skagit County Sheriff's Office posted the incident on Facebook, where it garnered thousands of shares and comments. The Sedro-Woolley Police Department expressed disappointment but will continue to respond to the business as requested.

Paula Deen faces another setback as QVC joins other major companies in cutting ties with her following her admission of using a racial slur. Deen, who has been under scrutiny since the revelation, issued a statement emphasizing her desire to "set things right" and earn forgiveness. QVC's CEO, Mike George, stated that the company is "troubled" by the allegations and is taking a pause in their relationship with Deen, emphasizing the importance of giving her a chance to address the issues. This latest development adds to a growing list of corporate partners who have distanced themselves from Deen, including Target, Home Depot, and Wal-Mart. Despite the setbacks, Deen's cookware line remains popular, and her "Paula Deen Cruise" has even added an extra departure in 2014 due to high demand.

Twin explosions targeted Syria's army command headquarters in Damascus, setting off hours of sporadic gun battles and a raging fire inside the heavily guarded compound, state-run media and witnesses reported. The blasts, one from a car bomb and another from an explosive device, caused heavy gunfire and chaos, with panicked soldiers reportedly shooting randomly. Syrian authorities claimed no military commanders or personnel were hurt, but an Iranian correspondent died in the ensuing exchange of fire. The attacks, part of the ongoing civil war, highlighted the rebels' growing efforts to target regime symbols. The explosions also disrupted traffic and access to the capital, with checkpoints set up. The conflict, which began in March 2011 with protests against the Assad regime, has claimed nearly 30,000 lives and intensified as rebels increasingly target security sites.

In the Jessica Ridgeway murder case, investigators have released a description of a man who attempted to abduct a 22-year-old woman near Ketner Lake on May 28, linking the two cases in hopes of uncovering a lead. The suspect was described as white or light-skinned, between 18 and 30 years old, with brown hair and a medium build, standing about 5 feet, 8 inches tall. He used a chemical-soaked rag in the attempt. Law enforcement is also examining other attempted abductions in the Denver metro area to see if they could be connected to Ridgeway's case. The public is encouraged to call Westminster police with any information.

Air Force Staff Sgt. Luis Walker, convicted of raping a female recruit and sexually assaulting several others, faces sentencing at Lackland Air Force Base. A military jury found him guilty on all 28 counts, including rape and aggravated sexual assault. Walker is accused of sexually assaulting 10 female recruits between October 2010 and January 2011. The case is part of a larger sex scandal involving 12 instructors at Lackland, who are accused of misconduct toward at least 31 female trainees. The Air Force is investigating more instructors, with another facing trial. The scandal highlights the rigorous hierarchical nature of the military, making it conducive to sexual abuse, and has led to new steps by the Pentagon to combat sexual assault.

Artist Ryan Mendoza saved Rosa Parks' Detroit home from demolition by moving it to Germany, where it was rebuilt and displayed. Now, Mendoza wants to return the house to the U.S., believing it should serve as a reminder of the civil rights movement. The home, once facing demolition, was dismantled and shipped to Berlin, where it was reconstructed to give visitors a more intimate sense of Parks' life. Mendoza plans to bring the house back to America as communities debate the fate of Confederate monuments and memorials. He has received support from the Nash Family Foundation and the vice chancellor of Germany, who wrote a letter to former first lady Michelle Obama. The house, which is about 21 feet wide and 21 feet long, has been visited by thousands of people, including some American celebrities, in Berlin. Mendoza hopes to find a suitable location in the U.S. to display the house, emphasizing its importance in the context of ongoing discussions about racial justice and equality.

Scientists at the University of Tokyo and Kyoto University have successfully grown human ear cartilage from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), marking a significant step in regenerative medicine. The process involves culturing iPSCs into cartilage cells, which are then shaped into tiny balls and placed into a tube. These tubes, resembling a human ear, are implanted onto a rat's back. After about two months, the tubes dissolve, leaving behind a human ear about 2 inches long. This breakthrough could potentially help individuals born without ears or with ear deformities. Clinical trials involving humans are expected to commence in about five years.

Florida Governor Rick Scott proposed a comprehensive plan to enhance school safety, including raising the minimum age to buy firearms to 21, strengthening background checks, and allocating $450 million for increased law enforcement presence and mental health resources. Scott's plan aims to keep guns away from dangerous individuals, particularly those with mental health issues, and does not include a ban on assault-style rifles. In response to the Parkland shooting, Scott emphasized the need to make it "virtually impossible" for those with mental issues or who pose a danger to themselves or others to obtain firearms. The plan also calls for mandatory active shooter training, enhanced school security measures, and a "see something, say something" hotline. Scott's proposal faces criticism from gun control advocates who argue that it falls short of addressing the root causes of gun violence and does not go far enough to ban assault weapons. Seven men have been charged in the 2014 hazing death of University at Albany student Trevor Duffy. The men, who say they were part of the Zeta Beta Tau fraternity, are accused of forcing Duffy to drink a 60-ounce bottle of vodka, leading to his death. The fraternity, based in Indianapolis, has released a statement denouncing the men, stating they are not part of the Epsilon Gamma chapter recognized by the university. Zeta Beta Tau is suing the men, claiming they falsely represented themselves and damaged the fraternity's reputation.

The Bramble Cay melomys, a small rodent endemic to a coral cay in the Great Barrier Reef, has been declared extinct, marking the first mammalian extinction linked primarily to human-induced climate change. Extensive surveys found no evidence of the species, with habitat loss due to rising sea levels and increased storm surges cited as the primary cause. This extinction highlights the severe impacts of climate change on biodiversity, particularly in low-lying coastal areas.

In a resignation letter, Sebastian Gorka cited "forces" that do not support President Trump's "MAGA promise" as being ascendant in the White House. Gorka, a deputy assistant to the president who was closely aligned with former chief strategist Steve Bannon, was ousted from the White House, officials confirmed. In his letter, Gorka wrote that outside of the president, the individuals who most embodied and represented the policies to "Make America Great Again" have been "internally countered, systematically removed, or undermined." Gorka's departure came one week after Bannon was fired. A White House official indicated that Gorka was forced out rather than resigning. Gorka's wife, Katie Gorka, an official at the Department of Homeland Security, may also leave the administration. The move is seen as part of new White House chief of staff John Kelly's effort to shape the president's staff. Gorka's departure was marked by controversy, with

The Amtrak train on its inaugural run through a faster railway route was traveling about 80 mph in a 30 mph zone before derailing, according to officials. The speed limit changes from 79 mph to 30 mph just before the curve where the crash occurred. Positive train control, which can prevent dangerous situations like excessive speed, was not operational on this stretch of track. The derailment killed three people and injured more than 70, with 10 suffering serious injuries. The new route, part of a $181 million project, was intended to cut travel time and reduce the need to slow down due to curves and single-track tunnels. The incident raised questions about the implementation of safety technology and the need for improved infrastructure.

A 5-year-old girl in Texas is being hailed as a hero after saving her unconscious mother from the bottom of a swimming pool. Tracy Anderwald, 34, had a seizure and sank to the pool's floor, but her daughter Allison, who has been swimming since age 2.5, realized her mother had not surfaced for over five minutes. Allison jumped in, pulled her mother to the shallow end, and helped her head stay above water. A sister, Tedra Hunt, heard the commotion and called 911. Tracy Anderwald was taken to the hospital, where doctors initially had low expectations for her recovery but later deemed her stable. Allison's actions are seen as a miracle, and the family hopes their story raises awareness about teaching children water safety and emergency response.

The U.S. ambassador to New Zealand, Scott Brown, has admitted to being investigated by the U.S. State Department over inappropriate comments made during his inaugural trip to Samoa to celebrate 50 years of the Peace Corps in the country. Brown, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, confirmed the official inquiry and stated that the complaints related to comments he made at a party in Apia, Samoa, where he told attendees they looked "beautiful" and could make hundreds of dollars working in the hospitality industry in the U.S. Brown and his wife, Gail Huff, expressed that they did not realize the comments would be considered offensive. The incident has raised questions about cultural sensitivity and the role of ambassadors.

A circuit judge in Baltimore ruled that the case against six police officers charged in the death of Freddie Gray will proceed in separate trials, with Baltimore State's Attorney Marilyn Mosby remaining as prosecutor. The officers face charges ranging from second-degree assault to second-degree "depraved-heart" murder. Outside the courthouse, protesters gathered to voice their support for Gray and demand justice, while police maintained order. The judge denied motions to dismiss charges and recuse Mosby, stating that trying the officers together would not be in the interest of justice due to differing evidence admissibility. The case has sparked widespread protests and become part of the national dialogue on police treatment of black citizens.

"LOL" is losing its popularity on Facebook as younger users opt for emoji to express laughter, according to a report. The term, once a staple of internet communication, is now used less frequently, especially by younger demographics, while "haha" and "hehe" remain more common. The shift highlights how language evolves rapidly online, with emoji emerging as the universal language. However, the decline of "LOL" may also be influenced by its ironic use or the difficulty older users face in finding the emoji keyboard.

A new study indicates that almost half of the edible seafood in the United States goes to waste, primarily due to consumer discard, with annual losses totaling 1.3 billion pounds. This waste, equivalent to the protein needs of over 10 million people, occurs at various stages of the supply chain, including distribution, bycatch, and consumer disposal. The research, published in the journal Global Environmental Change, highlights the urgent need to reduce seafood waste as dietary guidelines recommend increased seafood consumption, which could strain already threatened global seafood resources. The study suggests strategies such as smaller portion packaging and encouraging the purchase of frozen seafood to mitigate waste, aiming to support more efficient and sustainable seafood systems.

Ben Affleck's "Argo" won the Best Director and Best Picture awards at the 18th Annual Critics' Choice Movie Awards, held at Barker Hangar in Santa Monica. Affleck joked about the "academy" and thanked the Critics' Choice organization. Jennifer Lawrence won for best actress in an action movie and best comedic actress. Daniel Day-Lewis was named best actor for his role in "Lincoln." The Critics' Choice Awards, often a reliable predictor for the Oscars, also honored "Argo" as the best picture. Stars like Jessica Chastain, Anne Hathaway, and Bradley Cooper celebrated their nominations and wins. Judd Apatow received the Louis XIII Genius Award. The event, hosted by Sam Rubin, featured a mix of humor and serious acceptance speeches, with some stars expressing gratitude for their nominations and the recognition of their directors.

A powerful storm that hit northern Europe caused flooding and high tides, prompting evacuations along the eastern English coast. The Thames Barrier in London closed for a second time in two days to protect the city. Exceptionally high tides, similar to those in a 1953 flood, were expected in some areas, though flood defenses and warnings prevented major damage. In the U.S., a winter storm brought snow, ice, and freezing rain to the East Coast, causing travel disruptions and flight cancellations. The storm's effects were felt from Texas to New England, with low temperatures and icy conditions. In Dallas, temperatures dropped to 26 degrees, the coldest December high in 23 years. At least seven deaths were reported, mostly due to icy road conditions. The storm caused widespread travel issues and canceled flights, but travel was expected to improve by Monday.

Blue Ivy, while a nice name, might still cause some confusion in kindergarten, especially if her classmates are named Audio Science or Pilot Inspektor. Despite this, she won't be the wackiest baby name among Hollywood's offspring, as other celebs like Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin have given their children names like Moon Unit and Apple.

U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, recovering from a gunshot wound to the head, surprised her rabbi by singing "American Pie" and knowing all the words, demonstrating progress in her recovery. Her medical team encourages her to sing as part of brain rehabilitation exercises. Giffords, who was shot in the left forehead, is making slow but steady progress, though doctors caution that her recovery will be long and difficult. Her husband, astronaut Mark Kelly, remains by her side. Meanwhile, a Tucson firefighter's refusal to respond to the shooting incident due to "political bantering" may have caused a delay in the initial response, though the department later stated the delay was minimal. The firefighter, Mark Ekstrum, retired from his 28-year career after the incident, citing personal reasons.

Ben Bernanke's upcoming news conference on Wednesday is expected to address the Federal Reserve's decision to end its $600 billion bond-buying program as scheduled. Despite inflation picking up and a moderate economic recovery, the central bank remains concerned about the jobs market. The FOMC's key interest rate will remain at its historic low range of 0% to 0.25%, and it will adjust its holdings of Treasurys and mortgage-backed securities as needed. Attention now turns to Bernanke's first-ever press conference, where he will provide more details on the Fed's future policy outlook.

Oscar Pistorius, the double-amputee Olympian, appeared in court on Monday, showing emotion as graphic images of the night he killed his girlfriend, Reeva Steenkamp, were displayed. Pistorius, 27, maintains he mistook her for an intruder. The court showed a close-up of one of Steenkamp's wounds, prompting Pistorius to sob and cover his face. His defense called pathologist Jan Botha to testify, challenging the prosecution's timeline of events. The trial continues, with Pistorius offering a tearful apology to Steenkamp's family and friends.

China's official GDP figures are considered "man-made" and "for reference only," according to Li Keqiang, who is expected to become the next premier. Despite these caveats, the latest GDP report showed a 7.6% growth rate for the last quarter, the slowest in three years. Analysts and investors face challenges in interpreting these numbers, with some suggesting they may be artificially inflated, especially ahead of the upcoming leadership transition. The statistical system struggles to accurately measure the service sector and middle-class consumption. While industrial production and profits are better tracked, the overall reliability of GDP figures remains questionable. The government is working to improve data collection methods and transparency, but the process remains largely opaque. Despite the slowdown, there is optimism that the economy may have bottomed out, with the government having tools to ensure steady growth in the medium term.

When Americans gather for Thanksgiving, they typically enjoy the same traditional dishes: turkey, cranberry sauce, stuffing, and pumpkin pie. But how did these foods become the staples of the holiday meal? The first Thanksgiving in 1621 may not have included turkey, as the Pilgrims likely ate wild fowl. Turkey became the main dish due to its size and the lack of other suitable meat options. The cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie we know today did not appear until much later, with the first Thanksgiving lacking both. Venison, fish, and shellfish were more common at the meal. This article explores the history of Thanksgiving foods, revealing that many of our modern traditions are relatively recent developments.

A Wiltshire homeowner discovered a Roman villa in his backyard while installing electricity for a table tennis room. Luke Irwin, a rug designer, hit a mosaic layer 18 inches underground, leading to the identification of a grand villa built between AD 175 and 220. Archaeologists from Historic England and Salisbury Museum confirmed the site's national significance, uncovering well-preserved Roman artifacts including oyster shells, well, and a child's stone coffin repurposed as a flower bed. The villa, possibly belonging to a wealthy Roman family, is one of the largest ever found in Britain and offers insights into Roman and post-Roman life. The site's undisturbed state since the 5th century provides a unique opportunity for research.

British Prime Minister Theresa May announced the expulsion of 23 Russian diplomats in response to the nerve agent attack on a former Russian spy, Sergei Skripal, and his daughter in Salisbury. The UK believes the Russian government was behind the poisoning, using a Soviet-developed nerve agent called Novichok. President Donald Trump has yet to publicly weigh in on the matter, despite Secretary of State Rex Tillerson's more direct statements. US Ambassador to the UN Nikki Haley said the US stands in "absolute solidarity" with the UK and called for immediate concrete measures to address the situation. Russia denies any involvement and has dismissed the UK's accusations as "fairy tales." The expulsion of Russian diplomats is seen as a significant move, potentially degrading Russian intelligence capabilities in the UK for years to come.

A poll in Denmark shows strong support for banning male circumcision, with 74% of respondents favoring a full or partial ban. The upcoming parliamentary hearing on the practice may mark a step towards an eventual ban, with some parties, like the Red-Green Alliance and Liberal Alliance, already in favor. Despite a 2013 study by the Danish Health and Medicines Authority finding insufficient evidence to justify a ban or recommend the practice, the debate continues. Male circumcision is common among Jewish and Muslim communities and is prevalent in some countries like the United States and Canada.

President Barack Obama and Mitt Romney will resume their campaigns on Wednesday, but in different ways. Romney will hold events in Florida with prominent Republicans, while Obama will tour New Jersey with Governor Chris Christie to assess damage from Hurricane Sandy. Obama’s campaign argues that his focus on disaster response is politically beneficial, reinforcing a theme that the government plays a crucial role. Romney, meanwhile, will continue his aggressive campaign schedule. Both campaigns are balancing the demands of the presidential race with the need to show sensitivity in the wake of the storm. Obama’s response to Sandy could bolster his re-election efforts, while Romney aims to display his compassion and leadership. The campaigns are adjusting their events to stay positive and connect with voters amid the storm coverage.

President Donald Trump often uses Twitter to criticize the media, labeling it as "fake news." On Sunday, he tweeted about unfair treatment of his son Donald Jr. for meeting with a Russian lawyer, accusing the media of "distorting democracy." He also thanked Michael Caputo, a former campaign adviser with Russian ties, for defending the administration. Caputo, who advised on communications and has business links to Russia, denied discussing Russian involvement in the campaign. Despite ongoing investigations, Caputo remains loyal to Trump, denying any knowledge of collusion.

In a wide-ranging interview with Rolling Stone, Howard Stern discusses his recent divorce, plans to reduce his radio show to three days a week, and his thoughts on former sidekick Artie Lange's potential return. Stern also reveals his interviewing techniques and the impact of his show on his personal life. He expresses concern for Lange's well-being and the challenges of maintaining his show's freshness.

A group of 18 House Republicans has formally nominated President Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize, citing his efforts to denuclearize the Korean Peninsula and end the 68-year-old war between North and South Korea. In a letter to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, the lawmakers highlight Trump's administration's success in uniting the international community, including China, to impose sanctions on North Korea. The nomination comes after a landmark meeting between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korean President Moon Jae-in, where they agreed to work toward eliminating nuclear weapons from the Korean Peninsula and enter into talks with the U.S. to formally end the Korean War. Trump is set to meet with Kim at the end of May or in June, marking the first such encounter between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader in history.

" Eat Pray Love" offers a visually appealing journey of self-discovery with Julia Roberts, but falls short in delivering substantial spiritual enlightenment. The film, directed by Ryan Murphy and based on Elizabeth Gilbert's memoir, follows Liz Gilbert's quest for self-realization through food, meditation, and romance in Italy, India, and Bali. While Roberts' performance is warm and engaging, the narrative feels overly familiar and lacks the depth of Gilbert's original writing. The movie's structure is predictable, with each segment focusing on a different aspect of Gilbert's journey, but the characters and settings, though picturesque, remain somewhat superficial. Despite its shortcomings, " Eat Pray Love" may still appeal to audiences seeking a pleasant, if somewhat clichéd, exploration of personal growth.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for a special prosecutor to take over the Russia investigation, warning that the FBI Director's firing might be a cover-up. Schumer questioned the timing and reason for Comey's dismissal and expressed concerns about its impact on future FBI leadership. Republican senators, including Richard Burr and John Cornyn, also voiced disapproval, while some Democrats demanded a special committee to review the Russia allegations. The White House attributed Comey's firing to his handling of the Clinton email investigation, but critics saw it as politically motivated, comparing it to historical precedents like Watergate. The firing raised questions about the Justice Department's ability to oversee the Russia probe independently.

Special Operations Command is collaborating with industry, universities, and laboratories to develop a high-tech suit inspired by "Iron Man" for real-world combat. Dubbed TALOS, the suit aims to provide superhuman strength and enhanced protection. Key features include 360-degree night vision cameras, sensors for detecting injuries and applying wound-sealing foam, and a bulletproof exoskeleton made of magnetorheological fluids that can rapidly solidify upon impact. While the concept is promising, challenges remain, such as the need for a heavy hydraulic system or powerful batteries. The Army hopes to have a prototype by next year, with an advanced model following two years later. Despite skepticism from some, the project aims to significantly improve soldier survivability and performance in combat.

On a remote island off Western Australia, a new grave has been discovered, offering fresh insights into one of Australia's most notorious maritime tragedies. The Dutch East India Company ship Batavia, carrying 341 people, wrecked on Morning Reef in 1629. Survivors made it to Beacon Island, but a brutal mutiny ensued, resulting in the deaths of over 120 people, including women and children. This latest find, the 11th skeleton uncovered on Beacon Island since the 1960s, was discovered near two musket balls, suggesting a violent end. The skeleton, believed to be that of an adolescent, was found about 1.5 meters underground. Experts, including UWA archaeologist Professor Alistair Paterson, are excited by the discovery, which could provide new details about the mass murder. The Batavia's story, a dark chapter in Australian maritime history, continues to captivate researchers and historians.

Oakland, still celebrating its NBA championship, received a $34 million anonymous donation to benefit underserved residents through the San Francisco Foundation. The donation will fund 731 affordable housing units, create about 2,500 jobs, and support early-childhood education and African-American student achievement. Mayor Libby Schaaf thanked the "generous soul," emphasizing that government cannot do it alone. The donation, earmarked for nonprofits and specific neighborhoods, aims to address the city's housing and economic challenges, particularly in East Oakland, where rising rents are pushing out poor and lower-income residents.

About 1 million gallons of acidic mine waste turned the Animas River orange-brown, prompting the city of Durango to stop pumping raw water and close the river to public use. The EPA, working on a project to pump and treat contaminated water, accidentally triggered the discharge. The toxic plume, containing high levels of sediment and metals, flowed downstream, closing the river to recreational activities and prompting water conservation in Durango. La Plata County officials warned residents to avoid the river and conserve water. The impact on aquatic life was uncertain, with some fish potentially at risk.

A British chef who died fighting ISIS in northern Syria reportedly shot himself to avoid capture, according to Kurdish sources. Ryan Lock, 20, from Chichester, West Sussex, joined the Kurdish People’s Defence Units (YPG) militia as a volunteer after telling his family he was going on holiday to Turkey. During a battle for ISIS’s stronghold of Raqqa, Lock and four comrades were surrounded by ISIS fighters. Kurdish rights activist Mark Campbell praised Lock's "outstanding bravery" in potentially preventing a propaganda victory for ISIS. Lock's body was eventually transported to Iraq for repatriation to the UK. He became the third British man to die fighting alongside the Kurds against ISIS.

San Bernardino police are searching for a missing 22-year-old art student, Sahray Astina Barber, who was last seen early Monday morning. Her disappearance comes amid a series of violent incidents on the nearby California State University, San Bernardino campus, including an attempted kidnapping. Police have found some of Barber’s belongings scattered outside her apartment, and are questioning her ex-boyfriend and roommates. A search of the hills north of her apartment complex is ongoing. Police are concerned but have no concrete evidence linking her disappearance to the campus incidents.

Eminent economists Paul Krugman and Ben Bernanke are at odds over the Federal Reserve's approach to combating high unemployment and slow economic growth. Krugman, a Nobel laureate and New York Times columnist, argues that the Fed should aim for higher inflation to spur growth and job creation, while Bernanke, the Federal Reserve chairman, contends that such a strategy would be reckless. Bernanke believes that the Fed's commitment to low inflation helps maintain flexibility in monetary policy and supports economic recovery. Critics of Krugman's proposal warn that higher inflation could reduce purchasing power, increase saving, and lead to unpredictable financial market reactions. Despite the disagreement, the article suggests that the debate highlights the limitations of economic policy and the challenges in achieving economic recovery.

In his new book, "With Charity for All: Why Charities Are Failing and a Better Way to Give," Ken Stern critiques the American nonprofit sector, highlighting both fraudulent charities and those that, while seemingly legitimate, may not deserve their charitable status. Stern argues that obtaining nonprofit status from the IRS is overly easy, and state oversight is often weak or non-existent, making it difficult for donors to identify and avoid scams. He provides examples of non-profit hospitals and college football bowl games, suggesting that these entities may not be as charitable as they appear, and instead benefit primarily their donors. Stern emphasizes the importance for donors to be vigilant and to seek out truly effective charities through thorough research and reliable sources.

Two former bodyguards of Gisele Bundchen and Tom Brady have been jailed for five years for shooting at photographers during the couple's wedding celebrations in Costa Rica in 2009. A court found Miguel Solis and Alexander Rivas guilty of attempted murder after the bodyguards demanded camera memory cards from the photographers and one of them opened fire as the photographers drove away, though neither photographer was injured. Manuel Valverde, the third bodyguard, was acquitted. The court ordered the defendants to pay damages to the photographers.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average experienced a sudden drop of 145 points within minutes after a fake tweet from the Associated Press Twitter account claimed explosions at the White House and an injury to President Barack Obama. The tweet, which was quickly dismissed as a hack, caused the market to briefly turn negative but quickly recovered. White House Press Secretary Jay Carney confirmed the president's safety. The Associated Press suspended its Twitter account following the incident, which came after hackers attempted to steal journalists' passwords. The Syrian Electronic Army, an organization supporting Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, claimed responsibility for the attack.

A jury in White Cloud, Michigan, has found Glenna Duram, 46, guilty of first-degree murder and a felony firearm charge in the 2015 death of her husband Martin Duram. Martin was shot five times and found dead in their home in Ensley Township, while Glenna survived a bullet wound to the head. Family members claim their pet African grey parrot, Bud, seemed to replay the murder by mimicking an argument between voices. The prosecutor did not use the parrot as evidence but did not rule it out. Sentencing for Glenna Duram is set for August 28.

More than 35 people gathered in San Jose to officially file a notice of intent to recall Superior Court Judge Aaron Persky, who sentenced former Stanford swimmer Brock Turner to six months in jail for sexually assaulting an unconscious woman. The campaign, spearheaded by Stanford law professor Michele Dauber, aims to collect 58,634 valid voter signatures within 160 days to qualify the recall for the June 2018 countywide ballot. The statement filed with the county registrar of voters brands Persky as an apologist for rapists and batterers. District Attorney Jeff Rosen, a key supporter, noted the case has already had a significant impact, including the passage of a state law requiring a prison term for sexual assault of an unconscious or intoxicated person. Persky, a former Stanford athlete, faces criticism for his lenient sentence, with opponents arguing he has a history of awarding lenient sentences to athletes and upper-class defendants.
