President Obama faces criticism for his energy policies, particularly regarding gas prices, notes Charles Krauthammer. His "all-of-the-above" approach, which excludes drilling in certain areas, is seen as ideologically driven and ineffective. Obama’s veto of the Keystone pipeline and restrictive policies on drilling are highlighted as examples of his anti-oil stance. Krauthammer argues that these policies are politically motivated and ignore the reality of abundant domestic oil resources. He criticizes Obama’s focus on alternative fuels like algae, which he calls unrealistic. Krauthammer suggests that high gas prices are a political liability for Obama, serving as a reminder of his inflexible energy policy and its negative impacts.

Bayesian statistics, a method inspired by an 18th-century Presbyterian minister, can help refine the search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. By updating probabilities based on new information, such as flight path data and search results, statisticians can narrow the search area. This technique has been successfully used in previous aviation mysteries, like the Air France Flight 447 crash. However, the complexity of the Malaysia Airlines case, with new evidence suggesting a deliberate act, complicates the Bayesian calculations. Despite the challenges, Bayesian methods can provide a structured approach to adapting to new information, potentially improving the search's effectiveness.

A fossil hunter in Sussex, UK, discovered a brown pebble over a decade ago, which has now been confirmed as the first example of fossilized dinosaur brain tissue. The specimen, likely from a species related to Iguanodon, shows preserved meninges, capillaries, and parts of the cortical tissue. Found near Bexhill, this brain tissue was likely preserved due to the dinosaur's head falling into a highly acidic, low-oxygen body of water shortly after death, allowing soft tissues to mineralize before complete decay. Researchers from the University of Cambridge and the University of Western Australia used scanning electron microscopy to identify these structures. The preservation provides a rare glimpse into dinosaur brain anatomy, potentially revealing insights into their cognitive abilities. However, scientists caution against drawing definitive conclusions about dinosaur intelligence from this single specimen, emphasizing the need for further study.

Ignite Restaurant Group, the parent company of Joe’s Crab Shack, is testing a no-tipping policy at 18 of its 131 locations to address the controversy surrounding federal minimum wage policies. The policy, which raises wages for restaurant workers, is seen as a way to reduce employee turnover and avoid the "fray" of minimum wage discussions. Joe’s operates two restaurants in Orange County, but they are not part of the pilot. The test locations, spread across several states, have increased the fixed hourly rate of workers, though specific salary details are not disclosed. The company is not adding service charges to checks, though there have been small menu price increases. This move follows Danny Meyer’s announcement of eliminating tipping at all of his New York City restaurants, with price hikes to ensure fair compensation for all workers.

Susan Carland, wife of The Project host Waleed Aly, channels daily hate tweets into donations to UNICEF. As a Muslim sociologist, Carland faces constant abuse on social media, including racial slurs and accusations of being a "filthy traitor." To combat this, she donates $1 for every hateful tweet she receives, benefiting UNICEF. Carland explains her approach is rooted in her faith, which instructs her to respond with good in the face of evil. This method has not only raised over $1000 but also helped her feel more secure in her identity.

A 12-year-old student opened fire at Berrendo Middle School in Roswell, New Mexico, on Tuesday, injuring two students. The suspect, Mason Campbell, a seventh-grader, was arrested after a teacher and a school supervisor talked him into dropping his 20-gauge shotgun. One 11-year-old boy was in critical condition, while a 13-year-old girl was in satisfactory condition at a hospital in Texas. The shooter had warned several students not to come to school. School staff had participated in active shooter training and responded appropriately. A prayer vigil was held for the community.

UPMC is investigating potential links between fungal infections and the deaths of two heart transplant patients who stayed in the same cardiothoracic intensive care unit (CTICU) where mold was recently found. The patients, who had infections of rhizomucor and lichtheimia, died in October 2014 and June, respectively. Mold was discovered in the CTICU earlier this month, leading to its closure for cleaning. While the role of the mold in the patients' deaths is uncertain, the hospital has notified their families. The investigation is ongoing, and the source of the mold remains unknown.

Scientists have discovered a bizarre sea creature in Morocco that lived 480 million years ago and could grow up to seven feet long. Dubbed Aegirocassis benmoulae, this ancient arthropod is part of an extinct group known as anomalocaridids and is the largest of its kind found to date. It lived during the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event and had an elaborate net-like structure of spikes to catch plankton. The well-preserved fossils show that early arthropods had upper limb flaps for swimming, which are precursors to the double-branched limbs seen in modern arthropods. This discovery provides insights into the evolution of arthropod limbs and the rich plankton ecosystem of the time.

Auto makers aim to make 2014 the year of the connected car, partnering with tech giants like Google to bring advanced smartphone features into vehicles. Google's Open Automotive Alliance, launched at the International Consumer Electronics Show, includes automakers such as General Motors, Honda, and Audi, aiming to modernize infotainment systems and keep up with smartphone alternatives. This move challenges traditional automotive practices, as companies face pressure from the rapid evolution of mobile technology. While carmakers have developed custom software systems, partnerships with tech companies offer access to newer technology and lower costs. Cutting-edge automakers like Tesla have already embraced the computerized car concept, while new companies like CloudCar are working on devices to bridge the technology and automotive realms.

A white Texas police officer faces a murder charge in the shooting of 15-year-old Jordan Edwards, who was killed leaving an unruly house party. Former officer Roy Oliver was fired earlier in the week for violating department policies. Oliver turned himself in on Friday and was released on a $300,000 bond. The Dallas County Sheriff's Office stated the warrant was issued based on evidence suggesting Oliver intended to cause serious bodily injury. Edwards and his two brothers and two other teenagers were leaving the party when Oliver fired a rifle at their car, fatally shooting Edwards. Police initially said the car was backing up aggressively, but later body camera footage showed the vehicle driving away. The arrest and charges have renewed national discussions on police bias and overreactions. Jordan's family attorney expressed hope that this case would not be swept under the rug as in the past.

An unusual, cave-style house in Malibu listed at $3.5 million offers a unique living experience with vaulted ceilings, glass walls for ocean views, and a wine cellar. The property, situated on nearly 23 acres, was owned by the ageless television personality Dick Clark and his wife. Clark, known for hosting "American Bandstand" and other shows, sold his production company for $175 million in 2007. The house, with one bedroom and two bathrooms, combines modern amenities with a prehistoric aesthetic, attracting potential buyers with its distinctive design.

Beyoncé has revealed that Jay-Z will be a hands-on father and will change Blue Ivy's diapers, contrary to the notion that he will be a distant celebrity dad. "He will change diapers, of course he will," she told Star magazine. "He's going to be a very hands-on father and he is going to be so good at it." Despite rumors of a lavish hospital stay, Beyoncé clarified that security was tight for Blue's safety, though some details were exaggerated. Kelly Rowland is among the babysitters waiting to care for the little girl.

A Florida lawyer, Jeff Herman, has filed a lawsuit against "X-Men" director Bryan Singer and Gary Goddard, alleging sexual abuse of a teenage client. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Los Angeles, claims that Singer and Goddard, along with others, groomed and sexually assaulted the plaintiff, now 25, during a 2006 "Superman Returns" premiere in London. Photos and emails allegedly showing the plaintiff with Singer and Goddard before the alleged assault were presented at a press conference. Singer and Goddard have denied the allegations and accused Herman of using the cases to gain publicity. Herman plans to file more lawsuits and claims the incidents are part of a broader sex ring in Hollywood.

President Obama returned to the debt ceiling debate, offering no clear solution but urging citizens to contact their representatives to demand a "balanced approach." He criticized Republicans for risking economic crisis and rejected Boehner’s proposed short-term debt ceiling hike, arguing it would only delay the inevitable. Obama emphasized the need for spending cuts, defense reductions, and tax increases from the wealthy. He highlighted the origins of the deficit, blaming tax cuts, wars, and prescription drug programs. Obama’s speech aimed to appeal to independent voters, framing the issue as a center-right debate, while Boehner’s address was seen as more aligned with the right-wing base, though his plan faced significant opposition.

A 22-year-old Spanish golfer, Celia Barquín Arozamena, was found dead with multiple stab wounds on an Iowa golf course, leading to the arrest of a homeless man, Collin Daniel Richards, who faces first-degree murder charges. Barquín, a star athlete at Iowa State University and a European Ladies' Amateur champion, was finishing her civil engineering degree. Her death came just weeks after the murder of another Iowa student, Mollie Tibbetts. Richards, known to local police for past offenses, was found with scratches on his face and a laceration on his hand. He reportedly told an acquaintance of his "urge to rape and kill a woman." Barquín's teammates and university mourned her loss, with Iowa State withdrawing from a tournament to return to Ames and honor her. The European Golf Association and Spanish officials expressed shock and sadness at her passing.

A total lunar eclipse will occur on January 31, 2018, visible from Australia and western USA. This event is special as it will be a Supermoon and a Blue Moon, making it the first total eclipse of a Blue Moon in over 150 years. The Virtual Telescope Project will partner with astrophotographers in Australia and the USA to live-stream the event, starting at 11:30 UT. Additionally, a Supermoon rising above Rome will be shown later in the day, starting at 16:00 UT. The eclipse will be visible in the evening for western parts of the world, while eastern regions will see it during sunset. For North America, the total phase begins at 4:51 a.m. PST, with the duration of the total phase being 77 minutes. The next total eclipse of a Blue Moon will occur on December 31, 2028.

A high school teacher in Visalia, California, has been arrested after video surfaced showing her forcibly cutting a student's hair in class. Margaret Gieszinger, a 52-year-old chemistry teacher, allegedly declared it was "haircut day" and began cutting a student's hair while singing the "Star Spangled Banner." The student ran to the main office for help, but Gieszinger chased after him with scissors. Other students intervened, and Gieszinger stopped teaching for the day. She was arrested on suspicion of felony child endangerment and faces a $100,000 bail. The Tulare County Office of Education is investigating the incident and has sent counselors to support affected students.

Florida's coral reefs are facing a severe multi-year disease outbreak, affecting numerous species across a large portion of the Florida Reef Tract. The disease, which began in fall 2014 near Key Biscayne, has spread north to St. Lucie Inlet and south to Looe Key in the Florida Keys. Efforts to combat the disease include documenting its distribution, identifying pathogens, understanding environmental factors, and experimenting with treatments. Despite ongoing challenges, raising healthy corals in labs and transplanting them onto reefs is seen as a critical strategy to help recovery.

Yahoo, once a dominant player in the internet landscape, is being sold to Verizon for $4.8 billion, marking the end of its independent run. The deal, which includes Yahoo's core web assets but excludes its stakes in Alibaba and Yahoo Japan, will see Verizon combine Yahoo with AOL, the company Verizon acquired in 2015. Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer, who has faced criticism for her tenure, will leave the company with a significant severance package. Verizon sees the acquisition as a way to strengthen its position in mobile media and digital advertising, potentially challenging the dominance of Google and Facebook. The combined entity aims to leverage Yahoo's large user base and AOL's advertising technology to boost Verizon's revenue streams.

Lady Gaga performed her Oscar-nominated song "Til It Happens To You" at the 2016 Academy Awards, a poignant moment that highlighted her personal journey as a survivor of sexual abuse. The performance, which featured several rape survivors writing messages of resilience on their arms, was a powerful statement against sexual assault. Surprisingly, some family members, including her grandmother and aunt, were unaware of her past until after the performance. Gaga, who first revealed her abuse in a 2014 Howard Stern interview, expressed deep gratitude to the survivors who stood with her on stage, stating that their bravery lifted a weight off her shoulders and allowed her to no longer hide. She also celebrated her fiancé, Taylor Kinney, for his unwavering support.

While much attention has been paid to the fiscal cliff and federal legislation, thousands of new state laws took effect quietly at the start of 2013. California hunters can no longer use dogs to chase bears or bobcats, and New Yorkers face a $1,000 fine for selling even electronic cigarettes to minors. Illinois banned motorcycle wheelies, while North Carolina made stealing unused cooking oil a felony. Massachusetts outlawed plastic bottles, and Kentucky prohibited the release of wild pigs into the wild. California and Illinois banned shark fin soup, and Illinois required strip clubs to charge $3 and donate proceeds to charity. These laws, ranging from the ridiculous to the serious, reflect public concerns and legislative efforts across the states.

Ontario has a new premier, Doug Ford, the brother of former Toronto Mayor Rob Ford. Ford's Progressive Conservatives won a majority government, defeating the Liberals after 15 years in power. Ford, a populist with ties to his controversial brother, capitalized on a desire for change and promised tax cuts and reduced government spending. Despite some organizational chaos and last-minute headlines, his campaign was effective. The election results reflect a shift in Ontario politics, with the NDP making gains and the Liberals suffering significant losses. Ford's victory was seen as an "ideal candidate" to win the election, leveraging his brother's legacy and appealing to small-c conservative voters.

Rachel Uchitel, famous for her affair with Tiger Woods and subsequent $10 million settlement, is expecting her first child with her current husband, Matt Hahn, 26. The couple, who got married in Nevada in October after dating for several months, is eagerly anticipating the arrival of their baby. Uchitel, 36, shared a photo of Hahn touching her growing belly, tweeting, "Expecting big things for 2012... Five down, Four months to go."

A beef recall involving over 6.5 million pounds of products due to possible salmonella contamination has been issued by JBS Tolleson, Inc. The products, including ground beef and beef patties, were packaged between July 26 and September 7 and distributed nationwide. Health officials have linked 57 cases of salmonella illness in 16 states to these products. Consumers are advised to check for the "EST.267" mark and discard or return any affected items. Symptoms of salmonellosis include diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and fever.

Danish radio station Radio24syv sparked controversy by killing a baby rabbit on air to highlight the hypocrisy of those who claim to be animal lovers but eat meat. Host Asger Juhl hit the rabbit with a bicycle pump and later prepared and ate it with his family. The station defended the stunt, arguing it exposed the everyday reality of meat consumption. However, the act drew widespread criticism, including death threats, and was compared to the controversial killing of a giraffe at the Copenhagen Zoo. While Juhl justified the method as humane, others found it disturbing, highlighting the complex ethical issues surrounding meat consumption.

A version of Edvard Munch's "The Scream," one of the most iconic images in art history, sold for $119,922,500 at Sotheby's, breaking the record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction. The 1895 pastel on board, the only version still in private hands, was sold to a telephone bidder. Munch created four versions of "The Scream," with the other three now in Norwegian museums. The painting, depicting a man screaming under a blood-red sky, has become a symbol of human anxiety and has been widely reproduced in popular culture. The previous record holder was Picasso's "Nude, Green Leaves, and Bust," which sold for $106.5 million in 2010. Proceeds from the sale will fund a new museum, art center, and hotel in Hvitsten, Norway.

Anonymous author "O: A Presidential Novel" set during the 2012 election buzzes with speculation over its identity. Publisher Simon & Schuster hints at the author's close ties to Barack Obama, fueling theories ranging from Joe Klein to Rahm Emanuel. Politico's Ben Smith leads a hunt, gathering denials from potential suspects. The book, a mix of fact and fiction, offers a fast-paced campaign narrative, though its anonymity adds intrigue. Speculation centers on the author's possible roles, from political reporter to press staffer, with clues pointing to specific individuals and events.

US senators demand that Pakistan pardon a surgeon sentenced to 33 years in prison for helping in the hunt for Osama bin Laden, warning that the decision could jeopardize US assistance. The tribal court in Khyber sentenced Shakeel Afridi for treason after he agreed to collect DNA for US intelligence to verify bin Laden's presence. Senators Carl Levin and John McCain called Afridi's sentence "shocking and outrageous," urging Pakistan to pardon and free him immediately. The United States has provided Pakistan with over $18 billion since joining the war in Afghanistan, but US officials have long worried about support for extremists within Pakistan's establishment. The US is also pushing Pakistan to re-open supply routes to NATO forces in Afghanistan, which were closed after a NATO air raid killed 26 Pakistani troops. Tensions between the US and Pakistan have risen over a range of issues, including US drone strikes, which are seen as violations of sovereignty.

Ukraine's President Petro Poroshenko canceled a planned visit to Turkey due to escalating tensions in the Donetsk region, where Russian troops are reportedly involved. Poroshenko called for an urgent UN Security Council meeting and an emergency EU Council session. Meanwhile, rebels have taken control of Novoazovsk, a town crucial for connecting Russia to Crimea, raising concerns about a new front in the conflict. Russian-backed separatists claim to have 3,000-4,000 Russian citizens fighting alongside them. Ukraine reports withdrawing its forces from Novoazovsk to reinforce defenses in Mariupol. The OSCE is convening a special meeting to address the situation.

An anonymous person dropped a coin worth $1,200 into a Salvation Army red kettle during a local fundraiser at a Tega Cay Wal-Mart. The coin was appraised at a local Brownlee Jewelers store and will likely be sold, with all proceeds going to the Salvation Army.

The U.S. Air Force is promoting the slogan "Loose Tweets Destroy Fleets" to remind military personnel about the risks of sharing sensitive information on social media. This modern twist on the World War II slogan "Loose Lips Sink Ships" aims to highlight the potential dangers of posting details about military operations and personal information that could be exploited by adversaries like ISIS sympathizers. The Air Force emphasizes the importance of maintaining operational security (OPSEC) by using appropriate privacy settings, checking with supervisors before posting work-related content, and being cautious about what is shared online. Recent threats from a group calling itself the "Islamic State Hacking Division" have underscored the need for heightened awareness.

German police believe an iron gate stolen in 2014 from the Dachau concentration camp has been found in Norway. After receiving an anonymous tip, Norwegian police discovered a gate with the Nazi slogan "Arbeit Macht Frei" ("Work sets you free"). Bavarian police say it is "highly likely" to be the stolen gate. More than 40,000 people were murdered at Dachau, which opened in 1933 and was liberated by US troops in 1945. The original gate was stolen in 2014, sparking outrage, with German Chancellor Angela Merkel calling it "appalling."

A hammer-wielding man attempted to steal a Magna Carta from Salisbury Cathedral, setting off alarms when he tried to break through the glass box protecting the document. The suspect, a 45-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of attempted theft, criminal damage, and possession of an offensive weapon after being wrestled to the ground by staff. The incident occurred just before Evensong near closing time at the visitor centre. The Magna Carta, considered one of Britain's most influential legal manuscripts, is claimed to be the best preserved of four original copies. The document was removed for safekeeping, and a facsimile copy will be displayed while the case is refurbished. No one was injured, and the original Magna Carta remained undamaged.

Minnie Driver, now 42, reflects on her career and personal life in a hotel room in West Hollywood. Despite being once hailed as Hollywood's "hottest young thing," she has never fully achieved leading-lady status. Her latest film, Hunky Dory, a small British indie, showcases her strong performance and Welsh accent but faces budget constraints. Driver discusses her past, including the negative press surrounding her, and her unconventional upbringing as one of two children born out of an affair. She reveals that her son, Henry, was fathered by a writer on her TV show The Riches, whom she now feels comfortable disclosing. Driver expresses a desire to return to the small screen and work with directors like Danny Boyle and Martin Scorsese, while also enjoying her role as a mother.

Ted Cruz criticizes the Drudge Report for its recent coverage, accusing it of becoming a propaganda site for Donald Trump's campaign. Cruz claims Drudge now focuses almost exclusively on attacking him, posting old articles and ignoring election results when Cruz wins. Drudge responds by linking to positive comments Cruz made about the site in the past and articles defending Colorado's delegate selection process. The dispute highlights the growing influence of conservative media in shaping the Republican race narrative.

An 8-year-old girl testified in court against her mother, Jessica Dutro, during her murder trial for the death of her 4-year-old brother, Zachary Dutro-Boggess, in 2012. The girl recounted how her mother and her 24-year-old boyfriend, Brian Canady, would beat the children, including Zachary, for misbehaving. Zachary was taken to a hospital with severe injuries, but he died two days later. Canady pleaded guilty to manslaughter. Prosecutors argue that Dutro feared Zachary was gay, which motivated the abuse. Evidence includes a Facebook message from Dutro to Canady detailing the abuse and her fears. The girl and her surviving siblings now live with relatives.

In "The Other Guys," Will Ferrell and Mark Wahlberg star as desk-jockey detectives who get their moment to shine in a buddy police comedy. Directed by Adam McKay, the film features a mild-mannered forensic accountant, Allen Gamble, and his reluctant partner, Terry Hoitz, who must prove their mettle when a major case arises. Their incompetence becomes the stuff of legend, providing plenty of laughs through a mix of verbal sparring and broad slapstick. Supporting actors Dwayne Johnson and Samuel L. Jackson add to the chaos, while the film's nonsensical zone of verbal riffing and slapstick humor delivers some good laughs.

An Egyptian court has sentenced a little-known singer, Shaimaa Ahmed, to two years in prison for "inciting debauchery" after a music video featuring her suggestively eating a banana was deemed too sexually explicit. Ahmed, known professionally as Shyma, was arrested last month and found guilty along with the video's director, who was sentenced to two years in absentia. The video, titled "I Have Issues," showed Ahmed dancing in underwear and making suggestive gestures. Ahmed expressed surprise at the backlash, stating she did not intend for the video to be interpreted in an inappropriate manner. This case follows similar incidents where other female singers have faced charges for provocative content, highlighting ongoing issues with freedom of expression and censorship in Egypt.

A 61-year-old New Hampshire woman found herself stuck in her backyard pool after the ladder broke, unable to climb out and with no one else home. She posted a "911" message on a community Facebook page, and within minutes, neighbors arrived to help. Despite trying various methods, they couldn't fix the ladder or safely retrieve her. Finally, using a step ladder, she managed to climb out. The incident highlighted the positive impact of social media in emergencies and the community's willingness to assist.

Citigroup faces approval hurdles for a shareholder payout after failing U.S. stress tests, while other banks like JPMorgan and Wells Fargo received green lights. Citigroup CEO Vikram Pandit aims to return capital to shareholders but the Federal Reserve objected to its plan, citing a capital ratio below the minimum requirement. The stress tests, which simulate severe economic conditions, revealed that Citigroup and others may need to adjust their capital actions to meet regulatory standards. Citigroup shares fell 3.2% following the news, while JPMorgan and Wells Fargo saw minor fluctuations. The tests also affected Ally Financial and SunTrust Banks, both of which will resubmit plans. The results highlight ongoing challenges for banks in managing capital and meeting regulatory expectations post-crisis.

New Jersey Democrats will decide today who will be their nominee for the U.S. Senate, with Cory Booker, the 44-year-old Newark mayor, leading in the primary. Booker won the Democratic primary easily, taking 59% of the vote against two U.S. congressmen and the speaker of the New Jersey State Assembly. His opponent in the October general election will be Republican Steve Lonegan, a former mayor of Bogota, N.J. Despite criticisms from some progressive Democrats that Booker is too aligned with Wall Street and Silicon Valley, his poll numbers remain high. Booker's supporters argue that his pragmatic approach and record in Newark make him a valuable advocate. His opponents see him as an elite politician who may not prioritize the needs of the working class. Regardless, Booker is likely to win the general election and become the fourth African American U.S. senator.

Colin Kaepernick's decision to kneel during the national anthem has sparked a broader movement, with Seattle Seahawks players considering joining the protest. Cornerback Jeremy Lane has already sat during the anthem, and linebacker Bobby Wagner and receiver Doug Baldwin may follow suit. The Seahawks organization and coaches will not dictate what the players do, allowing them to make their own decisions. Coach Pete Carroll supports Lane's action, stating it is up to him to handle the responsibility. The team's approach emphasizes unity over individual actions, with players expressing the importance of coming together rather than acting alone. The Seahawks face the Miami Dolphins in their opener on September 11, potentially drawing attention to their stance.

The retired King of Belgium, Albert II, 84, faces a DNA paternity test order from a Brussels court regarding his alleged daughter, Delphine Boël, 50. Boël seeks to prove Albert as her father, challenging an earlier test that ruled out Jacques Boël, a wealthy industrialist. Albert abdicated in 2013, losing his legal immunity. The test, if not completed within three months, could legally presume Albert as Boël's father. Boël's lawyers are pleased with the court's affirmation of the "child's best interests" principle.

Democratic Senator Jon Tester won Montana's U.S. Senate race against Republican Representative Denny Rehberg, emphasizing the need for Congress to address pressing issues like the federal deficit, taxes, and economic challenges. Tester, a farmer from Big Sandy, led Rehberg by 16,000 votes, with some counties still counting ballots. Rehberg, a rancher from Billings, conceded the race, praising Tester and acknowledging their shared love for Montana and America. Tester called for transparency in political spending, criticizing the influence of outside money in elections. The race was the most expensive in Montana history, with significant spending from both candidates and outside groups.

Pro-independence candidate Tsai Ing-wen won Taiwan's presidential election, taking a commanding lead over the ruling KMT party's Eric Chu, who conceded defeat. Tsai, leading the Democratic Progressive Party, is poised to become Taiwan's first female president, marking a significant shift in the island's political landscape. With about 60% of votes counted, Tsai's victory introduces new uncertainty in the complex relationship between Taiwan and mainland China, which claims the island as its own territory. Tsai has promised to maintain the status quo in relations with China, emphasizing mutual respect and cooperation. Chu's defeat signals the end of the KMT's nearly 70-year monopoly on power, with the party losing its majority in the legislature for the first time. The election results reflect growing concerns among Taiwanese voters about economic dependence on China and the preservation of Taiwan's sovereignty and democracy.

The driver of a Spanish train that derailed, killing at least 80 people, is under police guard in hospital, facing investigation for excessive speed. The eight-carriage train derailed, hit a wall, and caught fire near Santiago de Compostela, a pilgrimage destination. The crash, one of Europe's worst rail disasters, occurred on the eve of St. James' feast day, leading to the cancellation of local festivities. The driver, Francisco Jose Garzon, who had 30 years of experience, was reportedly traveling at 190 km/h (120 mph) in a 80 km/h (50 mph) zone, though Renfe stated the train had undergone a routine inspection that morning. Garzon, who had previously boasted about speeding on social media, is not under arrest but is being formally investigated. The accident left 95 people hospitalized, with 32 in critical condition. A 22-year-old Disneyland employee has been arrested in connection with a dry ice bomb explosion in the park's Toontown section, authorities said Wednesday. Christian Barnes, who worked as an outdoor vendor, was booked on suspicion of possession of a destructive device and is being held on $1 million bail. The explosion, which occurred in a trash can, forced the evacuation of Toontown but caused no injuries. Anaheim police believe Barnes placed dry ice in a plastic bottle to create the explosion. Disneyland is working closely with authorities, and Barnes claims it was an isolated incident.

King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia warns that extremist groups could attack Europe and the U.S. if there is not a strong international response to terrorism in Iraq and Syria. The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) has seized a wide territory across both countries, prompting concerns that the group could spread its influence further. Saudi Arabia, a U.S. ally, has taken an increasingly active role in criticizing ISIS and has tightened restrictions on its citizens who fight in Syria and Iraq. The U.S. is considering expanding its military campaign against ISIS to include Syria, where it has ordered surveillance flights. Meanwhile, a suicide bomber in Iraq killed 11 people, including four soldiers, at an army checkpoint, and a video of the beheading of a Lebanese soldier captured by ISIS was posted online.

Cell phones in Broadway theaters have become a persistent issue, with incidents ranging from a young man plugging his phone into a fake outlet during a performance of "Hand to God" to Patti LuPone snatching a phone from a texting audience member during "Shows for Days." The behavior highlights a growing divide between traditional theater etiquette and the increasing use of mobile devices, particularly among younger audiences. Producers and performers are increasingly frustrated, with LuPone even suggesting she might stop performing due to the disruption. The incidents, while amusing to some, underscore the challenge of maintaining a distraction-free environment in the digital age.

TEXAS CITY — Four pit bulls attacked and killed a 10-year-old beagle in October, leading the dogs' owner to sue the beagle's family for up to $1 million in damages. The incident occurred when the pit bull owner entered the Baker family's backyard to retrieve her dogs, which had entered through a hole in the shared fence. The lawsuit claims the pit bull owner suffered "serious injuries" and ongoing medical treatment. However, the dog's owner, Steve Baker, said he decided not to sue, stating that justice had already been served through the city declaring the dogs dangerous and raising awareness. The dangerous dog ordinance requires owners to secure their dogs in an at least 6-foot-high enclosure with a mechanical locking device and to post signs and maintain $100,000 liability insurance.

A detective testified at a preliminary hearing for 18 Penn State fraternity brothers accused in the hazing death of Timothy Piazza, describing surveillance video showing Piazza looking like a corpse after a pledge event involving heavy drinking. The video, shot at the Beta Theta Pi fraternity house, depicted Piazza's injuries and his being left alone, with fraternity members eventually finding him unconscious and carrying him upstairs. Piazza, a 19-year-old from New Jersey, died from a traumatic brain injury and severe abdominal bleeding two days after the incident. The fraternity chapter faces various charges, including involuntary manslaughter and felony aggravated assault. Penn State has permanently banned the fraternity due to a pattern of excessive drinking, drug use, and hazing.

Residents of the Big Island of Hawaii faced a tense Friday as a magnitude 6.9 earthquake jolted their homes, adding to the ongoing threats from a volcanic eruption that shows no signs of slowing. Multiple new volcanic vents opened, with at least one home and another structure destroyed by lava. Civil Defense Administrator Talmadge Magno reported that the activity continues and does not appear to be slowing down. Hundreds of people were evacuated from Leilani Estates and Lanipuna Gardens, with some allowed to briefly return to collect belongings. The eruption has caused widespread concern, particularly due to high levels of sulfur dioxide, which can be dangerous for the elderly and those with respiratory issues. The Hawaii National Guard was called in to assist with evacuations and security. The situation remains volatile, with residents urged to stay alert and prepared for potential further developments.

Hailey Glassman insists she's not back on the market despite Jon Gosselin's recent tweets suggesting otherwise. Glassman tweeted, "Yes, I am semi-single, but definitely NOT YET ready to mingle," and that she needs "Hailey time and regroup myself and my life." Meanwhile, Gosselin has been busy apologizing and seeking forgiveness, tweeting, "Going home to see my kids,-excited, but i'll miss Hailey," and thanking her for helping him reform. Gosselin also claimed he and Glassman aren't splitting up but slowing things down to avoid making the same mistakes with her that he did with his ex-wife, Kate. A source close to Gosselin says Hailey's recent TV appearance was staged to attract attention for a potential reality show, while Gosselin was actually considering a deal with Octomom, Nadya Suleman.

No winning tickets were drawn for the growing Mega Millions jackpot, pushing the estimated prize to $502 million for the next drawing on Friday. The winning numbers from Tuesday's drawing were 7, 25, 43, 56, 59, and the Mega Ball 13. This is the fourth time in the game's history that the jackpot has surpassed $500 million. The next drawing will be on Friday, March 30. The estimated jackpot is the fourth-largest payout in Mega Millions' 16-year history. Mega Millions can be played in 44 U.S. states, Washington, D.C., and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Since the last winning jackpot on January 5, there have been 33 winners of $1 million or more.

A U.S. Senate candidate's Super Bowl ad portraying a young Asian woman speaking broken English has sparked controversy and accusations of racial insensitivity. Michigan Republican Pete Hoekstra's ad, which features the woman riding a bike near rice paddies and thanking "Debbie Spenditnow" for spending too much American money, is facing criticism from Asian-American groups and political opponents. Hoekstra's campaign spokesman argues the ad is satirical and meant to highlight Democratic overspending. The ad is part of a broader campaign strategy targeting Michigan's economic concerns, particularly job losses to China. Democratic Senator Debbie Stabenow and her allies are using the ad to raise funds and criticize Hoekstra's record. Hoekstra defends the ad, stating it is fact-checked and factually accurate, but faces growing criticism from even some Republicans.

The vampire genre has become increasingly popular, and Daybreakers, set in a future where vampires have taken over the world, offers a fresh take with its corporate setting and blood substitute plot. Critics find the film's visual flair and clever ideas appealing, though the plot eventually becomes predictable. Ethan Hawke plays a vampire hematologist working to create a blood substitute for a corporate boss, while encountering a human resistance led by Willem Dafoe. The movie balances black comedy with horror elements but struggles with a lack of action in its latter half. While inventive, the film's familiar world and apocalyptic chase elements may leave audiences feeling unsatisfied.

A mother's request for a specific shirt for her autistic daughter went viral, garnering over 22,000 shares. Deborah Skouson of St. George needed a pink flowered top from Target for her 10-year-old daughter Cami, who has been fixated on this shirt for five years. The original shirt had become unwearable, and Skouson couldn't find duplicates, even on eBay. She posted a plea on Facebook, asking for someone to sell her the exact shirt, offering to pay for shipping. The post quickly spread, and Skouson received or was promised over 135 shirts from all over the world. "It’s been very, very touching," Skouson told 2News, expressing her gratitude for the overwhelming support.

Danish inventor Peter Madsen has been sentenced to life in prison for the premeditated murder and sexual assault of Swedish journalist Kim Wall on his private submarine. Judge Anette Burkoe and two jurors found Madsen guilty of premeditated murder, aggravated sexual assault, and desecrating a corpse. Madsen, 47, had denied murder and claimed Wall died accidentally inside the submarine, but he confessed to cutting up her body and throwing the parts into the sea. The court believed the prosecution's theory that Madsen had sexually tortured Wall to fulfill a violent sexual fantasy, as evidenced by tools and text messages found on his computer. Wall, 30, was last seen on August 10, 2017, during a two-hour trip on Madsen's submarine. Her mutilated remains were found in the waters near Copenhagen over the next several weeks. A CTA bus jumped a curb during rush hour on Michigan Avenue, killing one woman and injuring eight others, including the bus driver, during a Tuesday evening crash. The bus, an articulated Route 148 Clarendon/Michigan Express, struck two pedestrians and four cars before jumping the curb and landing on the sidewalk. Aimee Coath, 51, was trapped under the bus and later pronounced dead at Northwestern Memorial Hospital. The bus driver, 48, suffered minor injuries and was also hospitalized. At least 10 ambulances responded to the scene. The bus driver was cited for not stopping at a red light and "failure to exercise due care." Police are continuing to investigate the cause of the crash, and CTA officials are reviewing footage from the bus. Parts of Michigan Avenue and Lake Street were closed for several hours, and the CTA rerouted several buses around the crash site.

Two people and two dogs are traveling the country in a 98-square-foot utility trailer, part of the tiny house movement. Kelly Tousley and Curtiss O’Rorke Stedman left their home in Juneau, Alaska, to hit the road for a year, pulling the trailer with a truck for a yearlong trip through Alaska and the Lower 48. The trailer, costing $8,600, has vinyl hardwood floors and a queen-sized bed that folds out from a bench. It runs on solar power and has a small kitchenette and a bathroom separated by a curtain. Curtiss, a high school English teacher and musician, and Kelly, who worked with autistic kids, decided to quit their jobs and travel indefinitely. They faced mixed reactions from friends and family but are embracing the downsizing and do-it-yourself approach to home ownership.

Rescue efforts continue in Turkey after a 7.2-magnitude earthquake hit the eastern Van region, killing at least 265 people and injuring 1,140. Nearly 1,000 buildings were destroyed, with the town of Ercis hit hardest. Survivors were pulled from rubble, including one man who called for help via mobile phone. Rescue teams and heavy machinery are working to free trapped individuals, but the death toll is expected to rise. In Ercis, thousands slept outdoors in freezing temperatures. Deputy Prime Minister Besir Atalay reported that 970 buildings collapsed, and tents and food were being distributed. Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan emphasized the vulnerability of mud-brick buildings in outlying areas. The earthquake, centered 16 km northeast of Van, triggered about 200 aftershocks, including one of magnitude 6.0. Turkey, located on major fault lines, has experienced significant quakes

Funny or Die has launched a dedicated channel for 2012 presidential election coverage, featuring impersonations of the candidates. Comedians like Mike Tyson as Herman Cain, Darrell Hammond as Rick Perry, and Reggie Brown as President Obama, deliver humorous messages directly to the internet. The platform uses comedy to engage with the online audience, highlighting the candidates' unique traits and generating light-hearted content.

A former Stanford University swimmer, Brock Turner, sentenced to six months in jail and three years of probation for sexually assaulting an unconscious woman, is set to be released three months early on September 2. Turner's sentence, which sparked outrage for perceived leniency, will see him serve just three months before release due to good behavior. His early release is due to the county jail policy of allowing inmates to serve 50% of their sentences if they maintain a clean disciplinary record. Turner blamed his actions on Stanford's "party culture" and expressed that he felt his life was ruined by "20 minutes of action." His father also defended the leniency, stating it was a "steep price" for Turner's actions.

Swedish chemistry professor Charlotta Turner received a distressing text message from her student Firas Jumaah in 2014, who was in Iraq and feared for his family's safety amidst the ISIS threat. Jumaah's wife and children were in the next-door village when ISIS took over, killing men and enslaving women. Turner, deeply concerned, contacted the university's security chief, Per Gustafson, who orchestrated a daring rescue. Four heavily-armed mercenaries in Landcruisers rescued Jumaah and his family from a disused bleach factory, bringing them to safety in Erbil Airport. Jumaah completed his PhD in Sweden and now works for a pharmaceutical company in Malmö, while the family has repaid the university for the rescue operation. This unique event highlights the university's willingness to intervene in life-threatening situations to protect its students.

Warner Bros. plans to produce 10 DC Comics movies between 2016 and 2020, aiming to rival Marvel's success but potentially over-saturating the market. The studio's strategy includes solo films for Wonder Woman, The Flash, Aquaman, Shazam, and Cyborg, along with Justice League sequels and a Suicide Squad movie. While Marvel's superheroes often feature humor, Warner's characters tend to be more serious. The upcoming glut of movies could hasten the superhero genre's decline, as box office numbers for recent superhero films have shown a downward trend. Critics argue that the saturation might be short-sighted, suggesting that the superhero era may not last indefinitely.

Netflix is partnering with Leonardo DiCaprio to release the documentary "Virunga," which focuses on park rangers protecting endangered mountain gorillas in Virunga National Park, Democratic Republic of Congo. The film, directed by Orlando von Einsiedel, will debut in select theaters and on Netflix on November 7. DiCaprio serves as executive producer, and Ted Sarandos, Netflix's chief content officer, emphasizes the film's potential to engage global audiences. This collaboration highlights Netflix's growing presence in the film distribution landscape, potentially intensifying the conflict with theater owners.

Former Secretary of State Colin Powell, a retired four-star general and Republican, criticized Donald Trump as a "national disgrace" and "international pariah" in leaked personal emails, according to Buzzfeed News. Powell also dismissed Trump's overtures to African-American voters and slammed the repeated investigations into the 2012 Benghazi attack as a "witch hunt." The emails, obtained by DCLeaks.com, a site believed to have ties to Russian intelligence, also reveal Powell’s reluctance to endorse Hillary Clinton for the presidency, despite previous support for Barack Obama.

Michael Lohan, 49, has proposed to Kate Major, 27, whom he describes as a "friendship" of five years. Lohan, who is encouraging his daughter Lindsay to enter rehab, says he waited for the "situation with Lindsay to resolve" before asking Major. They plan to have children together, and Major, who is already planning the wedding, tells UsMagazine.com she is "really happy." The couple plans to get married later this year at Oheka Castle in New York, and Major says the ring is "gorgeous."

Netflix's "House of Cards" is ending with its sixth and final season, the streaming giant confirmed less than 24 hours after actor Anthony Rapp accused Kevin Spacey of sexual misconduct. The decision to conclude the series was made months ago and was not in response to the allegations, according to Netflix. Production on the final season began earlier this month, despite Netflix not officially confirming a sixth season order. The show's co-showrunners previously hinted at an end date, noting a significant creative pivot at the conclusion of Season 5. House of Cards will premiere in 2018.

Secretary of State John Kerry said on Sunday that the separatists in Ukraine are likely responsible for the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 and may have received help from Russian forces. Kerry stated that new intelligence indicates that a convoy of military equipment, including rocket launchers and artillery, crossed the Russian border into Eastern Ukraine and was turned over to separatists within the last month. He also mentioned evidence of separatists receiving training from Russians and tampering with the crash site. Kerry emphasized the need for full access to the crash site and expressed concern that the investigation has been "seriously compromised." Kerry also discussed the ongoing conflict in Gaza, where Israel is conducting a military operation against Hamas. Kerry criticized Israel's limited scope assurances and expressed frustration, suggesting a need to go to the region immediately.

The United Nations food agency, the World Food Programme (WFP), is pushing for immediate access to Myanmar’s troubled northern Rakhine state amid accusations that a critical report revealing desperate hunger among the persecuted Rohingya population was shelved. A July assessment by the WFP warning that over 80,000 children under five in majority-Muslim areas were "wasting," a potentially fatal condition, was removed from public view at the request of the Burmese government. The six-page document was replaced with a statement saying Myanmar and WFP were "collaborating on a revised version," and the report should not be cited. Despite this, WFP’s executive director, David Beasley, directed that the original report be republished. The revelation adds to criticisms that the UN did not push hard enough for the rights of 1.1 million Rohingya in Myanmar. The WFP’s in-country team was reportedly nervous about the report’s attention due to concerns that it might cause harm and damage

Orange County Sheriff Sandra Hutchens announced five arrests Wednesday in connection with the escape of three inmates from the Orange County Central Men's Jail. The inmates—Hossein Nayeri, 37, Jonathan Tieu, 20, and Bac Duong, 43—were awaiting trial for violent crimes. Hutchens believes the five arrested are part of a larger group that helped in the escape and more arrests are expected. The inmates escaped Friday by cutting through steel bars, squeezing through plumbing ducts, and rappelling off the roof. Hutchens described the escape as "every sheriff's nightmare" and said it took 16 hours before the inmates were noticed missing. Changes have been made to jail head count policies to prevent future escapes. A $200,000 reward has been offered for information leading to the inmates' arrests.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, chairwoman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, says there is no evidence of terrorism related to the missing Malaysia Airlines flight, which disappeared en route to Beijing over three weeks ago. "So far, there's been none," she told CNN's Candy Crowley on "State of the Union." The search, involving many nations, has turned up only minor clues, making it a difficult mission, Feinstein noted. She was hesitant to speculate on the fate of the airliner or the search's difficulties. Russia's ambassador to the United States, Sergey Kislyak, stated that Russia will not leave Crimea, asserting it is now part of the Russian Federation. He rebuffed questions about a potential Russian excursion into Ukraine, emphasizing that Russian forces are conducting exercises within their own territory. Kislyak also pushed back against President Obama's characterization of Russia as a "regional power acting out of weakness," highlighting Russia's importance in the global region from Europe to Asia.

Freedom Industries Inc., facing legal challenges and investigations following a coal-cleaning chemical spill, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January. The company's assets and liabilities range from $1 million to $10 million, with at least 200 creditors and $3.66 million owed to top creditors. The leak, which contaminated the state's largest water system, is believed to have been caused by a hole in the storage tank possibly due to freezing ground from a nearby water line break. Residents were initially told to use water only for flushing toilets, with some businesses and schools closing for several days. The storage tank had not been inspected by state officials since 2001, when it was owned by a different company.

Loch Ness, Scotland, experiences subtle tidal movements influenced by the North Sea, with the ground beneath the lake shifting as the tide comes in, creating a wobbly effect similar to a carpenter's level. Researchers from the National Oceanography Centre in the UK and the University of Porto, Portugal, used pressure sensors to measure depth changes in the 35 km (22 mi) long loch with an accuracy of 0.1 mm (0.004 in). These measurements reveal that the loch's depth varies by up to 1.5 mm (0.06 in) at its different ends due to the tidal loading from the North Sea, demonstrating Loch Ness as one of the world's most accurate tiltmeters.

Former National Security Adviser Susan Rice requested the identities of U.S. persons in raw intelligence reports related to the Trump transition and campaign, according to U.S. officials. These requests were part of a broader review of the "unmasking" policy by the National Security Council. The identities of Trump officials, when unmasked, were disseminated to key officials including Rice’s deputy, Ben Rhodes, and others at the National Security Council, Defense Department, and intelligence agencies. This practice, while legal, has raised concerns among civil libertarians and sparked investigations by the House and Senate intelligence committees. House Intelligence Committee Chairman Devin Nunes has been criticized for viewing classified documents at the White House, while Democrats have remained silent on the issue. The revelation adds a new dimension to the ongoing scrutiny of the Obama administration’s surveillance practices and their potential political motivations.

President Obama, in his final address to the United Nations General Assembly, called for a "course correction" in globalization to ensure that nations and their peoples do not retreat into a more sharply divided world. He warned against the forces of globalization exposing "deep fault lines" and urged nations to work together to address the refugee crisis, terrorism, and breakdown in basic order in the Middle East. Obama also criticized Russia for attempting to recover "lost glory" through force, and highlighted the benefits of free markets over markets resisting globalization. He emphasized the need for democracies to speak out forcefully for freedom and dignity, and acknowledged the growing gap between the rich and poor, arguing that policies such as expanding labor unions and increasing education would help address these disparities. Obama defended his administration's achievements, including normalizing relations with Cuba, reaching a nuclear agreement with Iran, and agreeing with nations on goals to reduce emissions and fight climate change. While live streaming herself playing League of Legends, Twitch user AnaPlaying accidentally set her hair on fire after casually playing with a lighter. She didn't notice for a few seconds, but quickly put out the flames and laughed it off, appearing unharmed. The incident highlights the unpredictable nature of life, much like a video game.

Justice Anthony Kennedy’s retirement, coming after the contentious process following Justice Antonin Scalia’s death, highlights the broken process for selecting Supreme Court justices. Senate Republicans blocked President Obama’s nominee, Merrick Garland, in 2016, leading Democrats to filibuster Neil Gorsuch. This tit-for-tat has resulted in a process where the minority party holds no power over Supreme Court picks, and seats often remain unfilled. The stakes are high, with terms potentially lasting 40 years, leading to extreme candidates and unpredictable confirmation battles. To de-escalate these fights, some suggest limiting terms to 10 years, making the process more predictable and less partisan.

On a Tuesday morning in Doral, Florida, McDonald’s drive-thru cashier Pedro Viloria jumped through the ordering window to help an off-duty Miami-Dade police officer who suddenly became unconscious while driving her SUV to order breakfast for her children. Viloria noticed the woman struggling and, seeing her foot slip from the brake, immediately leaped out to pull her from the moving vehicle. Paramedics and a second McDonald’s employee assisted in reviving the woman at the scene. McDonald’s praised Viloria’s bravery, stating he is an excellent employee who took immediate action to save the woman.

Hungary faces its worst floods ever as the Danube is expected to reach record levels, with water levels set to peak near Budapest over the weekend. Nearly 400 people have been evacuated so far, and the Hungarian military is working on dams along the river. Concerns grow about a toxic waste reservoir in Almasfuzito, near Komarom, potentially leading to water pollution. Meanwhile, the swollen Elbe River threatens Saxony-Anhalt in eastern Germany, with thousands of people evacuated. Flood defenses in Dresden saved the historic city center, but outlying areas remain under water. The flooding has caused at least 15 deaths across the region. In the Czech Republic, about 20,000 people have been evacuated, and attention now shifts to the clean-up operation.

A Las Vegas judge dismissed charges against Kirstin Blaise Lobato, who spent over a decade in prison for the 2001 killing of a homeless man whose penis was cut off. Lobato, 35, was twice convicted but maintained her innocence. The Innocence Project, which took her case, presented evidence that cast doubt on the state’s timeline of events, showing Lobato was in Panaca, Nevada, at the time of the crime. District Attorney Steve Wolfson chose to dismiss the charges, ending Lobato's wrongful conviction. Lobato's release is pending, with her advocates working to secure her immediate freedom.

A new study from South Korea, where instant noodle consumption is high, found that women who ate instant noodles at least twice a week were 68% more likely to have metabolic syndrome, a cluster of symptoms including abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. This effect was not seen in men. The study, published in The Journal of Nutrition, analyzed data from 10,711 adults as part of the Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey IV. While the overall dietary patterns of "traditional" and "meat and fast-food" did not independently link to metabolic syndrome, the frequent consumption of instant noodles was associated with a higher risk in women. The researchers suggest that the high sodium and saturated fat content in instant noodles may contribute to this increased risk, though they caution that more research is needed to confirm these findings.

A dispute over folding chairs at a wedding reception in Ellanor C. Lawrence Park in Chantilly, Virginia, escalated into the stabbing death of 35-year-old Tyonne Johns, a caterer and chef. Kempton Bonds, 19, a seasonal employee of the Fairfax County Park Authority, allegedly stabbed Johns after an argument over the chairs. Bonds, who was also working the wedding, allegedly used a pocketknife to stab Johns in the upper body. Police found Bonds at the scene and charged him with second-degree murder. The park authority has fired Bonds pending the investigation.

Facebook is introducing face recognition technology to assist users in tagging photos of friends, aiming to make the tagging process easier. The new feature, set to roll out next week, will not alter existing privacy settings, allowing users to confirm or reject suggested tags. Facebook emphasizes that tagging remains opt-in and that only friends can be tagged. The technology is expected to improve accuracy by comparing photos against a smaller subset of frequently communicated friends. While the reliability of face recognition remains a challenge, Facebook's implementation includes a "human in the loop" approach, enhancing user control. The feature will be gradually rolled out, initially in the United States.

"Sausage Party" debuted with a robust $33.6 million, providing a welcome boost for Sony Pictures and serving as a reminder of the appeal of original ideas in a summer dominated by reboots and spinoffs. The R-rated animated film, backed by Annapurna Pictures, features Seth Rogen, Kristen Wiig, and Edward Norton in voice roles and holds the record for the largest August opening for an animated film. It scored an A- CinemaScore from audiences and an 82% rating on Rotten Tomatoes. In contrast, "Suicide Squad" continued its decline, earning $43.8 million for a 67% drop from its opening weekend, though it has amassed a substantial $222.9 million domestically. "Pete's Dragon," a Disney remake, opened to $21.5 million, underperforming expectations for a family-friendly film. "Jason Bourne" added $13.6 million, bringing

The Curiosity rover is set to land on Mars at 1:31 a.m. Eastern time, with confirmation expected about 13 minutes later. If successful, the landing will be a moment of intense anticipation, with confirmation or silence indicating the rover's fate. Direct communication from Curiosity to Earth will be challenging due to the rover's position relative to Mars Odyssey, a necessary relay for initial signals. If Odyssey is unable to relay the signals, a second orbiter will record the data, with results available hours later. Engineers at Mission Control will be powerless to intervene during the descent, maintaining a stance of "rational confidence and emotional terror." The landing is a critical test for the rover's advanced landing system, with worldwide attention focused on the outcome.

The University of Alberta initially scheduled a workshop on "Spoon Bending and the Power of the Mind," which was later cancelled. The event, to be presented by Anastasia Kutt, an Edmonton "energy healing therapist" and "registered reiki master," aimed to teach participants how to bend cutlery using meditation and energy transfer techniques. The workshop was part of Pediatric Integrative Medicine Rounds, highlighting the integration of pseudoscientific practices with conventional medicine. Critics argue that such events undermine scientific integrity and highlight a lack of skepticism within academic medical institutions. The cancellation of the workshop, while a step in the right direction, underscores the ongoing challenge of combating quackademic medicine.

The search for Christopher Dorner, a former Los Angeles police officer suspected of a killing spree, continued in the snow-covered San Bernardino Mountains on Friday. More than 100 officers were involved in a meticulous search, slogging through deep snow and checking homes and cabins, as authorities hoped to find definitive evidence of his location. Dorner, described as 6 feet tall and 270 pounds, is accused of killing three people and wounding others in a revenge campaign against those he blamed for his 2008 dismissal. His manifesto, published on Facebook, threatened "unconventional and asymmetrical warfare" against police and their families. Despite warnings and false sightings, the hunt remained intense, with authorities guarding over 40 people mentioned in the manifesto. Cold weather posed a significant threat to Dorner's survival, and speculation arose about his plans and whereabouts.

Rebels in the Central African Republic declared Michel Djotodia as the new president after seizing the capital Bangui, forcing President Francois Bozize to flee. The African Union suspended the country and imposed sanctions on rebel leaders. International leaders condemned the coup and called for respect of a January peace deal. Djotodia pledged a power-sharing government and democratic elections within three years. The rebels accused Bozize of reneging on the peace agreement, but the future remains uncertain for the impoverished nation.

Natalie Portman and Benjamin Millepied tied the knot in an intimate ceremony in Big Sur, California, on August 4, with only 60 family and close friends in attendance. The traditional Jewish ceremony, held after sundown, featured a stunning Rodarte tea-length cocktail dress for Portman. Celebrity guests included Diane Sawyer, Ivanka Trump, and Macaulay Culkin. The couple, who met on the set of "Black Swan," celebrated with a vegetarian meal and dancing until 2:30 a.m. The wedding was a personal and happy occasion for the couple.

Oscar Pistorius, the former Olympian convicted of culpable homicide in the death of his girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp, is expected to be released from prison in August after serving 10 months of his five-year sentence. A family member confirmed to Reuters that Pistorius will be released on parole. Pistorius, known as the "Blade Runner," shot Steenkamp through a locked bathroom door in his home on Valentine’s Day 2013, claiming he mistook her for an intruder. He was initially found guilty of culpable homicide but the state is appealing for a murder conviction, which could result in a minimum 15-year sentence. Pistorius has been in Pretoria Central Prison since his conviction last fall and is set to be released on August 21.

Insurance company Pacific Life announced it is pulling its advertisements from Fox News' "Tucker Carlson Tonight" after the host made comments about the "immigration crisis" making America "poorer and dirtier and more divided." The company's ad, promoting its 150 years of protecting families, appeared on the show following Carlson's controversial statements. Pacific Life stated it disagrees with Carlson's views and will reevaluate its relationship with the program. A Fox News spokesperson defended the network, calling the controversy an "unfortunate and unnecessary distraction." Critics on social media are calling for other sponsors to follow Pacific Life's lead.

Amazon's Prime Day, now one of the company's biggest sales events, is set to kick off on July 10, 2017, at 9 PM Eastern time, running for 30 hours across 13 countries. The event aims to attract more Prime subscribers, offering over 100,000 deals with new ones launching every 5 minutes. However, Prime Day is not the only day for deals; Amazon's regular sales and the company's Alexa devices also offer exclusive deals. To keep track of deals, Amazon's Shopping App, Alexa, Amazon Assistant, CamelCamelCamel, SlickDeals, and Facebook can be used. Despite potential issues with sales tax in states where Amazon collects it, Prime Day presents opportunities for significant savings.

A Laurel County man facing murder charges admitted to shooting and killing his wife early Wednesday morning, stating it was her final wish to end her suffering from terminal cancer. Ernest Chumbley called 911 after the shooting and claimed he complied with his wife's request to stop her pain. Neighbors described the couple as having a long and loving marriage, but noted the cancer had significantly impacted his wife's quality of life in recent years. Chumbley pleaded not guilty and is in jail on a $200,000 cash bond, with a preliminary hearing scheduled for September 5th.

Brazil's Senate impeached and removed Dilma Rousseff, the country's first female president, on Wednesday, marking the end of 13 years of leftist governance by the Workers' Party. The Senate vote of 61 to 20 found Rousseff guilty of manipulating the federal budget to hide economic issues. However, her removal went beyond a judgment on her leadership; it reflected the declining fortunes of Latin America's largest economy. Interim President Michel Temer was sworn in following the impeachment. Rousseff, accused of budget mismanagement and economic misrepresentation, testified for 14 hours. Despite the impeachment, she can still run for office again in the future.

A 19-year-old University of Kentucky student, TeNiya Elnora Jones, is missing after getting caught in a rip current while swimming in the Mediterranean Sea near Tel Aviv, Israel. The students involved called Israeli officials, and UK officials are coordinating with the US Embassy and CIEE, the education abroad provider. Jones' mother and grandfather are traveling to Tel Aviv, and UK Education Abroad officials are arranging for the other students to return to Amman, Jordan. The program, which began in June, is scheduled to end this week.

Scientists have unearthed evidence suggesting that early humans in East Africa developed sophisticated stone tools and trading networks around 320,000 years ago, much earlier than previously thought. This discovery, reported in three papers in the journal Science, challenges the notion that modern human behaviors such as complex tool-making and long-distance trade emerged only with Homo sapiens. The oldest Middle Stone Age tools found in Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin are the earliest of their kind, dating back 320,000 years. These tools, including smaller, more specialized implements, indicate a shift from the earlier Acheulian hand axes. The presence of obsidian, a material sourced from 25 to 55 miles away, suggests the development of social networks and long-distance exchanges among early human groups. Additionally, the discovery of red and black pigments indicates early symbolic behavior. These findings suggest that the development of modern human behaviors began much earlier and may have occurred in multiple hominin

CareerCast has identified the 10 best and 10 worst jobs in America for 2017. Among the top 10 best jobs, speech pathologists, occupational therapists, and software engineers rank highly, with median annual wages of $73,410, $80,150, and $100,690, respectively. Mathematicians and university professors (tenured) also make the list, with median wages of $111,100 and $72,470. These jobs are characterized by high salaries, strong job security, and projected growth rates exceeding the national average. Conversely, newspaper reporters and other low-paying, declining occupations like taxi drivers and pest control workers are among the worst jobs. The best jobs often require advanced skills and are in fields like healthcare and technology, while the worst jobs are frequently associated with dangerous or low-paying roles.

At least 100 people died when a military plane carrying soldiers crashed shortly after takeoff in northern Algeria on Wednesday, officials said. Emergency services rushed to the scene near the Boufarik military base. The Soviet-designed Il-76 plane was heading to a base in Bechar, southwest Algeria, with stops in Tindouf and Boufarik. The crash site was in an agricultural area with no nearby residents. The cause of the crash remains unclear, and an investigation has been launched.

The overall suicide rate among children aged 5 to 11 in the United States remained stable from 1993 to 2012, but this stability masked significant racial disparities. The rate increased for black children and decreased for white children during this period. Hanging/suffocation was the most common method, followed by firearms. The study highlights the need for further research to understand the factors influencing these trends and to develop targeted prevention strategies.

Antarctic notothenioid fishes, which thrive in icy waters, use antifreeze proteins (AFPs) to prevent their blood from freezing. However, these same proteins inhibit ice melting, potentially leading to the lifelong accumulation of ice crystals within the fish. Despite summer warming, which should theoretically help melt the ice, notothenioid fishes in McMurdo Sound, Antarctica, still contain ice even when temperatures exceed the expected equilibrium freezing/melting point. This phenomenon, termed "superheated ice," suggests that AFPs not only prevent ice formation but also hinder its natural melting process. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, reveals that while AFPs are crucial for the fishes' survival, they come with the risk of internal ice accumulation, highlighting the trade-offs inherent in evolutionary adaptations.

The U.S. economy shed 33,000 jobs in September due to Hurricanes Harvey and Irma, marking the first decline in nearly seven years. The unemployment rate fell to 4.2%, the lowest since February 2001, as job growth is expected to rebound as businesses reopen and construction companies increase repair work. Job losses were heavily concentrated in the restaurant and bar sector. Despite the weather-related job losses, the proportion of adults with jobs rose to 60.4%, the highest since January 2009. Average hourly wages increased by 2.9% year-over-year, though this figure may be artificially inflated due to the loss of lower-paid workers. Other economic indicators suggest a solid recovery, with services and manufacturing sectors expanding at their fastest pace in years. Auto sales also saw a significant increase, potentially leading to higher production levels.

In Nice, a vigil marks the second night of mourning after the Bastille Day truck attack that killed 84 people. Well wishers have left flowers, bears, and toys as tributes. Police have cordoned off the area to shield the growing crowd from passing cars. Survivors recall the horrific events, with one couple noting they were alive because they let families with children go up the promenade first. French authorities are widening the investigation to include potential accomplices of the 31-year-old attacker, Mohamed Lahouaiej Bouhlel, who has been described as a troubled loner inspired by terrorist organizations. Lahouel's text message, sent shortly before the attack, was found on the rented truck. Security-camera footage showed him driving the truck on the promenade two days before the attack. The attack was the third major terrorist assault in France in 18 months, following the Charlie Hebdo and Bataclan attacks. Despite the outpouring of solidarity

U.S. President Donald Trump has indicated he would potentially intervene in the extradition case against Huawei finance executive Meng Wanzhou if it could aid in securing a better trade deal with China or serve national security interests. Meng, who faces charges of misleading banks about Iran-linked transactions, was arrested in Canada on December 1 at the request of U.S. authorities. Trump's comments have raised concerns among analysts about the arrest's political motivations, coming as diplomatic tensions between China and Canada have escalated with the detention of a Canadian diplomat in China. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau has stated his government is taking the situation of a Canadian detained in China very seriously and is offering consular assistance to the family.

Inheritance tax, imposed on the value of a deceased person's estate transferred to beneficiaries, varies in rate depending on the heir's relationship to the decedent. Rates in Pennsylvania include 0% for transfers to a surviving spouse or parent of a child under 21, 4.5% for direct descendants and lineal heirs, 12% for siblings, and 15% for other heirs, excluding charitable organizations, exempt institutions, and government entities. Jointly owned property between spouses is exempt. Effective for estates of decedents dying after June 30, 2012, certain farm and agricultural land may be exempt if transferred to eligible recipients, with details available in Notice 2012-01. Inheritance tax payments are due upon the decedent's death, with a 5% discount for payments made within three months.
