Relief efforts in Tacloban, the hardest-hit city in the Philippines after Typhoon Haiyan, are struggling to keep up with the scale of the disaster. Eight people died in a stampede at a rice warehouse as thousands of survivors tried to grab supplies, reports the AP. Meanwhile, looting and lawlessness are rampant, with residents breaking into homes of the dead and digging up water pipes for drinking water. The official death toll stands at 2,275, but aid workers fear it could rise. The U.S. military has delivered nearly 274,000 pounds of supplies, including plastic tarps, hygiene kits, and medical supplies. However, logistical challenges remain, with many remote areas still lacking aid. The U.S. is sending 300 Marines to bolster the relief effort, and other countries are also providing assistance. Despite the aid, the situation remains dire, with many residents desperate for food and water and facing the risk of disease outbreaks

Donald Trump's Republican National Convention in Cleveland is set to feature a lineup of sports stars and leaders from various industries, aiming to deviate from the typical politician-heavy events. During a radio interview, Ivanka Trump highlighted the diverse speakers, including business leaders, athletes, and coaches, emphasizing that the convention will not be "a ho-hum lineup of the typical politicians." However, securing these top sports figures has faced challenges. Mike Tyson, former heavyweight champion, and NASCAR CEO Brian France both announced they would not attend. Former Indiana University basketball coach Mike Ditka expressed willingness but stated he had not been invited. The sports figures' roles at the convention are yet to be finalized, and it is uncertain if any will speak on stage. Meanwhile, third-party groups have booked musicians like Journey, Bret Michaels, and Rascal Flatts to perform at venues throughout Cleveland during the convention. Trump has previously boasted about endorsements from sports personalities, aiming to present a "winner's" convention.

A tornado that struck Joplin, Missouri, on Sunday killed at least 126 people and left over 230 missing, according to updated figures. Emergency workers searched for survivors as Sally Adams, 75, was found to be alive after being mistakenly listed as missing. The Red Cross reported that at least nine of the unaccounted-for were confirmed dead. The death toll rose to 126, with some victims identified through personal effects like wallets and cell phones. Identification efforts, slowed by a previous misidentification incident, involved DNA testing and other forensic methods. Residents and families faced the daunting task of checking the missing list and calling authorities to confirm their status.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft, after 35 years of exploration, has entered a new region near the edge of our solar system called the "magnetic highway." This area allows charged particles to move freely, both from inside and outside the heliosphere, the bubble created by the sun's solar wind. Scientists believe this is the final region Voyager 1 has to cross before reaching interstellar space. Voyager 1's instruments detected a five-fold increase in high-energy particles and a 1,000-fold drop in low-energy particles, indicating it may be exiting the heliosphere. However, the spacecraft's magnetic field reading suggests it remains within the sun's influence, with no change in the magnetic field direction expected until it truly leaves the solar system. Voyager 1 is about 122 AU from Earth, and while scientists can't predict exactly when it will exit, they expect it to take a few months to a couple of years.

Fox News hosts Sean Hannity and Megyn Kelly are at odds, with Hannity accusing Kelly of supporting Hillary Clinton. Hannity's tweet came after Kelly criticized both Trump and Clinton for avoiding tough interviews, saying Clinton has a "presidential protection program" and Trump only appears on Hannity's show. The spat has sparked a Twitter storm, with many noting the feud's timing as Fox News celebrates 20 years since its launch. Some see this as a preview of future conflicts as Fox News navigates the post-Ailes era.

A heartwarming photo of an elderly widower dining at In-N-Out Burger with a picture of his late wife has gone viral, showcasing a 55-year love story. Twitter user Madina Bashizadah shared the image, while imgur.com user "soulrose" provided the backstory. The couple met at 17 but lost touch when he went to war and her family moved. He searched for her for 10 years and never dated. One day, at a barber shop, he recognized his daughter, who had been searching for him. They were married for 55 years until her passing in 2009. The man always carries a photo of his beloved, sharing that "I was a very rich man. Not with money, but with love" and advising others to "Tell your wife that you love her everyday."

Floyd Mayweather's legal team requested his release from jail due to health concerns from low-quality food and water, but a judge denied the request, stating Mayweather should eat and drink the provided meals and has sufficient space for physical activity. Mayweather, 35, pleaded guilty to reduced domestic battery charges and began a three-month sentence, with his lawyer arguing he might never fight again due to his condition in solitary confinement. His personal physician reported he was consuming fewer than 800 calories a day instead of his usual 3,000 to 4,000 calories and was dehydrated. The judge dismissed these claims, emphasizing Mayweather's condition was self-induced.

Divers have found the head and legs of Swedish journalist Kim Wall, who went missing after boarding a privately built submarine with its Danish inventor, Peter Madsen, on August 10. Madsen is accused of killing Wall and denies the charges, claiming her death was an accident. Danish police identified Wall's headless torso that washed ashore later in August. The body parts, a knife, and some of Wall’s clothes in bags weighted down by metal pieces were found in Koge Bay. Police are still working to determine Wall's cause of death, focusing on her neck and throat area. Madsen remains in custody while the investigation continues.

Sean Spicer, former White House press secretary, expressed regret over his infamous January 2017 press conference where he disputed accurate reports of President Obama's larger inauguration crowd. Spicer's latest comments came after his appearance at the Emmys, where he mocked his own initial remarks. James Corden on "The Late Late Show" playfully denied kissing Spicer at the after-parties, suggesting he kissed many others instead. Spicer's admission of regret and his Emmy performance reflect his attempt to rehabilitate his image and secure future speaking engagements.

A 16-year-old boy wielding two kitchen knives went on a stabbing rampage at Franklin Regional High School in Murrysville, Pennsylvania, early Wednesday, before being tackled by an assistant principal. Twenty students and a security officer were either stabbed or slashed. The attacker, Alex Hribal, faces charges including four counts of attempted homicide and 21 counts of aggravated assault. Hribal's attorney described him as a "nice young man" who has never been in trouble. Assistant Principal Sam King tackled the teen, and a school resource officer handcuffed him. Students used their hoodies as tourniquets to help stop bleeding. The attack, which began shortly before the start of classes, left at least five students in critical condition. The motive remains unclear, but the district attorney said the teen made statements indicating he wanted to die. The incident has rattled the small, residential town of Murrysville, where the high school is located.

Arnold Schwarzenegger is set to return to the film industry, tweeting that his talent agency can now take offers seriously after a seven-year wait. The former California governor, best known for his roles in "Terminator" films, plans to explore new acting opportunities, acknowledging his need to adapt roles to his age. He previously considered a script where he would play a kind-hearted Nazi soldier, returning children to safety. Schwarzenegger emphasizes his willingness to learn and adapt, comparing himself to Clint Eastwood. His last significant film roles were cameo appearances in "Around the World in 80 Days" and "The Expendables."

John Thune has decided not to run for president, stating he is better positioned to fight for America's future in the Senate. Thune, who has been considering a presidential bid for months, cited his role in the Senate, his family's concerns, and the timing as key factors in his decision. He plans to seek reelection in 2014 and will focus on his current Senate duties, including his new role on the Finance Committee. With Senate Minority Whip Jon Kyl set to retire, Thune may have opportunities to advance his leadership position in the Senate.

Pressure is building on the Metropolitan police to expand their phone-hacking inquiry to include Jonathan Rees, a notorious private investigator accused of targeting politicians, members of the royal family, and high-level officials. Rees, who worked for the Mirror Group and the News of the World, is alleged to have hacked into the bank accounts of the Duke and Duchess of Kent, Prince Edward, and Kate Middleton, among others. He is also accused of stealing confidential data from MI6 agents and using a computer hacker to breach the data of a former British intelligence officer. The Metropolitan police is believed to have collected extensive evidence on Rees, but it is unclear whether these allegations fall within the scope of their ongoing investigation. News International, the parent company of the News of the World, denies the allegations.

A 50-year-old man from Spokane faces assault charges after allegedly attacking his neighbor with a sword during a dispute over garbage cans, court documents show. The incident occurred when the victim's wife accused the neighbor, Carlo M. Cerutti, of throwing garbage into her can. Cerutti allegedly rushed out with a large, multi-bladed sword and attempted to swing it, prompting the victim to block and wrestle the weapon away. Another neighbor witnessed the altercation. Cerutti was arrested at his NorthTown Mall duplex.

Germanwings flight 4U 9525, an Airbus A320 carrying 150 people, crashed in the French Alps on March 24, 2015, killing all on board. The plane was en route from Barcelona to Düsseldorf when it descended rapidly, with no distress call sent. Rescue efforts were hampered by the remote and rugged terrain. Families of 16 German high school students and two teachers, who were on a language exchange program in Spain, were devastated. The crash site, strewn with debris, was difficult to access due to snow and poor weather. French authorities recovered a black box, which will be analyzed to determine the cause of the crash. The incident shocked the aviation industry and prompted calls for improved cockpit security and mental health screening.

Robin Williams' suicide topped Google's list of 2014's most searched topics, beating out events like the Ebola outbreak and the World Cup. Flappy Bird, an addictive mobile game, also made the top 10. Other global searches included Conchita Wurst, ISIS, and the Winter Olympics. In the U.S., Michael Brown's shooting in Ferguson and the conflict in Ukraine garnered significant attention. Google's data reflects broader search trends, while rivals Yahoo and Bing offer more specialized categories.

PayPal has banned Infowars, claiming the site promotes "hate and discriminatory intolerance," a move seen as politically motivated and aimed at financially crippling the influential media outlet weeks before mid-term elections. Infowars was given 10 days to switch payment processors, with the ban based on a vague "acceptable use policy." Critics argue the decision is part of a broader effort to silence conservative voices, citing similar bans by other tech giants and alleging political collusion. The ban raises questions about the role of private companies in regulating speech and commerce, potentially setting a dangerous precedent. Infowars is considering legal action and urging support from its audience.

A French court ordered Air France to pay damages and a fine for forcibly removing a pro-Palestinian activist, Horia Ankour, from a flight to Tel Aviv because she was not Jewish. The court fined Air France 10,000 euros and required the airline to pay 3,000 euros to Ankour and her legal fees. Ankour, a nursing student, attempted to fly to Israel to participate in a "Welcome to Palestine" campaign in April 2012. She was taken off the plane in Nice after an Air France employee questioned her about her Israeli passport and Jewish identity. French prosecutors supported Ankour's case, calling it a case of discrimination. Air France claimed her name was on a list of undesirables provided by the Israeli government.

Renowned Swiss climber Erhard Loretan, known for summiting all 14 peaks above 8,000 meters, died in a climbing accident on the Gruenhorn in the Swiss Alps on his 52nd birthday. Loretan, who began climbing at age 11, fell with a client at 3,800 meters, with Loretan dying at the scene and his client in serious condition. Loretan was one of three climbers to reach the summits of all 14 8,000-meter peaks. His career was marred by a 2001 conviction for manslaughter after he shook his 7-month-old son to death, a case that led to new research on infant shaken injuries.

Jerry Seinfeld's return to web series with "Comedians in Cars Getting Coffee" offers a casual, unscripted format where Seinfeld drives his famous friends around in vintage cars, stopping for coffee and conversation. The first episode, featuring Larry David, showcases Seinfeld's humor in discussing trivialities like cigar smoking versus cigarette smoking. The show's format, while reminiscent of other travel and talk shows, stands out as a web-only production, allowing Seinfeld to explore comedy in a more relaxed, spontaneous manner. This approach aligns with the growing trend of established Hollywood stars leveraging the internet for creative freedom, away from traditional television constraints.

President Donald Trump responded to reports of an FBI informant in his 2016 campaign by suggesting the truth would only come out if lawmakers gain access to documents currently being withheld. On Saturday, Trump tweeted, "If the FBI or DOJ was infiltrating a campaign for the benefit of another campaign, that is a really big deal." Earlier, he had tweeted about a possible FBI informant, maintaining any such action was politically motivated. Trump emphasized that the truth could only be revealed with the release or review of documents requested by the House Intelligence Committee and Senate Judiciary Committee. This comes amid ongoing tensions between congressional Republicans and the Justice Department over access to sensitive investigation materials.

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg has drawn criticism for her politically charged comments about presumptive Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump. Ginsburg, known for her candor, told CNN in a recent interview that Trump is a "faker" and lacks consistency. She elaborated, saying he "really has an ego" and "How has he gotten away with not turning over his tax returns?" Her comments, made during a previously scheduled interview related to her research on Chief Justice John Roberts, have sparked controversy. Trump himself responded by calling for Ginsburg to resign, tweeting, "Justice Ginsburg of the U.S. Supreme Court has embarrassed all by making very dumb political statements about me. Her mind is shot - resign!" Critics argue that Ginsburg's remarks, while expressing her political views, may have crossed the line and compromised her impartiality as a Supreme Court justice.

An Egyptian man was charged with fraudulently collecting insurance payouts after driving his severely autistic children to their deaths when he sped off a pier into the Port of Los Angeles. Ali Elmezayen, 44, allegedly plotted for over two years before driving his Honda off a commercial fishing dock in San Pedro, turning the car abruptly and accelerating towards a parking space. He surfaced within 30 seconds and swam to a ladder on the pier, while his partner and two boys, aged 8 and 13, drowned. Elmezayen collected over $260,000 in insurance proceeds and was held without bail, facing charges of mail and wire fraud.

Scientists have discovered a new genus and species of shrew rat in the high-altitude moss forests of Sulawesi Island, Indonesia. This unique rat, named Hyorhinomys stuempkei, has a large, flat, pink nose with forward-facing nostrils, extremely large ears, and long white incisors. It represents a new genus due to its distinct morphological features, including the loss of the coronoid process on the dentary bone, which suggests a diet of soft-bodied prey like earthworms and beetle larvae. The discovery, made by researchers from Australia, Indonesia, and America, highlights the biogeographic complexity of Sulawesi, where many new species continue to be found despite limited previous scientific exploration.

A 6-year-old girl named Lexi, who has a tiny fraction of Native American heritage, was removed from her California foster family of four years due to a legal ruling under the Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978. Despite strong opposition from her foster parents and their supporters, who gathered thousands of signatures on a petition, the court ordered Lexi to live with relatives in Utah. The Pages, her foster parents, have three other children and are seeking to adopt Lexi, arguing that she considers them her family. However, the court ruled that Lexi's best interests are served by being placed with her relatives, as the law prioritizes keeping Native American children with their families. The removal was carried out by social workers, with Lexi crying and clinging to a teddy bear as she was taken away. The case highlights the complex and often emotionally challenging application of the Indian Child Welfare Act.

Bill Cosby's wife, Camille, faced intense questioning during a six-hour deposition in February as part of a defamation lawsuit filed by seven women who accuse Cosby of sexual assault. Camille invoked spousal privilege numerous times, often refusing to answer questions. She stated she had no opinion on whether her husband was deceitful or acted with a lack of integrity. The deposition, which lasted about eight hours with frequent breaks, was contentious, with Camille leaving the room at one point. Despite the judge ruling she could refuse to answer certain questions, Camille maintained her stance, citing marital privilege. The transcript reveals that Camille was questioned about her husband's alleged actions, including giving Quaaludes to women, but she refused to comment. The legal proceedings continue as Cosby faces multiple civil and criminal cases related to sexual misconduct allegations.

A Spanish court ruled that a doctor stole a newborn child nearly five decades ago, one of many abducted during Spain's 20th-century dictatorship, but cleared him because the statute of limitations had expired. The Madrid court found 85-year-old gynecologist Eduardo Vela responsible for abducting Madrigal in 1969 and forging official documents, but could not convict him due to the expired statute of limitations. This is Spain's first ruling in the "stolen babies" scandal, which involved taking children from poor families, prisoners, or political enemies and giving them to pro-Franco families or the church. Madrigal, now 49, considers the verdict "bittersweet" and plans to appeal. The trial was a test case for thousands of families affected by the illegal practice, which began shortly after Franco's victory in the civil war and continued until his death in 1975.

McDonald's is giving away 10,000 bottles of its special sauce to promote the launch of new Big Mac variations, the Mac Jr. and the Grand Mac. The giveaway, a first in the U.S., aims to boost sales amid a 1.3% dip in U.S. sales over the last quarter. The Mac Jr. is a smaller version of the Big Mac, while the Grand Mac features larger beef patties. The move comes as the company seeks to attract younger customers, with internal data showing only one in five Millennials have tried the classic sandwich.

An eastern South Dakota farm with 1.3 million egg-laying chickens has become the first in the state to be infected with a deadly flu virus, despite extensive biosecurity measures. Dakota Layers, which produces over 90,000 dozen eggs daily, noticed an unusual number of dead birds and confirmed the presence of the highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza virus. The state veterinarian plans to euthanize the chickens, with the virus affecting over 33 million birds in the Midwest. Egg prices have surged due to the outbreak, with liquid eggs prices doubling in three weeks. The U.S. Department of Agriculture forecasts a drop in egg production for the first time since 2008.

Award-winning musician Prince will play a concert in Baltimore to promote peace following violent protests over the death of Freddie Gray. The concert, scheduled for Sunday at the Royal Farms Arena, will feature Prince's new song "Baltimore," addressing socio-political issues and the unrest in Baltimore and across the country. Attendees are asked to wear something gray in tribute to those lost in the violence. Prince's song, which includes lyrics like "Peace is more than the absence of war" and "Maybe we can finally say enough is enough, it's time for love," is a direct response to the current situation. The event aims to bring people together in a spirit of healing and reflection.

"The Lovely Bones," directed by Peter Jackson, is a film that straddles multiple emotional and narrative tones, making it a mixed success. The story, based on Alice Sebold's novel, follows the murdered 14-year-old Susie Salmon (Saoirse Ronan) as she observes her family and the killer, George Harvey (Stanley Tucci), from a special in-between state. Ronan's performance is praised for bringing naturalness and radiance to the role, while Tucci's portrayal of the murderer is unsettling and effective. However, the film's attempt to balance the dark and the fantastical elements often feels uneven. Jackson's direction, known for its intricate and imaginative visuals, is put to use in creating the in-between world, which, while visually stunning, sometimes overshadows the emotional core of the story. The film's handling of the killer's character and the overall narrative structure are criticized for being overly simplistic, particularly in comparison to the novel. Despite these shortcomings

Poland's Senate approved a controversial bill making it illegal to accuse the Polish nation or state of complicity in the Nazi Holocaust, with fines or up to three years in jail as punishment. The bill must be signed by President Andrzej Duda before becoming law. Israel is outraged, with Israeli MPs seeking to strengthen their own Holocaust denial laws. The bill states that accusing the Polish nation or state of complicity in Nazi crimes is illegal, except in artistic or scientific contexts. The bill passed with 57 votes to 23. Poland has long objected to phrases like "Polish death camps," which suggest shared responsibility for Nazi camps. The bill's more contentious point is whether it will outlaw references to individual complicity by Poles with the Nazis. Israel is furious, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu calling it an attempt to rewrite history. The U.S. State Department urged Poland to rethink the bill, citing concerns it could undermine free speech and strategic relationships. Poland's conservative ruling Law and Justice

Imagining a bathroom suite made entirely of chocolate? That's the quirky idea behind a collaboration between Bathrooms.com and U.K.-based chocolatiers Choccywoccydoodah. The Maderno Sweet bathroom set includes a 210,000-calorie chocolate bidet, a 210,000-calorie chocolate basin, an 8 million-calorie chocolate bath, and a 980,000-calorie chocolate toilet, totaling 9.4 million calories. The entire set is listed for $133,040 on Bathroomsweets.com, with individual pieces also available for purchase. While the set is designed for display rather than use, it promises to add a unique, sweet flavor to any bathroom. However, it's not recommended for actual bathroom use due to its sensitivity to heat and moisture, with a shelf life of six months or longer if kept at room temperature.

Notre Dame football star Manti Te'o claims he is the victim of a hoax after it was revealed that his girlfriend, Lennay Kekua, never existed. Katie Couric's show has released recordings of voicemails left by who Te'o believed was Lennay, suggesting he spoke to Ronaiah Tuiasosopo, who posed as Lennay over the phone. Phone records show numerous, lengthy calls to a single number, believed to be Lennay's.

The New England Holocaust Memorial in Boston was vandalized for the second time in two months when a 17-year-old suspect shattered a glass panel with a rock. The teenager, from Malden, was quickly apprehended by bystanders and is due to appear in court. Police are investigating whether the incident was a hate crime. The vandalism occurred just two days after a violent white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and less than two months after a 21-year-old shattered a glass panel at the same memorial. Boston Mayor Martin J. Walsh condemned the act, stating that Boston stands against hate. Police are posting an officer at the memorial throughout the night.

The International Court of Justice has rejected claims of genocide by Serbia and Croatia against each other during the Croatian war of secession from Yugoslavia, dismissing both the Croatian claim and the Serbian counter-claim. About 20,000 people died during the 1991-1995 war, mostly Croats. The court ruled that neither side had provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate the specific intent required for acts of genocide. The ruling, which is final, may stoke political tensions in both countries as they seek to justify their wars. The court's decision is unlikely to find Croatia or Serbia liable for genocide if no individuals from either country have been convicted of the crime.

Democratic candidate Dan Adler is generating buzz with his unconventional campaign ads, which some find bizarre and potentially offensive. In one, Adler interacts with a diverse group, highlighting his appeal to Asian voters through a marriage to a Korean and his Jewish background. A Korean immigrant woman, spoken in a heavy accent, awkwardly interrupts, asking what "mensch" means. Another ad features former child star Patty Duke declaring "Dan Adler: He Gets Shit Done." The most shocking ad has Adler's young son deliver the same catchphrase, followed by a special effects-assisted basketball dunk that rivals professional athletes.

A mummified monk found in Mongolia's Songinokhairkhan province is believed to be in a deep meditative state known as "tukdam," not dead, and potentially a teacher of Lama Dashi-Dorzho Itigilov, a Buryat Buddhist Lama who died in 1927. Forensic examinations are underway on the 200-year-old remains, which were discovered wrapped in cattle skin. Dr. Barry Kerzin, a physician to the Dalai Lama, suggests the monk may have achieved a rare spiritual state that helps preserve the body. The monk was reportedly stolen by a man planning to sell him on the black market, but was arrested by Mongolian police. The body is now guarded at the National Centre of Forensic Expertise in Ulaanbaatar.

President Obama was interrupted during his O'ahu vacation on Monday when the son of one of his friends suffered a minor injury on the beach in Kailua. The first family was unharmed, according to White House spokesman Bill Burton. Obama left the Luana Hills Country Club golf course abruptly to ensure the child was with his parents and returned to his vacation home in a dramatic motorcade. After confirming the injury was minor, Obama returned to finish his golf game, which he completed before sundown. The incident initially caused concern among the press and locals, but the White House later clarified that no stitches were needed.

A scuba diver, Christopher Le Cun, is suing Florida Power and Light after being sucked into an intake pipe at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant in 2015. Le Cun and his friend Robert Blake were scuba diving off Hutchinson Island when they encountered a yellow buoy marking three large submerged structures. Despite no warnings, they swam towards the structures and Le Cun was suddenly pulled into the pipe. He spent five minutes tumbling through darkness before emerging into sunlight. Le Cun survived but was seriously injured, contemplating death. A similar incident occurred in 1989, also resulting in a near-fatal experience for William Lamm. Florida Power and Light claims there are safety measures in place, including a protective cap and buoy, but Le Cun disputes their effectiveness.

All roads through Valley Forge National Historical Park were closed Tuesday due to a massive raw sewage spill from a broken pipe, estimated at 5 million gallons. The break occurred near Routes 252 and 23 in Tredyffrin Township, Chester County, and affected multiple townships sharing the sewer main. Overnight crews worked to replace the pipe, with new sections expected to arrive Wednesday. Several park roads remain closed for days as repairs continue, impacting traffic and access. The spill poses no human health risk but could harm wildlife.

Ricky Gervais and Mel Gibson faced off during the 2010 Golden Globes, leading to an awkward moment. Gervais joked about Gibson's alcohol problem, but preferred spending time with him over Bill Cosby. Gibson responded with a quip about getting a colonoscopy, creating a memorable interaction. Gervais' hosting style was acerbic, with memorable jabs at Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, and "The Martian" being mistaken for a comedy. His 2011 monologue was particularly harsh, targeting stars like Johnny Depp, Charlie Sheen, Cher, and Robert Downey Jr. In 2012, Gervais toned down his act but still managed to offend with a homophobic comment about Jodie Foster and a crude remark about Salma Hayek and Antonio Banderas. ISIS has released a new propaganda video featuring two deaf-mute militants using sign language to call for more recruits from the Islamic world, threatening to slaughter enemies. The video, subtitled in Arabic and English, shows the fighters working as traffic police in Mosul and ends with them launching rockets at nearby Peshmerga fighters, suggesting that disability is no excuse for not joining the fight.

Researchers have sequenced the genome of the tammar wallaby, the third marsupial to have its genome mapped, after the Tasmanian devil and the South American opossum. This milestone provides insights into the evolution of marsupials and mammals. Key findings include identifying a gene responsible for the kangaroo's distinctive hopping ability and genes crucial for the survival of young wallabies in their mother's pouch, which is external and vulnerable to pathogens. The study also examines how genes are expressed at different stages of the wallaby's life cycle and in various parts of its body, potentially offering insights for future human disease treatments. Led by Australian scientists, this project has been a long-term endeavor, adapting to advances in genome sequencing technologies.

Tim Tebow canceled a scheduled appearance at the Dallas megachurch of controversial pastor Robert Jeffress, citing personal and professional reasons. Tebow, who was set to deliver sermons at the $130 million building of First Baptist Dallas Church, tweeted about the cancellation, emphasizing his commitment to bringing faith, hope, and love. The church responded, stating that Tebow contacted Pastor Jeffress to avoid controversy and expressed interest in speaking at a future date. Tebow's decision to cancel drew criticism, with some suggesting he should have issued a stronger statement against Jeffress' beliefs. However, Tebow's polite cancellation is seen as a principled stand against intolerance. The church claims Tebow was unjustly pressured by the media to back out, citing misrepresentations of Pastor Jeffress' past comments on homosexuality, AIDS, and other religions.

Elton John and David Furnish plan to get married in a quiet registry office ceremony in May, marking the first day gay couples can legally wed in England. The pair, who entered a civil partnership in 2005, will take their two children, Zachary and Elijah, with them for the ceremony, which will also include a few witnesses. John, 67, and Furnish, 51, believe it's important to take advantage of the new legislation, despite not feeling the need for a large party. They have been together for 21 years and entered the civil partnership as a symbolic gesture to support the movement and acknowledge their commitment. The couple believes the civil partnership changed their relationship more than they anticipated, providing a sense of commitment and happiness they didn't expect.

Republican presidential contender Ben Carson maintained a business relationship with Alfonso A. Costa, a close friend convicted of health care fraud, despite advocating for harsh penalties for such crimes. Costa's dental practice was found to have charged for procedures not performed, resulting in a loss to insurance companies. Carson testified on Costa's behalf, helping to secure leniency, which contradicts Carson's 2013 stance advocating for at least a decade in prison for health care fraudsters. The article details Carson's close friendship with Costa, their joint business ventures, and the ongoing business ties despite the conviction.

A 19-year-old suspect, Erich Nowsch, has been arrested in connection with the fatal shooting of Tammy Meyers, a mother of four, in a road rage incident. Nowsch faces charges of murder, attempted murder, and discharging a gun from a vehicle. The shooting occurred after Meyers was confronted by an angry driver earlier that night while driving her daughter home from a driving lesson. After returning home, Meyers and her armed 22-year-old son went out to look for the driver involved in the earlier incident. When they returned to their cul-de-sac, a silver or gray car pulled up, and someone inside began shooting. Meyers' son returned fire, and Meyers was found shot in the head. Nowsch's arrest came after a brief standoff at a home a block away from the scene. Meyers' husband, Robert, said the family knew Nowsch and that his wife had been trying to help him. The

As the controversy over the death of Cecil the lion continued, two Zimbabwean men who allegedly assisted an American tourist in killing the famous lion appeared in court to face poaching charges. Theo Bronchorst and Honest Trymore Ndlovu, a landowner, were granted bail and ordered to return for further proceedings. The men are accused of luring Cecil outside Hwange National Park using bait, in violation of hunting regulations. Cecil, a 13-year-old lion known for his black mane and as a tourist attraction, was shot with a bow and arrow and later killed with a gun. The hunters are alleged to have tried to destroy Cecil's GPS collar, which was part of a research project. Zimbabwean authorities are investigating and have charged Bronchorst and Ndlovu with poaching offenses. Walter James Palmer, the American dentist accused of killing Cecil, has not been contacted by authorities but may face charges. A 37-year-old female caretaker was fatally mauled by a Bengal tiger in a zoo in Benidorm, Spain. The incident occurred around 5 pm when the worker was inside the tiger's cage at Terra Natura zoo. Local reports suggest the door may have been left open accidentally. Emergency services, including the Red Cross and medics, were called but found the victim already deceased. The tiger was sedated to allow recovery of the body. The zoo was open at the time but the cage was not visible to visitors. Staff are "appalled and deeply affected" by the tragedy. The park, described as an "immersion zoo," houses over 1,500 animals from 200 species. This incident follows another fatal attack at a UK zoo where a Sumatran tiger killed a 24-year-old employee.

A stretch of the Bronx River Parkway near the Bronx Zoo has been dubbed the "Bermuda Triangle" due to multiple fatal accidents, according to attorney Eric Buckvar, who sued the city and state over a 2006 crash. Seven people died in a recent accident where a speeding driver clipped a highway divider, causing her SUV to plunge off the road and into a ravine. The crash killed three generations of a family, including three children. The area has seen at least one other serious accident in the past year, highlighting ongoing safety concerns on this section of the highway.

More than 6,400 tins of Heinz baked beans with sausages were stolen from a parked lorry while the driver slept in the cab. Thieves cut a large hole in the curtain-sided vehicle, targeting an entire pallet and part of a second pallet on the A441 near Redditch, Worcestershire. Police are appealing for information, especially about anyone trying to sell large quantities of Heinz baked beans in suspicious circumstances.

A nine-year-old boy named Kieran, born without fully formed ears, underwent a groundbreaking surgery at Great Ormond Street Hospital to receive new ears crafted from his own rib cartilage. Kieran, who was also born deaf, has been gradually able to hear thanks to previous operations and a hearing aid. His father, David Sorkin, said the procedure was "on cloud nine" and would boost Kieran's confidence. The surgery, led by Neil Bulstrode, involved harvesting cartilage from Kieran's ribs, shaping it, and grafting it onto his head. Kieran's reaction was overwhelmingly positive, and he is now able to wear sunglasses and earphones. Researchers are also exploring the use of stem cells from a child's own fat to create new ears, potentially making the procedure less invasive.

A 1928-built wooden racing schooner named Nina, with a crew of seven including six Americans and one Briton, went missing in the Tasman Sea while en route from New Zealand to Australia. The vessel, equipped with modern tracking and communication devices, ceased contact in early June. Despite a tracking device and emergency buoy, no signals were received after the last known communication on June 4. Family members alerted New Zealand authorities in mid-June, leading to extensive searches including aerial reconnaissance, but no trace of the Nina or its crew was found. The ship left New Zealand on May 29 and was last heard from 370 nautical miles west of the country. Authorities are considering various scenarios, including communication failure, drift, or a catastrophic event leading to the vessel's sinking.

Rapper 50 Cent faced backlash after posting offensive memes mocking actor Terry Crews, who testified about sexual assault before the Senate Judiciary Committee. The memes, which suggested Crews could not be sexually assaulted due to his size, received numerous critical comments. Despite the controversy, Crews maintained a positive stance, stating, "I prove that size doesn’t matter when it comes to sexual assault." His testimony highlighted the challenges faced by sexual assault survivors and the need for better support systems.

In Northern California, the Tubbs Fire unleashed a series of fire tornadoes that flipped cars, uprooted trees, and ripped homes apart, according to fire scientists. Powerful winds, reaching up to 73 mph, fueled the fire, creating a vortex of air that circled at hurricane-force speeds. This phenomenon, known as a fire whirl, occurred in Santa Rosa neighborhoods, particularly in Fountaingrove and Coffey Park, where homes burned rapidly. The heat from the fire rose, pulling in wind and creating a vortex that caused significant damage. Fire experts compare the situation to the 2003 Cedar Fire and the 1991 Oakland Hills Fire, which also created their own weather patterns. The Tubbs Fire, which killed at least 22 people and burned 36,432 acres, demonstrated the destructive power of fire whirls in an unprecedented manner.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has agreed to allow nuclear inspections and to permanently close a key missile test site in the presence of international experts, subject to final negotiations. Kim also pledged to close the country's main Yongbyon nuclear complex if the United States takes reciprocal actions. During a summit with South Korean President Moon Jae-in, the two leaders agreed to establish a joint military committee, reconnect rail and road links, and allow South Korean citizens to visit the Mount Kumgang tourist region for the first time since 2008. Kim expressed a desire to visit Seoul in the near future, making him the first North Korean leader to do so. The United States welcomed the developments, with Secretary of State Mike Pompeo inviting North Korea's foreign minister to meet in New York. However, critics remain skeptical about the progress toward irreversible denuclearization.

American rock band Bon Jovi's first concerts in mainland China have been cancelled due to the band's inclusion of a picture of the Dalai Lama in a video backdrop during a concert in Taiwan five years ago. The decision, made by China's Culture Ministry, marks the band as the latest to fall victim to Chinese sensitivities surrounding the Tibetan spiritual leader, who is seen as a "splittist" and "wolf in monk's robes" by the Chinese government. Other artists, including Björk and Maroon 5, have also faced bans or cancellations for similar reasons. Bon Jovi's frontman, Jon Bon Jovi, had previously described the band's music as about "individual freedom and expression." The cancellations come amid heightened tensions over Tibet as China celebrates the 50th anniversary of the region's direct control.

This year's Oscar nominations brought both surprises and snubs, with some notable absences despite strong performances and box office success. Martin Scorsese's "Silence" and "Finding Dory" failed to secure any nominations, while actors like Amy Adams, Annette Bening, and Hugh Grant were left out. Notably, "Hidden Figures" and its star Taraji P. Henson missed a best actress nomination, though Octavia Spencer was recognized. Despite critical acclaim and BAFTA nods, "Sully" and its lead Tom Hanks were not nominated. The inclusion of actors of color, such as Denzel Washington and Mahershala Ali, marked a step towards diversity, but the overall nominations list still faced criticism.

Twitter has promised to improve its policies after Robin Williams' daughter, Zelda, was bullied off the platform following her father's suicide. The company will update its policies to better handle tragic situations, including expanding rules on self-harm and private information. However, Zelda Williams' experience is just a small part of the broader issue of abuse on Twitter. Imani Gandy, a legal analyst, describes facing constant harassment due to her race, gender, and medical condition. Twitter's tools for reporting abuse are often insufficient, as persistent attackers can easily create new accounts. Critics argue that Twitter's commitment to free expression may overlook the impact of harassment on certain users.

An oil platform exploded and caught fire off the Louisiana coast, but no significant oil leak was found, according to the Coast Guard. All 13 crew members were rescued wearing "Gumby suits," bright orange survival gear. The platform, owned by Mariner Energy, was producing oil and gas from seven active wells when the fire broke out. Despite initial reports of an oil sheen, no spill was detected upon further investigation. The incident occurred in shallower waters compared to the Deepwater Horizon disaster, making cleanup easier. Mariner Energy has a history of safety violations, with 10 accidents reported in the Gulf of Mexico over four years. The Coast Guard continues to monitor the situation, while BP prepares to remove the failed blowout preventer from the seafloor.

Seth Meyers shared the dramatic story of his second son, Axel Strahl, being born in the lobby of his apartment building on his show. Meyers, 44, welcomed the baby boy with wife Alexi Ashe on April 8. He recounted how the baby made his entrance just as Meyers called 911, with the NYPD helping to cut the cord and neighbors providing towels to keep the baby warm. Meyers thanked the emergency responders and his neighbors, and even showed a photo of the birth, depicting his wife holding their son as emergency personnel assisted her. The proud new dad joked about his bravery, despite getting choked up. Social media users congratulated the couple on their new addition, praising the heartwarming story. Axel's middle name honors his grandparents, who met in a hospital in Austria after being liberated from a concentration camp. The U.S. military has no plans to suspend any more major military exercises with South Korea, according to Defense Secretary Jim Mattis. This comes after President Trump unilaterally halted the drills as a good-faith gesture following his summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Mattis stated that no decisions have been made about major exercises for next year, and that smaller, exempted exercises are ongoing. The decision to resume the exercises suggests a potential shift in the Trump administration's approach, indicating a lack of progress in negotiations with North Korea. The U.S. and South Korea's traditional exercise calendar typically hits a high point in the spring with the Foal Eagle and Max Thunder drills. Despite the halted exercises, the U.S. maintains about 28,500 troops in South Korea.

More than 50 women have accused Harvey Weinstein of sexual misconduct, with allegations spanning decades and including claims of rape, sexual assault, and harassment. Among the accusers are well-known actresses and models, such as Ashley Judd, Rose McGowan, and Gwyneth Paltrow, who describe uncomfortable and unwanted encounters with the producer. The accusations detail instances where Weinstein allegedly forced women to perform oral sex, groped them, or attempted to pressure them into sexual encounters. Some women, like Asia Argento, claim they were raped, while others, like Mira Sorvino, describe feeling violated during auditions. The article highlights the pervasive nature of Weinstein's alleged behavior, affecting women from various stages of their careers and backgrounds. Despite his denials, Weinstein has faced legal charges and lost his position at The Weinstein Company. The #MeToo movement has brought these allegations to the forefront, sparking a broader conversation about sexual harassment and assault in the entertainment industry.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren grilled Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf during a Senate Banking Committee hearing, accusing him of "gutless leadership" and calling for his resignation and a criminal investigation. Warren highlighted the bank's cross-selling scandal, where millions of customers were enrolled in unwanted financial products, and questioned Stumpf's role in driving this unethical behavior. Stumpf defended his actions, stating that cross-selling was about deepening customer relationships. Warren produced transcripts of Wells Fargo earnings calls from 2012 to 2014, showing Stumpf repeatedly citing cross-selling as a key factor for the company's success. She accused Stumpf of profiting from this unethical practice, with his stock holdings gaining over $200 million during the period. Stumpf's stock price dipped slightly during the hearing, but recovered by midday.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have shared details of their upcoming wedding, including the roles of their parents and plans to honor Princess Diana. Meghan's parents, Doria Ragland and Thomas Markle, will visit the British royal family before the ceremony and Thomas will walk Meghan down the aisle. The bride will spend her last night as a single woman at an undisclosed hotel. The couple will marry at St. George's Chapel in Windsor Castle on May 19 at 12:00 p.m. Harry's mother's family will also be involved, with one of Diana's sisters giving a reading. Meghan will not have a maid of honor, and all bridesmaids and pageboys will be children. The couple will not leave for their honeymoon immediately after the wedding and will make their first public appearance as a married couple during the following week.

The Navy has recommended including any available police reports, even if they did not result in charges or convictions, in future security reviews after the shooting deaths of 12 Navy personnel by a gunman with an honorable discharge and a Secret-level clearance. The gunman, Aaron Alexis, had a 2004 arrest involving a firearm, which was not mentioned in a federal personnel report. The Office of Personnel Management interviewed Alexis about the incident, but he did not disclose the involvement of a weapon. The Navy cleared Alexis based on the information available at the time. The recommendation aims to address missed opportunities by the Navy and Alexis' civilian employer to address his violent tendencies and apparent mental illness.

Over the holiday weekend, a group of predominantly white militiamen occupied the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge headquarters in Oregon, sparking a tense standoff with law enforcement. Media outlets initially treated the events as a peaceful protest, using terms like "armed protesters" and "peaceful resolution," despite the group's stated willingness to use violence if police attempted to remove them. This contrasted with how similar events involving minority groups were covered, with more alarmist and racially charged language. Social media users and some critics pointed out the perceived double standards in media coverage, arguing that the same level of concern and scrutiny would not have been applied if the protesters were black or Muslim. The article highlights how implicit biases might influence media coverage, potentially leading to different treatment of similar events based on the racial identity of the protesters.

A Florida gun shop declared a "Muslim-free zone" after its owner, Andy Hallinan, faced a lawsuit from the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR). Hallinan's store was sued for allegedly discriminating against Muslims, violating federal public accommodations law. CAIR's lawsuit aims to prevent the gun shop from segregating people based on religion. Hallinan's decision to ban Muslims followed the Chattanooga shootings, where a gunman killed four Marines and a Navy sailor. Hallinan's attorney called the lawsuit "frivolous" and "bogus," arguing that the store's policy was for public safety. CAIR officials emphasized that American Muslims have the right to purchase and handle firearms without discrimination.

A new study suggests that proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), commonly used to control heartburn, might increase the risk of dementia in seniors. Researchers analyzed data from 73,679 patients aged 75 or older, finding a 44% higher risk of dementia among those regularly using PPIs compared to non-users. The study, published in JAMA Neurology, supports previous findings that PPIs may increase levels of amyloid plaques in the brain, linked to dementia. However, the study does not establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship, and more research is needed through randomized, prospective clinical trials. Experts advise that the findings should prompt clinicians to reassess PPI prescriptions, aiming to avoid overuse. While the risk is concerning, doctors recommend that patients consult with their healthcare providers before making any changes to their medication regimen.

President-elect Donald Trump has been criticized by some Republican leaders for his apparent indifference to the CIA's assessment that Russia tried to influence the U.S. election to his advantage. Trump has dismissed the intelligence community's findings, saying "These are the same people that said Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction." Meanwhile, Obama is pushing for a definitive report on Russia's cyber-intrusions before leaving office, while congressional Republicans are divided on how to respond, with some calling for investigations and others defending Trump. The situation could lead to a potential conflict between Trump and his own party, as well as between the U.S. and Russia. Congress may use hearings, sanctions, or public criticism to try to steer Trump towards a tougher stance on Russia, but the outcome remains uncertain.

President Obama emphasized the need for a thorough investigation of the Secret Service prostitution scandal during a news conference at the Summit of the Americas. He highlighted the importance of dignity and probity for the Secret Service agents and all U.S. personnel serving abroad. If the allegations prove true, Obama expressed anger, stating that the agents must uphold the highest standards. The scandal, involving 11 Secret Service agents and five military personnel, has overshadowed the economic summit, drawing criticism from lawmakers and the public. The incident, which came to light after a dispute over payment, has raised questions about the effectiveness of security measures and the potential for future breaches.

Donald Trump is set to receive his first classified briefing as the Republican Party's presidential nominee tomorrow, according to sources. The briefing, led by career staffers from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (DNI), will cover major global threats and is expected to take place in a secure room at the FBI's New York Field Office. Accompanying Trump will be New Jersey Governor Chris Christie and retired Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn, both of whom have publicly supported Trump. The decision to include these individuals in the briefing could fuel speculation about potential Cabinet positions. Despite concerns from some critics about Trump's fitness to handle classified information, the DNI and White House maintain that providing briefings to both major-party candidates is a longstanding tradition. Each candidate is expected to receive two or three briefings before the election.

A 49-year-old woman with the last name of Crook was arrested on Friday for allegedly stealing ladies' undergarments from a Kohl's store in Alhambra. Police say she used an empty purse to conceal the items and failed to pay for them. She was taken into custody around 7:15 p.m. and booked at the Alhambra Police Department. Crook's bail was set at $20,000 and she is scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday.

Over 1,000 meters of overhead cabling were stolen in Lincolnshire, causing a village blackout. The theft occurred overnight on the A1133 near Newton-on-Trent and left residents without power for several hours. This is the second such incident in the area, with a similar theft at Normanby-Le-Wold in August. Police warn of the dangers involved and are seeking tips from the public, who can contact them at 0300 111 0300.

A group of Russian hackers infiltrated Dow Jones & Co.'s servers, potentially seeking stock tips, according to Bloomberg. The Federal Bureau of Investigation, Secret Service, and Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating. Dow Jones stated it has received no information from authorities about the alleged hack and is looking into the report. The breach is considered more serious than a previous lower-grade intrusion disclosed a week earlier, where hackers sought contact and payment information of about 3,500 customers. The hack investigation highlights the evolving challenge of insider trading in cyberspace, where market-moving information is increasingly targeted by cyber-criminals.

Katie Holmes, after filing for divorce from Tom Cruise, has kept a busy schedule, including working on a film about a single mother, appearing on Project Runway, and maintaining a public profile through shopping trips with her daughter Suri. Her career appears to be moving forward, with upcoming projects and a return to fashion week. Meanwhile, Tom Cruise, before embracing Scientology, studied for the priesthood at St. Francis Seminary in Cincinnati. His time there, marked by both discipline and occasional trouble, provided a stark contrast to his later life. Cruise's decision to leave the seminary and pursue acting was influenced by his tumultuous personal life, including an abusive childhood and a brief stay with his former manager, Eileen Berlin. Despite his early promise and the support of Berlin, Cruise's career and personal life have been marked by challenges and controversy, including his eventual involvement with the Church of Scientology.

A limited edition Karlbox, combining Karl Lagerfeld’s innovative spirit with Faber-Castell’s fine art and graphic products, has been launched. This unique art supply storage box, designed by Lagerfeld, features 350 premium drawing and painting tools, including Albrecht Dürer and Polychromos color pencils, highly pigmented Pitt Artist ink pens, and Castell 9000 graphite pencils. The elegant black lacquered box, with a removable drawer system, holds a carefully selected range of colors, from soft pastels to vibrant hues. Only 2,500 Karlboxes have been produced, each with a unique serial number and certificate of authenticity, priced at $2,850. The collaboration symbolizes the symbiosis of fashion, art, and design, with Lagerfeld noting Faber-Castell’s long-standing reputation for quality.

Archbishop Charles Chaput of Philadelphia has issued new guidelines for Catholics, including those in same-sex relationships and divorced and civilly remarried individuals, in line with Pope Francis' call for greater acceptance. The guidelines, effective July 1, state that gay Catholics should strive to live chastely, while priests are advised to help those with same-sex attractions find chastity challenging. For divorced and civilly remarried Catholics, the archdiocese requires abstinence from sexual intimacy to receive Holy Communion. Cohabitating unmarried couples are also instructed to refrain from sexual intimacy. The guidelines emphasize that those in "irregular" relationships may not hold positions of responsibility within the church. While the document acknowledges the complexity of these issues, it upholds traditional church teachings and disciplines.

An adult film star who partied with Charlie Sheen hours before his hospitalization claims Sheen was splattered with wine stains, had "tennis ball size" chunks of cocaine delivered, and consumed so much alcohol and drugs she feared he was on a "suicide binge." Sheen is in rehab and production on his sitcom "Two and a Half Men" is on hold. The star's publicist said he was rushed to the hospital with "severe abdominal pains" Thursday. Sheen offered the adult film star a deal to move into a mansion with him and babysit his children. His ex-wife, Denise Richards, has barred him from being alone with their daughters until he completes rehab.

A study by researchers at Nationwide Children's Hospital found that 75% of breast milk samples purchased online were contaminated with high levels of bacteria, including disease-causing bacteria and fecal matter. The samples were collected from a public milk-sharing website and compared to unpasteurized breast milk donated to non-profit milk banks, which follow strict guidelines and pasteurize their milk. The online-purchased milk had significantly higher bacteria counts and more disease-related bacteria, despite the fact that the milk bank samples had not yet been pasteurized. The study suggests that the contamination likely resulted from poor hygiene during collection, storage, or shipping. While some bacteria in breast milk are beneficial, high levels can pose health risks, especially to infants. The researchers advise against purchasing breast milk online and recommend using milk banks for safe, screened milk.

A blood test can detect the buildup of beta-amyloid plaques in the brain, potentially signaling a future Alzheimer's diagnosis. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis developed this test, which measures the relative amounts of different beta-amyloid types in the blood, indicating whether plaques are forming. This could allow for earlier detection and treatment, similar to cholesterol tests for heart disease. However, further validation is needed, and experts advise that a positive test does not definitively mean Alzheimer's will develop. The test could help identify those at risk and guide preventive lifestyle changes.

Parents in Windsor, Vermont, expressed shock and concern after their fifth-grade children took a survey asking about sexual history, orientation, and gender identity. Vanessa Beach, whose 10-year-old daughter participated, found the questions inappropriate for her child's age. The survey, conducted by WISE, a domestic violence prevention group, was distributed without Beach receiving the opt-out form. While Beach supports discussions on gender identity and sexuality, she believes the survey invaded her daughter's privacy. School administrators and WISE officials are addressing parental complaints, emphasizing that students have the option to decline participation.

The Jon2012girls, the daughters of presidential candidate Jon Huntsman Jr., recently had a karaoke-themed photo shoot in a Chinese restaurant on the Lower East Side. Despite their celebrity status, their campaign remains a marginal effort. The trio, Liddy, Abby, and Mary Anne, are known for their social media presence and unfiltered support for their father. They discuss using new technology to reach disillusioned young voters and explain that their parents raised them with a philosophy of giving back. The article mentions a past encounter between Mary Anne and Kris Humphries, now Kim Kardashian's ex, after seeing Elf together. While the encounter is not newsworthy, it adds a personal touch to the story.

A suspect in five homicides in Ohio contacted a local television reporter before his arrest, according to police. George Brinkman, 45, exchanged Facebook messages with a WOIO-Channel 19 reporter in the hours before and during a nine-hour standoff, which ended with his arrest. Brinkman, identified as a suspect in the deaths of a North Royalton mother and her two daughters, as well as a Lake Township couple, was house-sitting for the John couple when they were found dead. He was also ex-boyfriend to the mother of the North Royalton victims. Brinkman was in custody facing murder charges. The murders occurred after a nearly 9-hour standoff in Brunswick, where officers used a stun gun on Brinkman after he was found holding a gun.

Republicans pulled their Obamacare repeal bill just before a scheduled vote, dealing a significant setback to President Donald Trump and House Speaker Paul Ryan. Despite Trump's ultimatum for House Republicans to support the bill or live with Obamacare, GOP lawmakers decided they could live with the current law for now. A Republican leadership aide reported that Trump and Ryan spoke by phone, with the president asking the speaker to cancel the vote. Ryan admitted his team had been losing support all day and was not close to passing the American Health Care Act. Democrats remained steadfast in their opposition, while conservative outside groups opposed the bill from the start. Trump acknowledged he was short of the necessary votes, about 10 to 15, and Ryan insisted the president had done his best. The Freedom Caucus, which had previously brought down Speaker John Boehner, refused to compromise, believing the bill did not sufficiently dismantle Obamacare.
