A British Army lieutenant has become the youngest person to reach the South Pole solo, completing a 702-mile trek through extreme conditions. Scott Sears, 27, from the First Battalion Royal Gurkha Rifles, pulled a sled and supplies for 38 days in temperatures as low as -50°C and winds up to 150mph. His journey, which ended on Christmas Day, took more than five weeks and raised over £33,500 for the Gurkha Welfare Trust and schools in Nepal. Sears, brother-in-law to tennis star Andy Murray's wife, Kim, faced dangerous crevasses and a physical wall on his final day but persevered, celebrating his achievement with a message of pride and relief.

Kenneth Starr, a financial adviser to wealthy clients, was arrested and charged with running a $30 million fraud scheme. The complaint alleges Starr, his son, his wife, a former politician, and a law firm partner were involved in the fraud. Clients include celebrities and businesspeople, though specific names were not disclosed. Starr was detained without bail and faces charges of wire fraud, investment adviser fraud, and money laundering. His wife and son were also named in a civil complaint by the SEC. Co-defendant Andrew Stein, a former New York City Council president, was released on bail. Clients reportedly included actress Uma Thurman and former talent agent Jim Wiatt. The case highlights a complex web of alleged financial misdeeds involving high-profile individuals and raises questions about the extent of Starr's network of clients and associates.

The United States men's national team suffered its most embarrassing defeat in history, losing 2-1 to Trinidad and Tobago on the final day of CONCACAF World Cup qualifying, thus missing out on the 2018 World Cup. The loss, despite the U.S. needing only a point, highlighted a poor qualifying campaign with three wins in ten games. Key issues included a lack of urgency, poor team selection, and tactical errors. The U.S. will face significant scrutiny, with potential changes at the top of the soccer federation. The broader failure points to systemic issues in player development and youth soccer, leaving the sport in a weakened state heading into the next World Cup cycle.

Two police reports from the night George Zimmerman shot Trayvon Martin detail Zimmerman's injuries and witness accounts supporting his version of events. The reports state Zimmerman had a bloody face and nose, and two witnesses described a struggle with a hoodie-clad figure straddling Zimmerman. The case, which sparked national outrage and racial debates, is part of a trove of documents released by Florida's state attorney. The documents include a 911 call where Zimmerman speculated the teen looked suspicious, and an autopsy revealing Martin had THC in his system. Martin's father disputes the voice on 911 calls, claiming it was his son. Zimmerman, charged with second-degree murder, claims self-defense.

The Sentinelese, a tribe believed to be the last pre-Neolithic people in the world, have remained isolated for thousands of years, rebuffing all attempts at contact with the modern world. They are known to fire arrows at anyone who approaches their island, and their hostility is rooted in centuries of violence and exploitation by outsiders. In 2004, the Sentinelese survived the devastating Asian tsunami, a feat that initially left their fate unknown. Despite their isolation, the Sentinelese have adapted by using metal from shipwrecks to make tools and weapons. Their way of life, marked by a lack of community structure and a primitive form of art, reflects their long-standing separation from the outside world. Efforts to protect the Sentinelese from the same fate as other Andaman tribes, who have suffered from exploitation and disease, have led to stricter policies against outsiders. However, the debate continues on how best to ensure their survival and well-being

Secret US military files reveal a complex and often strained relationship between the United States and Pakistan, highlighting mutual suspicions and accusations of complicity in the war against terrorism. The documents, obtained by WikiLeaks and published by the New York Times, detail American frustrations with Pakistan’s perceived lack of cooperation in combating militant groups and allegations of Pakistani intelligence working alongside Al Qaeda. American officials have accused Pakistan’s Directorate for Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) of running a “double game,” appeasing certain American demands for cooperation while supporting insurgent networks. Behind-the-scenes accounts show American anger at Pakistan’s unwillingness to confront attacks near its border posts and the movement of insurgents across the frontier. The reports suggest that Pakistan’s spy agency has been involved in suicide bombing networks and Taliban offensives, though direct evidence of ISI complicity in major attacks is limited. American officials have confronted top Pakistani military officers with accusations of ISI involvement, but denials from Pakistan’s military and intelligence officials persist. After 180,000 bedbug bites and eight years of study, Simon Fraser University scientists have developed a new bedbug trap. Biologist Regine Gries, along with her husband Gerhard Gries, a biology professor, and chemist Robert Britton, led the research. Regine Gries acted as a host for over a thousand bedbugs to identify pheromones that attract the pests. The trap emits a combination of chemical attractants, including histamine, which signals "safe shelter" to bedbugs, keeping them in place. This technology, developed with Contech Enterprises Inc., aims to help detect and monitor bedbug infestations effectively and affordably.

Kanye West has been discharged from UCLA Medical Center after a week of treatment for a mental breakdown, Us Weekly reports. West, 39, is now back at home with his wife Kim Kardashian and their children. Kim has been by his side throughout his hospitalization, as well as his personal physician, Dr. Michael Farzam, who called 911 when West was admitted. The breakdown was reportedly triggered by the anniversary of his mother's death and the stress of his 63-date Saint Pablo tour. Kim Kardashian, 36, struggled to feel safe after being robbed at gunpoint in Paris, while West returned to the tour. Their relationship faced challenges due to West's workaholic tendencies and his behavior during his hospitalization. Kim feels relieved that West is getting the help he needs, hoping it will strengthen their marriage. West's concert promoter, Live Nation, has canceled the remaining dates of his Saint Pablo Tour.

New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg will officiate at the wedding of his chief policy adviser, John Feinblatt, and consumer affairs commissioner, Jonathan Mintz, on July 24, the first day same-sex marriages are legal in New York. This marks the first time Bloomberg, who has only performed two marriages since taking office in 2002, will officiate at a same-sex wedding. The ceremony will take place at Gracie Mansion, and Bloomberg stated that Feinblatt and Mintz, who have been together for fourteen years and have two daughters, helped him "see the issue of marriage equality in very clear terms." The city extended the hours of the City Clerk's office on that Sunday to accommodate same-sex couples wishing to marry. New York, the sixth state to legalize gay marriage, saw its governor, Andrew Cuomo, sign the bill on June 24, making it possible for an estimated 42,000 same-sex couples to marry.

Saudi Arabian billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal, detained since early November as part of a wide-ranging corruption crackdown, was released on Saturday after reaching a financial settlement with the attorney general. His release, along with several other prominent businessmen, suggests the main part of the probe is winding down. Prince Alwaleed, who maintains his innocence, expects to keep full control of his global investment firm Kingdom Holding Co. and has been able to communicate with business executives while detained. The decision to free him and others appears aimed at signaling a move towards other economic reforms and addressing foreign investor concerns. Prince Alwaleed described his confinement as a "misunderstanding" and expressed support for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's reform efforts. While he appears thinner and greyer than before, he maintains he has nothing to hide and is comfortable in his suite at the Ritz-Carlton in Riyadh. His release is seen as a step towards normalcy in Saudi Arabia's business and political landscape.

Casey Affleck will not present the Best Actress award at the 2018 Oscars and will not attend the ceremony, according to Deadline. Affleck's decision stems from concerns that his presence could create controversy amid ongoing sexual harassment allegations. In 2010, two women who worked on Affleck's film "I'm Still Here" accused him of sexual harassment, including unwanted physical contact and verbal abuse. Affleck has denied the claims, stating that the cases were settled to his satisfaction. His absence from the Oscars aims to focus on the performances of the nominated actresses.

A mother and son in New Mexico face up to 18 months in prison if found guilty of incest. Monica Mares, 36, and her son Caleb Peterson, 19, have declared their love for each other and plan to fight the charges. They claim to be "madly in love" and are appealing for public support to fund their legal defense. The couple's relationship, driven by "Genetic Sexual Attraction," has drawn attention to the complexities of such close relationships. Despite facing legal and societal opposition, they vow to remain together, with Mares willing to give up her other children if necessary. The case highlights the challenges and emotional depth of such relationships, as both parties express their commitment to each other.

Caitlyn Jenner faced a naming dilemma for her new child, considering her Kardashian family's K-heavy names. Jenner, formerly Bruce, chose "Caitlyn" after watching the Miss America pageant and liking names like Heather and Cathy. Her assistant, Rhonda, suggested "Caitlyn," which Jenner loved. Jenner decided to break the Kardashian tradition, opting for a "C" instead of a "K." Meanwhile, Kim Kardashian is pregnant with twins, a secret she's keeping close to her chest. Kim, 34, had in vitro and two embryos are fertilized, waiting to see if both will "stick." She's lying low about the pregnancy, planning a family outing with Caitlyn that could be filmed by paparazzi. Caitlyn's mother, Esther, met her daughter and is adjusting to the name change, still calling her "Bruce" for now. The 65-year-old Olympian shared her transition journey in the promo for E!'s documentary series

American Joshua Holt, 26, a Mormon missionary from Utah jailed in Venezuela's notorious El Helicoide prison, has posted an emotional video plea for his release, saying his life is in danger amid an ongoing inmate riot. Holt, who married his wife Thamara Candelo in 2016 after meeting online, has been in custody for two years without charge, following accusations of weapons possession in their apartment. In two 20-second videos, Holt appeals to the U.S. government and citizens for help, stating, "Please, my fellow Americans, don't allow me to continue suffering in Venezuela." Holt's prison is under control of the inmates, who claim to be protesting torture and human rights violations. The U.S. embassy expressed concern, warning that Holt could be lynched by Maduro's regime agents. Venezuelan authorities have stated the situation has "normalized," but inmates dispute this claim.

David Goldberg, CEO of SurveyMonkey and husband of Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg, passed away unexpectedly. The couple met in 1996 while working in Los Angeles and later married in 2004. Goldberg sold his first start-up for $12 million and grew SurveyMonkey into a billion-dollar business. He emphasized a work-life balance, encouraging his team to leave work by 5:30 p.m. and himself to spend time with his children. Goldberg believed in hiring great people and allowing them to fail, holding regular meetings but also valuing informal conversations. His death has left a significant impact on both his professional and personal life.

Saudi Arabia, frustrated with the international community's response to Middle East issues, including the Syrian conflict and the Israeli-Palestinian dispute, announced it would not take up its seat on the United Nations Security Council, citing the body's failure to effectively resolve conflicts and promote peace. The decision, a departure from Saudi Arabia's traditional low-key diplomatic approach, reflects its anger at the perceived double standards in the Security Council and the U.S.'s rapprochement with Iran. Saudi officials argue that the Security Council has failed to address key issues such as the Syrian civil war and nuclear proliferation in the region. The move comes as Saudi Arabia seeks to assert a more public and assertive stance on international issues, though some analysts suggest it may be a strategic decision to avoid constraints on backing the Syrian opposition.

Leonardo DiCaprio, star of Inception, reveals he suffers from anxiety over trivial matters, despite his successful career. He describes his stomach churning over "really stupid stuff" that shouldn't cause anxiety. DiCaprio, who rose to fame with Titanic, admits he "got to be wild and nuts" after its success but avoided the pitfalls that claimed the lives of some of his peers, including Jonathan Brandis and River Phoenix. The actor, known for his breakout role, says he had better success meeting girls before Titanic, noting that there wasn't a perception of him solely for his fame.

Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas announced plans to seek full UN membership during his upcoming UN General Assembly address, setting up a potential diplomatic clash with Israel and the United States. Abbas stated his intention to present a membership bid to the UN Security Council, aiming for recognition of a state with 1967 borders. He emphasized that this move is not intended to delegitimize Israel but to advance negotiations from a position of equality. The decision comes as the Obama administration faces an acute dilemma, as it supports direct talks while Arab countries rally behind the Palestinian cause. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized Abbas's approach, maintaining that peace cannot be achieved through a unilateral UN campaign. Hamas, the Palestinian faction controlling Gaza, dismissed Abbas's move as a futile attempt to justify ongoing negotiations with Israel. The United States has vowed to veto the bid, and the process faces procedural challenges, potentially delaying a final decision. Abbas's strategy may aim to create time for alternative negotiation frameworks to develop, but most analysts fear it

A study published in the journal Health, Behavior and Policy Review found that happier individuals are twice as likely to have better heart health compared to those who are less optimistic. The research, which analyzed data from over 5,100 adults, showed that higher levels of optimism correlated with improved cardiovascular health metrics, including blood pressure, body mass index, and physical activity. Even after adjusting for socio-demographic factors and poor mental health, the association between optimism and heart health remained significant. The findings suggest that a positive outlook on life could be a valuable tool in cardiovascular health management, potentially offering a new approach to prevention strategies.

"Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales" sailed into first place at the domestic box office with a three-day total of $62.2 million from 4,276 locations, marking the lowest opening for a Pirates movie since the original. The film, with a $230 million production budget, is expected to make $270.6 million overseas, highlighting the franchise's reliance on international audiences. Meanwhile, "Baywatch" struggled, earning only $18.1 million in its first three days, far below early estimates. "Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2" maintained its success, adding $19.1 million in its third weekend. Fox's "Alien: Covenant" and Warner Bros.' "Everything, Everything" rounded out the top five, with modest performances. Disney continued its strong showing, becoming the first studio to earn over $1 billion in 2017.

Protesters and the NYPD were on a collision course Friday over the cleaning of Zuccotti Park, with Occupy Wall Street vowing to resist eviction. The city said protesters could return after the cleanup but without sleeping bags, tents, and tarps. "We see this as a pretext to shut the occupation down," said a protester. They planned to form a human chain to block the cleanup and potentially face mass arrests. Brookfield Properties, the park owner, cited unsanitary conditions. Mayor Bloomberg assured protesters they could return after the cleanup, but Police Commissioner Kelly said camping gear would not be allowed back. Council members rallied to support the protesters, calling on the mayor to protect the demonstrations. The protesters had already begun cleaning the park themselves.

Donald Trump's former personal driver, Noel Cintron, has sued the Trump Organization for unpaid overtime and alleged underpayment over a 20-year period. Cintron, who worked for Trump from 1994 to 2016, claims he was only given two raises in 15 years, with the second raise coming with the loss of health benefits, which saved the Trump Corporation approximately $18,000 annually. He also alleges he worked about 3,300 hours of uncompensated overtime during his last six years on the job, potentially owed $178,000 in back pay. The Trump Organization denies the claims, stating that Cintron was paid "generously and in accordance with the law."

An American woman missing since April while walking a famous Christian pilgrimage route in northern Spain has likely been found dead on a rural property. The body discovered on a small farm near the Camino de Santiago, also known as the St. James Way, is believed to be that of Denise Thiem, 41, of Arizona. Thiem was last seen on April 5 in the town of Astorga, which is on the pilgrimage route leading to the cathedral in Santiago de Compostela, believed to house the remains of St. James, one of Jesus' apostles. The 39-year-old prime suspect, Miguel Angel Munoz, was arrested in the town of Grandas de Salime, 200 kilometers north of Astorga, after a police operation. Munoz led investigators to his property where the body was found. The FBI cooperated in the search, which involved about 300 officers and military personnel. Thousands gathered in Soho on Monday night to honor the victims of the Orlando shooting at Pulse nightclub. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and London Mayor Sadiq Khan were among those in attendance. Attendees stood in silence, holding Pride banners, before releasing 49 rainbow balloons and singing "Bridge Over Troubled Water" with the London Gay Men's Chorus.

Rush Limbaugh recently urged listeners to call Congress on air, an unusual move for the conservative radio host. Limbaugh, who typically does not mobilize listeners for political action, recalled only doing so once before in the 1990s for a U.S. News & World Report profile. Limbaugh demonstrated the impact by tying up the Capitol switchboard and explained his current action as a response to the health care legislation, emphasizing the need for the American people to voice their opposition.

A New Jersey couple on their way to a wedding in Pittsburgh died in a chain-reaction crash on Interstate 78 in Berks County. Kathryn Schurtz, 35, and her fiancé Joseph Kearney were killed when their vehicle was struck by a tractor-trailer and pushed into another, setting off a crash involving five tractor-trailers. The couple was driving to their wedding in Pittsburgh when the accident occurred. Schurtz worked as the Head of Platform Partnerships for Oracle Data Cloud in New York City. A visitation will be held at Immaculate Heart of Mary R.C. Church in Scotch Plains, New Jersey, and donations can be made to the Kathryn M. Schurtz Scholarship Fund at Union Catholic High School.

New York Giants players and fans are celebrating their Super Bowl victory with a parade through the city, starting at Battery Place and Washington Street, ending at City Hall Plaza where Mayor Michael Bloomberg will present the Key to the City. The event is drawing large crowds, and the Giants are in attendance. The celebration comes as some question whether honoring veterans should wait until conflicts are over, potentially sending a mixed message about the ongoing efforts of U.S. servicemen and women.

Attorney General Eric Holder announced plans to provide guidance to banks to facilitate transactions with legal marijuana businesses, addressing the challenges faced by these businesses due to cash-heavy operations. Holder emphasized the need for these businesses to use the banking system for security and public safety reasons. The guidance, being developed jointly by the Justice and Treasury departments, aims to prevent large amounts of cash from accumulating in these businesses, which poses security risks. While the guidance will not grant banks a green light to accept deposits, it will instruct prosecutors not to prioritize cases involving legal marijuana businesses that use banks. This move comes in the wake of Colorado and Washington state legalizing marijuana for recreational use, creating legal tensions as the drug remains federally illegal. The details of the guidance remain unclear, and its application is uncertain, potentially affecting only states where marijuana is legal for recreational use or medical purposes.

North Korea fired a short-range missile into the Sea of Japan on Sunday, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency. This comes after three short-range guided missiles were launched into the sea on Saturday. South Korea has increased monitoring and is maintaining a high level of readiness. Tensions in the region have eased since last month, when North Korea threatened war and conducted a nuclear test. Short-range missile launches are not uncommon, but given recent rhetoric, they have raised security concerns. The United Nations Secretary General called for North Korea to refrain from further launches and return to nuclear talks. South Korea criticized the missile tests and urged dialogue over a suspended inter-Korean industrial park.

Israel's cabinet authorized the mobilization of up to 75,000 reservists, preparing for a possible Gaza invasion after Palestinians fired rockets toward Jerusalem and Tel Aviv. Hamas claimed responsibility for the attacks, which marked the first time Jerusalem faced rocket fire in decades. Israel's air and missile strikes killed 30 in Gaza, while three Israeli civilians were killed by a rocket. The Israeli military reported 97 rockets hit Israel, 99 intercepted by Iron Dome. Tanks and self-propelled guns were seen near the border, and 16,000 reservists were already called to active duty. Israel's Prime Minister Netanyahu warned Hamas would face an "intolerable price" if it continued attacks. Hamas vowed to retaliate, saying Israel should expect "more surprises." Egypt's Prime Minister Hisham Kandil visited Gaza, denouncing Israeli aggression and pledging to mediate a truce. The conflict has killed 30 in Gaza and three in

A Florida woman, Felicia Nevins, called the Pasco County Sheriff's Office for help after forgetting to remove a rubber O-ring from a thermos containing sperm and dry ice, fearing it might explode. The sheriff's office posted details of the incident on Facebook, leading to widespread sharing and Nevins feeling mortified. Despite not using her name, enough details were shared for her to be identified, causing her distress and embarrassment. The sheriff's office defended its action, emphasizing the importance of safety information, but Nevins felt her privacy was violated and expressed her dissatisfaction with the social media strategy.

French nuclear safety institute IRSN suggests an accident occurred at a nuclear fuel treatment site or center for radioactive medicine in Russia or Kazakhstan in late September, based on measurements of ruthenium-106 in the atmosphere across Europe. The release, estimated at 100 to 300 teraBecquerels, was likely in a zone south of the Ural mountains, between the Volga and Ural rivers. Russian authorities deny any accident on their territory. IRSN ruled out a reactor accident or satellite crash as sources. Concentrations of ruthenium-106 in Europe posed no health or environmental risks. IRSN simulations indicate the release occurred during the last week of September, with no specific location identified.

Soylent, the liquid meal replacement popular among tech-savvy millennials, is expanding its retail presence by partnering with 7-Eleven. Starting July 10, 18 7-Eleven stores in the greater Los Angeles area will sell three flavors of Soylent—Cacao, Cafe Coffiest, and Cafe Chai. This marks the first time Soylent will be available in a traditional brick-and-mortar store, previously only sold online and through Amazon. The company aims to test this distribution model as part of a broader retail strategy. Soylent advertises its products as nutritious and convenient, catering to busy lifestyles. However, the company has faced criticism and recalls due to digestive issues reported by some users.

Hillary Clinton's doctor released a letter detailing her mild bacterial pneumonia diagnosis and overall good health, aimed at addressing concerns about her recent illness. The letter, from Clinton's personal physician, Lisa Bardack, confirms the pneumonia diagnosis and notes that Clinton is halfway through her antibiotic treatment. It also includes information about her medications, including Coumadin, a blood thinner, and her normal vital statistics, such as blood pressure and cholesterol levels. Clinton canceled several campaign events after becoming severely dehydrated and leaving a 9/11 memorial service early. The revelation comes as both Clinton and Trump's campaigns have faced scrutiny over their handling of health information, with Trump also releasing some of his own medical records during a recent television appearance.

Why did Facebook's IPO face a rocky start? Reuters reports that Morgan Stanley, the lead underwriter, unexpectedly delivered negative revenue forecasts to major clients during the IPO roadshow, just days before the offering. This sudden caution, coming as an investor roadshow was underway, was a big shock to some investors and may have contributed to the weak performance of Facebook shares, which fell more than 18% below the IPO price on their second and third days of trading. The underwriter's analysts, required to operate independently of the marketing team, are expected to have lowered their forecasts after Facebook amended its prospectus to warn about the impact of mobile users on revenue growth. While JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs also revised their estimates, Morgan Stanley's actions were seen as highly unusual and potentially problematic. The company declined to comment on who was informed about the revised forecasts.

A key phone call led U.S. intelligence to Osama bin Laden's hideout in Abbottabad, Pakistan, where Navy SEALs killed the world's most wanted terrorist. The breakthrough came from a trusted bin Laden courier, identified through years of CIA work. The courier's call, monitored by U.S. intelligence, revealed his location, allowing the SEALs to storm the compound and kill bin Laden. The operation, which took about 40 minutes, was meticulously planned to avoid detection and ensure bin Laden's death could be confirmed. Bin Laden's body was later buried at sea in a traditional Islamic ceremony aboard a U.S. warship. The successful raid was seen as a defining moment in the war on terrorism.

The New York Times Book Review faced criticism for recommending a book by David Icke, a controversial author accused of antisemitism. In an interview, Alice Walker, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author of The Color Purple, mentioned Icke's work "And the Truth Shall Set You Free" among books on her nightstand. Critics, including Tablet magazine's Yair Rosenberg, condemned this recommendation, calling Icke's book an "unhinged antisemitic conspiracy tract." The Times defended its decision, stating that the recommendation does not imply an endorsement by editors. However, this incident highlights the ongoing issue of cultural figures promoting antisemitic content without proper scrutiny.

The owner of a Frisco hospice company, Brad Harris, is accused of ordering nurses to administer excessive doses of morphine to hasten patients' deaths and boost profits, according to an FBI affidavit. Harris, an accountant who founded Novus Health Services in 2012, allegedly instructed employees to "make this patient go bye-bye" via text messages and directed nurses to overdose patients to avoid Medicare and Medicaid payment penalties. The company faced a raid in September 2015, and Harris has not been charged. Novus has filed lawsuits against several former employees for violating non-compete agreements and for allegedly taking company money as they left.

Herman Cain faces growing doubts in New Hampshire, where he trails Romney, Ron Paul, and Newt Gingrich in the polls. Cain's recent controversies, including sexual harassment allegations and a gaffe about Libya, have dampened his chances. Despite high hopes, Cain's campaign decided to cancel a scheduled meeting with the influential Union Leader newspaper, missing an opportunity to secure its endorsement. Cain defended himself by emphasizing the importance of leadership over deep foreign policy knowledge. However, the Union Leader's decision to headline Cain's no-show highlights the challenges he faces in the state. With just seven weeks until the primary, Cain's campaign must navigate these obstacles to maintain momentum.

Lorde, the 16-year-old New Zealand singer, has been named VH1’s You Oughta Know artist for September. Her hit song “Royals” topped the Billboard Alternative charts and has been called the fastest charting alternative song in years. Inspired by a National Geographic photo of a baseball player wearing a “Royals” shirt, Lorde also drew from her fascination with historical royalty to create the song. Despite its popularity, a San Francisco radio station has banned the song from its airwaves until the San Francisco Giants win the World Series, with the station’s program director responding that they removed the song “as of 4pm today” until the end of the World Series.

President Obama ordered flags at the White House and other federal buildings to fly at half-staff in honor of five armed forces members killed in Chattanooga last week, amid criticism over the delay. The flags will remain at half-staff through Saturday as a mark of respect. Obama's decision came after Speaker John Boehner ordered flags at the U.S. Capitol to be lowered. Conservatives criticized the president for the delay, with Rep. Mac Thornberry calling it "unconscionable" and Rep. Duncan Hunter urging immediate action. The White House and U.S. Capitol both lowered their flags by Tuesday afternoon, resolving the discrepancy.

The former U.S. Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr. and his wife, former Chicago Ald. Sandi Jackson, were sentenced to prison for their misuse of campaign funds. Jesse Jackson Jr., 48, received 2.5 years, while Sandi Jackson, 49, was sentenced to one year. Both expressed remorse and cited personal struggles, but the judge rejected their pleas for leniency. The sentencing marks the end of a political dynasty and highlights the Jacksons' misuse of nearly $750,000 from Jesse's campaign fund. The judge emphasized the need for equal justice and rejected arguments for probation, sentencing the couple based on their actions rather than their status.

A rat infestation closed down a government office in Kissimmee storing donations for Puerto Rico, contaminating supplies that were never sent. The Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration’s executive director Carlos Mercader stated the office lacked funds to ship the items and previous efforts to distribute through other organizations were unsuccessful. Mercader plans to conduct an inventory to identify suitable items for Puerto Rican evacuees. The office, managed by Mercader since the recent resignation of Frances Ortiz, was infested since August, a month before Hurricane Maria hit. The reports come amid other administrative failures in aid distribution to Puerto Rico, including a $156 million contract awarded to a small company that delivered only 50,000 of 30 million promised meals, according to CNN.

Texas teen Ethan Couch, now 18, admitted to using drugs and drinking alcohol frequently in a newly-released deposition, revealing details of his privileged life before a fatal 2013 drunk driving crash that killed four people. Couch, who was 16 at the time, barely remembers the night he crashed his father's pickup truck with three times the legal limit of alcohol in his system. His parents, Tonya and Fred Couch, testified that they sometimes allowed their son to stay unsupervised in the family’s second home and let him drive before he was of age. The psychologist who testified in his criminal case, Dr. G. Dick Miller, used the term "affluenza" to describe Couch's upbringing, suggesting he was spoiled and lacked consequences for his actions. Couch was sentenced to 10 years of probation and treatment instead of jail, a decision that outraged the victims' families. Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana, faced significant backlash after the restaurant's owners declared they would not cater a gay wedding, aligning with the state's Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The owners, Crystal and Kevin O'Connor, received death threats and had to close the business for a time. Despite the controversy, they received over $600,000 in donations from supporters, allowing them to reopen. However, the ordeal led to the restaurant's permanent closure. Many reviews on Yelp reflect the polarized opinions, with some praising the pizza and service while others criticize it harshly due to the owners' stance. The incident sparked a debate on freedom of religion and discrimination, with supporters of the O'Connor family arguing their right to uphold their beliefs, while critics accused them of bigotry.

Amazon is expanding its delivery services to include business customers, launching a new "Shipping with Amazon" service in Los Angeles, according to the Wall Street Journal. This move could put Amazon in direct competition with established delivery giants like FedEx and UPS. The service is expected to offer competitive pricing, potentially undercutting rivals. Shares of FedEx and UPS saw a significant drop in pre-market trading. UPS maintains it remains a partner with Amazon, stating it will continue to support the e-commerce giant and other customers without commenting on specific business strategies.

Canned foods may contain bisphenol A (BPA), which can leach into the food from the liner. Two new studies link chemicals like BPA and phthalates, commonly found in processed and packaged foods, to obesity and insulin resistance in adolescents. In one study, higher levels of DEHP, a phthalate found in processed foods, were associated with increased insulin resistance, a condition that can lead to Type 2 diabetes. However, the study does not prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Another study found that children with higher urinary BPA levels had double the risk of being obese compared to those with lower levels. Both studies suggest a link but caution that further research is needed to establish causality. The findings highlight the potential health risks of consuming processed and packaged foods and suggest that reducing exposure to these chemicals may help prevent obesity and related conditions.

The U.S. economy grew at a modest 1.3% rate in the second quarter, down from the initial estimate of 1.9%, and the first quarter's growth was revised down to 0.4%, the weakest pace since the recession ended. Higher gas prices and reduced consumer spending contributed to the slower growth. The 2007-2009 recession was even worse than previously thought, with the economy shrinking 5.1% from the start of the recession to its end in June 2009, 1 percentage point worse than the previous estimate. Among the previous 10 postwar recessions, only two had larger declines in output. The government attributed the bigger declines in output to weaker consumer spending and business investment. Growth in 2010 was slightly stronger than initially estimated, with the economy growing 3% instead of 2.9%.

A 911 call reporting shots fired at Virginia College in Spartanburg on April Fool's Day led to a full-scale law enforcement response, with multiple patrol cars and deputies rushing to the scene. The call was reportedly made by Angela Timmons to her daughter, who then called 911 after not receiving a response from Timmons. Timmons claims it was a harmless April Fool's joke between her and her daughter, but the Spartanburg County Sheriff's Office charged her with disturbing schools, aggravated breach of peace, and two counts of unlawful use of telephone. Sheriff Chuck Wright expressed disappointment in Timmons' poor judgment, stating that deputies were prepared for a serious situation like Columbine or Sandy Hook. Timmons faces up to 30 days in jail and a fine of up to $1,000. Virginia College's vice president of marketing issued an apology for the incident, stating that it was a poor judgment call that does not reflect the institution.

President Donald Trump is escalating his criticism of Attorney General Jeff Sessions, suggesting the Justice Department's recent indictments of two popular Republican congressmen, Rep. Duncan Hunter and Rep. Chris Collins, may have jeopardized Republican midterm prospects. Trump tweeted, "Obama era investigations, of two very popular Republican Congressmen were brought to a well publicized charge, just ahead of the Mid-Terms, by the Jeff Sessions Justice Department." He added, "Two easy wins now in doubt because there is not enough time. Good job Jeff......" The indictments, which began in 2016 and 2017, have raised hopes for Democrats, though both seats are likely to remain in GOP hands. Trump's comments highlight his disregard for the Justice Department's independence and his view of the department as an extension of his personal and political interests. Sessions' chief of staff has stated he has no intention of resigning despite Trump's constant criticism.

Israeli airstrikes and tank shells targeted parts of Gaza, killing a 4-year-old girl and injuring others, while a Gaza sniper killed a Bedouin Israeli citizen near the border fence. Israeli warplanes and tanks struck al Qassam Brigades camps, reportedly killing 11 people. Hamas claimed the killed Israeli was a soldier, but the military said he was a civilian. The Israeli military blamed Hamas for the sniper attack and vowed a strong response. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon condemned the violence and deaths. Israel tightened restrictions on Gaza workers near the border fence, citing security concerns. Israeli officials warned Hamas to prevent further attacks and stressed the need for quiet in the south.

The captain of the Costa Concordia, Francesco Schettino, apologized for the accident that claimed 32 lives and said he was distracted when the ship struck a rock. In his first full television interview since the January 13 disaster, Schettino acknowledged his responsibility as captain but insisted others should share the blame. He admitted to being distracted and not having command of the ship at the time of the accident. Schettino denies charges including manslaughter and causing a shipwreck. He broke down when discussing the youngest victim. The captain claims he saved lives by steering the ship into shallow water.

Protesters clashed at a Trump rally at the Minnesota State Capitol, with five masked individuals, including Woody Kaine, a son of Democratic vice presidential nominee Tim Kaine, arrested for allegedly throwing a smoke bomb. Kaine resisted officers, requiring a knee strike to subdue him. The incident occurred during a rally where both pro- and anti-Trump groups disrupted the event. The Ramsey County attorney’s office declined to file charges, citing insufficient evidence for felony-level riot, though a misdemeanor charge remains under investigation. Political questions arose regarding the decision, with the Republican Party chairman suggesting political motives influenced the decision.

German police have recovered over 100 items stolen from John Lennon's estate, including three diaries, two pairs of his signature round glasses, a cigarette case, and a handwritten music score, reports the BBC. The items were stolen from Yoko Ono in 2006 and recently displayed at Berlin police headquarters. A 58-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of handling stolen goods, and another suspect, living in Turkey, remains unattainable. The items, including a tape recording of a Beatles concert, were confiscated from an auction house in Berlin and returned to Ono, though a timeline for their full return is uncertain.

North Korea launched an unidentified projectile from its capital Pyongyang that flew over Japan, officials said, escalating tensions in the region. The South Korean and U.S. militaries are analyzing the launch, which landed in the Pacific Ocean with no reported damage. This comes days after North Korea fired three short-range ballistic missiles and a month after testing an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the U.S. mainland. North Korea typically reacts with anger to U.S.-South Korean military drills, which are currently underway, and the country's U.N. ambassador described the exercises as "provocative and aggressive."

New York lawmakers are negotiating a deal to expand the state’s DNA database, which could include collecting DNA samples from all convicted criminals. This move is part of broader legislative efforts addressing the state budget, redistricting, and a new pension plan. The current database, created in the 1990s, only covers certain crimes and has been expanded three times since then. The state’s DNA database could be expanded to include all convicted criminals, potentially leading to more convictions and exonerations. However, there are concerns about access to the database by defense lawyers and the potential for wrongful convictions. The governor is proposing a new pension plan, but lawmakers are considering dropping a controversial 401(k) option. Negotiations are moving quickly, with a federal court deadline for redistricting and a state budget requirement by April 1st.

The Union Street Guest House in Hudson, NY, offers a unique stay but faces significant criticism, particularly over its controversial $500 fee for negative online reviews. Guests have reported issues such as poor cleanliness, noisy neighbors, and rudeness from staff. Despite some positive reviews praising the vintage decor, many guests warn potential visitors to seek alternatives. The hotel's strict review policy has sparked outrage, with some calling it unethical and comparing it to intimidation tactics.

Hillary Clinton criticized FBI Director James Comey's decision to inform Congress about new emails related to her private server, calling it "unprecedented" and "deeply troubling." Clinton urged Comey to release more information and accused Republican rival Donald Trump of trying to mislead voters. The Clinton campaign accused Comey of being "light on facts" and "heavy on innuendo." Campaign chairman John Podesta and manager Robby Mook called for Comey to explain his actions, suggesting they may have entered political territory. Meanwhile, Trump continued to use the issue to attack Clinton, questioning her loyalty to Huma Abedin. The FBI's investigation into Anthony Weiner's laptop may not reveal new information, according to Clinton aides.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds were spotted sharing a friendly dinner at Blue Ribbon restaurant in New York City, just one week after announcing their divorce. They were seen laughing and smiling, contradicting rumors of a reconciliation. "They just wanted to connect and have a friendly chat," a source says. "They aren't reconciling. This was just two people who were married being civil and friendly." The couple, who married in 2008, have no children and Reynolds was in New York for a photo shoot during a break from filming "The Change Up." Their public dinner highlights Scarlett's intention to show that exes can remain civil and that divorce does not mean an end to friendship.

Travelers can now enjoy a deeper, more restful sleep with the Gravity blanket, a high-tech weighted blanket designed to reduce stress and anxiety by simulating the sensation of being hugged. The blanket, which uses "deep pressure touch stimulation" therapy, is made with high-density plastic poly pellets designed to relax the nervous system by targeting pressure points on the body. These pellets are meant to be between seven and 12 percent of the user’s weight, with three weight sizes available: 15 lbs, 20 lbs, and 25 lbs. The blanket features a soft fleece cover and a cotton inner shell, ensuring comfort and breathability. According to its designer, John Fiorentino, the Gravity blanket can be used to treat a variety of conditions, including insomnia, post-traumatic stress disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump launched a broad attack on Hillary Clinton's experience, honesty, and foreign policy expertise during a 40-minute speech. His claims were fact-checked, revealing numerous inaccuracies. Trump accused Clinton of single-handedly destabilizing the Middle East, but her tenure did not initiate the conflicts in Libya, Syria, or Iran. He also exaggerated Clinton's role in the Benghazi attack, despite her having no direct military decision-making authority. Trump claimed Clinton wanted to resettle hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of Middle Eastern refugees, but the actual U.S. budget for refugee resettlement is much lower. Other false claims included Trump's business success, the value of his assets, and Clinton's acceptance of expensive gifts from Brunei. Fact-checkers also debunked Trump's assertions about the U.S. trade deficit with China and the effectiveness of Obamacare. Trump's proposed tax cuts were criticized for potentially increasing government debt and interest rates.

A Texas couple, Forrest and Donna Sanco, both 56, who reconnected and fell in love after high school, went missing while on a private plane trip to the Bahamas. They were planning to elope on their final destination, Rum Cay. No one heard from them after they left Freeport, Bahamas, on September 26. Their niece, LeeAnn Burger, says they landed in North Eleuthera and purchased fuel but never made it to Rum Cay. The couple had a Cessna 150, which was recently purchased by Forrest. Despite a GoFundMe campaign to hire private search crews, the couple remains missing. The search continues, with authorities leading the effort, but the family is facing resistance and frustration.

Caitlyn Jenner, the former Olympic gold medalist and reality TV star, has undergone gender reassignment surgery as part of her transition from male to female, as detailed in her new memoir, "The Secrets of My Life," which is set to be released on April 25. Jenner, 67, confirms in the book that she had the surgery in January 2017, nearly two years after publicly revealing her identity as a trans woman in a Diane Sawyer interview. She states the surgery was successful and that she feels "wonderful and liberated." Jenner decided to disclose the information to end the constant inquiries about her anatomy. "I am telling you because I believe in candor," she writes. "So all of you can stop staring. You want to know, so now you know. Which is why this is the first time, and the last time, I will ever speak of it."

Millions of Americans take proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) for acid reflux and heartburn, but new research suggests these widely used medications may increase the risk of ischemic stroke. In a study presented at an American Heart Association conference, researchers found that overall stroke risk increased 21% among patients taking PPIs. At the highest doses, the risk increased by 79% for Protonix patients, 50% for Nexium patients, and 33% for Prilosec and Prevacid patients. The study, conducted in Denmark among 250,000 patients, adds to growing concerns about the cardiovascular safety of PPIs, which have been linked to heart attacks, kidney disease, and dementia. While the drugs are generally considered safe and effective, the findings raise questions about their long-term use and the need for re-evaluation by the pharmaceutical industry and regulatory agencies.

During the U.S. Women's World Cup final victory over Japan, some fans began relating the win to Japan's 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, sparking a Twitter debate. Hashtags like "Pearl Harbor" trended, with users making references to the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. While some supported the comments, many condemned them as insensitive. The original tweet received over 8,500 retweets, but the majority of reactions were critical, with users urging respect for historical tragedies.

Last year, Harvard University appointed its first female president. Now, the institution is set to celebrate another milestone: the installation of the first black female as dean of Harvard College. Harvard President Drew Gilpin Faust, who became the first woman to lead the university after nearly four centuries of male presidents, announced the appointment of Evelynn Hammonds, Harvard’s senior vice provost for faculty development and diversity, to the top post in Harvard College. Hammonds, 55, will be the first female and first black person to hold this position. Her appointment comes as Yale administrators are launching efforts to encourage more racial diversity within their upper ranks. Hammonds’ role will cover a wide range of responsibilities, including academic affairs, student life, and general administration. She expressed readiness to tackle challenges with her colleagues’ help. This appointment marks the second milestone for Harvard in breaking gender barriers, following the appointment of Faust as the first female president. Hammonds’ background includes a history of promoting faculty diversity

Fifteen former members of the Church Committee, which investigated CIA activities in the 1970s, have written to President Obama and Attorney General Loretta Lynch, urging leniency for Edward Snowden. They argue that Snowden’s disclosures led to significant reforms, including changes to the Patriot Act and enhanced privacy protections for foreigners. The letter cites past leniency shown to officials like former CIA Director David Petraeus, who received a reduced sentence for leaking classified information. The authors suggest negotiating a plea agreement with Snowden, rather than a full pardon, as a way to balance public benefits with legal consequences.

A new national investigation by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution has uncovered 450 cases of doctors who were brought before medical regulators or courts for sexual misconduct or sex crimes in 2016 and 2017. In nearly half of those cases, the AJC found, the doctors remain licensed to practice medicine, no matter whether the victims were patients or employees, adults or children. Even some doctors criminally convicted are back in practice, demonstrating that a system that forgives doctors—first exposed by the AJC in 2016—has not changed. Examples include Dr. Anthony Bianchi, who was disciplined but allowed to continue practicing under a settlement requiring therapy and a five-year probation. The leniency of penalties for sexually abusive doctors is aggravated by the personal nature of the doctor-patient relationship, with victims often feeling their cases are not adequately addressed. Pope Francis, the 266th Supreme Pontiff, has captured the world’s imagination with his humility and pastoral approach, making him TIME’s 2013 Person of the Year. As Archbishop of Buenos Aires, he frequently visited impoverished neighborhoods, emphasizing the church’s role as a field hospital for the wounded. His papacy has shifted the focus from doctrinal policing to mercy and service, addressing issues like poverty, the role of women, and gay rights. Francis has also restructured the Vatican, appointing a dynamic Almoner to engage more directly with the poor. His actions, from washing the feet of prisoners to advocating for mercy, reflect a new direction for the Catholic Church. While facing criticism for his cautious approach to some issues, Francis’s popularity and reforms have made him a symbol of hope and change.

Lena Dunham, known for her body-positive approach, celebrated Glamour magazine for not Photoshopping her cellulite out of their February 2017 cover. In an Instagram post, Dunham thanked the magazine for letting her be real, stating that her body isn't "fair game" and that it's time for women of all sizes, colors, and gender identities to be recognized as beautiful. Dunham, who has been vocal about her imperfections, highlighted the importance of normalization and inclusivity in popular culture. She also shared that as the creator of Girls, she sometimes felt left out on set but learned to treasure collaboration. Dunham's post received widespread support, with many agreeing that it's time for a more inclusive and positive approach to body image in media.

Truckers are planning to protest by backing up the Capital Beltway around Washington, D.C., to draw attention to their frustrations with regulations and the overall political climate. The group "Truckers for the Constitution" hopes to highlight issues such as low wages, high gas prices, and government spying, framing their protest as a necessity to get lawmakers' attention. They aim to present demands to Congress, including the arrest of officials they believe have violated their constitutional oaths. The protest, scheduled for October 11, could significantly impact D.C. traffic and has garnered significant support, with close to 50,000 likes on a Facebook page.

A new report from the Syrian Centre for Policy Research (SCPR) reveals that the death toll from the five-year conflict in Syria is far higher than previously estimated, with 470,000 deaths, compared to the UN's figure of 250,000. The report also highlights the severe economic and humanitarian impact, estimating $255 billion in overall economic losses and noting that 45% of the population has been displaced. Life expectancy has dropped from 70 in 2010 to 55.4 in 2015, and 1.9 million people have been wounded. The report's findings are more alarming than previous UN estimates and suggest that indirect deaths due to lack of healthcare and resources are significant. A new study of Southern California high school seniors over two decades shows that while cigarette smoking has declined, the combined use of e-cigarettes and cigarettes among 12th graders in 2014 was higher than the rate of smoking alone in 2004, when e-cigarettes were not available. This suggests that e-cigarettes are not merely substituting for cigarettes but are also attracting a new group of users who would not have smoked if e-cigarettes were not available. The study, published in the journal Pediatrics, indicates that e-cigarettes may be contributing to nicotine addiction and potentially leading to increased smoking rates among youth. Researchers found that never-smoking e-cigarette users were six times more likely to start smoking cigarettes within a year compared to those who had never used e-cigarettes. The findings raise concerns that e-cigarettes could be a gateway to traditional smoking, especially among those who might not have otherwise taken up the habit.

A Blue Angels F/A-18 fighter jet crashed near Nashville, Tennessee, killing the pilot just days before a weekend air show. The pilot, Marine Capt. Jeff Kuss, was the only casualty, and no civilians were hurt. The Navy said the pilot was beginning to take off during an afternoon practice session when the crash happened. Five other F/A-18 jets landed safely moments after the crash. Adm. John Richardson, the Navy's top officer, expressed condolences and promised a full investigation. This crash comes a day after a U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds jet crashed in Colorado, with the pilot ejecting safely.

CNN's Jim Acosta apologized on Friday for sending a direct message with the words "F– You" to a Twitter user, later revealing he had mistaken the person for an old friend from the campaign days. The incident began after Acosta criticized the loud music at a Trump campaign rally, leading to a back-and-forth with a GOP consultant and former aide to Melania Trump. Acosta blocked the consultant after sending the message. Acosta has often clashed with the Trump administration, with the president previously calling him "fake news" and press secretary Sarah Sanders engaging in sharp exchanges with him.

Dennis Rodman, the former NBA star turned amateur diplomat, has criticized President Trump for his frequent Twitter attacks on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rodman, who calls Kim his friend, expressed a desire for Trump to call him and ask about Kim's character, stating that he has never met Kim or spoken with his people. Rodman, who has visited North Korea several times, hopes to broker peace between the two leaders but has not spoken with Trump in a while. Rodman's representative acknowledged that alcoholism has been a struggle for him and that he is currently dealing with personal issues. Rodman was recently arrested for DUI in Newport Beach, having failed a field sobriety test and tested over the legal limit, spending 7 hours in jail before being released.

The Obama administration aims to cut food waste in half by 2030 as part of efforts to combat climate change. This initiative, led by the USDA and EPA, involves partnerships with private sector, charitable organizations, and local governments to reduce food loss and improve overall food security. The goal is to address the significant environmental impact of food waste, which accounts for a substantial portion of U.S. methane emissions. By reducing food waste by just 15%, the U.S. could feed an additional 25 million people annually. The USDA will launch a consumer education campaign and continue initiatives like the U.S. Food Waste Challenge to promote food loss and waste reduction. Support from food companies, including Albertson's and FreshDirect, highlights the potential for significant impact through these collaborative efforts.

A cattle roundup on public land in southern Nevada was abruptly halted by federal land managers to avoid potential violence, returning about 300 head of cattle to the rancher Cliven Bundy. The BLM cited safety concerns for employees and the public. The controversial situation, which drew armed militia supporters, ended with the closure of northbound lanes of Interstate 15 near Bundy's ranch. U.S. Senator Dean Heller urged calm and appealed for supporters to return home. The dispute, centered on grazing rights on federal land, has been ongoing for decades, with Bundy claiming his family has been ranching in the area since the 1800s. The BLM asserts Bundy owes about $1 million in back fees for illegal grazing.

A top North Korean diplomat who served as the ambassador's deputy in London has defected to South Korea, marking the highest-ranking North Korean official to do so in nearly two decades. The diplomat, Thae Yong-ho, 55, was part of North Korea's efforts to promote a positive image of the regime in the West. He recently arrived in South Korea with his family, expressing disillusionment with North Korea's increasingly isolated government under Kim Jong-un. South Korean officials say Thae cited his disgust with the regime, admiration for South Korea's democratic system, and concerns for his family's future as reasons for his defection.

Actor Jeffrey Tambor, best known for his role as Maura Pfefferman in the critically acclaimed series Transparent, has faced significant backlash following allegations of sexual harassment from co-workers Van Barnes and Trace Lysette. Despite denying the claims, Tambor has acknowledged his past outbursts and temperamental behavior, expressing regret for his actions. His firing from Transparent and subsequent public apology have sparked discussions about the #MeToo movement, the challenges faced by transgender actors in Hollywood, and the complex dynamics within the entertainment industry. Tambor's current focus is on learning from his experiences and ensuring he behaves more appropriately on set in the future.

Tyra Banks will host the 12th season of "America's Got Talent," taking over from Nick Cannon after eight years. The show, featuring a variety of talents competing for a $1 million prize, will air live from the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles this summer with judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Heidi Klum, and Howie Mandel returning.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) has revealed that its database was hacked by a Russian group, Fancy Bear, which posted confidential medical data of several US Olympic athletes online, including tennis stars Serena and Venus Williams, gymnastics champion Simone Biles, and basketball player Elena Delle Donne. Wada claims the hackers accessed passwords through a spear-phishing attack. The group has accused the athletes of using "illicit strong drugs" with Therapeutic Use Exemptions, but US Anti-Doping Agency chief Travis Tygart says the athletes have followed the rules. Wada director-general Olivier Niggli expressed concern over the breach, which he said undermines the global anti-doping system. The hack comes amid ongoing doping controversies, including the ban of Russia's track and field team from the Rio Olympics.

The Israeli military launched a ground offensive into Gaza, stepping up its 11-day-old operation against Palestinian militants. Troops and tanks entered Gaza to target Hamas infrastructure, with Israel calling up 18,000 more reservists. Gaza's health ministry reported 24 Palestinians killed, including a five-month-old child, and 200 injured. Israel confirmed killing 14 "terrorists" and suffered its first military fatality. Palestinian officials said 1,370 homes were destroyed and 18,000 displaced. The ground operation followed 10 days of airstrikes and bombings. Hamas condemned the Israeli action, warning of a "heavy price." The operation aims to destroy Hamas tunnels and show that Israel will not tolerate attacks. Palestinian leaders called for a truce, as Egypt mediated talks in Cairo. A temporary ceasefire allowed aid distribution but was violated by both sides. Israel warned Gaza residents to evacuate areas of operation.

Donald Trump's Republican National Convention lineup includes two daytime soap opera stars: Kimberlin Brown and Antonio Sabato Jr. Brown, known for her roles in "The Young and the Restless" and "The Bold and the Beautiful," will speak during the Tuesday evening session and is introduced by Ben Carson. The inclusion of these actors, alongside other unconventional choices like Dana White and Natalie Gulbis, reflects Trump's "showbiz" approach to the convention. Kimberlin Brown's excitement for her speaking role is evident in her recent social media posts. The convention theme "Make America Work Again" will feature speakers emphasizing economic themes, including Trump's business background and his promise to revive the economy. Other notable speakers include Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, House Speaker Paul Ryan, and former rivals Chris Christie and Ben Carson, who are now supporting Trump. The convention aims to unify the party and highlight Trump's readiness for the presidency.

The controversy surrounding Sandra Bland's death in a Texas jail cell continues, with some questioning whether she was already dead in her mugshot. Forensic experts, including Dr. Michael Baden, who conducted a family-requested autopsy for Michael Brown, dismiss the idea as "ridiculous." Bland, 28, was found hanging in her cell three days after being arrested for failing to signal a lane change. While the medical examiner ruled her death a suicide, some social media users have pointed to inconsistencies in her mugshot, such as the positioning of her shoulders and the background color matching the cell floor. However, forensic pathologists emphasize that it's impossible to determine if someone is alive or dead from a photo alone, and Bland's appearance in the mugshot is consistent with a living person. The case has sparked debate over the circumstances of her arrest and death, with family members and supporters calling for a thorough investigation.

Donald Trump faced backlash over a tweet featuring a photo of Hillary Clinton with a Star of David overlaid, which critics said was anti-Semitic. The tweet was later deleted and replaced with an image using a circle instead of the Star of David. The original image was traced to a white supremacist message board. Trump's campaign attributed the image to an anti-Hillary Twitter user, but critics argue this explanation is inconsistent with the campaign's usual practice of attributing sources. The Anti-Defamation League condemned the tweet as evidence of extremist sympathies within the Trump campaign. Trump's supporters defended the tweet, while his former campaign manager argued it was a simple star. The incident raised concerns about the campaign's handling of potentially offensive content and its ties to extremist views.

President Obama urges "meaningful action" to prevent gun violence in his weekly radio address, following the tragic shooting at a Connecticut elementary school that killed 26 people, including 20 children. He calls on the nation to come together and take steps to prevent such tragedies, though he does not specify any particular actions. New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg criticizes Obama for not showing enough leadership on gun control. Obama expresses grief for the families affected and emphasizes the need for support. House Speaker John Boehner cancels the Republican weekly address to show solidarity with the nation's mourning.

The youngest son of the late shah of Iran, Prince Alireza Pahlavi, was found dead in his Boston home on January 4, 2011, after allegedly shooting himself. His brother, Reza Pahlavi, announced the death, attributing it to years of sorrow over the loss of his father and sister. Alireza Pahlavi, 44, had struggled with depression following his sister Leila's 2001 death from a drug overdose. The Pahlavi family, once a symbol of Iran's monarchy, has since lived in exile, with Reza Pahlavi taking a public role in opposing Iran's current regime. Alireza's death was marked by a military-like precision, reflecting his disciplined nature. The community of Iranian exiles in the U.S. expressed condolences, though the extent of support for a potential return to monarchy remains unclear.

Vice President Joe Biden officiated the first same-sex wedding at the Naval Observatory, marrying longtime White House staffers Brian Mosteller and Joe Mahshie. Posting a photo on Twitter, Biden expressed happiness for the couple, noting their long-time employment at the White House. His wife, Jill, also tweeted her support. Biden had publicly endorsed same-sex marriage in 2012.

Poland has summoned the U.S. ambassador and demanded an apology over comments on the Holocaust by FBI director James Comey. The foreign ministry said Comey's suggestion in a Washington Post article that some Poles were accomplices was an "insult to thousands of Poles who helped Jews." President Bronislaw Komorowski and Prime Minister Ewa Kopacz both criticized the comments, emphasizing Poland's victim status during World War II. U.S. envoy Stephen Mull clarified that the U.S. believes "Nazi Germany alone" was responsible. Mull stated that any suggestion that Poland or other countries shared responsibility for the Holocaust is "a mistake, harmful and insulting." The article highlights the tension between Poland and the U.S. over historical narratives and the importance of accurate historical representation.

Gigi Hadid, the 22-year-old supermodel, was named one of Glamour's 2017 Women of the Year, joining a class that includes Nicole Kidman, Solange Knowles, Patty Jenkins, and Maxine Waters. Hadid, known for her commercial success and vocal advocacy for issues like gun control and women's personal safety, was praised for her work ethic and kindness. A video of Hadid staring into the camera for four minutes was posted by Glamour, described as "weirdly mesmerizing." The video, while aimed at generating engagement, was criticized for its simplicity and lack of substance, highlighting the challenges magazines face in adapting to a video-first digital landscape.

Scientists have discovered that up to 25% of people infected with Ebola show no symptoms, suggesting the recent West African Ebola epidemic was more widespread than previously thought. A study in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases found that in a Sierra Leone village, 14 out of 187 individuals who were likely exposed to Ebola but not known to have the disease, tested positive for Ebola antibodies. This indicates that a significant portion of Ebola transmission events may have gone undetected during the outbreak. The findings suggest that the definition of Ebola survivorship should be reconsidered, as it could include individuals with minimally symptomatic infections. Further research is needed to understand the potential risk of transmission and clinical sequelae in such individuals.

A dead goose fell from the sky and struck a waterfowl hunter, knocking him unconscious during a hunting party near the Miles River in Dorchester County. The incident occurred around 5 p.m. when the group was shooting at geese. The hunter, Robert Meilhammer, 51, suffered head and facial injuries and was airlifted to Maryland Shock Trauma.

Six people were shot dead in the Russian city of Belgorod on Monday afternoon, with a 14-year-old girl among the victims, reports suggest. The gunman, identified as Sergey Pomazun, 32, opened fire near an arms shop before fleeing in his vehicle. Law enforcement has deployed special forces to search for Pomazun, who has a criminal record and is believed to be armed. The incident has prompted heightened security measures and a reward for information leading to his capture. President Vladimir Putin is informed of the situation, and the city declares days of mourning.

Pope Francis on Sunday emphasized the need for Christians to seek forgiveness from marginalized groups, including gays, during a press conference aboard the papal plane returning from Armenia. He stated, "I repeat what the Catechism of the Catholic Church says: that they must not be discriminated against, that they must be respected and accompanied pastorally." Francis added, "The Church must ask forgiveness for not behaving many times—when I say the Church, I mean Christians! The Church is holy, we are sinners!" The Pope's remarks were seen as a significant shift, with some calling it a "groundbreaking moment." Francis also mentioned the need for apologies to the poor, exploited women, and children exploited for labor, and even for blessing weapons. His comments came in response to a German cardinal who suggested the Catholic Church should apologize for being "very negative" about gays. The Pope's approach reflects his more merciful stance towards marginalized groups, though he did not change the church's doctrine

A study of over 400 men followed for 20 years found no significant link between long-term marijuana use and later physical or mental health issues such as depression, psychotic symptoms, or asthma. The research, published in Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, analyzed data from the Pittsburgh Youth Study, which tracked boys from adolescence into their mid-30s. Participants were divided into groups based on their marijuana use patterns, from low or non-users to early chronic users. Despite tracking health outcomes for over two decades, the study found no differences in health between marijuana users and non-users, suggesting that chronic teenage marijuana use does not necessarily lead to adverse health effects in adulthood. However, the study acknowledges limitations, such as its focus on male participants and the need to consider individual differences in susceptibility to marijuana's effects.

In Mountain View, a police officer stopped a Google self-driving car for traveling at 24 mph in a 35 mph zone, backing up traffic on El Camino Real. The car, operating under the Neighborhood Electric Vehicle Definition, was lawfully traveling at the speed limit. The officer educated the operators about impeding traffic but no ticket was issued. Mountain View Police regularly meet with Google to ensure safe vehicle operation. Google capped its prototype vehicle speed at 25 mph for safety and to make the cars feel approachable. The company has never been ticketed in 1.2 million miles of autonomous driving.

When and how long a baby looks at other people’s eyes offers the earliest behavioral sign to date of whether a child is likely to develop autism, according to a new study. Researchers using eye-tracking technology found that children who were later diagnosed with autism at age 3 looked less at people’s eyes when they were babies than children who did not develop autism. However, the difference was not apparent at birth and emerged between 2 and 6 months of age. By contrast, babies who did not develop autism looked increasingly at people’s eyes until about 9 months old, and then kept their attention to eyes fairly constant into toddlerhood. The eye-tracking differences are not something parents and pediatricians would be able to perceive without the technology and expertise of an autism clinic. The study, published in the journal Nature, involved 110 children, from 2 months to 2 years of age, who were assessed 10 times while watching videos of friendly women acting like playful caregivers. More than 200 people attended an unveiling ceremony for a new Confederate monument in Alabama's Crenshaw County on Sunday. The modest stone marker commemorates "unknown Confederate soldiers" who died in the Civil War but have been forgotten by history, particularly those from Crenshaw County and the surrounding area. The memorial, located in a confederate memorial park, stands among existing monuments, replica cannons, and tall flagpoles flying Confederate and other flags. Attendees, many wearing Confederate attire, gathered to honor the soldiers and support the ongoing movement to remember their sacrifices. The event, organized by the Sons of Confederate Veterans, was not seen as a response to recent racial discord but rather as a way to preserve heritage and history. Despite ongoing debates about Confederate monuments, this ceremony aimed to celebrate and remember the soldiers' contributions.

A 106-year-old woman named Virginia McLaurin danced with joy during a visit to the White House with President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama for Black History Month. McLaurin, visibly elated, squealed and laughed upon meeting the Obamas. The president exclaimed, "She's 106!" Michelle Obama hugged McLaurin and said, "Oh, my goodness! I want to be like you when I grow up." The trio then danced together in the Blue Room, sharing laughter. McLaurin expressed her happiness, saying, "I thought I would never live to get in the White House. And I tell you. I am so happy: A black president."

The Islamic State's advance in northern Iraq has left thousands of Yazidis trapped on Mount Sinjar, facing the choice between descending to certain death at the hands of the Sunni extremists or remaining on the mountain and risking dehydration and starvation. Reports indicate that between 10,000 and 40,000 civilians, primarily Yazidis, are stranded on the mountaintop. The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) has confirmed that at least 40 children have died due to the harsh conditions and displacement. Iraqi politician Vian Dakheel, a Yazidi, described the situation as a "total disaster," with children dying from thirst and lack of food. The Yazidis, followers of an ancient religion, are considered "devil worshippers" by the Islamic State and face execution or enslavement if they do not convert.
