The price of EpiPens, a life-saving device for severe allergies, has surged by over 480% since 2009, prompting outrage and scrutiny. Despite the device containing only a few dollars' worth of epinephrine, the manufacturer, Mylan, charges hundreds of dollars for it. Mylan acquired the EpiPen in 2007 and has capitalized on aggressive marketing and lobbying to maintain a near-monopoly. The company argues that price increases reflect the value of the product and significant investments in support. However, families face financial strain, with some opting to buy cheaper alternatives or refuse the treatment due to cost. Critics, including Senator Bernie Sanders, argue that the price hike is unethical and unnecessary.

Republican New York gubernatorial candidate Carl Paladino faced criticism for remarks he made about homosexuality, telling Matt Lauer on NBC's "Today" show that discrimination against gays is "horrible" and "terrible." Paladino, a Tea Party favorite, had previously given a speech to Orthodox Jews in Brooklyn where he sharply criticized homosexuality, saying children should not be exposed to it. He also criticized his Democratic opponent, Andrew Cuomo, for participating in a gay pride parade. Paladino's campaign manager defended his views, stating they reflect those of the Catholic Church. Cuomo's spokesman called Paladino's comments "stunning homophobia" and "a glaring disregard for basic equality." Paladino's stance on gay rights and his personal life have become issues in the campaign, with polls showing he faces challenges in gaining support.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Ingraham v. Wright that the Eighth Amendment's prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment does not apply to disciplinary corporal punishment in public schools. The Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment does not require prior notice and a hearing before imposing corporal punishment, as long as it is within the common law privilege. The Court noted that public schools are open institutions, subject to community supervision, and that common law remedies provide adequate protection against abuse. The Court emphasized that the risk of error in school disciplinary processes is minimal, and that requiring prior hearings would significantly burden the use of corporal punishment as a disciplinary measure.

President Trump defended his approach to staffing key positions at the State Department, arguing that the quality of his decisions mattered more than the quantity. He stated, "The one that matters is me, I'm the only one that matters because when it comes to it that's what the policy is going to be." Trump also faced questions about potential vacancies in the State Department, with some positions remaining unfilled. He downplayed the importance of having a fully staffed department, saying, "We don't need all the people that they want," and citing cost-saving measures as a reason. Trump maintained that Secretary of State Rex Tillerson was working hard and doing his best, despite reports of low morale. Trump blamed Senate Democrats for more nominees not being approved, but acknowledged that he had focused on nominating fewer people. He emphasized that the Senate had been obstructive, saying, "Schumer and the Democrats are just obstructing. You can't get anything through."

The MPAA and NATO have adopted a zero-tolerance policy against wearable technologies like Google Glass in movie theaters. Moviegoers must turn off and put away any such devices or risk being asked to leave. Theater staff may call the police if they suspect illegal recording. This new rule applies to all recording devices, including phones.

Hugh Hefner is countering Crystal Harris's claims about their sex life on "The Howard Stern Show." Harris told Stern that sex with the 85-year-old Playboy founder lasted "like two seconds" and that she was "grossed out." Hefner, however, tweeted that the first night's sex was "good enough" to keep her for more. Harris, 24, has been spotted with Dr. Phil's son Jordan McGraw, raising questions about her intentions after their breakup.

For individuals with coronary artery disease, repeatedly losing and regaining weight, or "yo-yo" dieting, may significantly increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and death, according to new research. Analyzing data from 9,509 men and women with stable coronary artery disease over five years, the study found that those with the highest weight variability faced a 78% higher risk of new-onset diabetes, 117% higher risk of heart attack, 136% higher risk of stroke, and 124% higher risk of death compared to those with the lowest weight variability. The findings, published in The New England Journal of Medicine, suggest that maintaining a stable weight is crucial for those with pre-existing heart conditions. Dr. Sripal Bangalore, lead author from NYU Langone Medical Center, emphasizes the importance of not only losing weight but also keeping it off to prevent severe health consequences.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is investigating reports of seizures in infants and children who used homeopathic teething products, which may contain "natural" compounds but are not regulated as drugs by the FDA. Consumers should seek immediate medical care if their child experiences seizures, difficulty breathing, lethargy, excessive sleepiness, muscle weakness, skin flushing, constipation, difficulty urinating, or agitation after using these products. Instead, doctors recommend giving babies a firm object to chew on, such as a teething ring or hard, unsweetened teething crackers. The FDA does not support the use of homeopathic teething tablets and gels, as there is no proven health benefit, and some products may contain toxic substances.

A man armed with an AR-15 rifle intervened to stop a knife attack during an argument in Oswego, Illinois. The incident occurred at an apartment building on Harbor Drive when someone attacked another person with a knife. Neighbor Dave Thomas witnessed the attack, retrieved his AR-15, and ordered the suspect to stop. No shots were fired, and the suspect was eventually arrested while the victim was taken to the hospital. Thomas, who has a valid firearm owner's identification card and a concealed carry permit, stated that the AR-15 is his preferred weapon for home protection and that the larger gun played an intimidation role in stopping the attacker.

Apple offers free recycling of its products across the United States and provides details for independent recyclers to handle specific components. The company's annual environmental report highlights the recovery of over 61 million pounds of materials, including 2,204 pounds of gold, worth approximately $40 million at current gold prices. This gold is sourced from millions of recycled iPhones and other devices, each containing small amounts of gold in their internal components. Apple emphasizes its commitment to recycling and recovering valuable materials from old electronics to prevent them from ending up in landfills.

Whale-watching trips may be putting marine mammals at risk, according to conservationists who presented findings at the International Marine Conservation Congress in Glasgow. While the activity is traditionally seen as green tourism, researchers are concerned about its potential to disturb cetaceans, causing behavioral changes such as reduced feeding and increased energy expenditure. Boat collisions are a lesser concern. Studies show that minke whales in Iceland and bottlenose dolphins in New Zealand exhibit stress responses to whale-watching boats. The number of whale-watching participants has grown significantly since the 1990s, with an estimated 13 million people joining trips in 119 countries in 2008. Guidelines to minimize disturbance exist but are often inadequate. Boat collisions and the stress from whale-watching can harm marine mammals, potentially leading to population declines. Conservationists advocate for better management and stricter guidelines to protect the animals.

Two people are dead and one woman is in good condition after a shooting Saturday morning at Melbourne Square mall. The shooter, Jose Garcia-Rodriguez, 57, of Palm Bay, shot his wife, 33-year-old Idanerys Garcia-Rodriguez, who worked in the mall's food court, and another man before taking his own life. Idanerys Garcia-Rodriguez is in good condition at a local hospital. About 100 people were inside the mall when the shooting occurred, and gunshots were still being heard when officers arrived. Police believe the incident may stem from a domestic-violence incident. The mall was closed for the remainder of the day but is expected to reopen Sunday. Multiple agencies, including the FBI, were involved in the investigation.

Most people take breaks during their workdays, but are they taking the best type of breaks? A new study from Baylor University researchers Emily Hunter, Ph.D., and Cindy Wu, Ph.D., suggests that breaks earlier in the day, involving activities preferred by the employee, and more frequent shorter breaks are more beneficial for energy, concentration, and motivation. The study, which surveyed 95 employees over a five-day workweek, found that mid-morning breaks are most effective, while non-work-related activities are not necessarily more beneficial. Taking more frequent, shorter breaks can help prevent fatigue and boost productivity. The findings suggest that employees should take breaks more often and engage in activities they enjoy to improve their health and job satisfaction.

Democratic heavy hitters, including Bill Clinton, are quietly trying to woo a new candidate to challenge Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell. Actress Ashley Judd is considering a star-studded campaign, but some Democrats fear her potential candidacy due to her liberal views and lack of political experience. The focus is shifting to 34-year-old Alison Lundergan Grimes, the Kentucky secretary of state, who lacks political baggage and has the Clintons' support. However, it's uncertain if Grimes will enter the race. The situation highlights the divide among Democrats over taking on McConnell, with concerns about the risk of a messy primary battle or a weak performance by Judd.

Eva Longoria and José Bastón welcome their first child, Santiago Enrique Bastón, born on June 19 in Los Angeles. The 43-year-old actress shared the first photo of her newborn with HOLA! USA, showing her cradling the baby. This addition will join Bastón’s three children from his previous marriage. Eva stayed active during her pregnancy and supported the Time's Up movement. The couple celebrated their two-year wedding anniversary in May.

Russian skier Maria Komissarova underwent a successful 6.5-hour surgery after breaking her spine during a training crash at the Sochi Olympics. The 23-year-old, who was training for the ski cross competition, suffered a fractured and dislocated T12 vertebra. She was immediately taken to Krasnaya Polyanskaya Hospital No. 8 for emergency surgery. Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Komissarova in the hospital. Komissarova's best career result was finishing second in a World Cup event in 2012, but she was not expected to be a medal contender in the Sochi Games. The injury highlights the risks in freestyle skiing, a discipline that was added to the Winter Olympics in 2010.

Global central banks took coordinated action Wednesday to ease financial strains, sending stock markets higher. The European Central Bank, U.S. Federal Reserve, Bank of England, Bank of Canada, Bank of Japan, and Swiss National Bank made it cheaper for banks to access U.S. dollar liquidity and set up temporary swap lines for other currencies if needed. This move aims to bolster liquidity support to the global financial system and mitigate effects on credit supply to households and businesses. Stock markets, particularly Germany's DAX and Dow futures, saw significant gains following the announcement. Concerns remain over Europe's debt crisis, which has raised fears of a broader financial shock.

Dustin Snyder, 19, with a rare form of cancer and weeks to live, is set to marry his high school sweetheart Sierra Siverio. The couple, who reconnected after Dustin's diagnosis, are planning a wedding despite his terminal condition. Dustin's sister Brittany Hails launched a GoFundMe page to cover costs, which has received over $13,000 in donations, including a wedding dress, tuxedo, and venue. Dustin and Sierra are focusing on making their final moments together as happy as possible, emphasizing the importance of living life to the fullest.

Zynga Inc. priced its initial public offering at $10 per share, signaling strong investor demand for the social games maker. The company will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ZNGA. Zynga priced 100 million shares at the high end of the expected range, raising about $1 billion. This is the latest in a series of high-profile Internet IPOs this year, following LinkedIn and Groupon. The deal values Zynga at $8.9 billion, lower than the $20 billion expected earlier. Zynga makes games played primarily on Facebook, with popular titles like "CityVille" and "FarmVille." For the nine months ended September 30, the company reported total revenue of $828.9 million and net income of $30.7 million.

Barack Obama's former Harvard Law professor, Roberto Unger, has publicly urged voters to defeat the President in the 2012 election, despite their past professional relationship. Unger, a Brazilian politician and author, claims Obama has failed to advance the progressive cause and has spent trillions of dollars to benefit the wealthy while neglecting workers and homeowners. He criticizes Obama's healthcare reform, suggesting it has prioritized access over broader economic and educational opportunities. Unger's video, posted on YouTube, argues that Obama's policies have been ineffective and that a second term would be detrimental to the United States.

Forensic technology from South Africa was used to analyze residue from tobacco pipes found in the garden of William Shakespeare, revealing evidence of various substances smoked in early 17th-century England. Chemical analyses identified cannabis in eight samples and cocaine in two samples from the pipes. Shakespeare’s garden yielded pipes containing cannabis, suggesting he might have preferred this mind-stimulating plant over cocaine. Literary indications, such as Sonnet 76, hint at Shakespeare’s potential use of cannabis for creative writing and his possible avoidance of strange drugs. The findings raise questions about the atmosphere in which Shakespeare’s plays were performed, possibly in a smoke-filled environment with his contemporaries like Sir Francis Drake and Sir Walter Raleigh.

Only about 2% of commercials featuring men depicted them doing domestic tasks. Women often feel the need to maintain a clean home, believing it provides a sense of safety, even if they work full-time. However, men are less likely to clean, partly because they fear being judged for a messy house and because women still receive more credit for keeping it tidy. This disparity persists despite the desire for gender equality in chores. Philosophy professor Alexandra Bradner suggests couples assess their division of tasks, while Jenny Anderson advocates for dividing chores based on comparative advantage. Another approach is lowering one's standards of cleanliness. Some suggest making cleaning more enjoyable, though this may not fully address the issue. The article concludes that viewing housework inequality as solely a result of men's laziness may overlook women's higher standards of cleanliness and the subjective nature of domestic tasks.

Bruce Jenner, now Caitlyn, reveals her transition to living as a woman, sharing her journey in a Vanity Fair cover story. The article details Jenner's internal struggles and the impact on her family, including her children from two marriages. Despite the support of some, others, like Kris Jenner, express disappointment and disagreement over Jenner's reality TV series. Caitlyn's decision to go public and her plans for the upcoming E! series aim to raise awareness for the transgender community. Her transition marks a new chapter, bringing both challenges and opportunities for connection and advocacy.

Google's parent company, Alphabet Inc., has deployed Project Loon balloons to provide internet access to remote areas of Puerto Rico affected by Hurricane Maria. Two Project Loon balloons, HBAL199 and HBAL237, are currently delivering basic internet services to AT&T customers with compatible handsets. The balloons, located over 60,000 feet above the ground, use solar power and navigate by adjusting their altitude to optimize signal delivery. Additional balloons are on their way, with Alphabet authorized to launch up to 30 to serve the area. While still experimental, Project Loon has previously provided temporary internet in Peru following floods. The deployment aims to assist in communication and information access during the recovery from Hurricane Maria, which has significantly impacted Puerto Rico's infrastructure.

Democratic strategists have urged President Obama to regain control amid a series of controversies, including the IRS targeting of conservative groups and the Benghazi attack. Obama responded by releasing emails and documents, requesting the resignation of the acting IRS commissioner, and planning to appoint a new commissioner. While Republicans criticized these actions, Democratic operatives believe the White House has regained some momentum. The controversies, though, are seen as tier one issues, prompting calls for congressional investigations. Republicans are advised to handle the situation carefully, avoiding overreliance on scandal for political gain.

Pop star Justin Bieber spent some time on FaceTime with Malala Yousafzai, the young activist who survived a Taliban attack in Pakistan. Bieber, 20, shared a photo of the call on Instagram, expressing his admiration for Yousafzai's work advocating for girls' education. He wrote that he can't wait to meet her in person and support her and the Malala Fund. This comes after Bieber was involved in a dispute with actor Orlando Bloom, posting photos of Bloom's ex-wife, model Miranda Kerr, on Instagram. Yousafzai, 17, has been working to send girls to school worldwide, particularly in light of the recent kidnapping of Nigerian schoolgirls.

Astronomers studying the star KIC 8462852 have concluded that its unusual dimming patterns are likely due to a swarm of comets rather than an alien megastructure. Iowa State University researchers, using data from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, found no significant excess of infrared light, which would have been present if the dimming were caused by a catastrophic event like a planetary collision. The irregular and deep dimming of the star, observed by NASA's Kepler mission, is more consistent with a family of comets traveling on a long, eccentric orbit around the star. The leading hypothesis is that a large comet passed in front of the star in 2011, causing a significant dimming event, followed by smaller comets in 2013. The comets have since moved away, leaving no infrared signature. This conclusion does not rule out the alien megastructure theory but provides a more plausible natural explanation for the star's behavior.

Trend-chasing coffee giant Starbucks is diving into the unicorn craze with a new Unicorn Frappuccino, set to debut on April 19. Rumors of the pink-and-blue drink have been swirling on social media, with baristas on Reddit discussing its arrival and early tasters sharing their experiences. Descriptions of the flavor range from a "sour raspberry" taste to "Tropical Skittles." The drink is expected to be a limited-time offering, adding another whimsical twist to the Frappuccino line.

Sen. John McCain's opposition to the latest GOP Obamacare repeal bill has complicated the future of the health care law. Some Republicans still push for repeal, but it appears more likely that the debate will move into a new stage. Democrats are pushing for bipartisan talks in the Senate Health Committee, and there are signs that Trump may be open to working with Democrats. A key issue is addressing cost-sharing reductions that help insurers provide coverage to low-income people. Without bipartisan action or a final repeal attempt, Obamacare, which has extended coverage to about 20 million people, will likely remain in place. Democrats warn that repeal is still a "very real threat" and accuse the administration of trying to sabotage the law. McCain's opposition is a significant blow to the seven-year effort to repeal Obamacare, and it almost certainly dooms the current legislation.

Thousands of documents purportedly leaked from inside ISIS provide a detailed look at the terror group's recruitment and management processes, including a 23-question form used to vet potential fighters. The forms, obtained by several media organizations, ask for personal details such as name, blood type, education, and previous fighting experience, as well as more sinister questions about willingness to become a suicide attacker. Among the names listed are well-known jihadis and some previously unknown recruits from at least 51 countries, including the UK, France, Germany, and the United States. German intelligence officials believe the documents are authentic and see potential in using them to prosecute individuals who joined ISIS and returned home. The leak, attributed to a disillusioned ISIS fighter, could offer critical information to intelligence agencies and serve as a deterrent to potential recruits.

PizzaNet, launched in 1994, was a pioneering attempt to order pizza online, marking one of the first instances of purchasing a physical product over the World Wide Web. Despite its innovative concept, PizzaNet's integration of online ordering with traditional delivery methods felt somewhat half-baked. Customers needed Internet access, a version of Mosaic, and a customized menu to place their orders. The transaction process involved transmitting data to Pizza Hut headquarters, followed by a phone call to verify orders. While PizzaNet's launch was significant, it missed the mark by not fully leveraging the interactivity and customization potential of the internet. The article suggests that future iterations could allow customers to design their pizzas online, creating a more engaging and valuable experience.

About 10 people fell ill after a suspicious package arrived in the mailroom of a downtown IRS building in Kansas City, Missouri, on Friday. Fire Department spokesman James Garrett reported that two individuals required hospitalization but were in good condition. The Fire Department isolated the package and did not evacuate the building, which continued its operations. The investigation has been handed over to the IRS and other federal authorities.

Tiger Woods faces a new setback as mainstream publications like Golf Digest suspend bylined articles featuring him, reflecting the widespread impact of his scandal. The magazine will not publish Woods' instruction articles during his indefinite break from professional golf, citing respect for his family-focused decision. This move, surprising given athletes' usual resilience within their sport, underscores the depth of his marketing crisis. Woods, who earns an estimated $110 million annually in endorsements, has lost several major sponsors, including Accenture, Gatorade, and Gillette. Despite the backlash, Tag Heuer publicly supports him, re-posting his image on their website with a message of solidarity.

The U.S. Under-23 national team was eliminated from Olympic qualifying after a 3-3 tie with El Salvador in a match that featured a dramatic stoppage-time goal. Despite a strong start and a one-goal lead, the U.S. could not secure the victory, allowing El Salvador to equalize and advance to the semifinals. The U.S. led 3-2 with minutes left but conceded a late goal, ending their hopes of qualifying for the 2012 Olympics. The match was marked by a series of key moments, including a first-minute goal by Terrence Boyd, two quick goals by El Salvador, and a late equalizer by Jaime Alas. The U.S. missed out on a spot in the Olympics for the second time in three attempts, leaving a bitter taste for the team and its supporters.

More than half of terminally ill cancer patients receive chemotherapy in the last few months of their lives, according to a new study from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. These patients are more likely to die in a hospital intensive care unit, hooked to a ventilator, rather than at home as they would have preferred. Chemotherapy did not prolong survival but increased the likelihood of a more medicalized death. Patients receiving chemotherapy were also less likely to have discussed their end-of-life wishes with their oncologist. Doctors often avoid these conversations, fearing they might make patients feel their doctors are giving up on them. The study, published in the British Medical Journal, suggests that doctors need to be more proactive in discussing end-of-life care with their patients.

UN human rights investigators have gathered evidence suggesting Syrian rebels may have used sarin nerve agent, while government forces have not yet been found to have used chemical weapons, according to Carla Del Ponte, a member of the commission. The investigation into rebel use of sarin is separate from the stalled UN inquiry into government chemical weapon attacks. The ongoing civil war has claimed over 70,000 lives and displaced millions within Syria and abroad. Meanwhile, Israeli air strikes near Damascus have targeted Iranian-supplied weapons meant for Hezbollah, drawing Syrian accusations of aggression, though Israel denies direct involvement in the civil war.

Courtney Stodden, 21, has announced her pregnancy with her first child, confirming to FOX411 after a video of her with a positive pregnancy test was shared. The reality star's estranged mother, Krista Keller, revealed on The Mother/Daughter Experiment that she has feelings for her daughter's husband, Doug Hutchison, 55. This adds another layer of complexity to Stodden's already unconventional relationship with Hutchison, who is 34 years her senior. The couple, who tied the knot in 2011, have faced numerous challenges, including a brief separation in 2013. Stodden expressed that the pregnancy is a bittersweet experience, coming at a time of significant personal stress.

Scientists from Imperial College London believe they have made significant progress in understanding the genetic basis of human intelligence. Intelligence, while largely influenced by genetic inheritance, has not been linked to a single gene. Instead, two networks of genes, M1 and M3, each containing hundreds of genes, may control cognitive abilities such as lateral thinking, mental arithmetic, and strategic planning. These networks also play roles in neurodevelopmental disorders like epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism. The researchers hope that understanding these genetic networks could eventually lead to methods to modify human intelligence, such as through targeted drug therapies. The study involved analyzing data from mouse brains, human brain samples, and large-scale health studies, using advanced computational techniques to identify the genes involved. While the exact mechanisms and key players are still unclear, the findings could contribute to better treatments for neurodevelopmental diseases.

Sen. Ben Cardin of Maryland attributes General Motors' recent plant closures and job cuts to President Trump's trade policies, including tariffs on steel and aluminum. Cardin's comments echo those of Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, who cited the tariffs as a reason to remove trade barriers between the two countries. Cardin expressed concern over the impact of tariffs on American jobs and called for unity in dealing with China. The summary also mentions the positive developments in U.S.-China trade relations and the newly signed United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Missouri Republican Sen. Roy Blunt agreed that the China truce was encouraging but called for more details.

International Women’s Day on Thursday is marked by corporate campaigns and product launches aimed at celebrating women’s achievements and promoting gender parity. Brands like Mattel, Nike, Uber, and Facebook roll out ads and initiatives, while McDonald’s flips its golden arches upside-down to form a W. Despite the push for female empowerment, some initiatives face criticism. Mattel’s new Barbie dolls, while featuring inspiring role models, are criticized for their uniform, rail-thin body shapes. Similarly, McDonald’s W symbol is panned as an empty gesture. The #MeToo movement adds urgency to these efforts, but brands must ensure their actions go beyond superficial gestures to meaningful change.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov blamed Western governments for encouraging the fighting in Ukraine, warning that the situation was "getting out of control." Protesters in Kiev clashed with police, leaving vehicles burning in the streets. Opposition leaders, including Vitali Klitschko, attempted to negotiate with President Viktor Yanukovych but were unsuccessful. Lavrov criticized the protesters for using violence and called their behavior a "complete violation of all European standards of behavior." Meanwhile, Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov said the government would use force if clashes in Kiev do not cease. Protesters faced off against police, with some capturing and questioning individuals they believed were hired by pro-government forces to create chaos. The situation remains tense, with little hope for a peaceful resolution.

A 40-year-old nurse serving a life sentence for murdering two patients in northern Germany is now suspected of killing at least 84 other people, police say. Niels H, as he is referred to under German reporting rules, was convicted of attempted murder in 2006 and murder in 2015. His victims received lethal drug doses at units where he worked. Relatives of patients who died in clinics where he worked had urged police to investigate further. A commission was set up in 2014 to investigate the scale of his crimes, potentially making him Germany's worst post-war killer. The medication caused heart failure or the collapse of patients' circulatory systems. During his 2015 trial, he admitted applying the drug to about 90 people at an intensive care clinic in Delmenhorst. Police say the abnormalities stretch back to 2000 at another clinic in Oldenburg. President-elect Donald Trump’s election offers a potential multibillion-dollar tax windfall to America’s wealthiest families, particularly those who stand to benefit from the elimination of the estate tax, often referred to as the “death tax.” Trump’s administration and congressional Republicans are pushing for sweeping tax reforms that would significantly benefit the wealthy. The estate tax, which applies to estates worth more than $5.45 million for individuals and $10.9 million for couples, could be repealed, saving estates like Trump’s and those of his cabinet nominees substantial amounts. For instance, Trump’s estate could save $564 million, and Wilbur Ross, his pick for Commerce Secretary, could save $545 million. The plan also includes lowering the corporate tax rate to 20 percent and small business tax rates to 25 percent, with the potential for further cuts. The Second Amendment, originally ratified to preserve slave patrol militias in the South, is now being used by weapon-manufacturing corporations to protect their "right" to sell assault weapons. Thom Hartmann argues that the amendment's primary purpose is to ensure a "free state" by allowing citizens to defend themselves against tyranny, not just for self-defense against criminals. He points out that the memory of British attempts to disarm colonists in 1775 was still fresh when the Constitution was written, and the Bill of Rights in England included language about the right to bear arms for defense. Hartmann suggests that the 30-round magazine limit might be too small if the amendment truly protects citizens from their own government. He warns that as the President proposes gun restrictions, he should remember Justice Robert Jackson’s opinion in West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, emphasizing the importance of protecting individual freedoms.

Senate Democrats failed to advance a defense authorization bill containing a repeal of the "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" policy, falling 3 votes short of the 60 needed. Despite support from key Democrats and military leaders, Republicans blocked the bill, citing procedural concerns. In response, Sens. Joe Lieberman and Susan Collins announced plans to introduce a stand-alone repeal bill, with Majority Leader Harry Reid promising to support it. The vote dealt a blow to President Obama's efforts to repeal the ban, and advocates criticized the political maneuvering. A new vote on the repeal is expected during the lame duck session.

Secret files revealing evidence of widespread suspected match-fixing at the top level of world tennis, including at Wimbledon, have been uncovered by the BBC and BuzzFeed News. Over the past decade, 16 players who have ranked in the top 50 have been repeatedly flagged to the Tennis Integrity Unit (TIU) over suspicions they have thrown matches. Despite these warnings, all of the players, including winners of Grand Slam titles, were allowed to continue competing. The TIU, which was set up to police the sport, claims it has a zero-tolerance approach to betting-related corruption. However, critics argue that the unit has failed to act on credible evidence and that players implicated in suspicious matches have not been properly investigated. The TIU's decision not to pursue past corruption cases, citing legal advice, has been criticized as a missed opportunity to clean up the sport. A cyclospora outbreak has sickened 397 people in 16 states, with Iowa and Nebraska linking the illnesses to prepackaged salad mix, though other states are unsure of the culprit. The parasite, rarely seen in the U.S., causes watery diarrhea and other symptoms. The investigation, criticized for its pace, struggles to identify the exact source due to the short shelf life of packaged lettuce and laws protecting agricultural producers. Despite efforts, the CDC and FDA have not yet pinpointed the contaminated product, leaving many sickened individuals and food safety experts concerned.

Rolling Stone, a half-century-old magazine synonymous with rock 'n' roll journalism, is up for sale, its co-founder Jann Wenner announced. Wenner, 71, stated he loves his job but sees selling as the "smart thing to do." The magazine, known for iconic covers and influential writers, faced a significant blow when it retracted a 2014 article about a gang rape at the University of Virginia, which was found to have fundamental journalistic failures. This retraction led to three libel lawsuits, one resulting in a $3 million jury award. Financially, Rolling Stone suffered from declining print advertising and newsstand sales, exacerbated by Wenner's skepticism towards digital media. The sale of Us Weekly and Men's Journal, key revenue sources, further diminished Wenner Media's financial health. This sale marks Wenner's denouement, ending his unlikely rise from a Berkeley dropout to a media mogul.

The leaders of the Republican and Democratic national committees weighed in on the prospect of an independent presidential run by Michael Bloomberg. DNC Chairwoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz suggested that Bloomberg's priorities are already "well cared-for" in the Democratic platform, while RNC leader Reince Priebus welcomed the idea, framing Bloomberg as a spoiler who would siphon votes from the Democratic nominee. Bloomberg, who recently criticized the level of discourse in the campaign, is considering a run and has assembled a team to explore the possibility. Priebus dismissed the likelihood of a Bloomberg candidacy, predicting that Paul Ryan would choose the Republican nominee if the race went to the House of Representatives for a decision.

Older fathers appear to have geekier sons, according to a new study. By analyzing the cognitive and behavioral data of over 15,000 twin pairs, researchers found that boys born to older fathers scored higher on a "geek index" that measures non-verbal IQ, focus on interests, and social aloofness. The effect was strongest in boys, with geek traits appearing more frequently after the father was 45. These geeky boys performed better in school, especially in STEM subjects, suggesting they might be more successful in their careers. However, the study's authors caution that the geek effect may not extend beyond secondary education and future success remains uncertain. They also note that the findings do not imply men should delay fatherhood to have geekier children. The study's lead author, Magdalena Janecka, suggests that older fathers might have more stable careers and better educational backgrounds, which could encourage their children's geeky traits. Sen. Bernie Sanders is considering a 2020 presidential run, likely as the best candidate to defeat President Trump, though he remains uncertain. Sanders, who ran in 2016 and garnered support among progressives, now faces a more challenging political landscape. His team is mapping out a 2018 plan to position him for a potential 2020 campaign, including extensive travel to support Democratic candidates. Sanders faces criticism for his age and past criticisms from within the party, but he believes his ideas are now mainstream. His digital media operation is more ambitious than that of any other politician, and he has used it to popularize his platform. Despite his influence, Sanders remains uncomfortable with the political process and the pressure of his newfound popularity. He is wary of potential rivals, particularly Senator Elizabeth Warren, and is considering the symbolic power of stepping aside for a younger leader. The passenger in the car with Walter Scott before he was shot by a South Carolina police officer says Scott didn't deserve to die. Pierre D. Fulton, who was in the vehicle during the April 4, 2015, traffic stop, released a one-paragraph statement through his lawyer, calling Scott a "dear friend" who helped him become a better man. Fulton expressed confusion over why Scott ran from the officer, Michael Slager, who is charged with murder. Slager shot Scott eight times as he fled, and the incident was captured on video. Fulton asked for prayers for Scott and his family while respecting his privacy.

Billionaire Michael Bloomberg has pledged to provide $15 million to help cover the funding shortfall the United Nations will face due to the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement. Bloomberg, a former New York City mayor and philanthropist, stated that Americans are not walking away from the agreement and that non-state actors, including cities, states, businesses, and civil society, will continue to drive U.S. climate action. His offer to the United Nations underscores the shift in leadership in the fight against climate change from the federal government to other sectors. Bloomberg's contribution could be included in future reports on the progress made by signatories of the Paris deal.

A 3-year-old boy drowned during a family vacation in Fort Morgan, Alabama, highlighting the silent and swift nature of drowning. His mother, who had taken water safety seriously, found her son face-down in the deep end of a pool, mere moments after they had shared a brownie. Despite immediate medical intervention, including CPR and intubation, the child could not be saved. The tragedy prompted the mother to create a non-profit, Levi’s Legacy, dedicated to preventing drowning. She emphasizes that drowning can occur in non-swimming situations and calls for increased awareness and education on the topic, urging the American Academy of Pediatrics to prioritize water safety in their resources for parents.

A 40-year-old woman, Andrea Giesbrecht, faces charges of concealing the bodies of six infants in a U-Haul storage locker. The grim discovery was made when U-Haul employees cleared out the locker due to unpaid rental payments. Police initially believed there were three or four bodies but later confirmed six. The infants are believed to be newborns. Giesbrecht, who has a gambling addiction and a history of fraud, was arrested outside her home in north Winnipeg. She faces six charges of concealing a body and one charge of breaching probation. The state of the remains was such that it took time to determine the number and age of the infants. Forensic investigations are ongoing, and no homicide charges have been filed yet.

Austrian daredevil Felix Baumgartner faces weather delays in his attempt to break the world record for the highest-ever skydive. Scheduled to leap from a balloon nearly 23 miles (37 kilometers) above southeastern New Mexico, Baumgartner aims to plummet to Earth, shattering the sound barrier and setting multiple records. However, a cold front with gusty winds and cooler temperatures on Monday forced a one-day postponement. If conditions clear by Tuesday, Baumgartner will ascend in a 55-story-tall helium balloon, reaching an altitude of 120,000 feet (36,576 meters) before stepping into the void. The 43-year-old's jump, sponsored by Red Bull, marks the culmination of five years of planning and training. Despite the risks, including potential blood boiling and brain damage, Baumgartner remains confident. His mentor, former U.S. Air Force Colonel Joe Kittinger, will guide him

Star Wars creator George Lucas is mourning the loss of his longtime friend and leading lady Carrie Fisher, who died at 60 after suffering a heart attack during a flight from London to Los Angeles. Fisher, known for her role as Princess Leia, was in stable condition when her family shared the news. Other Star Wars stars, including Harrison Ford and Mark Hamill, paid tribute to Fisher's legacy. Fisher had completed filming for "Star Wars: Episode VIII" before her death, and it is unclear how her passing might affect future films in the franchise.

Four U.S. senators are betting on the outcome of the NBA Finals, with California Sens. Kamala Harris and Dianne Feinstein backing the Golden State Warriors against Ohio Sens. Sherrod Brown and Rob Portman, who are rooting for the Cleveland Cavaliers. Victory for the Warriors would require the Ohio senators to deliver a case of beer and a case of California Chardonnay to the California senators, while the Cavaliers' win would see Harris and Feinstein receive a case of beer from Portman and a case of Great Lakes Brewing from Brown. The series is closely watched, with the teams having faced each other in every NBA Finals since 2015.

The US military's takeover of emergency operations in Haiti has sparked diplomatic tensions with countries and aid agencies, as flights were redirected, causing frustration. Brazil and France lodged official protests, with Brazil warning it would not relinquish command of UN forces in Haiti, and France complaining the airport had become a US "annexe." The UN was feeding 40,000 people and aimed to increase that to 1 million within two weeks. However, aid distribution faced challenges, with 200 flights daily at the congested airport, mostly for US military. The Haitian government, struggling to function, signed a memorandum transferring control of the airport to the US. The UN confirmed the deaths of three senior officials, including the secretary general’s special representative. Coordination issues persisted, with aid agencies accusing the US of prioritizing securing the country over feeding the population. Fuel shortages and damaged infrastructure further hampered efforts. Despite progress, aid workers remained frustrated with the lack of orderly distribution and the need

The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader, directed by Michael Apted, is a largely dreary installment in the Narnia franchise, with a new cast of characters and a directorial style that prioritizes blandness over excitement. Will Poulter's performance as Eustace Scrubb, a grumpy cousin of the Pevensie siblings, is a highlight, adding depth to the story. The film's action sequences, while not striking, have a game energy. However, the faith-based messages and generic plot elements can be seen as a letdown for both the faith group and the general audience. The special effects, including a transformation scene, offer moments of human touch. Despite its shortcomings, the film is a decent family adventure, suitable for a cold Saturday morning but likely to be forgotten by Sunday.

The recent assault on the National Security Five highlights the fear our elites have about discussing and understanding radical Islamists. Rep. Michele Bachmann and four other Republican congressmen accused Hillary Clinton's aide, Huma Abedin, of being a secret agent for the Muslim Brotherhood, sparking a rush to silence questions in Washington. This aggressive push to stop inquiries is reminiscent of the Cold War era, when unpleasant surprises shocked even experts. The article questions why elites fear an honest discussion on radical Islamism, suggesting it might reveal a more confrontational strategy is needed. It also criticizes Politico for giving Newt Gingrich 5,000 words to defend Bachmann's accusations, which included zero evidence. The piece argues that Islamophobic practices aimed at marginalized Muslims have not provoked similar outrage, and highlights Israel's exclusion from the Global Counterterrorism Forum and its omission as a terrorism victim in a State Department speech.

Justin Trudeau jokingly challenged Matthew Perry to a rematch after Perry's "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" segment about beating up a younger Trudeau in elementary school. The incident, which Perry claimed pushed Trudeau into politics, led to Trudeau's tweet: "I've been giving it some thought, and you know what, who hasn't wanted to punch Chandler? How about a rematch Matthew Perry?" While the challenge came on April Fools' Day, many were excited about the possibility of seeing the two fight, even for charity.

Norwegian Air Shuttle plans to offer one-way tickets to Europe for $69 by 2017, flying from U.S. airports with low fees, according to CEO Bjørn Kjos. The airline aims to serve smaller U.S. cities like New York's Westchester County Airport and Connecticut's Bradley International Airport, which are currently under-served. Average round-trip fares on such routes are expected to be around $300, significantly lower than Norwegian's current fares due to lower airport fees. These plans are part of Norwegian's strategy to challenge traditional flag carriers by offering direct flights to smaller cities. Kjos believes such services will become common within five years, posing a threat to airlines like Lufthansa. Norwegian has 100 Boeing 737 MAX jets on order, suitable for transatlantic flights to smaller airports. Regulators must approve customs stations at U.S. regional airports to handle international traffic.

Support for the death penalty in the United States has fallen below 50%, according to a new Pew Research Center poll. Just 49% of Americans now favor capital punishment, the lowest level since 1971. Support has declined steadily since 1994 when it peaked at 80%. The poll also found that 42% of Americans oppose the death penalty. Political affiliation significantly influences support, with 72% of Republicans favoring it and only 34% of Democrats. For the first time, independents are as likely to oppose the death penalty as to support it. Support varies by demographic factors, with men more likely to back the death penalty than women, and whites more supportive than blacks and Hispanics.

Hostess Brands is recalling 710,000 cases of snack cakes and donuts due to possible undeclared peanut residue from their supplier, Grain Craft. The recall affects specific varieties like Ding Dongs, Zingers, and Chocodiles, and includes single-serve and multipack boxes. Consumers with peanut allergies are advised to discard or return the products for a refund. No serious health issues have been reported so far. For more details, visit the FDA’s website or Hostess’ official site.

In the southeastern United States, an increasing number of people are developing a life-threatening meat allergy after being bitten by the Lone Star Tick. This allergy, known as alpha-gal syndrome, causes severe reactions like hives, stomach cramps, and in the worst cases, difficulty breathing and even death. The allergy is triggered by a sugar called galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal) found in mammal meat, including beef and pork. Researchers believe the tick spreads the allergy through its bite, possibly by introducing alpha-gal into the body or altering the immune system. Cases of this allergy have been reported in new areas, including Pennsylvania and New York, raising questions about whether the tick's range is expanding or if other tick species are involved. While the exact mechanism remains unclear, scientists are working to understand the spread of this allergy and develop potential treatments.

Turkish prosecutors are seeking over four years in prison for NBA player Enes Kanter on charges of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan through tweets. Kanter, a vocal supporter of Fethullah Gulen, claims the potential indictment is not a concern and focuses on his basketball career. He hopes the Knicks' playoff success will be a form of retaliation against the Turkish government. Kanter has faced travel restrictions and was detained in Romania due to canceled travel documents.

Donald Trump's campaign has been marked by relentless attacks and a refusal to back down, as evidenced in a recent Rolling Stone cover story. During a sit-down with writer Paul Solotaroff, Trump commented on Republican rival Carly Fiorina, saying, "Look at that face! Would anyone vote for that?" He added, "I mean, she's a woman, and I'm not supposed to say bad things, but really, folks, come on. Are we serious?" This outburst highlights Trump's tendency to push boundaries and face backlash, a trait that has both bolstered his base and drawn criticism. The article notes that Trump's unyielding nature, while effective in maintaining his lead, has also landed him in disputes with ex-wives, business partners, and media outlets. Despite the controversy, Trump remains unfazed, viewing these moments as opportunities to gain media attention.

CNN is investigating claims that its star correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, misled viewers about his role in saving an earthquake victim in Nepal. During a report on the 7.8 magnitude quake, Gupta was shown performing a craniotomy on an eight-year-old girl. However, the Global Press Institute reports that Gupta actually helped with an operation on a 14-year-old patient, and the eight-year-old girl had not suffered serious injuries. CNN has acknowledged errors in their reporting, with Gupta conceding that the patient may have been a different girl. The incident raises questions about the role of celebrity journalists in covering disasters and the ethics of filming medical interventions.

Apple is expected to announce a new subscription plan for newspapers, potentially providing a new revenue stream for publications as they struggle with declining print revenue. However, sources suggest Apple may take a significant cut of subscription and advertising revenue, sparking concerns among publishers. Publishers hope tablets like the iPad can help stem losses, but are unhappy with Apple's terms, which require them to use Apple as an intermediary with subscribers. While some see this as a short-term risk, others believe it could benefit Apple and publications by enabling sophisticated and lucrative ads.

Nearly two dozen workers, mostly Hispanic, lost their jobs after participating in the "A Day Without Immigrants" protest, according to KTUL. The workers, employed at I Don't Care Bar and Grill in Catoosa, were fired for skipping work, despite their intention to support the national movement. The restaurant owner, Bill McNally, stated he has a "zero tolerance policy" for no-shows and fired the 12 kitchen staff members via text message. Meanwhile, 18 employees at Bradley Coatings, Incorporated in Tennessee were also terminated for joining the same protest. Both companies maintained their actions were based on attendance policies, not the workers' participation in the protest.

Brown University has sanctioned two fraternities for hosting unregistered parties that facilitated sexual misconduct, including one incident where a female student was reportedly drugged with a date-rape drug. The sanctions include probation, suspension of social and university privileges, and loss of housing for one fraternity, while the other faces a comprehensive review of its alcohol policy and social event regulations. The university aims to prevent sexual assault by addressing the campus climate and ensuring adequate security measures for events.

Comedian Bill Cosby is alive despite rumors circulating on social media that he had died. On Monday, Cosby took to Twitter to address the rumors, writing, "Again, I'm rebutting rumors about my demise." This isn't the first time Cosby has had to respond to such rumors; in February, he tweeted, "As you well know, a dead person cannot rebut. Therefore, I am rebutting to tell you that when I heard the news I immediately began rebutting and went into denial." Cosby clarified that "rebutting" can be used as a verb, though he added, "I don't care, because I'm alive."

Heavy fighting in South Sudan's capital, Juba, has led to hundreds of deaths and raised concerns of a return to full-scale civil war. Aid workers report that the situation is dire, with thousands displaced and humanitarian facilities damaged. Despite a ceasefire, tensions remain high, and the international community calls for swift, safe, and unhindered access for aid organizations. The conflict appears to be fueled by longstanding ethnic tensions, with some pointing to the influential power of former SPLA chief of general staff, Paul Malong, who may be behind recent events. The future of South Sudan looks grim, with the potential for further violence and a breakdown in peace efforts.

Three people died and at least six were injured early Thursday when gunshots fired from a black Range Rover caused a fiery crash on the Las Vegas Strip. The incident began with a dispute at a nearby hotel, escalating to sporadic gunfire from the SUV as the vehicles traveled north on Las Vegas Boulevard. The Maserati, driven by Kenneth Wayne Cherry Jr., was hit and crashed into a taxi, which exploded into flames. The taxi driver and his passenger were killed, while Cherry also died at a hospital. Cherry's passenger was injured. Police are seeking the black Range Rover, which fled the scene with tinted windows and paper dealer plates. The area was closed for hours as crime scene investigators collected evidence. The Las Vegas Strip, known for its safety, experienced this unusual and violent event, which marked the latest in a series of incidents in recent weeks.

Guinness is planning to become vegan-friendly for the first time, aiming to stop using isinglass, a fish product used for yeast clarification, by introducing a new filtration system by 2016. This follows years of campaigns and petitions from vegan beer enthusiasts who noted that Guinness and similar breweries do not need to disclose isinglass usage on their products.

Spring allergies are at their peak in certain cities, with Louisville, Kentucky, topping the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America's list of 2014 Spring Allergy Capitals. The city's river basin effect, temperate climate, and high pollen counts contribute to the issue, with local clinics seeing a 20% increase in visits over the past three years. Dr. Nancy Snyderman notes a longer growing season and new plant growth exacerbate the problem for the estimated 40 million Americans suffering from seasonal allergies. Avoiding allergens by limiting outdoor activities during peak pollen times can help alleviate symptoms. Other cities in the top 10 list include Memphis, Tennessee; Baton Rouge, Louisiana; and Oklahoma City.

A TV crew investigating car break-ins in San Francisco inadvertently became victims themselves, as thieves broke into both their bait car and camera van, Inside Edition reports. The crew left a $250 speaker and a Michael Kors purse in a car parked at Alamo Square, rigged with GPS trackers. The items were quickly stolen by a couple who fled on a bus. Meanwhile, while interviewing a local resident, the crew's van was broken into, resulting in thousands of dollars' worth of equipment being stolen. The resident's security camera captured the first break-in, which lasted about 20 seconds. Inside Edition's Lisa Guerrero confronted the suspects but they refused to return the speaker. The incident highlights the prevalence of car break-ins in San Francisco, with only 2% of 31,000 reported cases resulting in arrests in 2017.

The gunman who killed a UCLA professor in a murder-suicide left behind a "kill list" that led police to the body of his estranged wife in Minnesota, authorities said. Mainak Sarkar, 38, allegedly shot and killed engineering professor William S. Klug before turning the gun on himself. Days before the shooting, Sarkar had killed his wife, Ashley Hasti, 31, in Brooklyn Park, Minnesota. The "kill list" found in Sarkar's apartment included the names of Klug, another UCLA professor, and Hasti. Sarkar, who had two semi-automatic pistols and multiple rounds of ammunition, drove from Minnesota to Los Angeles, where he also intended to kill the second professor. The motive for the shootings appears to be linked to Sarkar's belief that Klug had stolen his intellectual property. Police are searching for Sarkar's 2003 Nissan Sentra with Minnesota license plate 720KTW.

Edward Snowden's father, Lon Snowden, arrived in Moscow to visit his son, who is living in Russia after leaking details of government surveillance programs. Lon Snowden expressed gratitude that his son is safe and secure, though he is unsure if Edward will return to the U.S. The younger Snowden, who faces espionage charges in the U.S., has been granted asylum in Russia and is living in a secret location. His lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, stated that Edward is seeking employment and has run out of savings, relying on donations. Edward Snowden has met with four former U.S. security officials who presented him with an award for his actions. Lon Snowden defended his son, calling him a whistleblower, and thanked Russian authorities for granting asylum. Edward himself has not spoken publicly about his situation.

The new head of the British Army, General Mark Carleton-Smith, has warned that Russia now poses a greater threat to the UK's national security than Islamist extremist groups like al-Qaeda and Islamic State (IS). Carleton-Smith, in his first interview since being appointed Chief of the General Staff, emphasized the need for Britain and its allies not to be complacent about the threat Russia poses. He highlighted Russia's efforts to exploit vulnerabilities in non-traditional areas such as cyber and space. The Russian Embassy responded with a tweet mocking the comments, stating "Army chief doesn't care about [IS]? Great global strategic vision!" Carleton-Smith's remarks come amid heightened tensions between the West and Russia over issues including Ukraine, election meddling, cyberattacks, and the poisoning of a Russian double agent and his daughter in Britain.

Oscar Pistorius' ex-girlfriend Reeva Steenkamp expressed fear and dissatisfaction in text messages sent to Pistorius weeks before her death, according to testimony in his murder trial. Steenkamp accused Pistorius of being jealous and throwing tantrums, while Pistorius admitted to being "tired and sick" but denied using jealousy as an excuse. The trial also heard from a neighbor who reported hearing gunshots and screams on Valentine's Day, the night Steenkamp died. The defense questioned the accuracy of the neighbor's testimony. The trial, originally expected to last three weeks, has been extended until mid-May.

An advertisement depicting Michelangelo's David holding an American-made AR-50A1 rifle has sparked outrage in Italy, with the culture minister demanding the ad be immediately removed. The image, part of a "Work of Art" campaign by ArmaLite, an Illinois-based small arms company, shows the famous statue brandishing the large rifle instead of its traditional slingshot. The Italian cultural establishment, including the superintendent of Florence's historical heritage and a city councillor, have criticized the ad as offensive and illegal. However, an art critic argues that certain cultural icons belong to everyone and that such depictions are akin to playful, tongue-in-cheek images.

North Korea granted journalists a rare peek at its preparations for a controversial rocket launch, set to mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of Kim Il Sung. The launch, scheduled between April 12 and 16, is seen by some as a cover for a long-range missile test, breaching U.N. Security Council resolutions. North Korea insists the operation is for peaceful purposes, aiming to launch a satellite to gather information on forestry, natural disasters, and weather. While international leaders urge cancellation, Pyongyang refuses to back down. Journalists were shown the control center and the satellite, noting the rocket's 30-meter length. Weather conditions will determine the exact launch date, with tensions heightened by potential nuclear test preparations at the Punggye-ri site.

A Blue Moon, the second full moon in a calendar month, will occur on July 31, 2015, creating a rare celestial event. Typically, most years have 12 full moons, one per month, but some years, like 2015, have 13. The Blue Moon label is applied to the third full moon in a season that has four. The term "Blue Moon" has a long history, with its origins in an old English term meaning "betrayer," and it was used in the Maine Farmers' Almanac for the third full moon in a season with four. In 1946, Sky & Telescope magazine published an article misinterpreting the older definition, defining a Blue Moon as the second full moon in a calendar month, which has since become the most widely accepted definition. 57 people, including 22 crew and 35 passengers, spent Christmas trapped in ice off the coast of Antarctica aboard the Russian-operated Akademik Shokalskiy. The ship, built for oceanographic research, became stuck 1,500 nautical miles from Hobart, Tasmania, and issued a satellite distress call. Australian maritime officials say the vessel is not in immediate danger, but rescue ships are at least two days away. Passengers are reported to be in good spirits, with one tweeting, "All are well and spirits are high. Happy Christmas." The ship is part of a research expedition commemorating the centenary of Douglas Mawson's exploration. Three ice-breaking ships have been tasked with the rescue, but the nearest is a two-day sail from the stranded vessel.

Inorganic mercury in skin creams can lighten skin but is harmful to health and the environment, with its use banned. Norwegian studies reveal many illegal products in the market containing mercury without proper labeling. Mercury is absorbed through the skin, building up slowly and potentially causing kidney damage, skin rashes, and other health issues. Children can also be exposed by touching treated skin. Mercury exposure can lead to symptoms like tremors, memory problems, and numbness. The FDA warns against using mercury-containing products, which are often sold illegally and can cause mercury poisoning. Consumers should avoid such products and seek medical advice if exposed.

Texas Governor Rick Perry announced he will not seek re-election for a fourth term, but he left open the possibility of running for president in 2016. Speaking at a Caterpillar dealership in San Antonio, Perry said he would spend the next 18 months working to create jobs and determine his future path. His decision clears the way for Attorney General Greg Abbott to run for governor, who is considered the likely frontrunner. Perry's announcement comes after a successful but controversial 13-year tenure as governor, including a disastrous 2011 presidential campaign. Perry hinted at a potential presidential bid, saying, "Certainly, that's an option out there," but emphasized that he had a lot of work to do in Texas.

Mitt Romney's defense of Obamacare in his Ann Arbor speech faced criticism for reinforcing the individual mandate's justification, which conservatives oppose. Romney argued that the mandate was to address the "free-rider" problem, similar to ObamaCare, but this only solidified the Republican Party's view of the mandate as an infringement on individual freedom. His speech also highlighted his lack of self-awareness and failed to convince conservative primary opponents, who see Romneycare and Obamacare as infringing on individual freedom and increasing government healthcare costs.

Fans faced website crashes and errors as they tried to secure presale tickets for "Star Wars: The Force Awakens" on Monday. The highly anticipated film, directed by J.J. Abrams and featuring actors like Oscar Isaac, Daisy Ridley, and John Boyega, opens in theaters on December 18.

Mike Evans, a Tampa Bay Buccaneers wide receiver, donated $11,000 to the family of Gregory Hill, who was shot and killed by a St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy in 2014. The jury found Hill 99% responsible for his death and the department 1% responsible, awarding the family $4 in damages, with Evans' donation helping to raise nearly $100,000. Gregory Hill, a 30-year-old father of three, was shot after officers responded to a noise complaint. The jury's verdict left the family with just 4 cents.

Nintendo's President Satoru Iwata announced the company is considering a new business model after forecasting a 25 billion-yen annual loss due to weak demand for the Wii U console. The company cut its Wii U console sales forecast to 2.8 million units from 9 million and its Wii U game sales to 19 million units from 38 million. Nintendo's shares fell 17% to $14.90 in New York, their biggest decline since September 2001. The company also cut its forecast for operating income to a 35 billion-yen loss from the prior 100 million-yen profit. Iwata is trying to address the decline in family-focused content's appeal as titles were delayed and as casual gamers migrate to mobile devices. Zynga, the social gaming company that has struggled since its 2011 IPO, has named Don Mattrick, former head of Microsoft’s Xbox division, as its new CEO. Mattrick will take over from Mark Pincus, who will remain as chairman and chief product officer. This move follows a series of layoffs and office closures at Zynga, as the company attempts to pivot to mobile gaming. Pincus, who has held the top job since the company’s founding, sees Mattrick as the right leader to revive Zynga. Mattrick’s experience in game development and business management could be crucial as Zynga seeks to develop successful mobile games. Zynga’s stock rose about 9% following the announcement.

European scientists have determined the "perfume" of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko by analyzing the chemicals in its coma, the fuzzy head surrounding the nucleus. Using the Rosetta spacecraft's onboard instrument, scientists have detected a mixture of molecules including ammonia, methane, hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen cyanide, and formaldehyde. The aroma is described as a mix of rotten eggs, horse stable, alcohol, and bitter almonds, making it an unpleasant scent. As the comet approaches the Sun, the mixture of molecules is expected to become stronger, providing valuable insights into the comet's composition and the early solar system.

Jared Fogle is challenging his sentence, arguing that he should not be punished for his fantasies. His lawyers are appealing the judge's decision, which sentenced him to more than 15 years in prison, saying the judge exceeded the maximum sentencing guideline. Fogle's attorneys claim the judge considered his fantasies, which are not a crime, in imposing the sentence. They argue that fantasies should not form the basis of a criminal sentence and that the judge abused her authority. Fogle's appeal asks for a resentencing where his actions, not his thoughts, are the focus.

Saturday Night Live's latest episode was a mixed bag, with Steve Carell hosting for the third time and bringing his usual blend of listlessness and uninspired sketches. Carell's monologue was peppered with former Office cast members pleading for a reboot, but the offer was ultimately a non-starter. The cold open mocked Fox News, with Kate McKinnon delivering a pitch-perfect Laura Ingraham impression. Weekend Update focused on voter fraud conspiracy theories, with Cecily Strong as Jeanine Pirro adding a touch of absurdity. Steve Carell's Amazon sketch, where he portrayed Jeff Bezos, was a series of Trump burns, but the overall episode felt flat and unoriginal, with many sketches failing to land. The space station sketch, featuring Carell's clueless dad character, was a particular disappointment, with its explanatory dialogue and lackluster execution. The episode ended on a low note with a poorly executed commercial about a GPS voice that could be set to "drag

Paul Manafort, facing charges including money laundering and bank fraud, is being held in solitary confinement for 23 hours a day ahead of his July 25 trial, citing safety concerns. His legal team argues this prevents adequate preparation for his upcoming trials and seeks his release, but prosecutors from Robert Mueller’s office oppose, stating such limitations are common for defendants awaiting trial. Manafort has been in the “VIP” section of Virginia’s Northern Neck Regional Jail since June 15.

Acting DEA Administrator Chuck Rosenberg sent a memo to agents instructing them to maintain core values of respect and compassion when dealing with suspects, contradicting President Trump's comments that suggested police should be "rough" with suspects. Rosenberg, in his memo, emphasized the DEA's commitment to "rule of law, respect and compassion, service, devotion, integrity, accountability, leadership and courage and diversity." Trump, during a speech in New York, advised police not to be "too nice" when arresting suspects, drawing criticism from law enforcement agencies. Attorney General Jeff Sessions pledged to prosecute officers for abusing their authority.

DIY microwave popcorn is easier and healthier than store-bought varieties, which can contain harmful chemicals and high levels of saturated fat, trans fats, and sodium. Store-bought microwave popcorn bags may contain perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), linked to cancer and reduced vaccine effectiveness, and diacetyl, a chemical that can cause 'popcorn lung' when inhaled. Trans fats, which raise bad cholesterol and increase heart disease risk, are also found in many microwave popcorn flavors. Sodium content can exceed daily recommendations. Making popcorn at home by popping kernels in a paper bag or air-popper is a safer and healthier alternative, allowing for custom seasoning and avoiding harmful chemicals.

President Barack Obama delivered a strong speech at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation dinner, urging African-Americans to vote for Hillary Clinton in the upcoming election. Obama emphasized that the progress made during his presidency is at stake, highlighting issues such as tolerance, democracy, and justice. He criticized Donald Trump, calling him a "nasty, hateful charlatan" and warning that his candidacy poses an existential threat to the black community. Obama highlighted Trump's history of questioning his birthplace and his divisive rhetoric, contrasting it with the progress and resilience of African-Americans. He encouraged the audience to vote and register more voters, emphasizing the importance of their participation in the election.

Three lawsuits have been filed against Trump University, alleging the real estate seminar business misled students with promises of learning from Donald Trump's investment techniques. The lawsuits, including a $40 million civil suit by New York's attorney general, accuse the program of deceptive practices and false claims about Trump's involvement. Former employees and students have criticized the business for unethical sales tactics and unqualified instructors. Despite Trump's claim of innocence, the cases have resulted in some setbacks, including a New York court ruling that Trump University and Trump were liable for running an unlicensed school. Trials for these cases may continue into the post-election period.

Canada faced a "brutal and violent attack" on Wednesday when an armed gunman shot and killed a soldier at the National War Memorial before storming Parliament, where he was eventually shot dead by the House of Commons sergeant-at-arms. Prime Minister Stephen Harper vowed that Canada would not be intimidated, stating, "For the second time this week, there has been a brutal and violent attack on our soil," and emphasizing, "But let there be no misunderstanding — we will not be intimidated, Canada will never be intimidated." The slain soldier was identified as Cpl. Nathan Cirillo, 24, a reservist from Hamilton. MPs and other witnesses reported 30 to 50 shots fired inside Parliament. NDP Leader Tom Mulcair and Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau condemned the attacks and pledged support for the government.
