Passengers restrained the flight attendant, who spoke about the plane crashing and alluding to 9/11. The incident lasted about 15 minutes and involved three or four passengers. Two flight attendants were injured and taken to the hospital. The plane eventually departed for Chicago, arriving more than an hour late.

White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, 50, revealed on the "Charlie Rose" show that he would like to run for mayor of Chicago someday, despite previous attempts to quash such speculation. Emanuel stated he would support Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley if he seeks re-election but would run for mayor if Daley does not. Emanuel moved his family to Washington and took on the role of chief of staff when Obama tapped him, giving up a safe House seat. While Emanuel expressed a desire to reconnect with constituents, he emphasized his loyalty to President Obama and his commitment to serving until the end of the year, though he left the door open for an extension.

Local federal agents arrested a 19-year-old man, Sergio Morales Soto, just before he tried to leave the country on a flight to Guatemala. Soto was on a delayed flight on April 5 when agents located and apprehended him. They boarded the aircraft and took him into custody, according to Gregory Wiest, Deputy Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Atlanta. Soto will face six felony sex assault charges in Maryland. Agents at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport can quickly identify and arrest suspects, even those booked on flights, Wiest said. U.S. Customs Border Protection's Port Director Carey Davis stated that they arrest over 20 suspects daily.

Summary:
The article reveals that despite President Obama's supposed antagonism toward Wall Street, the financial industry continues to support Democratic lawmakers, including House Financial Services Committee member Gary Ackerman, who received significant contributions from the sector. While Mitt Romney has become a darling of Wall Street, Obama still receives substantial funding from financial services, indicating that the industry is not abandoning the Democratic Party. The New York congressional delegation, dominated by Democrats, receives substantial support from Wall Street, with Kirsten Gillibrand, a pro-Wall Street advocate, receiving more campaign contributions than her conservative Republican opponent. This suggests that Wall Street is more focused on maintaining its influence through established relationships rather than aligning strictly with one political party.

Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton chose Virginia Senator Tim Kaine as her running mate, a decision that drew mixed reactions from party members and liberal groups. Kaine, a former governor and chairman of the Democratic National Committee, was seen as a safe but potentially less enthusiastic pick compared to progressive alternatives like Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren. While Kaine received praise for his experience and ability to appeal to moderates, some Sanders supporters were disappointed, citing his support for trade deals and regulatory policies favored by big banks. Kaine's selection was seen as crucial for winning swing states like Virginia, where he has a strong base. Despite criticism from progressive organizations, Kaine's supporters highlighted his strong record on workers' issues and his fluency in Spanish. His pick also aimed to showcase Clinton's ability to unite the Democratic Party, though it raised concerns about potential divisions with the left.

Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli's tweet about wishing to be one of the 72 Virginians Osama bin Laden is supposedly "hanging out" with since his death sparked confusion and speculation. Cuccinelli wrote, "How much would I give to be one of the 72 Virginans Osama is 'hanging out' with since Sunday?" This tweet, referencing a joke about bin Laden's post-death experience, led to questions about Cuccinelli's intentions and whether he was referring to the Virginia-based Navy SEALs who killed bin Laden. The tweet also highlighted the political pitfalls of social media, as Cuccinelli had to clarify his statement and link to the joke to avoid misunderstanding.

A six-member medical board has decided to start a multi-stage plastic surgery on Abul Bajandar's hands in about three weeks. The 26-year-old, nicknamed "Tree Man" due to bark-like warts on his hands and feet, is still too weak for immediate surgery. Doctors plan to remove extra flesh from his thumb and index fingers to regain some functionality. Medical examinations, including blood tests and biopsies, will begin soon. Foreign doctors and researchers have expressed interest in his case, offering assistance. Bajandar, who has been suffering from the rare condition for 10 years, is hopeful about the upcoming surgery. He and his family are currently at Dhaka Medical College Hospital, with his wife and three-year-old daughter set to join him.

Kanye West, rapper, fashion designer, and member of the Kardashian family, is in need of financial support, as he claims to be $53 million in debt. A fan, Jeremy Piatt, created a GoFundMe page titled "Get Kanye Out of Debt," hoping to help the "greatest living artist" achieve his full potential. While some fans have contributed, the amount raised is minimal. West has also publicly asked tech billionaires Mark Zuckerberg and Larry Page for $1 billion each to support his ideas. Despite his financial struggles, West continues to release new music and fashion collections.

Amazon is launching a new in-store promotion this holiday season, allowing users of their Price Check app to get up to 5% off selected products by scanning barcodes with their smartphones. The deal, which runs from December 9th at 9 PM PST to December 10th at 11:59 PM PST, encourages customers to use the app in physical stores and take advantage of Amazon's generally lower prices. By offering this additional discount, Amazon aims to boost awareness of their Price Check app and drive more sales, while also providing customers with an incentive to shop with them. The promotion highlights the growing trend of price transparency and mobile shopping, as more consumers use their smartphones to compare prices in physical stores. However, brick-and-mortar retailers may face increased competition, as Amazon's strategy could draw customers away from traditional shopping experiences.

A 600-year-old dog meat festival in Zhejiang Province, China, has been canceled after intense protests from animal rights activists and online campaigns. Traditionally, thousands of dogs were slaughtered and served during the three-day event. Activists, including a blogger from Guangdong who started a campaign on Sina Weibo, highlighted the cruelty involved. The festival, which included dogs being stabbed, strangled, and boiled alive, faced backlash from both local residents and celebrities. Local officials eventually decided to cancel the event, citing public opinion and the need to respect animal rights, despite some villagers' attachment to the tradition.

Sen. Marco Rubio's response to President Obama's State of the Union Address was overshadowed by a moment where he had to pause to take a drink of water, sending social media into a frenzy. The Florida senator's quick sip from a bottle of Poland Spring water, near the end of his speech, was GIF-ified and tweeted about extensively. Social media users mocked Rubio, with Abby Huntsman and Ana Marie Cox making jokes about the timing of his water break. Rubio himself responded by tweeting a photo of the empty water bottle, acknowledging the moment. The incident led to a spike in Twitter activity, with the hashtag #watergate trending. Some Republicans defended Rubio, while others suggested better staff support.

President Trump's post-election press conference focused on the Mueller investigation and his response to the midterm election results. Trump suggested he could have ended the Mueller probe at any time and criticized Attorney General Jeff Sessions for recusing himself, leading to Sessions' resignation. Trump named Matthew Whitaker as the new acting attorney general, who has been critical of the investigation. Democrats regained control of the House, while Republicans maintained their majority in the Senate. Trump celebrated Republican Senate gains but faced criticism for his hardline immigration rhetoric. Democrats vowed to investigate Trump and his administration, with calls for Whitaker to recuse himself from overseeing the Mueller probe. Sessions' departure marked the end of a tumultuous tenure, with Trump and Sessions' relationship strained due to the Russia investigation.

North and South Korea will hold a summit in Pyongyang in September, both countries announced. It will be the third in-person meeting between South Korean President Moon Jae-in and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The two first met in April, pledging to forge closer relations and work to formally end the Korean War. High-level talks between officials from Pyongyang and Seoul at the DMZ confirmed the date, though a specific time has not been set. South Korean President Moon will be the third South Korean president to travel to the North Korean capital, and the first in more than a decade. The Winter Olympics helped warm relations between Pyongyang and the rest of the world, paving the way for the April inter-Korean summit and US President Donald Trump's meeting with Kim in Singapore. Both sides discussed denuclearization during their talks, but North Korea has continually rejected Washington's proposals, calling them "gangster-like."

Community leaders in Cleveland plan to file affidavits seeking charges against two police officers involved in the 2014 shooting death of 12-year-old Tamir Rice. The group, including clergy and civil rights activists, will hold a press conference to announce their intention to bypass the grand jury process and ask a judge to issue arrest warrants. The case currently rests with the Cuyahoga County Prosecutor's Office, which will present evidence to a grand jury. The community leaders argue that justice has not been served and that the criminal justice system has failed to provide answers or accountability in Tamir Rice's death.

A 34-year-old man, Jonathan Carlyle Merkley, was killed after lying down in front of a car driven by a friend who left his birthday party just after midnight in San Diego. Witnesses said both had been drinking alcohol with friends before the incident. Merkley tried to prevent the woman from leaving by walking into the path of her BMW and laying down in front of the moving car. The woman did not stop, ran over Merkley, and drove away. He suffered major chest trauma and died about 45 minutes later at a hospital. Police have not yet arrested the BMW driver, who has not been identified.

The Last Station, directed by Michael Hoffman and starring Christopher Plummer and Helen Mirren, offers a vivid and emotionally rich portrayal of the final year of Russian literary giant Leo Tolstoy's life. Mirren delivers a powerhouse performance as the jealous and tempestuous Countess Sofya, while Plummer brings warmth and humanity to Tolstoy, a man torn between his spiritual convictions and his love for his wife. The film, based on Jay Parini's novel, is a testament to great acting and filmmaking, blending historical drama with personal drama. Critics praise the performances, the lush landscapes, and the intricate plot, though some find the structure a bit uneven. Overall, The Last Station is a deeply satisfying and unforgettable cinematic experience.

Three years ago, Christine O'Donnell, a Delaware Senate candidate, spent the night in a Philadelphia man's apartment after a night of drinking. O'Donnell, who was in her late 30s at the time, ended up in bed with the man but claimed to be a virgin. The man, who approached Gawker anonymously, described O'Donnell's anatomy in detail, leading to backlash against both the story and the anonymous writer. Gawker defended the piece as a "great story" that highlighted the contrast between O'Donnell's public persona and her private life. The incident sparked debate on the treatment of women in politics and the media's focus on personal scandals.

Islamic State militants have released a new video purportedly showing the execution of five men accused of spying for the UK. The 10-minute film features a masked man with a British accent threatening attacks in the UK and targeting David Cameron. A young boy, believed to be around six or seven years old, also appears, speaking about killing "unbelievers." The video cannot be independently verified, but British authorities are examining its content. The release of the video comes after the recent loss of control over parts of the Iraqi city of Ramadi, potentially aimed at shifting Western attention. British Prime Minister David Cameron condemned the video as "despicable," while intelligence agencies are hunting for the identity of the masked man, who is being called the "new Jihadi John."

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC) suggested during a recent speech that as president, he would use the military to force Congress to reverse defense and intelligence budget cuts. In audio obtained by BenSwann.com, Graham stated he would "literally use the military to keep them in if I had to" until defense and intelligence cuts are restored. His office later clarified that this was meant as over-the-top humor. However, the proposal raises concerns about a potential self-coup, where a president uses military force to override the legislative branch. While Graham's spokesperson has since stated the comments were not meant literally, the suggestion has sparked debate over constitutional separation of powers.

Hope Solo's career with the U.S. Women's National Team is effectively over after she was suspended for six months and had her contract terminated following her controversial comments during the Rio Olympics. In a new documentary series called Keeping Score, viewers can witness the moment Solo learns about the harsh punishment. The series, produced by Fullscreen, offers an intimate look at the lives of three top female athletes, including Solo, Megan Rapinoe, and Crystal Dunn, as they prepare for and compete in the Olympics. The documentary captures their personal journeys and the challenges they face, including the fight for equal pay. Solo's reaction to the news is emotional, as she expresses disbelief and anger. The series, set to air on September 2, provides a unique perspective on the lives of these professional athletes.

The remains of the Civil War-era steamer Planter, once commandeered by enslaved African Americans and piloted to freedom by Robert Smalls, have likely been found off the coast of South Carolina. NOAA researchers identified a probable location in 2010, with large concentrations of iron consistent with a sunken ship buried under 10-15 feet of sand and water. The shipwreck is situated within an environmentally sensitive area of Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge. NOAA's discovery aims to highlight African-American contributions to maritime history and inspire future generations. The Planter's escape in 1862, where Smalls and his crew commandeered the ship and delivered it to the Union Navy, made Smalls the first African-American captain in the U.S. Navy and a member of Congress. Despite its historical significance, the ship's remains may not be salvaged due to environmental concerns.

Legendary Pennsylvania jockey Jose Flores, 56, died Thursday after suffering a headfirst fall during a race at Parx Racing in Bensalem. Flores, who had won 4,650 races and earned over $64 million, was riding 14-1 shot Love Rules in the ninth race when the horse went down, causing Flores to hit the ground headfirst. He was placed on life support but was officially pronounced dead at 12:42 p.m. on Thursday. Flores' longtime agent, Dave Yanuzzi, said Flores would have likely reached 5,000 wins had he not suffered several serious injuries in the last 3 1/2 years. The accident happened on Monday, and racing was canceled on Tuesday but planned to resume on Saturday. Flores leaves behind a wife and three sons.

Avicii, the Swedish DJ known as Tim Bergling, died by cutting himself with broken glass, according to sources familiar with his death. Found dead in Oman, Avicii's family stated he struggled with existential questions and could not go on. Despite his success with hits like "Wake Me Up," Avicii battled health issues, including acute pancreatitis from heavy drinking, and quit touring in 2016. Known for his generosity, Avicii donated millions to charities, including $1 million from his 2012 House for Hunger tour. His death came after a life of intense touring and personal struggles.

Three former WWE wrestlers passed away in separate incidents: Brian Christopher, son of WWE Hall of Famer Jerry "The King" Lawler, died after hanging himself in a Tennessee jail cell; Nikolai Volkoff, known for his iconic villainous character as Nikolai Volkoff, died at 70 due to heart problems; and Brickhouse Brown, a wrestler known for his time in various wrestling promotions, died at 57 from cancer. The wrestling community mourned the losses, with many expressing condolences and remembering the contributions of these wrestlers.

Tesla's sales in Hong Kong halted in April following the government's elimination of tax breaks for electric vehicles, highlighting the company's dependency on such incentives. With the tax waiver capped and only applicable to first-time owners, the cost of Tesla models significantly increased, reducing their appeal compared to other brands. Tesla registered 2,939 first-time EV registrations in March before the policy change, a stark contrast to the absence of new Tesla registrations in April. As Hong Kong's EV market shifts, Tesla is focusing on mainland China, where it aims to establish a manufacturing facility to avoid high import taxes and capitalize on growing demand for electric vehicles due to government efforts to combat air pollution.

Malcolm Gladwell's argument that the revolution will not be Tweeted has been challenged by the backlash against Gap's new logo. Social media users successfully pressured Gap to revert to its classic blue box logo, proving that online activism can drive real change. Gap's decision to crowdsource a new logo design and then backpedal faced criticism, with social media users mocking the new logo and demanding a return to the old one. This incident highlights the power of social media in shaping public opinion and influencing corporate decisions, contradicting Gladwell's skepticism about the effectiveness of online activism.

O.J. Simpson was banned from the Cosmopolitan Hotel in Las Vegas after reportedly being removed for unruly behavior. Simpson's lawyer, Malcolm LaVergne, denies claims that Simpson was drunk and disruptive, stating he was there to eat chicken wings and was a social drinker. LaVergne says no reason was given for the ban, and Simpson left quietly after being notified. The hotel has not issued a statement regarding the incident, which some reports claim involved broken glasses and a dispute with staff. Simpson, released from prison last month, is allowed to consume alcohol in moderation as part of his parole conditions.

At least nine people, including two children, were killed and dozens injured as violent storms and tornadoes swept through parts of the Midwest on Friday evening, officials said. The storms, which brought peak rainfall of 7.9 inches in Oklahoma, caused widespread damage, including overturned vehicles and destroyed homes. In Oklahoma City, a mother and child died in a vehicle, while seven fatalities were reported in Canadian County. The storms also hit Missouri and Illinois, damaging a high school gym and several homes. Three people drowned in Missouri due to flooding. Emergency officials surveyed the damage, with power outages affecting over 86,000 customers. The storms, which followed a powerful EF5 tornado that struck Moore, Oklahoma, two weeks earlier, left residents reeling.

Donald Trump's visit to Mexico City as the Republican presidential nominee garnered mixed reactions. After a closed-door meeting with President Enrique Peña Nieto, Trump emphasized mutual respect and the shared interests of the two nations. Trump stated that both countries should respect each other's right to build a border wall, though he did not discuss the issue of Mexico paying for it. Peña Nieto challenged Trump's characterization of the border situation, noting that illegal immigration has decreased, and highlighted the importance of trade and mutual respect. The meeting was seen as a strategic move by Trump, aiming to project a more diplomatic image ahead of his immigration-focused speech in Arizona. Despite the invitation from both Trump and Hillary Clinton, Peña Nieto's decision to meet with Trump was criticized by some Mexican leaders, who found it puzzling given Trump's past negative rhetoric towards Mexico.

Celebrities are seriously considering moving to Canada or other countries if Donald Trump wins the presidency. Lena Dunham, Miley Cyrus, and Whoopi Goldberg have all expressed their intentions to leave the U.S. if Trump is elected. Other notable figures like Jon Stewart, Chelsea Handler, and Raven-Symone have also made similar declarations. Trump's sons, Eric and Donald Jr., responded by offering to buy their airfare. A website called "Cape Breton If Donald Trump Wins" even offers these celebrities a new home on a Canadian island.

A new drug, nalmefene, now available in the UK, helps people reduce their alcohol intake, particularly those consuming at least half a bottle of wine or three pints a day. This drug, suitable for those drinking above the World Health Organization's threshold of 7.5 units a day for men and 5 units for women, can be prescribed alongside counseling. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) has approved its use, making it accessible to patients who meet specific criteria. Nalmefene, costing £3 per day, aids in gradually cutting back on alcohol consumption, making it unsuitable for severe cases requiring immediate cessation. Experts suggest it is appropriate for individuals who might not recognize their alcohol dependency. The drug is expected to benefit around 35,000 people in the first year, though uptake may be lower due to patient preferences.

Arizona's March 22 presidential primary saw long lines and late voting hours at many polling places, with some voters waiting up to four hours and others until nearly 1 a.m. to cast their ballots. Maricopa County, which has 2 million registered voters, reduced the number of polling sites from 400 in 2008 to 60 this year, leading to significant delays. The U.S. Justice Department is investigating potential voting rights law violations, requesting details on the number of polling places and their impact on minority voters. Secretary of State Michele Reagan certified the results, opening a five-day window for legal challenges, particularly as Bernie Sanders' campaign considers contesting the outcome due to issues with provisional ballots.

Nearly a million jars of peanut butter from a bankrupt New Mexico plant are being dumped at a landfill to expedite the sale of the facility. The plant, once a major producer of organic peanut butter, was shuttered after a 2012 salmonella outbreak linked to 41 cases in 20 states. Bankruptcy trustee Clarke Coll faced the dilemma of selling the peanut butter to Costco, repackaging it, or donating it, but Costco rejected the product. Instead, Coll opted to destroy the peanut butter, valued at $2.6 million, by hauling it to a Curry County landfill. A Canadian company's last-minute $25 million bid to purchase the plant's assets has been accepted, potentially benefiting creditors by settling more of Sunland's debt.

Maine Department of Transportation is running a contest to select humorous safety messages for highway signs, with 2,000 entries submitted. Voting will begin soon for the public to choose from finalists, and winners will get their message displayed and prizes including a ride to Penobscot Narrows Bridge & Observatory, Maine State Ferry tickets, and a state park vehicle pass. Six winning messages, split into small and large sign categories, showcase clever safety themes like "Put Down UR Cell — Or You May End Up In One" and "Be Protected — Not Projected – Buckle Up." These signs will blink across Maine's interstates, changing every two weeks.

A barroom brawl erupted at the Republican political gathering on Mackinac Island, involving aides for Sen. Marco Rubio and Sen. Rand Paul. Paul's aide, John Yob, alleged that Rubio's deputy campaign manager, Rich Beeson, punched him at Horn's Bar. Police are investigating the incident, with a grainy security camera video provided by Yob as evidence. The Mackinac Republican Leadership Conference, hosting six GOP presidential hopefuls, is ongoing. Beeson did not comment.

A mother is suing an anti-abortion group and the ad company that created a controversial billboard featuring her 4-year-old daughter's photo. The billboard, which appeared near the Holland Tunnel in Manhattan, displayed the message "The most dangerous place for an African American is in the womb," alongside a picture of the young girl in a sun dress. The mother claims the ad violated the terms of a contract she signed for stock family photos, which stated the image should not be used in "unflattering or unduly controversial" ways. She argues the ad caused emotional distress and may have damaged her daughter's modeling career. The ad company and anti-abortion group have not responded to comments.

The Federal Reserve took no new steps to support the economy in September, but said it was ready to act if job growth did not improve. The statement, released after a meeting of the Fed’s policy-making committee, indicated that the rate of economic growth had slowed and was likely to remain moderate. The central bank deferred any effort to improve the situation at least until the committee’s next scheduled meeting in mid-September. The absence of action disappointed some equity investors, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones indices experiencing slight drops. However, the Fed’s statement was seen as stronger than in previous meetings, suggesting a willingness to act if necessary. The market’s attention now turns to the September meeting, where the Fed will update its economic projections. Some analysts believe the Fed may still opt for action, assuming growth remains sluggish, but the statement keeps the debate open.

Britain sent a Royal Air Force plane carrying one million euros to Cyprus on Tuesday as a contingency measure for emergency loans for British military personnel, in case banks there stop giving out money due to the island's banking crisis. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is asking personnel if they want their salaries paid into UK bank accounts instead of Cypriot ones. The MoD stated, "An RAF flight left for Cyprus this afternoon with one million euros on board as a contingency measure to provide military personnel and their families with emergency loans in the event that cash machines and debit cards stop working completely." The MoD will consider further shipments if needed. The announcement comes amid reassurances to British troops posted in Cyprus that they will be fully compensated for any losses from the planned levy on savings as part of a bailout deal.

Regular caffeine consumption from coffee, tea, or chocolate does not appear to cause heart palpitations or irregular heartbeats, according to a new study. Researchers from the University of California San Francisco found no difference in instances of these heart disturbances, regardless of how much caffeine-containing products participants consumed daily. This challenges the long-held belief that caffeinated drinks can lead to dangerous heart rhythm disorders. The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, suggests that doctors should reconsider advising against regular consumption of caffeinated products, as they might have cardiovascular benefits. However, higher doses of caffeine can be deadly, and children should avoid excessive caffeine intake.

German prosecutors have indicted two former Nazi SS guards, both in their 90s, on charges of being accessories to murder for their service at the Stutthof concentration camp during World War II. The men, who served from June 1942 to May 1945, are accused of supporting hundreds of killings as guards. About 65,000 people died at Stutthof, with victims killed by gas chambers, shootings, and injections. The indictments, based on new German legal reasoning that allows prosecution of former camp guards without specific evidence of a crime, are part of an ongoing effort to bring justice to those responsible for atrocities committed during the Holocaust.

Police in Italy have deciphered a coded text that reveals details of a secretive mafia initiation process used by the 'Ndrangheta, a crime network based in southern Italy. The document, found during an investigation into a high-profile murder in Rome, is said to be part of the oath-taking process for new members of the "San Luca" clan. It was the first such document discovered in Rome and was deciphered by two policemen who spent weeks working on the code. The text, rich in symbolism, describes how to recognize a "Man of Honour" and is written in a special alphabet combining elements of Arabic, Cyrillic, and Chinese script. The 'Ndrangheta is now considered Italy's most powerful mafia, having surpassed Sicily's Cosa Nostra in power and influence.

Boeing's stock took a hit after a fire broke out on an Ethiopian Airlines 787 Dreamliner at Heathrow Airport, causing temporary runway closures. The incident, involving an empty plane, is being treated as unexplained by British police. Shares of Boeing fell 6.5% to $99.58. This comes after the entire fleet of 787s was grounded in January due to battery issues, with the latest modifications approved in May. The 787, marketed as a fuel-efficient aircraft, has faced production and technical challenges since its delayed entry into service in 2011. Boeing is working to understand the cause of the fire and address the situation.

A white man opened fire during a prayer meeting inside a historic black church in downtown Charleston, killing nine people in what authorities described as a hate crime. The shooting took place at Emanuel AME Church, a congregation with a long and tumultuous history, including a failed slave rebellion led by one of its founders. The victims included a state senator and pastor, several church leaders, and community members. President Obama and other officials called for healing and justice, while the community mourned and sought answers. The suspect, identified as a white male in his early 20s, was still at large as police and FBI agents searched for him.

The United States continued its strong performance in the London Olympics, setting a record with a victory in the women's 4x100-meter relay. The U.S. now leads both the gold and overall medal counts, having surpassed China for the top spot. With two more relays and other events to come, the U.S. could exceed its projected 30 medals. Away from track and field, Britain excelled in rowing and track cycling, securing its best medal performance in over a century. South Korea surprised with 13 gold medals, while Japan and Australia underperformed. The U.S. Olympic flagbearer, Bryshon Nellum, carried the flag at the closing ceremony after his remarkable journey from injury to Olympic success.

President Trump's nominee for secretary of the Navy, Philip Bilden, withdrew from consideration on Sunday, citing ethical concerns that would require significant financial sacrifices. Bilden, a former military intelligence officer who managed a private equity firm in Hong Kong, stated he could not satisfy the Office of Government Ethics requirements without "undue disruption and materially adverse divestment" of his family’s private financial interests. This withdrawal follows a similar situation with Vincent Viola, Trump’s previous nominee for Army secretary, who stepped down due to conflicts of interest. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis will now recommend a new nominee to Trump.

A 16-year-old Memphis teen named Chauncy Jones Black caught the attention of Matt White after Chauncy asked to carry groceries in exchange for donuts at a Kroger store. Chauncy, a straight A student, lives with his disabled mother in a home with no furniture and sleeps on pallets. Matt took Chauncy shopping and then drove him home. A GoFundMe page was set up to help Chauncy get a lawn mower and basic needs. The campaign has raised over $92,000, far exceeding the initial $250 goal. Matt is also working to provide new clothes and furniture for Chauncy and his mother, and to help them move to a safer neighborhood.

Lady Gaga's new album "Born This Way" sold 1.1 million copies in its first week, a record for digital downloads. This success, while impressive, came with a caveat: Amazon's 99-cent promotion for the digital version significantly boosted sales. Amazon, aiming to promote its Cloud Drive service, offered the album at a loss, with 440,000 downloads over two days. This strategy, while boosting Gaga's sales, raises questions about the true value of the album's success. Despite the controversy, the album's marketing campaign, spanning months and including various promotional appearances and tie-ins, underscores the evolving role of the album in the modern music industry.

Hispanic communities are grappling with increased anxiety as federal authorities implement President Trump’s immigration policies. The deportation of Guadalupe Garcia de Rayos, a working mother with U.S.-born children, has heightened concerns. Trump initially promised a deportation force targeting dangerous criminals but has since shifted to prioritizing "bad hombres." His executive orders have expanded the scope of enforcement, targeting so-called "sanctuary cities" and redefining "criminal aliens" to include minor offenses. This has led to widespread raids and detentions, raising fears among both undocumented and legal residents. Activists warn that indiscriminate enforcement could harm communities and potentially allow dangerous criminals to evade detection. Community organizations are working to inform and support immigrants but acknowledge limited tools to alleviate the current uncertainty.

A British study published in Science Translational Medicine offers a promising new pathway for future drug treatments of Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative diseases. The research, conducted at the Medical Research Council's Toxicology Unit at the University of Leicester, focuses on blocking a faulty signal in brains affected by such diseases, which shuts down the production of essential proteins, leading to brain cell death. The study tested a compound that inhibits an enzyme, known as PERK, which activates a defense mechanism that stops essential proteins from being produced. In mice with prion disease, the compound restored protein production, protected brain cells, and halted disease progression, improving memory and behavior. While the compound caused side effects like weight loss and mild diabetes in mice, scientists remain optimistic about developing a drug that could protect the brain without these issues. Experts believe this breakthrough could be a turning point in the search for medicines to control and prevent Alzheimer's, though human trials are still years away.

If Donald Trump wins the presidency, more Americans are considering moving to Canada. A new dating site called Maple Match aims to help them by connecting them with potential Canadian partners. CEO Joe Goldman says interest is high, with over 35,000 hits and 4,500 signups in just four days. The site's slogan, "Making dating great again," plays on the idea of escaping a Trump presidency. While some may view it as a joke, Goldman insists it's a serious attempt to help people find love before making a big move. With Canada offering attractions like universal healthcare and low business taxes, the site taps into the growing desire to escape a potential Trump presidency.

This recent comprehensive examination of Hollywood salaries by THR reveals some surprising earnings disparities among stars. Robert Downey Jr. earned $75 million from the Iron Man series, while Leonardo DiCaprio made $25 million for The Wolf Of Wall Street, compared to Jonah Hill's $60,000. Jennifer Lawrence earns $35 million from The Hunger Games, compared to Jennifer Aniston's $15 million. Product endorsements can be incredibly lucrative, with Robert Downey Jr. earning $12 million from an HTC endorsement, and Jennifer Aniston making as much from Aveeno and Smartwater as she does from starring in major films. Liam Neeson reportedly got $20 million for Taken 3. TV stars like Ashton Kutcher, Mark Harmon, and the main cast of The Big Bang Theory make substantial salaries. Alex Trebek earns $10 million annually for hosting a TV show. Jon Stewart's late-night show pays him $25 to $30 million annually

A Republican lawmaker, Rep. Ron DeSantis, has proposed an amendment that would halt funding for the special counsel’s Russia investigation 180 days after the amendment becomes law. The amendment also restricts the special counsel, Robert Mueller, from investigating matters occurring before June 2015, the month Trump announced his presidential bid. This comes as federal investigators are focusing on President Trump's role in crafting a response to a published article about a meeting between Russians and his son Donald Jr. at Trump Tower in 2016. The White House confirmed that Trump "weighed in" on the response, which was later revised to downplay the significance of the meeting. The amendment is part of an upcoming spending package and faces uncertainty in the Senate.

The Great Bear Rainforest, a vast wilderness area in Canada, is home to the spirit bear, a rare black bear with white fur due to a genetic variation. This remote region, difficult to access, is also rich in wildlife, including whales, wolves, and eagles. However, it faces a significant threat: a proposed oil pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia, which could transform the spirit bear’s habitat into a superhighway for supertankers. Conservationists and First Nations people are fighting this project, seeing the spirit bear as a symbol of their efforts to protect the rainforest. To raise awareness, a team of conservation photographers, including Thomas Peschak, Jack Dykinga, and Paul Nicklen, documented the spirit bear and the rainforest’s biodiversity. Their work aims to highlight the ecological and cultural significance of the spirit bear and the Great Bear Rainforest, urging public support to preserve this unique ecosystem.

A study published in Nature Climate Change projects that Antarctica's 600,000-strong emperor penguin population will decline by at least 19% by 2100 due to climate change, with two-thirds of colonies projected to decline by more than half. The iconic birds, which breed on sea ice, are vulnerable as sea ice becomes less secure. Satellite images have made it easier to estimate emperor populations, especially droppings from colonies visible from space. The study urges governments to list the birds as endangered, potentially imposing restrictions on tourism and fishing. The research fills a gap in understanding climate change and wildlife in Antarctica, with implications for other penguin species.

Fighting continues in South Sudan's key northern oil town of Malakal, with government forces battling rebels in the streets, reports state. The battle for Malakal, now in its second month, has seen tank battles in the town, according to the United Nations. The army denies rebel claims of taking control, while rebels say they have "recaptured" the town. The conflict, between President Salva Kiir's Dinka forces and those of ex-vice president Riek Machar, has displaced over 400,000 civilians and claimed thousands of lives, including over 200 civilians who drowned while fleeing the fighting. Meanwhile, government troops are advancing on Bor, the last major town held by rebels. Peace talks, overseen by the East African regional bloc IGAD, are ongoing in Addis Ababa, but a ceasefire remains elusive.

Selena Quintanilla's father, Abraham Quintanilla Jr., has filed a lawsuit to halt a planned television series about his daughter's relationship with her husband, Chris Perez. The project was announced just weeks after Endemol Shine North America agreed to develop it. Quintanilla Jr. claims only the singer's estate has the right to her name, image, and the commercial exploitation of her life story. Perez signed an agreement in 1995, two months after Selena's death, granting Quintanilla Jr. exclusive rights to all entertainment properties related to the late star. The lawsuit alleges Perez's book and potential TV series are unauthorized and in breach of contract.

The New York Review of Books editor Ian Buruma, who was forced out of his position amid controversy over publishing an essay by Jian Ghomeshi, has defended his decision. Ghomeshi, a former Canadian radio host, was acquitted in 2016 of sexual assault charges but faced multiple allegations of violent behavior from women. In his essay, Ghomeshi maintained the accusations against him were "inaccurate." Buruma, who faced intense backlash and pressure from advertisers, described his situation as ironic, noting he had previously published a theme issue on individuals convicted by social media. Buruma characterized his ouster as a capitulation to social media and university presses, and he stood by his decision to publish the essay, despite facing criticism for giving Ghomeshi a platform to defend himself.

In a New York Times Book Review, Douglas Brinkley reviewed Jodi Kantor’s book "The Obamas," describing it as "chick nonfiction" and focusing on the First Marriage rather than politics. This characterization drew criticism, with some arguing it reflects a double standard in how women authors are perceived. Jodi Kantor, a New York Times reporter, documented Michelle Obama’s influence on her husband’s agenda and her conflicts with White House staff. The review acknowledged the book’s strengths but also highlighted its perceived flaws, sparking debate about gender bias in journalism.

President Trump asked then-FBI Director Comey in February to stop investigating ousted national security advisor Michael Flynn, according to memos Comey recorded. House Oversight Chair Jason Chaffetz has requested these memos from the FBI, and Democrats are claiming obstruction of justice. The firing of Comey has slowed or stalled Republicans’ policy agenda on Capitol Hill, with health care and tax reform being pushed off the front-burner. Democrats are demanding more answers about the timing of the firing and the FBI’s investigation into possible ties between the Trump campaign and Russia, and are threatening to block the confirmation of any new FBI director until a special counsel is appointed. The controversy has already eaten into the rest of their work, with Senate Republicans holding meetings on the matter and struggling to maintain focus on their policy agenda.

Demi Moore has emerged from rehab and is back at work, executive producing "The Conversation" in Beverly Hills. She's using her Twitter handle @MrsKutcher, which may surprise followers given her recent divorce from Ashton Kutcher. Meanwhile, Ashton has been spotted dining with Mila Kunis, potentially reigniting speculation about a new relationship.

A dentist, Rashmi Patel, was charged with criminally negligent homicide and tampering with evidence in the death of a 64-year-old patient, Judith Gan, who stopped breathing during a dental procedure. Gan was under conscious sedation to have 20 teeth extracted and several implants installed when her oxygen levels dropped dangerously low. Patel ignored signs of distress from his assistants and continued the procedures, only stopping when Gan was declared "flat lining." She was rushed to the hospital but died. Patel's license was suspended and he was barred from performing conscious sedation, but he disputes the charges and urges them to be dropped.

David Letterman is launching a new Netflix talk show series called "My Next Guest Needs No Introduction with David Letterman." The first episode, set to debut on January 12, 2018, will feature an interview with Barack Obama, marking the former president's first on-camera talk-show chat since leaving office. Other guests include George Clooney, Malala Yousafzai, JAY-Z, Tina Fey, and Howard Stern. Each episode will explore in-depth conversations with Letterman's chosen guests, both inside and outside a studio setting, with field segments related to the featured guest. The show aims to bring together influential figures for intimate and humorous discussions.

Pastor Marrion P'Udongo, known as the "Schindler of Congo," has faced a new crisis after suffering severe kidney failure. Working tirelessly to save and nurture lives in war-torn northeastern Congo, P'Udongo has provided shelter, hope, and medical care to thousands. His most notable act came in 2003 when he sheltered over 70 people from ethnic Lendu militia, securing their safety through his own bravery and the intervention of a former congregant. Despite his heroic efforts, P'Udongo now requires a kidney transplant, estimated to cost around $76,000. After a successful initial transplant, his body rejected the new kidney, leaving him in critical condition. His friends and colleagues are now fundraising to cover the costs of another transplant and ongoing medication. P'Udongo's return to the St. Kizito orphanage and his community is hoped to continue his vital work, offering hope and

With Kate Middleton experiencing severe nausea and vomiting due to hyperemesis gravidarum, medical experts suggest she might be expecting twins. The Duchess of Cambridge, already expecting her third child, is in a London hospital managing the rare condition that impacts 2 percent of pregnant women, leading to weight loss and dehydration. While the condition traditionally indicates a healthy pregnancy, it could signal the birth of twins. Gamblers have placed bets on potential names, with "Elizabeth" topping the list of favorites, reflecting a possible return to traditional royal naming conventions.

Uganda's parliament has passed a stringent anti-homosexuality bill that could see repeat offenders jailed for life, despite international condemnation. The bill, championed by lawmaker David Bahati, bans the promotion of homosexuality and criminalizes the failure to report gay individuals. US President Barack Obama and human rights groups have criticized the measure as "odious" and a "grave assault on human rights." President Yoweri Museveni must now sign the bill into law. The vote comes amid a broader crackdown on perceived moral offenses, including an anti-pornography bill that bans sexually suggestive clothing and behavior. Ugandan gay activists express outrage and fear, warning of increased persecution.

George Papadopoulos, a former foreign policy adviser to President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign, pleaded guilty to making false statements to the FBI. Papadopoulos admitted to lying about his interactions with Russian officials, including claims that Russia had “thousands of emails” related to Hillary Clinton. The guilty plea, unsealed on October 30, 2017, marks the first public case related to Robert Mueller’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders downplayed Papadopoulos’s role, calling it “extremely limited” and a “volunteer position.” Papadopoulos’s guilty plea could have implications for the broader investigation into potential collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia.

The four children of Charles Vacca, a gun instructor killed in an incident at an Arizona gun range involving a nine-year-old girl, released a video message to the girl. In the video, Vacca's 11-year-old son Christopher and 15-year-old daughter Elizabeth addressed the unnamed girl, urging her to move forward and not let the tragedy define her. They expressed a hope to meet her someday and offer support. Vacca's legal representative, James Goodnow, appeared at the end, noting the family's awareness of the broader national discussion on gun culture but emphasizing the personal tragedy for both families.

North and South Korea will march together under a unified flag at the Winter Olympics opening ceremony, and field a joint women's ice hockey team, marking a diplomatic breakthrough following talks between the two countries. The unified team will compete in the Pyeongchang Games, while North Korea will send a 550-member delegation, including cheerleaders, artists, and taekwondo players for a demonstration. Prior to the Olympics, the teams will train together and perform a joint cultural event. The move comes after a thaw in relations, but some of Seoul's allies remain cautious about North Korea's intentions, with Japan warning against easing pressure on the North. The two Koreas have been in talks since last week, the first since 2015, amid heightened tensions over North Korea's nuclear and missile programs.

Snoop Dogg, the cannabis icon, has launched a new platform called Merry Jane, a comprehensive lifestyle site focusing on all aspects of marijuana. The site, which includes video and editorial content, aims to be the ultimate resource for both novices and seasoned users. Merry Jane will feature various show series, such as cooking shows and celebrity interviews, and will also delve into the business and politics of the cannabis industry. Users can search for specific strains and connect with local dispensaries. The platform also plans to allow dispensaries to manage their own digital storefronts. Snoop Dogg sees Merry Jane as a way to help people come out of the closet about their cannabis use. Meanwhile, other celebrities, including Jared Leto, Jessica Alba, and Justin Bieber, are investing in various tech and business ventures, reflecting a trend of stars diversifying their business interests beyond entertainment.

President Trump during a solo press conference after his summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un touted North Korea's potential in real estate, suggesting the country could benefit economically by developing its coastline with top-tier hotels. Trump mentioned that Kim showed interest in video simulations of possible projects, though he noted Kim was interested in a smaller scale version. Trump also emphasized North Korea's agreement to denuclearize and work towards peace on the Korean Peninsula.

Donald Trump's inauguration on January 20, 2017, will feature a ticketed ceremony with viewing locations in Washington D.C., and a parade open to the public. Trump encouraged his supporters to set an attendance record, but organizers expect about 800,000 people, fewer than Obama's first inauguration. The ceremony will include performances by Three Doors Down, Toby Keith, and the Mormon Tabernacle Choir. Trump's speech is expected to focus on unity and promise keeping, with a potential nod to previous inaugural addresses by Kennedy, Reagan, and Nixon. The parade will follow Pennsylvania Avenue and pass by Trump's hotel. The inaugural weekend will also include balls, a wreath-laying ceremony, and a prayer service, with both pro- and anti-Trump protests anticipated.

Grambling State won the Celebration Bowl 10-9 by blocking North Carolina Central's extra-point kick after the Eagles' quarterback was penalized for excessive celebration. North Carolina Central's Quentin Atkinson scored a 39-yard touchdown with 2:14 left, but the extra point was negated, and Grambling blocked the subsequent attempt. The win is Grambling's 15th national championship in black college football history.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein says she's open to holding public hearings on the NSA’s surveillance programs, noting she's held classified sessions and defended the programs as helpful in thwarting terrorist attacks. However, she acknowledges it's difficult to detail specific successes due to the classified nature of the information. She cited cases involving David Headley and Najibullah Zazi to support her stance.

The U.S. military has decided to exhume the possible grave of Arthur "Bud" Kelder, a World War II prisoner of war, from an anonymous grave in a Philippine war cemetery. Kelder's family has long fought to get him identified, even suing the Pentagon. Using historical records, a family cousin discovered clues suggesting the grave labeled "X-816" might be Bud's. Despite some support from military experts, the Joint Prisoners of War/Missing in Action Accounting Command (JPAC) refused to exhume the grave for DNA testing. Now, the military plans to exhume not only X-816 but also the remains of 10 other unknowns from the same grave. The family hopes this will finally bring closure, but remains frustrated by the delay and calls for reforms in the MIA accounting process.

First lady Michelle Obama will attend the funeral of Hadiya Pendleton, a 15-year-old honor student and band majorette from Chicago, who was fatally shot about a mile from the Obamas' home. The funeral is set for Saturday at Greater Harvest Baptist Church. Obama will be accompanied by Valerie Jarrett, a senior adviser to the president, and Secretary of Education Arne Duncan. The first lady expressed her heartbreak over the senseless gun violence that took Hadiya's life, which occurred just days after she performed at President Obama's inauguration. Hadiya's family, including her cousin Shatira Wilks, appreciate the gesture but want the funeral to be a celebration of Hadiya's life. The funeral will also feature a visitation on Friday and a wake before the service. Governor Pat Quinn, a Chicagoan, will speak at the funeral, emphasizing the need for tougher gun control measures.

Charlie Sheen's political one-liners and ego-driven comments at DAR Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C., drew mixed reactions from the audience. He joked about running for president with Nicolas Cage, made controversial remarks about President Obama's birthplace, and proposed radical changes to federal spending and drug laws. The event, part of his "Violent Torpedo of Truth" tour, highlighted Sheen's unpredictable and often entertaining persona, though his late arrival due to legal issues added to the chaotic atmosphere.

Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner faced backlash after tweeting in Spanish with a mock Chinese accent, replacing "r"s with "l"s, which has been shared over 1,500 times. To address the controversy, she later tweeted that the situation's absurdity could only be handled with humor. The tweet came during her visit to China, where she aimed to boost investment in Argentina's economy. Her government has also been dealing with the investigation into the death of prosecutor Alberto Nisman, who accused the President of covering up Iran's involvement in a 1994 bombing.

Donald Trump faced criticism for his interview on The Tonight Show, where he mocked an NBC reporter's question about his language use, calling him "so politically correct." The interview drew backlash for its light-hearted tone, especially given Trump's history of using offensive language. Meanwhile, during a QVC segment, Trump's steaks, once a major product line, received overwhelmingly negative reviews from customers, highlighting the disparity between his public persona and actual product quality. Trump's various business ventures, including Trump University, Trump Airlines, and Trump Vodka, also faced legal challenges and poor performance, further undermining his reputation as a business genius.

The Bombay High Court may grant a temporary reprieve to Renuka Shinde and Seema Gavit, the first women convicts set for hanging in independent India, as their advocate plans to challenge the rejection of their mercy petitions. The sisters, along with their mother and husband, were convicted in 2001 for kidnapping and killing nine children between 1990 and 1996. Their execution, scheduled for this Saturday, could be delayed pending a court decision. Meanwhile, the sisters' health has deteriorated significantly, and their lawyer argues they should not be executed due to their poor physical condition.

A rare annular solar eclipse was visible across a narrow path stretching from Asia to the western United States, creating a "ring of fire" effect. Viewers in Tokyo, Japan, and other cities along the path enjoyed spectacular views, while heavy clouds marred the view in Hong Kong. In the U.S., thousands attended parties in northern California and southern Oregon to witness the first annular eclipse in the region since 1994. Experts warned against looking directly at the sun without proper viewing equipment. The eclipse, which occurred when the moon was at its farthest point from Earth, was visible for about four minutes in Tokyo around 7:32 a.m. local time. The next annular eclipse will be visible over northern Australia on November 13.

An Ohio man scheduled for execution on Thursday is set to be put to death using a never-before-used lethal drug combination. Dennis McGuire, convicted of the 1989 rape and fatal stabbing of Joy Stewart, was moved to the Southern Ohio Correctional Facility in Lucasville on Wednesday. His attorneys argue he is at risk of experiencing "air hunger," a terrifying sensation of struggling to breathe, while the state disputes this scenario. Documents show McGuire attempted to become an organ donor but was denied a reprieve by Governor John Kasich. The state plans to use intravenous doses of midazolam, a sedative, and hydromorphone, a painkiller, for the execution. The method has been on the books since 2009 but has never been used before. A federal judge sided with the state, allowing the execution to proceed. McGuire's last words were, "I'm going to heaven, I'll see you there when you come."

The Libyan government has confirmed the death of Muammar Gaddafi, ending his 42-year rule. Gaddafi was reportedly found hiding in a drain outside Sirte, where his convoy was hit by NATO airstrikes. His body was reportedly dragged through the streets of Sirte, and he was shot in the head and both legs according to NTC officials. Confusion surrounds the fate of other Gaddafi family members, with reports suggesting his sons Mutassim and Saif al-Islam may have been killed or captured. Gaddafi's spokesman Moussa Ibrahim and cousin Ahmed Ibrahim were reportedly captured. NATO is expected to formally decide to end its mission over Libya, marking a significant milestone in the transition to a new government.

Three Idaho Republican lawmakers refused to attend a Hindu prayer delivered by guest chaplain Rajan Zed before the Idaho Senate on Tuesday, while the majority of senators remained for the invocation. Zed, president of the Universal Society of Hinduism, gave a lengthy prayer in both English and Sanskrit, focusing on selflessness and peace. Senators from both parties shook his hand and thanked him afterward. Vick, Nuxoll, and Den Hartog cited their religious beliefs as reasons for missing the prayer, with Nuxoll also expressing a desire for a Christian prayer to be included. Zed had previously offered the invocation to Senate Pro Tem Brent Hill.

Anthony Weiner's campaign faces another setback as his campaign manager, Danny Kedem, resigns, leaving the already struggling operation without a leader. Kedem informed Weiner of his decision in the last 24 hours, citing the recent revelations about Weiner's continued inappropriate online behavior. Weiner's campaign, already short on experienced staff, now faces further challenges. Political strategist David Axelrod and Republican congressman Peter King both call for Weiner to drop out of the race, citing his "pathological problem" and suggesting he is not psychologically qualified to be mayor.

Protesters opposed to China’s territorial claims in the South China Sea marched on the Chinese embassy in Manila, escalating tensions with the Philippines. The small, rocky Huangyan Island, about 220 kilometers from the Philippine mainland, has become a focal point of the dispute. The Philippines accused Chinese vessels of illegally fishing in their territory, leading to increased tensions. Chinese officials blamed the Philippines for complicating the situation and demanded effective measures to protect Chinese nationals. Smaller protests also took place in Beijing. The standoff has affected trade, with 1,200 containers of Philippine bananas held in customs due to quarantine concerns. Civic groups in the Philippines plan more protests outside Chinese missions in New York, Singapore, and Rome. Both countries claim the Scarborough Shoal, known as Panatag Shoal to Filipinos or Huangyan Island to the Chinese, and the dispute has drawn mass support in the Philippines.

A 34-year-old substitute teacher was arrested for indecent exposure after performing a cartwheel in a high school choir class with no underwear on, police allege. Lacey Sponsler, while substituting at Pawhuska High School, exposed herself to students in the junior high choir room, according to a probable cause affidavit. Sponsler's actions were captured on video by a student. When questioned, Sponsler initially denied the incident but later admitted to performing the cartwheel. She faces charges of indecent exposure. Sponsler has a history of legal troubles, including previous convictions for marijuana possession and drug paraphernalia.

Forcing a smile when feeling unhappy can make you feel worse, according to a study by Anirban Mukhopadhyay from Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. Smiling frequently may link to negative emotions, leading to unhappy memories. The best strategy is to wait until you feel better before attempting to smile. This research suggests that the motivation behind smiling significantly impacts emotional well-being.

Miley Cyrus has quit smoking marijuana, stating she hasn't done it in three weeks, the longest she's gone without it. Cyrus, now 24, is promoting her upcoming album, "Malibu," set to release its first single on May 11. She discusses her relationship with fiancé Liam Hemsworth, noting they had to "refall for each other" after their 2013 breakup. Cyrus also talks about her political activism, including her initiative #HopefulHippies, and her evolving music style, which will feature more country elements. She emphasizes the importance of reaching out to different audiences and creating real change through compassionate communication.

Pope Francis delivered the first papal address to a joint session of Congress, urging lawmakers to address climate change, poverty, and the refugee crisis. His speech emphasized the need for a "culture of care" and an integrated approach to combating these issues. Francis highlighted the importance of protecting human life at every stage and called for an end to the arms trade, advocating for the rehabilitation of criminals over capital punishment. He also addressed the family, expressing concern that it is "threatened, perhaps as never before, from within and without," but did not explicitly mention abortion or same-sex marriage. The historic event drew a mix of applause from Democrats and silence from Republicans, with some conservative lawmakers boycotting the speech due to disagreements on climate change.

A 2-year-old Tennessee boy named Owen Torti is living with a rare genetic disorder called LCHAD, which means his body cannot break down certain fats for energy. He must eat every hour to avoid his body breaking down muscle for energy, a process that can lead to serious health issues like kidney or liver problems. Owen was diagnosed with the disorder as a newborn, and his parents, Kayla and Tyler Torti, are raising awareness and funds to help other families dealing with LCHAD. They organized a Ragnar Relay run, raising $15,000 to support Owen and his medical expenses. The Tortis hope their efforts will help spread awareness and provide hope to other families facing similar challenges.

Four people died when a small propeller-driven plane crashed into two houses in East Haven, Connecticut, on Friday. The victims include 13-year-old Sade Brantley, 1-year-old Madisyn Mitchell, and the pilot, 54-year-old former Microsoft executive Bill Henningsgaard, and his 17-year-old son. Emergency repairs were made to the damaged homes to allow for the recovery of the bodies. A vigil was held at Margaret Tucker Park, attended by the children’s mother, Joann Mitchell, who wrote on Facebook about her loss. The mayor and governor praised the community’s support. The plane, a Rockwell International Turbo Commander 690B, was making its first approach to Tweed New Haven Airport when the crash occurred. Henningsgaard had previously survived a crash in 2009, where he and his mother were rescued from the Columbia River. His family and the Social Venture Partners foundation expressed their condolences.

The price of Bitcoin continues to surge, reaching $250, with some speculating that it could go much higher. However, many view Bitcoin as a speculative bubble that could crash. Despite its potential risks, the rapid rise in value has made many early investors rich. The lack of regulation and the potential for fraud and hacking also pose significant risks. Some argue that Bitcoin's limited supply and its potential as a global currency could support its value, but others warn that its complexity and lack of mainstream acceptance could lead to its downfall. The future of Bitcoin remains uncertain, with both bullish and bearish perspectives coexisting.

The family of Thomas Eric Duncan, the first person diagnosed with Ebola in the United States, visited him at the hospital but declined to view him via video, finding it too upsetting. Duncan, 42, is in critical condition and on a ventilator and receiving kidney dialysis. His nephew expressed optimism about his condition, saying they hope to see him soon. Health officials are monitoring 48 people who had contact with Duncan, with 10 considered high risk. None of the monitored individuals have shown symptoms. Duncan's care is expected to cost around half a million dollars, with the hospital unlikely to collect the full amount due to his lack of insurance. The case highlights the challenges and costs of treating Ebola patients in the U.S.

The Pacific coast's sardine population is in severe decline, raising concerns for the marine ecosystem and commercial fishing. This critical forage fish, essential to species like salmon, tuna, and seabirds, has seen its numbers drop by 72% since 2006. The Pacific Fishery Management Council (PFMC) should set conservative catch limits and prohibit unregulated fishing on similar, abundant forage species. The decline is partly due to a naturally occurring climate cycle, but its exact cause remains unclear. If sardines do not recover soon, the West Coast's marine life and fishing industry could suffer. Conservation groups advocate for halting sardine fishing entirely when populations are low to prevent further decline. The sardine's boom-bust nature and its role as a key food source highlight the need for cautious management and further scientific study.

The Federal Communications Commission's (FCC) net neutrality rules, which aimed to ensure equal treatment of all internet traffic, have been struck down by a federal appeals court. This decision allows internet service providers (ISPs) like Comcast and Verizon to potentially prioritize certain content by charging content providers for faster delivery, or by blocking or discriminating against websites they dislike. Critics warn that this could lead to a two-tiered internet, where only those who can afford to pay for faster access will enjoy smooth streaming and fast load times, while smaller websites and services struggle. The FCC now faces the challenge of finding a way to maintain an open internet, possibly by reclassifying ISPs as common carriers, a move that could face significant political resistance. Without net neutrality, the internet may evolve into a system where ISPs can favor their business partners and hinder competition, potentially raising prices for consumers and stifling innovation.

President-elect Donald Trump questioned outgoing CIA Director John Brennan's credibility on Twitter, suggesting he might be the "leaker of Fake News." Trump's tweets came after Brennan warned Trump about the Russia threat and criticized his lack of understanding regarding Russia's actions, including Syria, Crimea, Ukraine, and nuclear build-up. Trump also criticized intelligence agencies, previously calling their actions comparable to those of Nazis.

A new species of praying mantis has been named after Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in honor of her work for gender equality. Scientists from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History and Case Western Reserve University named the Madagascar species Ilomantis ginsburgae, recognizing Ginsburg's advocacy and her appreciation for the jabot, a decorative neck accessory resembling the mantis's neck plate. This research, published in Insect Systematics & Evolution, marks the first time female genitalia have been used to classify a new species of praying mantis, addressing the historical reliance on male genitalia characters. The study involved analyzing 30 praying mantis specimens from three museums, highlighting the importance of considering both sexes in scientific investigations.

New satellite images released by the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea show steady growth in a prison camp on the northeast coast, with Camp 25 expanding 72 percent between 2009 and 2010 alone. The report indicates the camp now includes several new buildings, agricultural fields, and almost two dozen guards, housing about 5,000 prisoners. While North Korea claims to have closed down some of its political prison camps, the expansion of others, such as Camp 25, suggests ongoing human rights abuses. The reasons for the growth are unclear, but may be linked to increased crackdowns on defectors and political opponents.

ATM manufacturers Diebold Nixdorf and NCR have warned of a rise in "jackpotting" attacks, where criminals install malware or specialized hardware to force ATMs to dispense large amounts of cash. These attacks, previously more common in Europe and Asia, have now been reported in the United States, with the U.S. Secret Service issuing warnings to financial institutions. The attacks typically involve gaining physical access to the ATM and using an endoscope to connect a laptop to the machine's internal components. Once control is gained, cash can be dispensed at a rapid rate. Diebold Nixdorf has confirmed that Opteva series ATMs are targeted by the Ploutus.D malware, and the Secret Service warns that further attacks are planned. Financial institutions are advised to update their systems and take steps to protect their ATMs.

Dozens were shot over a 24-hour period in Chicago, with five fatalities, during a weekend that included the Lollapalooza music festival. The violence was concentrated on the West and South sides, with the heaviest incidents between midnight and 3 a.m., when 30 people were shot. Multiple mass shootings, each involving three or more victims, occurred in areas like the Gresham neighborhood, where eight people were wounded. Chicago Police Chief of Patrol Fred Waller blamed gangs for the violence, stating that the weekend was one of the city's most violent in recent memory. Despite heightened security for Lollapalooza, the festival did not divert police resources, according to Waller. The surge in violence strained hospital resources, with Stroger Hospital limiting visitation to immediate family members. The community and local officials expressed frustration and called for a collective effort to address the issue.

US Defense Secretary James Mattis issued a stern warning to North Korea on Wednesday, urging the regime to "cease any consideration of actions that would lead to the end of its regime and destruction of its people." This came a day after President Donald Trump threatened to unleash "fire and fury" on Pyongyang. Mattis called for North Korea to "stop isolating itself and stand down its pursuit of nuclear weapons," emphasizing that the US military response would be "grossly overmatched" if North Korea initiated conflict. Despite the escalating rhetoric, Mattis stressed his preference for resolving issues through diplomacy rather than military action.

President Barack Obama's convention speech, the shortest acceptance speech by an incumbent in 36 years, was workmanlike and focused on reiterating his achievements and defending his record, though it fell short of being historically memorable. Obama's speech was criticized for not offering a clear second-term agenda and for feeling more like a State of the Union address. While it failed to sway undecided voters, it did send convention-goers back to their home states excited about the final 60 days of the campaign. Among the highlights, Gabby Giffords' recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance was an emotional high point, and John Kerry's scathing assessment of Mitt Romney's foreign policy credentials was well-received. However, some speakers, like Brian Schweitzer and Caroline Kennedy, were underwhelming. Overall, Obama's speech was seen as average, neither a triumph nor a failure.

Focus, a caper film starring Will Smith and Margot Robbie, fails to deliver a coherent plot or impactful relationship, despite its promising premise and talented cast. The movie, directed by John Requa and Glenn Ficarra, is a con in itself, with a convoluted narrative and absurd scenes that leave the audience questioning the logic of the story. Smith's Nicky Spurgeon, a master of confidence and pickpocketing, and Robbie's Jess, a quick study in the art of deception, form an unlikely partnership. However, the emotional core of their relationship lacks depth, and Smith's performance, while charming, is overshadowed by the film's lack of substance. The writers and directors, who initially considered a star-studded cast, ultimately chose Smith and Robbie, creating a dynamic that, while not revolutionary, offers some entertaining moments. Despite its flaws, Focus manages to maintain a light-hearted tone and a few clever scenes, making it a watchable, if not memorable,

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, facing a scandal involving the shutdown of traffic lanes on the George Washington Bridge, sought to reconnect with the Republican base at the Conservative Political Action Conference. His speech, though uncharacteristically low-key, praised Republican governors for getting things done and contrasted their actions with the perceived inaction in Washington. Christie emphasized the importance of defining the GOP as the party of ideas and entrepreneurship, urging conservatives to focus on positive messaging. He defended his own record, highlighting budget cuts and anti-union efforts, and sought to distance himself from the dysfunction in Congress. Christie also addressed the media, stating that the GOP should not let it define the party’s agenda. His appearance at CPAC marked a thaw in his relationship with the Republican establishment, which had previously snubbed him.

Jim VandeHei, co-founder of Politico, in a Wall Street Journal op-ed, calls for a "true outsider" to disrupt Washington, suggesting a military leader or a third-party candidate with military experience as running mate. He advises exploiting fear and using muscular language on terrorism, referencing drone technology. However, his piece is criticized for its simplistic solutions and potential authoritarian undertones, especially in light of recent political climate. VandeHei's call for exploiting fear and militarizing politics is seen as problematic, given the current political landscape.

Nikki Sixx, 55, the bassist of Mötley Crüe, married model Courtney Bingham on March 2 at Greystone Mansion in Los Angeles. The couple, who have been together for over three years, celebrated with a gothic rock meets French countryside-themed wedding in front of family and friends. Bingham's custom-made wedding dress was designed by her aunt and inspired by Jennifer Lawrence's Oscar dress. The couple's celebration included a triple berry cake from Sweet Lady Jane. This is Sixx's third marriage, following divorces from Playboy playmate Brandi Brandt and actress Donna D'Errico.

Arizona Governor Jan Brewer hailed the Supreme Court's ruling as a "victory for the rule of law" and a "legal victory" for her state, while President Barack Obama praised the decision to strike down key provisions of the controversial Arizona immigration law. The Supreme Court upheld one provision allowing police to check the immigration status of individuals they stop or arrest if there is reasonable suspicion of illegal presence, but struck down three other provisions. Governor Brewer emphasized that the state's efforts to protect its citizens and secure its borders had been "vindicated," while President Obama highlighted the federal government's supremacy in immigration matters. Both sides claimed victory, with the governor stressing non-racial profiling and the president focusing on comprehensive immigration reform.

MPs are set to approve the introduction of compulsory lie detector tests for monitoring high-risk sex offenders in England and Wales starting next year. The tests, which measure physiological responses to determine truthfulness, will be used for around 750 serious offenders who have been released from prison. These offenders will be monitored to ensure they do not breach the terms of their release or pose a risk to public safety. The move follows a successful pilot scheme in the Midlands, where polygraph tests were found to increase honesty among offenders. The National Probation Service will utilize this technology as part of a comprehensive approach to managing high-risk offenders. The tests, though not admissible in court, are expected to enhance the effectiveness of community supervision and reduce the risk of reoffending.

A hayride accident in Chunky, Mississippi, on Halloween killed three people and injured several others. The crash occurred around 7:45 p.m. on Highway 80 when a Ford F-150 rear-ended a trailer carrying adults and children. Three helicopters and multiple ambulances rushed to the scene, and two died at the scene while a third died waiting for a helicopter. The victims were all related, but their names and ages were not released. The cause of the crash is unknown. Chunky, a small town with about 325 residents, is near the Chunky River and is located about 80 miles east of Jackson.

Two children died after the car they were in was hit by a speeding driver on U.S. Highway 175 near Pine Street in South Dallas. Kelvin Walker, 23, was driving a Range Rover SUV at high speed when he struck a Honda sedan carrying a family of five. Two of the children in the sedan, a 12 or 13-year-old boy and a 13-month-old baby, were ejected and the 12-year-old boy died at the scene. The baby was taken to Children’s Medical Center but later died. The baby and the 12-year-old boy were not identified. The children’s parents and another child were treated for minor injuries.
