Walker, who has a criminal history, faces vehicular manslaughter charges and is being held in jail. Three other people died in separate flooding incidents in North Texas over the holiday weekend.

CNN producer Mohammed Tawfeeq, an Iraqi national and permanent legal resident of the U.S. since 2013, has filed a federal lawsuit challenging President Trump's executive order on immigration, which bars people from seven Middle Eastern countries, including Iraq, from entering the U.S. for 90 days. Tawfeeq was detained at Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport in Atlanta for additional screening upon his return from Baghdad, delaying his entry. The lawsuit claims the executive order violates the Immigration and Nationality Act and the Administrative Procedure Act, increasing uncertainty for lawful permanent residents like Tawfeeq. It seeks a declaration that the ban does not apply to legal permanent residents and an order preventing its application to those individuals.

Tunisia's leadership changed hands twice in less than 24 hours as the country grappled with chaos following the ouster of President Zine el Abidine Ben Ali. Fouad Mebazaa, the former president of the lower house of parliament, was sworn in as interim president, vowing to consult with all political parties before holding elections within 60 days. The rapid succession of leaders and the ensuing violence have raised questions about constitutional propriety and the stability of the new government. Amidst the turmoil, security forces and ordinary Tunisians worked to quell unrest, with army tanks positioned in the capital. The events in Tunisia have inspired hope for change across the Arab world, but also raised concerns about potential chaos and the role of former regime loyalists in the ongoing violence.

The body of Carmine Carini, 35, a reputed member of a local mob family, was found in cement overshoes in the waters off Brooklyn. Carini's father, also named Carmine, is an associate of the Colombo crime family. The victim died from blunt-force trauma to the head and had also been stabbed. He was identified through fingerprints. Carini had a criminal history, including multiple robbery arrests and a drug-possession charge. His father was previously imprisoned for the 1983 killing of a Bay Ridge record shop owner but was later freed in a plea deal.

A man named Frank Romano is searching for his 6-year-old bull terrier, Ty, who went missing from a cargo area at LAX after a Delta Airlines flight. Ty escaped from his pet carrier, but Romano questions how this could have happened. The situation becomes more confusing when Romano is told the kennel would appear in baggage claim, but it never did. Romano has called Delta multiple times, but the airline has not provided clear answers. This case is not isolated; Delta has a history of losing pets, as evidenced by several other incidents, including a German Shepherd that died after being lost in Atlanta. The airline's handling of these cases has raised concerns about their commitment to safe pet travel.

A Thai surrogate mother, Pattaramon Chanbua, who was left with a Down syndrome baby boy named Gammy after his Australian parents took his healthy twin sister home, says she would be willing to take back the twin girl if the reports about her alleged Australian father being a convicted sex offender are true. Gammy, who also has a heart condition, has been cared for by Chanbua since his birth. The Australian couple has not publicly commented on the case, with one of them denying intentional abandonment and claiming they did not know about the twin. An online campaign has raised over $215,000 for Gammy's medical expenses.

Meghann Foye, a 38-year-old author, felt envious of co-workers who got to leave early for maternity leave and parents who left early to pick up their children. Inspired by these observations, she proposed the concept of "meternity" leave, which she defines as a sabbatical-like break allowing women, and to a lesser extent men, to focus on personal life outside of work. Foye believes this leave could benefit women who follow a traditional career path and men who have been in the workforce for a decade or more. She argues that such a leave would help women learn to self-advocate and prioritize their family needs, potentially leading to a more balanced life. Foye's own "meternity" leave, though not related to having children, taught her to live on her own terms and advocate for what works for her. She emphasizes the need for both parents and non-parents to support and not judge each other in achieving work-life balance

President Donald Trump claimed without evidence on Tuesday that Moscow will be "fighting very hard" to help Democrats win in the 2018 midterm elections, contradicting Russian President Vladimir Putin's statement that he wanted Trump to win in 2016. At a hearing on election security, lawmakers, including some of Trump's closest GOP allies, criticized Russian interference and pointed to an indictment of 12 Russian intelligence officers for breaking into Democratic email accounts and attempting to penetrate state election systems. Despite U.S. intelligence agencies' warnings of continued cyberattacks, Trump's comments drew criticism from Democrats, who urged more questioning, documents, and funding for states to secure their election infrastructure. The decentralized nature of state election systems provides some protection, but Homeland Security officials are working to identify vulnerabilities and offer security clearances and reviews. Democrats also called for continued funding, while the Senate introduced bipartisan legislation to impose new Russian sanctions.

Former President George W. Bush remains comfortable with his decision to invade Iraq, despite the absence of weapons of mass destruction. He hopes his presidential library and museum will provide historians with the same facts he had access to during his presidency. Bush's post-presidency focuses on issues like fighting AIDS in Africa and empowering women in the Middle East. The museum, centered around the "Decision Points Theater," aims to educate visitors on the pressures and decisions faced by the president. Bush's approval ratings have improved, with 47% of Americans now viewing his presidency as a success. He advocates for his brother Jeb Bush to run for president in 2016 and has found solace in painting. The dedication of the George W. Bush Presidential Center also marks the arrival of his first grandchild, with Bush joking he plans to be called "El Jefe."

Twitter has permanently banned the accounts of right-wing conspiracy theorist Alex Jones and his "Infowars" show for violating the company's abusive behavior policies. The ban follows a heated exchange between Jones and a CNN reporter, where Jones live-streamed a rant on Periscope, criticizing the journalist and even the Twitter CEO, Jack Dorsey. This action comes weeks after Jones' accounts were suspended or removed by other major tech companies, including Apple, Facebook, and YouTube. Jones will not be able to recreate his presence on these platforms under another account.

A 2.5-year-old child at Mweya Safari Lodge in Queen Elizabeth National Park, Uganda, has been killed by a leopard. The child, Elisha Nabugyere, was left in the care of a nanny at the unfenced staff quarters when he was snatched and taken by the leopard on Friday around 7:30 pm. The child's father, SSP Francis Manana Nabugyere, says efforts to rescue the child were unsuccessful, and only the child's skull and some bones were recovered. The child's mother, a park ranger, was not present at the time. UWA communications manager Bashir Hangi described the incident as unfortunate and stated that efforts are underway to track down the leopard, considering relocation as an option due to the risk of the leopard preying on humans again. The father challenges UWA to improve security measures for staff and their children.

Authorities in northern Mexico are searching for 20 people, including 15 members of the Colombian-style band Kombo Kolombia and their crew, who went missing after a private performance at a bar. Family members reported losing contact and found the band's vehicles still parked outside the venue. Local residents heard gunshots early Friday morning. The band, known for playing vallenato music, has not been linked to narcocorridos, which celebrate drug traffickers. Over 70,000 people died in drug-related violence in Mexico last year, prompting new police initiatives.

The worst flu season in a decade continues, with 13 new child deaths reported, bringing the total to 97 this season. Despite a slight decline in visits to doctors for flu-like symptoms, the flu remains widespread in 48 states, with health officials predicting the season could last until mid-April. The flu vaccine is only 36% effective overall but can significantly decrease the risk of a heart attack. For children, the vaccine is 59% effective, while for adults, it is about 25% effective against the dominant H3N2 strain. Health officials still recommend getting vaccinated, as it can reduce the severity of the illness. The process of making flu vaccines using eggs is criticized for its limitations, with experts working on alternatives like cell-based vaccines to improve effectiveness.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved Yescarta (axicabtagene ciloleucel), a cell-based gene therapy, for treating adult patients with certain types of large B-cell lymphoma who have not responded to or relapsed after at least two other kinds of treatment. This approval marks the second gene therapy approved by the FDA and the first for specific types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). Yescarta, a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, involves collecting a patient’s T-cells, genetically modifying them to target and kill lymphoma cells, and infusing them back into the patient. The therapy has shown a 51% complete remission rate in clinical trials. However, it comes with significant risks, including severe side effects such as cytokine release syndrome and neurologic toxicities, leading to a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy. The FDA is requiring hospitals to be specially certified and trained to manage these potential

A new driver claims to have completed a lap of Manhattan in a record time of 24 minutes and 7 seconds, setting a new unofficial record. The route starts on FDR Drive at 116th Street, passing under several bridges and through the Battery Park Tunnel before cutting through West Street and Midtown. Despite stopping at six red lights, the driver managed to beat the previous record set in 2010. The video, shot from the dashboard of a 2006 BMW Z4, shows the driver weaving through traffic and managing to save time by passing on the right and cutting people off. While supporters praise the feat, others criticize the reckless driving. The NYPD is investigating and using license plate readers to help catch the driver.

Tesla is facing scrutiny after one of its electric vehicles caught fire on a busy street in Los Angeles. Actress Mary McCormack shared cellphone video of the incident, noting it occurred "out of the blue" while her husband was driving on Santa Monica Blvd. Tesla is investigating the unusual event, which they describe as extraordinarily rare. The company emphasizes its battery architecture is designed to protect passengers in such incidents. While no injuries were reported, the event has sparked concerns and questions about the safety of Tesla vehicles. The incident comes amid other challenges for Tesla, including production issues and negative headlines.

Edward Snowden made a surprise appearance at the 2014 TED conference in Vancouver via a video chatbot controlled from his undisclosed Russian location. During the interview with TED curator Chris Anderson, Snowden stated that more revelations are yet to come from his cache of National Security Agency documents. He called on tech companies to make SSL encryption the default setting for web browsing to protect internet freedom. When asked about his status as a hero or traitor, Snowden maintained that his actions were for the American people and to protect their rights. He emphasized the importance of privacy and criticized the NSA's practices, arguing that they make the U.S. and the world less safe. Tim Berners-Lee, inventor of the World Wide Web, joined the interview and supported Snowden, calling him a hero. The audience largely supported Snowden, with only a few disagreeing.

NASA's New Horizons spacecraft is set to make history by flying past Pluto on Tuesday, after a journey of 3 billion miles and 9.5 years. The spacecraft, traveling at over 30,000 miles per hour, will get within 8,000 miles of Pluto, providing the first detailed images of the dwarf planet. New Horizons will observe Pluto and its five known moons, capturing features as small as the lakes in New York City’s Central Park. The mission aims to reveal insights into Pluto’s terrains, composition, geologic activity, and atmosphere, as well as clues about the formation and evolution of the Pluto system. After passing Pluto, New Horizons will continue its journey into the Kuiper Belt, potentially studying another icy world within the next five years. The first high-resolution images from the flyby are expected to be released on Wednesday, with the full dataset taking about 16 months to transmit back to Earth.

Mitt Romney secured a significant victory in Florida's Republican primary, defeating Newt Gingrich and taking a major step toward the GOP nomination. Romney's win, with 47% of the vote compared to Gingrich's 32%, gave him all 50 Florida delegates and bolstered his status as the front-runner. Despite the setback, Gingrich vowed to continue the campaign. Romney's victory demonstrated his appeal across various voter demographics, including strong support among women and the Latino community. Gingrich's momentum faltered after Romney's aggressive campaign tactics and superior financial resources. The result may diminish arguments against Romney's ability to unite the party, while Gingrich faces a challenging path to recovery, particularly in February contests.

President-elect Donald Trump has continued to question the intelligence community's findings on Russian hacking, tweeting that an intelligence briefing on the topic was delayed and that a 14-year-old could have hacked John Podesta's email. Trump's skepticism has drawn criticism from intelligence officials and lawmakers, who see his comments as adversarial. Despite Trump's doubts, evidence suggests Russia was involved in the hacking campaign. Trump's tweets come as he prepares to receive a more comprehensive intelligence briefing on Russian hacking, which is scheduled for Friday. Trump has also promised to hold a press conference to reveal what he claims to know about the situation, though the exact timing remains unclear.

BP shareholders rejected a 20% increase in Chief Executive Bob Dudley's total remuneration package for 2015, amounting to nearly £14 million, at the company's annual general meeting. Despite BP's $5.2 billion loss and job cuts, Dudley's pay rise was seen as excessive, with over 59% of investors voting against the decision. This non-binding vote highlights growing shareholder opposition to high executive pay, especially in challenging economic conditions. BP Chairman Carl-Henric Svanberg acknowledged the strength of feeling and promised to review future pay terms. The vote could influence corporate governance practices in the UK and put pressure on BP to adjust its executive compensation policies.

Israel's Shin Bet security agency announced the arrest of three Palestinians, including two from Jerusalem and one from the West Bank, who were allegedly recruited by an al-Qaida operative in Gaza to carry out a series of attacks. The suspects were planning to target multiple locations in Israel, including the Jerusalem Convention Center, a bus traveling between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, and the U.S. embassy in Tel Aviv. Security forces monitored communications between the suspects and their handler, who was identified as Ariv Al-Sham, an al-Qaida operative in Gaza. The suspects were planning to use a suicide truck bomb, firearms, and possibly foreign militants to execute their attacks. The swift recruitment and preparation process, facilitated through online communications, highlight the ongoing threat posed by global jihadi elements in Gaza and their attempts to expand into Jerusalem and the West Bank.

Single and proud? Consider these unique rings designed for the modern, independent individual. The 925 Sterling Silver Ring, featuring Venus and Mars symbols, symbolizes attraction and can be worn on any finger. For those seeking closure after a divorce, the Wedding Ring Coffin offers a symbolic final resting place. Meanwhile, the Ah Ring, a $350 band with diamonds, promotes singlehood and can be worn by anyone. My Single Ring, available for $40, has attracted both male and female customers, serving as a discreet way to signal availability. Other options include the Ms. Taken ring, a $30 gag gift, and specialty rings for same-sex couples, like those from LoveAndPride.com. The resale market for used engagement and wedding rings is also on the rise, with sites like IDoNowIDont.com and ExBoyfriendJewelry.com catering to those looking to part ways with their jewelry. Frenchman Tancrede Melet, 32, a skilled slackliner, base jumper, and wing-suiter, died while preparing for a hot air balloon stunt in southern France. According to reports, Melet was stuck in the basket of the balloon and fell to his death. He was part of a group called the “Flying Frenchies,” known for their daring high-line walks and stunts. His death leaves behind his partner and young child.

Spanish riot police clashed with protesters in Barcelona on Sunday, attempting to halt a disputed independence referendum in Catalonia. The Catalan government had planned to hold the vote despite a court order declaring it illegal. Police fired rubber bullets and used force to enter polling stations, while some voters defied orders and cast ballots in schools and other locations. Catalan President Carles Puigdemont condemned the police actions, stating, "Police brutality will shame forever the Spanish state." The Spanish government and security forces have been working to prevent the referendum, sealing off many voting centers and seizing ballot boxes. The vote, which was backed by Catalan regional authorities, was scheduled for Sunday and was expected to be declared invalid by the Spanish Constitutional Court.

An outbreak of crown of thorns starfish on the Great Barrier Reef could become the worst on record, with estimates suggesting the number of starfish could soar from four to 12 million to 60 million by 2020, according to a report commissioned by WWF-Australia. These starfish, already responsible for the loss of around 60,000 hectares of live coral over the past 30 years, thrive in waters rich with harmful chemical fertilizers from agricultural runoff. Conservationists argue that reducing pollution could prevent future outbreaks and allow the reef to rebuild its coral cover. Current government investment has fallen short of achieving even modest targets, and more funding is needed to address the issue. If the current pattern continues, coral cover could be reduced to below 10 percent.

The Sesame Street YouTube channel was hacked, resulting in the removal of its content and the replacement of the banner with a pornographic video. The hack, which lasted about 20 minutes, featured a 7-minute adult film. The channel's profile description claimed responsibility for the hack, attributing it to two YouTube users, MrEdxwx and MrSuicider91. MrEdxwx later denied involvement, stating he is an honest YouTuber who respects community guidelines. Neither PBS, YouTube, nor Google has commented on the incident.

A French Apple Store in Dijon was destroyed by an angry customer using a steel ball, typically used in the game pétanque, sparking a rampage and causing significant damage. The incident, captured on video, appears to have been triggered by a refund dispute, as the customer, speaking in French, claimed Apple "violated" European consumers' rights and refused to reimburse him. After causing extensive damage to iPhones, MacBooks, and iPads, the customer was apprehended by security and arrested. The French word for Apple, "pomme," which means "apple" and is also related to "pummel," might have contributed to his confusion.

The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to Donna Strickland of Canada, along with Arthur Ashkin from the United States and Gerard Mourou from France, for their groundbreaking work in laser physics. Strickland, the third woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physics, shared half the 9 million kronor ($1.01 million) prize with Ashkin for developing optical tweezers that use laser light to manipulate tiny objects without damaging them. Mourou and Strickland were honored for their development of chirped pulse amplification (CPA), a technique that has revolutionized high-intensity lasers and found applications in fields such as laser eye surgery. This marks the first time a woman has won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 55 years, highlighting the advancement of women in science.

Gisele Bündchen, Tom Brady's wife, revealed that Brady suffered a concussion during the 2016 season in an interview with Charlie Rose on "CBS This Morning." The NFL and the NFL Players Association reviewed the matter and stated that there were no records indicating Brady had a head injury or exhibited concussion symptoms. Brady has not been listed as having a concussion in his professional career, though the Patriots did report leg, thigh, and ankle injuries. Brady, 39, has expressed a desire to continue playing until his mid-40s, but Bündchen is concerned about the long-term effects of brain trauma from football. She advocates for environmental issues and believes that living a plant-based diet has improved Brady's health.

The family of 17-year-old Johran McCormick, who was fatally shot in his girlfriend's bedroom, wants criminal charges filed against the girl. McCormick's mother and father believe he was in bed with the 16-year-old when her father came into the room around 2:30 a.m. The father shot McCormick, claiming he thought the boy was reaching for a weapon. McCormick's family and supporters, led by Community Activist Quanell X, want the girl charged for her role in the shooting, believing she intentionally lied to her father. The Harris County Grand Jury will decide if charges should be filed against the father, but many think the girl should also be held accountable.

Superhero sequels often follow a familiar formula, but "Deadpool 2" pushes the boundaries with its self-aware, over-the-top humor and unconventional plot. The film, starring Ryan Reynolds as the wisecracking antihero, delivers nonstop raunchy jokes and absurd action sequences. Reynolds' portrayal remains charismatic and entertaining, though the script relies heavily on familiar tropes and Reynolds' own commentary. The story, while simple on the surface, delves into themes of pop culture, gun violence, and celebrity cameos. Despite its flaws, "Deadpool 2" remains a must-see for fans of the series, offering a mix of laughs and surprises.

Casual-dining restaurants Applebee's and IHOP are planning to close up to 160 locations, with 105 to 135 Applebee's and 20 to 25 IHOP sites potentially shutting down. The closures are part of a strategy to focus on improving franchisee financial health and enhancing the supply chain. Despite the closures, the companies plan to open 125 new restaurants globally. Applebee's and IHOP are facing increased competition from quick-service restaurants like Panera Bread and Chipotle Mexican Grill, which market themselves as offering healthier and more upscale food. The closures are part of a normal course of business in the industry, with DineEquity aiming to improve the overall brand experience.

A new Dartmouth study confirms the authenticity of the famous backyard photo of Lee Harvey Oswald holding the same type of rifle used to assassinate President John F. Kennedy. The findings refute claims that the photo was faked due to Oswald's physically implausible pose. Using a 3-D model of Oswald and advanced digital image forensics, researchers determined that his pose is stable, the lighting and shadows are consistent, and the rifle's length matches the one used in the assassination. This study, published in the Journal of Digital Forensics, Security and Law, aims to resolve long-standing debates about the photo's authenticity.

As night fell on Baltimore on Tuesday, thousands of police and National Guard troops patrolled the city to enforce a new curfew and prevent further violence. More than 3,000 police from other states and National Guard members supported Baltimore’s 620,000 residents, who had experienced rioting, looting, and fires following the funeral of a 25-year-old black man who died in police custody. The mayor faced criticism for her cautious response, which included a one-week curfew and a focus on avoiding a heavy-handed approach. The death of Freddie Gray, who died a week after sustaining spinal injuries in police custody, reignited protests and highlighted long-standing issues of police misconduct and racial tensions. The city’s response was seen as a delicate balancing act between maintaining order and avoiding escalation.

At least eight people died and 44 were injured in a single-vehicle rollover crash on U.S. Highway 83 south of Laredo, Texas, on Saturday. The OGA Charters bus, bound for a casino in Eagle Pass, lost control and rolled over. The driver survived but was among the injured. The crash is one of the deadliest in Texas in recent years. The National Transportation Safety Board sent a team to investigate. OGA Charters, based in the Rio Grande Valley, had faced brake and emergency exit issues in previous inspections.

President Trump on Friday dismissed concerns about escalating tensions with North Korea, stating, "I think you know the answer to that" when asked if the U.S. is going to war. He refused to rule out a military intervention in Venezuela, where civil strife has turned violent, saying, "I'm not going to rule out a military option." Trump's comments came as Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Nikki Haley echoed the president's unified stance on the North Korea crisis, emphasizing the need for a diplomatic solution. Trump also doubled down on his "fire and fury" rhetoric, warning North Korea of "big, big trouble" if it targets Guam. Meanwhile, tensions in Venezuela have escalated, with the U.S. imposing fresh sanctions on President Nicolas Maduro and threatening military action. Latin American countries have strongly criticized Trump's military threat, with Peru, Mexico, and Colombia among those rejecting the idea. Venezuela's government, led by Maduro, has dismissed the threats

The 59-year-old man who opened fire at a Lafayette, La., movie theater on July 23, 2015, killing two and injuring nine before taking his own life, has been identified as John Russel Houser, a "drifter" from Alabama who had been in the Lafayette area since early July, according to police. Houser, described as having a history of erratic behavior and mental health issues, had previously lived in Phenix City, Ala., and was involved in several past incidents, including arson and speeding violations. He had also sought a protective order against his wife in 2008 due to his volatile behavior. The shooting occurred during a showing of "Trainwreck," with the gunman standing up about 20 minutes into the movie and firing 13 times. Authorities found wigs and other disguises in his motel room. A witness described hearing popping noises and seeing muzzle flashes before evacuating the theater.

Colorado's top state prison official, Tom Clements, was shot and killed at his home, sparking a manhunt and raising questions about potential motives related to his position. Governor John Hickenlooper, while expressing shock, did not immediately link the killing to a broader attack. The FBI and Colorado Bureau of Investigation joined the investigation. Clements, who had overseen state and private prisons, was shot around 8:30 p.m. Tuesday in Monument, north of Colorado Springs. Authorities are searching for a dark-colored "boxy" car seen near the scene. Clements' killing occurred a week after he denied a Saudi prisoner's request to be sent to his home country. The incident has prompted increased security for top state officials and at the governor's mansion. Colorado has seen several high-profile killings, including the 2008 murder of prosecutor Sean May. Flags were ordered lowered to half-staff at public buildings until after Clements' funeral.

China warned it will retaliate if Washington imposes new trade penalties, following reports the Trump administration plans to propose increasing the tariff rate on an additional $200 billion of Chinese imports. A foreign ministry spokesman said Beijing is ready for "dialogue and consultation" but will "definitely fight back" if the US escalates the situation. The US has already imposed 25% tariffs on $34 billion of Chinese goods, with China responding in kind. The US plans to raise pending tariffs on $200 billion in Chinese goods to 25% from 10%, though this is not finalized. US and Chinese officials are trying to restart talks to avert a full-blown trade war, with private conversations ongoing. Complicating the situation, US Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer has taken a harder line than Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, who is leading the negotiations. The US aims to secure certain concessions, while China vows to respond with the same amount of tariffs

The American Psychiatric Association released the DSM-5, its fifth major revision of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, coinciding with the APA's annual meeting in San Francisco. This long-awaited update includes several significant changes, such as the consolidation of Asperger's syndrome, childhood disintegrative disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified under the broader autism spectrum disorder category. Other notable changes include the introduction of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, which is intended to address concerns of over-diagnosing bipolar disorder in children. The manual also removes the bereavement exclusion for major depressive disorder, recognizing that grief can last longer than two months and can trigger depression. The DSM-5 also updates criteria for conditions like post-traumatic stress disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and major and mild neurocognitive disorders. While the APA emphasizes the DSM-5 as a guide for clinicians, critics argue that it may over-diagnose mental disorders and lacks a focus on underlying biological factors

About two hours into a Singapore Airlines flight from Singapore to Milan, the pilot announced an engine oil warning and the plane turned back to Changi Airport for safety. Passengers on the Boeing 777-300ER, including Amit Jain and Ms. Lee Bee Yee, noticed vibrations and a fuel-like smell. Upon landing, they witnessed the plane's right engine catching fire, with flames reaching a meter high. Firefighters quickly extinguished the blaze, ensuring all 222 passengers and 19 crew members disembarked safely. The plane was towed away, and a new flight with a new crew departed for Milan after 10 am. Singapore Airlines offered passengers the option to defer or reschedule their travel.

American sprinter Manteo Mitchell broke his left fibula during the men’s 4x400 relay at the London Olympics, but continued to run the remaining 200 meters, finishing in 46.1 seconds. His teammates went on to qualify for the final. Doctors diagnosed the injury after the race. Mitchell initially downplayed the injury, saying it was just a cramp, but an X-ray revealed the break. His determination to finish the race, despite the intense pain, is praised for his resilience.

Unlike his boss and other Cabinet members, Vice President Joe Biden will hold off on taking a pay reduction in solidarity with government workers hit by the sequestration budget cuts, his office said. Biden will take a pay cut if and when his staff is affected. President Obama, Secretary of State John Kerry, and others have pledged to return a portion of their salaries. The $85 billion in sequestration cuts were designed to force agreement on a budget, but after failure, the cuts took effect on March 1. The impact on government agencies is still unclear, and furloughs of federal workers will take time to implement. Biden's decision highlights the varying financial situations of Cabinet members and the political pressures surrounding the sequester.

Google admitted to mistakenly collecting data from unsecured Wi-Fi networks using its Street View cars, a practice it previously said only gathered network names and MAC addresses. The company has halted the data collection, isolated the affected data, and plans to hire a third party to review the software. While the collected data was minimal, potentially raising legal concerns, Google expressed regret and vowed to improve internal controls to prevent future errors.

Gil Scott-Heron, often hailed as the "godfather of rap," passed away at the age of 62. His most notable work, "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised," has been influential in the hip-hop community and beyond. Born in Chicago, Scott-Heron spent his formative years in Tennessee and New York, eventually settling in Manhattan. His career spanned several decades, with a significant hiatus before his 1994 album "Spirits," which included the track "Message to the Messengers." This piece warned the hip-hop generation to use their power responsibly. Despite struggles with substance abuse, Scott-Heron made a comeback in 2010 with the critically acclaimed album "I'm New Here." His unique blend of poetry and music left a lasting impact on the cultural landscape.

Mitt Romney secured a significant victory in the Illinois primary, outpolling Rick Santorum by 48% to 34% of the vote. This win, Romney’s largest in a large state since Florida, further solidifies his delegate lead. Santorum acknowledged the loss, while Romney emphasized the broader political landscape in his favor. Exit polls indicated that voters prioritized electability over ideological purity, with 37% of respondents citing electability as the most important quality in a nominee. Santorum campaigned outside Illinois, focusing on Pennsylvania and Louisiana, while Romney maintained a presence in the state. Santorum’s speech highlighted his conservative credentials and criticized his rivals, particularly Romney, for changing positions on issues like global warming and health care. Despite the loss, Santorum expressed confidence in upcoming primaries, particularly in Pennsylvania, where he aims to make a strong showing.

The parents of Charlie Gard, an 11-month-old with a rare genetic condition, have established The Charlie Gard Foundation to help other children with mitochondrial diseases and rare childhood illnesses. They aim to increase clarity for families and hospitals regarding parental rights and medical treatment access. The foundation will serve as a hub of information for parents facing similar situations. The Gard family has also been advised by GoFundMe to donate £10,000 towards the foundation. Charlie, who passed away, had attracted global attention and support, highlighting the ethical debate between parental rights and medical decisions.

Scientists have long debated whether human intelligence is linked to brain size, with some suggesting a strong correlation for over 150 years. A recent review of 88 studies involving more than 8,000 participants found a small but significant positive association between brain volume and IQ. However, this association is weak and does not imply causation. The researchers argue that brain structure and integrity are more critical for cognitive abilities than brain size, which may work as a compensatory mechanism for cognitive functions. Despite publication bias, the association remains robust and independent of sex and age. The study concludes that brain volume plays only a minor role in explaining IQ test performance, emphasizing the importance of brain structure in understanding cognitive differences among individuals.

Utah lawmakers passed a bill eliminating the statute of limitations for lawsuits against child sexual abuse perpetrators, allowing victims to file civil actions regardless of when the abuse occurred. Co-founder of the Foundation for Survivors of Abuse, Deondra Brown, expressed excitement for the change, stating it provides victims time to heal and pursue legal action. The bill, sponsored by Rep. Ken Ivory, aims to hold abusers accountable, as current law limits civil actions to four years after a victim’s 18th birthday. Victims can now have a four-year window from the time of discovery or remembrance to file a lawsuit, overcoming emotional obstacles that often prevent them from taking action.

Federal authorities have determined that 13 bald eagles found dead on Maryland's Eastern Shore did not die of natural causes, ruling out diseases such as avian influenza. The deaths are now being investigated as potentially human-caused, with a focus on poisoning. No signs of trauma were found on the eagles, suggesting they may have consumed poisoned animal carcasses. The incident, the largest single die-off of bald eagles in the state in at least three decades, occurred in Federalsburg in February. The owner of the farm where the eagles were found told NBC Washington that he did not use poison. A $25,000 reward has been offered for information leading to a conviction. Bald eagles are still protected under federal law, and killing one can result in severe penalties.

A 36-year-old woman from Florida sought medical attention two months after her honeymoon in Belize due to an itchy skin lesion on her groin. Initially, doctors suspected an insect bite and prescribed antibiotics, but the lesion persisted. Upon further examination, a surgeon suspected the presence of a living creature under the skin. A 5-millimeter incision revealed a human botfly larva, which was removed and identified by a pathology lab. The larva, about 27 to 128 days old, had burrowed into her skin, causing itching. The woman's lesion resolved completely within a week after the larva was removed. Human botflies are rare in the U.S. but common in tropical regions, where they lay eggs on other insects that can transfer the larvae to human skin.

The British government is preparing for the potential fallout of a Greek exit from the eurozone, with Bank of England Governor Sir Mervyn King warning that Europe is "tearing itself apart." Capital flight from Greece has intensified, with €3 billion withdrawn in less than a week following the election. A Greek departure could cost the EU $1 trillion, 5% of its output. British Prime Minister David Cameron will stress the eurozone's need for a stable solution at the G8 summit. The Bank of England, the Treasury, and the Financial Services Authority are drawing up plans, viewing a Greek exit as potentially as damaging as the Lehman Brothers collapse. Officials warn that a disorderly collapse could cost 2% of EU GDP, while a more structured exit might result in a 5% drop. The European Central Bank could face hundreds of billions in losses, with Germany and other countries potentially needing to recapitalize. The IMF and other institutions may also be exposed, with the potential for hundreds

President Donald Trump addressed the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, emphasizing the resurgence of a strong and prosperous America. Trump highlighted the creation of 2.4 million jobs since his election and the stock market's record-breaking performance. He stressed that the U.S. is open for business, boasting about significant tax cuts and regulatory reductions. Trump also discussed his administration's commitment to free and fair trade, though he emphasized the need for reciprocity. He underscored America's role in global security, mentioning efforts against terrorism and North Korea's nuclear program. Trump's speech aimed to attract international investment and business, positioning the U.S. as a competitive and welcoming environment for growth. Despite criticism from some attendees, Trump maintained a positive tone, focusing on economic achievements and the benefits of his policies.

Nathan "Bodie" Barksdale, the former Baltimore gangster who inspired characters in "The Wire," died in a federal medical prison in North Carolina on Saturday. He was 54. Barksdale, known as "Bodie," was a notorious criminal in the 1980s, running a violent heroin-dealing operation in the Murphy Homes public housing complex. He was shot more than 20 times and had to have his right leg amputated below the knee. Barksdale later worked with the anti-violence Safe Streets program. However, he was arrested in 2014, pleaded guilty to participating in a heroin conspiracy with members of the Black Guerrilla Family gang, and was sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison. Despite his criminal past, Barksdale claimed to have made amends and worked to counsel young people on avoiding similar mistakes.

A Florida man, Joseph Schreiber, 32, was arrested for setting fire to the Islamic Center of Fort Pierce, a mosque damaged in the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history. Schreiber admitted to the arson and expressed embarrassment over the crime. The fire occurred on the 15th anniversary of 9/11 and during the Muslim holiday Eid al-Adha. Surveillance video and anti-Islamic social media posts linked Schreiber to the crime. He faces at least 30 years in prison if convicted, and the case is being prosecuted as a hate crime. Federal authorities are also investigating.

Amal Clooney visited Yazidi refugees in a Greek camp, advocating for their plight and the prosecution of ISIS. Clooney, a human rights lawyer, aims to gather evidence and push for the International Criminal Court to hold ISIS accountable for genocide against the Yazidis. She met with survivors, including 23-year-old Nadia Murad, who escaped after being enslaved and raped by ISIS. Together, they seek to bring the perpetrators to justice, despite diplomatic challenges.

Brussels officials have blamed "mice" for the city's chronic traffic jams, claiming that the original plans to improve underground tunnels were eaten by rodents. This excuse has been made during an investigation into the state of Brussels's 7.1 miles of underground traffic tunnels, which have become dilapidated due to years of decay. The plans were reportedly stored in a concrete pier for 20 years before being moved to a proper storage room in 2010, but were then reportedly eaten by mice. The state of Brussels's infrastructure has become a political issue, with an estimated bill of €1 billion to repair the tunnels. Despite warnings about the need for deeper renovation, budgetary constraints and traffic chaos have hindered progress.

Julian Assange said he would accept arrest by British police if a U.N. working group on arbitrary detention decides that his three years in the Ecuadorian Embassy does not amount to illegal detention. Assange, who sought asylum in the embassy to avoid extradition to Sweden over rape claims, tweeted that if the U.N. finds against him, he will turn himself in to police at noon on Friday. However, he added that if the U.N. finds in his favor, he expects his passport to be returned and further arrest attempts to be terminated. The U.N. panel is due to publish its findings on Friday, which are expected to conclude that Assange is "arbitrarily detained." Swedish and British governments have different views on the matter, with the Swedish foreign ministry noting that the U.N. panel's decision differs from their stance. Assange's lawyers are calling for the Swedish extradition request to be dropped immediately if the U.N. panel rules in his favor.

A lawsuit filed in Dallas County District Court accuses the Boy Scouts of America of negligence leading to the death of 15-year-old Reid Comita, who died from heat stroke during a hike at Buffalo Trail Scout Ranch in June. The Comita family argues that Reid was sent on an aggressive hike in extreme temperatures without proper training or adult supervision. They claim the Boy Scouts failed to notify them promptly of Reid's death. The lawsuit also highlights communication issues and the absence of required adult supervision during the hike. Reid was on the verge of achieving the Eagle Scout rank. The Boy Scouts of America have stated that the safety of youth members is their top priority and that they are keeping the family in their thoughts and prayers.

Warren Buffett, one of the world's wealthiest investors, sees Japan's recent market downturn as a buying opportunity. Despite the devastating earthquake and nuclear crisis, Buffett believes Japan's economic future will recover. He stated, "If I owned Japanese stocks, I would certainly not be selling them." Buffett's optimism is echoed by Yoji Takeda, who noted overseas investors bought Japanese stocks last week. While the disaster's impact on the global economy is expected to be limited, reconstruction spending could eventually boost the economy. Shares of construction companies have already seen a surge.

President Donald Trump is reportedly considering firing Robert Mueller, the special counsel overseeing the Russia investigation, according to Newsmax CEO Christopher Ruddy. While Trump has not discussed this with Ruddy, who based his claim on comments from one of Trump's lawyers, the White House denies any such talk. Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein stated he has not seen good cause to dismiss Mueller and emphasized that only Mueller can be fired for legitimate reasons. Senate Democrats criticized Attorney General Jeff Sessions for canceling his planned testimony at a hearing and sending Rosenstein instead.

Rare photographs from Nirvana's first concert in March 1987 have surfaced, shared by Maggie Poukkula, daughter of Tony Poukkula, who hosted the band's inaugural show in his basement. The photos, found tucked away in her father's biographies of Cobain and Nirvana, show young Kurt Cobain and Tony Poukkula jamming with the band, including a guitar appearance by Poukkula for Led Zeppelin covers. The set list includes early versions of songs that would later become Nirvana classics. These images, along with other rare artifacts, have been featured in Brett Morgen's documentary, Montage of Heck, which is set to return to theaters starting August 7th.

Gwyneth Paltrow, known for her wellness brand Goop, has expanded into the beauty industry with makeup products and her own skin-care line. Despite her involvement in alternative therapies, a 55-year-old woman died after an allergic reaction to live bee acupuncture, a treatment Paltrow promoted. The incident highlights the risks of such therapies, even for those who have previously not shown allergies.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie stated that a New Jersey Transit train crashed into the Hoboken station at high speed, killing one person and injuring 108. The train engineer was hospitalized but later released. The National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation. Christie emphasized not speculating on the cause. The structural integrity of the Hoboken station needs evaluation, with no estimated reopening time. PATH service is expected to resume later. Passengers described the crash, noting the train's speed seemed normal before impact. Chaos ensued as passengers escaped through broken windows, and the scene inside the station was chaotic with damaged infrastructure.

At Yahoo's shareholder meeting, the company's annual gathering under CEO Marissa Mayer, the event was largely uneventful. Shareholders re-elected all directors and endorsed the executive compensation plan. Mayer highlighted progress, such as a 70% increase in mobile email usage and a 50% rise in Flickr photo uploads. Despite the lack of major events, a crass shareholder asked Mayer, "I'm Greek and a dirty old man, and you look attractive," then inquired about a dividend. Mayer handled the question professionally, deflecting other off-topic queries. Yahoo shares rose over 3% in trading following the meeting.

President Obama is allowing other nations to take the lead in addressing the Libyan conflict, a strategy that reflects his desire for a more multilateral approach to foreign policy but also exposes him to criticism for seeming weak during a crisis. Obama has not made many public statements on the situation, focusing instead on private diplomacy and military planning within NATO. His cautious approach is influenced by the challenges of dealing with a secretive country and the uncertainty of the situation on the ground. Critics argue that only strong American leadership can effectively challenge brutal regimes like that of Moammar Gaddafi. France has taken a more assertive stance, recognizing the rebel leadership and pushing for a no-fly zone, while other nations like Britain and Germany are taking a more cautious approach. The conflict continues to rage, with loyalist forces making gains in several cities. The international community is considering various options, including humanitarian aid and a no-fly zone, but any action would require careful consideration and regional support.

Tobacco giant Reynolds American Inc. agreed to acquire Lorillard Inc. for $25 billion, creating a formidable competitor to Altria Group Inc. in the U.S. market. The deal, which includes Lorillard's popular Newport menthol brand, aims to reshape the U.S. tobacco industry, leaving only two major competitors controlling 90% of the market. However, the transaction faces antitrust challenges, prompting Imperial Tobacco to acquire Lorillard's e-cigarette brands and other assets. The combined company will have significant market share and aims to leverage cost savings and next-generation tobacco technologies to boost earnings. The deal, though risky, reflects the industry's ongoing consolidation amid declining cigarette sales and growing e-cigarette markets.

Whitney Houston had a deadly mixture of Valium, Xanax, and alcohol in her system when she died at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, according to a source close to the situation. Valium and Xanax were found in her hotel room. The coroner is awaiting final toxicology results to determine the major contributing factor of her death, which is likely to be the sedatives and alcohol, as her heart stopped due to respiratory suppression. Houston's final days were marked by scandal, including an altercation at a Hollywood nightclub where she thought another woman was flirting with her boyfriend, Ray J. She appeared disheveled and intoxicated, with blood on her leg, after leaving the nightclub. The final toxicology results should be released in the coming weeks. Additionally, Bobby Brown, Houston's ex-husband, is reportedly planning to sell a tell-all book about his life with her, despite a confidentiality agreement signed during their divorce.

Uber faces a major setback in London after Transport for London rejected its application for a new license, citing concerns over corporate responsibility and safety. The company's chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, acknowledged the "high cost of a bad reputation" but vowed to appeal the decision. Despite the ruling, Uber plans to continue operating in London until the appeals process is exhausted. The move has sparked criticism from users and some government officials, while supporters argue it could harm 40,000 drivers and 3.5 million users. Uber's loss of the license in London could have broader implications for the gig economy, with some viewing it as a warning to companies like Deliveroo.

With just six days before the July 20 deadline, Iran's nuclear talks seemed to be faltering as U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry arrived in Vienna on Sunday. Despite efforts to mend ties with Germany amid its espionage dispute and handle the ongoing crisis in Israel and Gaza, no breakthrough was produced by the end of the day. The P5+1 group, including the U.S., UK, France, China, Russia, and Germany, seemed keen on getting a deal done by July 20, but representatives suggested any extension would be relatively short. Major gaps remained, including questions about Iran's uranium enrichment level. On Monday, Secretary Kerry and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif held in-depth discussions, but the talks were complicated by regional crises and diverging interests. While the U.S. and Iran have found some areas for cooperation, such as in Afghanistan, their nuclear negotiations remained challenging, with significant differences on key issues. An extension of the deadline appeared increasingly likely,

The acting director of the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has been reassigned following a series of security failures at major airports where undercover agents were able to smuggle mock explosives or banned weapons through checkpoints in 95% of tests. Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson announced that Melvin Carraway will be moved to the Office of State and Local Law Enforcement at DHS headquarters, while Acting Deputy Director Mark Hatfield will lead the TSA in the interim. Johnson directed TSA leadership to revise standard operating procedures to address the specific vulnerabilities identified by the inspector general’s testing and ordered training for all TSA officers and supervisors. He also plans to conduct more random covert testing at checkpoints and urges the Senate to confirm the nomination of Coast Guard Vice Admiral Pete Neffenger as the next TSA administrator.

A video and photos posted on Reddit by a Golden Corral employee have sparked outrage over alleged poor kitchen conditions and improper food storage practices. The employee, Brandon Huber, claims raw and cooked foods are kept near the dumpster in preparation for a health inspector's visit. Golden Corral denies any of the food was served to customers and states the manager was terminated for failing to follow food handling procedures. Huber's father attempted to sell the video for $5,000, but the offer was declined. The incident highlights how social media can quickly spread allegations against restaurant chains, potentially damaging their reputations.

Comedian Joan Rivers remains on life support at Mount Sinai Hospital five days after a near-fatal heart and lung failure during a doctor's visit. Her daughter, Melissa, issued a brief statement expressing gratitude for the support and stating that Rivers is still on life support. Melissa and Rivers' grandson, Cooper, flew to New York to be by her side. Doctors hope to assess any brain damage caused by the incident. Despite conflicting reports, sources suggest Rivers is showing small positive signs of recovery. Joan's condition is described as stable but critical. Fans and colleagues have been sending messages of support on social media.

In the first presidential debate, Hillary Clinton effectively challenged Donald Trump's perceived weaknesses while he struggled to defend himself, appearing wimpy and defensive. Clinton's well-prepared attacks on his business practices, net worth, and past comments about women and minorities contrasted sharply with Trump's unprepared and often meandering responses. His attempts to deflect questions about the birther controversy and his tax returns backfired, while Clinton's attacks on his business ethics and failure to release tax returns resonated with voters. Despite Trump's initial defensiveness, his supporters seemed disappointed, while Clinton's team appeared relieved. This debate highlighted the importance of preparation and the potential impact of effective attacks on an opponent's perceived strengths.

A U.S. Secret Service agent who suffered a stroke while working to protect President Donald Trump during his trip to Scotland died in a Scottish hospital on Sunday. The 42-year-old agent, identified as Special Agent Noel E. Remagen, was found unresponsive by colleagues at Trump's Turnberry resort on Saturday night. He was quickly attended to by a White House doctor and Secret Service colleagues before being rushed to the hospital, where he passed away. Special Agent Remagen, who had served for 19 years, leaves behind a wife and two small children. President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump departed to visit the agent's family.

President-elect Donald Trump has sparked confusion and concern with his recent comments about nuclear weapons, suggesting the U.S. should engage in an "arms race" and "outmatch" potential adversaries. During an interview with MSNBC's "Morning Joe," Trump stated, "Let it be an arms race, we will outmatch them at every pass, and outlast them all." However, White House press secretary Sean Spicer quickly backtracked, clarifying that these remarks were from a private conversation and that there will not be an arms race. Trump's statements appear to contradict longstanding U.S. nonproliferation policies and could potentially violate arms control treaties. Experts are alarmed by the potential consequences of such a policy shift and warn that it could lead to a nuclear arms race.

A majority of pediatricians and family physicians often or sometimes agree to parents' requests to spread out vaccines for their children under two years old, despite believing such decisions put children at risk for diseases like measles and whooping cough, according to a new survey. In a typical month, 93% of respondents reported some parents requesting to delay vaccines, and 21% reported more than 10% of parents making such requests. Most doctors thought these parents were putting their children at risk (87%) and that spreading out vaccines was more painful for children (84%). However, 82% believed agreeing to these requests would build trust with families, and 80% thought families might leave their practice if they did not. Forty percent reported this issue had decreased their job satisfaction. Physicians often agreed to spread out vaccines (37% often/always, 37% sometimes), with 2% often/always and 4% sometimes dismissing families for requesting it.

Ohio Governor John Kasich postponed the execution of Ronald Phillips until July 2014 to investigate the possibility of organ donation. Phillips, sentenced to death for the 1993 murder of a 3-year-old, sought the delay to donate his organs to his mother and sister. The execution was originally set for January 16, 2014, using a new lethal-injection drug cocktail. Phillips' execution has drawn attention due to the untested combination of midazolam and hydromorphone. Dennis McGuire, another death-row inmate, may become the first to be executed using this new method.

Demi Lovato has candidly shared her struggles with drug and alcohol addiction, admitting she would smuggle cocaine onto airplanes and use it in the bathroom. In an interview with Access Hollywood, Lovato revealed she hit rock bottom at 19 after completing a rehab program in 2010. She described how she couldn't go more than 30 minutes to an hour without cocaine and would wait for passengers to fall asleep on flights to use the drug. Lovato's mother, Dianna, also opened up about her own eating disorder and the family's journey to recovery, stating they became closer after both sought help.

Matthew Inman, creator of The Oatmeal, launched a Kickstarter campaign for the card game Exploding Kittens, aiming to raise $10,000. The project quickly surpassed its goal, reaching over $100,000 within an hour and nearing $1 million at the time of writing. The game, inspired by Russian roulette, involves players drawing cards until someone picks an exploding kitten, causing them to "explode" and lose. Strategic cards allow players to avoid or force others to draw the kitten. Each card features Inman's signature Oatmeal-style illustrations, including elements from his past comics. The team behind the game includes Inman, Elan Lee, and Shane Small. If you enjoy card games or want to support a quirky project, backing this Kickstarter could be a fun choice.

The NHS medical director in England, Prof Sir Bruce Keogh, has called for hospitals to stop burning aborted foetuses as clinical waste and instead cremate or bury them, following revelations that some NHS trusts have been disposing of foetal remains in this manner. Health minister Dr Dan Poulter has also ordered a ban on the practice, stating it is "totally unacceptable." Keogh's letter to NHS trusts emphasizes that incineration is inappropriate and that other methods offer more dignity. The Human Tissue Authority has been asked to provide clearer guidance. The Care Quality Commission will investigate the issue, and Sands, the stillbirth and neonatal death charity, advocates for cremation over incineration. Thousands of miscarried and aborted babies have been incinerated without parents' knowledge, with 15,500 foetal remains incinerated by 27 trusts over two years.

After FBI Director James Comey sent a letter to congressional leaders stating that the FBI found no new evidence to change their previous conclusion that Hillary Clinton would not face criminal charges related to her use of a private email server, Twitter erupted with reactions. Democrats who had criticized Comey earlier now praised him, while Republicans who had supported him turned against him. The Trump campaign and its surrogates criticized Comey, calling his actions a distraction and a sign of political pressure. Democrats like Bill Kristol defended Comey's decisions, while Republicans like Newt Gingrich accused him of being politically motivated. The revelation that the FBI's review of new emails did not change their conclusion about Clinton's email use did not fully undo the damage of the previous letter, but it did help Clinton's campaign to focus on other issues.

Wonder Woman maintained its lead at the box office, earning an estimated $57.2 million in North American theaters during its second weekend, outpacing Universal's The Mummy, which debuted with a weak $32.2 million. The DC Comics superhero film has amassed over $205 million domestically in just two weeks. The Mummy, part of Universal's Dark Universe, struggled to launch a new monster franchise. Meanwhile, A24's horror film It Comes at Night performed well with a modest $6 million debut, targeting more discerning horror fans. Other entries in the top 10 include Captain Underpants: The First Epic Movie and Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, which saw further declines.

A new study by computer scientist Jon Kleinberg of Cornell University and Facebook engineer Lars Backstrom reveals that the shape of a person’s social network can be a powerful indicator of their spouse or romantic partner. Analyzing data from 1.3 million Facebook users, the researchers found that the dispersion of mutual friends, rather than embeddedness (the number of mutual friends), is a better predictor of romantic relationships. The dispersion algorithm correctly identified a user’s spouse 60% of the time, and couples with high dispersion were less likely to break up. This research highlights the importance of a partner’s role in expanding one’s social network, suggesting that relationships characterized by a diverse and interconnected social circle are more likely to endure.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reacted sarcastically to a question about the firing of FBI Director James Comey during a visit to the State Department. Lavrov quipped, "Was he fired? You're kidding," before leaving the room. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson was more measured, stressing that the purpose of Lavrov's visit was to continue dialogue on a broad range of topics. The meeting came as scrutiny intensified over investigations into the Trump campaign’s possible ties to Russia. President Donald Trump met with Lavrov at the White House, emphasizing his hope for better relations with Russia. The meeting also included Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak, whose role in the investigation into former National Security Adviser Michael Flynn was critical. Lavrov and Tillerson discussed issues including Syria, Ukraine, and de-escalation zones in Syria. Lavrov dismissed concerns about Russian involvement in the 2016 U.S. election, stating it was "an internal affair."

A teenager in West Palm Beach, Florida, was caught posing as a doctor at St. Mary's Medical Center for a month. He wore a white coat with the hospital's logo and was seen by security guards and patients. When interviewed, the teen claimed to have been a doctor for years and had family support. Hospital staff stated he never interacted with patients but was seen in secured areas of the hospital. The teen's mother said he was under medical care but refusing medication. Police and hospital officials decided not to press charges.

A 20-year-old mother has applied to the Family Court to overturn a ruling that bans her from breastfeeding her 11-month-old son due to her recent tattoos. The mother, referred to as Ms. Jackson, had tattoos done without disclosing her breastfeeding status, prompting concerns about the risk of blood-borne diseases like HIV and hepatitis. The court ruled that the mother should have primary care of the child but ordered her not to breastfeed due to these risks. Judge Matthew Myers stated that the benefits of breastfeeding must be weighed against the potential harm to the child if he contracted HIV. The mother, diagnosed with post-natal depression, is appealing the decision, which has sparked debate among breastfeeding advocates about the balance between health risks and maternal rights.

Al-Jazeera America, after a decade of trying, is set to launch on Tuesday, aiming to provide in-depth news content in a 24-hour cable news world dominated by sensationalism. The network will be available in nearly 50 million U.S. homes, replacing Current TV, and has hired many experienced U.S. journalists. It promises less opinion and more in-depth reporting, though it faces challenges such as lower commercial breaks and the need to cater to American tastes without appearing anti-American. Al-Jazeera America's launch comes with a large staff of 900 employees, including 400 in the newsroom, and 12 U.S. bureaus. Despite initial skepticism, the network hopes to compete with established news channels by offering quality journalism and a broader range of stories.

President Trump defended Russian leader Vladimir Putin against accusations of being a "killer," stating, "We’ve got a lot of killers. What, do you think our country’s so innocent?" during an interview with Fox News. Trump's comments sparked criticism from Florida Senator Marco Rubio, who tweeted, "When has a Democratic political activist been poisoned by the GOP or vice versa? We are not the same as Putin." The conversation highlights ongoing tensions between Trump's approach to Russia and concerns raised by some lawmakers and the intelligence community regarding Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election.

Hillary Clinton is likely to win the 2016 presidential election, given the current political landscape and trends. Her candidacy is seen as a safe bet, with the Democratic Party holding a slight advantage in the Electoral College and among swing voters. The economy, while not booming, is stable, which benefits Clinton as the incumbent. The "Emerging Democratic Majority" theory suggests that demographic shifts and changing voter behavior favor Democrats. Clinton’s favorability ratings, while break-even, are not significantly worse than those of other candidates. Her well-known status and strong organizational support are assets. The Republican field is fragmented, with candidates struggling to differentiate themselves. Unless the economy worsens or a major scandal emerges, Clinton’s path to victory appears clear.

A valedictorian at Portsmouth High School in New Hampshire orchestrated a surprise flash mob to Taylor Swift's "Shake It Off" during his graduation speech, turning the ceremony into a viral sensation. Colin Yost, along with friends Georgina Head and Lauren Gagne, choreographed the dance and rehearsed it over five scheduled graduation rehearsals. Yost's speech, which encouraged embracing one's inner nerd, ended with the line, "all you have to do is shake it off," prompting the seniors to break into dance. The performance, viewed over 270,000 times on YouTube, brought national attention to the class of 2015, with Yost, who plans to attend Princeton University, feeling proud of the positive message conveyed.

A North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea has been found to have anthrax antibodies in his system, raising concerns about the rogue state's biological weapons capabilities. According to a South Korean intelligence official, the soldier, who defected in 2017, was either exposed to or vaccinated for anthrax, indicating the North's possession of the deadly disease. Anthrax can be fatal within 24 hours if not treated with antibiotics or a vaccine. South Korea's military plans to develop an anthrax vaccine by the end of 2019. North Korea has been suspected of developing biological weapons, as evidenced by the works of the Pyongyang Biological Technology Research Institute, which is run by the Korean People's Army Unit 810. The institute claims to specialize in pesticide research, but analysts suggest it may be producing biological weapons. Concerns have also been raised about the U.S. military's testing of live bacteria at bases in South Korea.

Jennifer Lawrence revealed she's considered "obese" by Hollywood standards but vows to never starve herself for a role. "I eat like a caveman, I’ll be the only actress who doesn’t have anorexia rumors," she told Elle magazine. The Hunger Games star worked hard to set a good example for young fans when getting in shape to play Katniss Everdeen. "That’s something I was really conscious of during training, when you’re trying to get your body to look exactly right. I was trying to get my body to look fit and strong, not thin and underfed." Lawrence also opened up about her boyfriend Nicholas Hoult, who she met on the set of X-Men: First Class. The pair, who have a decidedly unglamorous lifestyle, enjoy watching TV and eating Cheetos together. "He’s my favourite person to be around and makes me laugh harder than anybody," she said.
