Bloomingdale’s, a luxury department store owned by Macy’s, faces criticism over an ad in its holiday catalog that some interpret as encouraging date rape, reports the Wall Street Journal. The ad features a woman laughing with her head turned as a young man looks her way, and the text reads: “Spike Your Best Friend’s Eggnog When They’re Not Looking.” Over the past 48 hours, 3,868 comments on social media have criticized the ad, with many calling it “creepy.” Bloomingdale’s has apologized, stating the copy was inappropriate and in poor taste. Marketers are under pressure to stand out amid an increasing number of advertising messages, but the risk of controversy grows with each attempt.

A Maine mother, Hallie Twomey, used social media to scatter her son CJ's ashes in over 100 countries, including space, after he tragically took his own life at age 20. Twomey started the "Scattering CJ" Facebook page to share her son's ashes with strangers who would scatter them in places CJ never got to see. His ashes have traveled from Antarctica to the Galapagos Islands and even to space. Twomey hopes this journey will keep CJ's memory alive and help her cope with her guilt.

Scientists have investigated the phenomenon of resting bitch face (RBF) or Bitchy Resting Face, finding that faces with this expression register more than 3 percent underlying emotion, with "contempt" being the key factor. Behavioral researchers Jason Rogers and Abbe Macbeth used a software tool, FaceReader, to analyze faces of celebrities like Kristen Stewart, Queen Elizabeth, and Kanye West, confirming that RBF is not a predominantly female issue but rather a social norm where women are expected to be more smiley and happy. The study offers a way to self-assess RBF through the Noldus Information Technology website, but advises against getting stressed over the findings.

Walt Disney CEO Bob Iger disclosed that hackers claiming to have access to a Disney film threatened to release it online unless the studio paid a ransom in Bitcoin. Iger stated during a town hall meeting that Disney refused to pay and is working with federal investigators. The film in question is rumored to be Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales, though Disney did not confirm the name. This incident follows other Hollywood targets like Sony Pictures and Netflix, highlighting the growing threat of ransom demands in the film industry.

U.S. Rep. Trey Radel, a Florida Republican and tea party freshman, was arrested for cocaine possession in Washington D.C. on October 29. He faces a maximum of 180 days in jail and a fine of up to $1,000. Radel, 37, was charged with misdemeanor cocaine possession and is scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday. He apologized, stating he struggles with alcoholism and needs help for his family and constituents. Radel has missed recent votes in the House. Speaker John Boehner’s spokesman said members should be held to high standards, and the case will be handled by the courts. Radel’s arrest has raised questions about his re-election prospects, with some local officials expressing disappointment.

A 19-year-old Israeli with dual American and Israeli citizenship was arrested in connection with a series of bomb threats targeting Jewish institutions worldwide, including in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand, according to Israeli police. The suspect used advanced camouflage technologies to cover his tracks and was arrested after an international investigation involving the FBI. The threats were spread across 33 states and most came in five waves. The suspect's lawyer stated he had a history of behavioral issues and an inoperable brain tumor. The arrest was seen as a relief by Jewish leaders, who expressed concern that the suspect was Jewish. U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions praised the cooperation between the FBI and Israeli National Police.

In a pretrial hearing, evidence emerged linking Jesse Matthew to the 2014 disappearance and death of University of Virginia student Hannah Graham. A former detective testified that a police bloodhound detected traces of Graham inside Matthew's apartment and on the passenger side door of his car. The dog also found her scent at an industrial site about a mile from downtown Charlottesville, suggesting she may have been attacked there. Matthew, who is charged with capital murder in Graham's case, also faces first-degree murder charges in the 2009 death of Virginia Tech student Morgan Harrington.

European airlines are questioning the need for a blanket flying ban over much of Northern and Central Europe, as test flights by Air France-KLM and Deutsche Lufthansa showed no damage to aircraft. EU transport ministers are set to hold emergency talks to discuss easing the travel crisis, with the ban costing airlines $200 million a day. The volcanic ash cloud, stretching from the Arctic to the French Mediterranean, has canceled 63,000 flights and affected over 6.8 million passengers. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) urges flexible airspace openings. Spain suggests using its airports as entry points for stranded travelers. British Airways fears it may not resume normal services until Thursday. The UK has extended its airspace ban until at least Monday evening, with Ireland, Germany, and the Netherlands keeping their skies closed until midday. The ash cloud, while easing slightly, remains a concern for aviation safety.

A disturbing shrine was discovered in the backyard of Jared Lee Loughner, the 22-year-old accused of shooting U.S. Rep. Gabrielle Giffords and 19 others in Tucson, Arizona. Inside a camouflage tent, investigators found a miniature altar with a human skull replica, along with candles and potting soil. This shrine, combined with Loughner's anti-government rhetoric and odd behavior at Pima Community College, raises questions about his motives and mental state. Loughner, who had been suspended for disruptive behavior, showed signs of mental instability and a fascination with lucid dreaming. His friend, Bryce Tierney, recalls Loughner's obsession with Giffords, whom he perceived as a "fake," and his belief in an alternate reality where words and government have no meaning. The discovery of the shrine and Loughner's online postings suggest a complex psychological profile that may have contributed to the tragic shooting.

A 23-year-old man and his 62-year-old mother were found dead in their home in east Wichita on Saturday night. Police were called to the 7500 block of East Huntington around 11 p.m. and found the bodies of Cody Ha and his mother, Huong Pham. Ha's friend, Ashley Martinez, who was playing video games with Ha at the time, heard popping noises that sounded like gunshots and reported the incident to police. Ha's mother had conflicts with other people in the past, but the connection to the murders is unclear. The house, where Ha and his family had lived for at least 10 years, had frequent visitors, sometimes for the purchase of prescription drugs. Ha worked at his mother's dry cleaning business during the day and played video games at night. Friends describe Ha as easy-going and inclusive. Police are seeking tips to solve the case.

A New Mexico middle school math teacher faces felony charges after allegedly threatening a student with a knife during a pop quiz. According to police, Benjamin Nagurski, 63, was removed from his classroom by school officials after the incident. The criminal complaint states that Nagurski threatened a student with a knife, telling him to stop talking to another student. When confronted, Nagurski allegedly said, "Maybe next time I'll pull a machete on you." Nagurski is charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and possession of an unlawful weapon. He was arrested and booked into jail, facing a $10,000 bail. The principal reported that Nagurski had a steak knife and another knife with a sharp tip and wooden handle. The Bernalillo Public Schools superintendent did not immediately comment on the case.

A 9-year-old girl, Jordan Landon, survived a car accident that killed her father, Douglas Landon, in Craven County, North Carolina. The crash occurred on Friday, with Jordan trapped inside the 1995 Chevrolet Monte Carlo. She managed to survive for two days on Pop-Tarts, water, and Gatorade. Jordan's mother, Cissy Leohmann, filed a missing person report and searched for her daughter and father, but crashed her own car during the search. Jordan was finally found and rescued on Sunday evening, after a man spotted the overturned car. She endured the cold and was trapped by a seatbelt, but remained calm. Troopers believe the car was traveling over 100 mph at the time of the accident, and no mechanical failure was involved. Jordan suffered non-life-threatening injuries and is expected to recover fully.

The Islamic State claimed responsibility for the truck attack in New York City that killed eight people and injured 12, according to its weekly newsletter. President Donald Trump responded by tweeting that the suspect, Sayfullo Saipov, should receive the death penalty. Saipov, an Uzbek national, was charged with providing material support to ISIS and other crimes. He had reportedly watched ISIS videos and followed the group's playbook, leaving a note at the scene expressing allegiance to the group. While Saipov's actions appear to be inspired by ISIS, there is no evidence of direct involvement from the group. The attack prompted New York to install concrete barriers on the affected bike path to prevent similar incidents.

A final search vessel, the Dutch-owned Fugro Equator, has departed for what is likely the last mission in the hunt for missing Malaysia Airlines flight MH370. The search, which has spanned over 46,000 square miles of the Indian Ocean and cost an estimated $150 million, is set to end early next year if no new evidence is found. Four ships have been combing the area, but none have uncovered any trace of the Boeing 777, which disappeared in March 2014 with 239 people on board. Despite the extensive search, families of the victims have called for the beach search to continue, as several pieces of debris confirmed to be from MH370 have washed up on coasts in East Africa and Madagascar. The search area, which includes some of the world's roughest seas, is expected to be completed by early 2017, pending weather conditions.

President Donald Trump made an unannounced visit to Dover Air Force Base to honor the remains of Navy SEAL William "Ryan" Owens, the first U.S. combat casualty since Trump took office. The SEAL's death highlights the human costs of ongoing military campaigns, with more than 8,400 U.S. troops training and advising local forces in Afghanistan, over 5,100 in Iraq, and about 500 in Syria fighting the Islamic State. Trump's trip to Delaware was shrouded in secrecy, with the president and his daughter, Ivanka, traveling in the presidential helicopter. The SEAL's family requested privacy for the visit and the return of his remains. Melania Trump, the president's wife, has not yet moved to Washington and is putting together her staff, raising questions about her role as first lady. She confirmed plans to move to D.C. at the end of the school year, with her son Barron finishing his studies in New York.

Mirror, Mirror, a modern retelling of the Snow White story, opens March 30, offering a lighter, more comedic take on the classic tale. Directed by Tarsem Singh, the film features Julia Roberts as the vain and self-absorbed Queen, Lily Collins as the spirited Snow White, and Armie Hammer as the handsome Prince Alcott. The story updates the original, giving Snow White more agency and a sword for self-defense. Tarsem Singh, known for his visually stunning films, brings a colorful and elaborate world to life, but critics note that the plot can be slow and the dialogue occasionally flat. The film aims to balance traditional fairy tale elements with contemporary humor, though some find it lacking in depth and emotional resonance.

A 30-year-old man was ordered to vacate his parents' Syracuse-area home after a legal battle in court. State Supreme Court Justice Donald Greenwood ruled that Michael Rotondo must move out, and ordered an investigation by adult protective services due to concerns about his living situation. Rotondo's parents had given him multiple eviction notices, but he refused to leave. His parents' lawyer sought a court order enforceable by sheriff's deputies. Rotondo argued for an additional six months, citing legal research, but the judge found his request "outrageous." Despite the order, Rotondo vowed to appeal and planned to stay in the house, taking only necessary items. His parents had offered financial assistance but Rotondo claimed it was insufficient. The case has garnered national and international attention.

A Florida state appeals court overturned the murder conviction of former FBI agent John J. Connolly Jr. on Wednesday, ruling that jurors relied on a flawed charge against him in the 1982 killing of Boston businessman John Callahan. By a 2-to-1 decision, the Miami appeals court ruled that Connolly's conviction of second-degree murder with a firearm should be overturned because he did not carry or discharge the gun used to kill Callahan. The court faulted prosecutors for using a firearms charge that skirted Florida's statute of limitations. Connolly, who had been 1,500 miles away in Boston when hitman John Martorano killed Callahan, could now be freed. The ruling raises the possibility that the 73-year-old, a former handler of notorious Southie mobster James "Whitey" Bulger, could be released. Connolly's wife and children celebrated the decision, while victims' families expressed outrage. The Florida Attorney General is considering

A Pakistani railway minister has personally offered a $100,000 reward for the death of the filmmaker behind an anti-Islam movie, drawing criticism from the US state department. Ghulam Ahmad Bilour made the offer at a news conference, inviting the Taliban and al-Qaeda to carry out the "sacred duty." The minister's party, the Awami National Party, has distanced itself from his comments, stating they do not represent the party's stance. Prime Minister Raja Pervez Ashraf's office has dissociated itself from the minister's announcement. Meanwhile, protests against the film continue worldwide, with clashes and deaths reported in Pakistan, Nigeria, Greece, and Turkey. The US has urged citizens not to travel to Pakistan and has aired TV ads showing President Obama and Secretary of State Clinton condemning the film. Anti-Western sentiment has also been fueled by recent caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad in a French satirical magazine.

A Canadian Olympic gold medalist and his team were kicked out of a curling tournament in Alberta for poor behavior, including drunkenness and breaking brooms. Ryan Fry, who won gold at the 2014 Winter Olympics, and his teammates Jamie Koe, Chris Schille, and DJ Kidby forfeited their final game after complaints from opponents and spectators. The team apologized for their actions and promised to improve their behavior in the future.

Beijing authorities have dismantled over 500 illegal outdoor barbecues in an effort to combat air pollution, which often reaches hazardous levels and can lead to long-term health issues like rising lung cancer rates among the city's 20 million residents. The barbecues, operated by ethnic Uighur Muslims from Xinjiang, are considered a significant source of PM2.5, tiny particles that can enter deep into the lungs. State media reports show workers cutting up the barbecues, while citizens online have mocked the move, suggesting the government should focus on larger sources of pollution. Emergency measures like car restrictions and school closures are in place when pollution is particularly heavy.

Republican presidential candidate Ted Cruz is benefiting from a feud with The New York Times, which has excluded his memoir "A Time for Truth" from its bestseller list despite strong sales. Cruz's campaign claims the Times is using "strategic bulk purchases" as an excuse to exclude the book, while HarperCollins denies any such practices. The controversy has boosted sales and media attention for Cruz, with his campaign calling for the Times to release evidence supporting its claims. Despite the exclusion, "A Time for Truth" ranked high on other bestseller lists, including Nielsen Bookscan, The Wall Street Journal, and Barnes and Noble. Cruz's campaign sees the dispute as a chance to drive readers to his book and increase its visibility.

An American Airlines pilot died mid-flight during an overnight "red eye" flight from Phoenix to Boston, causing the plane to divert to Syracuse. The co-pilot took over and landed the plane safely around 7:10 a.m. The captain's condition became "incapacitated" about four hours into the flight, according to air traffic control recordings. American Airlines confirmed the pilot's death and expressed condolences to the family. The airline stated that one of the flight attendants, who is a nurse, assisted the ill pilot. The flight, which had 147 passengers and five crew members, was delayed for four hours in Syracuse before continuing to Boston with a new crew.

Green Bay, WI — A local filmmaker has stepped forward to claim responsibility for the "creepy clown" sightings that have been causing concern in the area. Adam Krause, who created the Gags - The Green Bay Clown Facebook page, revealed himself as the creator of the phenomenon, stating it was part of a 10-day marketing plan for his upcoming short film. Krause explained that the photos used were taken in May 2016 and that no one was in danger during the photo shoots. Police received a few calls about the clown but have limited options as the person is not breaking the law by walking in a clown costume. The viral Facebook page and sightings continue to cause a stir among residents.

This fall, several celebrities will be back on campus. James Franco, Emma Watson, and the actor from Home Alone 3, along with an Olympic gold medalist, will be studying at various universities. Check out the slideshow for more names and details.

Amanda Knox, dubbed "Foxy Knoxy," has found a new love in classical guitarist James Terrano, a fellow student at the University of Washington. Knox, 24, and Terrano, 24, have known each other since childhood and have been seen together in Seattle, despite Knox's efforts to return to a "normal" life post-conviction. Knox's family and friends have been supportive, but Knox herself has remained tight-lipped about the relationship. Meanwhile, Raffaele Sollecito, Knox's former boyfriend and co-defendant, has broken his silence in an Italian TV interview, expressing that their relationship was "overdue" due to the "cruel injustice" they both suffered. Sollecito says he wishes Knox well and may visit her in Seattle, though he is unsure when.

Researchers have identified a microscopic, sack-like sea creature, Saccorhytus coronarius, as the earliest known ancestor of humans, dating back 540 million years. Found in central China, these fossils, "exquisitely well preserved," reveal insights into the primitive beginnings of a broad range of species, including vertebrates. Saccorhytus, about a millimeter in size, likely lived between sand grains on the seabed, with a large mouth relative to its body, possibly used for engulfing food. The creature's body was bilaterally symmetrical, covered with a thin, flexible skin, and may have moved by wriggling. Notably, Saccorhytus lacked an anus, suggesting waste material was expelled through the mouth. A Russian passenger plane carrying 71 people crashed near Moscow shortly after taking off from Domodedovo Airport, killing all on board. The Antonov An-148 airliner, operated by Saratov Airlines, disappeared from radar screens a few minutes after departing. Wreckage, including at least one engine, was found in fields near the crash site. President Vladimir Putin offered condolences and ordered a special investigative commission. The plane, manufactured in 2010, had been in service for two years before being put into storage due to a parts shortage and re-entered service in 2017. Investigators are considering all possible causes, including weather conditions and technical issues. More than 70 people died, and emergency services deployed over 150 workers to the scene.

A service dog named Presley, who attends school with her owner Joseph "Seph" Ware in West Monroe, Louisiana, has gained attention after being included in the yearbook at Good Hope Middle School. Seph, 14, has Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a condition that causes progressive muscle weakness. Presley, a 5-year-old golden doodle, has been by Seph's side for four years and helps him with daily tasks. When picture day came around, school officials decided to include Presley in the yearbook with the other students. Seph's mother, Lori Ware, says her son's reaction was, "Why not." The administrators' gesture has been well-received by the students, who adore Presley and often sneak pets in the hallways. Presley's inclusion in the yearbook has drawn significant attention online.

The main fugitive from the November Paris attacks, Salah Abdeslam, has been arrested in Brussels after four months on the run, according to French police officials. Abdeslam, 26, was captured in a major police operation in the Molenbeek neighborhood of Brussels. Belgian authorities also found his fingerprints in an apartment raided earlier this week, suggesting he had been using the location as a hideout. During the raid, a man believed to be an accomplice of Abdeslam was shot dead, while two suspects escaped. Salah Abdeslam is believed to have played a key logistical role in the Paris attacks and was one of the attackers who killed 130 people. His arrest comes as Belgian and French authorities continue to investigate the Paris attacks and their links to Brussels.

A baby girl born with her heart outside her body in Britain has survived after undergoing three operations, making her the first known case in the UK to do so. Vanellope Hope Wilkins, born with the rare condition ectopia cordis, had her heart relocated to inside her chest within an hour of birth. The surgery, performed by a team of 50 medical staff at Glenfield Hospital in Leicester, is believed to be the first of its kind on a newborn in Britain. The condition, which affects about five to eight babies per million, usually results in stillbirth or termination due to high infection risks. Vanellope's parents, Naomi Findlay and Dean Wilkins, decided against termination, opting to continue the pregnancy despite the bleak prognosis. The family named Vanellope after a Disney character to symbolize her resilience. Despite the challenges, Vanellope continues to recover, facing the risk of infection as she adjusts to her new condition.

Raffaele Sollecito, freed from prison after being cleared of Meredith Kercher's murder, plans to visit Amanda Knox in Seattle. Sollecito, speaking to Oggi magazine, expresses a strong desire to see Knox and reconnect, stating they speak and write to each other daily. Sollecito says they need each other to understand what happened and look toward a future together. The pair spent four years in what Sollecito describes as a "circle of hell," suffering greatly and ruining their lives. Sollecito plans to visit Knox before Christmas, though he is open to going earlier.

Film critic Roger Ebert, who battled thyroid and salivary gland cancer, died at 70. His career spanned 46 years at the Chicago Sun-Times and 31 years on television, where he co-hosted "Sneak Previews" with Gene Siskel. Ebert was the first film critic to win a Pulitzer Prize and became a cultural icon. His reviews were known for their scholarly wit and entertainment value. Ebert's autobiography, "Life Itself," detailed his life and career, including his diagnosis and subsequent recovery. He continued to work, attending film festivals and producing "Ebert Presents at the Movies" with his wife, Chaz. Ebert's honesty and dedication to his craft inspired admiration and respect.

Wonder Woman's Gal Gadot reportedly earned the same upfront salary as Henry Cavill for Superman, according to a source familiar with both negotiations. The salary discrepancy reported by Elle magazine was based on a mix of salary information from various publications and did not differentiate between upfront salary and bonuses. Warner Bros., the studio behind both movies, declined to comment. While low- to mid-six figures are standard for Hollywood tentpole debuts, especially for actors with short track records, box-office bonuses and sequel negotiations can significantly increase earnings. Producer Jon Peters took home $80 million to $85 million for his role in jumpstarting the Superman franchise in the 1990s.

In the Beach to Beacon 10K, Jesse Orach, a 23-year-old Gorham native and University of Maine alumnus, faced a sudden heat stroke during the race. He collapsed just before the finish line but was helped to his feet by his top competitor, Robert Gomez, and both finished the 6.2-mile course together in 31 minutes, 31 seconds. Despite Orach's condition, Gomez insisted he ran a better race and deserved to win. Orach, who had won the Maine division last year, was the first Maine man to repeat as champion since 2009. His mother, Brenda, was present to witness his victory. Both runners were commended for their sportsmanship.

Researchers have made significant progress in growing bone for human use by creating a scaffold from cow bone and populating it with stem cells from pigs. This personalized approach, tested in 14 pigs, resulted in new bone that integrated well with the animals' existing jaw structure. The technique involves 3D imaging to create a scaffold matching the missing bone, followed by culturing stem cells in a bioreactor for three weeks. Implanted in the pigs, the seeded scaffolds showed better mechanical strength and integration compared to unseeded ones or those left to heal naturally. This method, if proven safe and effective in humans, could offer an alternative to painful and complex autografts. Clinical trials are at least three years away.

The University of Wisconsin's Archive-It partnership includes two sub-collections: the UW-Madison Collection and the Stem Cell Research Archives Project. The UW-Madison Collection captures various aspects of the university's life, while the Stem Cell Research Archives Project focuses on stem cell research and its reactions in Wisconsin. Meanwhile, Hong Kong has overtaken New York as the city with the largest super-rich population, with a significant increase in ultra-high-net-worth individuals (UHNWIs) due to its booming stock market and growing financial links with China. Asia, particularly China, is catching up with the United States in terms of wealth creation, with the number of UHNWIs in Asia rising by 20% last year. However, China faces challenges such as a trade war with the U.S. and high levels of debt in its financial system.

A former New York City schoolteacher and her 4-year-old son were found dead in her Manhattan apartment, leading to the arrest of the woman's ex-lover on murder charges. Isaac Duran Infante, 23, confessed to killing the 36-year-old teacher, Felicia Barahona, and their son, Miguel. Barahona was strangled with an electrical cord, and her son was found unresponsive in a bathtub. Duran Infante was arrested and confessed to the killings, citing dissatisfaction with how their son was being raised. The couple's relationship began when Duran Infante, then a student, had a sexual relationship with Barahona, who was later fired from her teaching job. Neighbors described Barahona as protective of her son, and the case has shocked the community.

On Father's Day, an 18-year-old man was shot four times by his father in New Smyrna Beach. Eugene Blackwell Sr., 46, shot his son Eugene Blackwell Jr. after an argument with his wife, who mentioned a possible divorce. The son intervened when his father choked his mother. The elder Blackwell shot his son in the abdomen, leg, hip, and arm. Eugene Blackwell Jr. was critically injured and taken to the hospital. His father fled the scene but turned himself in later, facing attempted first-degree murder charges. He was held without bond.

President Donald Trump escalated a global trade dispute by threatening to impose a retaliatory tax on car exports from the European Union, in response to new tariffs on steel and aluminum imports. In a tweet, Trump stated, "If the E.U. wants to further increase their already massive tariffs and barriers on U.S. companies doing business there, we will simply apply a tax on their cars which freely pour into the U.S." This move could impact popular European brands like Volkswagen and BMW, which manufacture many vehicles in the U.S. and export them to Europe. In 2016, the EU exported over 6 million cars, with the U.S. being its largest market, absorbing more than 1 million of those vehicles. The U.S. has a significant trade deficit with the EU, amounting to over $151 billion in 2017. European leaders, including Jean-Claude Juncker, responded by threatening to impose retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products

Kim Kardashian was caught off guard at a launch event for her new fragrance when a fan threw a bag of flour on her, leaving her covered in white powder. The reality star handled the situation gracefully, retreating to clean up and returning to the event. Her sisters Khloe and Kourtney chimed in on social media, with Khloe wishing she had been there to see the incident and Kourtney speculating about the flour-bomber's motives. Kim's security quickly escorted the perpetrator away, and the local fire department confirmed the powder was safe. Despite the unexpected attack, Kim maintained her composure and continued with the event, earning praise from fans for her poise.

A Chinese woman spent over $1,100 to rescue 100 dogs from a dog meat festival in Yulin, a city that holds an annual event on the summer solstice. Animal activists have long criticized the festival, with some activists traveling to Yulin to purchase and save dogs from being slaughtered. The festival, which is not illegal, has faced increasing backlash from celebrities and the public, with some cities like Guangzhou closing dog meat restaurants. Critics argue the festival promotes cruelty, poses a rabies risk, and violates food safety regulations. Despite local government attempts to distance themselves, the festival continues, with business booming for traders.

In the wake of a film festival premiere, the comedy "Get Hard" starring Will Ferrell and Kevin Hart faced backlash for potentially offensive content. During a Q&A at the South By Southwest Film Festival, audience members questioned the film's portrayal of race and homosexuality, leading to harsh criticism from marketing executives. Early reviews further scrutinized the movie's handling of sensitive topics, with some deeming it perpetuating stereotypes. However, the film's stars and producers defended it as a satire of existing attitudes and misconceptions. They argued that the movie aimed to provoke and mirror real-world issues, such as income inequality and racial prejudice. Despite the controversy, the film's popularity with audiences and the goodwill of its stars may mitigate any negative impact on its box office performance.

Romney pollster Neil Newhouse argues that the key to the election is unemployment and food stamps, not convention bounce. Newhouse contends the race remains tight, with Romney close in several swing states. Despite Obama's post-convention bump, Newhouse believes the "Obama economy" will ultimately turn voters against him. Newhouse highlights Romney's grassroots efforts and financial advantage, predicting a Romney victory.

A baby shower in Stoughton, Massachusetts, turned into a chaotic brawl involving approximately 200 people, including children, at a local social club. The situation escalated so severely that Stoughton police had to call in backup from three additional local police departments, the state police, and the sheriff’s department. The crowd, which had initially gathered for a baby shower, became unruly, surrounding officers and throwing bottles and chairs at them, prompting the use of Tasers by the officers. Four individuals, including three men and a teenager, were arrested and charged with assault and battery on a police officer. The club, which caters to the Portuguese community, had rented the room for a private party but never anticipated such a violent turn of events. Police expressed concern over the presence of children at the party, though injuries were non-serious.

Dwight Yoakam performed "Seven Spanish Angels" at the 50th annual CMA Awards, where Garth Brooks won the top prize, beating out Carrie Underwood, Chris Stapleton, Keith Urban, and Luke Bryan. Brooks, who returned to music after a 13-year break, expressed gratitude, saying, "We are so damn lucky to be part of this thing called country music." Beyoncé and the Dixie Chicks performed "Daddy Lessons," receiving mixed reactions on social media. The night featured memorable performances, including Dolly Parton's honor and a tribute to the CMA Awards' 50th anniversary. Chris Stapleton won male vocalist and music video of the year, while Underwood took home female vocalist of the year. Other winners included Thomas Rhett, Kenny Chesney, and Little Big Town. Paisley and Underwood hosted the show, delivering political jokes.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement on Friday, retracting his previous accusation that a Palestinian cleric, Haj Amin al-Husseini, convinced Adolf Hitler to exterminate Jews during World War II. Netanyahu clarified that the decision to implement the "Final Solution" was made by the Nazis independently, without external influence. He maintained that the Nazis saw al-Husseini as a collaborator but did not need him to decide on the systematic destruction of European Jewry, which began in June 1941. Netanyahu's statement aimed to clarify that he never intended to absolve Hitler of his responsibility for the Holocaust.

Seven-year-old Grayson Powell bowled an impressive game to win a youth bowling tournament in St. John's but was disqualified for wearing the wrong color of pants. The rule, according to the tournament, is to wear black pants, and Grayson's faded black jeans did not meet the standard. Despite performing well, Grayson was informed of the disqualification after his team won the championship. His father, Todd Powell, was critical of the decision, feeling it was unfair and undermining the spirit of the game. The governing body defended the rule, stating it had been in place for decades, but Powell Sr. argued that the disqualification should not have been enforced after Grayson had already competed.

The University of Texas at Austin will relocate the statue of Jefferson Davis to the Dolph Briscoe Center for American History, while leaving statues of Confederate generals Robert E. Lee, Albert Sidney Johnston, and others on the South Mall. President Gregory Fenves cited Davis's unique role in Confederate history as a reason for the move. The Davis statue will be removed in the next two days and relocated within 18 months. The university will consider adding plaques to the remaining statues to provide historical context. The decision follows recommendations from a 12-member advisory panel that received over 3,100 public opinions. The move is part of a broader national discussion on Confederate monuments and their place in public spaces.

A new genetic blood test shows promise in detecting early-stage cancers, potentially improving survival rates, reports HealthDay. The test, developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, scans blood for DNA fragments released by cancerous tumors, focusing on 58 "cancer-driver" genes. Among 200 patients with colon, breast, lung, or ovarian cancer, the test detected stage 1 or 2 cancers between 59% and 71% of the time. It also successfully screened out cancer-free individuals, with no false positives. The test identified early-stage ovarian cancer, often missed, with 68% accuracy. While promising, researchers need to validate the test in larger studies and improve its detection rate. The ability to distinguish between life-threatening and non-life-threatening cancers will also be crucial.

Firefighters in the Grande Prairie area rescued 10 horses that broke through thin ice on a slough, using chainsaws and specialized equipment. Three horses died during the rescue due to exhaustion and injuries. The incident highlights the dangers of thinning ice, as regional fire chief Trevor Grant warns that conditions can change rapidly. Seven horses were successfully rescued and are expected to recover.

A 19-year-old Chicago woman named Ruth Ann Steinhagen shot and nearly killed former Cubs first baseman Eddie Waitkus in 1949, inspiring the novel and movie "The Natural." Steinhagen, known as a "Baseball Annie," lured Waitkus to a hotel room with a note and shot him with a .22-caliber rifle. Waitkus survived, and Steinhagen was committed to a mental hospital. After being deemed sane and released, she lived quietly for decades, rarely speaking about the incident. She died in 2013 at 83, having lived a life of anonymity despite her infamous crime.

For over 25 years, the Picasso painting "Woman in Red Arm Chair" at Houston's Menil Collection remained untouched. However, a vandal spray-painted the 1929 masterpiece, stenciling a bull and the word "Conquista" before fleeing. The museum swiftly repaired the damage, and the incident is under active investigation as a criminal mischief case. The painting, one of nine by Picasso in the Menil collection, has an excellent prognosis. Museum officials are urging anyone with information to come forward.

Researchers at Flashpoint suggested that "script kiddies," or inexperienced hackers, likely carried out the massive DDoS attack on Dyn, which disrupted access to numerous popular websites. The attack, involving millions of internet-connected devices like DVRs and cameras, targeted Dyn's Domain Name System (DNS) services. While the primary target may have been a video game company using Dyn's services, Dyn has not disclosed the identity of the actual target. The attack utilized the Mirai malware, which can infect and control IoT devices. Dyn estimated that tens of millions of such devices were involved. The incident highlights the vulnerability of IoT devices to hacking and the difficulty in preventing such large-scale attacks. Dyn's analysis indicated that the Mirai botnet was the primary source of the malicious traffic. Senator Mark Warner expressed concern about the security of IoT devices, suggesting that ISPs should ban insecure devices from their networks to prevent future attacks.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump sparked controversy by suggesting women who have abortions illegally should face "some form of punishment." His rivals swiftly distanced themselves, with Ted Cruz calling his comments "horrific and telling." Trump later clarified that doctors and others performing illegal abortions would face legal consequences, not the women. The incident highlighted the stark divide within the Republican Party on abortion, with most candidates supporting overturning Roe v. Wade but differing on whether to allow exceptions for rape and incest. Trump's comments also reignited debates about his evolving stance on abortion and his ability to unite the party.

A group of friends visiting a haunted house in Nashville for Halloween had a terrifying encounter when one of the actors, believed to be an employee, handed a real knife to one of the women. The woman, thinking the knife was a prop, stabbed her friend in the left arm. When she pulled back, she realized the knife was real and the wound was severe, with blood squirting from the victim's arm. The friend was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment. The actor reportedly ran away after the incident, and the haunted house is now investigating and considering legal action.

A 25-year-old Israeli woman was allegedly gang-raped near Manali after accepting a ride from a vehicle in the early hours of Sunday. The woman, trying to reach Kaza in the Spiti Valley, was picked up by a car without license plates and taken to Manali. Two of the six men in the vehicle raped her at an unknown location before dropping her off in Manali. Police have registered a case and are examining CCTV footage to identify the suspects. This incident is the third reported rape involving a foreigner in the Kullu district in the past four years.

Coach is acquiring its rival, Kate Spade & Co., in a $2.4 billion deal, aiming to broaden its customer base to younger, trendier millennial shoppers. The transaction is expected to close in the third quarter of 2017 and will add to Coach's adjusted earnings in fiscal 2018. Shares of both companies saw significant increases following the announcement. Coach CEO Victor Luis highlighted Kate Spade's strong brand awareness among millennials. The deal is expected to generate $50 million in annual savings through combined inventory management and supply chains, boosting profitability.

A federal wrongful death lawsuit has been filed by the parents of Megan Rondini, a University of Alabama student who died after alleging she was raped by a wealthy Tuscaloosa man. The lawsuit names the alleged attacker, university officials, and law enforcement officers as defendants, accusing them of mishandling the case and driving Rondini to suicide. The parents claim Rondini was treated as a suspect rather than a victim by law enforcement, and that university officials failed to provide adequate psychological support. The lawsuit alleges that Rondini's rape kit was not tested, witnesses were not interviewed, and she was denied counseling services. The defendants deny the allegations, with the accused's lawyer stating the accusations are "false." The case highlights ongoing issues in handling sexual assault cases, particularly when the accused is from a prominent local family.

Investigators continue to search a South Carolina property for more remains after finding another body, bringing the total number of suspected victims to at least seven. Todd Kohlhepp, accused of a decade-long crime spree, was denied bond in a court appearance. Kohlhepp confessed to killing four people at a motorcycle shop in 2003 and pointed out additional burial sites on his property. The investigation has expanded to other properties Kohlhepp owns or used to own, with involvement from the FBI and Department of Homeland Security. Kohlhepp's case includes charges of murder, kidnapping, and multiple weapons offenses. Family members of the victims expressed a mix of emotions, including relief and a desire for justice. Kohlhepp's criminal history includes a 1987 conviction for kidnapping and sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl.

Mitt Romney secured a second consecutive victory in the Nevada caucuses, signaling a strong path toward the Republican nomination. His win over rivals Newt Gingrich, Ron Paul, and Rick Santorum highlighted Romney's ability to maintain momentum. Romney focused on criticizing President Obama's economic policies and emphasizing his own experience. Gingrich, Santorum, and Paul struggled to gain traction, with Santorum hoping to reset the race and Paul aiming for a strong showing in Minnesota. The results in Nevada are significant as the state is expected to be a key battleground in the general election.

On Tuesday night, get ready for a lunar occultation as the moon passes in front of the bright star Aldebaran, one of the most colorful stars in the sky. This event, visible in portions of Mexico, Central America, southeastern Canada, the eastern U.S., and southern Europe, offers a rare chance to observe the moon "play hide-and-seek" with a star. For viewers in the southern and eastern U.S., including parts of California, Colorado, and Minnesota, the waning gibbous moon, 85% illuminated, will occult Aldebaran, creating a spectacle visible through binoculars or a telescope. The event is part of a series of Aldebaran occultations that began in January 2015 and will end in September 2018, with the next visible from North America coming on December 12-13. President Trump unveiled a Republican tax reform framework in Indiana, proposing sweeping changes to the tax code. The plan includes reducing individual income tax brackets from seven to three (12%, 25%, and 35%), doubling the standard deduction to $12,000 for individuals and $24,000 for married couples, and slashing the corporate tax rate to 20%. Trump aims to benefit the middle class and American workers, though critics argue it primarily helps the wealthy. The plan eliminates the estate tax and allows for immediate write-offs of business investments. Trump seeks bipartisan support, but Democrats oppose tax cuts for the rich and worry about the plan's impact on the deficit. The framework is part of Trump's efforts to boost the economy and create jobs.

Beloit College's annual Mindset List highlights the cultural touchstones and experiences that define the entering class of 2014, born in 1992. Key points include their familiarity with digital technology, the rise of cable TV channels, and the normalization of various social and technological phenomena. The list, now in its 21st year, provides a snapshot of the world these students have grown up in, noting their lack of experience with cursive writing, the prevalence of email, and the constant availability of information through the internet. It also touches on their awareness of global issues and the changing landscape of technology and society.

RedState, an influential conservative website, fired several prominent writers on Friday, allegedly to purge the outlet of anti-Trump voices. The Daily Beast confirmed that top editors and writers Caleb Howe, Jay Caruso, Ben Howe, Patrick Frey (writing under the pseudonym Patterico), Neil Stevens, and Susan Wright, who often criticized the president, were among those dismissed. Fired staffers learned of their termination via locked email accounts or a memo from Townhall general manager Jonathan Garthwaite. The layoffs reflect a shift in the conservative movement, with some viewing it as a reflection of the drift during the Trump era. RedState's decision to retain pro-Trump writers while letting go of those critical of the president suggests a political motivation behind the layoffs, as writers' compensation was based on traffic generated.

A homeless man, Johnny Bobbitt Jr., is suing the couple, Kate McClure and Mark D'Amico, who raised over $400,000 for him through a GoFundMe campaign. Bobbitt claims the couple has mismanaged the funds, treating them as a "personal piggy bank." McClure and D'Amico deny wrongdoing, stating they withheld money due to Bobbitt's drug addiction. The lawsuit seeks undisclosed damages and an appointed receiver for the funds. A hearing is scheduled for Thursday. Bobbitt, a Marine Corps veteran, received help from McClure after she ran out of gas on Interstate 95, leading to a viral fundraising campaign.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford put up personal items, including a tie he wore when admitting to smoking crack cocaine, for auction on eBay. The items, such as moose print pajamas and a football jersey, are being sold with descriptions linking them to the Ford administration. However, the seller, operating under the handle "torontorobford," has a feedback score of 0, raising questions about the authenticity and legitimacy of the auction.

At a United Nations conference in Marrakech, Morocco, nearly 85% of countries, including Germany, agreed to a non-binding Global Compact on Migration aimed at ensuring safe, orderly, and humane migration. The pact, supported by German Chancellor Angela Merkel, encourages international cooperation and the protection of migrants' human rights. However, the deal faced opposition from the United States and several other nations, particularly those with anti-immigration policies. The agreement seeks to address the challenges of migration, which affect hundreds of millions of people globally, and aims to reduce the human cost of unregulated migration, such as the 60,000 lives lost since 2000.

Prosecutors in six California counties have combined charges against Joseph James DeAngelo Jr., suspected of being the Golden State Killer, for a single trial in Sacramento. DeAngelo, a 72-year-old former police officer, faces 13 counts of murder across multiple jurisdictions. The case, spanning the 1970s and 1980s, involved numerous murders, rapes, and home burglaries. After decades of stumped investigators, DeAngelo's DNA was linked to the 1980 crime scene of the Smiths' murders. By matching DNA from other crime scenes and using genealogy databases, authorities identified DeAngelo as the suspect. Surveillance and DNA collected from his trash confirmed the link, leading to his arrest in April. The unified prosecution aims to bring justice for the victims and their families.

Harper Lee, author of the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel "To Kill a Mockingbird," has filed a lawsuit in federal court in Manhattan against the son-in-law of her former literary agent, Samuel Pinkus. The lawsuit seeks to re-secure the copyright to "To Kill a Mockingbird" and to compel the forfeiture of commissions Pinkus received after Lee allegedly assigned the copyright to him and his company in 2007, when she was reportedly suffering from declining eyesight and hearing. Lee, now 87 and living in an assisted-living facility in Alabama, claims Pinkus took advantage of her infirmity to deprive her of royalties. Pinkus's wife, Leigh Ann Winick, and journalist Gerald Posner are also named as defendants. The case highlights the legal and ethical complexities surrounding the rights and interests of aging authors.

Eliot Spitzer choked up on "Morning Joe" discussing his five-year journey of change following a prostitution scandal that ended his governorship. Despite his emotional response, Spitzer's sincerity was questioned online. MSNBC hosts and guests debated whether his tears were genuine, with some finding them authentic. Spitzer emphasized the importance of the public's judgment, urging them to consider his entire career. Meanwhile, Spitzer's political comeback continues, as he seeks the position of New York City comptroller. This role, though less prominent than governor, offers significant influence over financial institutions and city pension funds. Spitzer aims to use this power to advocate for corporate governance reforms and oversight. His announcement to run for comptroller has sparked discussions about his ability to move past past scandals and whether voters will see a more reflective and humble candidate.

Fenway Park, the storied home of the Boston Red Sox for a century, is America's most beloved ballpark and the oldest in major league baseball. Its unique features, from the classic brick entrance to Pesky's Pole, make it a destination for baseball enthusiasts and a setting for iconic moments. The park's charm lies in its unchanged layout since 1912, hosting everything from baseball legends to political figures and musicians. Every significant moment in Red Sox history, from World Series victories to dramatic home runs, is etched into Fenway's lore, making it a symbol of Boston's baseball culture.

A 30-year-old man, Shannon Miles, appeared in court charged with capital murder for allegedly shooting and killing Harris County Sheriff's Deputy Darren Goforth at a gas station. Miles, who wore a yellow jumpsuit and shackles, did not enter a plea. Goforth, 47, was shot 15 times by Miles, who then stood over him and continued firing. Ballistics tests confirmed the .40-caliber Smith & Wesson found at Miles' home matched the shell casings at the crime scene. Deputy Goforth, a 10-year veteran with a family, was remembered with a vigil and donations exceeding $150,000. Miles has a history of run-ins with law enforcement, including past assaults and resisting arrest charges. His motive remains unclear, with authorities continuing to investigate.

A New Hampshire jury convicted Owen Labrie, a former St. Paul’s School student, of five counts, including a felony charge of using the internet to entice a minor, but acquitted him of more serious charges of aggravated sexual assault. Labrie, 19, at the time of the alleged May 2014 incident, faced a maximum sentence of 11 years, including registration as a sex offender. Labrie’s accuser, 15 at the time, testified that Labrie had forced himself on her, while Labrie claimed it was consensual. The verdict left both teenagers in tears. Labrie’s lawyer argued that the jury believed there was no intercourse but did not find the encounter consensual. Labrie was released on $15,000 bail. St. Paul’s School, whose alumni include Secretary of State John Kerry, faced criticism for allegedly fostering a toxic culture that left students at risk of sexual violence. Labrie’s accuser’s

Elon Musk decided against taking Tesla private after considering feedback from investors and board members. Initial plans suggested the process would be challenging and more time-consuming than anticipated, potentially distracting from Model 3 production and profitability. Musk and the board concluded that remaining a public company is the better path for Tesla's mission and financial sustainability.

Belgian officials are investigating whether doctors improperly euthanized a woman with autism, Tine Nys, in 2010, marking the first criminal investigation in a euthanasia case since the practice was legalized in 2002. Three doctors from East Flanders are facing charges, accused of having "poisoned" Nys, who was 38 and had been diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome, a mild form of autism, two months before her death. The case highlights concerns about the criteria for granting euthanasia to those with mental health conditions, as Nys' sister alleged irregularities in the process. The investigation stems from a civil complaint filed by Nys' family, who claim the doctors did not properly prepare the case and rushed the decision. The incident has sparked debates on the appropriateness of euthanasia for psychiatric reasons and the need for stricter oversight, with some experts calling for more rigorous checks and balances to protect patients.

The shooting at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh, which killed 11 people and wounded six, is believed to be the deadliest attack on the Jewish community in U.S. history, according to the Anti-Defamation League. The suspect, Robert Bowers, 46, faces 29 charges, including 11 counts of using a firearm to commit murder and multiple hate crime charges. Bowers reportedly told police that Jews were committing genocide and that he wanted all Jews to die. The attack occurred during Sabbath services, exploiting the synagogue's unlocked door for worship. Four police officers were also injured. President Trump ordered flags to be flown at half-staff, while Jewish leaders expressed heartbreak and called for increased security in synagogues. The incident has reignited debates on gun control and hate crimes.

Josh Hardy, a 7-year-old with a history of cancer and recent complications, is set to receive a potentially lifesaving drug after a long battle with a pharmaceutical company. Following intense public pressure and a plea from his parents, Chimerix agreed to provide brincidofovir for a clinical trial, with Josh as the first patient. The drug, previously denied to Josh, is part of an FDA-approved study to help other patients in need. This case highlights the ethical challenges and public scrutiny surrounding the use of experimental drugs for critically ill children.

Donald Trump resumed his attacks on Fox News host Megyn Kelly after her return from vacation. Trump criticized Kelly's interview with Cornel West and tweeted that he "liked The Kelly File much better without @megynkelly." He also retweeted comments referring to Kelly as a "bimbo." Kelly, however, stated that her vacation was planned before the controversy and that it was unrelated to the Trump debate. Fox News defended Kelly and expressed support for her journalistic work. Trump has not apologized for his comments, maintaining that Kelly owes him an apology for her questions.

The songwriter of "Electric Slide" clarified that the song is not about a vibrator, dispelling rumors that circulated online. In a statement to EDM.com, Neville Livingston, also known as Bunny Wailer, denied the claim, stating that the song was inspired by Eddie Grant's "Electric Avenue." The lyrics, which include phrases like "It's electric!" and "You gotta feel it," have led many to speculate about a hidden meaning, but Livingston maintains the song is about nothing more than dancing and fun. Despite the rumors, the song remains a popular choice for weddings and parties, leaving fans to wonder if their childhood memories will be forever altered.

US investigators wiretapped former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort under secret court orders before and after the election, sources tell CNN. The government surveillance continued into early 2017, including a period when Manafort was known to talk to President Donald Trump. Special counsel Robert Mueller's team, leading the Russia investigation, has been provided details of these communications. The FBI's interest in Manafort dates back to 2014, partly as an outgrowth of a US investigation of Viktor Yanukovych, the former Ukrainian president. Manafort's firm and other US consultants worked with Yanukovych's regime, leading to an investigation into their compliance with the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The FBI surveillance was discontinued for lack of evidence but restarted in early 2017 due to intercepted communications between Manafort and suspected Russian operatives. Manafort has denied communicating with Russian intelligence operatives during the election and participating in Russian efforts to undermine US interests. The White House and Manafort's representatives declined to comment.

Parents are discovering mold growing inside Sophie the Giraffe teething toys, raising concerns about the safety of a popular baby toy. A pediatric dentist found mold inside her child’s Sophie toy after noticing a musty smell. Despite following cleaning instructions, the mold persisted. Reviews on Amazon from other parents detail similar findings, with some sharing photos of black mold inside the toys. Mold can cause health issues, and experts recommend cleaning toys with vinegar, the dishwasher, or boiling water to prevent mold growth.

Ricki Lake's ex-husband, Christian Evans, passed away on February 11, 2024, after battling bipolar disorder. Lake revealed his struggles with the illness in an emotional Instagram post on February 14, sharing a photo of herself with Evans and expressing her love for him. Married for two years, Lake and Evans had eloped in 2012 and divorced in 2015 due to Evans's mental health issues, though they continued their relationship until recently. Lake emphasizes the importance of recognizing and treating bipolar disorder and honors Evans's memory by planning to scatter his ashes on their favorite beach.

China has demonstrated its ability to manipulate internet traffic, redirecting 15% of global internet traffic through its servers for 18 minutes in April, according to a report by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. This incident affected traffic to and from U.S. government and military sites, as well as commercial entities. While China denied intentional manipulation, the report suggests the potential for malicious use. The incident highlights the fragility of the internet and the need for improved security measures to protect U.S. interests.

Iowa state legislator Henry Rayhons faces a complex legal dilemma after being charged with sexually abusing his wife Donna, who was living in a nursing home with Alzheimer’s. The case highlights the challenges in determining consent when one party lacks the mental capacity to make decisions. Donna’s daughters, who became concerned about their mother’s well-being, moved her to a nursing home, where she reportedly had interactions with Rayhons that raised suspicions. The prosecution argues Rayhons had intercourse with his wife when she was unable to consent due to her dementia. However, Rayhons maintains he had a loving and consensual relationship with Donna. The case raises questions about the legal framework for handling such situations and the nuances of consent in the context of dementia.

Steven Avery, the subject of the Netflix series "Making a Murderer," has filed a wide-ranging appeal claiming authorities used an improper warrant and that a juror was out to get him, among other issues. The appeal, filed in an appeals court in Madison, includes numerous spelling and grammar errors and doesn't list Avery's new attorney. Manitowoc County Sheriff Robert Hermann hasn't seen the appeal but has previously stated the investigation was proper. Avery's new attorney, Kathleen Zellner, hasn't commented. The appeal argues that evidence from an improper search should be excluded and that a juror tainted others. It also claims Judge Angela W. Sutkiewicz made misleading statements and that Avery's lawyers were ineffective. Avery, 53, has been serving a life sentence for the 2005 murder of photographer Teresa Halbach, and his nephew, Brendan Dassey, is serving life as an accessory. South Korea approved a plan to send $8 million in humanitarian aid to North Korea, despite concerns from China, the United States, and Japan. The aid, to be distributed through UNICEF and the World Food Programme, aims to support children and pregnant women. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi warned that the situation on the Korean peninsula was getting more serious and called for calm. North Korea's foreign minister, Ri Yong-ho, dismissed Trump's threats, comparing them to "the sound of a barking dog." The aid decision, following new UN sanctions against North Korea, could affect President Moon Jae-in's approval rating. Trump is set to meet with Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and South Korean President Moon Jae-in, with North Korea expected to be a key topic.

Loretta Lynch, President Obama's nominee for attorney general, faced a rigorous confirmation hearing before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Despite her strong background as a federal prosecutor, she navigated a series of questions on controversial issues, including immigration and the Justice Department’s policies. Lynch maintained a stance of independence from the White House, emphasizing her commitment to upholding the rule of law. She faced tough questioning from Republican senators, particularly on immigration, but also on issues like the National Security Agency’s surveillance programs and the Obama administration’s executive actions. Democrats defended Lynch’s nomination, arguing that her confirmation should be based on her qualifications rather than the administration’s policies. Lynch’s hearing highlighted the ongoing tensions between the Justice Department and Congress, especially regarding issues like minority communities and law enforcement. Her responses, while careful, showed a determination to forge a new path as attorney general.

President Donald Trump's relationship with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell faces new challenges after Alabama's Senate race. Republican Roy Moore, who used McConnell as a campaign target, defeated Luther Strange, a candidate backed by Trump. This loss, coupled with McConnell's decision to abandon efforts to repeal Obamacare, has intensified criticism from Trump, who called McConnell "weak" during a private dinner with conservative activists. The defeat could also impact McConnell’s ability to secure legislative victories, as Trump may seek support from Democrats when needed. Despite the setback, personal loyalty to McConnell remains high among his colleagues, who credit him with securing Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch. The result highlights the ongoing tension between Trump and McConnell, with Trump's base believing he had little genuine affinity for Strange and more for Moore.

A new study suggests that older adults perform better on cognitive tasks in the morning compared to the afternoon. Researchers from the Rotman Research Institute at Baycrest Health Sciences and the University of Toronto found that older adults are more focused and better able to ignore distractions in the morning. This improved performance correlates with greater activation of the brain's attentional control regions, similar to younger adults. The study, published in the journal Psychology and Aging, involved 16 younger adults (aged 19-30) and 16 older adults (aged 60-82) who participated in memory tests between 1:00 and 5:00 p.m. Older adults tested in the morning were 10% more likely to focus on the distracting information and showed similar brain activity to younger adults. The researchers recommend scheduling mentally challenging tasks for morning to optimize performance.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford's refusal to resign over admitted drug use has left Toronto's City Council grappling with how to govern without him. Despite mounting pressure, Ford continues to defy calls for him to step aside, even as he signs bobblehead dolls for charity. Councilors are considering motions to limit his powers, but face challenges in removing him legally. Ford's core supporters remain loyal, but his political leverage has diminished. His actions and statements, including a recent war veteran refusing to shake his hand, highlight the ongoing controversy. Councilors are concerned about the impact on governance, particularly regarding public transit projects. Ford's defiance and the council's efforts to isolate him underscore the complex political landscape in Toronto.

Professor Will Brooker, from Kingston University, is immersing himself in the life and work of David Bowie for a year to better understand the pop icon. Brooker, who is writing a monograph on Bowie, adopts the singer's eating habits, outfits, and even listens only to music Bowie listened to. He plans to visit places significant to Bowie and watch films that influenced him. Brooker, who has already experienced Bowie's 1960s and 1970s personas, is next heading to Berlin. His goal is to inhabit Bowie's headspace at different points in his career while maintaining a critical perspective. He has replicated Bowie's eating and drinking habits, including consuming only red peppers and milk, and is learning to sing key Bowie songs. Brooker's project, while unusual, aims to provide unique insights into Bowie's creative process and personal life.

A 32-year-old woman, Cherie Amoore, has been charged with kidnapping after abducting a 7-week-old baby from the King of Prussia Mall. Amoore, who claimed to be pregnant, approached the baby's mother and engaged in conversation, eventually taking the baby from his stroller. The baby was found safe a few hours later, but Amoore was charged with multiple offenses including kidnapping and false imprisonment. Amoore expressed confusion over her actions, stating she never intended to steal a baby. Surveillance footage and tips from the public helped locate Amoore and the baby. The ordeal left the baby's mother, Malika Hunter, shaken and fearful for her children's safety.

The U.S. Embassy in Moscow faced restricted access to a recreational property on the outskirts of Moscow, as Russia blocked entry and closed a warehouse in a southern industrial area. This move is part of Russia's response to U.S. Congress approval of new sanctions against Moscow. Russia also ordered the U.S. to reduce its diplomatic staff by over 700. The U.S. Embassy complained of not being allowed access for two days, while a Russian official blamed the Americans for failing to obtain necessary permits. The incident reflects ongoing tensions between the two countries over alleged interference in the 2016 U.S. election and new sanctions.

A 53-year-old Arizona man has been arrested for leaving his five-year-old granddaughter alone in the desert with a loaded and cocked .45-caliber handgun, instructing her to "shoot any bad guys," authorities say. Paul Armand Rater was booked into the Fourth Avenue Jail in Phoenix on suspicion of two counts of felony child abuse and one count of felony child endangerment. Deputies say Rater and the child left their home in Buckeye, about 30 miles west of Phoenix, in a pickup truck early Sunday afternoon. Four hours later, the girl was found in the desert by her mother and an off-duty firefighter, holding the gun. Rater told deputies he left the girl under a tree because she was complaining she could not walk anymore, after the vehicle broke down. He admitted to leaving the girl with the gun while he went for drinks and a cheeseburger. The child was returned to her mother, and state child welfare authorities were alerted.

A shipwreck discovered off the coast of Texas, about 150 miles away, has been explored using robotic submarines. Artifacts retrieved include muskets, cannon, clothing, and a bottle of yellow ginger, suggesting the ship sank around 1800. The wreckage, situated 3000 feet below the surface, has attracted various sea life. Scientists from Texas A&M Galveston and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration are coordinating the salvage operation from a control room on land, using satellite communication to direct underwater robots. The shipwreck, believed to be from the early 1800s, may have been a warship or cargo vessel, possibly supporting the Mexican army during Texas' fight for independence. The exploration aims to uncover more clues about the ship's origin and purpose.

A fast-spreading brush fire north of Los Angeles forced hundreds of people to evacuate their homes on Friday and Saturday, as firefighters struggled against triple-digit temperatures and erratic winds to contain the blaze. The wildfire, named the La Tuna Fire, grew to over 5,000 acres within a day, threatening about 300 homes in Burbank, 250 in Glendale, and 180 in Los Angeles. By Saturday, the fire was 10% contained, with one home destroyed. Erratic winds and canyons posed significant challenges. Despite the efforts of over 1,000 firefighters, including those from Houston, the fire remained dynamic and difficult to control. The ongoing severe heat wave and strong gusts worsened the situation. Rain on Sunday brought moisture but also strong winds, complicating firefighting efforts.

Sears' largest shareholder, Edward Lampert, has proposed selling the company's Kenmore appliance brand and home improvement business to his hedge fund, ESL Investments, to raise cash and improve Sears' financial position. The proposal aims to unlock the value of these assets and provide liquidity to the struggling retailer. ESL Investments has offered a non-binding indication of interest to acquire the Kenmore and home improvement businesses for an enterprise value of $500 million. The deal would also include the potential sale of Sears' real estate, with ESL willing to assume $1.2 billion in debt obligations. Lampert believes that pursuing these divestitures will demonstrate the value of Sears' portfolio and help the company transform to better compete in the retail market.

Senate Democratic leaders are delaying debate on a comprehensive climate change bill until spring, citing economic concerns and the upcoming midterm elections. Key committee chairmen, including Max Baucus and Jay Rockefeller, advocate for a cautious approach, while others like Barbara Boxer and John Kerry push for quicker action. The delay may provide time for the Obama administration to focus on financial regulatory reform and job creation. Despite the setback, White House officials maintain that addressing climate change is crucial for economic growth and reducing dependence on foreign oil. The timing of the climate bill is seen as a strategic move to avoid a potential backlash from voters in industrial states, while the administration continues to work on an international climate accord.

French lawmakers have approved a new law granting the state sweeping surveillance powers, despite criticism from civil society groups who liken it to the "French Patriot Act." The bill, which passed with 438 votes in favor and 86 against, aims to prevent Islamist attacks and update surveillance techniques to modern communications technology. However, critics argue it threatens civil liberties and gives too much power to the state. The law will now be reviewed by the Senate.

Apple has reversed its policy, allowing marijuana-related apps in the App Store after previously removing them, at least for apps geo-restricted to states where marijuana is legal. The change comes as weed tech companies face challenges navigating Apple's App Store policies, which have been described as arbitrary and stifling the growth of the marijuana industry. MassRoots, an online community for marijuana users, was one of the apps that had been removed but is now back in the App Store. Other apps and companies in the marijuana tech sector are pushing for Apple to clarify and soften its policies, citing concerns over free speech and the potential to hinder the industry's growth.

Sienna Miller and fiancé Tom Sturridge, 26, welcomed their first child, a daughter, in London over the weekend. The couple, who have been dating for over a year, kept their pregnancy under wraps for several months before Miller, 30, revealed her engagement and pregnancy to British Vogue in April. The new addition will be second in line to her older brother, Mason, but is the first little girl for the famous couple. Scott Disick, 29, is also overjoyed, having passed on his fashion sense to his new baby girl. Kourtney Jenner, 33, gave birth naturally to a 7-pound, 14-ounce baby girl, with both parents and family expressing their joy.

Apple's cash pile topped $200 billion, with nearly 90% held offshore, pressuring CEO Tim Cook to find ways to use the funds without incurring U.S. taxes. Booming iPhone sales have fueled the cash hoard, adding to the pressure on Cook to return capital to shareholders. Apple advocates for U.S. tax reform to allow repatriation of overseas funds. The company's overseas cash has climbed 70% since 2013, now making up 89% of its total cash and investments. Apple's lobbying spending has increased, with a record $4.1 million in 2015. Activist investor Carl Icahn has called for Apple to return more cash to shareholders. Apple's tax strategy includes using offshore affiliates and lobbying for tax reform.

Sherri Papini, a 34-year-old mother of two from Redding, California, was found alive early Thanksgiving morning after going missing three weeks prior. She was located near Interstate 5 in Yolo County, bound with restraints, and was able to flag down a passing driver. Her husband, Keith, was immediately notified and reunited with her at a hospital. The Shasta County Sheriff's Office is searching for two armed Hispanic women driving a dark-colored SUV, based on Papini's description. Although she was injured, the extent of her injuries is not disclosed. Her sister, Sheila Koester, expressed relief and gratitude for the community's support. Koester stated that Papini is in a very emotional state and needs time with her family. The case remains under investigation, with more than 400 tips received but no arrests made.

Belgian authorities are searching for a top suspect in the country's deadliest attacks in decades, as Brussels awoke under guard and with limited public transport after 34 were killed in bombings at the Brussels airport and a subway station. Police circulated a photo of three men seen in the airport, suspecting their involvement in Tuesday's attacks. Belgian state broadcaster RTBF has identified two of the attackers as brothers Khalid and Brahim Bakraoui, who are believed to have blown themselves up. The third man is at large and has not been identified. A suicide bomber who attacked the Brussels airport left a written statement that has been discovered near an apartment where a taxi picked him up, according to the Belgian prosecutor’s office. The note included mentions of "being in a rush," "no longer knowing what to do," and that if he takes too much time, he risks finishing his life "next to him" in a jail cell.
