LulzSec announced its retirement after fifty days of hacking, releasing a data dump from various targets including AOL, AT&T, Battlefield Heroes, FBI, Hackforums.net, NATO-bookshop.org, US Navy, and several corporate office networks. The group's final statement suggests they are moving on, leaving behind inspiration, fear, and other emotions. Despite plans for an ongoing campaign, LulzSec now hopes to inspire a broader AntiSec movement. The data dump includes technical documents, user details, and internal company information, raising questions about the group's true intentions and whether they are on the run from law enforcement.

Sen. Rand Paul is seeking a bill in Kentucky to allow him to run for both the U.S. Senate and president in 2016, potentially hedging his bets. Kentucky Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer is considering the legislation, which would clarify a state law currently preventing candidates from running for two offices simultaneously. Thayer says Paul brought the issue to the Republican caucus last month. If the bill passes, it would allow Paul to run for both offices, though a Democratic-controlled House may block it. Paul has not officially announced his presidential intentions but is seen as a frontrunner.

A Tennessee high school student named Emily Gipson was given a two-day in-school suspension for posting an anti-bullying video critical of her school's administration. The video, titled "Welcome to Lebanon High School," gained nearly 600,000 views on YouTube after being posted on January 22. In the video, Gipson criticizes her peers and school officials, stating that "smiles are fake" and "suicide prevention is something to laugh at." She also accuses the school of not taking bullying seriously, saying, "Creativity is put down, where the people who make fun of others never get punished." Principal Scott Walters defended the punishment, attributing it to Gipson recording the video in a classroom without permission. However, Gipson's grandfather and guardian expressed pride in her for speaking out on a sensitive issue. Gipson responded by posting another video titled "Have I Made a Difference Yet?" encouraging other students to speak up.

The value of body parts in workers' compensation varies significantly by state, as illustrated by the cases of Jeremy Lewis and Josh Potter. Both men, married with young children and with similar tattoos, lost portions of their left arms in industrial accidents. Lewis, working in Alabama, received $45,000, while Potter, working in Georgia, could receive over $740,000 over his lifetime. Alabama’s benefits for amputations are among the lowest in the nation, leading to stark differences in outcomes for identical injuries. This disparity highlights the geographic lottery that governs compensation for workplace injuries in America, where states independently determine their own benefits with no federal minimums. The article also explores the historical and political factors behind these varied benefit schedules, revealing a complex and often unfair system that affects the lives of injured workers and their families.

Former Wells Fargo employees and customers are alleging a pattern of unethical practices and retaliation. Siham El-Dahan, a former business banker, reported her managers' favoritism, denied breaks, and threats to meet sales quotas. She claims she was fired in retaliation for complaining, citing a customer loan default as the reason. El-Dahan believes the firings were part of a system to silence whistleblowers. Frank Ahn, a convenience store owner, says Wells Fargo opened multiple unwanted accounts for him, despite his protests. He eventually had most fees reversed but found it difficult to switch banks due to his business's reliance on the account. Both El-Dahan and Ahn's experiences highlight issues of unethical behavior and potential retaliation within Wells Fargo.

An Indian marine engineer named Saddam, whose grandfather chose his name with hopes of positive outcomes, now faces significant challenges due to his namesake of the former Iraqi dictator. After graduating second in his batch from Tamil Nadu’s Noorul Islam University in 2014, Saddam has struggled to find employment with multinational shipping companies, with each of the 40 interviews ending in rejection. He has learned that his name is a deterrent, as potential employers fear operational complications, especially with frequent international travel. Changing his name legally to Sajid has been a complex process, with his educational certificates needing updates, leading to a court hearing to expedite the name change. Saddam feels he is an innocent victim of a historical figure's legacy, highlighting the ongoing impact of namesakes even decades after the original person's execution.

Emmis Digital held a "Hunger Games"-themed social media contest to select interns, pitting 25 applicants against each other over two weeks. The finalists, Jake Bouvy and Kelsey Halverson, both won the internship, combining their strengths in social media and creativity. This unconventional method highlights the increasing importance of digital skills and social media presence in job hunting. Companies are increasingly using social media to engage with potential employees and gauge their abilities beyond traditional applications.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, missing for over 60 hours, continues with no definitive evidence of the plane's location. Nine countries are involved in the extensive search across a vast area of the South China Sea. Malaysian officials remain puzzled by the plane's sudden disappearance, considering various theories including hijacking, and are investigating every angle. Two passengers were identified as using stolen passports, one Italian and one Austrian, raising concerns about security measures. Despite several reports of possible debris sightings, none have been confirmed. The search area has been expanded, and officials are urging patience and understanding from families of the 239 passengers on board.

For the first time in 146 years, Chicago recorded no snow on the ground in January and February, a record that some celebrated while others worried about climate change. The National Weather Service documented no snow on the ground on January 30 and February 25 due to small amounts that melted. However, severe storms brought large hail, winds, localized flooding, and tornadoes, with a tornado in Ottowa killing one person. More stormy weather was forecast for the week, including possible snow. Meteorologists linked the snowless period to climate change, noting that unusual weather events may become more common. The lack of snow affected trees, insects, and animals, potentially leading to economic damage for fruit growers. Despite the record, the overall effect on people was generally positive, with lower heating bills and increased outdoor activities.

Queen Elizabeth II emphasized the importance of family and friendship in her annual Christmas message, recorded before Prince Philip's hospitalization. The royal family attended a Christmas service at St. Mary's church on the Sandringham estate, with Prince Philip remaining in hospital recovering from a heart procedure. The Queen, dressed in a lavender coat, led the way into the church, followed by Prince Charles and Camilla. Prince William, Kate, and Prince Harry also attended the service. After the service, children gave the queen bouquets of flowers, which she handed to her granddaughters. The royal family then returned to the house for lunch. The Queen's message will focus on family and community, marking the rare occasion when she voices her own opinion without government consultation.

Thieves broke into a Parisian cellar using the city's extensive underground tunnel network and stole 300 bottles of fine wine worth €250,000 (£230,500) from a private residence near the Luxembourg gardens. The thieves drilled a hole through the cellar wall and then navigated the catacombs, a maze of tunnels beneath Paris. Police speculate that the thieves likely made multiple visits to plan the precise location of the hole. The 3rd District of the Parisian Criminal investigation department is handling the case. The catacombs, home to an estimated six million human remains, are a popular spot for thrill-seekers and parties, despite being off-limits.

Two men in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, are facing charges for allegedly operating a citywide prostitution ring involving multiple women, some possibly as young as 15. The investigation began after police received complaints of increased prostitution activity in the city, primarily centered around certain streets. One of the men, Randy Lambach, allegedly recruited women with drug addictions, photographed them, and advertised their services online. Lambach would set up meetings and collect fees, often taking a significant cut or paying in drugs. He also transported the women to appointments and threatened them if they tried to stop working. The other man, Joseph Van Wert, allowed some meetings to take place in his apartment in exchange for drugs and cash. Both men are charged with human trafficking and related offenses, with Van Wert also facing additional charges. The investigation is ongoing, and more charges may be filed.

A woman accused of killing her twin sister by driving their SUV off a cliff in Hawaii is fighting extradition from New York. Alexandria Duval, 38, was arrested in Albany and faces a second-degree murder charge in Hawaii. Duval's attorney argues the case is not strong enough for extradition. The sisters, known as Alison and Ann Dadow before changing their names, were involved in a tragic accident in May 2016 when their SUV plunged 200 feet off a cliff, with Anastasia Duval dying at the scene. Alexandria Duval was initially released on bail but was later re-arrested after a grand jury indicted her. An extradition hearing is scheduled for December 16.

A 21-year-old Army National Guard combat medic was shot several times during a burglary attempt at her home in Charlotte, North Carolina. Reco Latur Dawkins Jr., 23, was charged with attempted murder, felony breaking and entering, and conspiracy after turning himself in to the police. Semantha Bunce, who was feeding her baby when the intruders broke in, managed to shoot the intruders before they fled. The baby was not injured. Friends and family have established a GoFundMe page to help with Bunce's medical bills and other expenses. Dawkins has a history of breaking and entering charges. The incident has raised concerns in the neighborhood about crime.

A father mistakenly shot and killed his 14-year-old son, Georta Mack, at their home in East Price Hill, Cincinnati, thinking the teen was an intruder. The shooting occurred around 6:30 a.m. Tuesday when the father, who had dropped Georta off at the school bus stop, heard a noise in the basement and grabbed a handgun to investigate. Upon startling the teen, the father accidentally shot Georta in the neck. The boy was rushed to Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center but was pronounced dead shortly after 8:15 a.m. Police are investigating the incident and interviewing the father, who has been cooperative. The father's name has not been released. Cincinnati Police Chief Eliot Isaac called the shooting a "terrible, terrible tragedy" and emphasized the importance of gun safety in the home.

A Baltimore mother caught on video smacking her 16-year-old son repeatedly after finding him at a riot expressed her concern for his future. Toya Graham, a single mother of six, said she was only trying to protect her son from becoming another Freddie Gray. Graham, seen pulling her masked son away from a protest crowd and hitting him, told CBS News that her son knew he was in trouble and wanted to run when he saw her. She emphasized her strict parenting style, stating, "I'm a no-tolerant mother. Everybody who knows me, knows I don't play that." The incident drew attention from Baltimore Police Commissioner Anthony Batts, who praised Graham's actions. Commissioner Batts noted that many of the rioters were local high school students. At least 20 police officers were injured, and one person was critically hurt in a fire during the violence, which led to 235 arrests, including 34 juveniles. The National Guard was deployed,

British Prime Minister Theresa May narrowly survived a confidence vote from her Conservative party on Wednesday, with 117 lawmakers voting against her leadership. The vote came after May cancelled a parliamentary vote on her Brexit deal, which had faced significant opposition. May promised to step down before the 2022 election but said she would stay on to deliver Brexit. The outcome left her party deeply divided, with hardline Brexit supporters calling for her resignation. May faces a no-confidence vote if she loses the support of 159 Conservative MPs, with the result expected to shape the future of Brexit negotiations.

The Mo Ibrahim prize for African leadership did not award a winner this year, marking the second consecutive year with no recipient. The prize, valued at $5 million over 10 years plus an additional $200,000 annually for life, requires candidates to have governed well, raised living standards, and voluntarily left office. Committee member Salim Ahmed Salim stated that no candidate met the stringent criteria. Previous winners include Botswana's Festus Mogae, Mozambique's Joaquim Chissano, and Cape Verde's Pedro Verona Pires. Mo Ibrahim emphasized the importance of maintaining high standards, stating that compromising on the prize criteria would undermine its credibility.

The estranged wife of acclaimed concert pianist Vadym Kholodenko, Sofya Tsygankova, has been ruled mentally incompetent to stand trial for allegedly killing their two young daughters. Tsygankova, 32, charged with two counts of capital murder of a person under age 10, will be committed to a state mental health facility for 120 days of treatment, with the hope she will regain "a reasonable degree of rational understanding" to face justice. When Kholodenko arrived at his wife's home to pick up their daughters on March 17, he found Tsygankova covered in blood with cuts on her wrists and the two children dead in their beds. Tsygankova had visited a state mental health facility in Fort Worth a day before the incident. Kholodenko, 30, won the gold medal at the 14th Van Cliburn International Piano Competition in 201

At Alan Shephard Elementary School in Bourbonnais, IL, janitor Steve Weidner, known affectionately as "Mr. Steve," received an unexpected and enthusiastic welcome from students on the last day of school. On June 2, as students lined up to have him sign their yearbooks, the queue extended around the playground. The school reported that Weidner was both touched and amazed by the students' gesture, which quickly went viral on Reddit, garnering thousands of upvotes and comments.

A physics major at the University of Texas at Austin is suing to stop his expulsion based on an unproven accusation of sexual assault. The 21-year-old student, identified as John Doe, claims the encounter was consensual and argues the university is violating his due process rights. The alleged incident involved Doe having sex with two women after a night of heavy drinking. Doe's alleged victim later claimed she was unconscious during the encounter, but Doe maintains she was awake and involved. The case highlights the ongoing debate over how colleges handle sexual assault allegations, with critics arguing that accused students are often punished without sufficient evidence.

More than 100 former professional football players, including Jamal Anderson, Chris Doleman, and O.J. Santiago, have joined over 1,500 other players in lawsuits against the NFL, alleging that the league hid the dangers of concussions. The latest lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Atlanta, claims the NFL "repeatedly refuted the connection between concussions and brain injury" and failed to protect players from head injuries. The NFL has denied these allegations, stating that any claim of intentional misrepresentation is without merit. The lawsuit cites scientific studies linking concussions to chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a neurodegenerative disease diagnosed only after death. The case adds to similar lawsuits already consolidated for trial in Philadelphia, though a specific date has not been set. Former Green Bay Packer Dorsey Levens, who filed suit in December 2011, highlights the lack of awareness about long-term consequences during his playing days

A young mother from Pleasant Grove has been indicted for her newborn baby's heroin addiction, which required intensive care. Alexandra Nicole Laird, 21, faces a Class B felony charge of chemical endangerment of a child. Laird was initially arrested in 2015 and has remained free on bond. Her daughter was born in 2015 with opiates and amphetamines in her system and spent a month in the ICU. Laird admitted to using heroin weekly during her pregnancy. She is now pregnant again and back in custody on another child endangerment charge. Police argue that Laird's drug use endangers the unborn child.

India's top court has ruled that adultery is no longer a criminal offense, declaring the colonial-era law unconstitutional and discriminatory against women. A five-judge bench unanimously agreed that the law, which carries a maximum five-year prison sentence, is outdated and deprives women of agency. The court emphasized that "husband is not the master," quoting John Stuart Mill. Justice Indu Malhotra highlighted that the time when wives were invisible to the law has ended. This decision comes after the court recently decriminalized homosexuality, marking a series of socially progressive rulings. Some advocates view these decisions as acts of decolonizing India's criminal code. However, critics argue that the law serves as a deterrent against men abandoning their families, especially in areas where women have little power. The ruling is part of a broader trend of the court overturning archaic laws, including a 157-year-old law criminalizing gay sex.

A policy intended to ensure minority representation in class elections at a Mississippi middle school has led to segregated positions, with only white students eligible for class president in certain years. The practice, which has been in place for 30 years, has sparked controversy and outrage, particularly from a mother of mixed-race children who was informed her daughter could not run for class reporter due to her race. The Nettleton School District has since announced it will no longer use race in school elections, acknowledging the need to reflect the diverse student body. The changes may have come too late for some families, as the mother moved her children to another district. The situation highlights ongoing racial complexities and the challenges of achieving true equality in schools.

President Donald Trump announced Tuesday that the United States is withdrawing from the Iran nuclear deal, citing the agreement as "defective at its core" and threatening to impose "the highest level" of sanctions on Iran. Trump's decision, reversing a landmark pact seen as Obama's foreign policy achievement, raises concerns that Iran might resume its nuclear weapons program. The move also prompts questions about Iran's response and its impact on North Korea's willingness to denuclearize. Critics argue the decision is misguided and harmful to America's standing. Trump's announcement comes amid heightened tensions, with Israel on high alert and Iran preparing a televised response. The U.S. withdrawal leaves a significant gap in international negotiations, as Trump seeks to force a new deal with Iran abandoning its ballistic missile development and funding of terrorist groups.

The Trump administration has instructed officials at the Environmental Protection Agency to freeze its grants and contracts, a move that could affect everything from state-led climate research to localized efforts to improve air and water quality to environmental justice projects aimed at helping poor communities. An email went out to employees in the agency’s Office of Acquisition Management within hours of President Trump’s inauguration, instructing them to temporarily suspend all contract and grant awards, including task orders and work assignments. It is unclear whether the freeze is indefinite or temporary as the agency transitions fully to the new administration. The freeze could impact a significant part of the agency’s budget allocations and threaten to disrupt core operations. The move is likely to increase anxieties inside an already tense agency, as the incoming administration’s officials have made no secret of their goal of greatly reducing the EPA’s footprint and regulatory reach.

Eliot Spitzer faced two libel lawsuits totaling $90 million from former Marsh & McLennan executives over a column he wrote in Slate.com defending his own enforcement actions against the company. The column, published three months after a judge overturned the executives’ felony antitrust convictions, was seen as defamatory by the plaintiffs, who claimed Spitzer inaccurately portrayed their roles in the company’s alleged misconduct. Spitzer, former New York Governor and New York Attorney General, faced accusations of recklessly disregarding facts in his writing, while his critics argued that his statements were necessary to uphold justice and ethical standards in the marketplace. The lawsuits highlight the ongoing tensions between corporate leaders and regulators in the aftermath of the financial crisis.

Three men, including a sheriff's deputy, were arrested in York County after a major drug bust where 247 pounds of marijuana, valued at around $2 million, and $11,000 in cash were seized. Christopher Heath, 37, a drug task force agent with the Yuba County Sheriff’s Department, and Ryan Falsone, 27, and Tyler Long, 31, both from California, were charged with delivery of marijuana, criminal conspiracy to deliver marijuana, and possession with intent to deliver marijuana. The arrest was part of an ongoing investigation based on tips, and Heath had his badge and service weapon on him at the time of his arrest. The men were out on bail and the investigation is ongoing, with possible additional federal charges.

Joe Jackson, the father and early manager of the Jackson family, has died at 89 after a battle with cancer, reports CNN. Jackson launched the careers of his sons Michael and Janet, as well as The Jackson 5, in the 1960s. He managed the family's careers and was known for being strict, even disciplining his children physically. Despite criticism, Jackson believed his methods helped his children achieve success and avoid trouble. Jackson's daughter Janet honored him at a Radio Disney Music Awards, praising his role in her life. Joe Jackson was married to Katherine for over 60 years, though they lived apart for decades.

The Senate confirmed Sally Jewell as the next Interior Secretary, voting 87-11. Jewell, CEO of outdoor retailer REI, will oversee federal lands for recreation, conservation, and energy use, managing 500 million acres of national parks and 1 billion acres offshore. A former petroleum engineer and banker, Jewell promised to balance conflicting land uses. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chairman Ron Wyden praised her ability to bring people together. Jewell will replace Ken Salazar, who announced his departure in January.

A new study suggests that the founding population of Easter Island, known for its towering stone statues, may have had a more complex and collaborative society than previously believed. By analyzing the chemical makeup of stone tools used to carve the statues, researchers found evidence of cooperation among families and craft groups. The tools, made of volcanic basalt, were sourced from a single quarry complex, indicating that the people worked together to produce the statues. This challenges the long-held theory that the islanders destroyed their own society through infighting and resource depletion. While the society later faced decimation by colonists and slavery, the study highlights the sophisticated nature of the Rapa Nui people and their ability to collaborate on a large scale.

Alan Rickman's portrayal of Professor Snape in the Harry Potter films is widely regarded as one of his most iconic roles. Initially cast as a villain, Rickman's nuanced performance transformed Snape into a complex character with hidden depths and a tragic backstory. Rickman had to keep key information about Snape's true nature from the filmmakers and cast, including the producers and directors. He once revealed that J.K. Rowling provided him with a "little piece of information" that significantly influenced his performance, though she did not disclose the end of the story. Rickman's dedication to the role earned him widespread admiration, with his character's journey from antagonist to hero leaving a lasting impact on fans. He passed away at 69 after a battle with cancer.

Taller individuals face a slightly increased risk of cancer, according to new research. For every 10 cm over the average height, the risk of developing any cancer increases by about 10%. This aligns with previous studies showing a link between height and various health issues, including heart problems and diabetes. Leonard Nunney, a biologist at the University of California, Riverside, analyzed large cancer databases and found that taller people have more cells, which can accumulate mutations leading to cancer. The risk is more pronounced in women, with taller women 12% more likely to develop cancer compared to shorter women. Men are 9% more likely. Colon and kidney cancer show the strongest correlation. While the risk is small, it suggests that the sheer number of cells is a key factor. Other factors, such as growth hormones or environmental influences, may play a role in specific cancers like thyroid and melanoma, but the primary driver appears to be the number of cells. Heavy rains returned Sunday night, forcing a series of evacuations in parts of west and central Harris County. Flash flood watches were in effect, with up to 15 to 25 inches of additional rainfall possible over several days, potentially exacerbating already catastrophic flooding. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began releasing water from the Addicks and Barker reservoirs, which could affect thousands of homes. Voluntary evacuations were issued for areas near Cypress Creek, Inverness Forest, and McDade Estates. Fort Bend County also ordered mandatory evacuations for low-lying regions near the Brazos River. Residents were advised to leave by Monday morning to avoid being trapped by rising waters.

In real life, it's sedans and pick-ups that are most stolen, not the exotic cars from movies, reports ABC News. The Honda Accord has topped the list of most stolen and recovered vehicles for the fifth consecutive year, according to LoJack, a worldwide tracking and recovery system company. This reliability and longevity make Accords a popular target for thieves, who can sell parts for up to three times the vehicle's value. While the Accord is the most stolen, other common makes include the Honda Civic, Toyota Camry, and Toyota Corolla.

Residents of a Chinese village in Guangdong province appear to be nearing a compromise with local authorities after a nearly two-week standoff. The villagers, who have been protesting land seizures and the death of their negotiator in police custody, say some demands have been met in a meeting with a senior official. Villagers had planned a march through police barriers but instead met with officials who agreed to release three detained village leaders and return one development project's land. The situation in Wukan has attracted attention due to its scale, with thousands of protests over land grabs occurring in China each year.

Nearly a month after some SAT tests disappeared, Loudoun County school officials say the missing tests were found in a cart at the same school where students took the test. The 236 answer sheets were discovered at Broad Run High School in Ashburn, Virginia, at the bottom of a cart in the same package they were supposed to be delivered to UPS. The tests were hand-carried to the College Board in Princeton, New Jersey, and it looks like they will be validated. Over 200 students in Loudoun County are relieved as they will not have to retake the exam. Initially, administrators thought UPS had carried the tests out of the building, but video surveillance showed otherwise. A mix-up occurred when the boxes were moved from the school’s guidance office to the shipping area, leading to the tests being left behind. The school system will conduct an investigation into the loss of the tests and review how it handles the delivery of tests.

Just believing you had a good night's sleep can boost your cognitive abilities, according to a new study from Colorado College. Participants were told they had either above-average or below-average quality sleep, even though the sleep measurements were fabricated. Those informed they slept well performed better on attention and memory tests, suggesting the power of a positive mindset can enhance cognitive function.

Amarillo aviation enthusiasts captured images of what they believe to be a mystery aircraft, sparking interest in potential new military technology. On March 10, 2014, Steve Douglass and Dean Muskett, along with other photographers, noticed contrails of three high-flying aircraft at Amarillo International Airport. Initially thinking the planes were B-2s, they later realized the aircraft had a unique, boomerang-like shape with a trailing edge that didn't match the B-2's distinctive "W" back. Aviation expert Bill Sweetman and the Aviation Week team investigated the photos, concluding they likely show a real, stealthy aircraft. Douglass reached out to Whiteman Air Force Base but received no response, leaving the identity of the planes a mystery. The incident has sparked speculation about potential new military projects or even hidden testing bases.

Cuba's National Assembly will elect a new president on Wednesday, marking a historic political transition. President Raul Castro plans to step down and hand over the office to a younger successor, with 57-year-old First Vice President Miguel Diaz-Canel Bermudez seen as the overwhelming favorite. The selection will install someone from outside the Castro family in the country's highest government office for the first time in nearly six decades. Diaz-Canel, known for his uncharismatic image, gained prominence as the top Communist Party official in central Villa Clara province. As head of the Communist Party, Fidel Castro will remain the most powerful person in Cuba. The transition aims to ensure the government's grip on power amid economic stagnation and increasing disenchantment among younger generations.

A 34-year-old Utah man, Samuel Shaffer, was convicted and sentenced to 15 years to life in prison for raping an 8-year-old girl, becoming the co-leader of a doomsday cult called the Knights of Crystal Blade. The sentence requires Shaffer to serve a minimum of 26 years. His co-leader, John Coltharp, also pleaded guilty to child sodomy and child bigamy, with his sentencing set for August. Shaffer and Coltharp were found to be married to each other's daughters. During a police investigation, two girls were found in a trailer and two in 50-gallon water barrels, all minors. The girls were in poor health due to the cold and lack of food and water.

An 82-year-old man, Masafumi Nagasaki, voluntarily lived as a castaway on Sotobanari island in the Yaeyama Islands, Okinawa Prefecture, Japan, for nearly three decades. He arrived in 1989 and lived a solitary life, eventually becoming known as the "naked hermit" in 2012 at 76 years old. Nagasaki, who worked as a photographer before his voluntary exile, found his remote island home after a flight over polluted seas prompted him to leave civilization. He lived without clothes, braving typhoons and insects, and maintained a strict daily routine of beach cleaning and exercise. His only contact with the outside world was a weekly trip to a nearby settlement for food and money from his family. Nagasaki's wish was to die on the island, feeling it was the perfect place to end his life. However, authorities removed him in April 2018, returning him

At least 36 people are presumed dead after a Japanese volcano erupted on Saturday, with toxic gases and ash forcing rescue efforts to halt on Monday. Five more bodies were found near the summit of Mount Ontake, bringing the total to 36 presumed dead, as reported by police. The search was abandoned due to an increase in toxic gases and ash. Eight bodies were airlifted off the mountain before work was called off around 1:30 p.m. The eruption, the first fatal one in modern times at the 3,067-meter peak, occurred as hundreds of hikers were enjoying a beautiful fall day. About 250 people were initially trapped on the slopes, but most managed to descend by Saturday night. Rescue operations were hindered by knee-deep ash and the smell of sulfur. The volcano, 210 kilometers west of Tokyo, erupted shortly before noon, sending large white plumes of gas and ash into the sky.

Three people were injured in a shooting inside Washington Square Mall in Indianapolis on Wednesday evening. A suspect, known to one of the victims, approached him and opened fire, while two other victims were hit by ricochet bullets. The suspect fled the scene, and no one was in custody. The victims, two men and a woman, were transported to hospitals with non-life-threatening injuries, though one was in serious condition. Police believe the incident was not random and that the suspect and victim had a prior relationship, though the nature of their interaction remains unclear. The mall was put on lockdown, and witnesses described a chaotic scene with people running for safety.

A Philadelphia transit worker who found $15,200 in cash and turned it in to police has been given the money since no one ever claimed it. Bob Tracey, a 62-year-old SEPTA worker, found a black bag containing dozens of $100 and $20 bills in the middle of the road last March. He immediately called police and turned the money in. Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood believed the money should have gone to Tracey if nobody claimed it. After more than a year, a judge ordered the money returned to Tracey. Although a couple of people claimed the money, they had no proof. The bag also contained drug paraphernalia, making it unlikely the real owners would come forward.

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a document pledging "to work toward complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" during a four-hour summit in Singapore. The meeting, which included frequent photo opportunities, marked the first face-to-face encounter between a sitting U.S. president and a North Korean leader. Trump described the summit as "better than anybody could have expected" and said he and Kim had "developed a very special bond." Kim stated they had "decided to leave the past behind." The joint statement did not define "security guarantees" or "complete denuclearization," leaving many details unclear. Trump promised to provide security assurances to North Korea and invited Kim to the White House. The summit provided a historic moment but raised concerns about the lack of substantive details on how denuclearization would proceed.

Eleven Secret Service agents and five military personnel are under investigation for bringing prostitutes back to their rooms at a hotel in Cartagena, Colombia, before President Obama arrived for an international summit. Rep. Peter King, chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, said the incident involved 11 agents, who were part of an advance team tasked with securing the hotel. The agents allegedly paid for sex with women who were presumed to be prostitutes, and a dispute over payment led to a disturbance that alerted local police. The Secret Service immediately launched an investigation and recalled the agents to Washington. President Obama's confidence in the Secret Service remains intact, according to White House spokesman Jay Carney, who said the incident was more of a distraction for the press than for the president. The scandal overshadowed Obama's diplomatic mission to Latin America and threatened to undermine efforts to focus on boosting economic ties. The military is also investigating five service members who may have been involved in misconduct, including violating curfew.

The Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences, facing criticism for its overwhelmingly older, male, and white membership, has invited 683 new members, nearly half of them women and 41% people of color, as part of a major overhaul. The list includes a diverse array of directors and actors, aiming to address the industry's ongoing diversity issues. With the hashtag #OscarsSoWhite gaining traction, the Academy has taken steps to double the number of women and people of color by 2020, making this the largest and most diverse class of invitees to date.

The beheading of American journalist James Foley by ISIS was confirmed through a graphic video uploaded to YouTube. Foley's parents received a final email from his captors, stating he would be executed as a result of US airstrikes in Iraq. The email, published by GlobalPost, included inflammatory rhetoric against the US government. Foley's captors also threatened the life of another American journalist, Steven Sotloff. The executioner, known as "Jihadi John," is believed to be a British citizen and a member of a small group of foreign fighters who guard ISIS's foreign hostages. Foley was singled out for harsh treatment due to his nationality. Pope Francis offered condolences to Foley's family, praising their son as a compassionate individual.

Rescue efforts in northern Thailand are racing against time and worsening weather conditions to extract 12 boys and their soccer coach from a flooded cave. A medical assessment concluded that the group is too weak to attempt a physically demanding escape. The Thai Navy SEALs are pumping water out of the cave complex, aiming to reduce water levels enough for the boys to walk or wade out. However, the boys, aged 11 to 16, and their 25-year-old coach are weak from malnutrition and lack of movement. They are being trained in scuba diving, but experts warn the route through narrow, flooded tunnels is too risky. The boys are currently huddled on a steep, muddy rock about 2.5 miles from the cave entrance. Water levels have dropped, allowing rescuers to walk through a 1.5 km stretch, but heavy rains are expected to start on Friday, potentially flooding the area where the boys are located. The California Supreme Court has reversed a ruling that ordered improved conditions for elephants at the Los Angeles Zoo, dealing a blow to animal advocates who argue the intelligent animals are mistreated. In 2012, a judge ordered the city to stop using bullhooks or electric shocks and to exercise elephants regularly. However, the high court ruled that a taxpayer action cannot be used to enforce violations of criminal law, invalidating the injunction against the city. The zoo defended its practices, stating it provides the highest level of care for its elephants.

A new study reveals that 260 million Americans cross structurally deficient bridges daily, highlighting the aging infrastructure crisis. At least 66,405 bridges, or 11% of the total, are classified as structurally deficient, needing significant maintenance or replacement. The Federal Highway Administration estimates repairs would cost $76 billion. These bridges are not necessarily unsafe but require attention to prevent future issues. The report comes after the collapse of a bridge in Washington state, emphasizing the urgency of addressing the aging infrastructure. Experts note that while the overall system is improving, the shift in responsibility from federal to state funding may impact repair efforts.

One of the four "Zebra Killers" convicted of racially motivated murders in San Francisco during the 1970s was found dead in his cell at San Quentin State Prison. J.C.X. Simon, 69, was pronounced dead late Thursday night. He was serving a life sentence with no possibility of parole. Simon and three other black men—Larry Green, Manuel Moore, and Jessie Lee Cooks—were convicted of a six-month killing spree targeting white victims, resulting in 14 deaths and seven injuries. The men were part of the Death Angels, an offshoot of the Fruit of Islam. Simon's death leaves three of the Zebra killers still incarcerated in separate California prisons.

Kim Kardashian, along with her sisters Kourtney and Khloé, and their mother Kris Jenner, have built a significant branding empire encompassing fashion, fitness, fragrances, and skincare products. Despite her controversial beginnings, Ms. Kardashian maintains a positive image, ranking alongside Snooki at the top of a celebrity loyalty index. Many consumers see her as an entrepreneur and a symbol of ethnic sex appeal, inspiring young women who seek to emulate her success. Her brand, largely created through her public exposure since 2007 on "Keeping Up With the Kardashians," thrives by allowing fans to project their own images onto her. She focuses on social media and direct fan engagement, creating products that reflect her followers' preferences. While her products may not be distinctive, they appeal to various consumer demographics, making her brand a success.

People who sleep for more than eight hours a day have an increased risk of stroke, according to a study from the University of Cambridge. The risk doubles for older people who consistently sleep longer than average. The study, published in the journal Neurology, followed nearly 10,000 people aged 42-81 over 9.5 years and found that those sleeping over eight hours had a 46% greater risk of stroke compared to those sleeping six to eight hours. Participants who reported consistently long sleep or a significant increase in sleep duration over the study period had an even higher risk. The association remained significant even after adjusting for other risk factors. The study, involving a meta-analysis of 11 other studies, supports these findings. However, the exact reasons behind the link are unclear, and further research is needed to understand the relationship between sleep and stroke risk.

Jonathan Butler, a graduate student at the University of Missouri, initiated a hunger strike to force the resignation of President Tim Wolfe, citing a series of racial incidents and a lack of action from university administrators. The football team and other faculty members joined the protest, leading to Wolfe's resignation and the announcement of new initiatives to address racial tensions. These include hiring a diversity officer, providing support for victims of discrimination, and requiring diversity training. The protest highlighted longstanding issues of racism and inequality on campus, with Butler emphasizing the need for a safer and more inclusive environment.

Matthew Weiner, creator of the critically acclaimed AMC drama "Mad Men," has signed a long-term deal with Lionsgate, ensuring he will continue running the show for two more seasons, with an option for a third, taking "Mad Men" through its seventh season. The deal, worth $30 million, one of the biggest payouts of its kind in cable television, comes after past seasons of "Mad Men" faced uncertainty when Weiner's contract expired last October. Despite AMC's insistence on budget cuts and additional commercial breaks, Weiner's new contract stipulates that cast members will not be cut for financial reasons, only for creative ones. Episodes will run 47 minutes for the first and last episodes of each season, with the rest at 45 minutes for television, but 47-minute versions will be available for digital formats. Weiner expressed gratitude for the support from fans and the agreement to support the artistic freedom of the show.

Nashville police continue to search for Travis Reinking, the suspect in a Waffle House shooting that killed four people and injured four others. Reinking, 29, was seen nearly naked and armed with an assault-style rifle. A customer named James Shaw Jr. wrestled the gun away from the suspect, preventing further casualties. Reinking, who has a history of mental health issues and past incidents involving firearms, was added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's Top 10 Most Wanted list. Multiple reports from Illinois detail his paranoid behavior and previous encounters with law enforcement. The victims include Taurean Sanderlin, DeEbony Groves, Akilah Dasilva, and Sharita Henderson. James Shaw Jr. suffered minor injuries in the confrontation.

Famed oceanographer Robert Ballard's team, working with the Navy and NOAA, has revealed the first images in over six decades of the USS Independence, a World War II aircraft carrier scuttled in 1951 off the California coast. The 20-hour expedition, streamed live to thousands of viewers worldwide, captured the carrier's flight deck, a Hellcat fighter plane, anti-aircraft guns, and other details. The Independence, 623 feet long, saw combat in Wake Island, Okinawa, and Leyte Gulf and was part of atomic tests at Bikini Atoll. Despite sustaining major damage in the tests, it was sunk in 1951. The ship's condition is better than expected, with the name still visible on the hull.
