A 18-year-old student, Vladislav Roslyakov, killed 20 people and wounded dozens at a vocational college in Kerch, Crimea, before taking his own life. The attack, described as the deadliest school shooting in Russia since 2004, left the city of Kerch in mourning. Crimean authorities, while searching for possible accomplices, have not revealed much about Roslyakov's background. The school had no security guards, and Roslyakov had recently obtained a shotgun permit. Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed globalization for the attack, citing similarities to US school shootings. The incident raised questions about school security and gun control in Russia.

A statue of a copper bull atop a restaurant in Hurricane, Utah, had its most prominent feature removed after causing community outrage. The owner, Stephen Ward, decided to take off the bull's oversized genitalia, stating he felt it didn't look right and wanted the sculpture to look better. Residents had complained to the city council, asking for the business license to be revoked. Ward clarified that he was not bowing to community pressure but was making the change for himself. The incident has brought more attention to the restaurant, with some customers coming in just to see the controversy. Ward plans to sue the city and a local bank teller who allegedly started a petition against his business license renewal.

Dennis Rodman led former NBA stars in singing "Happy Birthday" to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un before an exhibition basketball game in Pyongyang. Rodman, known for his "basketball diplomacy," dedicated the game to his "best friend" Kim and aimed to build cultural connections. The game featured Rodman and other ex-NBA players, including Kenny Anderson, Cliff Robinson, and Vin Baker, playing against North Korean teams. While the event was meant to be friendly, it drew criticism from U.S. officials and human rights groups, who questioned Rodman's visits to North Korea and his silence on Kenneth Bae, an American missionary held in the country. Rodman's comments during a CNN interview suggested he believed Bae was responsible for his own captivity, sparking outrage from Bae's family and U.S. representatives.

The Trump administration has rejected Turkey's proposal to link the release of American pastor Andrew Brunson with relief for a Turkish bank facing U.S. fines, setting the stage for increased pressure on Turkey to free Brunson. Brunson, held for nearly two years on charges of links to banned groups in Turkey, faces up to 35 years in prison if convicted. The U.S. has imposed sanctions and tariffs on Turkey, amid concerns over Turkey's treatment of Brunson. U.S. officials are considering further sanctions and delaying negotiations on the Turkish bank Halkbank until Brunson is freed, highlighting the worsening crisis between the two NATO allies.

Johnny Manziel's ex-girlfriend, Colleen Crowley, provided details of an alleged assault by the former Cleveland Browns quarterback, which occurred in the Dallas area early Saturday. Crowley claims Manziel struck her several times and appeared "on some kind of drugs" during their altercation. The NFL stated they began reviewing the incident when it happened. Manziel denied the allegations, saying, "It didn’t happen." The Dallas Police Department stated they conducted appropriate investigative follow-up and determined the incident to be closed, with no criminal complaint filed. This was the latest in a series of incidents involving Manziel, who is not expected to return to the Browns next season. The team's executive vice president, Sashi Brown, stated that Manziel's continual involvement in incidents undermines the organization's reputation.

Chelsea Clinton said Thursday that Donald Trump's description of the country as one where she can't imagine raising her children is "far more upsetting" than attacks on her mother. She believes Republican attacks on women, minorities, Muslims, and immigrants are worse than anything directed at Hillary Clinton. Chelsea, who recently gave birth to her second child, expressed hope that her mother's nomination would be overwhelming for her as a mother. She will introduce her mother at the Democratic National Convention, aiming to highlight her mother's resilience and fighting spirit. Chelsea also addressed the challenge of overcoming negative perceptions of her mother and the importance of unity, especially in light of Bernie Sanders supporters.

AmeriCares continues to support the treatment of Ebola patients and protect health workers in West Africa, focusing on rebuilding and strengthening the health system to improve access to healthcare and prevent future epidemics. Since the outbreak began in early 2014, the virus has killed over 11,000 people and infected more than 26,900, with many doctors and nurses contracting the disease. AmeriCares has provided critical supplies, trained health workers, and established treatment centers in Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea. Ongoing shipments of medical aid, including protective equipment and medicines, have been sent to more than 100 partners in West Africa. The organization also supports WFP’s food assistance efforts to prevent a health crisis from becoming a food crisis in affected areas.

Germany failed to persuade Hungary and other Central European countries to accept a quota of migrants, as Germany now expects 800,000 migrants this year. German Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier called the crisis the greatest challenge the EU has faced. Germany is keen to discuss not only those already in the country but a fair quota of distribution for those still on the way. However, Eastern and Central European countries, which have not been immigrant destinations, have criticized the idea and emphasized that immigration policy is a matter of national sovereignty. Hungary's Prime Minister Viktor Orban warned that his country would take an even harder line, and tougher laws on immigration go into effect soon. The UN gave qualified support to the EU's plan but said it was still insufficient. The situation continues to deteriorate in Macedonia, where authorities are struggling to cope with an increase in the number of migrants.

Mindy Kaling posted a video on Instagram while vacationing in Montana, seemingly hinting that all may not be lost for her show, The Mindy Project, after Fox announced its cancellation. The video shows Kaling smiling and winking at her followers, while the caption suggests she is checking in to see if anything is happening in Los Angeles. Shortly after Fox's announcement, Variety reported that Hulu was in talks to save the show for multiple seasons.

Newly discovered remains of a horse-sized dinosaur named Timurlengia euotica are providing insights into how Tyrannosaurus rex became Earth's top predator. Fossils found in northern Uzbekistan fill a 20-million-year gap in the tyrannosaur fossil record, showing that these dinosaurs developed their large body size rapidly towards the end of the age of dinosaurs. Timurlengia, about the size of a horse, had a big brain and keen senses, which allowed it to become a fast and intelligent hunter. This suggests that the ancestors of T. rex, like Timurlengia, were smaller but already had advanced brains and senses. Only after evolving these traits did tyrannosaurs grow into the colossal sizes of T. rex, indicating that intelligence preceded physical size in their evolution.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Tesla CEO Elon Musk are investigating a series of fires in Tesla Model S cars following road debris strikes. NHTSA opened a formal investigation into two fires in Washington and Tennessee, where battery fires resulted from undercarriage strikes. Tesla shares initially fell but recovered, closing up 3.7% for the day. In response, Musk announced higher ground clearance for the cars, asked for a full NHTSA investigation, and extended the warranty to cover fire damage. Musk defended the car's safety, citing zero injuries from fires and a lower fire risk compared to gasoline vehicles. He also updated the air suspension to increase ground clearance at highway speeds and gave drivers control over ride height transitions.

In the wake of a failed military coup attempt in Turkey, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan blamed the Gülen Movement, led by the exiled cleric Fethullah Gülen, for orchestrating the plot. The attempted coup, which involved tanks, helicopters, and attacks on government buildings, resulted in the deaths of at least 265 people, including 161 civilians and pro-government security forces. Erdoğan vowed to purge the military and other institutions of Gülen supporters. The U.S. expressed support for Turkey’s democratically elected government while maintaining that any extradition request for Gülen would need substantial evidence. As the situation unfolded, Turkey’s allies and adversaries condemned the coup and rallied behind the government. The Turkish military and security forces worked to quell the unrest, with thousands of military personnel arrested and judicial officials dismissed. The crisis highlighted the deep divisions within Turkey and the ongoing tensions between Erdoğan and the Gülen Movement.

An Alaska Bureau of Land Management employee captured a mysterious object moving in the Chena River, sparking speculation online. The 22-second video showed an icy, 12-15 foot long form swaying in the current, leading to theories ranging from a giant sturgeon to a sea monster. The Alaska Department of Fish and Game suggested a simpler explanation: frazil ice stuck to a rope caught on a bridge pier. Despite the disappointing reality, the video garnered over 600,000 views and highlighted the enduring appeal of mysterious natural phenomena.

Executives at "Wheel of Fortune" are trying to clarify why a puzzle with the answer "The Fast and The Furious" appeared on the show, aired on about 200 local stations on Monday night. The show stated it was an "unfortunate coincidence," as the puzzle was taped weeks before actor Paul Walker's death in a car crash. Host Pat Sajak also addressed the timing, explaining that the puzzle was recorded long ago and distributed to stations days before Walker's passing.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) has issued new guidance recommending the use of "Best If Used By" on food labels to reduce consumer confusion and food waste. This guidance aims to standardize date labeling, which is currently voluntary and varies widely among food producers. The FSIS argues that "Best If Used By" conveys that the product will be of best quality if used by the date shown, while foods not exhibiting signs of spoilage should still be safe to consume. Other date-related phrases like "Sell By" and "Use By" are less clear and can lead to unnecessary food disposal. The FSIS estimates that 30% of the U.S. food supply is lost or wasted at the retail and consumer level. By providing clearer date labels, the FSIS hopes to reduce food waste, save money, and promote in-home food safety practices. The guidance is a recommendation and does not have regulatory force, but it builds on other

The Walt Disney Company is thriving, with its stock near an all-time high and earnings up 26% over the past nine months. CEO Robert Iger expects continued growth from park investments, cruise lines, and expansion in Asia. Much of Disney's success is driven by its film studio, evident in the transformation of California Adventure into a Pixar park, with hits like "Cars Land" drawing more visitors. To sustain this growth, Disney needs to keep producing big-budget films like "The Avengers," which generate substantial revenue from merchandise and TV spin-offs. However, this focus on blockbusters has squeezed mid-budget films, making it harder for filmmakers like John Waters and David Lynch to secure funding for their projects. The shift towards television and streaming services offers new opportunities but comes with its own challenges, as the scale and creative control of episodic work differ from feature films. The future of mid-budget cinema remains uncertain, with studios betting big on tentpoles and filmmakers adapting to new mediums or retiring.

A former North Korean soldier, Lee So Yeon, reveals that life in the country's military was harsh for women, with many stopping menstruating due to malnutrition and stress. Sexual abuse was common, with female soldiers often raped by superiors. Despite laws against such acts, perpetrators were rarely punished. Women faced additional hardships, like inadequate sanitation facilities and reused sanitary pads. The military's strict gender roles and lack of privacy further exacerbated their struggles. While some women volunteered for the army, others were forced to serve due to the severe economic situation. The North Korean government has acknowledged the issue but faces criticism for its handling of sexual abuse cases.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposed removing the Oregon chub, a small minnow native to Oregon's Willamette Valley, from the endangered species list. If delisted, it would be the first fish to recover and be removed since the 1973 Endangered Species Act. The chub was placed on the list in 1993 due to habitat loss and predation by non-native fish, with fewer than 1,000 fish in eight populations. Recovery efforts, including habitat restoration and careful monitoring, have increased the chub's population to over 150,000 across 80 sites. This move aligns with the delisting of other species like the Steller sea lion and Gray wolf, which have also recovered. The proposal will undergo a 60-day public comment period before finalization, with continued monitoring for nine years.

The first trailer for Peter Jackson's film adaptation of "The Hobbit" offers a glimpse into the new material being added to the story, including a side quest involving Gandalf, Galadriel, and other powerful figures. This extra content will be featured in both parts of the film, not just the second. Galadriel appears prominently, suggesting a significant role in the new narrative. The trailer reassures fans that Middle Earth remains true to its original look, with familiar locations like Hobbiton appearing unchanged. Concerns about the appearance of the dwarves are alleviated as they are depicted more authentically, with Thorin Oakenshield standing out as a heroic character. The film promises to incorporate more of Tolkien's songs, with a new song "Misty Mountains" featured in the trailer. The trailer's release is seen as a positive sign for the film's prospects, with many fans considering the opportunity to see the trailer in theaters as worthwhile.

Justice Clarence Thomas, who had not asked questions during oral arguments for a decade, posed several queries during a Supreme Court hearing on Monday. The case involved a challenge to a federal law that bans people convicted of domestic violence from owning guns. Thomas, known for his silence during arguments, surprised observers by engaging with Justice Department lawyer Ilana Eisenstein, pressing her on scenarios where a misdemeanor violation might suspend a constitutional right. His questions, which came during the second week of arguments following Justice Antonin Scalia's death, marked a significant shift and highlighted the impact of Scalia's absence on the court's dynamics.

A private Ohio airline, Flamingo Air, offers a unique service: private flights where couples can enjoy a romantic experience, including the option to join the "Mile High Club." Flamingo Air's president, David MacDonald, explains how the idea began with a bet among friends and has since become a successful business, offering flights for $495 that include champagne, chocolates, and a discreet pilot. MacDonald emphasizes marketing the flights as romantic adventures rather than sexual encounters, noting that it is often women who book the flights. The airline has been operating for 21 years, serving as the only such service in the United States and attracting couples from various backgrounds, including those celebrating anniversaries or simply looking for a private moment. Competitors, like Love Cloud in Las Vegas, have also entered the market, but both companies have found that emphasizing romance over explicit sexual content is key to success.

Scientists have discovered the largest "four-winged" dinosaur known, named Changyuraptor yangi, with exceptionally long tail feathers and feather-covered forelimbs and legs. This 125-million-year-old creature, unearthed in northeastern China, resembles a turkey with a very long tail. It lived in a forested environment, potentially capable of gliding or primitive flight. The find provides insights into how dinosaurs may have flown and suggests that feathers served multiple purposes beyond flight, including display and mating rituals. China continues to yield numerous feathered dinosaur fossils, with this discovery highlighting the region's importance in understanding dinosaur evolution.

Tech leaders, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, are urging California regulators to direct Volkswagen to focus on accelerating the rollout of zero-emission vehicles rather than fixing its emissions-cheating diesel cars. They propose releasing VW from its obligation to fix diesel cars already on the road in California, directing the company to invest the money it would have spent on repairs into R&D or new plants, and requiring a significant reduction in pollutant emissions. This approach, they argue, would be more effective in reducing emissions and promoting zero-emission vehicles, which present no opportunities for cheating and would benefit California's economy and the environment.

A Queensland high school student suspended for throwing a Vegemite sandwich at Prime Minister Julia Gillard has disputed the charges, claiming he was just trying to protect her from a second sandwich thrower. During a visit to Marsden State High School, Gillard was hit by a sandwich, leading to Kyle Thomson's suspension. However, Kyle maintains he only hit the sandwich out of another student's hand to prevent a second attack. His mother supports his version of events, calling for a further investigation. Despite the incident, Gillard handled it with humor, stating she would not use parliamentary powers to appeal the suspension. The event has sparked debate and conspiracy theories online, with some questioning the authenticity of the sandwich and the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The number of hate crimes reported to the FBI increased by about 17 percent in 2017 compared to the previous year, according to the Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program’s annual Hate Crime Statistics report. Law enforcement agencies reported 7,175 hate crimes in 2017, up from 6,121 in 2016, with approximately 1,000 additional agencies contributing data. The most common bias categories were race/ethnicity/ancestry (59.6 percent), religion (20.6 percent), and sexual orientation (15.8 percent). About 5,000 of these incidents were categorized as crimes against persons, such as intimidation or assault, while around 3,000 were considered crimes against property. The FBI is working with law enforcement to improve reporting, offering training and a new hate crimes webpage to assist in identifying and documenting bias-motivated incidents. Acc

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 continues as Australia's Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) completes five missions in the southern Indian Ocean, despite weather delays. The search area, larger than South Carolina, is expected to be completed by January 2017. Ministers from Malaysia, Australia, and China agreed in July 2016 that the search would be suspended if no credible new evidence emerges. The operation, funded by Australia and Malaysia, has covered over 70% of the 46,000 square mile zone. The only confirmed piece of the plane found so far is a flaperon that washed up on Reunion Island. A towfish, crucial for scanning the ocean floor, was lost after striking an underwater mud volcano, but recovery efforts are ongoing.

The South African government has initiated the process of seizing land from white farmers, particularly in cases where negotiations for compensation have stalled. Two game farms in Limpopo province are the first to be targeted, with the government offering a fraction of the asking price. Akkerland Boerdery, the farm owners, sought legal intervention to prevent eviction, but the Department of Rural Development and Land Affairs opposed their application. The government plans to test the ability to seize land under existing laws, aiming to address past injustices. The process has sparked controversy, with Afriforum, a group representing the white Afrikaner minority, releasing a purported list of 190 farms targeted for seizure. The government denies the authenticity of the list, while farmers and investors express concerns about potential economic impacts.

A first grader in Colorado was suspended for one day after pointing his finger in a gun shape and saying "You’re dead" to a classmate. The boy’s father, Austin Thurston, believes the suspension was excessive. The school district defended the suspension, stating it was appropriate under their zero-tolerance policy. The incident highlights the challenges of applying strict policies to young children’s play behavior.

Bristol Palin is facing a lawsuit filed by a man who heckled her in a Los Angeles bar, calling her mother "evil" and a "whore." Stephen Hanks, the 47-year-old who was filmed during the September 2011 incident at Saddle Ranch, claims Bristol defamed him by blaming their encounter for her decision to leave Los Angeles and return to Alaska. Hanks also alleges emotional distress and invasion of privacy, and is suing Bristol and the cable channel Lifetime, which included footage of the incident in Bristol's upcoming reality TV show. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. federal court in Los Angeles, seeks unspecified damages. Bristol's camp has not commented on the matter.

Bill O'Reilly is taking a vacation from his Fox News Channel show amid sponsor defections triggered by sexual harassment allegations. O'Reilly announced the break at the end of Tuesday's show, stating it was planned and long in the works, and he will return on April 24. While advertisers are fleeing his "no spin zone," viewers remain loyal, with his show averaging 3.71 million viewers over five nights. O'Reilly's vacation announcement comes as about 60 companies said they won't advertise on his show due to the allegations. A Fox News spokesperson refuted reports suggesting tonight's show could be his last. However, sources at the network indicate that 21st Century Fox CEO James Murdoch wants O'Reilly out, while his father, Rupert, and brother, Lachlan, are more inclined to keep him. The Murdochs are currently divided over how to handle the situation.

A series of nine small bombs exploded at a world-famous Buddhist temple in eastern India on Sunday, injuring two people. Four of the explosions took place at the Mahabodhi temple complex in Bihar state, a UNESCO World Heritage site believed to house the tree where Buddha attained enlightenment. While no group has claimed responsibility, suspicion falls on the Indian Mujahideen, an Islamist group designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S. State Department. The temple itself was not damaged, but windows and a door were broken. Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh condemned the attacks, stating that such incidents targeting religious sites will not be tolerated. The Bodh Gaya complex, one of the oldest Buddhist sites in India, is a significant location for Buddhists worldwide.

A truce between Israel and Palestinian militants in Gaza collapsed amid renewed air strikes by Israel, which blamed rocket fire from Gaza. Palestinian group Hamas claimed the wife and child of its military commander were killed in the strikes, while Israel reported about 50 rockets launched from Gaza, causing no injuries. Talks in Cairo aimed at ending the conflict broke down with no deal, and Israeli delegates left the negotiations. The US criticized Hamas for violating the cease-fire. Israel launched Operation Protective Edge on July 8 to stop rocket fire, and since then, nearly 2,000 Palestinians have been killed, mostly civilians, while 67 Israeli soldiers died. The latest cease-fire lasted less than a day, with both sides accusing each other of breaking it.

Intensified military exercises by Russia and NATO are fueling tensions in Europe, according to a report by the European Leadership Network. Both sides are preparing for possible confrontation, with Russia conducting large-scale exercises that could be seen as practicing for a conflict with NATO. NATO has stepped up its military presence in eastern Europe, while Russia has recalibrated its military goals toward the transatlantic alliance. The report suggests that better communication on exercise plans could help minimize tensions. However, the changed profile of exercises is contributing to a climate of unpredictability and fear in Europe. NATO argues that its exercises are defensive, while Russia sees them as provocative. The risk of accidental confrontation is high, as each side watches the other train and concludes that more military exercises are necessary.

The 2015 Emmys inadvertently spoiled the endings of several hit television shows in a pre-recorded montage, angering thousands of viewers who were left feeling betrayed. Host Andy Samberg joked about the "spoiler awards" during the show, acknowledging the frustration of those who had not yet seen the series' finales. Viewers expressed their disappointment on social media, with many feeling the spoilers ruined their ability to watch the shows with an innocent mindset. Despite the backlash, a few supporters defended the organizers, arguing that most of the shows had ended earlier in the year and had been widely discussed online. Jon Hamm won his first Emmy after eight years of losing, adding to the show's controversial moments.

President Donald Trump claimed Wednesday morning that he knew Republican Roy Moore, whom he endorsed, would be unable to win the Alabama Senate race because "the deck was stacked against him." Trump initially backed Luther Strange in the primary, but later endorsed Moore. Trump's support for Strange in the primary and his backing of Moore in the runoff drew criticism from some Republicans, including Sen. Lindsey Graham. Trump's tweet suggested he had been right about Moore's chances all along, but the state's conservative leanings made his claim questionable. Democrats celebrated the victory, seeing it as a statement of values and a rebuke to Trump's presidency.

German authorities are on high alert amid a series of security concerns, including a potential terror plot in Hanover and a raised threat level in Germany overall. The interior minister, Thomas de Maizière, faced criticism for not providing details about the alleged plot, which led to the cancellation of a Germany-Netherlands football match. Meanwhile, Christmas markets in North Rhine-Westphalia will increase security measures. Turkey arrested eight suspected ISIS members at Istanbul airport, planning to enter Germany as refugees. The German Police Union opposes the deployment of soldiers for police duties. The threat level remains high, with officials advising caution but not fear.

A Chinese author who paid £7,700 for a dram of 19th-century Scotch whisky has been refunded by a Swiss hotel after the drink was officially deemed a fake. The 0.67-ounce dram, believed to be one of the world's only known bottles of Macallan 1878 still in circulation, was bought at the Waldhaus Am See hotel in St Moritz. However, following a series of investigative and forensic tests, including carbon dating, the whisky was shown to date back no further than 1970, making it almost worthless as a collector's item. The hotel manager, Sandro Bernasconi, flew to China to refund the customer in full, stating that they had a duty to ensure the authenticity of their stock. The incident highlights the growing concern over fake vintage whiskies in the market.

SEOUL, South Korea — After decades of strained relations, South Korea and Japan reached a landmark agreement on Monday to resolve the issue of "comfort women," women forced to serve as sex slaves for Japan's Imperial Army during World War II. The agreement, announced in Seoul by the foreign ministers of both countries, includes a Japanese apology and a $8.3 million payment to be administered by the South Korean government for the care of the remaining survivors. The deal is seen as a significant step towards improving relations between the two nations, crucial allies to the United States. However, some former "comfort women" remain unsatisfied with the terms, arguing for direct compensation and a more explicit acknowledgment of Japan's responsibility. The agreement, while not perfect, is viewed as a milestone in the ongoing efforts to address this painful legacy of Japan's colonial rule over Korea.

Hostess Brands, known for iconic products like Twinkies and Wonder Bread, has filed for bankruptcy and plans to close operations, affecting nearly 18,500 workers. The company cites a strike by bakers over a new contract as the reason. Hostess will sell its assets, potentially allowing other companies to revive its brands. The shutdown will impact 33 bakeries, 565 distribution centers, and 570 outlet stores. While the sale of assets could bring new life to Hostess products, current employees will not regain their jobs. The company's bankruptcy is its second since 2004, and it is now controlled by investment firms. Hostess had annual sales of about $2.5 billion and was the No. 2 bread baker in the U.S.

About 10,000 people fled into Thailand from Myanmar on Monday to escape fighting between Myanmar government forces and a splinter group of rebels from the Democratic Karen Buddhist Army. The clashes, which began over Myanmar's controversial election, left at least three people dead and 10 wounded. Myanmar's first election in 20 years, widely criticized as a sham, saw the ruling military-backed party win most seats. Opposition parties accused the government of vote rigging and boycotted the election. The fighting, centered in the border town of Myawaddy, highlights the ongoing conflict between ethnic minorities and the central government.

The Senate Commerce Committee's report on major data companies reveals the extensive and often sensitive personal data these companies collect and sell. Privacy groups testified that data brokers own consumer profiles containing information on health conditions, financial habits, and more. Some companies, like Acxiom, Experian, and Epsilon, refused to disclose data collection methods and buyers, citing confidentiality clauses. Equifax, however, was noted for its cooperation. Data is categorized into detailed dictionaries with over 75,000 data points, including lists of rape victims, people with HIV/AIDS, and police officers' home addresses. These practices highlight the need for stronger government regulations to protect individual privacy.

President Trump identified the European Union as his "biggest foe globally" in an interview with "CBS Evening News" anchor Jeff Glor, emphasizing trade disputes and NATO defense spending. The EU's trade policies are seen as unfair, and Trump criticized Germany for a pipeline deal with Russia, calling it "ridiculous" and "not fair." During the NATO summit, Trump's tough stance on defense spending and criticism of Germany's pipeline deal with Russia drew backlash from German Chancellor Angela Merkel. Trump's upcoming meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Helsinki faces skepticism, with low expectations expressed by the president. Trump also defended his Supreme Court nominee, Brett Kavanaugh, on the issue of abortion and discussed his meeting with Queen Elizabeth II, praising her sharp intellect. He defended family separations at the border, citing Obama's similar policy, and highlighted the power and immediacy of Twitter. Trump's visit to the UK was marked by protests, with some demonstrating in his favor, and he expressed mixed feelings about the

President Obama has ordered the Pentagon to prepare for the possibility of withdrawing all U.S. troops from Afghanistan by the end of the year, due to Afghan President Hamid Karzai's refusal to sign a bilateral security agreement. The White House stated that Obama informed Karzai of this decision during a phone call, leaving open the option of a limited post-2014 presence for training and counterterrorism. However, the longer the agreement is delayed, the more challenging it will be to plan any U.S. mission, and the smaller the potential troop presence. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel will discuss these plans with NATO allies at a meeting in Brussels.

Russian fighter jets were intercepted by American and Canadian planes off the coast of Alaska on Wednesday, according to US defense officials. The planes, including two MiG-31 jets, entered the Air Defense Identification Zone but did not enter US airspace. Two Alaskan-based F-22 fighter jets and two Canadian CF-18 fighter jets were scrambled to intercept the Russian planes in two separate incidents. The incidents occurred up to 10 times a year and are not uncommon. Additionally, two Russian military aircraft crossed into Swedish airspace, prompting the Swedish Foreign Ministry to call it a "serious violation."

The U.S. Pentagon has studied the body movements of Russian President Vladimir Putin twice over the past six years as part of a program called the "Body Leads Project," aimed at predicting his decisions and actions. Since 1996, Pentagon researchers have analyzed the body language of 15 world leaders, including Putin, Saddam Hussein, and Osama bin Laden, but have not studied any American leaders. No current effort is underway to analyze Putin's body language regarding the Crimea crisis, despite tensions escalating in Ukraine. The program, run by the Office of Net Assessment, has spent $300,000 annually on outside researchers to study body movements for insights into decision-making processes and truthfulness. While the results are not classified, the Pentagon has no plans to release the reports publicly.

An Indiana man's selfie with a trooper after a traffic stop has gone viral, touching many with its message of respect. Greg Barnes Jr. was pulled over for speeding and decided to take a selfie with the officer, Trooper Shawn Cosgrove, to send a positive message. Barnes wrote that the interaction was respectful and highlighted the potential for positive police interactions. He emphasized the importance of treating each other as humans rather than based on race or profession. The post has sparked conversations and gained nearly 500,000 shares.

Conjoined twins Knatalye Hope and Adeline Faith Mata were successfully separated during a 26-hour surgery at Texas Children's Hospital. Born at 31 weeks, the girls were joined at the chest and abdomen, sharing several organ systems. A team of over 26 clinicians, including 12 surgeons, worked on the complex procedure. The surgery took approximately 18 hours, with 23 hours for Knatalye and 26 for Adeline. The girls are now in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit for recovery, with anticipated additional surgeries in the future. Their mother, Elysse Mata, expressed gratitude to the medical team and supporters.

Actress Abigail Breslin, known for her role in "Little Miss Sunshine," has released a song with the indie band Stargroves, titled "Westfjords." The track, a catchy collaboration between Breslin and songwriter Teddy Watson, showcases Breslin's musical talents. This is not the first time actors have ventured into music; Ryan Gosling, Michael Cera, and Christopher Mintz-Plasse have also formed bands, including Dead Man's Bones, Mister Heavenly, and The Young Rapscallions, respectively.

Michelle Williams, still struggling to find meaning in Heath Ledger's death, reveals in her first network interview since his passing in 2007 that she cannot find a meaning for the event itself. Despite her current success from "Blue Valentine" and working with Ryan Gosling, Williams notes that she once struggled with the idea that life can change in an instant. She finds comfort in a line from a book: "When you've truly lost everything, then at least you can become rich in loss." Williams also reflects on the surreal feeling of Ledger's death not seeming real and misses the year of magical thinking that followed. Gosling, her co-star, describes working with her as creatively fulfilling but maintains they are still just professionals.

A new study suggests that lethal violence is an evolutionary trait inherited from our primate ancestors, with humans having a 2% rate of lethal violence among our species dating back to the dawn of our species. Researchers from Spain examined the evolutionary family tree of mammals, analyzing data from over 1,020 species and 600 human populations to estimate the levels of lethal violence among our evolutionary ancestors. The findings indicate that while violence is part of our evolutionary history, societal structures can significantly reduce the rate of lethal violence. The study, published in Nature, highlights that while humans may have inherited a propensity for violence, modern societies can modulate this tendency through social organization and institutions.

Yahoo is offering inactive Yahoo email addresses to new users, allowing them to claim and use these addresses starting mid-July. However, this move could pose significant security risks. Users who haven't logged into their accounts for a year or more may have their addresses taken over by malicious individuals, potentially leading to unauthorized access to other accounts. Yahoo has stated it believes it can handle this transition securely.

Democratic frontrunner Hillary Clinton's campaign raised $28 million in the third quarter of 2015, narrowly outpacing Bernie Sanders' $26 million haul. Clinton's fundraising remains formidable, with a total of $75 million raised in the first two quarters, including $3 million from a joint fundraising committee. However, Sanders' online fundraising prowess, highlighted by a single-day $2.07 million haul, raises concerns about his ability to compete in a general election against a well-funded Republican. Clinton's campaign manager Robby Mook expressed gratitude for the support, noting 93% of third-quarter donations were under $100. Sanders' campaign reached its goal of one million individual online contributions, faster than Obama in 2008 and 2012, underscoring his momentum and fundraising strength.

A 6-year-old English Springer Spaniel named Hendrix was mistakenly put on a flight to Ireland instead of Phoenix on United Airlines. His owner, Edith Albach, received a call from the airline just before the wrong flight landed in Newark. United staff walked and fed Hendrix during his unexpected journey before reuniting him with his family in Newark. Hendrix eventually arrived in Phoenix, where he was greeted by his owner's daughter, Meredith Grant. United offered a full refund but faced criticism for the mishap, with Grant demanding accountability for the error.

Amazon has introduced an $59.99 AmazonBasics Microwave that integrates with Alexa, allowing users to control the appliance via voice commands. The microwave lacks built-in microphones and speakers but pairs with an existing Alexa system. By pressing an Alexa button, users can activate voice commands without saying "Alexa" and can control functions like cooking times. A notable feature is the automatic reordering of microwave popcorn when users frequently ask Alexa to make popcorn. This device aims to showcase Amazon’s Alexa Connection Kit, enabling easier integration of voice control into everyday gadgets. The microwave is set to ship later this year, offering a budget-friendly option for smart home enthusiasts.

The Miss America Organization faced a scandal involving offensive emails sent by CEO Sam Haskell and other board members, which detailed derogatory comments about former Miss America winners. Haskell, who had been leading the organization for nine years, sent an email to the lead writer of the Miss America pageant telecast, suggesting a change in how former winners were referred to, and received a reply that included vulgar language. Haskell’s behavior behind closed doors showed he regularly maligned, fat-shamed, and slut-shamed former winners, calling them shocking names and laughing at inappropriate comments. Two board members, Tammy Haddad and Lynn Weidner, served as a rubber stamp for Haskell’s behavior. Haskell was suspended pending an investigation, and he and Weidner resigned. President and COO Josh Randle also stepped down. The organization’s board promised to conduct an in-depth investigation and reaffirmed its commitment to the education and empowerment of young women.

In a debate with Democratic challenger Joe Donnelly and Libertarian Andrew Horning, Richard Mourdock, the Republican candidate for Indiana's U.S. Senate seat, faced criticism for his comments on abortion in cases of rape. Mourdock stated that pregnancies resulting from rape are "something that God intended to happen," despite the "horrible situation" from which they arose. Democrats, including Donnelly, condemned Mourdock's remarks, with Donnelly stating that the God he believes in does not intend for rape to occur. Mourdock attempted to clarify his comments, asserting that he believes God creates life but did not intend for rape to happen. Mourdock's stance on abortion has drawn comparisons to Todd Akin's controversial comments on "legitimate rape." Republicans, including Mitt Romney, have distanced themselves from Mourdock's statements, with Romney's campaign spokesperson Andrea Saul stating that Romney disagrees with Mourdock's comments. The debate took place amid a highly competitive race, with top Republicans and outside groups supporting Mourdock

The Texas Policy Evaluation Project (TxPEP) released a study indicating that at least 100,000 and as many as 240,000 Texas women between the ages of 18 and 49 have attempted to self-induce abortions since the state passed restrictive abortion laws in 2013. The study, based on a survey of nearly 800 women, found that the rate of self-induced abortions may be rising due to increased restrictions. TxPEP identified two key groups where self-induced abortions were more common: Latina women in rural areas and those with difficulty accessing healthcare. Women often used home remedies or obtained misoprostol from Mexico. Reasons for self-inducing included financial constraints, clinic closures, and fears of stigma. The study highlights the potential negative impacts of restrictive abortion laws on women's health.

A former CIA officer, Sabrina De Sousa, faces imminent extradition to Italy and potential imprisonment for her alleged role in the extraordinary rendition of Abu Omar, a radical Egyptian cleric, in 2003. Abu Omar, who was kidnapped in Milan by the CIA with alleged Italian assistance, now believes De Sousa is a scapegoat and should be pardoned. De Sousa, who has been convicted in absentia, argues that she played a minor role and was merely a translator in early discussions. The case has become politically complex, with the U.S. government not intervening publicly, and Italy facing pressure over its handling of an Italian citizen's murder in Egypt. De Sousa has appealed to Pope Francis for support, expressing fear of being silenced in prison.

Barbara Soper of Rockford, Mich., delivered her third child on 10-10-10, continuing a numerical coincidence with her first two children born on 8-8-08 and 9-9-09. Despite not planning for their births to coincide, the Sopers' three children share a pattern of being born on dates with repeated numbers. The first, Chloe Corrin Soper, was born full term on August 8, 2008, at Spectrum Health's Butterworth Hospital. Their son, Cameron Dane Soper, was born on September 9, 2009, due to complications from his sister's birth. Soper developed blood clots three weeks before her due date for their third child, Cearra Nicole Soper, who arrived on October 10, 2010. Statisticians note that while such a pattern seems rare, it's more common than one might think,

A new Trojan called "Sabpab" poses a threat to Mac users who run Java and Microsoft Word, warn security experts. To protect against this and other malware, users are advised to ensure their computers are up to date with the latest software patches from both Apple and Microsoft, and to employ anti-virus software. One version of Sabpab exploits a Java vulnerability, similar to the one used by the Flashback malware, which infected up to 600,000 Macs. Another version arrives via a suspicious email attachment. Mac users may be caught off guard as the malware installs itself without prompting for a username or password. Microsoft has confirmed that its 2009 security update for Microsoft Office for Mac users will address the vulnerability exploited by Sabpab. Graham Cluley, a senior technology consultant at Sophos, urges Mac users to install anti-virus software, noting that free options are available for home users. Miley Cyrus narrowly avoided a dangerous situation early Saturday morning when an intruder armed with scissors was arrested at her Studio City home. The 40-year-old man, identified as Jason Luis Rivera, was found hiding in bushes around the singer's property and claimed to be her husband, stating they had been friends for five years. Police used a taser to subdue Rivera after he did not immediately comply with their orders. Miley was not at home at the time, but someone inside called 911. Rivera is being held on $1,000 bail and faces charges of trespassing and burglary.

A 1999 photograph by German artist Andreas Gursky titled "Rhein II" has set a new record for the most expensive photograph sold at auction, fetching $4.3 million at Christie's in New York. The large chromogenic color print, face-mounted to acrylic glass, was part of an edition of six, with four already in major museums. The previous record holder was Cindy Sherman's "Untitled #96" from 1981, which sold for $3.8 million. Gursky is known for his disorienting, large-scale landscapes that aim to make viewers aware of their place in the universe.

Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette charged six more state employees in connection with the Flint water crisis, bringing the total to nine officials facing criminal charges. The charges, filed in district court, include misconduct in office, conspiracy, and willful neglect of duty. Schuette’s investigation, ongoing for nearly eight months, alleges that state Department of Environmental Quality and Department of Health and Human Services employees altered or buried reports showing high levels of lead in Flint's water and children. The new charges stem from alleged actions on or around July 28, 2015, when state employees allegedly manipulated water testing reports and concealed data to downplay the severity of the lead contamination. Schuette maintains that arrogance and viewing Flint residents as expendable were motives behind the alleged cover-up. The investigation is described as the largest in Michigan’s history and continues to explore potential coordination between the two state agencies.

On April Fools' Day, Forbes.com fell victim to a prank when a blog post falsely claimed Mitt Romney had dropped out of the Republican presidential race and endorsed Rick Santorum. Contributor Len Burman, an economics professor, wrote the satirical piece, which briefly spread on Twitter and claimed the top spot on Google News. Editors pulled the post down about half an hour later but not before it caused confusion. Burman defended his piece as satire, aiming to highlight issues within the Republican Party. The incident led to a ban on April Fools' Day humor at Forbes.com, and Burman learned a lesson about the internet's tendency to focus on headlines.

In a study comparing opioids to nonopioid medications for chronic back pain or hip/knee osteoarthritis, neither group showed significant improvement in pain-related function over 12 months. Both groups experienced similar levels of pain intensity, with nonopioid medications showing a slight but not clinically significant advantage. Opioids, however, led to more medication-related side effects. This suggests that for moderate to severe chronic pain, nonopioid treatments may be preferable, as they offer comparable pain relief with fewer risks.

A 48-year-old woman sentenced to four days in jail for hitting and killing a 79-year-old school bus driver in New Prague, Minnesota, while texting, has agreed to community service and a fine. Joe Tikalsky, a beloved school bus driver, was struck while collecting his newspaper on the morning of the crash. The Tikalsky family, choosing forgiveness over anger, met with the driver and asked for her to use her gift to become a force for change. The case highlights the growing issue of distracted driving, with Minnesota law banning text messaging for all drivers but rarely resulting in felony convictions. The Tikalskys are working to lobby for stricter laws and stronger consequences for distracted driving.

A villager in Gansu province won over $80,000 in compensation after being attacked by a wild panda. The panda bit the villager's leg, requiring seven hours of surgery. Local forestry officials and the Baishuijiang National Nature Reserve agreed to pay the compensation. The giant panda, though known for its cute appearance, can be dangerous due to its strong bite and weight. Wild panda attacks on humans, including one in 2008 where a man was mauled, are rare but do occur.

Vice President Joe Biden stated there is "no doubt" that Syrian President Bashar al-Assad was responsible for the August 21 chemical weapons attack near Damascus. Biden cited the Syrian regime's possession of chemical weapons, past use, and efforts to obstruct international investigations. The White House press briefing emphasized the need for a response to protect U.S. security interests, though President Obama has not yet decided on a course of action. Lawmakers have called for congressional authorization before any military strike.

Mercedes-Benz is launching the Maybach G-Class 650, an ultra-luxurious SUV priced at around $500,000, to capitalize on the popularity of high-end all-terrain vehicles. This vehicle features a V12 engine, a retractable fabric roof, and luxury amenities like heated and massaging seats and thermal cupholders. Limited to 99 units, it aims to appeal to ultra-wealthy customers, helping Mercedes-Benz maintain its position as the world's top-selling luxury marque. The Maybach brand, previously revived in 2014, now includes more opulent versions of popular models, and this new SUV represents Daimler's strategy of targeting high-margin markets to fund the development of electric cars and autonomous technologies.

Longtime Trump adviser Roger Stone appeared on Infowars to refute claims of inappropriate contact with Russian intelligence during the 2016 election, wearing a hot air balloon pilot costume. Stone has repeatedly denied any collusion with Russia and claims he has not spoken to the FBI. He doubled down on his assertion of no contact with Russian officials and denied claims of wiretapping Trump Tower, suggesting the FBI and intelligence community are politicized. Stone's public statements about WikiLeaks and Julian Assange have raised suspicions, but he maintains his communications were "benign." Stone also defended former Trump campaign figures and suggested he had a backchannel with Assange.

Ryan Reynolds is this year's Sexiest Man Alive, according to People magazine, just as the trailer for his upcoming "Green Lantern" role hits the web. The honor comes as Reynolds prepares to don the famous green suit, playing Hal Jordan, who learns new powers and overcomes his fears to protect the Green Lantern Corp. from the new enemy, Parallax. The trailer also reveals Blake Lively in the role of Carol Ferris, a fellow test pilot and love interest, and Peter Sarsgaard as the villainous Hector Hammond. Despite his chiseled abs, Reynolds remains humble, stating that his body naturally wants to look like Dick Van Dyke. His wife, Scarlett Johansson, was recently named GQ's "Babe of the Year," leading to a playful discussion about the couple's representation as "Agents of the Year."

CBS News' Lara Logan suffered a brutal and sustained sexual assault and beating in Tahrir Square, Cairo, on the day Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak stepped down. Logan, separated from her crew, was surrounded by a mob of over 200 people whipped into a frenzy. She was saved by a group of women and an estimated 20 Egyptian soldiers. Logan reconnected with her CBS team and returned to the U.S. on the first flight the next morning. She is currently recovering. CBS News and Logan's family request privacy. The attack was one of at least 140 suffered by reporters covering the unrest in Egypt since January 30, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.

When it comes to air travel in the U.S., there are two realities. Most passengers find flying to be the worst it's ever been, citing smaller seats, higher fees, and less comfort. Yet, industry experts argue that flying is objectively the best it's ever been, with cheaper fares, better safety records, and improved amenities for those who can afford them. This conundrum arises from the evolution of air travel post-deregulation, where airlines shifted from competing on comfort to competing on price. The result is a mix of experiences: while some enjoy affordable and convenient travel, others face increased inconveniences and costs. The socialization of hating flying has also contributed to the perception gap, with humor and shared complaints reinforcing the negative experience.

Rapper Malik Taylor, known as Phife Dawg from the critically acclaimed A Tribe Called Quest, passed away at 45 due to complications from diabetes. Many hip-hop artists honored him on social media, including Jill Scott and Chuck D. A WSB-TV Atlanta traffic reporter, Mark Arum, paid tribute by weaving Phife Dawg's lyrics into his traffic update, showcasing the rapper's memorable lines and impact on hip-hop.

British Prime Minister David Cameron cut short his holiday to address the Syrian chemical weapons attack, while U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry called the use of chemical weapons a "moral obscenity." Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis have failed, with UN inspectors facing sniper fire during their investigation. The UK is considering possible military action, and the U.S. is preparing naval forces in the Mediterranean. Russia and China warn against any military intervention, maintaining that such actions would violate international law. The UN team is set to continue its investigation, but the situation remains tense as evidence may have been compromised.

German authorities are considering using software similar to the music recognition app Shazam to identify neo-Nazi songs quickly, according to SPIEGEL. Dubbed "Nazi Shazam," the software could help police react immediately if such songs are played in public, acting as a "gateway drug" into far-right youth scenes. Interior ministers from Germany's 16 regions will discuss the proposal at a meeting this week. Currently, 1,090 pieces of music with far-right or racist messages are indexed by the Federal Review Board for Media Harmful to Minors, restricting their sale and access to minors. While experts approve of the initiative, some neo-Nazi groups have already adapted by using newer, non-indexed songs.

After Ethan Couch and his mother, Tonya, were captured in Mexico, the "affluenza" teen remains in a Mexican detention center as he fights deportation. Tonya Couch, who faces charges for helping her son flee, was deported to Los Angeles and is expected to be brought back to Texas soon. A relative of Tonya Couch is offering a $1,000 reward for their missing dog, Virgil, a half-shepherd half-wolf mix, which was last seen near the same intersection where the Couches were apprehended. Tonya Couch waived her right to extradition in a Los Angeles court, but her attorney expresses concerns about a fair trial. Meanwhile, Ethan Couch's return to Texas is pending, with Tarrant County Sheriff Dee Anderson stating that deputies are ready to retrieve him.

Otto Warmbier's parents, Fred and Cindy, shared harrowing details of their son's condition upon his return from North Korea in their first television interview since his death. Upon arrival, they witnessed their 22-year-old son, now blind and deaf, jerking violently and producing inhuman cries. Cindy described the scene: "We walked over to the plane; the engines are still humming, when we got halfway up the steps, we heard this howling, involuntary, inhuman sound. We weren’t really certain what it was. … Otto was on the stretcher across in the plane, and he was jerking violently, making these inhuman sounds." Fred added, "As we looked at him and tried to comfort him, it looked like someone had taken a pair of pliers and rearranged his bottom teeth." North Korea denied torturing Warmbier, but his parents insisted, "North Korea is not a victim. They’re terrorists. They kidnapped Otto. They

Harvard rescinded admission offers to at least ten students after discovering an offensive, private Facebook group chat where prospective freshmen shared sexually explicit and racially charged memes. The group, initially for sharing popular culture memes, evolved into an "R-rated" chat where students traded images mocking sexual assault, the Holocaust, and the deaths of children. University officials found out and informed ten students that their offers were withdrawn. The incident highlights the impact of social media on college admissions and the university's stance on maintaining high moral standards.

Comedy Central's roast of David Hasselhoff, scheduled to air on August 15, turned into a relentless barrage of jokes centered around his infamous down-on-the-floor drunk, cheeseburger-chewing video and his long-standing battle with alcohol. Roast master Seth MacFarlane and comedians like Jeffrey Ross, Hulk Hogan, and Pamela Anderson mocked Hasselhoff’s acting and singing skills, with Ross even suggesting he once got so drunk he "fucked K.I.T.T." Hasselhoff, who sat in a red, oversized lifeguard's chair, gamely laughed at most of the jokes, though he admitted it was a "long night." The roast, which Hasselhoff had been waiting to address, proved to be a mix of humor and personal reflection, with Hasselhoff's daughters in the audience.

Malaysia Airlines, facing financial difficulties and the aftermath of two major tragedies in 2014, is undergoing a significant restructuring. The airline will cut about 6,000 jobs, leaving 14,000 employees, and will focus on regional routes rather than long-haul flights to Europe. CEO Christoph Mueller, known for his previous job cuts at other airlines, announced these plans as the carrier is "technically bankrupt." The airline aims to stabilize its finances by the end of 2015 and hopes to start growing again by 2017. Malaysia Airlines plans to rebrand in September and will consider joint ventures to manage route reductions. The company's flagship route from London to Kuala Lumpur will remain operational.

Disney's "Christopher Robin" aims to reconnect an adult with his childhood memories through the whimsical world of Winnie the Pooh, but the film struggles to balance its somber, artsy tone with a more lighthearted, child-friendly narrative. Ewan McGregor portrays the grown-up Christopher Robin, now a harried businessman dealing with a potential job loss, who is unexpectedly visited by his childhood friend Winnie the Pooh and his forest friends. The film's first half delves into Christopher's grown-up life and his strained relationships, while the latter half shifts to a more playful, fantastical adventure in the Hundred Acre Wood. Despite strong voice performances, particularly from Jim Cummings as Pooh and Brad Garrett as Eeyore, the movie's disjointed tone and heavy-handed themes make it a mixed success, appealing more to adults seeking nostalgia than to children.

President Obama is poised to end a 20-year ban on offering Pell grants to state and federal prisoners, allowing them access to federal subsidies for college. This move could come as soon as this week, with Education Secretary Arne Duncan and Attorney General Loretta Lynch scheduled to announce the change at Goucher College’s Prison Education Partnership in Maryland. Duncan has highlighted the potential of experimental sites to make Pell grants available to incarcerated adults seeking higher education and job training. The change could benefit thousands of inmates, potentially reducing recidivism rates. Lawmakers from both parties have shown support for this policy, and House Democrats have introduced legislation to reinstate Pell eligibility for federal and state prisoners.

North and South Korea have agreed to resume high-level talks after a surprise visit by North Korean officials, including two men thought to be second and third in command behind Kim Jong Un. The delegation, led by Hwang Pyong So, a top political official in the Korean People’s Army, met with South Korean officials and agreed to hold further talks, perhaps even within the next few weeks. This is the highest-level North Korean delegation to visit South Korea since 2009, signaling a potential thaw in relations. The visit comes amid speculation about Kim Jong Un's health and as North Korea prepares for a summit with the U.S. in June.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called for a new FBI director to be free of political stigma and suggested the Senate should refuse confirmation until a special counsel is appointed to investigate potential collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia. Schumer also urged an independent investigation into any interference in the Russia probe. Former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper stated that U.S. institutions are under assault, both externally from Russian interference and internally from the Trump administration. Clapper emphasized the importance of checks and balances among the three branches of government. Lawmakers from both parties criticized Trump's firing of FBI Director James Comey, with some calling for a new director without political background. Trump has interviewed several candidates for the position but has not yet made a selection.

George Clooney's directorial effort "Suburbicon" is a flawed and underwritten satire of 1950s suburban life, criticized for its disjointed tone and lackluster performances. The film, set in a seemingly perfect community, delves into the dark underbelly of betrayal, deceit, and violence. Matt Damon plays Gardner Lodge, a husband and father navigating the town's hidden sins. Julianne Moore, appearing twice in the film, portrays his wife and her twin sister, both Stepford-like characters. The movie's central plot revolves around a family murder and a subplot involving the first African-American residents facing racist hostility. While Oscar Isaac offers a standout performance as an insurance agent, the overall film is described as irritating, faux-edgy, and tonally wack, with a single star rating.

Amid a presidential campaign marred by scandal and the rise of a far-right candidate, disillusioned French voters have launched a petition calling for former U.S. President Barack Obama to run in the French election. The petition, known as Obama17, aims to gather 1 million signatures by March 15th and has already attracted 30,000 signatures. While the petition's creators acknowledge that Obama cannot run due to French citizenship requirements, they argue that it serves as a statement against the status quo in French politics. The organizers, a group of four friends from Paris, hope to spark discussion about the need for change in French governance.

Tech entrepreneur Scott Jones, founder of ChaCha and inventor of voicemail, is opening his 27,000-square-foot Carmel, Indiana, mansion to the public for an estate sale in September. The sale, managed by Aether Estate Sales Co., will run from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on September 14-17. The home, built in an English country manor style and costing $20 million, features a 33-foot-high great room, an indoor tree house, a 25-foot-long saltwater aquarium, and an indoor basketball court. Jones, who has been living in Hawaii for the past two years, is selling off his eclectic collection, including a T-Rex skull replica, high-end art, antiques, custom-built furniture, and a Steinway grand piano. The asking price for the house itself is $4,995,000. Visitors can browse through the house as if

Missouri Governor Eric Greitens acknowledges an extramarital affair from before his campaign but denies allegations of blackmail. Greitens and his wife Sheena released a statement, while his attorney James Bennett disputed KMOV-TV's claims of blackmail. The TV station reported that the woman's ex-husband provided a recording of her detailing a sexual encounter with Greitens and saying he threatened to release photos if she exposed the affair. Greitens maintains there was no blackmail and that the matter has been resolved privately.

President Donald Trump departed from his prepared speech at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) to deliver a campaign-style address, focusing on familiar themes from his 2016 campaign. Trump emphasized his administration's accomplishments, including tax cuts and judicial confirmations, and warned of potential Democratic gains in the upcoming midterm elections, linking them to threats to the Second Amendment. The president also read "The Snake" lyrics, a campaign staple, to underscore his immigration rhetoric. Trump urged Republicans to maintain their enthusiasm and warned of Democratic policies, including gun control, which he vowed to oppose. His off-script approach highlighted his desire to connect with the conservative base, despite his role as the current Commander-in-Chief.

Nevada plans to execute Scott Dozier using fentanyl, a drug central to the US opioid crisis, marking the first time it has been used in an execution. Dozier, a double murderer, has waived his appeals and requested the execution. The state's new three-drug regimen includes midazolam, fentanyl, and cisatracurium, with details of the protocol remaining largely secret. Civil rights lawyers argue the lack of transparency and the use of untested drugs could violate Dozier's constitutional rights. Questions also arise about how Nevada obtained the fentanyl, with concerns over potential legal violations and the role of pharmaceutical distributors. The execution, set for Wednesday, highlights the ongoing challenges states face in obtaining lethal injection drugs and the controversial methods they employ.

Cory Monteith, the star of Glee, was found dead in a hotel room in Vancouver, days after spending time with friends. Just two days before his death, Monteith enjoyed a relaxed dinner with his manager and a casting agent, appearing healthy and in good spirits. He had recently completed a stint in rehab for substance abuse, but his girlfriend, Lea Michele, was unaware of his ongoing struggles. The cause of death remains unknown, with no evidence of foul play. Monteith's death has left his co-stars and fans devastated, with many expressing shock and sadness. His passing comes after a year of battling addiction, including a second rehab stay in 2013. Monteith had previously spoken openly about his substance abuse issues, dating back to his teenage years. His death has raised questions about the risks faced by those in recovery, particularly when they return to their regular lives.

A 20-year-old man from Rockaway, New Jersey, fell to his death Wednesday evening while climbing scaffolding at the 52-story Four Seasons Hotel in Manhattan. Connor Cummings, a photography enthusiast and University of Massachusetts Amherst student, was trying to take pictures from the hotel's scaffolding when he slipped and fell nine stories, landing on a lower rooftop. His 18-year-old friend, Dimitri Olivares, was with him but managed to escape and was later interviewed by police. Hotel officials stated that Cummings and his friend were not guests and had accessed the restricted rooftop. Cummings's family and fraternity brothers expressed shock and grief over his death, describing him as a loving and passionate individual. No charges were filed against Olivares.

A San Antonio day care operated out of an unlicensed home was shut down after an infant suffered 27 bite marks from another child, KENS 5 reports. The day care, run by a woman who has not been criminally charged, was operating without a license for eight years. The baby, whose parents did not wish to be identified, was rushed to a hospital after the bite marks did not fade away. The case is under investigation by the sex crimes unit of the San Antonio Police Department, though it does not appear to be a sexual crime. The operator could face charges of child neglect or injury to a child by omission. The incident highlights the importance of licensing and regulation in child care centers.

A suspect in a downtown Buffalo shooting that killed four people and wounded four others has been cleared by law enforcement, who now believe they may have the wrong person. Erie County District Attorney Frank A. Sedita III announced he plans to dismiss charges against Keith D. Johnson, 25, who was arrested Saturday in connection with the shooting. Sedita stated they have "serious second thoughts" and "serious reservations" about the arrest, citing new video evidence and witness interviews. The shooting occurred outside City Grill on Main Street, where a skirmish between patrons and a gunman with a 9mm handgun took place. Four people, including Danyell Mackin, Tiffany Wilhite, Shawn-Tia McNeil, and Willie McCaa III, were killed. Demario Vass, James Robbs Jr., Shamar Davis, and Tillman Ward were wounded, with Vass in critical condition. Johnson, who was released from prison just two and a half weeks prior, was initially

Edward Snowden's decision to seek refuge in Hong Kong has placed his fate in a complex political landscape. Hong Kong's extradition treaty with the United States includes exceptions for political crimes, giving Beijing the right of veto if it deems the extradition would harm national interests. Snowden's choice reflects Hong Kong's relatively free press and political dissent, contrasting with mainland China. While Snowden denies his move was a vote of confidence in Chinese human rights, the territory's unique status under "one country, two systems" offers a degree of protection. The ongoing relationship between the United States and China, particularly regarding cybersecurity, could influence Beijing's decision. Snowden's legal status remains uncertain, balancing the legal obligations of the extradition treaty with political considerations.

Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Wendy Davis, in her upcoming memoir "Forgetting to Be Afraid," reveals she terminated a pregnancy in the 1990s due to a severe fetal abnormality. The book, set to release next week, details Davis's decision after doctors informed her the baby would suffer and likely be incompatible with life. She also mentions ending an earlier ectopic pregnancy, which she considered sharing during her famous 13-hour filibuster but felt it might overshadow the day's events. The revelations come as Davis trails in polls against Republican Attorney General Greg Abbott. While the story of her pregnancy with the abnormality hasn't surfaced in the race, it adds personal depth to her narrative and complicates efforts to attack her on the abortion issue. Davis's memoir includes details of her hardscrabble childhood and her journey to Harvard Law School, highlighting her resilience and personal struggles.

Chicken Offsets

Love Chick-fil-A's chicken sandwiches but feel guilty about supporting the company's stance against same-sex marriage? D.C. lawyer Ted Frank has created ChickenOffset.com to help. For $1, you can buy an "offset" that supports gay rights organizations, while still enjoying your Chick-fil-A meal. Frank promises to donate at least 80% of the proceeds to It Gets Better and the Williams Institute, ensuring more money goes to gay rights causes than to anti-gay organizations. The site went live recently and has already seen some interest, with about $100 in offsets sold by Monday afternoon.

Catalonia's regional parliament voted to establish an independent Catalan Republic, despite opposition from the Spanish government, which is preparing to take control of the region's autonomous powers. The vote was approved with 70 in favor, 10 against, and two blank ballots. Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy called for calm and urged the Senate to grant his government special constitutional measures to halt the independence bid. The measures could include sacking Catalonia's regional president and ministers, and curtailing the authority of the region's parliament. Outside the parliament, thousands of supporters celebrated the vote, while opponents criticized the move as a violation of democracy. The Spanish government is set to implement the measures, which could lead to a deeper conflict between Catalonia and Spain.

Two New Mexico State University students, McKinnah Sinclair, 18, and Charlie Daniels, 19, who went missing after attending a concert in El Paso, have been located in Idaho. According to Las Cruces Police, the girls were found in a red Ford Focus driven by Daniels, with Sinclair as the passenger, in Nampa, Idaho. The car had a fake license plate, which Daniels had reportedly switched before embarking on their trip. The girls' families have made arrangements to bring them back to New Mexico. Sinclair and Daniels were seen on surveillance footage in Beverly Hills, California, and Las Cruces Police are still unclear about their whereabouts and reasons for leaving without informing their families.

A Brazilian woman, Adriana, who had been searching for her birth mother for decades, found her through a radio show. During the reunion, she was shocked to learn that her husband, Leandro, was actually her brother, sharing the same birth mother, Maria. Adriana and Leandro, who had been married for seven years and had a six-year-old daughter together, were unaware of the family connection when they met and fell in love. Despite the revelation, they decided to stay together, believing their love was meant to be.

Lego has announced the creation of a new set celebrating five pioneering women in NASA's history, selected from a proposal by Maia Weinstock, deputy editor of MIT News. The set, titled "Women of NASA," features iconic figures such as Margaret Hamilton, Mae Jemison, Katherine Johnson, Sally Ride, and Nancy Grace Roman. Weinstock's project was submitted to LEGO Ideas and received 10,000 votes within 15 days, leading to its official selection. The set aims to inspire young girls and adults to pursue careers in STEM fields, highlighting the significant contributions of women in space exploration. Weinstock hopes the set will help improve the perception and visibility of women in these fields, encouraging more girls to explore science, technology, engineering, and math.

Seven-year-old Bana Alabed, known for her tweets from besieged Aleppo, wrote an open letter to President Donald Trump, appealing for action to help Syrian children. Bana, now in Turkey, asks Trump to "do something for the children of Syria" and emphasizes that they deserve peace. Her mother shared the letter with the BBC. Bana, who witnessed the destruction of her school and the deaths of friends, contrasts her current peaceful life in Turkey with the suffering of millions of Syrian children. Trump's position on Syria remains unclear, with his admiration for Russian President Putin complicating potential cooperation. Meanwhile, a ceasefire agreement involving Russia, Iran, and Turkey is struggling to hold.

Michigan officials have reported a significant increase in Legionnaires' disease cases in Genesee County since 2014, raising concerns about potential links to the Flint water crisis. From June 2014 to November 2015, 87 cases were confirmed, including 10 deaths, compared to 6 to 13 cases in previous years. While the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) cannot definitively link the increase to the Flint water source, a water treatment expert suggests the Flint River's lack of proper corrosion control and large buildings' plumbing systems may have contributed to the outbreak. The MDHHS has not changed recommendations for bathing or showering, stating the water is safe for these activities. The increase in Legionnaires' cases adds to the ongoing Flint water crisis, which has already led to lead contamination and other health issues.

Fierce winds in Southern California fueled a rapidly growing wildfire that forced thousands of residents to evacuate their homes and threatened nearby cities. The blaze, which broke out east of Santa Paula, a city of 30,000 people about 60 miles northwest of Los Angeles, expanded to more than 15 square miles within hours. The fire's intensity and speed surprised authorities, who described the growth as "exponential." Santa Paula and the city of Ventura, with 106,000 residents, were at risk as the winds pushed the fire westward. Thomas Aquinas College, a nearby school with about 350 students, was evacuated. One person died in an accident related to the evacuation, and at least two structures were destroyed. Over 40 mph winds, with gusts up to 60 mph, hampered firefighting efforts, causing planes to be grounded late Monday night. Thousands of homes lost power in the affected area.

Visiting Honolulu? Better keep your phone down when crossing streets. The City Council passed a bill banning pedestrians from using mobile devices in crosswalks, with fines ranging from $15 to $99. The law, which could take effect in October, does not apply to talking on the phone. Critics say it's intrusive, while supporters argue it holds pedestrians and motorists responsible for actions on the road. The bill now goes to Mayor Kirk Caldwell for approval.

God's Little People Cat Rescue on the Greek Island of Syros is seeking a live-in caretaker. The job includes free housing and a salary, according to a post on the organization's Facebook page. "PAID JOB OFFER WITH CATS! (this is genuine and NOT a joke — friends, please feel free to verify!)," the posting reads. "A very special position and living circumstance on offer on a little Greek island called Syros (a small paradise no less!)" (Syros is located in the Aegean Sea to the Southeast of Athens, Greece.)

To celebrate the launch of the all-new 2012 CR-V, Honda released a Super Bowl commercial featuring Matthew Broderick reprising his role as Ferris Bueller from the 1986 film. The ad, directed by RPA, serves as a homage to the original movie, with Broderick skipping out on a day of acting work to enjoy a day of slacking in his new CR-V. The commercial includes over two dozen references to Ferris Bueller's Day Off, some obvious and others very subtle, challenging viewers to spot them all. The ad aims to relive movie history while promoting the new CR-V model.
