Two executives from a Chinese bank have been suspended after a video circulated online showing bank employees being publicly spanked as punishment for poor performance during a training session. The video, filmed on a mobile phone, shows a man with a stick spanking eight employees, including four women, in front of around 200 colleagues. The bank president and another executive have been suspended, and the trainer has apologized, admitting that his methods may not be acceptable to everyone. The bank claims the spanking was part of a training session aimed at improving employees' thinking and competitiveness, though many criticized the punishment as a violation of employees' rights.

Jon Stewart's "Rally to Restore Sanity" on the National Mall this Saturday has sparked debate among fans and critics alike. Some worry Stewart is losing his outsider credibility, while others hope the event will boost Democratic electoral prospects. However, Stewart's rally is fundamentally a platform for his own brand, with Stephen Colbert as co-host. The event carries risks, including the potential for Stewart to overstep his role as a comedian and enter the political arena. Stewart's recent interview with President Obama, where he critiqued the administration's cautious approach, highlights his desire to maintain his outsider status while engaging with political issues. The rally aims to address political divisions and mobilize a moderate audience, potentially serving as a publicity stunt for his Comedy Central shows.

RAF jets have been scrambled twice this month in response to potential terror threats over UK airspace, revealing the serious nature of counter-terrorism measures in place since 9/11. Eurofighter Typhoons were dispatched from Coningsby in Lincolnshire after United Airlines flight warnings of "ransom" and "hostage" were overheard. Typhoons circled over Kent as the plane cleared UK airspace, while on 2 March, Typhoons intercepted an American Airlines flight with a distressed passenger, showing the rapid response required. Both incidents were false alarms, but highlight the potential for a decision to shoot down a civilian airliner, a choice to be made by the prime minister or designated cabinet members. These procedures are part of a Strategic Defence Review amid calls for budget cuts, with the RAF, Royal Navy, and Army competing for funding.

Thirty years after a 14-year-old girl's body was found on Torrey Pines State Beach, San Diego homicide investigators identified two suspects in her murder, one of whom was a former San Diego Police criminalist. Claire Hough, a teenager visiting her grandparents, was brutally killed in 1984, with evidence suggesting she was beaten, strangled, stabbed, and had one breast severed. In 2012, DNA evidence linked Kevin Charles Brown and Ronald Clyde Tatro to the crime. Brown, who worked as a criminalist from 1982 to 2002, was found dead in apparent suicide in 2014. Tatro died in a boating accident in 2011. Both men were identified through DNA analysis, though they had no known connection to the case at the time of the murder. The investigation also mentions a similar unsolved murder from 1978.

A New Hampshire couple, Lindsay and Lamar Austin, faced a difficult decision when their nine-months-pregnant wife went into early labor on New Year's Eve. Lamar chose to miss his part-time security guard job in Manchester to drive his wife to Concord Hospital. Their son, Cainan, was born on New Year's Day at 7:44 a.m., making him the first baby born in Concord that year. Lamar, a 30-year-old Army veteran and father of three, felt it was crucial to be present for his son's birth, even if it meant losing his job. The couple, now with four children, expressed gratitude for the support they received and hope for better labor laws to protect working parents.

An EgyptAir flight carrying 66 passengers and crew went missing over the Mediterranean Sea early Thursday, shortly after entering Egyptian airspace on its way from Paris to Cairo. Egyptian and Greek officials say the plane likely crashed into the sea. Debris and body parts have been found, but the plane's black boxes have not yet been located. The cause remains unclear, with terrorism being a possible explanation. France and other nations have joined the search efforts. Among those on board were 30 Egyptians, 15 French, two Iraqis, and passengers from other countries including Sudan, Chad, Portugal, Algeria, Canada, Belgium, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia. The plane was an Airbus A320 with a pilot and co-pilot who had extensive flight experience. EgyptAir and Airbus have provided statements regarding the incident.

A 9-year-old girl and her twin 6-year-old brothers were killed when a pickup truck struck them as they crossed SR 25 to board their school bus near Rochester, Indiana, on Tuesday, October 30, 2018. The siblings, Xzavier and Mason Ingle, and their sister Alivia Stahl, were students at Mentone Elementary School. An 11-year-old boy not related to the siblings was also hit and is in critical condition. The driver, Alyssa Shepherd, 24, has been charged with three counts of reckless homicide and one misdemeanor count of disregarding a stop sign and causing injury. The crash occurred around 7 a.m. as the children were boarding the bus with its stop-arm deployed. The Tippecanoe Valley School Corporation has relocated the bus stop and established a transportation safety review committee. Indiana Governor Eric Holcomb expressed his sorrow and urged prayers for the families.

A theft of at least 70 works of art, valued at over $1 million, has been reported from the National Museum of Fine Arts in Havana, Cuba. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has issued a list of the missing pieces, mostly paintings by Cuban artist Leopoldo Romañach from the "Turn of the Century" period. Cuban authorities found no signs of violence but noted the frames were carefully repositioned, suggesting the theft was planned. The Cuban Minister of Culture was dismissed following the theft, though no reason was given. Law enforcement in both Cuba and the United States are investigating the case, with a Miami art dealer, Ramon Cernuda, first reporting the theft after purchasing a painting registered to the museum. Cernuda believes the theft is significant due to its rarity in Cuba, where museums are well-guarded. The FBI is involved in the investigation, and there is hope the stolen art will be returned to Cuba.

A list of alleged campus rapists has appeared in multiple women's bathroom stalls at Columbia University, drawing attention and controversy. The latest version, found in a Butler women's bathroom, lists the same four names as previous versions, written in silver marker. Campus media have reported on the incidents, with some outlets publishing photos and descriptions of the alleged rapists. Public Safety has begun closing down the bathrooms to remove all traces of the names. The incident echoes a similar event at Brown University in 1990. Columbia University administration has not yet commented on the situation.

A new study finds that people are more empathetic towards abused puppies and dogs than to adult human victims, but show similar levels of empathy for abused children. Researchers from Northeastern University surveyed 240 college students, who read fictional news articles about a brutal beating with the victim being either an infant, an adult in their 30s, a puppy, or a 6-year-old dog. Participants showed higher empathy for the child, puppy, and dog compared to the adult. The study suggests that adult dogs are viewed as dependent and vulnerable, similar to children, while adults are seen as capable of self-protection. Women in the study were more empathetic than men.

Several hundred relatives of Jang Song-thaek, who was executed for plotting to overthrow the North Korean state, have been arrested and sent to political prison camps. A source in Pyongyang told the Daily NK, a defector-run newspaper, that armed men from the Ministry of State Security arrived in the Pyongchon area of Pyongyang on December 13, the day after Jang's execution, to take away relatives, both close and distant. The scale of these arrests highlights the extent to which Kim Jong-un is eradicating his uncle and former mentor from North Korea's history. Jang was accused of 24 crimes, including undermining party unity and engaging in irregularities and corruption. His relatives and associates now face severe punishment, with execution likely for the closest relatives or political allies, and others destined for labor colonies. Some relatives have volunteered for self-imposed punishment, but the Daily NK suggests they will still face severe consequences.

Starting November 3, random CTA train riders will be asked to hand their bags to Chicago police officers for explosive screening at some stations, as part of a federal counter-terrorism initiative. Passengers will be selected at random before passing through turnstiles. Police will swab bags for explosive compounds using a machine that takes about 30 seconds. If a bag fails the test, police may inspect it. Those who refuse to be screened will be ordered to leave the station. The screenings are expected to have no significant impact on commutes. While there is no known terrorist threat, police say the measure is a proactive step to enhance safety. The initiative is fully funded with a portion of a $3.5 million federal anti-terrorism grant.

Actress Jamie Denbo, 43, tweeted about being told she was "too old" to play the wife of a 57-year-old actor in a TV project. The characters have an 18-year-old daughter, making Denbo "too old" to be the mother. Denbo's tweet highlights the persistent issue of ageism in Hollywood, where older actresses struggle to get roles that don't fit the "younger than their partner" stereotype. Denbo's comments come as part of a broader conversation about age discrimination in the film and television industry, with other actresses like Maggie Gyllenhaal and Helen Mirren previously sharing similar experiences. Denbo's tweet aims to draw attention to the absurdity of age-based casting decisions and the need for more diverse and realistic representation of women of all ages.

If only "John Carter" had avoided the toxic buzz surrounding it before release, it might have been more easily accepted as a mildly entertaining, old-school adventure. However, the $250 million budget and the switch from animation to live-action directing by Andrew Stanton have fueled criticism. Despite its flaws, the film exudes the charm of a tall tale, with Taylor Kitsch bringing depth to the role of John Carter, a former Confederate soldier who finds himself on Mars. The 3D effects are less than stellar, but the visual backdrop of Mars is impressive. Willem Dafoe and Lynn Collins deliver strong performances, while the Tharks and other alien races add color. However, the convoluted plot and missed opportunities for innovation leave the film feeling stale.

U.S. Senator John McCain released a statement expressing disappointment with the Syrian regime's complaint to the United Nations regarding McCain's 2013 visit with Syrian rebels. McCain stated that the Assad regime's focus on his visit, rather than its mass killings, is "a sad but unsurprising truth." He emphasized the regime's responsibility for the deaths of over 200,000 people and contrasted it with his own concerns over his diplomatic engagements with the rebels.

A South Carolina serial killer, Todd Kohlhepp, who is already serving life in prison for seven slayings, claims to have two additional victims buried near an interstate. Spartanburg County Sheriff Chuck Wright is bringing Kohlhepp to the county to lead investigators to the supposed locations. Wright is unsure of the identities or exact locations of the supposed victims, and the claims are being investigated. Kohlhepp's crimes were uncovered in 2016 after Kala Brown was rescued from a storage container where she was held captive for two months. He admitted to killing four people at a motorcycle shop in 2003 and has served seven consecutive life terms plus 60 years. The search for the additional victims has not yet turned up any evidence.

The Norwegian man charged with the attacks left behind a 1,500-page manifesto outlining his plans and calling for a Christian war against Muslim domination. Anders Behring Breivik, 32, is described as a right-wing fundamentalist Christian who had been planning for months. The manifesto, titled "2083: A European Declaration of Independence," details his preparations, including buying chemicals and making explosives. Breivik claimed to be part of a group aiming to seize political and military control of Western European countries. He predicted a conflict that would kill or injure over a million people, stating that "the time for dialogue is over" and "armed resistance has come." The attacks, which killed at least 92 people, targeted government buildings and a youth camp, both associated with the Labor Party. Breivik's lawyer said he confessed but denied criminal responsibility, while investigators are looking into the possibility of accomplices. The attacks raised questions about whether Norwegian security agencies had

Ashley Madison claims that business fundamentals remain strong despite a data breach that exposed highly personal details for over 30 million users. The company states that hundreds of thousands of new users, including 87,596 women, signed up in the week following the breach. Ashley Madison disputes claims that the site has few genuine female users, stating that women sent over 2.8 million messages on the platform last week alone. The company's executives also announced that CEO Noel Biderman had left the company by mutual agreement.

Law enforcement officials suggest that the Aurora, Colo., theater shooter had likely practiced extensively before the massacre, based on his "unusually high" hit rate and the complexity of his attack. The gunman, James Holmes, used an AR-15 assault rifle, a shotgun, and a Glock pistol. His apartment was found booby-trapped with explosives. Authorities are searching for evidence of a gun range receipt or related information, which could indicate premeditation and a deliberate plan. Holmes' state of mind and potential insanity defense are under scrutiny. The official believes such evidence would support the prosecution's case against him.

Texting while walking could lead to fines in Fort Lee, New Jersey. The borough, with about 35,000 residents, plans to issue $85 tickets to pedestrians caught using their phones as they walk. Chief Thomas Ripoli of the Fort Lee Police Department says it's a safety issue, citing three fatal pedestrian accidents this year. However, some residents disagree, arguing that they still look around while walking and find the fines too expensive. The Stony Brook University study found that texters are 60% more likely to veer off course than non-texters, highlighting the dangers of multitasking while walking.

Sixteen U.S. Postal Service workers in the Atlanta area were sentenced to federal prison for accepting bribes, some as low as $250, to deliver cocaine on their routes. The U.S. Attorney's Office said these postal workers were bribed by drug traffickers to deliver packages of drugs, which they did in exchange for money. Federal agents learned of the scheme in 2015 while dismantling a drug trafficking organization. Postal workers were willing to deliver packages of cocaine and marijuana for such small bribes. All defendants received sentences between three and nine years in prison, and were ordered to pay restitution or forfeiture.

The Texas State Board of Education approved a resolution requiring publishers to correct a "pro-Islamic/anti-Christian bias" in future world history textbooks. Passed 7-6, the resolution aims to ensure more balanced coverage of Christianity and other non-Muslim faiths. Critics argue the measure is politically motivated and could undermine the board's reputation. Board members cited past instances of perceived bias and warned publishers against future prejudicial submissions.

The Bernie Sanders campaign and the Democratic National Committee (DNC) engaged in a heated dispute over voter data access, escalating tensions within the Democratic primary. The Sanders campaign accused the DNC of sabotage, while the DNC cut off Sanders' access to his own voter files, claiming the data breach was due to a software glitch. After negotiations and discussions with a federal judge, the DNC agreed to restore access to the data, but the Sanders campaign vowed to pursue legal action. The controversy highlighted long-standing suspicions among Sanders supporters that the DNC was favoring Hillary Clinton, and it threatened to disrupt the campaign's field operations. The Sanders campaign fired a staffer involved in the breach and accused the DNC of using the incident as a political tool. Both campaigns accused each other of data theft, with the Clinton campaign arguing that the Sanders team had improperly accessed valuable voter information. The dispute underscored the contentious nature of the Democratic primary and raised questions about the fairness of the nomination process.

Lea Michele and her 'Glee' co-stars posed for a racy shoot in the new issue of GQ, stepping away from their family-friendly image. "I've never been shot in so little clothing," Michele, 24, said. "I don't know how they got me to do half the stuff I did." The cover story also delves into the lives of the 'Glee' cast and the show's fanbase, known as "Gleeks." Michele recalls being told to get a nose job early in her career but refused, saying, "Barbra Streisand didn't get a nose job. You're not getting a nose job." 'Glee' co-creator Ryan Murphy discusses his approach to creating the show, aiming for a responsible family-friendly version. The article highlights a surreal moment for the cast, performing at the White House Easter Egg Roll, where they felt like they could be shot at any moment.

The White House continued to monitor Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli leaders, despite a promise to limit surveillance on friendly heads of state after Edward Snowden's leaks. The NSA intercepted private conversations involving members of Congress, raising concerns about potential legal and political ramifications. The administration feared Netanyahu might launch a surprise attack on Iran and later became worried about his intentions regarding the Iran nuclear deal. Intercepts showed Israel's knowledge of the negotiations and attempts to undermine the deal. To avoid accusations of spying on Congress, the White House left it to the NSA to handle the information, which was then sanitized. The White House defended its actions, stating that surveillance is conducted only for specific national security purposes. The Israeli embassy denied the allegations, while some U.S. officials and lawmakers expressed skepticism.

Elton John has reignited his long-standing feud with Madonna, calling her a "fucking fairground stripper" in an interview. The comments were triggered by Madonna's criticism of Lady Gaga, whom Elton considers a friend and godmother to his son Zachary. Elton also criticized Madonna's recent MDNA world tour and her career, stating her "career is over." He believes Madonna should have focused on making "great pop records" instead of dance music. The comments come after Madonna accused Lady Gaga of copying her hit "Express Yourself" in "Born This Way." Elton's wife, David Furnish, had previously called Madonna "embarrassing" and "desperate" after she won the Best Original Song award at the Golden Globes.

New York caffeine addicts now have a novel way to stay awake: Perky Jerky, the world's first caffeinated beef jerky. Invented by Matt Keiser after spilling Red Bull on a jerky snack, Perky Jerky combines the savory meat with a 60 mg caffeine hit, equivalent to a small cup of coffee. Available in 1 oz. ($2.99) and 2 oz. ($4.99) bags, the jerky has hit the market and will be sold in Sports Authority shops. While some find it unappetizing, others appreciate its unique energy boost. Perky Jerky positions itself as a natural, protein-rich snack for active lifestyles, offering a taste experience unlike any other.

After customer complaints, Lululemon blamed a Taiwanese supplier for producing see-through black yoga pants, but the supplier denied any issues. The dispute highlights Lululemon's quality control problems, which have included color bleeding and transparency issues in recent years. Analysts suggest Lululemon needs better oversight of its supply chain. The company cut its first-quarter sales forecast by around $20 million and offered refunds, leading to a 5% drop in its stock price.

Tiger Woods, 37, has reportedly started a new romance with Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn, 28, after his divorce from Elin Nordegren in 2010. The pair, who met through their children's skiing, have been dating for two months and spent a romantic vacation in Antigua. However, Lindsey's friends are worried about dating a man with a history of cheating. Tiger has been seen pulling out all the stops to win Lindsey over, despite his past indiscretions.

Fame, fortune, and power can be fleeting, as evidenced by the recent fall from grace of 50 well-known individuals from various fields, including television personalities, CEOs, financial wizards, and politicians. This list, compiled by 24/7 Wall St., highlights the rapid decline in status and influence of these public figures, showcasing the volatility of power in American culture. Highlights include Anthony Scaramucci, fired from his role as White House Communications Director; Chris Christie, former Governor of New Jersey with plummeting approval ratings; James Comey, former Director of the FBI abruptly terminated by President Trump; Mark Fields, former CEO of Ford Motor Company dismissed amid financial struggles; and Tiger Woods, once the top-ranked golfer in the world, now facing personal and professional challenges.

Juneau police defended their response to the death of newly elected mayor Stephen "Greg" Fisk, who was found bruised and bloodied at home. The case garnered national attention, with speculation that foul play was involved. Police deferred ruling out foul play until autopsy results came back, stating they had to consider all possibilities. Preliminary results indicated natural causes and injuries consistent with falling or stumbling. Police chief Bryce Johnson noted the initial assumption was an assault due to the injuries, but they had to rule out all possibilities. Fisk, a fisheries consultant, had a history of heart issues and was sworn in as mayor in October. His adult son, Ian, found him after missed appointments. The family is grieving privately.

Lady Gaga honored David Bowie with a technologically enhanced performance at the 2016 Grammys, featuring special effects, costume changes, and Nile Rodgers. The tribute included songs like "Space Oddity," "Changes," and "Heroes," showcasing Bowie's eclectic career. Gaga's performance, powered by Intel, highlighted her deep admiration for Bowie, who inspired her artistic journey.

Robin Williams, who died at 63, left an indelible mark on multiple generations, particularly those in their mid-to-late 20s and early 30s. His career transitioned from edgy comedy and dramatic roles to voice acting in children's films, notably as the Genie in "Aladdin." Williams' performance as the Genie was a triumph, bringing imaginative expansiveness to Disney's story. His willingness to abandon his recognizable face for the role of the Genie, and his commitment to entertaining children, exemplified his generosity and humility. Williams often played characters who were childlike or trapped in a child's body, reflecting his own sense of innocence and unselfishness. Despite his Oscar nominations and public profile, Williams was remembered for his ability to bring joy to his young audiences, making his legacy as much about his impact on childhood as his filmography.

A premature infant named Oakleigh Nance, born at 3 pounds, has been battling a severe UTI and a sudden fever, leading to the discovery of stage 3 kidney reflux and a dangerous, antibiotic-resistant Pseudomonas infection. She has also been diagnosed with heart conditions, including moderate ASD and pulmonary stenosis. Oakleigh is scheduled for a 4.5-hour surgery to address her kidney issues, followed by further testing for her heart conditions. Her family, thankful for the support, hopes for Oakleigh's recovery and is raising funds for her medical expenses.

Donald Trump acknowledged during a South Carolina town hall that he "could have" signaled support for invading Iraq in a 2002 interview with Howard Stern, though he was against the war by the time it started. Trump criticized former President George W. Bush for launching the war and has been dominating South Carolina polls. The town hall also featured Trump's confrontations with Jeb Bush and John Kasich over the Pope's comments, with Trump calling the Pope a "wonderful guy." Trump continued to attack his closest competitor, Ted Cruz, and defended his fast food consumption habits. The event highlighted Trump's tendency for colorful, unfiltered language and his ability to switch between being politically correct and not. Other candidates, including Jeb Bush and John Kasich, discussed their foreign policy views and personal experiences, with Bush expressing frustration with the pace of the campaign.

Men in Black III, 15 years after the original and 10 since the sequel, is surprisingly better than the first installment. The plot involves Agent K (Tommy Lee Jones) and Agent J (Will Smith) facing an alien threat, with J traveling back in time to prevent K from being killed. The film's most impressive aspect is the casting of Josh Brolin as the young Agent K, who uncannily resembles and sounds like the original. Despite some confusing and out-of-touch elements, the movie offers comic relief, intriguing time travel sequences, and a touching final scene. While the first Men in Black movie was entertaining, this sequel proves to be an enjoyable, if uneven, experience.

Attorney General Eric Holder denied any "cover-up" over "Operation Fast and Furious" during a House panel investigation, asserting he has nothing to hide and the probe is politically motivated. Holder stated there's no attempt at a cover-up and that he has shared extensive information. He denied authorizing controversial tactics and said no one has been disciplined yet, despite lost guns from the operation being linked to the death of U.S. Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry. Republicans accused Holder of withholding key documents and suggested firings and charges are likely. The hearing highlighted ongoing tensions between the Justice Department and lawmakers over the botched gun-running operation.

President Trump criticized Nordstrom for discontinuing his daughter Ivanka's clothing line, leading to a brief dip in Nordstrom's stock but ultimately resulting in a 5% increase by the end of the day. The White House accused Nordstrom of making a "direct attack" on administration policies, though the company stated the decision was based on poor sales performance. T. J. Maxx also dropped Ivanka's line, but no presidential tweets addressed this move.

Larry Villarin, a 62-year-old Californian, serves as America's oldest male sexual surrogate, helping clients overcome sexual dysfunction through one-on-one sessions. Since 1973, he has worked with over 100 clients, including disabled individuals, abuse survivors, and those from strict religious backgrounds. Larry's clients, ranging in age from 22 to 75, often seek his help to address emotional baggage, such as social anxiety or PTSD, before attempting real-life intimacy. Sessions involve non-sexual touch and exercises, with sexual activities gradually introduced. Larry uses techniques like blindfolded "trust walks" and mirror exercises to help clients open up. His work, though challenging, has led to significant personal growth and increased confidence for many clients.

Tunisians expressed particular joy at the downfall of the Trabelsi family, wife and relatives of ousted president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, who were widely seen as symbols of corruption and excess. The Trabelsis controlled significant parts of Tunisia's economy, including banks, airlines, car dealerships, and media, and were accused of using their influence to extort money and divide business profits. Following Ben Ali's departure, many of their properties and businesses were looted and burned, with some reports of violence against family members. The Trabelsis' influence and corruption played a crucial role in the regime's fall, reflecting broader public dissatisfaction with joblessness and political repression.

Tunisian towns have opened their homes to thousands of fleeing Libyans, mirroring a century-old pattern of Libyans seeking refuge from Italian colonizers. Since early April, about 30,000 Libyans have sought shelter with Tunisian families, who have shown remarkable generosity despite their own economic challenges. Local mayor Ali Mourou praised the community's response, noting that aid has flowed in from across Tunisia. However, the strain on resources is growing, with concerns about the economy and infrastructure. Meanwhile, the conflict between pro-Gaddafi forces and rebels has spilled over the border, with Gaddafi troops briefly occupying Tunisian territory and artillery shells striking the Tunisian side of the crossing. The situation in Misrata remains dire, with rebels accusing Gaddafi's forces of using larger rockets and civilians suffering from shelling. NATO's role in protecting civilians has come under scrutiny, as the military deadlock exposes growing international rifts.

A man who jumped the White House fence on Tuesday was apprehended by uniformed Secret Service officers who approached him with guns drawn, reports CNN. The incident occurred around 9 p.m. and was broadcast live on the network's "John King USA" program. The man, identified as James Dirk Crudup, 41, and homeless, was charged with unlawful entry and contempt of court due to a previous order to stay away from the White House. A backpack found near the fence was being examined. The White House was briefly locked down, but an all-clear was issued shortly after.

On Thursday, Jurgen Klinsmann, the coach of the U.S. national men's soccer team, dined with President Obama, Chancellor Merkel, Nobel laureates, and astronauts at a Berlin gala. The next day, Klinsmann faced criticism for recent losses that jeopardized his team's World Cup qualification chances. Despite this, Klinsmann defended his coaching record and expressed confidence in his position. However, on Monday, U.S. Soccer unexpectedly fired Klinsmann. The federation's president, Sunil Gulati, stated that while the team had quality players, their recent form necessitated a change in direction. Bruce Arena is expected to take over as Klinsmann's replacement.

Advisers to Mitt Romney defended his criticism of President Obama, arguing that the deadly protests in the Middle East would not have occurred if Romney were in office. Romney’s campaign emphasized the need for a strong American presence and leadership in the region, while Obama faced criticism for stating that Egypt was not an ally. Romney’s aggressive response to the situation was supported by influential foreign policy experts, who contrasted his approach with Obama’s. Romney’s campaign hopes to capitalize on this foreign policy debate, highlighting perceived weaknesses in Obama’s handling of crises and questioning his reliability as a global leader.

Four ordinary people—Bill Badger, Patricia Maisch, Roger Salzgeber, and Joseph Zamudio—became extraordinary heroes when they stopped a shooting rampage at a Tucson grocery store, preventing a greater catastrophe. Maisch, a 61-year-old grandmother, grabbed the magazine as the gunman tried to reload, while Badger, a 74-year-old retired Army colonel, and Salzgeber tackled the shooter. Zamudio, who was in a nearby store, helped hold the assailant down. The gunman, 22-year-old Jared Loughner, was armed with a 9-millimeter Glock semi-automatic. Federal charges were filed against him, including attempted assassination of a member of Congress. Pima County Sheriff Clarence Dupnik criticized the political climate and Arizona's gun laws, suggesting they may contribute to such incidents.

A substitute teacher was arrested for being drunk at Brookland-Cayce High School in Lexington, South Carolina, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Judith Elizabeth Richards-Gartee, 52, was found by an administrator who called a resource officer. The school district stated that Richards-Gartee is not an employee but works for Kelly Services, which contracts with the district to provide substitute teachers. She was charged with disorderly conduct and found in possession of an open container of alcohol. The sheriff's department will not release further details.

James Gandolfini, known for his role as Tony Soprano on The Sopranos, has died at the age of 51 from a possible heart attack while on vacation in Rome. Gandolfini, who won three consecutive Emmy Awards for his portrayal of the troubled crime boss, was set to participate in the 59th Taormina Film Festival in Sicily. His death sent shockwaves through the entertainment industry, with fellow actors and producers expressing their grief. Gandolfini's co-star Edie Falco called him "a man of tremendous depth and sensitivity, with a kindness and generosity beyond words." The Sopranos creator David Chase praised Gandolfini as "a genius" and "one of the greatest actors of this or any time." Gandolfini's career extended beyond The Sopranos, including roles in films like The Man Who Wasn't There and Zero Dark Thirty, as well as producing documentaries and working on

President Donald Trump declared the summit with North Korea's Kim Jong Un had gone better than expected after nearly four hours of talks in Singapore. The two leaders signed a document committing to work together for peace. Trump expressed optimism, while U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo cautioned about North Korea's sincerity regarding denuclearization. Staff-level meetings aimed to lay groundwork for the historic meeting, with discussions focusing on a peace-keeping mechanism and denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. North Korea's state-run media emphasized the summit's significance, though experts remain skeptical about the outcome.

France's National Assembly approved the government’s controversial same-sex marriage bill in a final vote on Tuesday, marking a significant step toward legalizing same-sex marriage. The law, which redefines marriage as a contract between two people rather than between a man and a woman, passed by a 329 to 229 vote, with 10 deputies abstaining. The bill must now be approved by the left-wing-controlled Senate, expected to pass it on April 2. France would join 11 other countries, including Spain, Sweden, and South Africa, in legalizing same-sex marriage. The legislation has faced strong opposition from the Roman Catholic Church and social conservatives, with large protests against the reform. While polls show a majority of French people support same-sex marriage, there is less agreement on adoption rights. The move is seen as France’s biggest social reform since the abolition of the death penalty in 1981.

Christina Grimmie's family expresses gratitude for the outpouring of love and support following her death, stating that her life was special to everyone she touched. Adam Levine of Maroon 5 offers to pay for Grimmie's funeral expenses, while a GoFundMe page set up by her manager has raised over $100,000 for the same purpose. Grimmie, 22, was shot and killed by a deranged fan at a concert in Orlando, Florida, on June 10. Her brother tackled the shooter, who then fatally shot himself.

Harrison Ford, 72, was injured when his vintage World War II-era plane crash-landed on a Los Angeles golf course. Ford reported engine trouble shortly after takeoff and attempted an emergency landing to avoid homes. He suffered moderate injuries, including a deep cut on his head, and was treated by doctors and paramedics on the scene. Ford's son, Ben, tweeted that his father was "battered, but OK" and expected to make a full recovery. The actor, known for his love of flying, has had several brushes with aviation incidents in the past.

The Food and Drug Administration has ordered 23andMe to halt sales of its genetic testing kit, citing concerns over the test's effectiveness and potential to mislead consumers. The company, founded by Anne Wojcicki, offers a Personal Genome Service that detects over 240 genetic conditions and traits, including heart disease and breast cancer risks. Despite multiple interactions with FDA officials, 23andMe has failed to provide the necessary scientific data to prove the test works as advertised. The FDA warns that false positive or negative results could lead to unnecessary or ineffective treatments. 23andMe has 15 days to respond with a plan to address the FDA's concerns or face regulatory actions such as civil fines or injunctions. The move highlights the FDA's growing oversight of direct-to-consumer genetic testing and the debate over individual access to genetic information.

An Egyptian blogger was sentenced to three years in prison with hard labor for claiming that 45% of married women are ready for "immorality" and could cheat on their husbands, reports CNN. His comments, made on a television show in December, sparked public outrage and led to his arrest. State-run newspaper Al-Ahram reported that the court found his statements would harm public peace and damage public interest. The blogger can still appeal the sentence. Critics argue that such cases reflect broader harassment and threats against non-political individuals under President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's regime. Similar incidents, like the expulsion of a parliament member for meeting with an Israeli diplomat, highlight how public opinion and pressure, rather than the law, often determine outcomes.

Rosemont authorities have closed the investigation into Kenneka Jenkins' death, ruling it accidental after reviewing surveillance video, interviewing witnesses, and conducting forensic analyses. Jenkins, 19, was found dead in a hotel freezer nearly 24 hours after going missing from a party. Police stated there was no evidence of foul play, though lawyers for Jenkins' mother argue the postmortem photographs, showing her body exposed, raise more questions than answers. The Cook County Medical Examiner's office had already classified Jenkins' death as accidental, caused by hypothermia and alcohol intoxication. Police also identified two individuals who booked the hotel room with a fraudulent credit card. The case has sparked social media speculation and conspiracy theories, with some questioning how Jenkins could have removed her own clothes while freezing to death.

A drunk passenger tried to enter the cockpit of an Indian aircraft on September 24, 2018, in Mumbai, to charge his phone, according to an airline spokesperson. The passenger was removed from the IndiGo flight 6E-395 bound for Kolkata and handed over to the police but was later released without charge. In another incident, a first-time flyer mistook a plane door for a toilet and attempted to open it mid-air during a GoAir flight from New Delhi to Patna on September 22. Passengers alerted the crew, and the man was taken to the police station after the plane landed safely.

The U.S. Olympic Committee (USOC) is set to hold a hearing that could lead to the dissolution of USA Gymnastics, the sport's national governing body, due to the organization's decision not to voluntarily surrender its status. In a statement, USOC CEO Sarah Hirshland said the USOC is moving forward with the process to revoke USA Gymnastics' NGB status, as the organization has not chosen to relinquish it voluntarily. The next step involves selecting a three-person panel to hear the USOC's complaint, with the panel expected to issue a report and recommendation to the USOC’s board of directors after the hearing. USA Gymnastics will continue to operate during this process, but if its NGB status is stripped, the USOC would take control of the elite programs until a new NGB is identified. The decision to proceed with the revocation process comes after USA Gymnastics faced criticism for its handling of the Larry Nassar sexual abuse scandal and subsequent

Adonis Johnson Creed, the son of Apollo Creed, seeks to follow his father's boxing legacy. After Apollo's tragic death in the ring, Adonis travels to Philadelphia to find Rocky Balboa and enlist his help. Balboa, now retired, takes Adonis under his wing, guiding him through training and preparing him for a title shot. The film, while formulaic, offers emotional depth and a satisfying conclusion, blending nostalgia with new characters and themes.

Tiger Woods is planning to return to the PGA tour in the spring, according to RadarOnline.com. He is currently undergoing rehab for sexual addiction at Pine Grove Behavioral Health and Addiction Services in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, a facility directed by Dr. Patrick Carnes. Woods hopes to have his life back on track and is not publicly revealing his plan to return to golf this spring, believing that going through rehab will help him convince everyone, including corporate sponsors, that he has changed. Tiger's wife, Elin, has not visited him during his treatment and has not filed for divorce, raising speculation about the future of their marriage. Woods has been romantically linked to at least 14 women during his marriage, with his most recent affair with Rachel Uchitel leading to his scandal.

The search continues for three missing children of the Hart family whose SUV plunged off a California cliff, killing five family members. Surveillance footage from a Safeway in Fort Bragg, California, taken a day before the crash, shows Jennifer Hart purchasing groceries, but authorities are unsure of the whereabouts of her wife and other children at the time. The California Highway Patrol believes the crash may have been intentional, with no skid marks found at the top of the dirt turnout where the SUV pulled off. Authorities are retracing the family's route based on cellphone pings and have pieced together that they were in the Newport, Oregon, area on March 24 before traveling south to Fort Bragg. A neighbor, Bruce DeKalb, reported to Child Protective Services that Devonte, one of the missing children, had been asking for food frequently, suggesting concerns about the family's treatment of their children. The Harts had faced past allegations of abuse, including a 2011 domestic assault conviction

The Tsarnaev brothers, immigrants from Chechnya, came to America seeking a new life. Tamerlan, the older brother, was a talented boxer who eventually quit college, got married, and had a child. Dzhokar, the younger brother, won a scholarship and wrestled in high school. Despite their American journey, hints of unhappiness emerged. Tamerlan expressed in a photo essay that he didn't have any American friends and struggled to fit in. He had a history of domestic violence and showed interest in radical Islamic websites. Dzhokar, on the other hand, was described by friends as quiet and grateful to be in the United States. The FBI interviewed Tamerlan in 2011 after receiving a tip that he was radicalizing, but found no evidence of terrorism. The brothers' uncle, Ruslan, described them as peace-loving and denied any connection to the bombings, suggesting someone else radicalized them. The tragic events that followed left

A new study in the BMJ suggests that playing golf can offer longevity benefits similar to those of high-intensity endurance activities like cycling and rowing. The research analyzed the mortality records of 9,889 Olympic athletes who competed between 1896 and 1936, across various disciplines with differing levels of exercise intensity. The findings indicate that athletes engaged in moderate or high cardiovascular intensity exercises did not have a significantly lower mortality risk compared to those who played sports with lower intensity, such as golf or cricket. However, athletes involved in sports with a high risk of bodily collision or intense physical contact had a higher mortality risk later in life. The study highlights that while high-intensity exercise may offer some health benefits, it may also come with potential long-term risks, especially for sports involving frequent collisions or intense physical contact.

The Eta Aquarid meteor shower, a result of Earth passing through debris left by Halley's Comet, will peak on May 5 and 6, offering a chance to see up to 10 to 20 meteors per hour from anywhere on Earth, provided skies are clear and free from light pollution. The meteors will appear to originate from the constellation Aquarius, rising in the early morning hours. NASA suggests the morning of May 5 might offer slightly better viewing conditions. For those unable to watch during these mornings, the Slooh Community Observatory will host a live show beginning at 8 p.m. EDT on May 5. This meteor shower is notable for producing "persistent trains," colorful, lingering streaks in the sky, due to the high speed of the meteors.

During the third night of the Democratic National Convention, Barack Obama surprised everyone by giving Jill Biden, his running mate Joe Biden's wife, a kiss on the lips. This incident sparked curiosity and speculation about whether it was a deliberate show of affection or an accidental peck. Obama has a history of smooching powerful women, including Diane Sawyer, Hillary Clinton, and Dr. Jill Biden. However, his attempts to kiss Carla Bruni, the French First Lady, were unsuccessful, leading to a handshake instead. The lack of a kiss between Obama and Bruni caused a stir in the media, with some speculating on the reasons behind the missed opportunity.

A former Dallas police officer, Amber Guyger, has been indicted on a murder charge for shooting and killing Botham Shem Jean in his apartment. The indictment came more than two months after Guyger's arrest in the September shooting, initially charged with manslaughter. District Attorney Faith Johnson stated that the murder charge was based on the evidence presented, which showed Guyger's actions as intentional at the moment of the shooting. Jean's family and legal representatives expressed satisfaction with the indictment, viewing it as a step toward justice. Guyger, who claimed she mistook Jean's apartment for her own, was fired by the Dallas Police Department and is now facing a more serious charge than initially presented.

Coca-Cola has launched its first alcoholic drink, a lemon-flavored alcopop, in Japan, marking a significant first for the company's 132-year history. The fizzy lemon drinks, ranging from 3% to 8% alcohol, hit the shelves on Monday and are aimed at a growing market of young drinkers, especially women. Modeled on popular Chu-Hi drinks, a mix of local spirit and fruit flavors, the new product is part of Coca-Cola's strategy to tap into new markets. However, there are no plans to introduce these drinks to markets outside Japan. The launch comes as alcopop drinks boomed in Europe and the UK in the 1990s, with brands like Smirnoff Ice and Bacardi Breezer becoming hugely popular.

After a dramatic finale, more than 190 countries adopted a set of agreements in Cancún that lay the groundwork for future climate change negotiations, restoring faith in the UN process but falling short of scientists' demands. The Cancun Agreements commit all major economies to greenhouse gas cuts, establish a "green fund" for climate change adaptation, and tackle deforestation. While the deal is seen as a significant turning point, it does not reduce temperatures as much as scientists say is needed. Bolivia, the only country to object, criticized the agreement as insufficient. The package, though not legally binding, paves the way for stronger measures in the future, with the next climate conference in Durban aiming to produce a legally binding global climate framework.

Researchers used human face recognition techniques to study guenon monkeys, finding that their distinctive facial features evolved to avoid crossbreeding. These monkeys, native to Central and West Africa, live in close proximity to multiple species, increasing the risk of interbreeding. By analyzing over 150 guenon monkeys, both in the wild and in zoos, the team discovered that facial patterns are remarkably similar within the same species but vary significantly between species. This visual diversity acts as a barrier to breeding, ensuring species remain distinct. The findings, published in Nature Communications, provide strong evidence that guenon monkeys use their unique appearances to recognize and avoid interbreeding with other species.

Mitt Romney and Sarah Palin lead the Republican field for the 2012 presidential nomination, but their broader prospects look vastly different. In a general-election trial heat, Romney runs evenly with Barack Obama among all Americans and slightly outpoints him among registered voters. However, Romney is the only Republican to do so well, with Obama leading other potential opponents like Palin, Newt Gingrich, Tim Pawlenty, Michele Bachmann, and Jon Huntsman. Palin faces significant challenges, with 64% of Americans saying they definitely will not vote for her, and 63% describing her as unqualified for the job. Romney, on the other hand, is strongest among those earning more than $100,000 a year and those with college degrees. The economy remains a major issue, with 89% of Americans saying it is in bad shape, and 57% saying it has not yet begun to recover. Obama's approval ratings have dropped, with

Sen. Dianne Feinstein of California accused the CIA of improperly searching a computer network established for Congress as part of an investigation into CIA abuse during the Bush era. CIA Director John Brennan denied the allegations, stating the agency was not spying on the Senate Intelligence Committee. The search of the committee's computers, according to Feinstein, may have violated the Constitution and federal laws, including the Fourth Amendment and an executive order prohibiting domestic surveillance. Feinstein called for an apology and acknowledgment from the CIA, but none was received. The matter has been referred to the Justice Department for possible criminal prosecution.

A new study from Cornell University reveals that adults consume nearly 92% of the food they place on their plates, suggesting that most people are part of the Clean Plate Club. Researchers analyzed data from 1,179 diners across eight developed countries and found that cultural and gender differences had little impact on this behavior. Children, however, ate only about 60% of what they served themselves, possibly due to uncertainty about their food preferences. This finding can help individuals be more mindful of appropriate portion sizes, as knowing they are likely to eat most of what they serve can influence their serving choices.

The Trump administration has reportedly reached a deal with Chinese telecommunications giant ZTE to ease penalties and allow the company to resume business with U.S. companies, including chipmaker Qualcomm. The deal requires ZTE to pay a $1.3 billion fine, implement U.S. compliance officers, and make management changes. However, top senators, including Democrats and Republicans, are urging the administration not to bend on ZTE, citing concerns about national security. ZTE, which was banned from buying U.S. technology components for seven years after violating sanctions against Iran and North Korea, has been accused of being a significant risk to U.S. national security and intellectual property theft. Despite the deal, many in Congress oppose it, fearing it rewards a company that poses a threat to U.S. interests.

An Ontario judge has acquitted animal activist Anita Krajnc of mischief for giving water to pigs on a truck heading to a slaughterhouse. Krajnc, founder of Toronto Pig Save, was charged after providing water to thirsty pigs in June 2015. The judge ruled that Krajnc did not interfere with the lawful use of the pigs' property, as they were eventually slaughtered. Despite the Crown's argument that Krajnc could have given the pigs an "unknown substance," there was no evidence of this, and the pigs were ultimately slaughtered without issue. Krajnc was not guilty of the charge, and the case has drawn international attention, with supporters seeing it as a victory for animal rights. However, farm groups remain disappointed, citing concerns about food safety and the potential for further confrontations.

A new ISIS media group called Zora has begun distributing guidelines for women supporting Isis fighters in Syria and Iraq. These guidelines, aimed at women already supporting Isis or preparing to join, provide advice on how to be "good wives of jihad," including roles in cooking, nursing, and creating propaganda. The Zora Foundation's social media accounts, established just over two weeks ago, have garnered over 2,000 followers. Analysts note this is the first time a media organization has officially provided guidance to women on their role in supporting Isis.

McDonald's Mighty Wings are back on the menu with a significant price reduction, now sold in packs of five for $3, or about 60 cents per wing, down from the original $1 per wing. National advertising for the bone-in chicken wings began this week, following poor sales during initial regional testing. McDonald's spokesperson Lisa McComb explains that the earlier pricing did not reflect broader customer preferences for the wings' price and spice level. The wings, introduced in September 2013, faced disappointing sales, leaving the company with about 10 million pounds of frozen wings by the end of 2013. McDonald's hopes the new, more affordable price will boost sales and recoup costs.

Pakistani security officials believe one of Osama bin Laden's sons may have gone missing after the Navy SEAL raid that killed the al-Qaeda leader. Three of bin Laden's wives, currently in custody, told interrogators that one of his sons was not seen since the raid. The disappearance of bin Laden's youngest son, Hamza, who was dubbed the "Crown Prince of Terror," has raised concerns. Initially, the U.S. claimed Hamza, 20, was killed in the raid, but later stated that his 22-year-old brother Khalid was killed. The uncertainty surrounding the identities and numbers of individuals in the compound where bin Laden was hiding for five years adds to the confusion. Bin Laden had at least 18 children, none of whom were groomed for leadership roles within al-Qaeda, according to former White House counterterrorism advisor Richard Clarke.

A massive ancient ocean once covered nearly half of Mars’s northern hemisphere, making the planet a more promising place for alien life to have emerged, NASA scientists say. This vast body of water, as large as the Atlantic Ocean on Earth, spread over about one-fifth of Mars’s surface and was up to a mile deep in some areas, holding more than 20 million cubic kilometers of water. The evidence comes from maps of atmospheric water and its deuterated form across Mars, revealing strong isotopic anomalies and a significant high D/H enrichment, indicating a substantial loss of water over time. The maps show that water ice in the polar reservoirs is enriched in deuterium to at least 8 VSMOW, suggesting an early Mars with a global equivalent water layer at least 137 meters deep. This finding, published in Science, supports the idea of Mars as a warm and wet world shortly after its formation 4.5 billion years ago, with long-standing bodies of water

Iran's morality police are enforcing a ban on Barbie dolls to protect the public from what they view as harmful Western cultural influences, shopkeepers report. The ban, part of a "soft war" against decadent cultural impacts, has forced toy shops to secretly sell the dolls while hiding them from plain sight. Despite a ban since 1996, Barbies have remained available, but now must be sold discreetly to avoid police closure. Official dolls like Sara and Dara, launched in 2002, have failed to gain popularity. Iranians continue their battle to purge Western culture, enforcing Islamic dress codes and banning Western music and satellite TV since the 1979 Islamic revolution. In another cultural response, an Iranian company plans to send a miniature model of the U.S. RQ-170 Sentinel drone to the U.S. government in response to a request to return the aircraft, which Iran claims entered its airspace illegally.

President Obama told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu the U.S. would reassess aspects of its relationship with Israel after Netanyahu's election campaign comments opposing a Palestinian state. The phone call, officially a message of congratulations, also carried a serious warning. Obama emphasized the U.S. commitment to a two-state solution. Netanyahu walked back his disavowal of a Palestinian state, stating he supports a two-state solution but conditions must change. He also addressed his campaign rhetoric about Arab voters, saying it was a "cynical Election Day tactic." The U.S. may reconsider its stance on a UN resolution supporting a Palestinian state. U.S. officials view Netanyahu's election campaign comments as a significant setback for U.S.-Israel relations, despite his reaffirmation of the two-state solution.

A sketchbook of drawings by Vincent Van Gogh, the post-Impressionist master, has been discovered and will be published in November by the French publisher Seuil. The artwork, titled "Vincent Van Gogh, Le Brouillard d’Arles" (The Fog of Arles), was known only to the owners and the publisher, Bernard Comment, who described the discovery as "stunning, dazzling." Details about the origin and discovery of the sketches remain undisclosed, with Seuil planning a press conference in Paris to reveal more information.

The smaller of twin giant panda cubs born to Mei Xiang at the Smithsonian's National Zoo died Wednesday afternoon, leaving the larger cub as the sole survivor. The smaller cub, weighing just 3 ounces at birth, showed signs of regurgitation and was having trouble breathing. Despite efforts to save it, including CPR, the cub went into respiratory and cardiac arrest. Mei Xiang, the 17-year-old mother, has been caring for the larger cub, which appears to be strong and healthy. This is the third time in three years that Mei Xiang has lost a cub, with the other two deaths occurring in 2012 and 2013.

At least 81 people, including 32 suspected militants and 23 hostages, died in a four-day hostage crisis at an Algerian gas plant, with five suspected militants arrested after the Algerian military ended the siege. The death toll is expected to rise as de-mining teams found more bodies. British, American, Filipino, and French workers were among those killed. The siege began when militants attacked buses carrying foreign workers and then took hostages at the facility. The Algerian government blamed the attack on Islamist militants seeking revenge for French intervention in Mali. Five suspected militants, including the alleged leader Mokhtar Belmokhtar, have been arrested. The crisis highlights the ongoing threat of terrorism in the region and the challenges faced by authorities in responding to such incidents.

Vatican officials are investigating a leak of Pope Francis' highly anticipated encyclical on the environment, with the full 191-page document published online three days ahead of its scheduled release. The Italian magazine L'Espresso posted the draft, which covers Francis' calls for radical changes to address global warming and protect the planet. The Vatican has indefinitely suspended the press credentials of L'Espresso's Vatican correspondent, Sandro Magister, who claims his editor obtained the document and decided to publish it. Several theories suggest the leak aimed to undermine the official launch, which includes discussions by a Catholic cardinal, an Orthodox theologian, an atheist scientist, and an economist. Some speculate the leak came from conservatives within the Vatican, opposing Francis' reform plans and his stance on climate change. The incident echoes past Vatican leaks, including the 2012 "Vatileaks" scandal, and highlights the ongoing challenge of maintaining confidentiality in the world's most secretive bureaucracy.

Poland's justice minister has criticized a controversial raid on the offices of news magazine Wprost, which published alleged private conversations involving top government officials. The raid, aimed at finding leaked tapes embarrassing to the government, has raised concerns about the breach of journalistic confidentiality and legal procedures. The tapes, which reportedly involved discussions about political appointments and economic crises, were obtained by an unnamed businessman and later provided to authorities. The incident has put Prime Minister Donald Tusk under pressure, with him suggesting a snap election if the crisis in confidence continues.
