Colgate Total® toothpaste has been a trusted choice for over two decades, backed by extensive clinical studies and endorsements from dentists worldwide. Formulated with 0.3% triclosan, it fights plaque germs that cause common oral health issues. With more than 90 clinical studies involving over 20,000 participants, Colgate Total® demonstrates superior efficacy in reducing gum disease-causing germs and providing 12-hour protection against plaque. It is clinically proven to be more effective than regular fluoride toothpaste in preventing gum disease, with studies showing a 22% reduction in plaque and gingivitis. The FDA supports its safety and effectiveness, noting that triclosan in Colgate Total® toothpaste is effective in preventing gingivitis. Unlike regular fluoride toothpaste, Colgate Total® also offers direct anti-inflammatory benefits, a crucial aspect of maintaining overall oral health.

Rep. Peter King demands a full investigation into a recent White House security breach, suggesting Congress may hold hearings. The New York Republican, a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, criticizes the incident as inexcusable, especially considering the current threat landscape. Meanwhile, Sen. Dianne Feinstein calls for a zero-tolerance policy on domestic abuse among NFL players, advocating for immediate suspensions and bans for convictions.

A California lawyer's "Sodomite Suppression Act" ballot initiative, which proposes executing gays with "bullets to the head," is forcing the state's Attorney General to allow it to circulate for signatures. Despite being unconstitutional and unlikely to gather the required 365,000 valid signatures, legal experts say Attorney General Kamala Harris is bound by law to prepare a title and summary by May. Critics argue this process undermines the integrity of the initiative process and calls for a "human rights exception" to block such proposals. Activist Charlotte Laws has responded by filing the "Intolerant Jackass Act," which would require the sponsor of the Sodomite Suppression Act to undergo sensitivity training and donate money to pro-gay organizations.

"Gravity," starring Sandra Bullock and George Clooney, soared past industry expectations, debuting with a robust $55.6 million, the biggest October opening ever, according to studio estimates. The 3-D space drama, directed by Alfonso Cuarón, attracted a predominantly older audience, with 59% over the age of 35, and received an average grade of A- from viewers. In contrast, "Runner Runner" flopped with a disappointing $7.6 million, indicating limited appeal to a younger demographic.

After the general election resulted in a hung parliament, Prime Minister Theresa May stated her commitment to stability. She said that if her Conservative Party won the most seats, she would take responsibility for delivering stability. The article outlines the process for forming a government in a hung parliament, detailing the roles of the Conservative Party, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), and other smaller parties. It explains the potential for a minority government and the importance of "confidence and supply" agreements. The article also covers the next steps, including the formation of a new government, the Queen's Speech, and the Brexit negotiations.

A 69-year-old woman in Cambria County may have died after accidentally coming into contact with drug paraphernalia while cleaning up from the suspected overdose death of her 45-year-old son, according to the coroner. Theresa Plummer found her son unresponsive in the bathroom on November 5 and took him to the hospital, where he died two days later. The coroner believes she likely absorbed a substance through her skin or had a reaction after handling the paraphernalia. Plummer began experiencing shortness of breath and was hospitalized, where she passed away on November 6. Authorities are cautioning people to be cautious when handling drug paraphernalia and to notify the proper authorities if they come into contact with any powder substances. Toxicology reports are pending.

It appears Europe's Schiaparelli probe likely crashed and was destroyed upon impact with the Martian surface, according to images from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. The orbiter's low-resolution images show a dark patch and a white parachute-like feature in the expected landing zone, suggesting the probe impacted at high speed, possibly due to its thrusters firing for too short a time. Despite the failure, the probe transmitted valuable data during its descent, including information on its heat shield, parachute, radar, and thrusters. This data will be crucial for improving the design of the 2021 ExoMars mission, which aims to land an ambitious six-wheeled rover on Mars. The European Space Agency emphasizes that the mission's Trace Gas Orbiter, which successfully entered Mars orbit, will continue its scientific operations, including studying the Martian atmosphere for signs of past or present life.

In the tiny Pacific nation of Palau, the bodies of six Japanese soldiers from World War II have been discovered in a recently reopened cave, marking the grim task of locating remains from one of the harshest conflicts in the war. The cave, located on the island of Pelileu, was used as a base by Japanese forces during their defense against U.S. troops in September 1944. Archaeologists and munitions experts have been clearing the way into the network of sealed caves to search for the remains of the 10,000 Japanese soldiers who died, with 2,600 still unaccounted for. The discovery comes ahead of a visit by Japan's Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko, as Palau and Japan work together to end a brutal chapter from the war. The cave remains sealed after the findings to prevent public access and preserve the site as a solemn reminder of the conflict.

Mary Kristene Chapa, 18, who was shot in the head alongside her girlfriend Mollie Judith Olgin, 19, is recovering "amazingly," her brother Hilario Chapa told NBCLatino.com. Chapa, a tech sergeant in the Air Force, says Kristene has made physical progress but doctors are still waiting for a response from the left side of her body. Portland police chief Randy Wright stated there is no evidence of a hate crime, though the Texas Rangers are assisting the investigation. Kristene's family, living in Sinton, Texas, has set up a WePay donation page to cover medical expenses. The families of both girls have received support from the community and the gay community, with a candlelight walk planned in memory of Mollie Olgin and to pray for Kristene's recovery. Olgin's father expressed confidence in justice being served for his daughter.

A concerned mother on the playground poses a question to the author: Could her son grow up to be gay? The author reflects on the common perception that boys who exhibit behaviors typically associated with girls might grow up to be gay. She shares her experience of guiding her gender-nonconforming son, who likes princesses and dislikes sports, through various stages of childhood. The author finds solace in Dr. Phil's advice, which reassures her that her son's interests are not a precursor to homosexuality. However, Dr. Phil's subsequent recommendations to restrict her son's access to "girl" toys and clothes raise questions about the pressure parents face to conform their children to traditional gender roles. The author contrasts Dr. Phil's approach with that of other parents, such as blogger Nerdy Apple Bottom, who allows her son to express himself freely. The piece delves into the broader societal issues surrounding gender identity and the potential harm of imposing rigid gender norms on children. It also touches on the historical and ongoing

A veteran set himself on fire in protest outside the Georgia Capitol in downtown Atlanta, according to the Georgia State Patrol. Identified as 58-year-old John Michael Watts, the Air Force veteran doused himself with flammable liquid and set off homemade incendiary devices before being extinguished by a trooper. Watts was rushed to Grady Memorial Hospital with severe burns. The Capitol and nearby buildings were evacuated, and multiple agencies, including the bomb squad, responded to the scene. No other injuries were reported. The incident occurred during a news conference about a new state law on hands-free driving.

Two young Tibetan monks set themselves on fire in western China to protest government religious controls, the third such protest this year, potentially sparking renewed tension in the unstable region. The monks, Kelsang and Kunchak, from the Kirti monastery, shouted slogans including "Long live the Dalai Lama" as they self-immolated. The incidents could lead to a fresh crackdown in Aba prefecture, a heavily ethnic Tibetan area. Chinese officials and state media downplay the events, with one official claiming ignorance and Xinhua calling it a "typical terrorist attack." The self-immolations come amid ongoing disputes over the reincarnation of the Dalai Lama and growing tensions between the Chinese government and the Tibetan community.

A shooting at Azana Salon & Spa in Brookfield, Wisconsin, left at least three dead and four wounded. Police searched for suspected gunman Radcliffe F. Haughton, who reportedly entered the salon armed with a gun, killing three women and injuring four more. Haughton's wife, Zina, a popular hair stylist, was a sought-after hairdresser who often spoke about her two daughters. She had obtained a temporary restraining order against her husband four days before the shooting and a four-year restraining order the week prior. Haughton's behavior raised concerns among his wife's customers, who described him as a troubled man. The shooting left the salon's tight-knit community shocked and confused, as Haughton was known to be warm and caring to his clients. The suspect was found dead later in the day, bringing an end to the manhunt.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai received a significant equity award valued at nearly $200 million, making him one of the world's highest-paid executives. In a recent securities filing, Alphabet announced that Pichai was granted 273,328 Class C Google stock units on February 3, with the grant vesting over four years. This new award brings Pichai's total holdings in Alphabet to over $650 million, though still significantly lower than the net worth of Google's founders, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, and former CEO Eric Schmidt. Pichai, who became Google's CEO in October following the company's reorganization into Alphabet, celebrated his award by watching the Super Bowl and meeting NFL legend Ronnie Lott.

In a remote community in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, the murders of three local residents—Heather Aldrich, Carrie Nelson, and Jody Hutchinson—shocked the small town. Kenneth Brunke, a drug dealer, and Garry Cordell, a former convict, were arrested for the triple homicide. Initially, confessions from both suspects implicated Brunke as the mastermind. However, after Marietta Carlson, Cordell's girlfriend, died in jail, Cordell changed his story, exonerating Brunke. Cordell now claims he and Carlson committed the murders, while Brunke was not at the scene. The prosecutor, Timothy Noble, allowed Brunke to plead to lesser charges in exchange for his testimony against Cordell. This deal angered the victims' families, who believe Cordell took the fall for Brunke. The case raises questions about the prosecutor's handling of the case and whether someone may have gotten away with murder.

The world's most famous dodo, which inspired Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, met a violent end, according to new research. Scientists used 21st-century forensic scanning technology to uncover that the Oxford Dodo, the only specimen with viable DNA, was shot in the back of the head with lead shot pellets. This discovery, made by researchers at the University of Warwick, challenges the long-held belief that the dodo died of natural causes. The dodo, native to Mauritius, was hunted to extinction by early European explorers and invasive species. The Oxford Dodo, a nearly 400-year-old specimen, is the most complete and well-preserved example of the extinct bird, containing soft tissue and skin. This rare dodo, usually kept under lock and key, was scanned using micro-CT technology, revealing the shocking evidence of its violent death. The researchers hope to conduct further analysis to determine the origin of the lead shot and potentially identify the dodo

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive. Flowing in every day, these data are added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. Actress Sean Young was released from the Hollywood LAPD police station after being taken into custody for reportedly slapping a security guard outside the Academy Awards' Governors Ball last night. Young claims she was there to take pictures with party guests for her Facebook page when security guards asked her to leave because she didn't have a ticket. She says the guard grabbed her arm and she struck him in self-defense. Young maintains it was the security guard who was in the wrong and the Academy's lawyer who should make a public apology. The Academy says it was not they who pressed charges.

Census director Robert Groves reported that the South and West experienced strong population growth over the last decade. The national count reached 308,745,538, marking the slowest growth since the Great Depression. The South had the fastest growth at 14.3%, followed closely by the West at 13.8%. The Northeast grew 3.2%, while the Midwest saw a 3.9% increase. Nevada had the largest population growth at 35.1%, while Michigan was the only state to experience a decline of 0.6%. Commerce Secretary Gary Locke declared the 2010 census a success, stating it saved $1.87 billion more than expected due to a high 74% participation rate in mailing back the 10-question form.

Pope Francis drew an estimated three million people to Rio de Janeiro's Copacabana Beach for a vigil, marking the largest gathering yet of his first international trip. The event, part of World Youth Day, aimed to inspire Catholics to adopt a more missionary mindset and serve the poor. Francis urged bishops to step out of their cathedrals and reach those on the periphery, while addressing intellectuals and leaders to promote dialogue and eliminate poverty in Brazil. The vigil, held under sunny skies, saw young Catholics from around the world camp on the beach, emphasizing faith and community. The pope's visit also included an impassioned plea for the downtrodden, reflecting his focus on social justice and the marginalized.

The leader of al-Qaeda's affiliate in Yemen released an audio message taunting President Donald Trump after a recent U.S. raid that killed 25 people, including 11 women and children. The U.S. military says a Navy SEAL was killed during the Jan. 29 raid. Qassim al-Rimi, the al-Qaeda leader, claims "dozens of Americans were killed and wounded" and describes Trump as the "White House's new fool." U.S. officials deny al-Rimi was a target, stating the mission aimed to gather intelligence. The raid, involving U.S. and UAE forces, resulted in the deaths of 14 al-Qaeda fighters, including two leaders, but Qassim al-Rimi survived.

Roseanne Barr drew criticism after tweeting an image of her discolored face, initially captioned as a "tussle" with Bill Cosby, before deleting and clarifying the post. The 62-year-old comic, who previously starred in The Cosby Show, defended her tweet, saying "13 to 1" believed her. She also called the Cosby scandal "the best and the worst thing," acknowledging its negative impact while praising the opportunity for truth. Despite the controversy, Barr is set to return to television with her new show Momsters: When Moms Go Bad on Investigation Discovery. Meanwhile, three more women have come forward to accuse Bill Cosby of sexual assault, adding to the 20 women who have already spoken out. Cosby's attorney dismissed the new claims as "ridiculous."

An explosion near a train station in Elizabeth, New Jersey, early Monday unintentionally detonated by a bomb squad robot caused no injuries but raised concerns. The backpack containing five devices, including one that exploded, was found in a nearby restaurant trash can by two men who noticed wires and a pipe. FBI agents are reviewing surveillance footage, and transit service has resumed after a suspension. The incident follows two other nearby explosions on Saturday, one in Manhattan that injured 29 people and another in Seaside Park, New Jersey. The FBI detained five people in Brooklyn for questioning related to the Manhattan explosion. Mayor Christian Bollwage warned of potential further explosions and suggested the devices might have been discarded by someone avoiding investigation.

The inventor of the Kalashnikov assault rifle, Mikhail Kalashnikov, expressed deep spiritual pain in a letter to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church before his death, questioning his moral responsibility for the many lives his weapon took. In a letter dated May 2012, published by Russia's pro-Kremlin newspaper Izvestia, Kalashnikov, who died in December 2013 at the age of 94, wrote that he was "a slave of God, the designer Mikhail Kalashnikov," and that his "spiritual pain is unbearable." He pondered whether he could be guilty of people's deaths, even those of enemies, through his rifle. The letter, typed on Kalashnikov's personal writing paper, was signed with a wavering hand. The Russian Orthodox Church, which received the letter, supports the creators and users of weapons that serve to protect the Fatherland, stating that Kalashnikov designed the rifle

Hollywood couple Emma Stone and Andrew Garfield cleverly turned paparazzi attention into a charitable effort by holding up signs promoting various organizations. In New York City, they promoted four charities, including Gilda's Club, Worldwide Orphans, Youth Mentoring Connection, and Autism Speaks. Their signs read, "Good morning! We were eating and saw a group of guys with cameras outside. And so we thought, lets try this again. We dont need the attention, but these wonderful organizations do," with Andrew's sign listing the web addresses. Their actions demonstrate how they use their fame to support causes they believe in, impressing fans with their initiative.

An Arkansas inmate who escaped 32 years ago is back in custody. Steven Dishman, 60, was found Sunday at a home in Springdale by the Arkansas State Police and Springdale Police Department and is now being held in the Varner Unit in Grady. Dishman originally escaped from the Benton Unit in May 1985 while serving a seven-year sentence for theft of property and burglary. He was located after an anonymous tip. Another inmate, Joel W. Lane, was also captured Sunday in Pine Bluff after a foot chase. Four prisoners remain at large as of Sunday.

The body of a Massachusetts honeymooner, Josh Byrne, 30, has been recovered after he was swept away by floodwaters in Costa Rica last week. Byrne and his wife, Bianca, were in Playa Dominicalito when their vehicle was caught in a flash flood while attempting to cross a bridge. Bianca was able to swim to shore, but Josh was swept away. His family concluded their search on Saturday after working around the clock. Byrne's father and brother traveled to Costa Rica to assist in the search. The family remembered Josh for his helpful and caring demeanor and his ability to make friends. They expressed gratitude to the local community, Massachusetts political leaders, the Red Cross, and the U.S. Embassy and State Department for their assistance. A GoFundMe campaign has been set up to help cover the costs of the recovery and services.

David Crosby, 73, was driving his 2015 Tesla near his California ranch when he accidentally hit a jogger, Jose Jimenez, 46, at the speed limit. Jimenez suffered non-life-threatening injuries and was airlifted to a hospital. Crosby expressed regret and relief that the injuries were not severe, wishing Jimenez a speedy recovery. The incident occurred because Crosby was blinded by the sun while driving.

A mysterious earthquake in Wyoming, known as the Wind River Earthquake, struck in 2013 with a magnitude of 4.7 and was one of the deepest of its type ever recorded. This quake occurred within the mantle, more than 75 km deep, which is unusually deep for the region, as the Earth's crust in the Wyoming Craton is typically no deeper than 40-50 km. The earthquake's depth challenges current understanding, as it doesn't fit typical patterns of crustal or mantle seismic activity. Scientists suggest the mantle might be more brittle than previously thought, but the exact cause remains uncertain. The unusual depth of the earthquake raises questions about the forces acting on the mantle in this region.

The U.S. government proposed removing most of the world's humpback whale populations from the endangered species list, citing their recovery over 45 years of protection. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Fisheries aims to reclassify humpbacks into 14 distinct populations, removing 10 from the endangered list. Two populations will be listed as threatened, and only two—the Arabian Sea and Cape Verde Islands—will remain endangered. Humpbacks were listed as endangered in 1970 after severe depletion due to whaling. NOAA Fisheries will accept public comments for 90 days, with the goal of finalizing the reclassification next year. Conservationists generally support the move but warn that some populations still face threats.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, whose campaign has been marked by controversial statements about Mexican immigrants, addressed crowds in Phoenix and Las Vegas, continuing to emphasize the need for stricter immigration policies. In Phoenix, Trump called for a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border and accused Mexico of sending criminals into the country, though he later expressed respect for the Mexican people. He also criticized Univision and other businesses that have cut ties with him, and mocked former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, calling him "weak on immigration." In both cities, Trump brought on stage a victim of crime to support his argument, though he faced interruptions from protesters. His speeches, which often veered between harsh rhetoric and more moderate statements, drew large crowds and generated significant backlash. Despite the criticism, Trump's campaign has gained momentum, with his tough stance on immigration resonating with a segment of the Republican base.

Astronaut nutrition is crucial for long-duration space missions, as evidenced by the research of Scott M. Smith, Ph.D., manager for NASA's Nutritional Biochemistry Lab. Ensuring proper nutrition is vital for mission success and astronaut health. Challenges in space, such as microgravity, higher radiation, and environmental factors, impact astronauts' dietary needs. Astronauts often eat less due to busy schedules and menu fatigue. The Biochemical Profile project examines nutritional markers to understand the effects of spaceflight on the body, including bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular issues, immune function impairment, and vision changes. Comparing Scott Kelly's nutritional status during his year aboard the International Space Station to his identical twin brother, Mark, on Earth, provides unique insights. Maintaining nutritional health is essential for astronauts' well-being during extended missions, with potential benefits for Earth-based health as well.

A suspect, described as a brunette in her 20s or 30s, stands 5-foot-8 and weighs about 130 pounds, is believed to have carried out six jewelry store robberies across Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, and North Carolina since April. The most recent incident occurred on Monday at a Jared Vault in Mebane, North Carolina, where she forced two workers into a back room at gunpoint, zip-tied their hands, and stole jewelry. Authorities also believe a male accomplice, described as a black man in his 30s or 40s, 6 feet tall, and weighing 250 pounds, may have been involved in some of the robberies. The suspect is considered armed and dangerous. Anyone with information is asked to contact the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI.

Microsoft's Surface tablet, with its sleek design and innovative features, offers a unique blend of tablet and laptop functionalities. The device, available in both RT and Pro versions, showcases a beautifully crafted magnesium body and a 10.6-inch, 1366x768-pixel screen. The RT model, running Windows RT, includes a preview version of Microsoft Office and a touch-friendly interface, but lacks compatibility with traditional Windows applications. The Pro version, powered by an Intel processor, supports full Windows 8 and a wide range of peripherals, making it more versatile but also more expensive. The Touch Cover keyboard, a key feature, provides a thin, magnetic attachment with a learning curve for typing, while the Type Cover offers a more conventional keyboard experience. Despite its innovative hardware, the Surface faces challenges with software, particularly the limited app selection in the Windows Store and the disjointed transition between the touch-centric and traditional desktop interfaces. The device's hardware is highly praised for its design

A dispute has emerged between Oprah Winfrey and a local resident over access to hiking trails near her new property in Telluride, Colorado. Retired physicist Charles D. Goodman claims that Winfrey's company and the town of Mountain Village secretly agreed to close trails that were previously accessible to neighbors. Mountain Village denies the accusation, stating that the correction to property records only cleared up ambiguities and that they intend to maintain trail access. Winfrey's plans for the property, including building a mansion and guest home, may require cutting down trees for wildfire mitigation.

Syrian rebels fighting against President Bashar al-Assad now align more closely with al-Qaeda, raising concerns about the future of the conflict. The merger between Jabhat al-Nusra, a powerful Syrian rebel group, and al-Qaeda in Iraq, forms a new entity called the "Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant." This move complicates the international effort to support moderate Syrian rebels, as al-Nusra is labeled a terrorist organization. The Obama administration faces challenges in deciding how to aid the Syrian opposition, given the potential for weapons to fall into extremist hands. Meanwhile, al-Nusra's leader Abu Mohammed al-Golani attempted to distance the group from the merger, emphasizing their commitment to overthrowing Assad. This development intensifies tensions within the Syrian opposition and highlights the difficulty in distinguishing between different rebel factions.

The owner of Eva Restaurant in Los Angeles is offering a 5% discount to customers who leave their phones at the door during their meal, aiming to encourage diners to connect with each other in person. This policy, which has gone viral, has resulted in numerous media requests and international attention. While it hasn't significantly boosted business yet, the restaurant hopes to foster a more intimate dining experience free from digital distractions.

European airlines, including Lufthansa, Air Berlin, and Air France, extended their flight cancellations to Tel Aviv due to safety concerns amid ongoing fighting between Israel and Hamas. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration initially banned American airlines from flying to and from Tel Aviv for 24 hours after a Hamas rocket landed near the airport. The European Aviation Safety Agency recommended avoiding Tel Aviv flights. British Airways, however, continued its twice-daily flights. Jerusalem Mayor Nir Barkat stated that Israel's security is "as good as it gets," while Michael Bloomberg, who arrived in Israel, praised the airport's security. Hamas hailed the flight cancellations as a victory. The incident has strained diplomatic relations and could affect Israel's economy, particularly its tourism industry.

The New York Jets cheerleaders, known as the Flight Crew, have reached a $325,000 settlement in a wage dispute with the team. Former cheerleader Krystal C. filed a class-action lawsuit in 2014, claiming the squad was paid only $150 per game and nothing for practice time. The settlement, covering the 2012-13 and 2013-14 NFL seasons, will give each of the 52 cheerleaders $2,500 per season, with an additional $400 for photo shoots. State Senator Diane Savino praised the settlement and called for the Buffalo Bills to follow suit, ensuring fair pay for their cheerleaders. The Jets deny the claims but agreed to the settlement to avoid litigation.

A New Mexico ob-gyn, Dr. Christopher Driskill, 42, faces suspension and potential license revocation after allegations of drinking on the job, having multiple sexual relationships with patients and staff, and abandoning women in labor. Driskill, who is married with four children and president-elect of the New Mexico Medical Society, allegedly kept alcohol at his workplace and left women unattended during childbirth. He also wrote inappropriate notes in patient charts and failed to disclose his termination from a job. His license is under review, and a hearing date has not been set.

A New Zealand father is raising funds to bring his Down syndrome baby, Leo, back to New Zealand after his Armenian mother abandoned him. Leo was born in Armenia on January 21, where it is common to abandon children with disabilities. Leo's father, Samuel Forrest, was given an ultimatum by his wife to give up the baby or face divorce. Forrest, who works as a freelance business contractor, set up a GoFundMe page to help him and Leo move to New Zealand. The page has received significant support, raising over $160,000. The Armenian government has fast-tracked Leo's citizenship and passport. Forrest hopes to find a part-time job to care for Leo and share his story to raise awareness about children with special needs.

George Zimmerman's auction for the gun he used to shoot and kill Trayvon Martin has concluded with a winning bid of over $120,000. The auction, hosted by United Gun Group, was initially marred by fake bids but managed to identify at least one verified offer. The highest verified bid was $138,900, though the identity of the winner remains confidential. Zimmerman, who plans to use the funds for "worthy causes," expressed gratitude for the successful auction and the support from United Gun Group. The gun, a Kel-Tec PF-9 pistol, still bears the case number from Zimmerman's trial.

PennLive/The Patriot-News will strictly limit op-Eds and letters to the editor in opposition to same-sex marriage, emphasizing the importance of civil discourse. The decision stems from the U.S. Supreme Court's ruling on Obergefell v. Hodges, legalizing gay marriage nationwide. The newsroom received backlash, with accusations of being "fascists" and violating the First Amendment. The editor apologizes for any unintended offense and clarifies that the policy aims to foster a respectful discussion, not suppress free speech.

Scientists using muon detection technology have discovered a mysterious void inside the Great Pyramid of Giza, raising questions about the pyramid's internal structure and potential hidden chambers. The cavity, located above the Grand Gallery, measures at least 30 meters and is comparable in size to the Grand Gallery itself. While its purpose remains unknown, it could be a structural element or a previously undiscovered corridor. The discovery, made by a team from Nagoya University and the Heritage Innovation Preservation Institute, is the first major internal structure found in the pyramid since the 19th century. Researchers are cautious about calling it a chamber and are seeking input from Egyptologists to develop hypotheses about its function. The team plans to use tiny flying robots, if approved, to explore the void further without damaging the monument.

Police pursued a stolen tractor through central Denver on Friday night, leading to a dramatic end when a police cruiser rammed into it. The tractor, towing an attachment, swerved through busy streets and sidewalks, striking several vehicles and buildings. The chase began near City Park and ended in Lower Downtown. Two officers were injured but treated and released. Witnesses reported the tractor driver was subdued with a Taser after the collision. No guns were fired during the pursuit. Police have not identified the suspect.

On Oahu, the mountains are dissolving from within due to groundwater, a new study reveals. This process will eventually transform the island into a flat, low-lying area similar to Midway. Researchers found that more material is dissolving from the island than being carried away by erosion. The study, conducted by comparing groundwater and stream water effects, shows that Oahu's weathering rates vary due to rainfall variability. While the island is currently growing, groundwater will eventually dominate, leading to its gradual flattening over about 1.5 million years.

Americans' frustration with Congress has reached an all-time low, with only 10% approving of the job Congress is doing, according to a Gallup poll. This is the lowest approval rating in nearly 40 years of Gallup polling. Even institutions and figures like Fidel Castro, Saddam Hussein, and Mark Fuhrman have been more popular. The article highlights several areas where public opinion is more favorable, including BP during the oil spill, socialism, waterboarding, abortion, President Nixon during Watergate, non-believers in Santa Claus, the Greek Prime Minister George Papandreou, and reality TV star Paris Hilton.

Supreme Court justices showed strong skepticism towards the Voting Rights Act's key provision during Wednesday's argument, suggesting the modern South has moved past its troubled past and questioning the legal burdens on covered states. Conservative justices, including Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Scalia, expressed doubts about the Act's necessity, while more liberal justices, like Justices Breyer and Sotomayor, defended its continuation. The outcome remains uncertain, but a potential ruling could make it easier for states to implement voting changes without federal approval, impacting nine states with a history of racial discrimination. The case, involving Shelby County, Alabama, challenges the Act's requirement for preclearance of voting changes, with the 2006 reauthorization based on outdated data.

The 26th annual Ig Nobel Prizes honored the most absurd and curious scientific research, with winners receiving a $10 trillion Zimbabwean bill as a symbolic prize. Nobel laureates handed out the awards at Harvard University, where scientists were recognized for a variety of studies. The reproduction prize went to Egyptian urologist Ahmed Shafik for his research on the effects of different types of trousers on rats' sexual activity. Mark Avis, Sarah Forbes, and Shelagh Ferguson won the economics prize for assessing the personalities of rocks from a sales and marketing perspective. The psychology prize was awarded to a team for their study on the frequency and detection of lies, while the peace prize went to researchers who explored the ability to recognize and detect pseudo-profound bullshit. Charles Foster and Thomas Thwaites shared the biology prize for their immersive experiences living as various animals, including a badger and a goat. Prime Minister Theresa May raised the UK's terror threat level to critical following a blast at Parsons Green station that injured 29 people, including a young boy. The explosion, which occurred during the morning rush hour, was treated as terrorism, and Islamic State claimed responsibility. May condemned the attack as "cowardly" and announced an increased armed police presence on transport networks. The hunt for the bomber is ongoing, with CCTV footage and images from the scene being analyzed. US President Donald Trump criticized May's comments about Scotland Yard's awareness of the bomber, but May dismissed such speculation as unhelpful. The blast involved an improvised explosive device that partially detonated, sending a fireball through a train carriage. Passengers described scenes of panic and chaos as they fled the station. London Mayor Sadiq Khan appealed for calm, stating the city would not be intimidated by terrorism.

Facebook users are rallying to boycott Spirit Airlines after the carrier refused to refund a dying veteran's flight cost. A campaign titled "Boycott Spirit Airlines" gained significant traction, with likes increasing from about 700 to over 18,000. Many current and former military members are joining the backlash, expressing disappointment in Spirit's policies. The airline did not respond to requests for comment. Additionally, the Veterans of the Vietnam War and the Veterans Coalition wrote a letter to Spirit Airlines, further highlighting the issue.

German police are on the hunt for thieves who made off with over 20 tons of Nutella and other chocolate treats from a refrigerated trailer, potentially worth $80,000. The theft occurred over the weekend in Neustadt, with police unsure if it was planned or opportunistic. They are also investigating a similar case where an empty trailer was stolen in Weimar around the same time. To prevent such thefts, local authorities advise reporting any large quantities of chocolate received through unusual means.

French and UN helicopters searched northern Mali for wreckage of an Air Algerie flight that crashed with 110 passengers, including nearly 50 French nationals, from Burkina Faso to Algiers. French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius said the plane may have encountered bad weather after the pilot requested a course change due to a storm. However, conflicting reports from Mali and Burkina Faso about the crash location complicated the search. Malian President Ibrahim Boubacar Keita and a Burkina Faso official reported finding wreckage in different areas. French President Francois Hollande cancelled a visit to overseas territories to focus on the search, promising to use all military means to locate the aircraft. The search is challenging due to the vast, sparsely inhabited region and the presence of Tuareg separatist rebels. Another plane crash in recent days has raised concerns over air safety.

A male student was fatally shot at a Mississippi State University residence hall Saturday night by three suspects who fled the scene, school officials said. Campus police were notified at approximately 10 p.m. and found the 21-year-old victim, John Sanderson, in grave condition; he died about 30 minutes later. The suspects are three black males who escaped in a blue Crown Victoria. The university is operating under advisory conditions and has set up a call center for parents. Mississippi State President Mark Keenum said this is the first such incident in the school's history. Mississippi Governor Phil Bryant expressed sorrow over the deaths of two college students in the state over the weekend, with one killed at Jackson State University in an off-campus apartment pool party.

A 37-year-old Oregon man faced multiple charges after reportedly becoming upset when a McDonald's restaurant in Sutherlin declined his order for 30 double cheeseburgers, the News-Review reports. Police arrested Jedediah Ezekiel Fulton on March 16, accusing him of second-degree disorderly conduct, second-degree criminal trespass, second-degree criminal mischief, and harassment. Fulton allegedly destroyed a banner and attacked the restaurant's arches. A witness, fearing for their safety, pulled out a gun. The Sutherlin Police Department states Fulton grabbed someone's shirt, though it's unclear if he has an attorney.

A 4-year-old girl led police to a burglary suspect hiding in her closet during a break-in at her family's home in Antioch, California, on May 11, 2015. The homeowner, holding her baby, fled the house when she saw an intruder enter through an unlocked door. Upon returning, she found her 4-year-old daughter at the top of the stairs. The girl told her mother the intruder was hiding in her closet, which police confirmed. After a brief struggle, 21-year-old Demaria Lopez was arrested and booked on charges of burglary and resisting arrest. No injuries were reported.

President Obama made a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room to discuss the acquittal of George Zimmerman in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin, emphasizing the importance of understanding the case through the lens of past racial discrimination. Obama stated, "Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago," highlighting the experiences and history that inform the African American community's interpretation of such events. He acknowledged the need for Americans to do some soul-searching about their inherent racial biases and suggested that individual Americans should reflect on whether they are doing enough to reduce these biases. Obama also called for a long-term project to bolster and reinforce African American boys, noting that many need positive reinforcement. He urged all Americans to respect the jury's verdict but also to understand the pain and frustration felt by the African American community.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has proposed new regulations to ban the use of sunlamp products (commonly known as indoor tanning beds) for minors under 18, aiming to reduce the risk of skin cancer and other health issues. These rules also require adult tanners to sign a risk acknowledgment certification every six months, acknowledging the potential health hazards. The FDA cites that indoor tanning increases the risk of melanoma by 59% and contributes to severe burns and eye damage. Approximately 1.6 million minors use indoor tanning facilities annually. The proposed measures include making warning labels more prominent, adding emergency shut-off switches, and improving eye protection. The FDA seeks public comments on these proposals, which could be enforced after a 90-day comment period.

PBS faced backlash after admitting it used pre-recorded fireworks footage in its live "A Capitol Fourth" broadcast, despite cloudy weather in Washington, D.C. Viewers complained on social media that the show was not truly live, with one tweet sarcastically asking, "How is using stock video patriotic?" PBS defended its decision, tweeting that it used footage from both this year and previous years to create "the best television show." However, many viewers remained upset, with one comment stating, "Not cool @pbs.... Fake footage of fireworks on the Fourth???? It's cloudy and rainy in DC."

British police are reviewing new information about the 1997 deaths of Princess Diana and Dodi Al Fayed in a Paris car crash. The Metropolitan Police is assessing the information's relevance and credibility but clarifies it is not reopening the investigation. In 2008, an inquest found the couple was unlawfully killed due to the driver's gross negligence and paparazzi pursuit. The force is working with officers from its specialist crime and operations command on the assessment.

The Journal News published an interactive Google Map with the names and addresses of gun permit owners in certain New York cities following the Newtown massacre. This sparked outrage and debate, with some arguing it could endanger gun owners. A Connecticut lawyer then posted the personal information of The Journal News staff, including the publisher's home address. The move has escalated into a debate about transparency and privacy, with open data being used for both democratic and partisan purposes.

A toxin produced by a common foodborne bacterium, Clostridium perfringens, may trigger multiple sclerosis (MS), a new study suggests. Researchers from Weill Cornell Medical College found that the epsilon toxin from certain strains of C. perfringens attacks cells involved in MS, including the brain's blood-brain barrier and myelin-producing cells. About 13% of food samples tested contained C. perfringens, and nearly 3% harbored the epsilon toxin. The study, presented at the American Society for Microbiology meeting, adds to growing evidence linking environmental factors to MS. If confirmed, a vaccine or treatment targeting the epsilon toxin could potentially prevent or halt the disease's progression.

An 11-year-old boy, Yonatan Daniel Aguilar, was found dead in a small closet in his Echo Park home, weighing just 34 pounds and covered in pressure sores from the tile floor. Court documents obtained by the Los Angeles Times reveal that Aguilar, 39, had been keeping Yonatan hidden in a locked bedroom closet for three years, sedating him with liquid sleep medication to keep him quiet. According to investigators, even Yonatan’s stepfather, Jose Pinzon, who lived in the home, was unaware of his presence. On August 22, 2016, Aguilar told Pinzon that Yonatan had died and led him to the closet. The boy’s three siblings and Aguilar were the only ones aware of his hiding place. Aguilar is now charged with murder and child abuse causing death and remains in jail on a $2 million bail.

An Egyptian man, described as "psychologically unstable," hijacked an EgyptAir flight from Alexandria to Cairo and forced it to land in Cyprus, where he surrendered with all passengers released unharmed after a six-hour standoff. The 59-year-old hijacker, Seif Eddin Mustafa, claimed to have explosives and demanded to speak to his ex-wife, who was brought to the airport. After realizing his demands would not be met, he left the plane, where he was immediately arrested. The incident, which involved 72 people on board, including 26 foreigners, raised concerns about Egyptian airport security following a Russian plane bombing in Sinai. The flight crew and passengers praised the crew's handling of the situation, with one flight attendant playing a role in convincing the hijacker to release the passengers. Mustafa is to face charges including air piracy and kidnapping.

Florida surpassed New York to become the third-most populous state, with an estimated 19.9 million residents, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. The state added about 300,000 new residents over the last year, while New York's population grew by only 51,000. Overall, the U.S. population increased by three-quarters of a percent to 318.9 million. Six states—Illinois, West Virginia, Connecticut, New Mexico, Alaska, and Vermont—experienced population declines, with Puerto Rico losing 1.3 percent of its population. North Dakota grew by 2.2 percent, the fastest rate among all states, due to an energy boom. Other rapidly growing states included Nevada, Texas, Colorado, Arizona, and Utah. Texas added the most residents at 451,000, followed by California, Florida, and Georgia, each gaining over 100,00

A 19-year-old Dutchman entered the headquarters of Dutch national broadcaster NOS, demanding airtime and threatening to detonate bombs at several locations. Wearing a black suit and tie, he carried a pistol but was later found to be holding a fake weapon. After a tense standoff, police arrested him without incident. The man claimed to be from a "hackers' collective" and said he was hired by intelligence agencies. NOS was off-air for about an hour during the incident. No one was injured, and the motive remains unclear. The broadcaster has increased security following the attacks on Charlie Hebdo in Paris.

A man who mistook a doll for an unresponsive infant in a parked truck called 911, leading to the recovery of a stolen truck and a 3-week-old baby inside, according to the Lumberton Police Department. The truck, a dark gray 2014 Ford F-150, was stolen from a home on the 1400 block of Mimosa Street. The mother was taking two other children inside when the theft occurred. Police issued an alert and the truck was abandoned in a nearby parking lot. A man noticed a window was down and saw a doll, calling 911. Deputies found the unharmed infant in the child-restraint seat. Two suspects are being sought, but no arrests have been made.

U.S. customs officials at Los Angeles International Airport intercepted 67 invasive giant African snails in a shipment from Lagos, Nigeria, marking the first such large quantity of these pests intercepted as a consumption entry, officials said. The snails, native to Africa and commonly used as a delicacy, can grow up to 8 inches long and 5 inches wide, living up to 10 years. They pose a significant threat to U.S. agriculture, public health, and the environment, as they can consume over 500 types of plants and even eat stucco and paint off houses. The mollusks are also carriers of several parasites harmful to humans, including one that can lead to meningitis. Due to their invasive nature, the shipment was transferred to the local plant inspection station for precautionary measures. Customs officials emphasized the importance of preventing the spread of such pests to protect the nation's agriculture and public health.

Tennessee state Senator Stacey Campfield drew criticism for posting a joke about pressure cookers being used as weapons one week after the Boston Marathon bombing. The post, titled "Here comes Feinstein again," featured a pressure cooker with labeled parts as weapons. When questioned about the sensitivity of the timing, Campfield responded that people should "lighten up" and criticized the focus on gun control following the Sandy Hook shooting. He also expressed frustration with perceived double standards in the gun control debate.

Flint's lead contamination crisis has expanded to pets, with two dogs recently testing positive for lead toxicity in Genesee County. State Veterinarian Dr. James Averill reports these are the first confirmed cases involving dogs in five years. Both dogs are alive but details on their condition, lead levels, and symptoms are limited. Averill advises residents to ensure pets only drink filtered or bottled water, similar to precautions for humans. He emphasizes monitoring pets for unusual behavior, as symptoms can vary widely and may mimic other illnesses. The state is working with local veterinarians, with free lab testing available for suspected cases. While lead poisoning in dogs is rare, Averill stresses the importance of protecting pets from Flint's contaminated tap water.

A global map of the world's hidden groundwater has been published, offering insights into the total volume and distribution of this vital resource. Led by Dr. Tom Gleeson of the University of Victoria, the study, published in Nature Geoscience, uses data and computer models to estimate that less than six percent and possibly as little as one percent of groundwater found close to Earth's surface is renewable within a human lifetime. The total volume of underground water is estimated at almost 23 million cubic kilometers, with 0.35 million cubic kilometers younger than 50 years old. This groundwater, ranging in age from months to millions of years, is crucial for managing water resources sustainably. Most modern groundwater is found in tropical and mountainous regions, with significant deposits in the Amazon Basin, Congo, Indonesia, and along the western borders of North and South America. The least amount is in arid regions like the Sahara. Understanding the age and distribution of groundwater helps in estimating how long it will

A Boulder father is offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to the recovery of his missing son, Ryder Johnson, who vanished more than seven months ago. Johnson, 21, was last seen after finishing his shift at Eldora Ski Resort near Nederland. His vehicle was found parked at Gross Dam in Boulder, over 20 miles from where he was last seen. The Boulder County Sheriff's Office has not found many leads so far. In January, the family offered the reward to find Johnson or identify those responsible, with the deadline set for January 17, 2017, the one-year anniversary of his disappearance. The father, Richard Johnson, continues to search and hopes for his son's safe return, stating, "Justice needs to be served, and I think it's time to bring him home."

In 1992, Morrad Ghonim, then 19, hired Leon Martinez, a drug dealer, to kill his 17-year-old wife, Vicki, at a park in La Mirada. Martinez testified that Ghonim wanted it to look like a robbery and offered $10,000. Martinez shot Vicki six times, including in the head, as she pleaded for her baby. He then fled with the money. Martinez was eventually convicted of the murder, while Ghonim, who fled to Antigua, was recently extradited and faced trial. Ghonim was found guilty of hiring Martinez, facing life in prison or the death penalty.

Celebrated novelist Junot Díaz adamantly denies sexual misconduct allegations from several women, including a claim of "forcible kissing" by writer Zinzi Clemmons. Díaz, who won the 2008 Pulitzer Prize for his novel "The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao," maintains he has not bullied or been sexually inappropriate. His accusers argue a broad range of behaviors should be addressed under the #MeToo movement. MIT and Boston Review, where Díaz teaches and edits, have conducted separate investigations, finding no evidence to restrict his roles. Critics and supporters debate the appropriate response, with some arguing for a nuanced approach to #MeToo allegations.

An Alabama man, Keith Maddox, who posted videos online complaining about bicyclists and making threatening remarks, was arrested and charged with reckless endangerment after cycling groups alerted authorities. In the videos, Maddox expressed his frustration and even threatened to run cyclists off the road. He was released on a $3,000 bond. Maddox later apologized on Facebook for his offensive videos, acknowledging his poor judgment and asking for forgiveness.

A new study suggests children living near the Fukushima nuclear meltdowns have been diagnosed with thyroid cancer at a rate 20 to 50 times higher than elsewhere, challenging the government's position that the increase is due to heightened screening. The study, led by Toshihide Tsuda of Okayama University, analyzed data from the Fukushima Health Management Survey, which has been monitoring children's thyroid health since the 2011 disaster. While some experts agree that the screening may have detected more cases, others argue the higher rate is real and not just due to increased vigilance. The findings could influence compensation and health policies for residents of the affected area.

World Cup organizers say vuvuzelas will not be banned from stadiums in South Africa, despite complaints. The plastic horns, likened to the sound of a thousand bees or stampeding elephants, have caused issues for players and fans. Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo and England's Jamie Carragher have voiced concerns, but FIFA president Sepp Blatter supports their use, calling them part of South African culture. A vuvuzela emits a sound of 127 decibels, louder than a drum or referee's whistle. While some argue the noise disrupts concentration and chanting, the England Supporters' Band sees it as part of the local culture and encourages fans to embrace it. Organizers will monitor the situation and may ban vuvuzelas if thrown onto the pitch or used as weapons.

A 36-year-old woman with special needs was found bound to a bed in the basement of a house on the 200 block of Linton Street in Philadelphia's Olney section. Police arrested Regina Bennett, 46, for threats and assault against a neighbor after discovering the woman in "unsuitable conditions." The victim, extremely thin and with sores, was taken to Albert Einstein Medical Center for evaluation. Police have not determined Bennett's relationship to the victim. Bennett faces multiple charges, including aggravated assault, kidnapping for ransom, and neglect of care. A neighbor described Bennett as "Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde," noting her erratic behavior and prejudice. The case is reminiscent of other similar cases involving the theft of Social Security checks from disabled individuals.

A Pennsylvania man applying to become a state trooper failed his polygraph pretest by admitting to having sex with an underage girl four years ago. Joseph Adam White, 29, of Hartstown, was at the Meadville barracks for his exam when he allegedly told the examiner about the consensual encounter with the now 19-year-old in 2011. Police charged White with four counts of unlawful sexual contact with a minor and 10 counts of corruption of minors after interviewing the woman and confirming the information.

Britain's Prince William and Kate have released a family photo of their 8-month-old son Prince George, taken at their London residence, Kensington Palace. The photo, taken by photographer Jason Bell, shows the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge with Prince George, who is wearing a light blue jumper with his name on it. The smiling duchess, 32, is holding Prince George on her knee, while William, 31, looks relaxed in a rolled-up-sleeves shirt. The family is looking out of an open window, with George focusing on their pet, Lupo, a black cocker spaniel. The Cambridges are set to embark on a 16-day tour of New Zealand and Australia, with Prince George's first official overseas tour. The itinerary includes stops in Wellington, Christchurch, Dunedin, and Sydney, among other locations. The tour will also involve commemorating the First World War and visiting areas affected by natural disasters.

Archaeologists have uncovered a medieval well in Rainhill, England, long believed to have healing properties and the ability to wash away sins. The well, named St Anne’s Well, was found on a private farm after a series of excavations by Historic England. The well, which dates back to the late Medieval Period, was likely built to honor Saint Anne, the mother of the Virgin Mary. It was used by pilgrims for bathing and healing, with a small structure built around it to accommodate caretakers. Despite its historical significance, the well had been buried under farmland for centuries. After careful excavation, researchers have secured the site to prevent further damage, ensuring its preservation for future study and appreciation.

Michael Phelps, the most decorated Olympian, is set to compete in his fifth Olympic Games, aiming to add to his 22 medals, including 18 golds. Phelps will participate in three individual events and potentially several relays. His previous Olympic performances, spanning from 2000 to 2012, showcased his dominance, setting numerous world records and winning eight gold medals in Beijing 2008. Phelps, now 31, will serve as Team USA’s flag bearer for the Rio 2016 Opening Ceremony, marking his significant role in representing the United States.

A 27-year-old man named Akayed Ullah detonated a crude pipe bomb strapped to his body in a crowded Manhattan subway passage on Monday morning, causing minor injuries to three commuters and prompting a massive police response. The attack, which left Ullah with burns and cuts, reignited debates about terrorism, public safety, and immigration. Ullah, who came to the U.S. in 2011 on a family-based visa, reportedly told investigators he was inspired by Islamic State propaganda. The FBI and NYPD were investigating, and charges were expected. The incident occurred just weeks after a truck attack in Manhattan, leading President Trump to call for reforms to the immigration system. Ullah's neighbors described him as a quiet individual who had worked as a cabdriver.

Verizon is rolling out its new "Share Everything" plans starting June 28, making shared data plans the default option for customers unless they maintain their existing plans and purchase new phones at unsubsidized prices. These plans allow family members to share a common data pool, offering savings for large families but potentially higher costs for individuals. The plans include unlimited voice and text messages, with data charges ranging from $50 for 1 GB to $100 for 10 GB. Monthly line access fees vary from $10 for tablets to $40 for smartphones. While the plans are beneficial for families, they may not be as cost-effective for individuals who use minimal voice and text services. The changes reflect a shift in how carriers measure and charge for data usage, potentially increasing revenue through a lump-sum approach rather than individual data limits.

North Dakota's Senate passed two highly restrictive abortion bills, one banning abortions as early as six weeks based on a detectable fetal heartbeat, and another prohibiting abortions due to genetic abnormalities or gender selection. If signed by Governor Jack Dalrymple, these laws would be among the strictest in the nation. The heartbeat ban could outlaw over 75% of abortions in the state, according to experts. Opponents argue the measures would be unconstitutional and could lead to legal challenges. Proponents aim to test the Supreme Court's Roe v. Wade ruling, which allows abortion until fetal viability, usually around 24 weeks. The bills passed with strong Republican support, while Democrats opposed them.

Despite Gwyneth Paltrow's efforts to prevent Vanity Fair from publishing a takedown piece, the influential magazine is moving forward with what many expect to be an in-depth article. Editor-in-chief Graydon Carter confirmed to The Times of London that the story is in progress. Paltrow had reportedly written an email to celebrity friends asking them not to speak to the magazine and advising them never to work with it again. Carter defended the magazine's coverage, stating that some famous people believe they live in a "cone of celebrity" that protects them, but such a bubble no longer exists in Los Angeles unless they stay in. The article also mentions that Paltrow recently moved back to Los Angeles from England and may face a more challenging environment there.

New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg praised President Barack Obama as a "credible, formidable candidate" for re-election, stating that the incumbent would be a "viable candidate" regardless of the Republican nominee. Bloomberg, an independent who has registered as both a Republican and a Democrat, also defended Rick Perry and Mitt Romney for actions that have hindered their campaigns, such as Perry's handling of the HPV vaccine and Romney's health care plan in Massachusetts. Bloomberg called New Jersey Governor Chris Christie "a good governor" and advised him to run for the Republican nomination if he wished. Additionally, Bloomberg criticized President Obama for using billionaire investor Warren Buffett as an example for increasing taxes on the wealthy, stating that Buffett's tax rate would be higher if his income came from ordinary income rather than capital gains. Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus mocked Obama's 2008 slogan, suggesting it won't resonate in 2012.
